title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article Il, Sec. 15 of the 1987 Constitution provides that: "The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.” It is the State's duty to provide safe, clean, accessible, and affordable drinking water, sanitation, and irrigation services to the public. It is of utmost importance that this is achieved through a well- coordinated, effective, efficient, and sustainable management of its water and sanitation resources. According to the 2019 World Water Development Report of the United Nations, 2 billion people live in countries with high water stress level. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that water scarcity affects four out of ten people in the world. World Vision stated that 800 children under the age of five die of diarrhea, every day, which is attributed to poor water and sanitation. Access to safe and potable drinking water as a basic right was recognized by the United Nations as one of its Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), and an essential part of the right to adequate standard of living A 2015 World Resources Institute study warned that the Philippines will likely experience a “severe water shortage” in the year 2040. This is not surprising given the fact that in the World Bank's 2003 Philippine Environment Monitor, it was already reported that as of year 2000, compared to other countries in Southeast Asia, the Philippines already ranked 2nd to the lowest in terms of annual renewable water resources per capita. More than 10 million people in the Philippines still get their water from unsafe sources. As to sanitation, more than 6 million people still lack access to proper sanitation facilities. Our country has been having recurring water shortages and droughts brought about by demand and supply factors and exacerbated by natural calamities, extreme weather events, global warming, and climate change. Population growth, migration, urbanization, and technological advances weigh in as demand drivers, while environmental factors influence supply. There have also been seasonal, occasional, and sometimes artificial supply shortages of fish and other seafood, affected by the same demand and supply factors that affect water resources, and result in compromising food security and raising prices of water and food sourced from the inland waters, the seas, and the Pacific Ocean. Ironically, the country has excess rainwater in the rainy months and acute water needs in the dry months. Meanwhile, the national government has many different agencies attending to compartmentalized although related water and fisheries concerns but lacks a coherent water and fisheries policy framework. These agencies were created one by one to address issues and problems as they arose over the many past decades. Neglected was the rationalization of the alphabet soup of agencies. The problem is once again brought to the forefront with the current problems involving local water districts and their partner service providers in many areas of the country. The Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA) has officially launched an investigation into the matter following mounting complaints over poor water distribution services and related issues. The investigation, ordered by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., will look into the water utility firms’ and their joint venture agreements with local water districts across the country. This bill seeks to establish the national framework for water resource management create the Department of Water Resources and the Water Regulatory Commission to provide a unified and coordinated service to all Filipinos with regard their human right to water. It seeks to establish a body that shall ensure safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply and improved sanitation services for all Filipinos and that this finite resource will be sustained. Following the lead of other countries who have found it wise to create a special department to manage this vital resource of water including Japan, Australia, China, and India, the availability of potable water in the Philippines and the continuing water supply for domestic, agricultural and industrial consumption may be ensured and the perennial problem that seriously affects the lives of the people in terms of health, sanitation, food security, and livelihood may be effectively addressed. This bill was previously filed in the 19" Congress but was not enacted into law due to lack of material time. Given the above premises, the urgent passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 3424
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is a vital yet finite resource essential for life, economic development, and environmental sustainability. While our country currently faces significant challenges in achieving water security, including the impacts of climate change, population growth, pollution, and fragmented governance, these obstacles also present us with an opportunity to innovate and collaborate. By addressing these issues proactively, we can develop strategies that ensure a sustainable water future for all. This proposed measure presents a valuable prospect to establish a comprehensive national framework for water resource management. By creating the Department of Water Resources (DMW) and the Water Regulatory Commission (WRC), we can promote the equitable, efficient, and sustainable management of our country's water resources, benefiting both the environment and our communities. This bill outlines a constructive roadmap to secure water as a shared national heritage. By centralizing authority within the DWR and WRC, we will harmonize policies, encourage sustainable practices, and uphold the right to water for all Filipinos. The timely passage of this legislation will not only help us prevent future water crises but also enhance our resilience to climate change and promote water justice for current and future generations. The Department will serve as the main entity within the Executive Branch of the government responsible for policy-making, planning, coordination, implementation, monitoring, and administration. Its focus will be on the comprehensive, sustainable, climate-resilient, and integrated development and management of the water resources in the Philippines. This includes the optimal allocation and use of these resources for domestic and municipal water supply, sanitation, irrigation, hydropower, industry, flood management, and recreational purposes. 1 By consolidating disconnected policies and agencies under a clear and unified national strategy, the Philippines could experience transformative benefits. This approach could lead to a more efficient and equitable distribution of water, enhance resilience to climate change-related disasters such as floods and droughts, and promote a sustainable future for the country's vital water resources. In view of the foregoing, the immediate consideration of this measure is hereby earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is facing an impending water crisis. Studies as early as the 2003 Philippine Environment Monitor have shown that the Philippines ranks among the lowest in Southeast Asia in terms of annual renewable water resources per capita. A 2015 World Resources Institute report further projected that the country would face a severe water shortage by 2040. Climate change hazards, rainfall variability, rising temperatures, sea level rise, will further aggravate this situation. PAGASA’s downscaled climate projections show that water resources will be among the most adversely affected sectors. With a growing population and continuing economic development, demand will intensify among competing users in domestic, agricultural, industrial, and ecological sectors. The United Nations recognized access to safe and potable drinking water as a basic human right in 2010, yet as of 2015, more than 12 million Filipinos still sourced water from unsafe supplies. Over 4 million lacked access to sanitary toilets and defecated openly. The Philippine Water Supply and Sanitation Master Plan warns that unsafe water and polluted sources have serious public health and economic consequences: 31% of recorded illnesses in the last five years were water-related, with the economic impact of poor sanitation estimated at US$1.4 billion or 1.5% of GDP in 2005, 72% of which (US$1 billion) stemmed from health costs. Episodes of red tides and fish kills have also caused substantial livelihood losses for fisherfolk, while events like the closure of Boracay in 2018 due to polluted waters demonstrate the severe impact on tourism revenues. Water governance remains fragmented. Over 30 government units at national and local levels manage separate and often overlapping mandates in water supply, sanitation, irrigation, Page | 1 REPRES Ox aN flood control, and water quality regulation. This structure hinders the development of an integrated, science-based, and sustainable framework for water resources management and puts at risk the attainment of Sustainable Development Goal targets for universal access to safe water and improved sanitation by 2030. This bill proposes the creation of a Department of Water Resources as the primary policy, planning, coordinating, implementing, and regulatory body for the country’s water resources. The Department will adopt Integrated Water Resources Management, harmonize river basin planning, ensure science-based water allocation, and work towards universal access to safe, adequate, and affordable water and sanitation services. This bill also establishes an independent Water Regulatory Commission to address poor economic regulation and service disparities. As of the 2015 Family Income and Expenditure Survey, while 87.2% of the population accessed water from formal providers, only 43.6% had piped connections, 11.2% relied on communal faucets, and 45.2% on point sources. The remaining 12.8% used alternative sources such as rivers, shallow wells, or vended water. On wastewater treatment, only 4% of the population was connected to sewerage systems, mostly in Metro Manila, leaving much of the country without proper septage management. By creating a strong apex body and a dedicated independent regulator, this measure seeks to safeguard the right to safe and sufficient water, promote public health, protect livelihoods, and ensure that this finite resource is managed sustainably and equitably for present and future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 3670
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT FOR THIS PURPOSE CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATINGS FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State is responsible for providing water security to all citizens and inhabitants of its country. The Philippines as a water-rich country needs to rationalize and streamline the implementation of its existing and sometimes overlapping policies, laws and regulations affecting its water resources including irrigation, sewage and sanitation. In President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s State of the Nation Address on 25 July 2022, the President called on Congress to pave the way for the creation of a Department of Water Resources to adopt an integrated water resource management and address the water supply issues in the country especially in the urban areas. The bill proposes to create the Department of Water Resources to serve as the primary agency responsible for national policy-making, coordination and management of all the water resources in the Philippines. All government agencies related to water shall be rationalized under this Department. Integrated Water Resources Management shall be adopted as the strategic framework for water management policy-making and planning in the country. The bill also proposes to create an independent Water Regulatory Commission to ensure the effective and adequate delivery of water and sanitation services throughout the country under a credible, transparent and accountable regulatory framework. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LORENZ R. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution declares water resources as State property, emphasizing the national government’s sole ownership and control over their exploration, development, and utilization. It also mandates the State to protect the right to a balanced and healthful ecology, including the preservation of water quality and the protection of marine wealth. This bill seeks to create a Department of Water Resources to address the fragmented water sector, ensure universal access to safe water and sanitation, mitigate water scarcity and climate change impacts like droughts and floods, and consolidate overlapping water management functions under a single, dedicated agency with a comprehensive national framework. This centralized approach is necessary because water resources are a shared national resource, not limited by political boundaries, and requires integrated planning and management to meet growing demand and protect vulnerable systems. In this measure also is the creation of the Water Regulatory Commission. The Commission will be an independent regulatory body tasked with overseeing the performance, compliance, and service delivery of all water service providers, whether public or private. It is also mandated to ensure that water resources are delivered efficiently, safely, and at a fair rate, while safeguarding consumer rights and promoting accountability. In view of the foregoing, passage of this bill is earnestly requested for. pada ATTY. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is a universal truth that water is life. Without it, life as we know it would be impossible. At a fundamental level, humans can go for up to one or two months without food, but we can only survive for a few days without water. The United Nations General Assembly explicitly recognized the right to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right that is essential for the full enjoyment of life and all other human rights. Without water security, we risk endangering the health and lives of our people. In 2020, the UNICEF and the World Health Organization recorded that only 47.46% of the entire population in the Philippines had access to safely managed drinking water.1 As of 2024, around 40 million Filipinos still lack access to formal water resources and are instead dependent on rainwater, rivers, or creeks for their daily needs, according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).2 Water scarcity limits our access to safe drinking water and prevents us from practicing basic hygiene. It could lead to failures in the sewage systems and a surge in diseases. The Philippines faces the recurring paradox of having too much water during the rainy season and too little during the dry months.3 Year after year, communities endure destructive floods that displace families and damage livelihoods, only to suffer water shortages and droughts in the months that follow. This cycle of crisis is made worse by the fragmented and outdated state of our water governance. As the effects of climate change intensify, the urgency to act grows even stronger. This bill seeks to fundamentally reform the governance of the Philippine water sector. The proposed measure establishes a comprehensive and coherent institutional framework for water governance through the creation of two new agencies: the Department of Water Resources (DWR) and the Water Regulatory Commission (WRC). This proposed legislation aims to: 1. Centralize policy and planning under a dedicated Cabinet-level department that will oversee integrated water resource management (IWRM), including the development of a National Water Resources Management Plan; 2. Establish a unified and independent regulatory body, the Water Regulatory Commission, to oversee licensing, tariff-setting, and performance standards for all water supply, sanitation, and sewerage service providers; 3. Rationalize and harmonize overlapping mandates of existing agencies; 4. Enable long-term sector development through socialized credit, public-private partnerships, and capacity-building programs, especially for missionary areas and low-capacity water districts; 5. title: AN ACT CREATING A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR INTEGRATED WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT, CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, an archipelagic nation rich in water resources, is currently facing a significant challenge in effectively managing and distributing these vital resources. Despite the abundance of water across the country, access to safe, reliable, and sustainable water supply remains a challenge for millions of Filipinos, particularly in rural and underserved areas. This situation is exacerbated by climate change, rapid urbanization, pollution, and insufficient infrastructure. In response to this, it is imperative that the government adopts a more cohesive and forward-thinking approach to water resource management. This bill seeks to establish a National Framework for Integrated Water Resource Management, which will serve as the backbone for the governance and protection of the country's water resources. It envisions a holistic and coordinated approach, ensuring that the management of water for various uses occurs in a sustainable and equitable manner. The bill also provides for the creation of the Department of Water Resources, a national agency tasked with overseeing and coordinating the development, conservation, and utilization of water resources across the country. Additionally, the bill proposes the creation of the Water Regulatory Commission, which will be responsible for regulating water supply and sanitation services to ensure that these essential services are efficiently delivered to the public, in accordance with standards of fairness, safety, and sustainability. In line with the Philippine government's commitment to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly Goal 6, which ensures universal access to safe water and sanitation, this bill will help address the country’s existing gaps in water access and service delivery. By creating a central, dedicated agency and regulatory body, this bill will improve the coordination of efforts between national and local governments, the private sector, and other stakeholders, creating an efficient and accountable water management system that can respond effectively to the needs of the Filipino people. The establishment of the Department of Water Resources and the Water Regulatory Commission is also aligned with the country’s existing water laws, such as the Water Code of the Philippines (Presidential Decree No. 1067), the Philippine Clean Water Act of 2004 (Republic Act No. 9275), and the National Water Crisis Act (Republic Act No. 8041). These laws have set the groundwork for water resource management, but the fragmented governance structures and lack of coordination have limited their effectiveness. By centralizing and streamlining water management functions under the DWR, this bill will bring the Philippines closer to realizing its constitutional mandate of ensuring that the needs of the people are met through the responsible and sustainable use of natural resources. This bill represents a vital step in addressing one of the most pressing challenges of our time, which is the provision of clean, safe, and sustainable water to every Filipino. With its passage, we will not only improve the management and protection of our country’s water resources but also move toward greater equity, sustainability, and resilience in our communities. The time to act is now, and it is incumbent upon us to ensure that future generations of Filipinos inherit a water-secure and prosperous nation. MARLYN L. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to clean, safe, and reliable water supply and sanitation services is fundamental to public health, economic development, and environmental sustainability. Despite ongoing efforts, many communities across the Philippines continue to face challenges in securing adequate water resources and efficient sanitation systems. These challenges are further compounded by the growing impacts of climate change, rapid urbanization, and increasing demands from various sectors. There is an urgent need for a comprehensive and integrated approach to managing the country’s water resources to ensure universal access and promote sustainable development. This bill seeks to address these pressing concerns by establishing the Department of Water Resources as the primary government agency tasked with the comprehensive identification, mapping, planning, policy formulation, and management of all water resources in the country, excluding fisheries or aquaculture. This department will serve as the central authority to coordinate efforts in water resource utilization, development, sustainability, protection, and infrastructure development. This bill aims to achieve the following objectives: (1) to ensure and accelerate universal access to water supply and sanitation services nationwide, thereby advancing public health and socio-economic well-being; (2) to encourage responsible private sector participation by fostering and prioritizing infrastructure and public works that incorporate innovative solutions and international best practices, particularly those that effectively address the challenges posed by climate change; and (3) to declare all water and water treatment infrastructure projects as projects imbued with national interest, thus expediting their implementation and safeguarding their integrity. Through the creation of a dedicated Department of Water Resources, this bill provides a clear institutional framework to harmonize policies, programs, and projects related to water resources management. It strengthens governance and regulatory oversight, promotes sustainable and climate-resilient water infrastructure, and enhances the country’s capacity to meet the growing and diverse water needs of its population. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is fundamental to public health, to any industry, and our ecosystems. The Philippines, being an archipelagic nation, surrounded by water, yet faces persistent and systemic problems in water supply, quality, resource management and climate resilience. These issues undermine development, increase costs, and expose communities to health and economic risks. The 2020 State of the Philippine Water Report by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) highlights that 40% of water supply systems in the country are either underdeveloped or inefficient. These inefficiencies lead to significant water losses, with some estimates suggesting that as much as 30% of water supplied in major urban areas is lost due to leaks, theft, or poor infrastructure. According to the 2024 Annual Poverty Indicator Survey (APIS) preliminary results, more than half of families (53.1%) had access to a safely managed drinking water service from an improved source. These data leave us of the fact that a significant number of Filipino families are still lacking basic access to a proper water supply. With the establishment of the Department of Water Resources, it shall serve as the primary agency responsible for the comprehensive identification, mapping, policy formulation, and management of all water resources in the Philippines. It shall oversee the ownership, appropriation, utilization, development, and protection of these resources to ensure their optimal use, sanitation, and management in accordance to every applicable industry such as flood mitigation, agriculture, irrigation, etc. Likewise, the Department shall lead in planning and policy- making to achieve universal access to safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply and improved sanitation services for all Filipinos. Last 19th Congress, the bill was approved on third and final reading at the House of Representatives, accumulating one hundred twenty seven (127) authors. The challenges in our water sector are real — from polluted rivers and shrinking watersheds to system losses and the growing impact of climate change. By creating a Department of Water Resources alongside an independent Water Regulatory Commission, we can bring together the focus, expertise, and strong regulation needed to secure clean and reliable water for every Filipino, while ensuring fair use for agriculture, industry, and the environment. With these 1 reforms, we take an important step toward a safer, healthier, and more sustainable future that we all deserve. Let us not lose the pure and life-giving quality that water brings to us all. Olaf, a famous Disney character once said, “Water has memories.” And just like every memory, we shall keep our waters like a part of our treasury. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is highly sought. JESUS “JESS” R. label: HB 5831
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is a paradox that the Philippines has more than 30 water-related agencies, yet the water sector remains a governance orphan. Overlapping agency mandates and functions produced inconsistent standards and spending inefficiencies. A 2024 World Bank assessment found that fragmentation of policymaking has prevented coordinated planning, allocation, and management of water resources.1 The proposed Department of Water Resources (DWR) Act responds to this institutional problem with structural clarity and regulatory coherence. First, it creates the DWR as the central policy, planning, and coordinating authority for the comprehensive and integrated development, allocation, protection, and climate- resilient management of water resources across basins and jurisdictions. Second, it establishes an independent Water Regulatory Commission (WRC) to promulgate and set just and reasonable tariffs; license, benchmark, and audit service providers; enforce service-quality and performance standards; and protect consumers through due process and transparency. Third, it consolidates financing under a Water Trust Fund to prioritize missionary areas, climate-resilient infrastructure, wastewater and septage management, and watershed rehabilitation, with audit safeguards and multi-stakeholder oversight. The measure also codifies the following principles: (1) water is a basic human right and a vital public resource; (2) all waters belong to the State and must be allocated equitably and efficiently; (3) responsible private participation must be encouraged without tolerating monopolies or anti-competitive behavior; and (4) water and water- related infrastructure are projects imbued with national interest, which must be streamlined, accountable, climate-smart execution. The World Bank, Philippine Water Supply and Sanitation Project, THE WORLD BANK, 2024, available at https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099052624232518179/pdf/P5042571bacf5e001a57316e17763b6f71.pdf By marrying policymaking with science, planning with budgeting, and regulation with consumer protection, this bill steers the country back on-track for the attainment of Sustainable Development Goals 6 and climate-resilient development.2 This much-needed reform recognizes the constitutional duty of the State as steward of our waters. Stewardship demands coherence, competence, and courage. As climate volatility intensifies droughts and floods, we can no longer maintain the status quo of a fragmented water policy. For equity, safety, and growth, the immediate passage of the “Department of Water Resources Act” is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is one of the most valuable resources essential to human life. Our bodies are mostly made up of water and we need water in our daily lives. It is essential for our survival. Although our country is an archipelago, and water resources abound, the recent acceleration of climate change has made it a priority to set up a system that will ensure its proper management, equitable distribution, and equal access by all. This bill seeks to enact a law that will endure and accelerate universal access to water supply and sanitation services, in a regulatory regime that encourages responsible private sector participation and shall foster and prioritize the establishment of infrastructure and public works that adopt innovative solutions and international best practices to address the challenges of climate change and that all water and water treatment infrastructure projects are hereby declared as projects imbued with national interest. The establishment of a national framework for water resource management will ensure the preservation of this valuable resource and balance human usage and its impact on the environment. It will also address the current problem of lack of proper infrastructure and facilities for the provision of clean water for usage and sanitation in various areas nationwide. This bill already passed the third reading in the 19th Congress and its passage in the 20th Congress is earnestly sought. JOSEPH “JOJO” L. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Access to safe drinking water and sanitation is a basic human right. In line with “Goal 6: Ensure access to water and sanitation for all” under the Sustainable Development Goals of the United Nations, it is imperative to demonstrate solutions that will empower citizens and communities with sustainable safe water and sanitation services. In 2024, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources reports that some 40 million Filipinos lack access to formal water resources. Many households continue to rely on rainwater, river, or creeks for their daily needs— highlighting the urgency of addressing water access in the country.! 1 Zaldarriaga, Joe, “Water access for all”, THE PHILIPPINE STAR, 27 Feb 2025, https:/ / www. philstar.com/ business /2025/02/27/2424412/water-access-all. 1 Further highlighting these challenges, a study by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies, “The Last Mile Challenge: Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) in the Philippines”, has identified significant gaps in existing water infrastructure and delivery systems. While the country has various types of water service providers, most supply water through Level I service, which frequently involve unsafe sources. Only 45% of water comes from safe sources, with 23% sourced from waterworks and 22% from shared communal faucets. The study also found that about 34% of water service providers are community-based organizations, while 31% are private and often unnamed entities that operate without formal management structures or reliable systems —conditions that compromise water quality and public safety. The study emphasized the need for a robust, integrated monitoring and evaluation framework to track progress, identify gaps, and guide effective interventions. It likewise underscored the importance of addressing governance and management issues to improve the efficiency and reliability of water supply and sanitation services.2 In response to these challenges, this proposed bill aims to develop a nationwide water supply, sanitation, and sewerage system that is orderly, rational, efficient, and responsive, while ensuring that rates remain reasonable. It further recognizes that the regulation and management of water resources must be carefully planned to secure long-term availability amid rising demand, population growth, and the threats posed by climate change. Effective water management also requires strong coordination across sectors, agencies, institutions, and stakeholders to harmonize relevant laws, policies, and initiatives. To achieve efficient, affordable, and equitable delivery of water supply, sanitation, and septage services, the State may enter into arrangements with the private sector, civil society, and community-based organizations based on the principle of beneficial use. As these arrangements constitute public service, they ? Accordingly, this bill proposes the establishment a National Framework for Water Resource Management through the creation of the Department of Water Resources and the Water Regulatory Commission—a unified policy and regulatory structure that promotes innovation and responsible private sector participation while ensuring environmental sustainability. Through rational, evidence-based, and integrated management of all water resources, this measure aims to guarantee that all Filipinos have access to safe, sufficient, and affordable water supply, sanitation, and septage services. label: HB 6848
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, more than three (3) million people continue to rely on unsafe and unsustainable water sources, while an estimated seven (7) million Filipinos lack access to improved sanitation facilities. Moreover, climate projections up to 2050 indicate that the country will experience rising temperatures, reduced rainfall during the dry season, and more intense rainfall events during the wet season, further increasing water scarcity, flooding, and water resource management challenges.1 Water is one of the most basic human needs, and access to safe and sufficient water is recognized as a universal human right by the United Nations. Ensuring reliable access to water supply and sanitation services is therefore a fundamental obligation of the State. At present, the management and regulation of the country’s water resources are fragmented among various government agencies, including the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), and the National Irrigation Administration (NIA). This fragmented governance structure has resulted in overlapping mandates, duplication of functions, weak coordination, and, in some instances, conflicting policies and programs. In view of these challenges, this bill proposes the creation of a Department of Water Resources. The proposed department shall serve as the central authority responsible for the integrated planning, management, regulation, and development of the country’s water resources. It aims to strengthen policy coherence, improve 1 Barkwith, Andrew. British Geological Survey. (10 June 2021). Improving water security in the Philippines Retrieved from: https://www.bgs.ac.uk/news/improving-water-security-in-the-philippines institutional coordination, and ensure the efficient and sustainable delivery of water supply and sanitation services. Ultimately, the establishment of the Department of Water Resources seeks to uphold the fundamental human right to water, enhance climate resilience, and accelerate the achievement of universal access to safe, affordable, and sustainable water and sanitation services for all Filipinos. For these reasons, the swift passage of the foregoing measure is earnestly sought. RICARDO S. CRUZ JR. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is one of the most important resources in the world. The Philippines, as an archipelagic country, is gifted with this resource in abundance. However, mismanagement and unsustainable consumption of water continues to be a major predicament of the country. In 2024, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources estimated around 40 million Filipinos do not have access to a formal water supply. This leads to various problems particularly on health and sanitation. An analysis conducted by the Philippine Statistics Authority revealed that between the years 2010-2019, fourteen (14) Filipinos die everyday because of water-borne diseases caused by contaminated water such as cholera, typhoid, and leptospirosis. The government needs to immediately address these concerns by providing comprehensive and long-term solutions. Congruent with the international efforts under the auspices of the WHO, the concerned government agencies should intensify its efforts to develop and implement water safety planning, to strengthen systems and capacity for drinking water quality surveillance and monitoring, and to improve water, sanitation, and hygiene. Such endeavor is consistent with Sustainable Development Goal 6 which seeks to provide clean water and sanitation for all. Among the targets under this SDG are the achievement of universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all; improvement of water quality by reducing pollution, eliminating dumping and minimizing release of hazardous chemicals and materials, halving the proportion of untreated wastewater and substantially increasing recycling and safe reuse globally; and implementation of integrated water resources management at all levels, including through transboundary cooperation as appropriate. The "National Water Act' seeks to rationalize the management of water resources, sewerage, and sanitation through the creation of the Department of Water Resources. The Department shall be the primary agency responsible for the comprehensive and integrated identification and mapping of all water resources, planning, policy formulation, and management of the ownership, appropriation, utilization, exploitation, development, and protection of water resources in the Philippines. The bill also establishes the Water Regulatory Commission which shall be placed under the administrative supervision of the Department of Water Resources. To ensure coherent and coordinated management of water resources, the economic regulatory units and functions of the Metropolitan Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS), National Water Resources Board (NWRB), and Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA) will be transferred to the Commission. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is highly recommended. NGGOY EJERCITO ESTRADA of tiK «. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE According to water.org, a global nonprofit organization working to bring water and sanitation to the world, out of 115 million Filipinos, 60 million lack access to safe water sources and 43 million lack access to a safe toilet. On top of that, our water sources are constantly on tremendous pressure due to the ever-increasing demand of our population and a burgeoning economy. This is more pronounced during the dry season when many of our dams and water sources reach critical levels. Aside from water sources problems, another issue that we face is the quality of water from our sources. The quality of water from many areas continue to deteriorate due to several factors, among them is pollution. These problems and issues are difficult to resolve when the government has more than 30 different agencies or units that have water-related functions or deal with water issues. To effectively implement the Philippines' roadmap to achieve universal water and sanitation services coverage by 2028 and achieve synergy and close coordination among agencies with water-related functions, it is imperative to have a department that will house all these agencies with water-related functions. This bill seeks to establish the Department of Water Resources. This Department once created, will be the lead agency to implement the country's policies and programs on water. It will have the whole-of-government approach in dealing with water issues. It will provide synergy, close coordination among government agencies and synchronize all the government's policies and programs on water. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is urgently sought. JUAN MIGUEL F. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, with the efforts of the public sector, private entities, advocacy groups, and local volunteers, has made significant progress in preserving our water resources. Safe and clean water has become more accessible for consumption through resolving water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) challenges and implementing sustainable water programs. However, recurring challenges in providing potable water still impact marginalized sectors and far-flung areas. According to a 2024 Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) study on the country’s progress on WASH,! some municipalities in the BARMM and MIMAROPA regions are still drinking surface water. Poor water management has also posed alarming risks to the health and safety of children. In 2019, 86% of diarrhea-related deaths were associated with inadequate WASH access, of which 35% of these deaths were among children under five. These ' Ulep, V. G., Talamayan, J. T., Casas, L. The Last-Mile Challenge: Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) in the Philippines. https://doi.org/10.62986/dp2024.19 real-life scenarios reflect the need for more accessible sanitation services, infrastructure, facilities, and awareness programs.’ Multiple government units and agencies are responsible for establishing the direction of water management in the country. Water related responsibilities are fragmented among various agencies. Aside from the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), as the primary agency for the water sector, other agencies like the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) have functions connected to water management. Local government units (LGUs) supervise water systems in their cities and municipalities, while other agencies address the need for consumption, supply, sewerage, agriculture, irrigation, and other water management purposes. With the recent flood control anomaly, a new problem emerges, the lack of coordination among agencies concerning flood mitigation and river basin and water system management. While the government’s enthusiasm for sustaining local water resources is evident, there comes an overlap and non-coordination in plans, objectives, and functions of these components. With the creation of this bill to establish the Department of Water Resources Management, there will be a coordinating agency to align all government programs, policies, and efforts concerning water management and water resource sustainability. This will include the management and maximization of the use of domestic and municipal water supply, sanitation, irrigation, hydropower, industry, navigation, flood management, storm water utilization and urban drainage. To further strengthen coordination, a National Water Sector Policy Council is created to ensure inter-agency coordination and policy harmonization among related and concerned agencies and departments such as the DENR, DOH, DA, DPWH, and DILG. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is a universal truth that water is life. Without it, life as we know it would be impossible. At a fundamental level, humans can go for up to one or two months without food, but we can only survive for a few days without water. The United Nations General Assembly explicitly recognized the right to safe and clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right that is essential for the full enjoyment of life and all other human rights. Without water security, we risk endangering the health and lives of our people. In 2020, the UNICEF and the World Health Organization recorded that only 47.46% of the entire population in the Philippines had access to safely managed drinking water.1 As of 2024, around 40 million Filipinos still lack access to formal water resources and are instead dependent on rainwater, rivers, or creeks for their daily needs, according to the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR).2 Inquirer.net. WHO-Unicef report: Nearly half of Filipinos get safe drinking water. Published on 07 July 2021. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1456912/who-unicef-report-nearly-half-of-filipinos-get-safe- drinking-water (Accessed on 26 June 2025). Philippine News Agency. Ensuring Water Access. Published on 25 February 2025. Available at https://www.pna.gov.ph/opinion/pieces/1018-ensuring-water-access (Accessed on 25 June 2025). Water scarcity limits our access to safe drinking water and prevents us from practicing basic hygiene. It could lead to failures in the sewage systems and a surge in diseases. The Philippines faces the recurring paradox of having too much water during the rainy season and too little during the dry months.3 Year after year, communities endure destructive floods that displace families and damage livelihoods, only to suffer water shortages and droughts in the months that follow. This cycle of crisis is made worse by the fragmented and outdated state of our water governance. Our current institutions lack the capacity, coherence, and coordination to manage water across its full cycle. As the effects of climate change intensify, the urgency to act grows even stronger. This bill seeks to fundamentally reform the governance of the Philippine water sector. The proposed measure establishes a comprehensive and coherent institutional framework for water governance through the creation of two new agencies: the Department of Water Resources (DWR) and the Water Regulatory Commission (WRC). This proposed legislation aims to: Centralize policy and planning under a dedicated Cabinet-level department that will oversee integrated water resource management (IWRM), including the development of a National Water Resources Management Plan; 2. Establish a unified and independent regulatory body, the Water Regulatory Commission, to oversee licensing, tariff-setting, and performance standards for all water supply, sanitation, and sewerage service providers; 3. Rationalize and harmonize overlapping mandates of existing agencies; 4. Enable long-term sector development through socialized credit, public-private partnerships, and capacity-building programs, especially for missionary areas and low-capacity water districts; Ensure transparency, accountability, and citizen participation in planning, regulation, and service delivery, while protecting consumers' rights. This proposed measure is not a mere exercise in administrative restructuring. It represents a long-overdue modernization of our national approach to water governance, shifting from a fragmented and reactive framework to one that recognizes water as a strategic and unifying policy priority. It calls for focused, science-based, and coordinated leadership, anchored in the principles of sustainability, equity, and accountability. The era of piecemeal and ad hoc reforms must come to an end. The time has come to build a future-ready, climate-resilient, and inclusive water sector. One that upholds the right of every Filipino to safe, adequate, and affordable water. Available at https://www.jircas.go.jp/sites/default/files/publication/intlsymp/intlsymp-13_41-52.pdf (Accessed on 25 June 2025). This version of the measure builds on the groundwork laid during the 19th Congress, based on Senate Bill No. 2771 under Committee Report No. 281. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 1976, then-President Ferdinand E. Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 1067, or the Water Code of the Philippines—di landmark decree that sought to codify how water, one of our most vital natural resources, should be allocated and protected. Nearly five decades later, the Philippines has yet to evolve a modern, unified, and fully functioning governance system that can meet the demands of a growing population, a warming climate, and a fractured institutional landscape. Since the early 2000s, at least five major attempts have been made to establish a Department of Water or create a national framework for water resource governance. The bills have changed names over the years — from the National Water Resources Management Framework Actto the Department of Water Act— but the core problem has remained: a fragmented, overlapping, and outdated governance structure that is failing to meet the needs of our people. With each Congress, the proposal was inherited, refiled, sometimes passed by the House, but never fully enacted. The problem, like water itself, kept slipping through the cracks. Today, the situation is no longer just inconvenient — it is unsustainable. As early as 2015, the Philippines has been classified as "water-stressed" by international standards, with per capita water availability dropping below 1,700 cubic meters per year.1 In a business-as-usual scenario, the World Resources Institute warns that vast portions of our archipelago will face extremely high water stress by 2050. This is not a future threat — it is a present emergency. Miliions of Fiiipinos still do not have reliable access to safe and clean water. According to the 2024 Annual Poverty Indicators Survey (APIS), 2.5% of househoids reiy on unsafe water sources, and 3.2% still practice open defecation, while over 12% have no access to basic sanitation facilities. Meanwhile, over 57% of major watersheds are critically denuded, worsening our vulnerability to floods, droughts, and degraded ecosystems. At the heart of the dysfunction is institutionai chaos. There are over 30 national government agencies involved in water resource management — each with its own mandates, plans, and standards. Coordination is minimal. Accountability is dispersed. Services are duplicated. And for the average Filipino, what this means is unpredictable bills, unequal service, dry taps, flooded streets, and unsafe water.2 This bill proposes a long-overdue solution—by creating two vital institutions: First, the Department of Water Resources (DWR), which shaii serve as the centra! coordinating body for all matters related to water policy, planning, infrastructure, data, and governance. It shall consolidate and rationalize the powers of several agencies, including the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), the Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), and the Water Resources Management Office (WRMO). The DWR wiil craft and lead the implementation of a unified Nationai Water Resources Management Plan grounded in the principles of Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM)—ensuring that water is managed as a finite, shared, and strategic resource. Second, the bill establishes the Water Regulatory Commission (WRC) — an independent economic regulator with powers to set tariffs, license all water service providers (WSPs), and enforce performance and service standards. At present, regulation is fragmented across NWRB, LWUA, MWSS, LGUs, economic zones, among other entities — resulting in inconsistent standards and rate-setting, weak oversight, and investor hesitation. LGU-run water providers, in particular, have underperformed, with studies from the Worid Bank and DILG citing poor governance, inadequate tariffs, and political interference. The WRC will streamline the regulatory landscape, provide predictability for investment, and protect consumers through rational pricing, consumer feedback, and performance monitoring. It wili also ensure that water is not just provided, but safely managed— meeting technicai and public health standards. 1 Kuzma, et.al, 2023. 2 According to the Integrated Water Resources Management Plan (IWMP), among the agencies involved in water governance include DEPDev, CCC, DENR (including NWRB, FMB, EMB, MGB, RBCO), LLDA, DILG, LWUA, MWSS, LGUs, WDs, DPWH, DA (including NIA and BSWM), DOH, NPC, and PEZA/TIEZA. This measure also includes a Socialized Credit Program, enabling public and community-based providers to invest in system upgrades and service expansion. It mandates clear rules for water rights allocation, supports data-driven planning through a centralized national water database, and promotes sustainability by integrating watershed protection, climate resiliency, gender equity, and disaster preparedness into national and regional water planning. What sets this version of the bill apart from previous attempts is not just its breadth — but its urgency, coherence, and momentum. In December 2023, the House of Representatives passed its counterpart bill on third reading. In February 2025, President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. convened a high-level sectoral meeting and ordered the refinement and advancement of the Executive version. Since then, the bill has undergone inter-agency harmonization and was formally endorsed to the Office of the President for certification as urgent. This is the closest the Philippines has ever come to finally reforming its water governance structure. We cannot allow this opportunity to slip away again. The next drought, flood, or water supply crisis will not wait for our laws to catch up. This is no ordinary bill seeking to create a department. This is an earnest attempt to secure our water future — to give every Filipino the right to clean water, to prepare our communities for the realities of climate change, to make water systems efficient and accountable, and to make one grand gesture to Mother Nature of our nation's recognition that water is a lifeblood that our people is willi

title: AN ACT CREATING THE WATER RESOURCES AND MANAGEMENT AUTHORITY, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, "The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them." Access to clean water is a basic human right. It is crucial in the sustenance of man and is used in almost every industry such as in irrigation, power generation, livestock raising, and fisheries, among others. According to a study funded by the US Agency for International Development (USAID), every single major city in the Philippines is expected to face some form of water shortage by 2025, prompting calls from environment advocates for the implementation of a nationwide water demand management program. With the onslaught of the pandemic in 2019, water, more than ever, proved to be the most essential public utility in promoting health and cleanliness. The cursory and forgotten habit of hand-washing has never been this critical, in certain instances in fact a matter of life and death. However, many Filipinos still do not have access to clean water. Some 40 million lack access to formal water resources in the Philippines, according to a 2024 report from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR). Many remain dependent on rainwater, rivers or creeks for their daily needs - highlighting the urgent need to address the problem of water access in the country. The management of water resources in the country used to be an exclusive function of the government through the Manila Waterworks and Sewerage System (MWSS) and its predecessors. Many laws have since been promulgated to address the water crisis, including the enactment of Republic Act No. 8041 or the "National Water Crisis Act of 1995" which recognized the need for the government to address the nationwide water management problem. In March 1996, Executive Order No. 311 was issued by President Fidel V. Ramos, encouraging the private sector's participation in the operation and facilities of the MWSS. As a result, the institutional arrangements in the Philippines' water sector have become exceedingly complicated, with overlapping functions of over 30 national government offices, local water boards and privatized water utility operators. Further, the recent spate of "man-made" flooding disasters has made the consolidation of these entities into a single coherent and comprehensive Water Resources and Management Authority urgent and critical. This bill seeks to finally establish the Authority as the sole government unit in charge of managing, integrating, and unifying policies pertaining to the use, distribution, and management of water resources in the country. In light of this, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR WATER RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF WATER RESOURCES AND THE WATER REGULATORY COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE One of Sustainable Goals of the United Nations is to ensure universal access to clean water and sanitation. Access to clean water and proper sanitation is the cornerstone of national development, public health, and environmental sustainability. According to the National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), 97.6% of Filipino families use improved drinking water sources and 84% have access to basic sanitation services. However, despite this progress, our country is still behind other Southeast Asian countries in terms of access to basic sanitation services. According to the 2020 Annual Poverty Indicators Survey (APIS), approximately 8.4% of Filipino households still rely on potentially unsafe sources of water, particularly unprotected wells, undeveloped springs, rivers, ponds, lakes, rainwater, or water purchased from tanker trucks and water peddlers. In 2022, APIS also reported that around 16% of households have limited or no access to sanitation facilities. The water sector in the Philippines is highly fragmented, with more than 30 government offices and instrumentalities involved in various aspects such as water supply, sanitation, irrigation, flood control, and water quality. This has resulted in overlapping functions, duplication of efforts, and unclear accountability. Furthermore, many water service providers are unregulated, water losses remain high, and long­ term planning is ineffective due to these institutional and governance gaps. 1 Moreover, faced with limited funding, local water districts often resort to partnerships with the private sector. However, it has been reported that some of these Public-Private Partnerships face issues such as declining service satisfaction, revenue losses, and concerns over long-term sustainability. In order to address the complex challenges faced by the water sector, this bill proposes the creation of the Department of Water Resources Management, a centralized agency responsible for the planning and policy formulation towards the attainment of universal access to safe, adequate, affordable, and sustainable water supply, and improved sewerage and sanitation services for all Filipinos. Alongside this, the bill also establishes the Water Regulatory Commission, an independent regulatory body tasked with overseeing the performance, compliance, and service delivery of all water service providers, whether public or private. The Commission is mandated to ensure that water services are delivered efficiently, safely, and at fair rates, while safeguarding consumer rights and promoting accountability. Towards this end, the purpose of this bill is to improve the quality of life of all Filipinos. Access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene is the most basic human need, essential to the health and well-being of every Filipino. It is for this purpose that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. FFYT. TULFO TWENTIETH CONGRESS OF THE ) REPUBLIC OF THE PHILIPPINES ) 2025 First Regular Session ) SENA TE S. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As a concrete step towards the sustainable exploration, exploitation and use of our country’s extensive marine and aquatic resources, the bill seeks to create a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR), which shall become the principal government agency responsible for securing our country’s fishery and aquatic resources. Although there are agencies attached to the Department of Agriculture that are currently performing functions related to marine resources, a centralized agency specifically created for such purpose can better discharge this duty. Towards this end, the DFAR shall have the power to administer, develop, conserve and utilize all fisheries and aquatic resources shail have the jurisdiction to take control over the production, capture, dispensation and promotion of fisheries and marine products in the country. The creation of the DFAR will be a significant move to ensure the protection of Philippine waters and marine resources and more importantly, the rights of local fish workers. Due to the foregoing reasons, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a country composed of more than 7,100 islands and a coastline extending 36,289 kilometers. As an archipelagic country, fishing is naturally a major source of livelihood for a lot of Filipinos. The fisheries industry employs some 1.4 million Filipino fishing operators nationwide as of May 2022. In 2021, the fishing and aquaculture sector generated a gross value-added (GVA) amounting to around Php 223.2 billion, contributing about 12.6% to the GVA of the agriculture industry in the Philippines. In 2021, total fisheries production was recorded at 4,250.79 thousand metric tons (MT), which translates to a total production value of Php 302.83 billion. In 2018, the Philippines ranked as the 8th top fish producing country in the world, with a total production of 4.35 million MT of fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and aquatic plants (including seaweed). These figures reflect how the fisheries and aquaculture industry contribute significantly to the country's food security, employment, and foreign exchange earnings, as well as the importance of the industry in the country's economy and its potential to grow. Data from the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, however, show that the global position of the Philippines in aquaculture production has fallen steadily from 4th place in 1985 to 12th place in 2022, and the Philippines now contributes only a little over one percent (1%) of global farmed fish production compared to five percent (5%) originally. This downtrend in the country’s production of fisheries and aquatic resources poses a challenge for the State to find more ways on how to sustainably utilize our aquatic resources for economic growth and improved livelihood and employment, while preserving the health of the ocean ecosystem. This economic paradigm, which characterizes a sustainable management of marine resources and the marine-linked sectors in the economy, is referred to as the “blue economy.” Aside from fisheries, the blue economy also encompasses tourism, trade, and other economic activities related to the utilization of our ocean resources. In 2018, the share of the blue economy to the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was estimated at 4.3%, corresponding to a GVA amounting to Php 789.5 billion, which is higher by 7.7% compared to the 2017 record of Php 578.0 billion. In 2019, the blue economy recorded Page 1 of 20 a PhP 916.31 billion, accounting for 4.7% of the country’s GDP. In 2020, however, the blue economy declined by -32.6%, posting a GVA of Php 617 billion and accounting for 3.4% of the country's GDP. Among the ocean-based industries, ocean fishing remains as the largest contributor to the country's blue economy. As reflected in the said figures, the blue economy in the Philippines represents an important source of income and resources for the vast majority of the population. Thus, changes in policies and institutions to provide sustainable conditions to ensure the continuity of marine life and the prosperity of the blue economy are urgently needed. At present, the Department of Agriculture is the main agency in charge of managing and utilizing our marine and aquatic resources. However, the Department’s focus is primarily directed towards land-based agriculture to the prejudice of the blue economy and everything that it has to offer. Considering the extent of the blue economy’s activities and its contributions to society, it is time that the State provides for a focused and specialized department dedicated to the needs and concerns of the sector. The proposed measure seeks to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) in order to strengthen its institutional capacity as the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources. Creating a department solely dedicated to the needs and concerns of the fisheries and aquatic resources of the country will be a significant step in order to better protect, utilize, maximize, and conserve the nation's blue economy, as well as uphold the best interest of the fisher folk. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. RON P. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Given its geographical characteristics, the Philippines has been regarded as one of the major fish-producing countries of the world. The Philippines is blessed with some 220 million hectares of territorial waters, 18.46 million hectares of continental shelf area and 2.7 million hectares of coral reefs. Inland, the Philippines hosts about 246,063 hectares of swamplands, 253,854 hectares of fishponds and about 250,000 hectares of other inland resources. The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO UN) projected that the country would produce about 3.23 million tonnes of fish by 2030. The fisheries industry is a critical socioeconomic sector in terms of its role in production of food and generation of household income. On the one hand, an average Filipino household annually spends about P11,950 on fish and other seafood, and consumes about 17.79 kilogram of tuna, 11.11 kg of tHlapia, 10.13 kg of bangus, and 5.86 kg of galunggong. On the other hand, the fisheries and aquaculture sector contribute P248.27 billion to the national economy, or about 12.70% of the total Gross Value Added (GVA) of the Agriculture, Hunting, Forestry and Fishing in 2021. Despite the importance of the sector to Filipinos in terms of sustenance and livelihood, the Philippine fisheries industry experiences nominal growth without improvements in productivity. While the Gross Value Added (GVA) of fisheries and aquaculture increased by an average of 1.07% per annum from 2011 to 2021 in real terms, the volume of fisheries production actually declined by an average of 1.33% annually during the same period. This seemingly-ironic situation reveals a deep-seated problem in the sector ~ one where the price inflation is one of the primary drivers of ‘growth,’ This predicament calls for a stronger government agency to maintain sufficient and sustainable food supply, to improve the productivity of the fisheries industry, to conserve our marine and aquatic resources, and to protect the welfare of small-scale fishermen and local fishing communities, This bill seeks to create a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, a government agency distinct from the Department of Agriculture, to address the needs of the Philippine fisheries sector. Through this intervention, proper institutional focus, sufficient technical expertise and adequate government support and funding can be extended on matters concerning the Philippine fishery sector. Ultimately, this bill seeks to realize two noble objectives: ensuring sustainable livelihcod for Filipino fisherfolk, and maintaining an adequate food supply for the country in the years to come. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 7, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “The State shall protect the rights of subsistence fishermen, especially of local communities, to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources, both inland and offshore. It shall provide support to such fishermen through appropriate technology and research, adequate financial, production, and marketing assistance, and other services.” As an archipelagic state with 7,641 islands and over 2.2 million km 2 of highly productive seas, the Philippines enjoys vast oceans and seas surrounding its peripheral territories that are rich in various species of marine and aquatic resources. It was also recorded that in 2018, 927,612 of our labor workforce engage in capture fishing while 239,483 fisherfolk were engaged in gleaning, 209,058 in aquaculture, 106,644 in fish vending, 34,880 in fish processing, and 384,129 in other fishing activities.1 Despite the abundance of marine and aquatic resources, our fisherfolk remained to be one of the sectors with the highest poverty incidence in the country with a 26.2% rate in 2018. 2 Our fisherfolk, together with farmers, were consistently recorded to be the poorest among other basic sectors since the 2006 statistical year of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).3 These data clearly show that there is a huge disconnect in the strategic utilization of our resources and uplifting of the livelihoods of our coastal communities. Given this dilemma, this bill intends to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources which will be the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources in the country. While we recognize the existence of the current Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources attached to the Department of Agriculture (DA), the creation of a separate department would give the much-needed 1 https://www.rappler.com/environment/philippines-fisheries-sector-statistics/ 2 https://psa.gov.ph/poverty-press-releases/nid/162541 3 https://psa.gov.ph/poverty-press-releases/nid/120251 specialized attention to the needs and concerns of the fisheries and aquatic resources industry. In addition, this would allow DA to focus its efforts on land-based farming including crop production, poultry, and livestock that would transcend to increased country’s food self-sufficiency. The department will also be empowered not only to conserve, promote, and develop the industry but also to protect the rights of our local fishermen. Indeed, the creation of a new Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources would serve the best interest of the country’s fisherfolk and the conservation of our marine resources. The immediate passage of the bill is most earnestly sought. LUIS RAYMUND “LRAY” F. VILLAFUERTE, JR. MIGUEL LUIS R. VILLAFUERTE TSUYOSHI ANTHONY G. HORIBATA NICOLAS “NICK” C. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2018, the Philippines ranked 8th among the top fish producing countries in the world with its total production of 4.35 million metric tons (MT) of fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and aquatic plants (including seaweed). The production constituted 2.06% of the total world production of 211.87 million MT (FAO, 2020). In terms of aquaculture production, the country ranked 11th in the world with 826.01 thousand MT or 1.01% share of the total global aquaculture production of 82.10 million MT. The total value of the country’s aquaculture production including fish, crustaceans, and mollusks is USD 1.89 billion (FAO, 2020). The Philippines is also the world’s 4th largest producer of aquatic plants (including seaweed) having a total of 1.48 million MT or 4.56% of the total world production of 32.39 million MT (FAO, 2020). The fishing industry’s contribution to the country’s Gross Domestic Page 1 of 19 Product (GDP) is 1.52% at both current and constant 2018 prices. This translates to PhP 273.41 billion at current prices and PhP 266.22 billion at constant prices of the country’s GDP of PhP 17,939 billion (current prices). The industry also shared 12.27% (PhP 224.19 billion) and 12.54% (PhP 223.20 billion) for both current and constant prices of the Gross Value Added (GVA) in Aquaculture, Hunting, Forestry, and Fishing Group of PhP 1,827.01 billion (current prices) and PhP 1,780.54 (constant prices), respectively (PSA, 2021). According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), approximately 1.6 million Filipinos depend on fisheries and aquaculture for their livelihood. However, despite the sector's vastness, poverty incidence continues to remain high among fishermen - estimated at 34% in 2018, higher by 12.4% than the poverty incidence of the general population. In order to strategically develop and utilize the country's fisheries and aquatic resources, and curb poverty in the rural areas where most of the country's fishermen live, this bill proposes the creation of a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) which shall be responsible for the development and management of fisheries and marine resources in Philippine waters including the exclusive economic zone, as well as the protection and conservation of the nation's marine wealth. The department will also ensure that the needs and concerns of the fisherfolk are adequately addressed to ultimately help them move out of poverty. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The country is blessed by enormous bodies of water with abundant marine resources. Two-thirds of the territorial area of the Philippines is composed of water, covering a total area of 171 million hectares. For this reason, a significant number of Filipinos engage in fishing as their main source of livelihood. To ensure the preservation and proper development of the country's archipelago waters and marine resources, this bill proposes the creation of the Department of fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR). The DFAR shall have the power to manage, develop, protect, conserve and utilize all fisheries and aquatic resources of the country, except for municipal waters, which shall remain under the jurisdiction of local government units. The DFAR shall likewise regulate the production, capture, processing and marketing of fisheries and marine products in the country. This is to make sure that the country's marine wealth is to be exclusively used for the benefit of the Filipino people. The creation of the DFAR will be a significant breakthrough in providing utmost protection to Philippine waters and marine resources. This will help in pursuing the government's thrust to increase food production to meet the demands of the country's fast growing population and alleviate poverty among the fishermen. Thus, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. RUFUS B.
