title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THERFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The aquatic resources of the Philippines are broadly divided into marine resources and inland resources. Our country’s unique geographic feature as an archipelago promises abundance of these resources and opportunities for economic growth. For a long time, we have enjoyed these blessings. We thought they’re limitless, until scarcity and poverty started banging our doors. Based on the available data of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, the volume of our country’s fisheries production had been declining year after year, except for the years 2018 and 2019 wherein we saw slight recoveries. It means the growth of the fisheries industry which is attributed to production of aquaculture, the municipal capture fisheries, and the commercial capture fisheries, is on the negative. In 2020, our fishery export was at 261,495.23 MT but our total fishery import was at 405,570 MT. The importance of the aquatic resources in terms of the demands of our growing population and the country’s need to propel economic development cannot be undermined. The fishing industry is contributing Php266B to our economy. It shared 12.54% of the Gross Value Added (GVA) in the Aquaculture, Hunting, Forestry, and Fishing Group of our agricultural sector in 2021. Aside from the pressure of feeding 111M Filipinos, more than 2M fisherfolks rely on this industry. Over the years, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources has ballooned into nine (9) functional divisions and eight (8) technology centers. The need to elevate this Bureau into a Department, separate and distinct from the Department of Agriculture is not just a recognition of the enormous task we have lodged upon its shoulders but to acknowledge the importance of our aquatic resources in securing food security for today and tomorrow’s generation. As a Department, sufficient resources can be allocated to develop, manage, utilize, protect and conserve these valuable resources. Additionally, this legislative action, will address the poverty incidence besetting the aquatic industry sector. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this Bill is earnestly, sought. HON. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Philippines is globally recognized as one of the major contributors to the world's fisheries industry. In 2018, our country made a significant impact by contributing 1.89 million metric tons (MT) of fish, accounting for 2% of the global marine capture production and ranking 13th worldwide. Additionally, we are the 4th largest seaweed producer globally, as reported by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) in 2020. Our fisheries industry is comprised of three sectors: aquaculture, municipal fisheries, and commercial fisheries. In 2018, aquaculture alone accounted for 53% of the total production, with 2.3 million MT, focusing on the cultivation of species such as seaweeds, milkfish, tilapia, and shrimps/prawns. Municipal fisheries constituted 25% of the total production with 1.1 million MT, while the commercial fisheries sector contributed about 946 thousand MT, comprising 22% of the overall fisheries production. These numbers, sourced from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), highlight the immense potential of our fisheries sector. Furthermore, fisheries are a cornerstone of our nation's export earnings, contributing significantly to our economic stability. In 2018, the Philippines earned approximately US$1.6 billion through fishery exports. Our primary fishery exports include tuna, seaweeds, shrimps/prawns, crabs, octopus, grouper, round scad, cuttlefish and squid, sea cucumber, and ornamental fish, according to BFAR's 2019 data. To harness the full potential of our fisheries sector, it is crucial to establish a dedicated Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources. Such a department will enable us to consolidate efforts, streamline regulations, and implement policies that promote sustainable fishing practices, protect our marine environment, and support the livelihoods of our coastal communities and fisherfolks. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, being an archipelago with very rich marine resources, can be a marine powerhouse. Thus, it is logical that a Department that is focused and accountable for the development, management, and conservation of our country's aquatic resources and fishing industries be established. Fish and aquatic resources are some of the biggest blessings of God to the people. Filipinos have always relied on fish as a basic food resource and commodity. Our dependence on fish can be attributed to the archipelagic nature of the Philippines with its approximately 7,600 islands. Our national territory comprises all the islands and waters, including its territorial sea, seabed, subsoil, the insular shelves, and other submarine areas. The waters around and between the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines. The Department of Agriculture's Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DA-BFAR) notes that the Philippines' coastline extends to 36,289 kilometers, while total territorial water area (including the exclusive economic zone) is at 2,200,000 square kilometers, teeming with rich marine resources.1 As an archipelago, one of the major sources of livelihood in the country is fisheries. Based on the latest DA-BFAR statistics2, the number of registered fisherfolk engaged in fishery activities totaled to 2,078,913 in 2020. The fishing industry ranks as the 3>'d highest contributor in the agriculture sector with 12.27% gross value added contribution in 2020. Fisheries production from the same year is at 4.4 million metric tons, which translates to a total contribution of Php 273.5 billion in 2020. At constant prices, this equates to a 1.52% share to the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP). In the global context, the Philippines is considered to be one of the top fish producing countries in the world, ranking 8th in 2018 with a total production of 4.35 million 1 http://www.bfar.da.gov.ph/profile 2 https://www.bfar.da.gov.ph/wp-content/iiploads/2022/02/2020-Fisheries-Profile-Final.pclf metric tons. Similarly, we are also the world’s 4* largest producer of aquatic plants ^including seaweeds} having produced a total of 1.48 million metric tonss. Overall, these figures reflect the importance of the industry in the country’s economy and its potential to grow. Moreover, by investing in methods to increase yields offish and aquatic resources, it niakes the produce more accessible to all. It inadvertently encourages healthy dietary choices, which in turn lessens the expenses on medical or health-related issues later on. While we have very good people in the Department of Agriculture, the Department's priority is more on agriculture. It is time that the government provides for a focused, single-minded, specialised department responsive to the needs and concerns of the fisheries and aquatic resource industry. Given the above tremendous potential of fisheries and aquatic resources and the priority and resources made available to Departments, there is a need to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) in order to strengthen the institutional capacities of DFAR as the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources. As with any administrative agency, DFAR will serve public purpose, efficiency and the best interest of the industry. Hence, this will be a significant step in order to better protect, utilize, maximize, and conserve the nation's marine resources as well as uphold the best interest of the fisher folk. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this measure is sought. ALAN PETER “COMPANERO" S. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is an archipelago composed of 7,641 islands, with a total land area of 301,000 km², surrounded by major bodies of water: the Pacific Ocean to the east, the West Philippine Sea to the west, the Luzon Strait to the north, and the Celebes Sea to the south. Its territorial waters, including its exclusive economic zone (EEZ), cover a total area of 2,200,000 km², while its coastline extends for 36,289 km. These geographical features make the Philippines the world’s second largest archipelagic State and establish it as a major fishing nation, with fisheries serving as a significant contributor to the national economy. The latest foreign trade performance of the Philippine fishery industry indicates a positive trend in imports, with a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 6.3% from 2019 to 2023, accounting for 100% of total fish and seafood imports during this period.1 In 2021, the value of production in the Philippine fisheries sector was estimated at approximately 236.1 billion pesos, reflecting a decline compared to the previous year. Meanwhile, in 2022, tuna emerged as the country’s top fishery export, with a volume of about 106.92 thousand metric tons, followed by seaweeds, which recorded an export volume of around 48.89 thousand metric tons (Philippine Council for Agriculture and Fisheries, 2022). As of 2023, the fisheries sector contributes approximately 1.3 percent to the Philippines’ GDP and supports around 1.6 million jobs, representing about 4 percent of the national labor force, including many low-income families engaged in subsistence fishing. It also supplies over 50 percent of the protein consumed by Filipino households.2 Despite its critical role, the sector has struggled with significant challenges. Over the past decade, fish stocks have declined by an average of 20 percent, primarily due to overfishing, 1 Philippine Council for Agriculture and Fisheries. (2022). Phil Agri attachés report trade performance of country’s agri -fishery products. https://pcaf.da.gov.ph/index.php/2022/01/27/phil-agri-attaches-report-trade-performance-of-countrys-agri-fishery-products/ 2 World Bank Group. (2023). New Fisheries Initiative Will Benefit Over a Million People in the Philippines. https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2023/05/31/new-fisheries-initiative-will-benefit-over-a-million-people-in-the-phi destructive fishing practices, habitat degradation, and adverse impacts from land-based activities (World Bank Group, 2023). Moreover, although the country holds substantial potential for aquaculture development, aquaculture production has decreased by roughly 10 percent over the same period. Moreover, an estimated 20 to 40 percent of total fish caught and farmed is lost annually, largely because of inadequate post-harvest handling and processing (World Bank Group, 2023). The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), the primary government agency tasked with the development, conservation, management, and sustainable use of the country’s fisheries and aquatic resources, currently operates under the Department of Agriculture. While BFAR continues to diligently pursue its mandate, elevating it to a full-fledged department would provide greater authority, resources, and focus to advance the sector – ultimately benefiting the Filipino people. With robust research capabilities, technical expertise, and adequate government support and funding, the proposed Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources can drive the fisheries and aquaculture industry toward a more sustainable, resilient, and prosperous future. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. SHIRLYN L. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As an archipelagic country, the Philippines’ history and continuing existence is inextricably tied to its coasts, internal waters, and the marine bodies that surround it. Our territorial waters consist of 2,200,000 square kilometers including our Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), shelf areas, and coral reef areas, while our country’s inland resources total to 646,336 hectares, including swamplands, existing fishponds, and other inland resources. With 429 fishing ports and 821 commercial ports scattered across the Philippines, it cannot be denied that fisheries and aquatic resources are a critical part of many, if not all, of its regional economies. As of 2018, 927,612 Filipinos reportedly rely on capture fishing. Thus, it is safe to say that our national economy, not to mention a significant number of our population, largely depends on fisheries, marine, and aquatic populations for sustenance and survival. More than its profound significance to our economy and national identity, however, the fisheries, aquatic, and marine resources industry is a pool of potential for national economic development and global competitiveness. In 2018, the Philippines ranked 11th in marine capture worldwide, accounting for 2% of the world’s total marine capture production and 1% of global inland capture production. Pre-pandemic data from 2019 reports that the country produced 4.415 million metric tons of fisheries production, amounting to P281,652 Billion. 53.42% of that total number came from aquaculture, 25.49% from municipal fisheries, and 21.10% from commercial fisheries. In February 2022 alone, with the recent lifting of closed fishing season in various major fishing grounds, Philippine Fisheries Development Authority (PFDA) Regional Fish Ports (RFP) recorded 43,568.27 metric tons (MT) of fish and fishery products. It is thus incumbent upon the State to ensure that such a critical area of the country’s wealth and natural resources is utilized to primarily serve the interest of the Filipino people: by ensuring that marine and inland aquatic resources help ensure local food security and local employment and by ensuring that our industry remains globally competitive in terms of technology, efficiency, and sustainability. It is also the responsibility of the State that such resources be protected and reasonably conserved for the enjoyment of future generations, even as we use such resources to supply present needs. Achieving these goals of equal and significant importance is a matter which requires the independence, expertise, and resources of a stand-alone National Government Agency established for such a purpose. The establishment of such an institution is the Spirit of this Bill, the goal of which has been shared by similar Bills from previous iterations of the Esteemed Representatives of this House. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The aquatic resources of the Philippines are broadly divided into marine resources and inland resources. Our country’s unique geographic feature as an archipelago promises abundance of these resources and opportunities for economic growth. For a long time, we have enjoyed these blessings. We thought they’re limitless, until scarcity and poverty started banging our doors. Based on the available data of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, the volume of our country’s fisheries production had been declining year after year, except for the years 2018 and 2019 wherein we saw slight recoveries. It means the growth of the fisheries industry which is attributed to production of aquaculture, the municipal capture fisheries, and the commercial capture fisheries, is on the negative. In 2020, our fishery export was at 261,495.23 MT but our total fishery import was at 405,570 MT. The importance of the aquatic resources in terms of the demands of our growing population and the country’s need to propel economic development cannot be undermined. The fishing industry is contributing Php266B to our economy. It shared 12.54% of the Gross Value Added (GVA) in the Aquaculture, Hunting, Forestry, and Fishing Group of our agricultural sector in 2021. Aside from the pressure of feeding 111M Filipinos, more than 2M fisherfolks rely on this industry. Over the years, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources has ballooned into nine (9) functional divisions and eight (8) technology centers. The need to elevate this Bureau into a Department, separate and distinct from the Department of Agriculture is not just a recognition of the enormous task we have lodged upon its shoulders but to acknowledge the importance of our aquatic resources in securing food security for today and tomorrow’s generation. As a Department, sufficient resources can be allocated to develop, manage, utilize, protect and conserve these valuable resources. Additionally, this legislative action, will address the poverty incidence besetting the aquatic industry sector. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this Bill is earnestly, sought. HON. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFORE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 7, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution commands as follows “The state shall protect the rights of subsistence fishermen, especially of local communities, to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources, both inland and offshore” and “provide support to such fishermen through appropriate technology and research, adequate financial, production, and marketing assistance, and other services.” Philippines, as an archipelagic state, does not only boast its vast waters but also its abundant marine and aquatic resources. Despite the invaluable contribution of our fisherfolk to the country, they remain one of the poorest sectors in our country. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority, the poverty incidence of fisherfolks is at 30.6% — the highest among all basic sectors in the country. While there are ongoing initiatives to address the poverty in the fishing sector, including development plans and initiatives focused on sustainable fishing practices and improving livelihoods, only a line bureau under the Department of Agriculture, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), is given the mandate to spearhead the said initiatives. It is in this regard that this proposed bill seeks to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources which shall serve as the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources in the country, in lieu of the existing Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR). The proposed measure will not only streamline the bureaucratic functions related to the fisheries and aquaculture industry, but also empower an independent government agency that will not only conserve, promote, and develop the industry but also champion the rights of the local Filipino fishermen. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. HON. HAROLD JAMES T. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, AND THE FISHERIES COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) aligns with long- standing calls for a more specialized and science-driven approach to managing the Philippines’ rich but vulnerable aquatic ecosystems. Research shows that the country sits at the apex of the Coral Triangle, recognized as the global center of marine biodiversity. However, overfishing, habitat degradation, and climate change have placed immense pressure on these resources. Studies such as Tolentino-Zondervan (2022) highlight that sustainable fishery management is essential not only for environmental protection but also for achieving socio-economic goals like food security and poverty alleviation. The DFAR’s mandate reflects these priorities by emphasizing development, regulation, and conservation in coordination with other agencies and local government units. Evidence from community-based fisheries management models in the Philippines suggests that decentralization and local participation improve compliance and stewardship. The DFAR’s joint management approach with LGUs for municipal waters is supported by findings that local governance fosters better resource protection and more equitable benefit-sharing. Moreover, the department’s role in rationalizing blue economy activities is backed by recent policy studies that advocate for integrated marine spatial planning and inclusive governance to balance competing interests—from tourism and energy to biotechnology and conservation. The proposed Act establishes the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) as the primary national body tasked with overseeing the development, management, and regulation of the country’s fisheries and aquatic resources. This includes not only fish and marine life but also the ecosystems and activities that affect them. The DFAR is mandated to work closely with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and other agencies to ensure that its policies are aligned with national goals for environmental protection and sustainable resource use. In light of the foregoing, the immediate and favorable passage of this bill is respectfully sought. ITN T. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2018, the Philippines ranked 8th among the top fish-producing countries in the world with its total production of 4.35 million metric tons (MT) of fish, crustaceans, mollusks, and aquatic plants (including seaweed). The production constituted 2.06% of the total world production of 211.87 million MT (FAO, 2020). In terms of aquaculture production, the country ranked 11th in the world with 826.01 thousand MT or 1.01% share of the total global aquaculture production of 82.10 million MT. The total value of the country’s aquaculture production, including fish, crustaceans, and mollusks, is USD 1.89 billion (FAO, 2020). The Philippines is also the world’s 4th largest producer of aquatic plants (including seaweed), having a total of 1.48 million MT or 4.56% of the total world production of 32.39 million MT (FAO, 2020). The fishing industry’s contribution to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is 1.52% at both current and constant 2018 prices. This translates to PhP 273.41 billion at current prices and PhP 266.22 billion at constant prices of the country’s GDP of PhP 17,939 billion (current prices). The industry also shared 12.27% (PhP 224.19 billion) and 12.54% (PhP 223.20 billion) for both current and constant prices of the Gross Value Added (GVA) in Aquaculture, Hunting, Forestry, and Fishing Group of PhP 1,827.01 billion (current prices) and PhP 1,780.54 billion (constant prices), respectively (PSA, 2021). According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), approximately 1.6 million Filipinos depend on fisheries and aquaculture for their livelihood. However, despite the sector's vastness, poverty incidence continues to remain high among Page 1 of 15 fishermen, estimated at 34% in 2018, higher by 12.4% than the poverty incidence of the general population. In order to strategically develop and utilize the country's fisheries and aquatic resources, and curb poverty in the rural areas where most of the country's fishermen live, this bill proposes the creation of a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) which shall be responsible for the development and management of fisheries and marine resources in Philippine waters including the exclusive economic zone, as well as the protection and conservation of the nation's marine wealth. The department will also ensure that the needs and concerns of the fisherfolk are adequately addressed to ultimately help them move out of poverty. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is embedded in our 1987 Constitution, under Section 7, Article XIII that "The State shall protect the rights of subsistence fishermen, especially of local communities, to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources, both inland and offshore. It shall provide support to such fishermen through appropriate technology and services, adequate financial, production, and marketing assistance, and other.” The Philippines is known for its archipelagic state with 7,641 islands surrounded by over 2.2 million km. of highly productive seas rich in various species of marine and aquatic resources. As of 2022, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resource (BFAR) reported that there are are a total of 2,302,648 registered fisherfolk in the Philippines: 1,173,381 of them are capture fisheries, 259,448 are in aquaculture, 257,511 are in gleaning, 157,161 are in vending, and 45,148 are in processing. Our fisherfolk, together with farmers, are consistently recorded to be the poorest among other basic sectors since the 2006 statistical year of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) despite contributing 1.3% to 1.5% to the country’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Furthermore, they supply 50% of our daily protein as part of our daily sustenance. These data clearly show that there is a huge disconnect between the strategic utilization of our resources and uplifting of the livelihoods of our coastal communities. Therefore, to empower our fisherfolk, this bill aims to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources which will be the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources in the country. While we recognize the existence of the current Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources attached to the Department of Agriculture (DA), the creation of a separate department would give the much-needed specialized attention to the needs and concerns of the fisheries and aquatic resources industry with their own budget and autonomy to completely decide on their succeeding policies and measures on fisheries and aquatic resources. In addition, this would allow DA to focus its efforts on land-based farming including crop production, poultry, and livestock that would transcend to increased country's food self- sufficiency. The department will also be empowered not only to conserve, promote, and develop the industry but also to protect the rights of our local fishermen. One of the department's goals is to likewise address the declining rate of daily catches and annual losses due to illegal activities such as illegal fishing amounting to a loss of an estimated P37 billion. Indeed, the creation of a new Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources would serve the best interest of the country's fisherfolk and the conservation of our marine resources. The immediate passage of the bill is most earnestly sought. HON. TSUYOSHI ANTHONY G. HORIBATA HON. VINCENZO RENATO LUIGI R. VILLAFUERTE HON. MIGUEL LUIS R. VILLAFUERTE HON. TERRY L. file: data/raw_text/3 Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources/HB03423.txt
title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, AND THE FISHERIES COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As an archipelagic nation, the Philippines is defined by its vast marine and freshwater resources, which provide food, livelihoods, and ecological stability for millions. Despite this immense natural wealth, the country's fisheries are in a state of progressive decline, threatened by overfishing, illegal activities, and climate change. While the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) currently manages this sector, a compelling argument exists for elevating it to a full-fledged Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR). Such a move would provide the focused leadership, institutional power, and specialized expertise necessary to safeguard the nation's marine heritage and uplift its marginalized fisherfolk. The primary rationale for a new department stems from the need for a unified and specialized authority. Currently, BFAR operates as a bureau under the Department of Agriculture (DA), where its concerns can be overshadowed by the more dominant agricultural sector. This organizational structure often leads to fragmented policy-making and insufficient budget allocation for the unique challenges of marine resource management. As a standalone department, the DFAR would consolidate authority and resources, enabling it to formulate and enforce coherent policies without bureaucratic competition. This would be particularly crucial for addressing the contentious issues of illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, which proponents argue BFAR, with its limited manpower, is ill-equipped to handle on a national scale. Furthermore, a dedicated department could more effectively implement sustainable management strategies tailored to the Philippines' specific needs. The country's marine ecosystems, located within the global center of marine biodiversity, are especially vulnerable to destructive practices like dynamite fishing and trawling. A DFAR could prioritize the establishment and protection of marine protected areas and the regulation of fishing gear to preserve critical habitats such as coral reefs and seagrass beds. It could also provide targeted support to the country's over two million municipal fisherfolk, who often face direct competition from larger commercial vessels in their traditional fishing grounds. By focusing solely on aquatic resources, a DFAR would be better positioned to protect the rights of these small-scale fishers and ensure their role in the nation's food security. Finally, the creation of a DFAR would serve as a crucial investment in research and development. The Philippines' fisheries output has seen a significant decline in recent years, a trend that is exacerbated by the effects of climate change. A new department would have the mandate and budget to fund vital research on fish stock assessments, climate vulnerability, and post- harvest technologies to reduce waste and increase fisherfolk income. This dedicated focus on science and innovation would not only inform policy but also provide tangible benefits to fishing communities through training and support for sustainable practices and alternative livelihoods. Several legislative proposals to create the DFAR have been filed in the Philippine Congress, signaling a growing recognition of the urgent need for a more robust and responsive institutional framework. In conclusion, the creation of a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources in the Philippines is a logical and necessary step towards securing the nation's marine future. By establishing a centralized authority, empowering sustainable practices, and investing in dedicated research, such a department would provide the focused attention and resources needed to reverse the decline of aquatic resources. It would represent a powerful commitment to both environmental stewardship and the economic well-being of the Filipino people who depend on the sea for their survival and prosperity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, being an archipelago with very rich marine resources, can be a marine powerhouse. Thus, it is logical to establish a Department that is focused and accountable for the development, management, and conservation of our country’s aquatic resources and fishing industries. Fish and aquatic resources are some of the biggest blessings of God to the people. Filipinos have always relied on fish as a basic food resource and commodity. Our dependence on fish can be attributed to the archipelagic nature of the Philippines with its 7,641 islands. Our national territory comprises all the islands and waters, including its territorial sea, seabed, subsoil, the insular shelves, and other submarine areas. The waters around and between the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines. The Department of Agriculture’s Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DA-BFAR) notes that the Philippines’ coastline extends to 36,289 kilometers, while total territorial water area (including the exclusive economic zone) is at 2,200,000 square kilometers, teeming with rich marine resources.1 As an archipelago, one of the major sources of livelihood in the country is fisheries. Based on the latest DA-BFAR statistics, the number of registered fisherfolk engaged in fishery activities totalled to 2,299,127 in 2023. The fishing industry ranks as the 3rd highest contributor in the agriculture sector with 12.0% gross value-added contribution in 2023. Fisheries production from the same year is at 4.26 million metric tons, which translates to a total contribution of Php 328.74 billion in 2023. 2 In the global context, the Philippines is considered to be one of the top fish producing countries in the world, ranking 11th in 2022 with a total production of 804,292.15 metric tons. Similarly, we are also the world’s 4th largest producer of aquatic plants (including seaweeds) having produced a total of 1.55 million metric tons. Overall, these figures reflect the importance of the industry in the country’s economy and its potential to grow.3 1 https://www.bfar.da.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2022-Philippine-Fisheries-Profile.pdf 2 https://www.bfar.da.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2023-Philippine-Fisheries-Profile.pdf 3 https://www.bfar.da.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2023-Philippine-Fisheries-Profile.pdf 1 Ironically, fisherfolks remain to have the highest poverty incidence among basic sectors even if they contribute substantially to the country’s economy. In line with the policy adopted by its original proponent Senator Alan Peter “Compañero” S. Cayetano, this bill therefore serves as a counterpart measure. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind.” Matthew 13:47 The Philippines is one of the world’s top producers of fish and aquatic plants, with over 2.2 million square kilometers of territorial waters and 2.29 million registered fisherfolk. Yet despite their vital contribution to the economy, Filipino fisherfolk remain among the country’s poorest sectors. And though we have very good people in the Department of Agriculture, the department’s priority is more on farming on land. Hence, it is time to have a focused, single - minded, specialized department responsive to the needs and concerns of the fisheries and aquatic resource industry. The Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) is a government agency under the Department of Agriculture. It was reconstituted as a line bureau by virtue of Republic Act No. 8550 (Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998). The BFAR is responsible for the development, improvement, management, and conservation of the country’s fisheries and aquatic resources. It holds a rich history marked by evolution, reorganization, and legislative milestones. From its modest beginnings in 1901, BFAR has undergone significant changes, expanding its functional divisions and establishing technology centers that emphasize modern approaches and crucial roles in specialized areas. The Bureau’s ongoing initiatives reflect its adaptability to the dynamic needs of the industry, underscoring its enduring commitment to the responsible stewardship of the Philippines’ rich aquatic ecosystems. Under the proposed bill, the proposed department would replace the existing BFAR. The measure would not only streamline the bureaucratic functions related to the fisheries and aquaculture industry, but also empower an independent government agency that will not only conserve, promote, and develop the industry but also champion the rights of the local Filipino fishermen. The proposed measure also ensures that the State commits to safeguard the rights of small- scale fishermen, foster sustainable aquaculture and fisheries development, and support private initiatives in fish production, processing and trade. Finally, the proposed department would also oversee blue economy initiatives such as biotechnology, seaweed farming and marine ecosystem preservation. Overall, when passed into law, this measure would ensure food security, uplift the lives of our fisherfolk, and protect our marine ecosystems for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this measure is sought. JORGE DANIEL S. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES,
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is an archipelagic nation with more than 36,000 kilometers of coastline and one of the richest marine biodiversity in the world. Fisheries and aquatic resources provide livelihood to millions of Filipinos, supply essential protein requirements to our population, and contribute significantly to national food security, foreign exchange earnings, and rural development. Despite this immense potential, the fisheries sector continues to face critical challenges. Overfishing, destructive fishing practices, coastal degradation, climate change, and illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUV) fishing have reduced fish stocks and imperiled the welfare of fishing communities. Fragmented institutional arrangements and limited resources for fisheries management have hindered the State’s ability to address these problems comprehensively. Republic Act No. 8550, or the “Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998,” as amended by Republic Act No. 10654, sought to provide a framework for sustainable fisheries management. However, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), as a mere bureau under the Department of Agriculture, has lacked the institutional stature and capacity to discharge the wide-ranging responsibilities required of modern fisheries governance. This bill therefore proposes the creation of a Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) as the primary government agency mandated to oversee the development, management, regulation, and protection of the nation’s fisheries and aquatic resources. The new Department shall: 1. Exercise jurisdiction over fisheries and aquatic resources, including habitats and activities that affect them; 2. Ensure sustainable and science-based management of fish stocks and ecosystems; 3. Provide support services to fisherfolk, fish farmers, processors, and industry stakeholders; 4. Strengthen monitoring, control and surveillance against IUU fishing; 5. Promote research, innovation, and the blue economy; and 6. Rationalize overlapping mandates by consolidating fisheries-related functions currently dispersed across different agencies. The bill likewise establishes a Fisheries Commission, an independent regulatory and quasi-judicial body, to ensure effective enforcement of fisheries laws and adjudication of disputes. It further provides for the orderly transfer, abolition, and attachment of existing agencies and offices, and guarantees security of tenure for affected personnel in accordance with the Government Reorganization Law. By elevating fisheries governance into a full-fledged Department, the State will be better positioned to secure the long-term sustainability of our marine wealth, protect the rights and welfare of small-scale fisherfolk, promote food security and fish self-sufficiency, and enable the Philippines to harness the full potential of the blue economy for inclusive national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a country composed of more than 7,100 islands and a coastline extending 36,289 kilometers (22,549 miles) which makes it the fifth longest coastline in the world. As an archipelago, one of the major sources of livelihood among a lot of Filipinos is fishing. Accordingly, as of February 2025, employment in the fishing and aquaculture industry was recorded at 1.455 million while the 2022 census of agriculture and fisheries reported 830,954 households with fishing operators. The total registered fisherfolk nationwide in 2020 was at 2.08 million. In 2021, the fishing and aquaculture sector generated a gross value-added (GVA) amounting to around 223.2 billion pesos, contributing around 12.6% to the GVA of the agriculture industry. In the same year, total fisheries production was recorded at 4,250.79 thousand metric tons (MT), which translates to a total production value of 302.83 billion pesos. Back in 2018, the Philippines was ranked as the 8" top fish producing country in the world, with a tota! production of 4.35 million MT. The Philippines is also considered as the 11" largest seafood producer globally and the 4" largest producer of aquatic plants, including seaweed. These figures reflect the importance of the fisheries and aquaculture industry and how it significantly contributes to the country’s food production, employment, foreign exchange earnings and its huge potential to fuel the economy's growth and development. However, despite the invaluable contribution of our fisherfolk in the country’s economy, they remain one of the poorest sectors in our nation. According from the Philippine Statistics Authority, the poverty incidence of fisherfolks is at 30.6% which is the highest among all basic sectors in the country. While there are various initiatives to address poverty in the fishing sector, including drafting of national fishery plans geared towards sustainable fishing practices and improving livelihood methods, only a line bureau in the Department of Agriculture is responsible as the operational arm for the actual implementation and delivery of services concerning fisheries and aquaculture development, the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR). It is in this regard that this proposed bill seeks to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources which shall serve as the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources in the country, to replace the existing BFAR. The proposed measure will not only streamline the bureaucratic functions related to the fisheries and aquatic industry, but also equip properly a government agency, separate and distinct from the Department of Agriculture, to focus in the conservation, responsible utilization, and development of the full potential of our marine resources. Moreover, this proposed legislative measure is the consolidated version of the numerous bills previously filed during the Nineteenth (19") Congress which was deliberated by the Committee on Government Reorganization and the Committee on Aquaculture and Fisheries Resources. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. This will pave the way for a sustainable livelihood for the local fisherfolk or fish workers, an adequate food 1 supply for the country, and the sustainable development and protection of fisheries, marine and aquatic resources, and Philippine waters. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The country is blessed by enormous bodies of water with abundant marine resources. Two-thirds of the territorial area of the Philippines is composed of water, covering a total area of 171 million hectares. For this reason, a significant number of Filipinos engage in fishing as their main source of livelihood. To ensure the preservation and proper development of the country's archipelago waters and marine resources, this bill proposes the creation of the Department of fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR). The DFAR shall have the power to manage, develop, protect, conserve and utilize all fisheries and aquatic resources of the country, except for municipal waters, which shall remain under the jurisdiction of local government units. The DFAR shall likewise regulate the production, capture, processing and marketing of fisheries and marine products in the country. This is to make sure that the country's marine wealth is to be exclusively used for the benefit of the Filipino people. The creation of the DFAR will be a significant breakthrough in providing utmost protection to Philippine waters and marine resources. This will help in pursuing the government's thrust to increase food production to meet the demands of the country's fast growing population and alleviate poverty among the fishermen. Thus, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, AND THE FISHERIES COMMISSION, DEFINING THEIR MANDATES, POWERS, AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our fishing sector is in crisis. A crisis so severe, stakeholders, including many loca! government officials, warn that enforcement alone is not enough. Fisheries production data collected by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) for the last 20 years show a consistent decline in catch volumes of the top species. We are all aware that the recorded decline in commonly caught fish is caused by overfishing, habitat destruction, and widespread illegal fishing, including the intrusion of commercial fishing vessels into municipal waters. A multifaceted approach is therefore needed to address this crisis, including relentless and full implementation of vessel monitoring measures, stricter enforcement, application of existing laws, and, last but most important, the protection, preservation, and conservation of marine habitats. Against this backdrop, there is now the underlying need, long overdue in fact, to push for the creation of the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources, an institution that is separate and distinct from the Department of Agriculture (DA), abolishing for this purpose the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) reconstituted via Republic Act No. 8550, otherwise known as the “Philippine Fisheries Code”. The principles of rightsizing should be applied in the migration of BFAR into a full-pledged department so that the agency’s efforts to address the growing needs of the fishing sector, existing problems, issues, and concerns, are more focused and streamlined, equipped with the requisite resources and authority. This bill has been proposed in the 19" Congress and in every Congress before it. This proposed legislation is an iteration of the substitute bill that fell short of enactment due to a lack of material time. Food security is a priority of this administration, and has been for every administration prior; thus, the passage of this bill will greatly contribute to the attainment of this goal. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution provides that, “[t]he State shall protect the rights of subsistence fishermen, especially of local communities, to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources, both inland and offshore. It shall provide support to such fishermen through appropriate technology and research, adequate financial, production, and marketing assistance, and other services. The State shall also protect, develop, and conserve such resources.” According to the Philippine Fisheries Profile published by the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) in 2022, the country’s total territorial water area, including the exclusive economic zone, is 2,200,000 sq.km. while the country’s coastline stretches 36,289 km.1 As an archipelago composed of 7,641 islands, fishing and fishery-related livelihoods remain the primary form of livelihood for a total of 2,302,648 registered Filipino fisherfolk as of 2022.2 However, data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) have consistently shown that fisherfolk remain among the poorest sectors in the country, with a poverty incidence of 30.6% in 20213 and 27.4% in 2023.4 1 Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources. (October 2023). 2022 Philippine Fisheries Profile. (6 February 2026). 881 Cities and Municipalities Recorded Poverty Incidence of 20 Percent or Lower in 2023. Retrieved from https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/poverty. 1 In 2025, the total volume of fisheries production in 2025 was estimated at 3.96 million metric tons, indicating an annual average decline of 2.5% from the 4.06 million metric tons output in 2024.5 These decreases in production, as noted in commercial fisheries, marine municipal fisheries, and aquaculture, are part of an alarming trend of declining production of the fisheries sector over the years. Furthermore, according to international conservation group Oceana, Philippine capture fisheries have been losing an average of 45,472 metric tons of fish each year since 2010, which amounts to more than 591,000 metric tons of fish that are not wasted nor exported, but just never allowed to exist in the first place.6 This 591,000 metric tons refers to lost potential, or rather, fish that would have grown, reproduced, and sustained future harvests if stocks had been kept within sustainable limits.7 According to marine biologist Wilfredo Campos, the average annual loss of 45,472 metric tons of fish could have fed around 93,000 Filipino families experiencing food insecurity. 8 Unfortunately, in the Philippines, the yearly rate of overfishing, which causes ecosystems to lose the ability to replenish themselves, compounds the problem, thus continuously shrinking future catch even if the effort remains the same.9 Among the identified causes for this is the weak enforcement behind the great ambition of Republic Act No. 8550, or the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998. Republic Act No. 8550 laid down progressive principles, such as “food security as a national priority” and “preferential rights for municipal fisherfolk within the 15- kilometer municipal waters”, while providing conservation tools, such as marine protected areas and closed seasons.”10 However, at present, several of these principles, most notably the preferential rights of municipal fisherfolk to the 15- kilometer municipal waters, have been challenged or unenforced. Weak penalties, fragmented monitoring, and the persistence of illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing allowed pressure on fish stocks to intensify, thus leading to sustained overfishing.11 In recognition of the need to strengthen the implementation and address the gaps of Republic Act No. 8550, the amendatory law, Republic Act No. 10654, was enacted in 2015 to “prevent, deter and eliminate illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing,” promising “tougher penalties, faster adjudication, modern monitoring and science-based management meant to reverse decades of overfishing.”12 However, almost a decade after the enactment of the amendatory law, the data continue to show lagging implementation and declining fish stocks. title: AN ACT CREATING A DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES AND AQUATIC RESOURCES, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, being an archipelago with very rich marine resources, can be a marine powerhouse. Thus, it is logical to establish a Department that is focused and accountable for the development, management, and conservation of our country’s aquatic resources and fishing industries. Fish and aquatic resources are some of the biggest blessings of God to the people. Filipinos have always relied on fish as a basic food resource and commodity. Our dependence on fish can be attributed to the archipelagic nature of the Philippines with its 7,641 islands. Our national territory comprises all the islands and waters, including its territorial sea, seabed, subsoil, the insular shelves, and other submarine areas. The waters around and between the islands of the archipelago, regardless of their breadth and dimensions, form part of the internal waters of the Philippines. The Department of Agriculture’s Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DA-BFAR) notes that the Philippines’ coastline extends to 36,289 kilometers, while total territorial water area (including the exclusive economic zone) is at 2,200,000 square kilometers, teeming with rich marine resources.1 As an archipelago, one of the major sources of livelihood in the country is fisheries. Based on the latest DA-BFAR statistics, the number of registered fisherfolk engaged in fishery activities totalled to 2,299,127 in 2023. The fishing industry ranks as the 3rd highest contributor in the agriculture sector with 12.0% gross value-added contribution in 2023. Fisheries production from the same year is at 4.26 million metric tons, which translates to a total contribution of Php 328.74 billion in 2023.2 In the global context, the Philippines is considered to be one of the top fish producing countries in the world, ranking 11th in 2022 with a total production of 1 https;//www. bfar.da.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/2022-Philippine-Fisheries-Profile. pdf 2 https;//www.bfar.da.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/2023-Philippine-Fisheries-Profile.pdf 1 804,292.15 metric tons. Similarly, we are also the world’s 4th largest producer of aquatic plants (including seaweeds) having produced a total of 1.55 million metric tons. Overall, these figures reflect the importance of the industry in the country’s economy and its potential to grow.3 Ironically, fisherfolks remain to have the highest poverty incidence among basic sectors even if they contribute substantially to the country’s economy. While we have very good people in the Department of Agriculture, the Department’s priority is more on farming on land. It is time that the government provides for a focused, single-minded, specialised department responsive to the needs and concerns of the fisheries and aquatic resource industry. Given the above tremendous potential of fisheries and aquatic resources and the priority and resources made available to Departments, there is a need to create the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (DFAR) in order to strengthen the institutional capacities of DFAR as the primary policy and regulatory body on fisheries and aquatic resources. As with any administrative agency, DFAR will serve public purpose, efficiency and the best interest of the industry. Hence, this will be a significant step in order to better protect, utilize, maximize, and conserve the nation’s marine resources as well as uphold the best interest of the fisherfolk. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this measure is sought. ALAN PETER “COMPANERO” S. title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 6728, as amended by Republic Act No. 8545—collectively known as the “Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act” (E-GASTPE)—was enacted to provide financial support to students and teachers in private educational institutions. However, more than - two decades since its passage, the educational landscape has significantly evolved, rendering some of its provisions outdated and insufficient to address current challenges. Today, private educational institutions face mounting difficulties. Notably, during the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, enrollment in private schools plummeted by 48%, highlighting the sector’s vulnerability. Even before the pandemic, many students had already been transferring to public schools due to the exodus of private school teachers—often lured by better compensation and job security in the public sector. This shift has not only strained private schools but has also placed immense pressure on the public school system, which must absorb the growing number of transferees, often without commensurate resources. Given these circumstances, there is an urgent need to update and expand the scope of E-GASTPE. A new legislative measure is imperative—one that is responsive to the current realities, strengthens private education, and reinforces the complementary roles of public and private institutions in delivering accessible, quality basic education to all Filipino learners. This bill was filed by Representatives Roman T. Romulo, Ruth Mariano- Hernandez, Ron P. Salo, Yedda Marie K. Romualdez, and Jude A. Acidre, among others, during the Nineteenth Congress and was approved on Third Reading. It seeks to: a. Affirm the right to quality education — It recognizes the constitutional mandate to make quality education accessible to all and acknowledges the complementary roles of public and private schools in delivering this mandate. b. Institutionalize and improve the voucher program — By codifying the voucher program, the government aims to provide financial support to students—especially the underprivileged—to enroll in private basic education institutions when public schools are overcrowded or inaccessible. c. Create the Bureau of Private Education — A specialized bureau under the Department of Education (DepEd) will be established to oversee and regulate all matters related to private basic education, ensuring accountability and effective management of assistance programs. d. Ensure quality and equity — The bill sets quality assurance mechanisms, performance evaluations, and tracer systems to ensure that both students and schools meet national education standards. It also prioritizes financial aid to vulnerable and underserved sectors. e. Support teachers and institutions — The bill provides for in-service training, scholarships, and salary subsidies for private school teachers, and capacity-building programs for institutions. f. Align with national development goals — Through coordination with the DepEd, NEDA, and DBM, the bill aims to ensure that public investments in private education lead to measurable educational outcomes. g. Replace outdated laws — It repeals specific sections of RA 8545 and RA 6728 (laws on government assistance to students and teachers in private education), updating them to respond to present-day challenges in the education sector. This bill addresses the long-standing and emerging challenges faced by private basic education—such as enrollment decline, teacher migration, and resource limitations—while reinforcing equity, quality assurance, and institutional development. It promotes educational choice, empowers families, and alleviates overcrowding in public schools, thereby fostering a balanced, efficient, and inclusive education system. Through timely and strategic government intervention, this bill aims to sustain and uplift private education as a vital partner in nation-building, ensuring that no Filipino learner is left behind. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. FE ND WA G. ROMUALDEZ JUDE # ACIDRE ANDREW JULIAN K. title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is a constitutionally guaranteed right and a cornerstone of national development. Under Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, the State is mandated to “protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” However, despite substantial government investment in public education, many Filipino learners, particularly those from poor, remote, or underserved communities, remain unable to access quality basic education due to overcrowded public schools, lack of nearby facilities, or limited capacity of the public school system. The Department of Education (DepEd) reported that over 23.8 million students were enrolled in basic education, of which 10.92% (2.6 million) were in private schools. Many of these private schools help fill gaps in access, especially in areas where public schools are congested or unavailable. Yet, despite their critical role, private schools have seen declining enrollment largely due to financial hardship among families and limited government support. To address these challenges and uphold the State's duty to provide equitable and quality education for all, this bill proposes the establishment of the Private Basic Education Voucher Program, as well as the creation of a dedicated Bureau of Private Education (BPE) under the Department of Education. This proposed measure aims to institutionalize a national voucher system that supports Filipino learners from underprivileged and middle-income families to enroll in qualified private schools for kindergarten, elementary, and secondary levels. The voucher amount will be determined based on need, congestion levels of nearby public schools, and geographic accessibility, giving priority to students who otherwise would have limited educational options. Additionally, the proposed measure repeals selected provisions of Republic Acts No. 6728 and 8545 (GASTPE laws) to modernize and strengthen the legal framework of government assistance to students and teachers in private education. It also ensures that the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) can implement its own version of the program, while still coordinating with DepEd for technical assistance and national alignment. In a country where over 50% of public schools are considered overcrowded and where access to quality education remains highly unequal, this legislative measure will not only reduce the strain on public schools but will also protect educational choice for families, uphold teacher welfare, and revitalize the role of private institutions in nation-building. In view of the foregoing, the approval of thje Bil is earnestly sought. HON. EDVIC G. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION VOUCHER PROGRAM, PROVIDING FOR THE CREATION OF THE BUREAU OF PRIVATE EDUCATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 2, 3, 4(2), 4(3), 5, 6, 7, 12, 14, AND 15 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8545, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "EXPANDED GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO STUDENTS AND TEACHERS IN PRIVATE EDUCATION ACT", WHICH AMENDED REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6728, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO STUDENTS AND TEACHERS IN PRIVATE EDUCATION ACT"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution states in Article XIV, Section 1 that "[t]he State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all." For this reason, it is the responsibility of the state to create, support, and maintain a comprehensive, appropriate, and integrated system of education that is In line with the needs of the populace and society”. Anchored on the state’s mandate that no Filipino child should be deprived of quality basic education due to economic limitations or geographical challenges, this proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a Private Basic Education Voucher Program and establish the Bureau of Private Education, thereby strengthening the government’s commitment to accessible, equitable, and quality education for all Filipino learners. Through this education voucher program, we strategically address the chronic problem of overcrowding in public schools through a system of decongestion and redistribution of our learners and maximizing private schools which are ready to accommodate them with the support of the Government. This proposed policy is also consistent with the state’s mandate under Section 2(1) of Republic Act No. 9155, otherwise known as the Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001, which recognizes 1 the complementary roles of public and private educational institutions in the national educational system. Pursuant to the same legislative intent, the Department of Education (DepEd) significantly focused its efforts and resources in addressing the pressing concerns of the public school system. While the challenges confronting education delivery in public schools are substantial and warrants the attention of DepEd, it is equally important that the broader educational landscape be considered and taken into account. Education delivery in private schools, which serves as a vital complement in our system of education, faces its own set of issues and developmental needs that must be acknowledged and addressed. There have been reports that the current organizational setup assigns only one supervisor per division to oversee numerous private schools. In Metro Manila alone, there are nearly 2,000 private schools distributed across 16 divisions—yet only 16 supervisors are designated to monitor and support them. These same supervisors are also burdened with other tasks unrelated to private education, such as nutrition programs, monitoring activities, among others. This situation has led to a disproportionate allocation of time and resources for the private education sector, despite its significant contribution to the country’s overall educational landscape. It is therefore imperative to create a Bureau of Private Education that will exclusively focus on the development, regulation, and management of private elementary and secondary schools. The proposed Bureau shall serve as a centralized and dedicated body to address all concerns, initiatives, and programs relating to private basic education, thereby ensuring timely and responsive governance. Ultimately, the enactment of this measure shall institutionalize a learner- centered, inclusive, and future-ready education system that recognizes the integral role of private education in national development. It affirms the State’s duty to provide adequate support and regulation for all educational stakeholders and ensures that both public and private institutions are empowered to nurture the next generation of Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill was approved by the House of Representatives during the 19th Congress. Article XIV, Section l of the Constitution provides that “the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all”. Thus, education has always enjoyed the highest budgetary priority in the annual budget of government as mandated by the Constitution itself. However, the meager resources of government led to the stagnation of budgetary allocation across all sectors including education. As a result, the resources provided for education has not kept pace with the growing student population. Massive backlog in classrooms, textbooks, desks and even teachers has continued to plague the public education system. The passage of the Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education (GASTPE) Program in l989 and its subsequent amendment in l998 tapped the potential of the private education system to fulfill the Constitutional mandate to make education accessible to all Filipinos. It made use of the otherwise unutilized capacity of the private schools to cater to students which cannot be accommodated by the public education system. Since its inception in 1989, GASTPE has provided support to over 700,000 beneficiaries in private schools. It has helped more than 1,400 private schools which enrolled in the program. The program has been very successful but has not achieved full potential due to budgetary constraints. According to the Department of Education, at least P2 billion pesos is needed on top of the annual appropriations for the program to achieve the desired level of 500,000 beneficiaries at P4,000 per grantee. In addition to this, the scarce resource for the program has made its appropriation centered on the student beneficiary and has left little or none at all for teachers who are also intended to be provided with the proper training. This bill seeks to increase the funding for the GASTPE Program in order to address the deficiency in the public education sector. It allocates P1 billion pesos exclusively to teachers to upgrade their training skills for the delivery of quality education to students. In addition, it seeks to institute a voucher system in place of the current tuition fee supplement program to further improve benefits to students enrolled in private schools. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. RODRIGUEZ, JR. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION VOUCHER PROGRAM, PROVIDING FOR THE CREATION OF THE BUREAU OF PRIVATE EDUCATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 2, 3, 4(2), 4(3), 5, 6, 7, 12, 14, AND 15 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8545, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EXPANDED GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO STUDENTS AND TEACHERS IN PRIVATE EDUCATION ACT”, WHICH AMENDED REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6728, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO STUDENTS AND TEACHERS IN PRIVATE EDUCATION ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Private schools have long been key partners in expanding access to basic education, especially in areas where public schools are overcrowded or absent. For decades, government assistance to private education—through laws like RA 6728 and RA 8545—has helped bridge gaps and support Filipino learners. But the needs of our education system have changed. The COVID-19 pandemic exposed deep vulnerabilities in private education, with thousands of students transferring out and teachers leaving for better security in the public sector. Many private institutions remain at risk of closure, while public schools struggle to absorb the overflow. This bill responds to that growing imbalance. It proposes a stronger, updated framework for government support to private basic education, one that reflects present-day challenges and empowers both schools and students. Among its key reforms are the institutionalization of an expanded voucher program to assist students in need; the creation of a Bureau of Private Education under the Department of Education to ensure focused oversight of the private basic education sector; the provision of capacity-building initiatives and salary support for private school teachers; and the establishment of quality standards and accountability mechanisms for participating institutions. More than a financial measure, this bill affirms the right of every Filipino child to choose quality education—public or private—regardless of income or location. In light of the above, the swift passage of this bill is respectfully sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen and expand government assistance programs for students and teachers in private educational institutions, building upon the foundations of Republic Act No. 6728, as amended by Republic Act No. 8545 (the "Expanded Government Assistance to Students and Teachers in Private Education Act," or E- GASTPE), and Republic Act No. 10931 (the "Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act"). The necessity for this measure is underscored by the challenges faced by the Philippine education system. In 2020, during the initial year of the pandemic, private school enrollment saw a significant decline of 48%. This was further exacerbated by a substantial migration of teachers from private to public schools, impacting the quality and accessibility of education in private institutions. These circumstances highlight the urgent need for a more robust and responsive E-GASTPE program. This bill aims to: e Expand Coverage: !nclude kindergarten and elementary students, as well as students in higher education institutions, in private educational assistance programs. e Enhance Resource Accessibility: Provide support for textbook assistance programs and expand the existing Educational Service Contracting (ESC) scheme. e Invest in Human Capital: Fund initiatives for the upgrading of knowledge and teaching competencies and the upskilling of teachers in private basic educational institutions, through the Teachers’ Salary Subsidy Fund. e Promote Holistic Development: Provide government assistance to private basic educational institutions in areas such as academic leadership, good governance, school finance and administration, research and curriculum design, facilities and school improvement, and institutional development. By enacting these provisions, this measure, which passed on Third Reading in the 19" Congress, will significantly contribute to making quality education more accessible to all and ensure the continued flourishing of the entire education sector, particularly private institutions, which play a vital complementary role in achieving the nation's educational goals. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Mog. T Lom MARCELINO R. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION VOUCHER PROGRAM, PROVIDING FOR THE CREATION OF THE BUREAU OF PRIVATE EDUCATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 2, 3, 4(2), 4(3), 5, 6, 7, 12, 14, AND 15 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8545, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “EXPANDED GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO STUDENTS AND TEACHERS IN PRIVATE EDUCATION ACT”, WHICH AMENDED REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6728, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE TO STUDENTS AND TEACHERS IN PRIVATE EDUCATION ACT” 11 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 13 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Private Basic Education Vouchers Assistance Act”. 16 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the declared policy of the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. As part of its mandate, it is the State’s policy to establish and maintain a system of scholarship grants, subsidies, and other incentives which shall be available to deserving students, as determined by the guidelines, in both public and private schools, especially to the underprivileged. Likewise, the State recognizes the complementary roles of public and private educational institutions in the educational system and the invaluable contribution that the private schools have made and will make to education. 26 The State shall provide the mechanisms to augment the resources and enhance the quality of private basic education, specifically promoting the complementary roles of public and private schools and thus recognize the government’s priority of providing basic elementary and secondary education to all Filipino students. 31 SEC. 3. Coverage. – This Act shall cover all private basic education institutions that receive government assistance in the form of vouchers for qualified students, teachers and schools. This covers all the years of basic education.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every Filipino child deserves a fair chance at quality education—regardless of whether they are born into wealth or poverty, or whether they live in the heart of the city or in a remote province. Education is not a privilege for the few; it is a constitutional right enshrined in Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution, which mandates the State to “protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Yet, for many families in the country, access to quality basic education remains a struggle. Public schools, especially in urban centers, continue to suffer from overcrowded classrooms, limited teaching resources, and overstretched faculty. Meanwhile, private schools—which often have better facilities and smaller class sizes—remain out of reach for many middle- and low-income families due to high tuition fees. This bill aims to institutionalize a comprehensive voucher system that will allow Filipino learners, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds and congested communities, to enroll in recognized private basic education institutions with the help of government subsidies. By doing so, we not only decongest our public schools but also empower families with real choices in their children’s education. The Private Basic Education Vouchers Assistance Act is not just a reform; it is a commitment to fairness, equity, and genuine partnership. It reflects our shared hope that no Filipino child should ever be deprived of quality education simply because of where they were born or how much their family earns. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
