Philippine News Agency (2019). Sports tourism boosts tourist arrivals in Dumaguete. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1088794 hosting the 2023 FIBA Basketball World Cup created an economic impact of Php 17.8 billion.3 Projections for hosting a single future event like the Volleyball World Championship estimate a total economic impact of over USD 40 million and an alignment with a destination tourism market valued at USD 5.4 billion.4 Yet, despite our proven capability to host world-class events and earning praise for our people’s renowned hospitality, we fail to consistently translate this potential into lasting national success. For too many Filipinos, sports remains a dream rather than a viable and honored profession. It is a calling we deny to our own people because we lack the right systems, support, and structures. This systemic weakness is most evident in the Olympics. The long wait between the 1996 boxing silver medal by Mansueto Velasco and Hidilyn Diaz's historic gold in weightlifting in 2020 highlights the challenges faced by Filipino athletes in reaching their full potential on the world’s biggest sporting stage. The Philippine Sports Commission (PSC), established in 1990 through Republic Act No. 6847, is mandated to, among others, “provide the leadership, formulate the policies and set the priorities and direction of all national amateur sports promotion and development, particularly giving emphasis on grassroots participation.” However, its focus on grassroots participation may not fully address the needs of elite athletes to compete at the highest levels of sports competitions. In 2001, Republic Act No. 9155 or the “Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001” abolished the Bureau of Physical Education and School Sports (BPESS) and transferred “[a]ll functions, programs and activities of the Department of Education related to sports competition” to the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). While physical education remains in the curriculum, this shift has weakened overall sports development. This measure will address the perennial challenges that hinder the growth of Philippine sports. This bill proposes the creation of a Department of Sports, a cabinet-level agency that will provide focused leadership for national sports promotion and development, and address the needs of athletes, coaches, trainers, and sports officials across all levels. With a dedicated department, we can find comprehensive solutions to the problems besetting Philippine sports, particularly the lack of a coherent national sports program, the need to enhance the partnership with various sectors involved in sports, obsolete training methods, lack of modern and high-quality training facilities, equipment, and sports venues. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As the agency responsible for training and capacitating the country's workers, the Technical Education and Skills Education (TESDA) was established to encourage the full participation of and for the mobilization of the industry, labor, local government units and technical-vocational institutions in the skills development of the country's human resources. The COVID-19 pandemic brought the world to an unprecedented level of societal disruption. Many industries were immediately impacted by this: with the loss of markets came the loss of jobs. Prior to the pandemic, Asia Pacific had some of the highest economic growth rates in the world; but still afflicted with high levels of worker hardship, with 300 million workers living with their families in poverty and some 58 million in extreme poverty in 2019.1 Through the Employment Recovery Agenda of the National Employment Recovery Strategy (NERS) 2021-2022 Task Force, TESDA took part and facilitated trainings and introduced approaches to restart economic activities, restore business 1 https://www. iio.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/—dgrcports/—dcomm/— publ/documents/publication/wcms_795453.pdf and consumer confidence, upgrade and retool the workforce, and facilitate labor market access. It has assisted 2.08 million individuals and benefitted 129,000 establishments, with 780,119 jobs generated.2 In order to comply with the growing demand of labor resources, TESDA is developing strategies on Technical Vocational Education and Training (TVET) for global competitiveness and social equity. However, these strategies may not be attained if TESDA's organizational structure, its own manpower and ability to produce higher quality of learning and training materials are still among the primary hindrances that prevent the progress of TESDA. This bill seeks to create a Department of Technical Education Training and Certification, which will take the place and absorb the current TESDA. It is high time to empo wer TESDA and enable the agency to fulfill its mandate as the leading partner in the development of the Filipino workforce. ■ In lieu of the foregoing, immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought NLEGARDA ■■ t-t. i. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, REPEALING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE TESDA ACT OF 1994 AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) paved the way in providing millions of Filipnos with relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development in support of the development of high quality Filipino middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. In 2018 alone, there are more than 2 million who benefitted in the agency’s various Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) program. For twenty-five (25) years, after the passage of Republic Act No. 7796 or the TESDA Act which was enacted on August 25, 1994, continues to be in the forefront in ensuring that Filipinos have access to technical education and skills development (TESD) that is not only relevant and efficient, but also accessible and of high quality. Despite much progress and lives changed, the agency is facing various and enormous challenges in order to adapt to the ever- changing local and global environment that the organization needs to focus on. In order to meet world standards, TESDA must address the need for modern facilities and equipment to level with the requirements in addressing the challenges created by the 4IR (Fourth Industrial Revolution) and other advancements that may happen in the future. It must also be bestowed with the police powers to impose sanctions and penalties to erring TESD implementers. These are among the limitations to what TESDA can do which can be ultimately addressed if the agency will be elevated into a line Department of the government. This proposed Bill seeks to repeal R.A. 7796 or the TESDA Act of 1994 and to reinforce the powers and organizational function of TESDA by turning it into a Department. The proposed Department shall become the primary policy formulation, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulating and administrative entity of the government for technical education and training and certification policies, plans and programs. It shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries. Page | 1 With the proposed legislative measure, TESDA will be strengthened as an implementing and regulatory institution of the Technical and Vocational Sector of the country’s trifocal education system. This measure is made in the interest of the Filipinos who wants to regain new skills and improve their well-being, and will be achieved in greater capacity vision as the transformational leader in the technical education and skills development of the Filipino workforce. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. TESDA's mandate is relevant since skills and training are essential to the workforce. To properly support such relevant activities, there is a need to revamp the system. By elevating the authority into a department, adequate budgetary support, personnel, and resources will be provided to fUrther develop the projects and programs of TESDA.

explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7796 or the TESDA Act of 1994 was approved on August 25, 1994 which paved the way for the creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA). Sec. 2 of the law specifically mandated TESDA to carry out the government efforts in providing relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development in support of the development of high quality Filipino middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. By virtue of this law, the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical Vocational Education of the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Apprenticeship program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) were integrated into TESDA. The merger of these entities was based on the recommendation of the Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM) that had undergone a nationwide review of the state of the Philippine education and training system in 1991. Twenty-five (25) years hence, TESDA has been the leading authority in ensuring that technical education and skills development (TESD) is relevant, efficient, accessible, and of high quality. However, the agency has been facing enormous challenges due to changes in the local and global environment that the organization needs to focus on. There are limitations to what TESDA can do which can be addressed if it will be elevated into a line Department of the government. TESDA must address the need for modern facilities and equipment in order to be at par with the requirements of the challenge posed by the Fourth Industrial Revolution and other advancements that may happen in the future. The bill seeks to repeal R.A. 7796 or the TESDA Act of 1994 and to strengthen the powers and the organizational function of TESDA by elevating it into a Department. The proposed Department shall be the primary policy formulation, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulating and administrative entity of the government for technical education and training and certification policies, plans and programs. It shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries. Carrying out the functions of the new Department shall be done by the various bureaus, service offices and Regional/ Provincial/ District Offices. Implementation of direct training programs will be done by the technology institutions. With the proposed legislative measure, TESDA will be strengthened as an implementing and regulatory institution of the Technical and Vocational Sector of the country’s trifocal education system. The agency will have a better capacity to fulfill its vision as the transformational leader in the technical education and skills development of the Filipino workforce. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARK O. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) was established through the enactment of Republic Act No. 7796 otherwise known as the "Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994" with the aim to encourage the full participation of and mobilize the industry, labor, local government units and technical vocational institutions in the skills development of the country's human resources. The said Act integrated the functions of the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical-Vocational Education of the Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Office of Apprenticeship of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) as a result of a national review of the state of Philippine education and manpower development which was undertaken by the Congressional Commission on Education back in 1991. TESDA has been the leading authority managing technical skills education in the Philippines. Its major thrust is the formulation of a comprehensive development plan for middle-level manpower based on the National Technical Education and Skills Development Plan that includes apprenticeship, dual training system and other similar schemes. TESDA is also improving its language course offerings in partnership with foreign embassies and international organizations consistent with the strategy to reposition technical vocational education and training (TVET) for global competitiveness. The language-related courses —Arabic, Mandarin, Korean, Italian and French —will be added to the existing courses under its National Skills Language Center (NLSC). President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said in his inaugural address on June 30 that “sharpening the language skills” of Filipino workers, including Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), is important to give them the advantage to survive and thrive in foreign countries. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, PROVIDING FOR ITS POWERS, STRUCTURE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7796 or the Technical Education and Skills Education Act (TESDA) was passed into law in 1994. It was created to provide relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development of the country’s human resources. Over the years, TESDA has established itself as the nation's leading source of labor in highly technical disciplines. The agency’s purpose was all the more highlighted during the pandemic when TESDA launched its TESDA Online Program (TOP) and “TESDA Abot Lahat ang OFWs” program which aims to upskill and retool workers in order to recoup job losses.1 Nonetheless, the current system leaves much to be desired and it is evident that changes must be had in order to make technical and vocational education in our country more efficient. Thus, this bill seeks to create a Department of Technical Education Training and Certification, which will take the place and absorb the current TESDA with the end goal of providing more quality and accessible technical and vocational education for all. In line with the policy adopted by its original proponent Senator Loren Legarda, this bill therefore likewise serves as a counter-part House Bill. It is for the reasons stated above that the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTONIO B. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) on August 25, 1994, through the merger of the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical Vocational Education of the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Apprenticeship program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), was an offshoot of the trifocalization of education recommended by the 1991 Congresssional Education Commission or EDCOM. By virtue of Republic Act No. 7796 (TESDA Act of 1994), the TESDA is mandated to ensure the delivery of relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development and to develop high quality middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. However, after more than two decades of delivering relevant, accessible, and efficient technical education and skills development thoughout ther country, TESDA has been encountering many challenges and limitations that affect the performance of its functions, delivery of technical-vocational education and training (TVET) programs, and fulfillment of its vision. One of these is the need to sstrengthen its organizational structure and functions to keep pace with the advent of technology and the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR). The frequent transfer of the TESDA from one office to another has also affected its functions, programs and projects, and delivery of educational services. From an attached agency of the Department of Labor and Employment, TESDA was transferred to the Office of the President and now, to the Department of Trade and Industry through executive order signed by President Duterte. Moreover, under the TESDA Charter, the TESDA Director-General shall enjoy the benefits, privileges ad emoluments equivalent to the rank of Undersecretary. However, the current and past two Presidents of the Philippines appointed the TESDA Director General with a Cabinet rank position or equivalent to a Secretary. By elevating the TESDA into a department, it shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries and attain self-determination to ensure permanence and continuity of mandated programs. This will also strengthen the implementing, regulatory, and policy-making functions of the agency, as well as make it more responsive and agile in the era of the 4IR and digital economy. The proposed Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) will not only improve the resource/budget allocation for TVET programs, but will also ably represent the TVET sector as a whole, changing its “second class” perception. More importantly, the proposed DTESD will have a better capacity to fulfill its vision as the transformational leader in TVET in the country. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF THCHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSH REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERVISE KNOWN AS THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS I)EVELOPMENT AUTHORITY OR TESDA ACT OF 1994, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution of the Philippines Article XII, Section 14 provides that "The sustained development of a reservoir of national talents consisting of Filipino scientists, entrepreneurs, professionals, managers, high-level technical manpower and skilled workers and craftsmen in all fields shall be promoted by the State." The Constitution likewise asserts in Article XIV, Section 1 that "The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all." Also, Article XIV, Section 2 emphasizes the govemment's duty to ensure a complete and suitable education system that meets the needs of the people in an ever-changing environment. It also calls for support for students through scholarships and other aid, especially for those from underprivileged backgrounds. Additionally, it promotes alternative leaming approaches, including informal and community-based programs. Critical to the promotion of sustained development of a highly skilled work force, the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) was established through Republic Act No. 7796 (TESDA Act of 1994) on August 25,1994. Through the merging of National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), Bureau of Technical and Vocational Education (BTVE), and the Apprenticeship Program of the Bureau of Local Employment a3LE), TESDA is mandated to oversee skills development, set standards, accredit institutions, fund projects, and support trainer programs for the development of a top-quality middle-level manpower capable of adapting towards emerging issues and necessities of the Fourth Industrial Revolution. TESDA has aimed to set the direction, promulgate relevant standards, and implement programs geared towards a quality-assured and inclusive technical education and skills development and certification system for the country's technical-vocational education and training (TVET) system. The frequent transfer between various administrative entities has been driven by different factors, including changes in government priorities, administrative restructuring, and attempts to enhance coordination between TESDA and other government agencies. However, these transfers have often resulted in disruptions to TESDA's operations, delays in the implementation of programs, and challenges in maintaining continuity and coherence in policy and programmatic efforts. Recognizing the need for stability, coherence, and focused leadership in the promotion of technical education and skills development, this bill proposes the establishment of the Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) as a permanent and dedicated government agency. By elevating TESDA into a department, the bill aims to provide TESDA with the necessary institutional franiework, authority, and resources to effectively cany out its mandate in a sustained and coherent manner. The creation of the DTESD is envisioned to address the ever-changing labor landscape and its frequent transfers between different government offices. By consolidating efforts in TVET development under a single department, the bill seeks to streamline governance, enhance coordination, and ensure the continuity and effectiveness of policies and programs aimed at developing a skilled and globally competitive workforce in the Philippines. Approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution provides that: the State shall promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services, promote full employment, a rising standard of living, and improved quality of life for all (Sec. 9, Art. II); the State shall promote social justice in all phases of national development (Sec. 10, Art. II); the State shall give priority to education, science and technology, arts, culture, and sports to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development (Sec. 17, Art. II); the Congress shall give highest priority to the enactment of measures that reduce social, economic, and political inequalities (Sec.1, Art. XIII); the State shall encourage non-formal, informal, and indigenous learning systems, as well as self- learning, independent, and out-of-school study programs particularly those that respond to community needs (Sec 2[4], Art. XIV); and Science and technology are essential for national development and progress. The State shall give priority to research and development, invention, innovation, and their utilization; and to science and technology education, training, and services. It shall support indigenous, appropriate, and self-reliant scientific and technological capabilities, and their application to the country’s productive systems and national life (Sec. 10, Art. XIV). In this regard, the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) which was created by virtue of Republic Act 7796, otherwise known as the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994” is the government agency tasked to manage and supervise technical education and skills development in the Philippines. TESDA’s vision is a transformational leader in the technical education and skills development of the Filipino workforce, with a mission of setting directions, promulgating relevant standards, and implementing programs geared towards a quality-assured and inclusive technical education and skills development and certification system. Under the bill, the proposed Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) shall be the primary policy formulation, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulatory, and administrative entity of the government for technical education and training programs. With its gargantuan task, it is believed that by converting Page 1 of 15 it into a Department, TESDA will be strengthened as an implementing and regulatory institution of the technical and vocational sector. It will make this Agency in a better position to fulfill its vision and mission, believing in demonstrated competence, institutional integrity, personal commitment, culture of innovativeness, and a deep sense of nationalism. The early passage of this Bill, therefore, is earnestly requested. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) was established on August 25, 1994, by virtue of Republic Act No. 7796, otherwise known as the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994.” Since its creation, TESDA has remained an essential contributor to the National Government’s mission of providing Filipinos with quality-assured technical education and skills development programs, and mobilizing technical-vocational institutions across the country. Over three decades after its establishment, TESDA continues to serve as the leading government agency responsible for setting the direction of, and ensuring the efficient delivery of, technical education and skills development programs across various sectors nationwide. However, TESDA has also faced challenges and limitations, particularly in today’s ever-changing local and global environment. To address pressing concerns such as strengthening TESDA’s organizational structure and modernizing skills training facilities, the overall system of the Authority must be enhanced through an increased budget, as well as sufficient personnel and resources. Hence, this proposed measure seeks to repeal Republic Act No. 7796, or the “Technical Education and Skills Development Act of 1994,” and strengthen the powers and organizational functions of TESDA by transforming it into a full-fledged Department. The Department shall serve as the primary policy- making, planning, coordinating, implementing, regulating, and administrative entity of the government for technical education, training, and certification programs. It shall be headed by a Secretary, supported by four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries. Such a reform is necessary to address challenges and implement policies consistent with the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution and other global advancements. Through this proposed legislative measure, TESDA will be further strengthened as the implementing and regulatory institution for the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) sector within the country’s trifocal education system. Most importantly, this measure is being filed to promote the interests and meet the needs of the hardworking and highly skilled Filipino workforce. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JONATHA) T. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The creation of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) on August 25, 1994, through the merger of the former National Manpower and Youth Council (NMYC), the Bureau of Technical Vocational Education of the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports (BTVE-DECS) and the Apprenticeship program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE), was an offshoot of the trifocalization of education recommended by the 1991 Congresssional Education Commission or EDCOM. By virtue of Republic Act No. 7796 (TESDA Act of 1994), the TESDA is mandated to ensure the delivery of relevant, accessible, high quality and efficient technical education and skills development and to develop high quality middle-level manpower responsive to the country’s development goals and priorities. However, after more than two decades of delivering relevant, accessible, and efficient technical education and skills development thoughout ther country, TESDA has been encountering many challenges and limitations that affect the performance of its functions, delivery of technical-vocational education and training (TVET) programs, and fulfillment of its vision. One of these is the need to sstrengthen its organizational structure and functions to keep pace with the advent of technology and the demands of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR). The frequent transfer of the TESDA from one office to another has also affected its functions, programs and projects, and delivery of educational services. From an attached agency of the Department of Labor and Employment, TESDA was transferred to the Office of the President and now, to the Department of Trade and Industry through executive order signed by President Duterte. Moreover, under the TESDA Charter, the TESDA Director-General shall enjoy the benefits, privileges ad emoluments equivalent to the rank of Undersecretary. However, the current and past two Presidents of the Philippines appointed the TESDA Director General with a Cabinet rank position or equivalent to a Secretary. By elevating the TESDA into a department, it shall be headed by a Secretary, four (4) Undersecretaries and four (4) Assistant Secretaries and attain self-determination to ensure permanence and continuity of mandated programs. This will also strengthen the implementing, regulatory, and policy-making functions of the agency, as well as make it more responsive and agile in the era of the 4IR and digital economy. The proposed Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) will not only improve the resource/budget allocation for TVET programs, but will also ably represent the TVET sector as a whole, changing its “second class” perception. More importantly, the proposed DTESD will have a better capacity to fulfill its vision as the transformational leader in TVET in the country. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION, TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TESDA ACT OF 1994”, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, with its growing economy, faces a significant challenge in bridging the skills gap in its workforce. Technical-vocational education and training (TVET) play a crucial role in developing a skilled labor force capable of meeting the demands of modern industries. However, the country has long faced inefficiencies in the management and delivery of TVET programs. These challenges stem from fragmented governance, outdated curricula, underfunding, and mismatched industry needs, among others. The Philippine technical education system is divided among various government agencies, which results in inconsistent policies, misallocation of resources, and lack of coordination. TESDA oversees skills development, while DepEd handles secondary-level vocational programs. Higher education institutions (HEIs) also offer technical courses under the Commission on Higher Education (CHED). This fragmented structure complicates the implementation of nationwide reforms and makes it difficult to monitor and evaluate the quality of training programs. Likewise, the skills taught in many TVET programs do not always meet the evolving demands of industries. While TESDA has attempted to bridge this gap, there is still a lag in updating curricula and aligning programs with technological advancements and market needs. Many TVET institutions lack modern equipment, and instructors often receive inadequate training. These deficiencies hinder the development of a skilled workforce capable of competing in global markets. There are geographic and socioeconomic barriers that limit access to quality technical education. Many regions, particularly in rural areas, lack sufficient training centers and resources to support the growing demand for skilled workers. The establishment of a Department of Technical Education and Training (DTET) will centralize the management of technical education and training across various levels. This new department will be tasked with the integration of TVET programs under one cohesive strategy, improving coordination among government agencies, educational institutions, and industries. The DTET will streamline decision-making processes, ensuring that policies and programs are coordinated and aligned with national economic priorities. This unified governance will help resolve issues of duplication and inefficiency, leading to a more coherent and effective TVET system. The DTET will be empowered to work closely with industries and employers to identify current and future skill requirements. By fostering partnerships with private sector organizations, the DTET can ensure that TVET curricula are continuously updated to meet the demands of emerging industries such as digital technologies, renewable energy, and healthcare. Studies, such as those by the Asian Development Bank (ADB), have stressed the need for curricula reforms that align education with labor market needs to reduce the skills mismatch. The creation of a dedicated department will allow for better prioritization and allocation of resources toward upgrading infrastructure, purchasing modern equipment, and improving the professional development of trainers and instructors. This will ensure that TVET institutions are equipped to deliver high-quality education. Additionally, the DTET can advocate for more sustainable and long-term funding for technical education programs, ensuring their continuity and expansion. With a single department overseeing all aspects of TVET, the DTET will be able to implement nationwide strategies to expand access to training, especially in underserved regions. Through initiatives like mobile training units, partnerships with local government units (LGUs), and the expansion of online and blended learning, the DTET can ensure that technical education opportunities are available to all Filipinos, regardless of their geographic or socioeconomic background. The creation of the Department of Technical Education and Training in the Philippines is a vital step toward improving the country’s technical education system. By centralizing governance, aligning curricula with industry needs, improving resource allocation, and expanding access, the DTET will help produce a highly skilled and employable workforce capable of driving economic growth and meeting the demands of an evolving labor market. Through this proposed legislation, the Philippines can build a robust technical education system that supports both individual and national development. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. DALE B. title: AN ACT CREATING THE DEPARTMENT OF TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE TESDA ACT OF 1994 AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In an increasingly competitive and rapidly evolving global economy, the country must ensure that its workforce possesses relevant, high-quality, and industry-responsive skills. While existing systems under the Republic Act No. 7796 created the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), there is a growing need to elevate and strengthen this mandate into a full-fledged department to better address persistent issues such as job mismatch, unemployment, underemployment, and unequal access to skills training. Thus, this bill measure seeks to establish the Department of Technical Education and Skills Development (DTESD) as the primary government body responsible for the formulation, coordination, implementation, and regulation of policies and programs on technical education and skills development (TESD) in the Philippines. 1 The DTESD will be mandated to formulate a National Technical Education and Skills Development Plan (NTESDP) to guide the country’s manpower development strategy and ensure alignment with national development goals. Further, it will prioritize access to technical education for marginalized and disadvantaged sectors, including beneficiaries of the Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program (4Ps) under Republic Act No. 11310, to support poverty reduction and inclusive growth. By transforming TESDA into a full department, we can expect improvement in the quality and global competitiveness of Filipino workers, reduction in job-skills mismatch, expansion of employment and livelihood opportunities, strengthening of industry participation in workforce development and enhancement of social mobility. Finally, we recognize Rep. Mark O. Go of the Lone District of Baguio for filing a similar bill in the Nineteenth Congresses. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DEPARTMENT OF CULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The culture and the arts are not just mere forms of expression and entertainment, more importantly, they are essential tools for nation-building. Arts and Culture are integral to a nation’s struggle for national identity as they can evoke dialogue, induce reflection, and charter new relationships and ideas—all of which are essential to a healthy society. This is exemplified through the works of renowned Filipino artists during the Spanish and American Colonial Period, which have helped shape a sense of national identity among Filipinos. It is the policy of the State under Section 17, Article II of the Constitution to give priority to arts and culture so as to “foster patriotism nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development.” However, with the transfer of the administration of cultural agencies to the National Commission on Culture Arts from the then Department of Education, Culture and Sports, effective promotion of the culture and arts took the sidelines due to the limited powers and resources of the NCCA and attached agencies. To this end, this proposed measure seeks to reorganize the National Commission on Culture and Arts into an independent Department of Culture or Kagawaran ng Kultura which shall be the primary policy- formulating, planning, coordinating, implementing, and administrative entity of the executive branch of the National Government that will develop, manage and implement the pertinent provisions of the Constitution regarding culture and arts. With more powers and better resources, the creation of the Department of Culture would be better equipped for the enormous task of preservation of the Filipino heritage and the promotion and advancement of cultural education among Filipinos. On behalf of the people of Parañaque City’s Second District, and for the common good of the Filipino people, the approval of the said measure is earnestly sought. REP. GUSTAVO S. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DEPARTMENT OF CULTURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Culture is a key driver of inclusive development, soft power, innovation, and national identity. Deeply rooted in history and tradition, it shapes who we are as a people and unites Filipinos across regions and generations. The 1987 Constitution affirms this by mandating the State to prioritize arts and culture to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development. Culture empowers local and Indigenous communities, fosters participation and solidarity, and contributes to human development, community cohesion, and socio­ economic transformation. It also offers sustainable pathways for development through the conservation of heritage structures, the promotion of cultural tourism, and the revitalization of local economies. Yet despite this vast potential, the Philippines has yet to establish a dedicated Department of Culture, unlike many of its neighbors in Southeast and East Asia. This institutional gap has led to fragmented policy direction, chronic underinvestment, and missed opportunities to fully harness our rich cultural assets. While the National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) serves as the primary coordinating and policy-making body, it is not a line agency and lacks direct authority over many of the cultural institutions responsible for implementation. As a result, the cultural sector remains underprioritized in national development planning and falls short of its potential as a strategic pillar of growth and national unity. According to UNESCO, cultural and creative industries generate nearly US$2.3 trillion in annual global revenues, equivalent to 3.1 percent of the world's gross domestic product (GDP). Their contribution to national value added varies among G20 economies, ranging from 0.7 percent in Mexico to 3 percent in the United States. These industries also provide employment for approximately 6.2 percent of the global workforce.1 In the Asia-Pacific region, countries like Japan and South Korea have successfully institutionalized cultural governance, generating massive returns. In 2023, Japan's anime industry (including television and film productions, streaming distribution, merchandising, music, events, and overseas licensing), supported by Agency for Cultural Affairs (Bunkachd) under the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), reached an all-time high of ¥3.3465 trillion (approximately US$22.3 billion). Of the total revenue, ¥1.6243 trillion (around US$10.8 billion) came from domestic sources, while ¥1.7222 trillion (about US$11.5 billion) was generated from international markets.2 South Korea's cultural content industry (Korean Wave or Hallyu), supported by its Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, has steadily grown into a high value-added sector marked by robust domestic sales and expanding exports. South Korea's cultural content industry grew steadily from 2021 to 2023, with total sales rising from W137.5 trillion (US$105.8 billion)3 to W154.2 trillion (US$110.5 billion),4 and exports increasing from US$12.45 billion to US$13.3 billion during the same period. 1 UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD). Retrieved August 1,2025, from https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10468573 In contrast, the Philippines' creative economy reached PhPl.94 trillion (USD 34,64 billion) in 2024. This marked an 8.7 percent increase from the PhPl.78 trillion (USD 31.95 billion) recorded in 2023, reflecting continued expansion across key creative sectors such as digital media, advertising, symbolic content, and traditional cultural expressions,5 These data points underscore a vital truth: countries that invest in strong cultural governance and infrastructure reap significant returns, not only in terms of economic growth, employment, and exports, but also in global influence, innovation, and national unity. In contrast, the Philippines continues to operate without a dedicated Department of Culture, limiting its ability to fully harness the value of its diverse cultural assets. With the Philippines'creative economy already contributing 7.3 percent to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and growing, the absence of a dedicated department risks leaving our rich cultural capital under-leveraged and fragmented. This bill seeks to address that institutional gap. By establishing the Department of Culture, it provides the policy leadership, operational mandate, and organizational structure necessary to protect, develop, and promote Philippine culture, both as a heritage to be preserved and as a resource to be activated for inclusive growth. Among its key features are the following: 1. Centralized cultural governance through the integration of policy, regulatory, and programmatic functions currently dispersed across multiple agencies; 2. Capacity-building and education through national institutes dedicated to living traditions, heritage

title: AN ACT PROMOTING BEHIND-THE-METER SOLAR ENERGY GENERATION AND BATTERY ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS FOR OWN-USE, ESTABLISHING A STREAMLINED REGULATORY, SAFETY, AND CONSUMER PROTECTION FRAMEWORK, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 21 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Republic of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 24
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The Philippines continues to face the challenge of ensuring an electricity supply that is affordable, reliable, secure, and resilient. Advances in solar photovoltaic generation and battery energy storage technologies now provide households, businesses, health facilities, educational institutions, government establishments, and other electricity end-users with greater opportunities to generate and store electricity primarily for their own use. 22 Behind-the-meter (BTM) solar generation and battery energy storage systems (BESS) can enable consumers to reduce their dependence on electricity purchased from the distribution system, manage peak electricity consumption, improve energy resilience, and make greater use of electricity generated within their premises. Battery storage is particularly valuable because it allows electricity generated or purchased during periods of lower demand to be stored for use during periods of higher demand or interruptions in grid supply. 31 However, the adoption of these technologies should not be hindered by unnecessary or disproportionate regulatory requirements. At the same time, simplification must be accompanied by appropriate safeguards to protect consumers, electrical workers, distribution utilities, and the reliability and safety of the electric power system. 37 The Sariling Kuryente Act therefore establishes a proportionate and risk- based framework for BTM solar generation and BESS. It provides simplified regulatory treatment for standardized, low-risk systems and streamlines procedures for qualified zero-export systems, while preserving necessary technical, electrical, structural, fire, environmental, and distribution-system safety requirements. 6 The measure also strengthens consumer protection by requiring covered solar and storage equipment to comply with applicable Philippine National Standards and conformity-assessment requirements. It requires the installation and commissioning of covered systems to be undertaken by duly accredited installers and establishes appropriate accountability requirements, including mandatory liability insurance or other financial security, to protect consumers from unsafe installations, defective workmanship, and unqualified or unscrupulous service providers. 15 The bill further protects the ability of end-users to install BTM generation and energy storage systems on property they own or exclusively control, while allowing reasonable restrictions necessary for structural safety, public safety, and the protection of common property. 20 The bill also prioritizes energy storage as a means of increasing self- consumption, reducing peak demand, and supporting distribution-system reliability and resilience. It likewise recognizes the need to account for the adoption of BTM systems in electricity planning while preventing unreasonable cost shifting to consumers who do not have such systems. It also authorizes the development of appropriate financing programs, incentives, and targeted financial assistance for qualified end-users adopting BESS and integrated solar-plus-storage systems, with priority given to measures that support energy storage, reduce or shift peak demand, improve electricity reliability and resilience, and assist low-income or underserved consumers, subject to the availability of funds and applicable laws. 32 By reducing unnecessary regulatory barriers while maintaining appropriate safety, technical, environmental, and consumer-protection safeguards, the Sariling Kuryente Act seeks to make consumer-owned solar generation and energy storage simpler, faster, safer, and more accountable. 37 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 39 40 41 REP. label: HB 10747
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL FRAMEWORK FOR YOUTH DEVELOPMENT AND EMPOWERMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is a young nation. Around 32.4 million Filipinos aged 15 to 30—nearly three out of every ten Filipinos—are part of our youth population. They are students, workers, farmers, entrepreneurs, athletes, artists, volunteers, community leaders, and dreamers who are already shaping the country we will inherit. But being young in the Philippines should not mean being left to figure everything out alone. In January 2026, 14.0% of young Filipinos aged 15 to 24 were not in education, employment, or training, an increase from 11.7% a year earlier. Youth labor-force participation and employment also declined during the same period. These numbers are more than statistics. They represent young people who may be struggling to find a school, a job, a livelihood, a safe space, or simply a clear next step. Government already has many programs for the youth. We have scholarships, skills training, employment assistance, entrepreneurship programs, health services, sports programs, and opportunities for civic participation. The problem is that these opportunities are often scattered across different agencies and difficult to navigate. This bill seeks to change that. The Philippine Youth Development and Empowerment Act creates a stronger national framework that connects existing government programs and brings opportunities closer to where young people actually live. Most importantly, every barangay shall have a Youth Development Hub, managed by the Sangguniang Kabataan in partnership with the Barangay Government. Municipalities, cities, and provinces shall likewise have Youth Centers where young people can access information, referrals, training, leadership activities, employment and entrepreneurship opportunities, digital resources, sports, culture, and other development programs. Because youth development should not depend on where a young person was born. A young person in a far-flung barangay deserves the same chance as a young person in the city. The bill also creates the Department of Youth Development and Empowerment as the national institution responsible for bringing government efforts together—not to replace DepEd, CHED, TESDA, DOLE, DSWD, DTI, DA, DOH, and other agencies, but to make sure that their programs reach young people in a coordinated and meaningful way. The bill is built on a simple belief: When we invest in the youth, we are not spending for tomorrow. We are building today. Every scholarship can change a family's future. Every job opportunity can restore a young person's confidence. Every youth-led project can transform a community. Every safe space can give a young person a reason to stay, grow, and lead. The Filipino youth do not need another promise that someday they will have a place in nation-building. They need that place now. This measure seeks to give them the opportunities, spaces, support, and voice they deserve. Because the future of the Philippines should not merely be something that the youth inherit. It should be something they are empowered to build. The passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10748
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RIGHTS, PROTECTION, DEVELOPMENT, AND EMPOWERMENT OF OUT-OF-SCHOOL YOUTH, PROVIDING FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE AND OPPORTUNITIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Filipino youth deserve a second chance—not because they have failed, but because circumstances should never be allowed to define the limits of their future. The Philippine Statistics Authority's recent data continue to show the challenge of keeping young Filipinos connected to education and productive economic activity. In July 2025, 15.9% of Filipinos aged 15 to 24 were not in education, employment, or training (NEET), higher than the 13.9% recorded a year earlier. While NEET is not exactly synonymous with out-of-school youth, it reflects a serious disconnection between young people and the pathways that lead to learning, work, and economic participation. At the same time, government already has important programs for second-chance education, particularly the Alternative Learning System under Republic Act No. 11510. What is still needed is a stronger framework that connects education with the other realities of an OSY's life: skills, work, livelihood, health, social protection, digital access, and reintegration. This is the purpose of this bill. The proposed Magna Carta of the Out-of-School Youth Act recognizes OSYs as rights- holders and partners in nation-building. It provides a framework for ensuring that young Filipinos outside the formal education system are not excluded from opportunities available to their peers. The measure is patterned in substance after the policy direction of Senator Raffy T. Tulfo's Senate Bill No. 2064, which was filed in the 20th Congress on April 21, 2026, and carries the same short title and broad objective of providing a Magna Carta for OSYs. It likewise builds upon the earlier SBN 2059 filed by Senator Tulfo in the 19th Congress, which proposed rights protection, education, technical-vocational training, entrepreneurship, employment, social protection, and assistance for OSYs in especially difficult circumstances. The proposed House measure, however, seeks to make the framework more coordinated and implementation-oriented. It does not create parallel education, health, labor, social-welfare, or technical-vocational systems. DepEd remains responsible for basic education and ALS; TESDA for technical-vocational education and training; DOLE for employment and labor programs; DSWD for social protection and welfare; and other agencies retain their respective statutory mandates. Instead, the bill establishes mechanisms for access, referral, convergence, and accountability. It also brings the Magna Carta closer to the community through an OSY Development Hub in every barangay, using existing public facilities whenever possible. A young person should not have to travel to a national office simply to ask: “Saan ako puwedeng mag-aral ulit? Saan ako puwedeng mag-training? May trabaho ba para sa akin? May livelihood program ba? Sino ang puwedeng tumulong sa akin?” Government should have an answer. The bill further recognizes that not every OSY will take the same path. Some may return to school. Others may pursue ALS, TESDA training, employment, entrepreneurship, agriculture, digital work, or other productive opportunities. The State's role is not to force one path upon them, but to ensure that there is a path available. This is why the measure promotes skills recognition, employment and apprenticeship pathways, entrepreneurship, digital inclusion, health and wellness, social protection, and access to essential government documents. The bill also gives special attention to OSYs facing poverty, disability, displacement, geographic isolation, family responsibilities, homelessness, conflict, or other difficult circumstances. Most importantly, this measure seeks to change the way society sees out-of-school youth. Being out of school is a circumstance—not a permanent identity. A young person who left school may still become a skilled worker, entrepreneur, farmer, professional, artist, community leader, or public servant. What matters is whether we give that young person the opportunity to begin again. The State should not merely ask why a young Filipino dropped out. We should ask what we can do to help that young Filipino move forward. The Magna Carta of the Out-of-School Youth Act answers that call by providing rights, opportunities, protection, and pathways to reintegration. No young Filipino should be told that because they once left school, they have already been left behind. There is always another path. There should always be another chance. The passage of this measure is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10749
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A TWENTY-YEAR SPORTS EXCELLENCE ROADMAP TO STRENGTHEN GRASSROOTS SPORTS, DEVELOP WORLD-CLASS FILIPINO ATHLETES, AND PROVIDE A SUSTAINABLE PATHWAY FOR SPORTS EXCELLENCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sports can change a young person's life. For many Filipino children and young people, the barangay court, school field, public gymnasium, or community sports program is where confidence begins. It is where discipline is learned, friendships are built, talent is discovered, and dreams of representing the country first take shape. But talent alone is not enough. A Filipino athlete may have the ability to compete with the best in the world, yet lose the opportunity because there is no proper coach, inadequate equipment, limited competition exposure, insufficient nutrition, lack of sports science, or no clear pathway from grassroots competition to elite training. The Philippines therefore needs to stop treating sports development as a collection of short- term programs and start treating it as a long-term national investment. The Roadmap for Sports Excellence Act establishes a clear national pathway: Barangay → Municipality/City → Province → National Development → International Competition. It begins where Filipino talent is first discovered—the community. The bill strengthens grassroots sports by requiring every barangay, subject to available resources and existing facilities, to maintain or designate an appropriate space for sports and physical activity. It also establishes or designates Sports Development Centers at the municipal, city, and provincial levels to serve as venues for training, talent identification, competition, coaching, and athlete assessment. At the national level, the bill strengthens Sports Excellence Centers and creates a coordinated system for athlete development, sports science, sports medicine, nutrition, mental wellness, coaching, competition exposure, and education. Most importantly, the measure recognizes that an athlete is not just a medal-producing machine. Behind every medal is a young person who needs education, health care, mental wellness, protection from abuse, financial guidance, and a future beyond sports. For this reason, the bill provides for student-athlete protection, athlete scholarships and support, safeguarding mechanisms, and a post-career transition program. The measure also recognizes that sports excellence must be inclusive. A child's chance to become an athlete should not depend on whether he or she was born in Metro Manila or in a remote barangay. Young women, persons with disabilities, Indigenous youth, economically disadvantaged athletes, and other underserved groups must have meaningful access to sports opportunities. The proposed Twenty-Year Sports Excellence Roadmap will therefore provide government with something that Philippine sports has long needed: continuity. Athlete development takes years. Coaches take years to develop. Sports facilities require long-term planning. International competitiveness cannot be built within a single administration or a single competition cycle. The country needs a system that survives changes in leadership and remains focused on measurable outcomes. The goal is not simply to produce more medals. The goal is to build a country where every talented Filipino child has a chance to be discovered, developed, supported, and given the opportunity to compete at the highest level. A champion does not begin on the international stage. A champion begins in a barangay. This measure seeks to build the pathway from that barangay court to the world stage. The passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10751
title: AN ACT CREATING AN AGRICULTURAL PENSION PROGRAM TO PROVIDE SOCIAL SECURITY AND PENSION BENEFITS TO FARMERS AND FISHERFOLK
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sa bawat butil ng kanin na ating kinokonsumo, sa bawat isda o yamang dagat na ating nilalasap, may magsasakang tinitiis ang matinding init ng araw at may mangingisdang hinaharap ang mapanganib na alon ng dagat… Ngunit sa kabalintunaan, ang mga magsasaka at mangingisda ang mga sektor na nanatiling pinakaduha sa Pilipinas. Filipino farmers and fisherfolk hold the primary role in ensuring national food security in the country. They are the most indispensable yet most vulnerable sectors of the Philippine economy. Through their hard work, they feed millions of Filipino families every day despite unstable incomes, high production costs, climate-related disasters, and limited social protection. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) research showed that farmers and fisherfolk consistently have the highest poverty incidence among all basic sectors in the country. It further reported that in 2021, the poverty incidence among fisherfolk stood at 30.6%, higher than the national poverty incidence.1 This means that nearly one (1) in every three (3) Filipino farmers and fisherfolk continues to live below the poverty threshold despite their vital contribution to the country’s food supply. Critical sources of livelihood and employment still come from the sectors of agriculture and fishing. Around 22.36% of total employment in the Philippines in 2023 was generated by agriculture-related work, proving the continued dependence of millions of Filipino families on this sector for survival.2 The fisheries sector alone directly and indirectly supports the livelihoods of approximately 2.29 million Filipinos, including those engaged in capture 1Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), Fisherfolks and Farmers Remain to Have the Highest Poverty Incidences Among the Basic Sectors in 2021 (2023). 2 World Bank/ILO Data, Employment in Agriculture (% of Total Employment), Philippines (2023). fisheries, aquaculture, processing, transport, and related industries. 3 The latest records further reported that there are already more than 2.29 million registered fisherfolk in the country. 4 Filipino farmers and fisherfolk remain economically insecure, especially the elderly ones, despite their indispensable role in the country. Most agricultural workers belong to the informal sector and often lack adequate retirement savings, pension security, insurance protection, and stable access to social security benefits. Many continue to work even in old age because retirement is simply unaffordable and not an option. Studies and government reports indicate that the average Filipino farmer is now in their mid-50s, an indication of an urgent demographic concern over the sustainability of food production and the declining interest of younger generations in agriculture.5 Without a comprehensive and dedicated pension mechanism for agricultural workers, not only perpetuates poverty but also discourages younger Filipinos from entering the agriculture and fisheries sectors. Without institutional support, farming and fishing become occupations associated with poverty. This proposed measure seeks to address this longstanding inequity through the establishment of the Farmers and Fisherfolk Social Security and Pension Program, a comprehensive pension and social protection system designed to provide income security and retirement protection to farmers and fisherfolk through access to sickness, maternity, disability, retirement, death, and funeral benefits under the Social Security System (SSS), in coordination with the Department of Agriculture (DA) and the Philippine Crop Insurance Corporation (PCIC). Recognizing that poverty among farming and fishing households is often intergenerational, this bill further introduces an educational scholarship component for children of registered farmers and fisherfolk. Through this bill, the State empowers the next generation to break cycles of poverty while still honoring and uplifting families whose labor sustains the nation. Higit sa lahat, ang panukalang batas na ito ang nagpapamulat sa isang simpleng katotohanan: Na ang mga taong naghihirap at nagbabanat ng buto upang may makain ang ating bayan ay nararapat lamang na hindi magutom, maabuso at makalimutan. Napapanahon na upang magkaroon ng isang komprehensibo at matibay na social protection mechanism para sa ating mga magsasaka at mangingisda na malaki ang sakripisyo para sa ating bansa. Similar bills were filed such as in the 18th Congress authored by Rep. Florencio Gabriel “Bem” Noel, in the previous Congress authored by Rep. Patrick Michael Vargas, and in the Congress, filed by Rep. Nathaniel Oducado Given the considerations mentioned, this Representation respectfully seeks the passage of this proposed measure. JC M. label: HB 10752
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL AUTISM CARE PLAN, ESTABLISHING A SUB- COMMITTEE ON AUTISM UNDER THE NATIONAL COUNCIL ON DISABILITY AFFAIRS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Autism, or Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), is a lifelong, complex neurodevelopmental condition caused by differences in how the human brain functions1. Social communications and interaction challenges, as well as restricted and repetitive behaviors, are primarily seen in persons with ASD2. The Philippines still does not have an official and available registry of autism prevalence. Recent estimates indicate that approximately one (1) in every one hundred (100) Filipinos may be on the autism spectrum, translating to roughly 1.2 million Filipinos living with autism, including an estimated 350,000 Filipino children with ASD3. Despite these rising numbers, autism care in the Philippines is still inaccessible and expensive to most Filipino families. Support systems are very much inadequate and unevenly distributed in the country. For many low-income households, especially those in underserved and geographically isolated communities, access to developmental specialists, diagnostic services, and intervention programs is out of financial reach. In 2022, it was cited that the Philippines has 99 board-certified developmental-behavioral paediatricians, of whom more than half (52%) are situated in the National Capital Region4. These compel families from provinces to shoulder significant transportation and accommodation expenses merely to access consultations and therapy. The financial burden associated with autism care is substantial and, in many cases, heartbreaking to household stability. The United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) and the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) jointly conducted a study that concluded that raising a child with a disability requires expenditures approximately forty percent (40%) to eighty percent (80%) higher than raising a typically developing child. Moreover, poverty rates among households caring for children with disabilities are fifty percent (50%) higher compared to other households. The same study also showed that only one (1) out of five (5) children with disabilities possesses a Persons with Disability (PWD) identification card, limiting access to vital government 1 Definition from web (https://www.cdc.gov/autism/about/index.html) 2 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/ 3 Autism Society Philippines prevalence estimate (1 in 100 Filipinos with autism), as cited in Philippine policy materials andautism awareness publications; see also Capitol Medical Center, “National Autism Consciousness Week.” 4 Challenges in Philippine Developmental Paediatric Care. Rafael L G Valenzuela, Julian E D Mendoza, Ourlad Alzeus G Tantengco, Eric D B Ornos. 18 June 2022. Retrieved from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jpc.16055 1 assistance and concessions. More alarmingly, forty-three percent (43%) of disability subsidies are received by the richest income quintile, while the poorest quintile receives less than six percent (6%), underscoring persistent inequities in access to social protection5. According to a Philippine study published in Acta Medica Philippina, the average cost of interventions, such as therapy, education, medication, and developmental monitoring, is about Php38,868 during the first year of care, or about twenty-one percent (21%) of the monthly expenses of a household earning Php15,000. The total cost of diagnostic evaluations for autism ranges from Php1,356 to Php44,634. The same study further revealed that approximately forty-two percent (42%) of diagnosed children received no intervention after diagnosis, largely due to financial and accessibility barriers6. Hindi lamang ito mga numero o datos. Ito ay ang nakapanglulumong realidad ng mga magulang at primary caregivers na isinasakripisyo ang kanilang oras at panahon para lamang alagaan ang kanilang mga mahal sa buhay na may ASD. Ang kabawasan, lalo na ang kawalan ng oras, sa paghahanapbuhay ang s’yang nagpapalugmok sa kanila sa kahirapan. And despite the passage of landmark legislation such as Republic Act No. 7277 or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, Republic Act No. 11223 or the Universal Health Care Act, Republic Act No. 11036 or the Mental Health Act, and Republic Act No. 11650 or the Inclusive Education Act, there is still no comprehensive and coordinated national framework specifically devoted to autism care across the life course, from early childhood through adulthood. Sa pamamagitan ng pagbabalangkas at pagtatag ng National Autism Care Plan at pagsaayos ng isang dedicated inter-agency and multi-sectoral mechanism sa ilalim ng National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA), ang panukalang batas na ito ay hindi lamang tutugon sa mga isyu sa kalusugan… ito ay may hangaring solusyunan ang mga isyu sa kahirapan, panlipunang proteksyon at inklusyong pang-ekonomiya. By investing in early intervention, strengthening inclusive educational systems, expanding access to therapies, and creating networks for skills training, livelihood, and employment, the State empowers persons with autism to become more independent, self-reliant, and productive members of society. Equally important, this measure enables parents and caregivers to remain economically productive while reducing the long-term financial burden borne by families and local communities. The heart of this proposed legislation affirms the State’s obligation to ensure that access to autism care is not determined by geography or financial capacity, but made available to every Filipino family in need. The National Autism Care Plan advances the welfare of neurodivergent Filipinos while contributing to broader national goals of inclusive growth, family resilience, and poverty reduction. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 10753
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE SERVICE INCENTIVE LEAVE (SIL) OF EMPLOYEES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE ARTICLE 95 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes labor as a primary socio-economic force and mandates the State to protect the rights and promote the welfare of Filipino workers. Consistent with this constitutional duty, Article 95 of the Labor Code grants employees who have rendered at least one (1) year of service an annual Service Incentive Leave (SIL) of five (5) days with pay.1 Yet despite decades of economic change, rising costs of living, and evolving family realities, this minimum benefit has never changed. This proposed measure seeks to increase the SIL entitlement from five (5) days to ten (10) days with pay, recognizing that Filipino workers deserve not only protection in the workplace but also meaningful opportunities to care for their health, fulfil family responsibilities, and spend time with their loved ones. Today, millions of Filipinos endure the difficult reality of working far from home. While employment opportunities are still concentrated in urban centers such as Metro Manila, Region IV- A (CALABARZON), and Region III (Central Luzon), many workers come from provinces and leave behind their spouses, children, and elderly parents in search of better opportunities. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) recorded approximately 48.5 million employed Filipinos in 2025 2. More than 6.3 million workers are recorded in the National Capital Region (NCR), underscoring Metro Manila’s continued role as the country’s primary employment hub. “Rest days,” or taking time off, are considered a luxury for many workers, especially minimum- wage earners and rank-and-file employees. The existing five (5) days of SIL are indeed often insufficient to address illness, emergencies, caregiving responsibilities, government transactions, and much-needed family time. Most of the time, these workers are left with no choice but to accept meager wages rather than return home to their loved ones. Moreover, additional leave days have a meaningful impact on those who come from Bicol, Visayas, Mindanao, or any distant province. A chance for them to go home opens several doors for their 1 Book Three – Conditions of Employment, P.D. 442, Labor Code Title I – Working Conditions and Rest Periods. https://library.laborlaw.ph/p-d-442-labor-code-book-3/ 2 https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/labor-force-survey family: it means being present at a child’s graduation, celebrating a birthday, caring for an aging mother, or simply spending precious time with family members whom they only see a few times each year. This proposed increase in Service Incentive Leave also comes at a time when Filipino households continue to struggle with inflation and rising living costs. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported sustained inflationary pressures in recent years, reaching 7.2 percent in April 2026 from 4.1 percent in March 20263. This resulted in increased household spending on food, transportation, healthcare, and utilities. These economic burdens disproportionately affect workers who live paycheck to paycheck. PSA data also showed that the average annual income of Filipino families in 2023 was PhP353.23 thousand4. Because of this, they always choose to give up their personal or family needs instead of taking a leave. Furthermore, adequate rest and work-life balance are essential to maintaining productivity and preventing workplace burnout. International labor standards recognize paid leave as an important component of decent work, contributing to improved physical and mental well-being, higher morale, greater employee retention, and better overall productivity5. Workers who are given reasonable opportunities to rest and reconnect with family are ultimately more motivated, healthier, and more productive members of the workforce6. Increasing Service Incentive Leave from five (5) days to ten (10) days is neither excessive nor unreasonable. Rather, it is a practical and compassionate reform that reflects the realities faced by Filipino workers today. It recognizes that workers are not machines, but individuals carrying responsibilities both in the workplace and at home. This bill tells us a simple truth-- labor policies must strengthen the family by giving workers enough time to be with their loved ones. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M.
