label: HB 10754
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE TEACHING OF THE WEST PHILIPPINE SEA, THE 2016 SOUTH CHINA SEA ARBITRAL AWARD, AND THE PHILIPPINES' MARITIME RIGHTS AND ENTITLEMENTS AS PART OF THE PHILIPPINE HISTORY CURRICULUM IN BASIC EDUCATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2026, the Philippines commemorates the tenth anniversary of the landmark 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award, a historic legal victory that reaffirmed the country's maritime rights under the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The Award clarified the legal status of maritime features in the South China Sea and declared that China's expansive “nine-dash line” claim has no legal basis under international law. It is a defining milestone in the pursuit of a rules-based international order, providing a final and legally binding resolution to disputes over maritime entitlements. As emphasized by the National Maritime Council (NMC), the 2016 Arbitral Award remains the Philippines' strongest legal foundation for defending its rights in the West Philippine Sea. The Council described the Award as "not merely a legal victory" but "a beacon that guides our national policy and collective action in protecting our maritime rights and ensuring that the West Philippine Sea remains a source of peace, stability, and prosperity for present and future generations of Filipinos." The Council likewise stressed that the Award is final and legally binding between the Philippines and China and continues to guide the country's maritime policy and diplomacy while promoting the peaceful settlement of disputes.1 Beyond its legal significance, the West Philippine Sea is an integral part of the nation's history, identity, security, and economic future. It sustains the livelihoods of Filipino fisherfolk, serves as a vital maritime corridor for trade and commerce, and contains valuable marine and natural resources essential to national development. As such, every Filipino should possess a clear understanding of the historical, legal, and geopolitical issues surrounding the West Philippine Sea. Recent government efforts have shown that increasing public awareness, especially among the youth, helps foster a better understanding of the 1 Esguerra, D. J. (2026, July 12). 10 years on, PH arbitral win remains anchor for WPS rights. Philippine News Agency. https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1279257 country's maritime rights and national interests. This highlights the importance of introducing these topics in the basic education curriculum.2 Recognizing that an informed citizenry is essential to safeguarding the country's maritime rights, the present administration launched a transparency initiative to systematically document and publicize developments and unlawful activities in the West Philippine Sea. By exposing coercive actions at sea and grounding the Philippines' position in international law, the initiative has strengthened public awareness, reinforced domestic support, and garnered greater international solidarity behind the country's rules-based position.3 While the transparency initiative keeps the public informed of current developments, public awareness must be sustained through formal education. Institutionalizing the study of the West Philippine Sea and the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award in the Philippine History curriculum ensures that Filipino students acquire, as early as primary and secondary education, a factual and evidence-based understanding of the country's maritime history, legal rights, and national interests. In this way, the measure transforms public awareness into enduring civic education and equips future generations to appreciate and uphold the Philippines' sovereignty, sovereign rights, and maritime entitlements through peaceful and lawful means. Despite its significance, discussions on the West Philippine Sea and the 2016 Arbitral Award remain limited in the basic education curriculum. There is therefore a compelling need to institutionalize the teaching of these subjects to ensure that future generations are equipped with knowledge grounded in Philippine history, the Constitution, and international law. This measure seeks to integrate the study of the West Philippine Sea, the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award, and the Philippines' maritime rights and entitlements into the Philippine History curriculum in primary and secondary education. This bill seeks to ensure that every Filipino student understands the substance of this victory. It aims to cultivate historical awareness, civic consciousness, patriotism, and respect for the rule of law while encouraging students to appreciate the importance of safeguarding the country's sovereignty, sovereign rights, and maritime interests through peaceful and lawful means. By educating the youth on these matters, the State fulfills its constitutional duty to develop informed, patriotic, and responsible citizens who understand the nation's rights and responsibilities in the international community. label: HB 10755
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL BLOCKCHAIN-BASED LAND REGISTRATION AND PROPERTY RECORDS SYSTEM TO MODERNIZE AND DIGITIZE PROPERTY INFORMATION MANAGEMENT, STRENGTHEN PROPERTY RIGHTS, AND PROMOTE TRANSPARENCY, SECURITY, AND ACCOUNTABILITY IN LAND ADMINISTRATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to rely on fragmented and largely paper-based systems maintained by various national government agencies and local government units. Land records are often dispersed across multiple repositories, resulting in inconsistent information, delayed verification processes, costly reconciliation of records, and administrative inefficiencies. The loss, destruction, deterioration, or unavailability of land records due to natural disasters, accidents, and the passage of time has likewise led to lengthy and expensive title reconstitution proceedings that burden both property owners and government institutions. Land ownership remains one of the most important foundations of economic security, social stability, and wealth creation for Filipino families. Secure and reliable land records are essential to protecting property rights, facilitating investments, improving access to credit, supporting infrastructure development, enhancing local revenue generation, and promoting sustainable economic growth. The lack of an integrated and secure property information system also creates vulnerabilities to fraud, unauthorized alterations, duplicate records, and conflicting claims over land ownership. These challenges undermine public confidence in land administration, increase transaction costs, discourage investments, and impede the efficient delivery of government services. Recent advances in digital governance and blockchain technology provide an opportunity to modernize the country’s land registration and property records management systems. Blockchain technology enables the creation of immutable and verifiable digital audit trails that can significantly strengthen the integrity, security, traceability, and authenticity of land records. By recording and verifying transactions through tamper-resistant digital mechanisms, blockchain technology can reduce opportunities for fraud, facilitate faster verification of ownership records, and improve institutional accountability. The establishment of a National Blockchain-Based Land Registration and Property Records System will enable the integration, digitization, and verification of land and property information across relevant government agencies. The system will support more efficient land administration, facilitate the reconstruction and verification of lost or damaged records, improve disaster resilience, enhance transparency in property transactions, and provide citizens with more accessible and reliable land information services. Moreover, secure and trustworthy land records are critical to strengthening property rights and improving the country’s investment climate. A modernized land registration system can reduce transaction costs, accelerate property-related processes, improve tax administration, support financial inclusion through easier access to collateralized credit, and contribute to the overall ease of doing business in the Philippines. This measure seeks to establish a secure, interoperable, and future-ready framework for land registration and property records management through the strategic use of blockchain technology and digital information systems. By modernizing the country’s land administration infrastructure, the State can better protect property rights, improve governance, strengthen public trust, and support long-term national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10756
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE LIFETIME VALIDITY OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY IDENTIFICATION CARDS ISSUED TO PERSONS WITH PERMANENT DISABILITY, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR DISABLED PERSONS”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A government identification card ought to make it easier for a citizen to access their rights, not require them to repeatedly prove that they deserve them. For persons with permanent disabilities, the current requirement to periodically renew a Persons with Disability (PWD) Identification Card can turn a necessary government service into an unnecessary and repetitive burden. A person whose blindness, deafness, loss of a limb, or other disability has been medically established as permanent should not have to repeatedly secure certifications, undergo administrative procedures, travel to government offices, and spend time and money simply to prove once again what is already known to be permanent. For many persons with disabilities, every renewal may mean additional transportation expenses, physical exertion, time away from work or livelihood, dependence on companions, and navigating government facilities and procedures that may themselves present accessibility barriers. A process intended to facilitate access to benefits and privileges can, in practice, become another barrier to accessing them. This is why the law must distinguish between disabilities that are permanent and those that are temporary. The appropriate policy, therefore, is not to subject everyone to the same renewal requirement, but to establish a system proportionate to the nature of the disability. This bill seeks to establish that distinction between permanent and temporary disabilities. It grants lifetime validity to PWD Identification Cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities, upon certification by the appropriate Municipal or City Health Office, while retaining a two-year validity period and medical reassessment requirement for persons with temporary disabilities. These PWD Identification Cards shall conform to the universal design prescribed by the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) and adopted by local government units, and shall be issued free of charge. At its core, this measure advances a simple principle: government should not make persons with permanent disabilities repeatedly prove what the government has already certified as permanent. Instead, public systems should adapt to the realities of persons with disabilities by removing unnecessary administrative barriers while maintaining reasonable safeguards against fraud, misuse, and inaccurate records. These proposed reforms also affirm the Philippines’ obligations under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), particularly its commitment to eliminate barriers that prevent persons with disabilities from exercising their rights and participating fully and equally in society. Accessibility must extend beyond physical spaces to include identification systems, government procedures, and administrative requirements that directly affect the daily lives of persons with disabilities. By establishing lifetime validity for PWD Identification Cards of persons with permanent disabilities, maintaining appropriate reassessment for temporary disabilities, requiring universal design, and ensuring that the cards are provided free of charge, this bill seeks to make the PWD identification system more accessible, equitable, efficient, and humane. The proposed legislation will reduce unnecessary paperwork, repeated medical certification, transportation costs, and time spent on renewal procedures, while allowing local government units to focus their administrative and medical resources on cases that genuinely require assessment or reassessment. Most importantly, this measure recognizes that government systems should respond to the realities of persons with disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10757
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR OPTIONAL EARLY RETIREMENT FOR GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES WITH DISABILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM ACT OF 1997”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Persons with disabilities continue to make invaluable contributions to the Philippine civil service despite facing barriers and additional disability-related costs throughout their careers. Many government employees with disabilities devote decades of public service while managing expenses for rehabilitation, medicines, assistive devices, accessible transportation, personal assistance, and other support necessary to perform their duties and participate fully in society. While the Government Service Insurance System provides retirement benefits to qualified government employees, existing retirement laws do not recognize the distinct circumstances faced by persons with disabilities who often experience greater physical, financial, and health- related demands over the course of their employment. As more persons with disabilities enter and remain in government service through inclusive employment policies, there is a corresponding need to ensure that the country’s retirement system likewise becomes more responsive to their circumstances. This proposed measure seeks to provide qualified government employees with disabilities the option of early retirement upon reaching fifty-five (55) years of age and rendering at least ten (10) years of government service. The measure is entirely voluntary and does not compel retirement. Rather, it provides an additional retirement option for those who, after years of dedicated public service, choose to retire earlier in recognition of the unique circumstances associated with disability. The bill likewise reflects the Philippines’ commitment under the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), which calls upon States Parties to adopt appropriate measures that promote equality, inclusion, and social protection for persons with disabilities. By recognizing disability-responsive retirement as a reasonable and equitable social protection measure, the State affirms that equality sometimes requires policies that respond to different circumstances rather than treating everyone identically. This proposed legislation honors the dedication and sacrifices of government employees with disabilities by providing them greater flexibility and security as they transition from public service. It strengthens the government’s commitment to inclusive employment, responsive social protection, and the dignity and well-being of persons with disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10758
title: AN ACT EXTENDING THE SIX PERCENT REAL PROPERTY TAX CAPPING PERIOD AND THE TAX AMNESTY PERIOD TO FOUR YEARS UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12001, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "REAL PROPERTY VALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REFORM ACT", AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 29 AND 30 THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12001, also known as the Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act (RPVARA), was borne out of the need to optimize the government’s real property tax collection. Aside from promoting a nationally consistent real property valuation based on international standards and the market value as single base for tax assessment, it also mandates the development and maintenance of a comprehensive, up-to-date electronic database of real property transactions. Notably, it improves revenue generation at the local level, further enhancing local government units’ capacity to pursue projects and programs which are responsive to the needs of their constituents. The transition period, however, provided in the RPVARA may be too short. Concerns have been raised regarding the need to further study its impacts beyond property valuation, such as its possible effects on housing affordability, economic competitiveness, and property ownership, to name a few. With the transition period having already lapsed, the policy status quo could do more harm than good. Under the directive of President Marcos Jr. in his fourth Legislative-Executive Development Advisory Council (LEDAC) to ease the financial burden of the public, including private property owners and businesses, this measure proposes to extend the six percent real property tax capping period and the tax amnesty period to four years, to avoid the abrupt additional property costs and allow for smoother and gradual transition to the new valuation system. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFREDO “ALBEE” B. label: HB 10759
title: AN ACT PROMOTING AND SAFEGUARDING THE INSTALLATION AND OPERATION OF BEHIND-THE-METER ELECTRICITY GENERATION AND ENERGY STORAGE SYSTEMS FOR PERSONAL CONSUMPTION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Sariling Kuryente Act”. SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is the policy of the State to ensure the reliable, secure, affordable and environmentally sustainable supply of electricity, to accelerate the development of renewable energy resources, and to protect the interest of the consuming public. SEC. 3. Definitions. — For purposes of this Act: (a) “Behind-the-meter system” refers to a generation facility, an energy storage facility, or both, located on the premises of an end-user and connected on the end-user’s side of the metering point. (b) “Distribution utility” refers to any electric distribution utility as defined in Republic Act No. 9136, including electric cooperatives. (c) “Export-limiting device” refers to equipment, certified under standards recognized by the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), that prevents the flow of electricity from a behind-the-meter system into the distribution system, including reverse-power relays, zero-export controllers and equivalent means. (d) “Non-exporting system” refers to a behind-the-meter system equipped with a certified export-limiting device.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cumulative net-metered capacity stood at 157 megawatts as of May 2025, the yield of twelve years of the programme. Independent analysis of market generation data suggests that roughly 600 megawatts of rooftop solar were added in the twelve months to April 2026 alone. Households are now installing generation faster than the approval system can process it, and the greater part of that capacity sits outside the statutory scheme altogether. The framework no longer describes the industry it governs. This bill closes that gap through a single classification rule, drawn from the Electric Power Industry Reform Act, which ties regulatory obligation to sale into the market: an end-user who generates power for personal consumption is not a generation company. The operative architecture follows from that premise. Qualified non-exporting systems require no prior approval and no certificate of compliance. Distribution utilities may not demand technical studies, meter replacement, agreements or added charges. Notification follows installation rather than preceding it. And homeowners' associations, developers and property managers may not prohibit installations on property the end-user owns or exclusively controls. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 10760
title: AN ACT IMPOSING SAFETY-BY-DESIGN AND AGE ASSURANCE DUTIES ON SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORM PROVIDERS WITH RESPECT TO CHILD USERS, ESTABLISHING A MINIMUM AGE FOR SOCIAL MEDIA ACCOUNTS, PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “Social Media Safety for Children Act”. SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is the policy of the State to promote and protect the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual and social well-being of the youth, and to defend the right of children to special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation and other conditions prejudicial to their development. SEC. 3. Definitions. — For purposes of this Act: (a) “Child” or “minor” refers to a person below eighteen (18) years of age.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7610, Republic Act No. 10175, and Republic Act No. 11930 penalize the abuse and exploitation of children online after it has occurred. No existing Philippine statute regulates the conditions that produce the encounter. A platform is under no legal obligation to determine whether its user is a child, to apply protective default settings to that child's account, or to withhold engagement-maximizing recommendation systems from a minor. This bill addresses that specific gap and does not extend beyond it. This bill imposes safety-by-design obligations on every account a platform knows or ought reasonably to know belongs to a minor, independently of the minimum age requirement. The obligations therefore apply to children who evade the age requirement, and to children who migrate to smaller services with weaker moderation and no Philippine presence. It places the obligation and the penalty on the covered platform. No penalty attaches to a child or to a parent, and parental consent cannot be used to waive the minimum age. This conforms the bill to Republic Act No. 9344, which prohibits the imposition of penalties on minors for status offences, and follows the Australian scheme in force since 10 December 2025. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 10761
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, INSTITUTIONALIZING COORDINATED EDUCATION AND WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT GOVERNANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Philippine education has long relied on a tri-focalized structure, with the Department of Education (DepEd), Commission on Higher Education (CHED), and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) exercising distinct statutory mandates. While specialization has its virtues, without sustained coordination, it can also lead to fragmentation. This concern lies at the heart of the findings of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). In its Final Report Turning Point: A Decade of Necessary Reforms1, EDCOM II described a systemic “proficiency collapse.” Only 30.5% of Grade 3 students meet proficiency standards. This low baseline declines sharply to 0.40% by Grade 12.2 The Philippine Statistics Authority likewise reported that while 93.1% of Filipinos aged 10 to 64 possess basic literacy, only 70.8% are functionally literate3, revealing a substantial gap between the ability to read words and the ability to understand and use information. This documented learning crisis cannot be solved through isolated reforms within individual agencies. Early learning affects later achievement; teacher preparation affects classroom instruction; curriculum must connect with further education and training; qualifications must translate across learning pathways; and education itself must ultimately respond to the skills Filipinos need to participate meaningfully in society and the economy. EDCOM II found that while tri-focalization brought greater focus to the respective education subsectors, it did not produce corresponding improvements in learning outcomes.4 Research found no statistically significant improvement in education 1 Available at https://edcom2.gov.ph/media/2026/01/EDCOM-II-Y03-for-web-012626_final.pdf 2 Student proficiency rates plunge from 30% in Grade 3 to 0.47% in Grade 12, SECOND CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON EDUCATION, 16 January 2026, available at https://edcom2.gov.ph/student-proficiency-rates-plunge-from-30-in-grade-3-to-0-47-in-grade-12/ 3 For every 10 Filipinos, 9 have Basic Literacy, while 7 have Functional Literacy, PHILIPPINE STATISTICS AUTHORITY, 4 April 2025, available at https://psa.gov.ph/content/every-10-filipinos-9-have-basic-literacy-while-7-have-functional-literacy 4 Fixing the Foundations: A matter of national survival, EDCOM II Year Two Report, SECOND CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON EDUCATION, 2025, available at https://edcom2.gov.ph/media/2025/01/EDCOM-2-Year-2-Report-Fixing-the-Foundations-2025.pdf outcomes attributable to tri-focalization and underscored the need for stronger coordination and oversight. The problem is not the absence of coordinating bodies. It is the absence of a permanent center of coordination with sufficient authority and continuity to make policies, plans, data, investments, and reforms pull in the same direction. The Executive Branch has already recognized this need through the creation of the Education and Workforce Development Group under Administrative Order No. 36 (s. 2025). This bill seeks to institutionalize that whole-of-government approach through the creation of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) under the Office of the President, so that education reform does not depend on temporary administrative arrangements or begin anew with every change in leadership. Anchored on the National Education and Workforce Development Plan 2026– 2035, the NCCE shall serve as the primary mechanism for strategic coordination, policy alignment, convergence planning, and monitoring of education and workforce development reforms. It shall promote coherent policies across the education continuum, strengthen human resource and labor market planning, facilitate seamless learner pathways and lifelong learning, improve education-to-employment linkages, coordinate complementary programs, and advance secure and interoperable education and workforce data. This measure does not create another bureaucratic layer. It favors the use of existing mechanisms, provides for the rationalization of overlapping bodies, and succeeds to the coordinating functions of the existing Education and Workforce Development Group. The answer to fragmented government is not necessarily more government, but government that works together. Education is a continuum—from the first word a child learns to read to the skills a young person carries into work and adult life. Government should govern it with the same continuity. Our education system must learn to work as one system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A LANDSCAPE-LEVEL FRAMEWORK FOR THE CONSERVATION, PROTECTION, RESTORATION, CLIMATE RESILIENCE, AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT OF THE SIERRA MADRE MOUNTAIN RANGE, CREATING THE SIERRA MADRE CONSERVATION AND MANAGEMENT AUTHORITY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A mountain range stretching more for than 540 kilometers across ten provinces1 cannot be effectively managed one permit, one municipality, or one agency at a time. The Sierra Madre is the longest mountain range in the Philippines and one of Luzon’s most important ecological systems. Extending from Cagayan to Quezon, it contains forests, watersheds, headwaters, river systems, wildlife habitats, ancestral domains, settlements, agricultural areas, and infrastructure that cut across political and administrative boundaries. Its ecological value is substantial and increasingly under pressure. A satellite- based study reported that about half of the Philippines’ surviving old-growth forest is located in the Sierra Madre, while forest gains from 2001 to 2018 were offset by continuing losses of open and closed forests.2 More recent research in General Nakar, Quezon and Rodriguez, Rizal likewise documented declining forest cover from 2016 to 2022 and identified kaingin, infrastructure expansion, timber poaching, small-scale mining, charcoal production, and natural hazards among the reported pressures on forests.3 The stakes are especially concrete in Bulacan. The Angat Watershed, situated at the southern end of the Sierra Madre, supports significant biodiversity and performs functions vital to water security, agriculture, energy, and downstream communities. Studies in Norzagaray and Doña Remedios Trinidad have documented considerable amphibian, reptile, and bird diversity, including Philippine endemic and threatened species. 4 The Angat water system, meanwhile, supplies more than 90% of Metro Manila’s 1 Sierra Madre: Mountain Range of Resilience, CLIMATE CHANGE COMMISSION, 26 September 2024, available at https://climate.gov.ph/news/934 Perez, et. al., Reforestation and Deforestation in Northern Luzon, Philippines: Critical Issues as Observed from Space, FOREST (2020), available at https://www.mdpi.com/1999-4907/11/10/1071 3 Israel, et. al., Deforestation and Forest Degradation Analysis of Southern Sierra Madre, Philippines Using Google Earth Engine and Community Mapping, INTERNATIONAL ARCHIVES OF THE PHOTOGRAMMETRY, REMOTE SENSING AND SPATIAL INFORMATION SCIENCES (2023), available at https://isprs- archives.copernicus.org/articles/XLVIII-4-W8-2023/313/2024/isprs-archives-XLVIII-4-W8-2023-313-2024.pdf 4 McLeod, et. al., Amphibians and Reptiles of Luzon Island, V: The Herpetofauna of Angat Dam Watershed, Bulacan Province, Luzon Island, Philippines, ASIAN HERPETOLOGICAL RESEARCH (2011), available at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/221673728_Amphibians_and_Reptiles_of_Luzon_Island_V_The_Herpetofauna_of_Angat_Dam_Waters hed_Bulacan_Province_Luzon_Island_Philippines domestic water requirements, supports irrigation in thousands of hectares of farmland, generates hydropower, and contributes to flood management.5 The Sierra Madre is also frequently described as Luzon’s natural defense against tropical cyclones. Scientific studies found that the mountain range influences wind and rainfall patterns, but its effects vary depending on location and storm conditions.6 Its protection need not rest on the claim that it stops every storm. Its forests, watersheds, biodiversity, slopes, and ecological connectivity already provide compelling reasons for responsible management. The challenge is that these ecological systems are interconnected, while government authority and management over them is necessarily divided. Protected areas have their own statutory management bodies. The Department of Environment and Natural Resources exercises authority over forests and natural resources. Local government units perform land-use and development functions. Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples possess constitutionally and statutorily protected rights over ancestral domains and ancestral lands. Other agencies exercise mandates involving infrastructure, agriculture, energy, water resources, human settlements, and national development planning. These institutions perform necessary functions, but no single one is positioned to manage the Sierra Madre as an interconnected landscape. A watershed may span several municipalities. A biodiversity corridor may extend beyond protected-area boundaries. Forest degradation upstream may affect communities downstream. Several projects that appear manageable when evaluated individually may, taken together, impose significant pressure on the same watershed or ecological corridor. Environmental impacts do not cease to be cumulative simply because permits are issued separately. This bill addresses that governance gap by establishing the Sierra Madre Management Area (SMMA) as a common framework for integrated, landscape-level planning and management. It adopts differentiated management based on ecological conditions and lawful existing uses. Areas of exceptional ecological, biological, hydrological, or disaster-risk significance may be delineated as Core Conservation Areas and accorded heightened protection. label: HB 10763
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING THE FINANCIAL PROTECTION OF PUBLIC ASSETS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND VULNERABLE SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Disasters are unpredictable in timing, but they are hardly unexpected in the Philippines. We face recurring typhoons, floods, earthquakes, and other hazards that destroy public assets, disrupt livelihoods, interrupt essential services, and impose substantial fiscal costs. This recurring exposure makes financial preparedness as necessary as operational preparedness. The World Bank estimates that the country is expected to incur, on average, about US$3.5 billion in annual asset losses from typhoons and earthquakes alone.1 The experience of Super Typhoon Yolanda is a stark reminder of the scale involved: damages and losses were estimated at US$12.9 billion, equivalent to about 4.7% of the country’s 2013 gross domestic product.2 The country already employs contingency funds, contingent credit, sovereign insurance, and other disaster-financing instruments. In 2019, for example, the World Bank issued catastrophe bonds providing the Philippines up to US$225 million in protection against earthquake and tropical cyclone risks, with payouts tied to predefined disaster parameters.3 These instruments demonstrate that disaster risk can be planned for, priced, pooled, and transferred before a calamity occurs. Gaps, however, remain. In 2025, the Department of Finance, while updating the national DRFI Strategy, acknowledged the continuing need for cost-effective and accessible financial protection for vulnerable people and communities and identified greater use of prearranged finance, parametric insurance, microinsurance, and anticipatory financing as areas for further development.4 1 Signer, B.L. and Poulter, R., Disaster risk insurance: 5 insights from the Philippines, WORLD BANK BLOGS, 01 December 2021, available at https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/climatechange/disaster-risk-insurance-5-insights-philippines 2 The Philippines: Transferring the Cost of Severe Natural Disasters to Capital Markets, WORLD BANK GROUP, 13 April 2020, available at https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2020/04/09/the-philippines-transferring-the-cost-of-severe-natural-disasters-to-capital-markets. 3 World Bank Catastrophe Bond Transaction Insures the Republic of Philippines against Natural Disaster-related Losses Up to US$225 million, WORLD BANK GROUP, 24 November 2019, available at https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2019/11/25/world-bank-catastrophe-bond-transaction- insures-the-republic-of-philippines-against-natural-disaster-related-losses-up-to-usd225-million 4 DOF leads establishment of enhanced climate-disaster risk finance & insurance mechanisms for the PH, DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE, 28 August 2025, available at https://www.dof.gov.ph/dof-leads-establishment-of-enhanced-climate-disaster-risk-finance-insurance-mechanisms-for-the-ph/ This bill institutionalizes a Philippine Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Framework anchored on risk reduction, risk layering, prearranged and anticipatory financing, fiscal sustainability, and transparency. Instead of relying on a single source of financing for every disaster, the measure matches appropriate financing instruments to different levels of risk, from regular appropriations and contingency resources, to contingent financing and insurance, to parametric and catastrophe-linked arrangements for more severe risks. The measure also strengthens the National Asset Registry System, protects critical public assets, supports highly exposed and financially constrained local governments, and promotes financial protection for vulnerable and productive sectors. It does so principally through existing institutions, while requiring sound fiscal management, timely claims processing, accountability, and proper use of disaster-financing proceeds. The proposed Disaster Risk Financing Insurance Act forms part of the Common Legislative Agenda of the Executive and Legislative branches for the Twentieth Congress, reflecting a shared policy objective to provide stronger financial safeguards against calamities. Its passage would help turn disaster financing from an exercise in post- calamity improvisation into a deliberate system of preparedness, protection, and fiscal resilience. We may not know when the next disaster will strike. But with sound planning, we will be able to know how to finance the response, protect essential services, and help our communities recover. Disasters may remain unpredictable, but our financial preparedness should not. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10764
title: AN ACT DECLARING THE BOCAUE PAGODA FESTIVAL, ALSO KNOWN AS “PAGODA SA WAWA,” AS THE OFFICIAL CULTURAL FESTIVAL OF THE MUNICIPALITY OF BOCAUE, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, AND A MAJOR TOURIST ATTRACTION, PROVIDING FOR ITS DEVELOPMENT, PROMOTION, PRESERVATION, AND SAFE CONDUCT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Some traditions survive because they are written in books. Others survive because people continue to live them. For generations, the people of Bocaue have gathered along the river for the Pagoda Festival, or “Pagoda sa Wawa”, a celebration inseparable from the town’s history, identity, and devotion to the Holy Cross of Wawa. The pagoda, the Festival’s most enduring image, not only carries participants, but also memories, from one generation of Bocaueños to the next. A tradition of such consequence deserves more than passing recognition. It deserves preservation that is thoughtful, promotion that is responsible, and celebration that is safe. This bill seeks to declared the Bocaue Pagoda Festival as the Official Cultural Festival of the Municipality of Bocaue and a Major Tourist Attraction. It aims to recognize the Festival for its legitimate secular significance as cultural heritage, as living local history, as a source of tourism and livelihood, and as an important public gathering requiring proper planning and protection. Accordingly, this measure provides for the sustainable development and promotion of the Festival, the documentation and safeguarding of its traditions, and the preservation of its historical narrative. It brings together the appropriate expertise of the Department of Tourism and the Tourism Promotions Board in tourism development; the National Commission for Culture and the Arts in cultural heritage; and the National Historical Commission of the Philippines in historical research, documentation, and interpretation. Considering that the Pagoda Festival’s defining feature is that its procession takes place on water, this bill requires an annual Festival Safety and Fluvial Procession Management Plan, including vessel inspection and applicable clearances, enforceable passenger and load limits, adequate life-saving equipment, controlled boarding, rescue and medical capability, unified incident command, and a documented go/no-go safety determination before the procession begins. The Bocaue River has long carried one of Bulacan’s most distinctive traditions. As the pagoda continues to carry the memory and devotion of generations, this measure ensures that the tradition be preserved with fidelity, promoted with dignity, and celebrated with every reasonable safeguard for the lives entrusted to it. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10765
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE DIGITAL INCLUSION OF SENIOR CITIZENS, ENSURING ACCESS TO ASSISTED DIGITAL SUPPORT AND ESSENTIAL SERVICES, ESTABLISHING STANDARDS FOR SENIOR-FRIENDLY DIGITAL SERVICES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE More and more public and private services are moving from the counter to the screen. For many, this means greater convenience. For some senior citizens, however, it can also mean difficulty accessing government services, financial transactions, transportation, health services, and even benefits already granted by law. This challenge will only become more significant as the country ages. The 2024 Census of Population recorded 11.42 million senior citizens, or 10.2% of the household population, up from 8.5% in 2020.1 This demographic shift is unfolding alongside the rapid digitalization of essential services, even as many older Filipinos continue to face barriers in navigating digital technologies. The Philippine Institute for Development Studies has reported that digital literacy is particularly low among persons aged 65 years and above.2 Recognizing that digitalization must remain inclusive, Republic Act No. 12254, or the “E-Governance Act,” requires the continued availability of government services to persons without internet access and provides for alternative modes of delivery. The proposed Digital Inclusion for Seniors Act builds on this principle by addressing the particular needs of senior citizens as more public and essential services move online. The proposed measure ensures reasonable assisted digital support in government and essential services; promotes senior-friendly digital design; protects access to statutory senior citizen benefits in online transactions; and allows the use of digital identification without making a smartphone, application, or electronic credential the exclusive means of proving eligibility. The bill recognizes that difficulty with technology does not mean incapacity. A 1 Age and Sex Distribution in the Philippine Population (2024 Census of Population), PHILIPPINE STATISTICS AUTHORITY, 17 July 2026, available at https://psa.gov.ph/content/age-and-sex-distribution-philippine-population-2024-census-population 2 Fact Friday on Digital Literacy Skills of Filipinos, PHILIPPINE INSTITUTE FOR DEVELOPMENT STUDIES, 17 December 2021, available at https://www.pids.gov.ph/details/fact-friday-on-digital-literacy-skills-of-filipinos senior citizen may seek assistance from a family member, caregiver, or chosen support person without surrendering the right to decide, consent, or transact independently. Digital transformation should make life easier, not place another barrier between citizens and the services to which they are entitled. The queue may be moving from the counter to the screen, but no senior citizen should be left behind when it does. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10766
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING VOTER EDUCATION IN THE JUNIOR AND SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL CURRICULA
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The strength of any democracy rests upon an informed and discerning electorate. Each election cycle, millions of young Filipinos become eligible voters, and that is why it is urgent and imperative to prepare them for this life-changing civic participation. The rise of digital platforms has transformed the way Filipinos receive political information. Like a double-edged sword, technology has widened access to public discourse but has also exposed citizens, particularly the youth, to misinformation, disinformation, historical distortion, and political propaganda disseminated through social media and other online platforms. As stated in a research published in 20201, the Philippines has been in a “post-truth era,” wherein public opinion is often shaped less by verified facts and more by emotionally charged narratives, viral content, and algorithm-driven information consumption2. This development poses serious risks to democratic participation and electoral integrity. This phenomenon in the Philippines demonstrates the growing influence of digital misinformation in shaping political behavior. Numerous studies and reports3 identified the country as highly vulnerable to organized online disinformation campaigns, including the use of troll networks, fake accounts, and coordinated propaganda to manipulate public opinion and electoral discourse. More recently, researchers documented the continuing proliferation of fake and coordinated online activities surrounding the Philippine elections, emphasizing the need to strengthen citizens’ capacity to critically assess political information. 1 Post-truth era in the Philippines? Centeno, Kevin Stephon. 2020. Retrieved https://www.academia.edu/42741100/Post_truth_era_in_the_Philippines 2 https://www.academia.edu/42741100/Post_truth_era_in_the_Philippines 3 Democracy under Threat: Post-Truth Politics and Democracy in the Philippines.Sacramento et. al.Vol. 28. No. 2 (2025):July-December.Thammasat Review.Retrieved from https://sc01.tci-thaijo.org/index.php/tureview/article/view/241283 This concern has been really alarming, considering the growing electoral influence of the youth. Data show that young voters comprise a significant portion of the Philippine voting population, with millions of newly registered voters belonging to the youth demographic4. In 2021, Millennials and Generation Z were the majority of registered voters--proof that they are one of the most decisive forces in shaping the country’s future5. Despite the importance of civic participation, voter education among young Filipinos remains largely limited to election-period campaigns or shallow discussions in classrooms. Many first-time voters enter the electoral process without a clear understanding of democratic institutions, electoral systems, governance, media literacy, or the responsibilities accompanying the right to suffrage. This measure seeks to institutionalize voter education in the Junior High School and Senior High School curricula to cultivate politically aware, media- literate, and critically thinking Filipino citizens. By integrating age-appropriate lessons on democratic participation, electoral processes, responsible citizenship, fact- checking, digital literacy, and critical evaluation of political information, students will be better equipped to distinguish truth from propaganda and make informed electoral choices. More importantly, this bill recognizes that voting is not merely a constitutional right but a solemn civic responsibility. Schools must help prepare future voters not only to participate in elections, but to exercise discernment, resist manipulation, and uphold democratic values. Sa panahong mabilis ang pagkalat ng mga propaganda, tahasang pagsisinungaling at pagbabaluktot sa katotohanan at kasaysayan, mariin nating isinusulong na maturuan ang Kabataan na maging mapanuri, maalam, kritikal, at responsableng mamamayan ng ating bansa sa pamamagitan ng pagboto nang tama. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. JC ABALOS Representative 4Ps Partylist 4 Comelec logs 4M new voters aged 28 to 21. title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 20 AND 22 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11215, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “NATIONAL INTEGRATED CANCER CONTROL ACT (NICCA),” TO EXPAND THE ALLOWABLE USE OF THE CANCER ASSISTANCE FUND TO INCLUDE THE CONSTRUCTION, EXPANSION, UPGRADING, AND EQUIPPING OF REGIONAL CANCER CENTERS, PROVIDING FOR ITS BUDGETARY CLASSIFICATION, AND RECOGNIZING REGIONAL CANCER CENTERS AS A SOCIAL PROTECTION MECHANISM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cancer remains one of the most serious public health challenges faced by the Philippines. According to the 2022 GLOBOCAN estimates of the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC)1, the Philippines recorded an estimated 188,976 new cancer cases and 113,369 cancer deaths in 2022, with approximately 466,012 five-year prevalent cancer cases. Breast cancer was the most commonly diagnosed cancer among Filipino women, with an age- standardized incidence rate (ASIR) of 60.34 per 100,000, the second-highest rate in Southeast Asia after Singapore (72.61 per 100,000). Among Filipino men, lung cancer was the most commonly diagnosed cancer, while lung cancer was also the leading cause of cancer death when both sexes were considered together. Among Filipino men, lung cancer had an age- standardized mortality rate (ASMR) of 33.59 per 100,000— the highest male lung-cancer mortality rate among the Southeast Asian countries included in the comparison2. These figures underscore not only the scale of the disease burden but also the urgency of ensuring that Filipinos, regardless of where they live, can access timely diagnosis and treatment. In 2019, Republic Act (RA) No. 11215, otherwise known as the National Integrated Cancer Control Act (NICCA), was a landmark law that established the Philippine Cancer Center. This mandated the creation of regional and 1 International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), GLOBOCAN 2022 Philippines Country Fact Sheet, Global Cancer Observatory, World Health Organization. 2 Bhoo-Pathy, N., et al., "Cancer incidence and mortality estimates in 2022 in southeast Asia: a comparative analysis," The Lancet Oncology, 2025. 1 specialty cancer centers outside Metro Manila, and created the Cancer Assistance Fund (CAF) to help cover the cost of cancer medicines, treatment, and care. However, more than five years since its enactment, access to cancer care remains heavily concentrated in the National Capital Region (NCR). Of the 11 facilities currently recognized under the Network of DOH-Designated Advanced Comprehensive Cancer Centers, six are located in Metro Manila alone, while only five are distributed across the rest of Luzon, the Visayas, and Mindanao combined3. This means that patients from many regions must still travel, often at great financial and emotional cost, to Metro Manila or to another distant urban center simply to receive a diagnosis, undergo chemotherapy or radiotherapy, or access follow-up care. This travel burden is not merely an inconvenience. Studies4 on the economic impact of cancer in Southeast Asia have documented that a significant share of patients and their families face catastrophic health expenditure with costs exceeding a large portion of household income. This is only within 12 months of a cancer diagnosis, a burden that is compounded by transportation, lodging, and lost income when patients must seek treatment far from home. For indigent and geographically isolated patients, this often means delayed treatment, abandonment of care, or, in the worst cases, forgoing treatment altogether. While the CAF under RA No. 11215 already provides financial assistance for the direct cost of cancer treatment, the law as currently written does not clearly authorize the use of the Fund for the construction, expansion, upgrading, and equipping of the very regional cancer centers that RA 11215 itself mandated to be established. This has left the expansion of regional cancer care infrastructure dependent on ad hoc appropriations, with no dedicated, sustained, and properly classified funding stream for capital investment in these facilities. This bill, to be known as the "Cancer Patients' Welfare Act," seeks to bridge this gap by: 1. Expanding the allowable use of the Cancer Assistance Fund to explicitly include the construction, expansion, upgrading, and equipping of regional cancer centers, by splitting the Fund into two distinct windows: a Treatment Assistance Window for direct patient care costs, and a new Infrastructure Development Window 3 Philippine Cancer Center (philcancercenter.gov.ph), Network of DOH-Designated Cancer Centers. 4 Thomas, et al., J Oncol Res Treat 2025.Cancer Spending, Economic Burden and its Effect on the Household Welfare.Journal of Oncology Research and Treatment 2 dedicated to capital projects, with priority given to regions that currently have no comprehensive cancer care facility; 2. Establishing clear, transparent prioritization criteria for selecting sites for infrastructure development, based on objective factors such as cancer incidence and mortality data from the national cancer registry, population size, geographic accessibility, existing health system readiness, and local government support; 3. Providing for proper budgetary classification of the Fund, treating the Infrastructure Development Window as Capital Outlay separate from Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses, while creating a distinct Treatment, Assistance, Medicines, and Procedures (TAMP) Sub-Window to ring-fence funds intended directly for patient treatment and medicines from administrative and operating costs; and allowing multi-year obligational authority so that infrastructure projects are not derailed by the annual character of government appropriations; and 4. Formally recognizing regional cancer centers as a social protection mechanism under Section 22 of RA No. 11215, in the same manner as PhilHealth, the Malasakit Program, and other assistance mechanisms, in acknowledgment of the fact that a regional cancer center built close to where patients live directly reduces the travel, lodging, and lost-income burden that keeps many Filipinos from completing life-saving treatment. By ensuring that funding exists not only for treatment but also for building the facilities where that treatment is delivered, this bill takes a concrete step toward the equitable, nationwide access to cancer care envisioned under RA No. 11215 and the Universal Health C

label: HB 10771
title: AN ACT GRANTING MENSTRUAL LEAVE TO FEMALE EMPLOYEES, PROVIDING BENEFITS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 14 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the State shall protect working women by providing safe and healthful working conditions, taking into account their maternal functions, and such facilities and opportunities that will enhance their welfare and enable them to realize their full potential in the service of the nation. As of 2023, the labor force participation rate of women in the Philippines was at 53. 4% which was lower than the 74.7% recorded for men.1 Despite this, it cannot be overlooked that women still significantly contribute to the growth of the Philippine economy. The participation of women in the workforce also promotes workplace diversity, employee retention, and organizational development. However, women may experience health-related setbacks, including menstrual pain and other menstrual-related medical conditions, which may affect their ability to perform their work. In a study conducted in July and August 2022, involving 1,800 Spanish women, 72.6% reported experiencing menstrual pain, 45.9% required medication, and 34.3% reported that they had been unable to attend work activities or had requested sick leave because of menstrual-related discomfort.2 _________________ 1 Fact Sheet on Filipino Women and Men, October 2023. Available at https://pcw.gov.ph/assets/files/2025/12/2023-Fact-Sheet-on- Filipino-Women-and-Men.pdf 2 The effect of menstrual pain and symptoms on activities of daily living and on work absenteeism: A cross-sectional study. Available at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/373470835_The_effect_of_menstrual_pain_and_symptoms_on_activities_of_daily_livi ng_and_on_work_absenteeism_A_cross-sectional_study This proposed legislation seeks to grant female employees a maximum of three (3) days menstrual leave per month. The leave shall be non-cumulative, non-convertible to cash, and shall not be used as ground for demotion or termination, reduction of benefits, or non-renewal of contract. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10772
title: AN ACT GRANTING ADDITIONAL BENEFITS TO QUALIFIED BENEFICIARIES OF TEACHERS IN PUBLIC EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS WHO DIE BY REASON OF, OR IN CONNECTION WITH, THE PERFORMANCE OF THEIR OFFICIAL FUNCTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE There have been several reported incidents of violence in schools in which teachers have been injured and, in some cases, have died by reason of, or in connection with, the performance of their official functions. It is the policy of the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and to take appropriate steps to make education accessible to all. Consistent with this policy, the State must also provide reasonable assistance to the families and qualified beneficiaries of teachers in public educational institutions who die by reason of, or in connection with, the performance of their official functions. For purposes of this measure, teachers in public educational institutions include teachers in public elementary and secondary schools, local universities and colleges, and state universities and colleges. These teachers devote their time, knowledge, and service to educating the country’s future generations. Their functions extend beyond classroom instruction and may include the supervision and protection of students, the implementation of officially authorized school activities, service in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, and the performance of election-related duties. On October 24, 2010, Lorna Pulalon, a Grade 2 teacher at the Talisayan Elementary School, reportedly died while shielding her students during a stabbing incident at the school. Reports further indicate that she was a breadwinner of her family. This incident illustrates the risks that teachers may face while performing their duty to protect and educate their students. In July 2026, another teacher was reportedly assaulted by two minor students at Elizalde National High School in Maco, Davao de Oro, allegedly after reprimanding them for wearing earrings in violation of school policy. The teacher reportedly died two days after the assault. Many other teachers, particularly those assigned to geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDA), literally have to walk miles and cross perilous rivers to reach what the Department of Education calls the “last mile schools”. They endure the hardship of working away from their families and remote areas for months just to fulfill their duties and responsibilities as educators. In fact, a documentary entitled “Hanggang Huling Milya” reportedly featured teachers of Pulong Mindanao Elementary School in Sta. Maria, Laguna, who walk approximately forty-five minutes to one hour each day and cross nine rivers just to reach school. The same feature reportedly stated that, in 2023, 9,225 out of approximately 47,000 schools nationwide were classified as last-mile schools. It further reported that such school served fewer than 100 learners and that some teachers were required to adopt a multigrade teaching arrangement, in which learners from different grade levels are taught simultaneously. Teachers have also been designated to serve as poll workers or members of electoral boards during elections. In performing these functions, they undertake additional public responsibilities and may be exposed to risks beyond those ordinarily associated with classroom teaching. The proposed measure seeks to grant a separate and additional financial benefit to the qualified beneficiaries of teachers in public educational institutions who die by reason of, or in connection with, the performance of their official functions. The proposed benefit shall be without prejudice to survivorship, retirement, insurance, employees’ compensation, death, scholarship, and other benefits available under existing laws. By providing immediate financial and educational assistance, this measure recognizes the sacrifices of teachers and assists their families when the teachers’ public service results in death. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10774
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF BARANGAY HEALTH WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State has the primary responsibility for people's right to health. It is a declared policy of the State under Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution to protect and promote the right to health of the people and to instill health consciousness among them. It is further guaranteed under Article XIII, Section 11 stating that “The State shall “adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost. There shall be priority for the needs of the under-privileged, sick, elderly, disabled, women, and children. The State shall also endeavor to provide free medical care to paupers.” In the Philippines, even before the 1978 Alma Ata Primary Health Care Declaration, many non-government organizations (NGOs) had taken the lead in training community health workers and providing health services in the communities. The government later on joined the bandwagon to train barangay health workers (BHWs). 1 Community health workers and/or BHWs are an integral part of health service provision at the community level as they provide basic health care services to the community. They provide ﬁrst aid, collect vital statistics, maintain records, and make 1 Tan, M. “‘Health for All’ (replay).” Inquirer.net, 5 April 2019. Retrieved from https://opinion.inquirer.net/120569/health-for-all-replay 1 reports; participate in community meetings’ provide assistance to health center activities like nutrition education, monitoring and feeding; immunization education, monitoring, and dispensing family planning services, sanitation and hygiene promotion and education, and disaster relief and rehabilitation, among others. BHWs are among the front-liners in primary health care as they provide assistance and support to physicians, dentists, nutritionists, public health nurses, and midwives. Their role is indispensable to community health and wellness. Recognizing the important role of BHWs in primary health care, Republic Act 7883 Barangay Health Workers’ Benefits and Incentives Act of 1995 was passed into law granting benefits and incentives to accredited barangay health workers. RA 7883 provided incentives and benefits to BHWs including hazard allowance, subsistence allowance, training and education and career enrichment programs, civil service eligibility, free legal services, and preferential access to loan. Despite the passage into law of RA 7883, the issues and concerns besetting the BHWs and the barangay level health care persisted. The country still does not have enough BHWs. The Department of Health (DOH) admitted in 2019 that the present number of BHWs at 207,392 are not enough for the needs of the people and that we need 802,422 more. According to 2024 Field Health Services Information System (FHSIS),2 there are 285,530 active BHWs, wherein majority were hired by local government units. The DOH-Bureau of Local Health Systems and Development Maria Lourdes Gajitos claimed that it is not easy to fill the discrepancy because BHW work is "voluntary".3 But this “voluntary” nature of BHWs is used as a pretext to exploit them and grossly take them for granted. Like most of the barangay folks they serve, BHWs suffer from poor economic conditions, inadequate health services and facilities, and being subjected to political maneuverings of local politicians. Many BHWs have no regular jobs and rely on their allowances as BHW. But their allowances vary significantly, ranging from ₱1,000 to ₱12,000 per month depending on the LGU. Some barangay health workers need to slog through the ﬁelds just to conduct house-to-house visits in some areas, many have to shell out their own money for food, 2 “CY 2024 Field Health Services Information System (FHSIS) Annual Report.” Department of Health- Monitoring & Evaluation Division, 2023. Retrieved from https://drive.google.com/file/d/1c5tGpU9gyd7irdxbfhPZ6axiSic7DSNQ/view?usp=drivesdk 3 Hernandez, Z. “Barangay health workers sa bansa kulang pa: DOH.” ABS-CBN, 21 April 2019. Retrieved from https://www.abs-cbn.com/business/04/21/19/barangay-health-workers-sa-bansa-kulang-pa-doh 2 travel and reproduction of forms; some are exposed to many health and hazard risks while doing their tasks, and some lack up to date awareness on emerging health issues. Their services need not be at the expense of the depreciation of their labor for our poor communities. Since BHWs are accredited, registered and maintained by local health boards, they are at the mercy of LGUs. Some “lucky” BHWs get more allowances and benefits and are given all the support by their LGUs. Yet some others get inadequate allowances and support, and worse removed or forced to resign if another local official is elected. BHWs are being used by many local executives for their political and electoral campaigns. If not for the strong spirit of volunteerism and patriotism of many BHWs, many would have left this voluntary work. Yet for all their willingness to help and serve, they are calling for recognition, and support from the government. This Bill seeks to give our barangay health workers the due recognition that they deserve by granting them beneﬁts package, as well as protection from discrimination and undue dismissal and free education and training programs for barangay health workers. Such would not only encourage more people to become BHWs but would also contribute to the improvement of community health services and better people’s health. This Bill was first filed by Bayan Muna Reps. Ferdinand Gaite, Carlos Zarate, Eufemia Cullamat, ACT Teachers Rep. France Castro, Gabriela Women’s Party Rep. Arlene Brosas and Kabataan Partylist Rep. Sarah Elago during the 18th Congress as HB 6562, which was substituted by HB 10699 and was passed on third reading. The Makabayan Bloc refiled this Bill in the 19th Congress. The immediate passage of this Bill, thus, is earnestly sought.

label: HB 10781
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF YOUNG FARMERS AND FISHERFOLK
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines faces a pressing generational challenge in agriculture: the people responsible for producing the country's food are increasingly older, while relatively few young Filipinos are entering or remaining in farming. The 2022 Census of Agriculture and Fisheries recorded 7.72 million agricultural operators, with a median age of 49.7 years; only 8.9 percent were between 15 and 29 years old, while 49.3 percent were aged 50 years and above.1 The same demographic concern is evident in fisheries, where the 2022 Census recorded 921,096 fishing operators with a median age of about 43.7 years, while the number of younger fishing operators has declined in several regions.2 These figures demonstrate the need for a deliberate national policy that makes farming and fishing viable, dignified, and sustainable livelihoods for the next generation. The challenge is not merely one of succession but also one of poverty and unequal access to economic opportunities. In 2023, farmers had a poverty incidence of 27.0 percent while fisherfolk had a poverty incidence of 27.4 percent, among the highest recorded poverty incidences across the basic sectors monitored by the Philippine Statistics Authority.3 At the same time, agriculture, 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, 2022 Census of Agriculture and Fisheries (Final Results): Agricultural Households and Operators, April 8, 2026. 2 Philippine Statistics Authority, 2022 Census of Agriculture and Fisheries: Capture Fishing Operation (Revised), May 19, 2026. 3 PSA, Poverty Incidence Declined from 2021 to 2023 in Ten Basic Sectors, March 31, 2025. forestry, and fishing remained a major source of employment, accounting for 19.9 percent of total employment in May 2026, while agriculture, forestry, and fishing contributed 7.9 percent of the country's GDP in 2025.4 These figures underscore the contradiction confronting the sector: agriculture and fisheries remain indispensable to the Philippine economy and food supply, yet many of the people who depend on them continue to experience poverty and limited access to productive opportunities. This proposed measure therefore seeks to establish a comprehensive Magna Carta for young farmers and fisherfolk that addresses the structural barriers preventing young Filipinos from pursuing and sustaining livelihoods in agriculture and fisheries. It provides for their rights to education and training, productive resources, technology, credit and capital, farmland, market development services, environmental protection, cultural identity, legal protection, and meaningful representation in policymaking, while creating a National Young Farmers and Fisherfolk Council and a national roadmap to coordinate government interventions. By investing in the capabilities and security of the next generation of farmers and fisherfolk, the State can strengthen the continuity of food production, promote rural development, encourage sustainable and climate-resilient practices, and help ensure that agriculture and fisheries remain viable sources of livelihood for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10782
title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11036, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MENTAL HEALTH ACT,” BY STRENGTHENING WORKPLACE MENTAL HEALTH PROMOTION AND PROTECTION, PROVIDING FOR WORKPLACE MENTAL HEALTH PROGRAMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 11036, or the “Mental Health Act,” affirms the State’s commitment to promote and protect the mental health of all Filipinos. However, the law requires further strengthening to ensure that mental health promotion and protection are effectively institutionalized in workplace settings, where individuals spend a significant portion of their time and are exposed to various psychosocial risks. This measure seeks to amend the law by clearly defining key concepts necessary for workplace implementation, including “Workplace Mental Health Program” and “Mental Health Focal Person,” to ensure accountability and proper coordination within organizations. The bill introduces explicit obligations on employers, both in the public and private sectors, to adopt and implement workplace mental health policies and programs. These programs are required to include mental health promotion, stigma reduction, access to referral mechanisms, confidentiality safeguards, non-discrimination measures, early identification and intervention systems, reasonable accommodations, and capacity-building for supervisors and designated personnel. It also mandates the designation of a focal person to oversee implementation and compliance. To protect the rights of workers, the measure establishes clear standards on confidentiality and data protection, ensuring that any information related to an employee’s mental health condition or treatment is handled with strict privacy safeguards and in accordance with existing laws, including the Data Privacy Act of 2012. The bill further provides for fair and supportive return-to-work and rehabilitation procedures for employees recovering from mental health conditions, including reasonable accommodations and reintegration measures, while prohibiting discrimination on the basis of mental health history. Finally, the measure delineates the roles of key government agencies. The Department of Health is tasked to lead in policy formulation and technical guidance, while the Department of Labor and Employment and the Civil Service Commission are mandated to ensure compliance in their respective jurisdictions. Other relevant agencies are likewise encouraged to integrate mental health promotion initiatives within their systems. By establishing clear standards, responsibilities, and safeguards, this measure aims to create healthier, more supportive, and rights-based work environments across all sectors. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 10783
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A REVISED NATIONAL APPRENTICESHIP PROGRAM, CLARIFYING THE STANDARDS FOR TRAINING AND ENGAGEMENT OF APPRENTICES AND ACCREDITATION OF APPRENTICESHIP PROGRAMS, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE CHAPTERS I AND II OF TITLE II, BOOK TWO OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The National Economic and Development Authority (NEDA), through the Philippine Development Plan, has adopted a long-term vision that represents the aspirations of the Filipino people and describes the kind of life that people want to live, as well as how the country will look like in the coming decades. This vision emphasizes the importance of good quality employment and opportunities for Filipinos without leaving the country. According to studies supporting this national vision, 79% of Filipinos aspire for a simple and comfortable life which includes having opportunities for good quality employment. One of the challenges hindering the country from achieving this vision is unemployment and underemployment. Recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority shows that while there are thousands of jobs available for Filipinos, many of them do not possess the required qualifications for these opportunities, resulting in a persistent job-skill mismatch. This bill seeks to address the job-skill mismatch in the country and reform the existing national apprenticeship program by providing the youth with the appropriate skills and access to employment. A worker who is at least 15 years of age is qualified to be an apprentice. The proposed apprenticeship law recognizes the advantages of work-based training, which allows our young workers to learn from experienced workers. The proposal also sets the duration of the training according to the complexity of the skills to be learned by the apprentices, thus expanding the maximum training period of six (6) months under the existing apprenticeship programs. The proposed apprenticeship program provides young apprentices with the opportunity to earn while they learn as they are entitled to a training allowance which should not be below 75 percent of the applicable minimum wage. The bill also introduces a provision on the issuance of training certificates to apprentices who have completed the apprenticeship program comparable to the completion of a training program in a Technical-Vocational Education and Training institution, and the award of equivalent unit credits in the formal system of education. The apprentice may use the National Certificate should he desire to pursue tertiary education. As for the participating enterprises, they are entitled to get an additional deduction from the taxable income equivalent to one half of the value of training expenses incurred for developing the productivity and efficiency of apprentices. This initiative will not only increase the employability of the youth but will also provide Philippine enterprises with a mechanism to ensure a continuous supply of skilled workers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10784
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 2 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8187, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PATERNITY LEAVE ACT OF 1996, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the thrust of developing a strong and proud nation, the State must reinforce the values and spirit of the most basic unit of Filipino society- the family. Acknowledging the vital role of the husband in providing care for his wife before, during, and after the birth of their Child, the Republic Act No. 8187 or the Paternity Leave Act of 1996 was enacted. However, the law is still inadequate in addressing the necessities of the Filipino Family. Studies show that fathers who take paternity leave are more likely to take on active roles in child-care tasks, therefore establishing strong relationships with their children and active involvement in their lives. Furthermore, sufficient early-child interaction has long-term benefits for the child’s cognitive development. Companies also benefit by providing their employees with a paternity leave policy, as such policies help companies in attracting the best and the brightest people to their human resources. It is the hope of this measure to mainstream co-parenting and provide adequate benefits to fathers of every Filipino family. This bill seeks to provide paternity leave to all married employees, regardless of the nature of their employment, and lengthen the leave period to 15 days. The bill also gives father-employees an option to extend their leave for 15 days more without pay. Additionally, the paternity leave shall not be deducted from the employee’s annual leave credits. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10785
title: AN ACT REQUIRING HOSPITALS TO INSTALL CLOSED CIRCUIT TELEVISION (CCTV) CAMERAS IN SELECTED PORTIONS OF THE HOSPITAL AND PENALIZING THE PUBLICATION OF THE VIDEO TAKEN BY THESE CAMERAS WITHOUT A COURT ORDER
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Many Southeast Asian countries require the installation of closed- circuit television (CCTV) cameras in their hospitals. In Vietnam, medical establishments are compelled to have CCTV cameras to monitor the activities of their staff. In Malaysia, surveillance cameras are installed in operating rooms to ensure the safety of the patients. The installation of surveillance cameras in hospitals offers a number of advantages not only to the patients but also to the staff. First, footage of operations will be beneficial in cases of medical malpractice as both the patient and the doctor can refer to them to prove their cases. The instances of baby switching will also be minimized, if not completely avoided, when delivery rooms and nurseries have CCTV. Lastly, having CCTV cameras in hospital entrances and exits will provide additional security for all those in the hospital. Overall, cameras in hospitals prevent theft, smoking, and other various violations of the law on the premises. Furthermore, this bill makes it criminal for any person to leak footage captured by the hospital CCTV camera without a court order, thereby giving assurance to patients and medical staff that their privacy is protected. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D.
