label: HB 10786
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ONLINE VOLUNTEERISM OPPORTUNITIES FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Volunteerism is one of the ways citizens can participate actively in nation building. It encourages the involvement of the public in important social and civil affairs. Opportunities for volunteerism activities, however, mostly require service delivery in physical or face-to-face set-ups. While the State provides for the inclusion and integration of Persons with Disabilities into the mainstream of society, physical disability may limit a person’s capacity to participate in volunteer work. In the Philippines, about 2.5 million Filipinos are registered persons with disability1. To uphold the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities, Republic Act No. 7277 or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons was enacted in 1992. Throughout the years, RA 7277 has had its fair share of amendments to adapt to the times. Despite this, there remains a gap in making volunteerism opportunities inclusive to persons with disabilities. Fortunately, the digital age has brought forth great opportunities for persons with disabilities to further participate in social activities by breaking 1 2025 National Council for Disability Affairs. certain barriers of inaccessibility. With the help of assistive technology, persons with disabilities have become part of online conversations and engagements. Given the promise of the digital age, this bill seeks to provide persons with disabilities with opportunities to engage in worthy humanitarian activities and overcome barriers to inclusion through online volunteerism. These online opportunities will enable them to develop their skills and become part of communities that advance different advocacies and human development, as they participate in society on an equal basis with everyone else while helping their fellow people who face different challenges. Online volunteerism will serve as a platform for our siblings with disabilities to share their strengths, abilities, and skills from the comfort of their own homes while making a tremendous impact on the lives of others as well as their own. It is the hope of this measure to showcase not disabilities, but people’s different abilities with the end goal of achieving a more inclusive Filipino society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10787
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR DIGITAL X-RAYS AND SPUTUM TESTING LABORATORIES IN LOCAL PUBLIC HEALTH CENTERS NATIONWIDE TO MAINTAIN FREE X-RAY AND SPUTUM TEST SERVICES FOR THE ERADICATION OF TUBERCULOSIS IN COMMUNITIES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The World Health Organization reports that tuberculosis remains a major health problem in the Philippines, affecting about a million Filipinos. Despite having free anti-tuberculosis medication provided to the citizens, the country continues to be the third highest in prevalence rate of tuberculosis (TB) in the world. Although the Department of Health cites a decline in TB cases in 2025, the country still lags in diagnosis and precautionary measures. Proper treatment and prevention of infection rely heavily on early detection of infected persons. While anti-tuberculosis drugs are available in national and local government health centers, patients still require overall treatments that include multiple tests such as X-rays, blood tests, chest radiographs, sputum smears, and rapid molecular Diagnostic Tests that are costly. In accordance with Republic Act No. 10767, “An Act Establishing a Comprehensive Philippine Plan of Action to Eliminate Tuberculosis as a Public Health Problem and Appropriating Funds Therefor”, it is the mandate of the State to promote the universal right to health and instill health consciousness among them. Republic Act 10767 states that: “The State is mandated to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development. Towards the end, the State shall support and expand efforts to eliminate tuberculosis as a public health problem by increasing investments for its prevention, treatment and control, and adopting a multisectoral approach in responding to the disease.” This bill seeks to uphold this mandate by tackling barriers to public health services. Towards this end and to address this harrowing public health concern, this legislation moves to adopt a mandatory, comprehensive, and sustainable periodic X-ray and sputum test program for the detection and prevention of tuberculosis. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10788
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION AGAINST K TO 12 HIGH SCHOOL GRADUATES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article 2, Section 9 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides: The State shall promote a just and dynamic social order that will ensure the prosperity and independence of the nation and free the people from poverty through policies that provide adequate social services, promote full employment, a rising standard of living, and an improved quality of life for all. With the implementation of the K to 12 Basic Education Program of the Department of Education, our high school graduates are expected to be more competent than ever. The K to 12 curriculum is standard and competency- based and is built around the needs of the learners and the community. Coupled with the fact that the new wave of high school graduates will be two years older than their previous counterparts, this means these competent graduates will have more years of experience to be more employable. Due to economic conditions, some Filipino families would opt to send their young graduates to work instead of moving on to enroll in higher education. However, very few options are available to our high school graduates due to stigma and discrimination. Some employers require entry- level employees to have a college degree or be enrolled in college, regardless of whether the degree is related to the job opening, before they can apply. With the institutionalized K to 12 Program that matches competencies worldwide, higher levels of education should now be optional to everyone. It entails an additional amount of investment from the family to send their children to university. Some families incur debts just to be able to afford the tuition so their children can have a college degree, just so they can apply for jobs that require them. Requiring a college degree for the sake of merely having one is an undue burden that employers ask of their prospective employees and their families. In many situations, these entry-level positions are jobs that our high school graduates are perfectly capable of doing. Furthermore, a number of progressive companies now require training for their new employees before the latter perform actual work, regardless of whether they have college degrees or not. The discrimination that high school graduates experience when certain companies require a college degree for positions that ought not to require one, must be prohibited. In doing so, we will be able to provide a broader employment base for employers and more opportunities to our high school graduates. This bill seeks to prohibit discrimination against non-degree holders for purposes of employment. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 10789
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A WAGE EMPLOYMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR DISPLACED AND/OR VULNERABLE WORKERS INSTITUTIONALIZING FOR THE PURPOSE THE TULONG PANGHANAPBUHAY SA ATING DISADVANTAGE/DISPLACED WORKERS (TUPAD) PROGRAM OF THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Despite the continued recovery of the Philippine economy, many Filipino workers remain vulnerable to unemployment, underemployment, and sudden loss of livelihood. The labor market continues to face challenges from worker displacement, informal and seasonal employment, and limited access to stable and decent jobs. For families dependent on daily income, even a temporary loss of employment can have serious consequences. Recent labor force data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) underscore the continuing need for programs that can provide immediate assistance to workers who lose their source of income or have insufficient employment. While unemployment has significantly improved from pandemic-era levels, millions of Filipinos remain underemployed or engaged in vulnerable forms of work. A viable mechanism for addressing this concern is the Tulong Panghanapbuhay sa Ating Disadvantaged/Displaced Workers (TUPAD) Program of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE). TUPAD provides temporary employment to disadvantaged, displaced, underemployed, and seasonal workers through community-based projects, allowing beneficiaries to earn income while contributing to their communities. This bill seeks to institutionalize TUPAD as a permanent employment assistance and social protection mechanism for workers who are displaced, disadvantaged, or vulnerable to loss of livelihood. It authorizes DOLE to implement emergency employment projects motu proprio in areas experiencing significant worker displacement and ensures that qualified beneficiaries from both the formal and informal sectors are covered. Institutionalizing TUPAD will provide the government with a responsive mechanism that can be activated during economic disruptions, natural disasters, business closures, and other circumstances that result in significant worker displacement or loss of livelihood. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10790
title: AN ACT GRANTING EMPLOYEES THE RIGHT TO DISCONNECT FROM WORK- RELATED ELECTRONIC COMMUNICATIONS AFTER WORK HOURS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Technology has significantly advanced labor and employment. However, the growing reliance on electronic communications has blurred the boundaries between work time and rest time, especially when employees are expected to remain reachable after official working hours. This reality has highlighted long-standing labor concerns on reasonable working hours, rest periods, work-life balance, and the right to disconnect. International empirical studies consistently show that after-hours work-related communication is associated with work-life conflict, difficulty in psychological detachment, sleep disruption, stress, fatigue, and burnout. In the Philippine setting, legal commentaries emphasize that while the Labor Code does not explicitly prohibit after-hours contact, excessive communication outside work hours may violate an employee's implicit right to rest under existing labor protections. The Department of Labor and Employment has recognized that employees may disregard work-related communications after office hours without disciplinary action, describing the "right to disconnect" as a choice of the employee rather than an imposed duty. However, there is still no standalone statute codifying a general right to disconnect, leaving workers vulnerable to informal pressure to remain available beyond their regular working hours. This measure therefore seeks to establish the right of employees to disconnect from work-related electronic communications after work hours, subject to reasonable exceptions based on the nature of the work, emergency situations, and other circumstances that may be provided by law or appropriate workplace policies. To achieve these objectives, this Act proposes to amend Presidential Decree No. 442, otherwise known as the Labor Code of the Philippines, as amended, by expressly recognizing the right to disconnect from work-related electronic communications after working hours and by providing a framework for its implementation in the workplace. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10791
title: AN ACT TO ESTABLISH MAGNA CARTA FOR BARANGAYS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The barangay serves as the bedrock of local governance and the most fundamental political unit in the Republic of the Philippines. Currently, there are 42,001 barangays across the country, each functioning as the critical interface between the State and its citizens. Enshrined in the 1987 Constitution and operationalized by Republic Act No. 7160 or the Local Government Code (LGC) of 1991, these territorial subdivisions are guaranteed genuine local autonomy. This constitutional mandate empowers them to transform into self-reliant communities and indispensable partners in national progress. Consistently, Philippine jurisprudence has reinforced that meaningful decentralization must reach the barangay level to ensure that grassroots governance remains dynamic and effective. Functioning as the government's primary planning and executing body at the community level, the barangay acts as the frontline for public service delivery, dispute resolution, and participatory governance. The sheer scale of this civic engagement was evident during the 2023 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE), where over 828,000 candidates vied for leadership posts to represent their communities.1 It is within this foundational tier that the collective voice of the people is formalized into actionable initiatives. Under the bottom-up development model established by the LGC, barangay development plans serve as the crucial building blocks for broader municipal, provincial, and national socio-economic strategies. Despite their indispensable role in nation-building, barangay officials and workers are plagued by a systemic lack of institutional support, limited social protection, and severe economic insecurity. Under current provisions, such as DBM Local Budget Circular No. 63, minimum honoraria remain starkly disproportionate to the workload: set at a baseline of just PHP 1,000 monthly for the Punong Barangay and PHP 600 for Sangguniang Barangay members, though some local government units augment this based on available local funds.2 This meager compensation persists even as their responsibilities multiply. During the COVID-19 pandemic and amidst frequent natural disasters, barangay officials and Barangay Health Workers (BHWs) functioned as the ultimate frontliners, managing contact tracing, enforcing quarantines, distributing relief goods, and maintaining peace and order, often without hazard pay, 1 GMA News Online. The push for a comprehensive Magna Carta for Barangay Officials is a decades-old legislative battle. The earliest attempt dates back to 1987 with House Bill No. 6925, followed by a broader Senate measure in 2007 that sought to elevate barangay officials to regular government personnel status, entitling them to fixed salaries, insurance, retirement security, and capacity- building resources. For years, these measures stagnated at the committee level. A notable breakthrough occurred recently in August 2026, when the Senate successfully approved on the third reading the Magna Carta for Barangay Health Workers, guaranteeing at least PHP 3,000 in monthly benefits, hazard allowances, and free legal assistance.3 This recent legislative victory sets a strong precedent for passing the broader Magna Carta covering all barangay officials. This proposed measure seeks to permanently close this long-standing legislative gap. It reaffirms the State's constitutional duty to promote the general welfare of its citizens by first elevating the economic and social dignity of its grassroots public servants. By officially institutionalizing financial support, professionalizing the barangay workforce, and ensuring local communities have the basic facilities for a dignified life, this bill transforms barangays into true engines of inclusive and sustainable national development. The enactment of this Magna Carta is no longer just timely; it is a moral imperative. It stands as a long-overdue validation of the sacrifices made by our community leaders and a definitive step toward fulfilling the constitutional promise of genuine, robust local autonomy. label: HB 10792
title: AN ACT CONSOLIDATING ALL PERFORMANCE MEASUREMENT TOOLS AND REWARDS SYSTEMS FOR ALL LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS BY INSTITUTIONALIZING MERITOCRACY IN THE PHILIPPINES, AMENDING CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11292, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS "THE SEAL OF GOOD LOCAL GOVERNANCE ACT OF 2019"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a modified version of the Human Development Index (HDI) as a performance measurement tool for Philippine local government units (LGUs). It proposes to amend the Seal of Good Local Governance (SGLG) Act of 2019 by adding a system that will measure the progress of LGUs based on selected indicators of human development. Under the proposed system, LGUs will be assessed based on their progress and performance in these indicators. The assessment will focus on whether LGUs are able to improve the outcomes within their respective areas of responsibility. The indicators may also take into account the different circumstances and capacities of LGUs to provide a fair and practical basis for evaluation. The measure also provides for the recognition of LGUs that consistently perform well under the index. LGUs that meet the established standards may be given appropriate recognition and incentives. On the other hand, LGUs that experience sustained decreases in their performance indicators may be subject to appropriate interventions or disincentives, in accordance with existing laws, rules, and regulations. The proposed index is intended to complement the existing SGLG framework by giving greater consideration to actual development outcomes. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is respectfully sought. ANTOLIN A. label: HB 10793
title: AN ACT DECLARING JULY 12 AS THE NATIONAL WEST PHILIPPINE SEA VICTORY DAY IN COMMEMORATION OF THE PHILIPPINES'TRIUMPH BEFORE THE PERMANENT COURT OF ARBITRATION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On July 12, 2016, the Republic of the Philippines secured a monumental legal victory when the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) in The Hague ruled unequivocally in our favor, invalidating China's expansive and baseless "nine-dash line" claim over the South China Sea. The historic arbitral award firmly established the Philippines' sovereign rights over its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) in the West Philippine Sea under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). A decade later, this landmark ruling remains the unassailable bedrock of our maritime rights and territorial integrity. However, despite the final and binding nature of this international legal decision, the Philippines continues to face relentless and escalating acts of aggression within our own waters. Over the past few years, state-sanctioned incursions, violent blockades, and coordinated intimidation tactics against our maritime personnel and fisherfolk have intensified, demonstrating a blatant disregard for international law. The necessity of this legislation is underscored by a deeply troubling pattern of recent hostilities. In June 2024, a routine rotation and resupply mission to the grounded BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin Shoal escalated violently when China Coast Guard personnel, armed with axes and bladed weapons, attacked and boarded Philippine Navy vessels. This brazen assault severely damaged our communications equipment and tragically resulted in a Filipino Navy seaman losing his thumb. By late 2025, aggression expanded geographically and tactically, with Chinese vessels utilizing water cannons against civilian Filipino fishing boats near Sabina Shoal; an alarming escalation targeting the livelihoods of our citizens. Most recently, on July 20, 2026, just days after the tenth anniversary of our arbitral victory, Chinese forces once again subjected our personnel at Ayungin Shoal to unprovoked violence. During an unlawful intrusion by the China Coast Guard, a Chinese officer struck a Philippine Navy sailor on the head with a wooden baton. This physical violence was accompanied by a sophisticated psychological warfare campaign, including the circulation of an AI-generated, racist video by Chinese state media intended to distort facts and humiliate the Filipino people. These continuous illegal, coercive, aggressive, and deceptive (ICAD) activities highlight the urgent need for a unified national response. This proposed measure seeks to declare July 12 of every year as the National West Philippine Sea Victory Day, to be observed as a special working holiday. Establishing this national observance serves a multi-fold purpose: it preserves the legacy of our diplomatic and legal triumph, fortifies the patriotic resolve of the Filipino people, and institutionalizes a national consciousness that our sovereign rights cannot be diluted, coerced, or negotiated away. While several local government units across the country have already passed ordinances commemorating this victory, this bill elevates those grassroots initiatives to a national mandate, cementing the 2016 arbitral award into our permanent historical and cultural record. Celebrating this victory is not an act of hostility, but a steadfast affirmation of international law. It’s a constant reminder to our government and our citizens that right makes might, and that the West Philippine Sea undeniably belongs to the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “A. label: HB 10801
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A POLICY ON BLOODBORNE VIRAL HEPATITIS TESTING AND SCREENING
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Viral hepatitis remains a major public health problem worldwide. Updated estimates from the World Health Organization (WHO) indicate that in 2024, approximately 287 million people were living with chronic hepatitis B or C infection globally, and viral hepatitis caused about 1.3 million deaths in the same year.1 In the Philippines, viral hepatitis continues to pose a significant burden. National data show that around one in 10 Filipinos has chronic hepatitis B, while an estimated six in 1,000 have chronic hepatitis C. The prevalence of hepatitis B is highest among the 20–49 age group, which comprises mostly the workforce and reproductive-age population.2 The majority of people with blood-borne viral hepatitis are asymptomatic and could unknowingly transmit the disease. Nevertheless, measures are available to prevent transmission, primarily through limiting the exposure of uninfected individuals to infected blood and other bodily fluids. In addition, an effective vaccine for hepatitis B is widely available and has been included in the government’s Expanded Program on Immunization. An important aspect of preventing hepatitis B and C transmission is public awareness of this disease. 1 World Health Organization. Global Hepatitis Report 2026. 2 Department of Health. The Annual Prevalence of Hepatitis B Virus Infection in the Philippines 2025. Infection with blood-borne viral hepatitis has a significant social impact not just from the disease but from fear, stigma, and discrimination. It has been reported that Filipinos with viral hepatitis find themselves subject to discrimination in the workplace. There are instances when individuals with positive blood tests are terminated or are not considered for employment even for jobs that have very low risk of disease transmission. The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Department Advisory No. 05 (Series of 2010), also known as the Guidelines for the Implementation of a Workplace Policy and Program on Hepatitis B, was issued to protect the rights of workers with HBV and HCV. Despite this, cases of discrimination against HBV and HCV-positive individuals persist. This situation highlights the need to revise our policy on hepatitis B and hepatitis C testing to ensure that the rights of all Filipinos to privacy and confidentiality when it comes to their health conditions are protected and to improve access of HBV and HCV positive individuals to quality health care. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10802
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE INSTALLATION OF CARBON MONOXIDE DETECTORS IN SCHOOL BUILDINGS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cases of Carbon Monoxide (CO) poisoning have been associated with prolonged use of electric generators, mostly during power outages. In the last few years, several cases of death and injuries due to CO poisoning have been tallied, whether in schools or enclosed homes of the victims. Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless toxic gas that poses an extreme danger to people when inhaled, for it can kill people within minutes. Carbon monoxide poisoning is a result of inhalation of carbon monoxide gas that can affect the memory, brain function, behavior, and cognition of humans, and in extreme cases, exposure to this toxic gas results in death. If inhaled, it can kill people within minutes. Early symptoms include drowsiness and headache, followed by unconsciousness, respiratory failure, and death. First aid for a victim of carbon monoxide poisoning requires access to fresh air; administration of artificial respiration and, if available, oxygen; and as soon as possible, medical attention. In accordance with the State policy of protecting the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being of the Filipino youth, we must ensure that our students are not susceptible to this toxic gas, especially in places of learning. As such, this bill requires the installation of carbon monoxide detectors in all school buildings where there is a substantial risk of exposure to the gas. Furthermore, this bill will allow authorities to detect CO levels in schools which are also used mostly as evacuation areas in times of calamities, thereby promoting the safety of other users of school buildings. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT MANDATING AN ACCIDENT AND LIFE INSURANCE COVERAGE FOR CONSTRUCTION WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution embodies our country’s commitment to protecting the rights and welfare of our workers, providing that "The State shall afford full protection to labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized, and promote full employment opportunities for all." The extensive Labor Code of the Philippines or Presidential Decree No. 442, as amended, also provides for the institutionalization of protection to labor and employment. Among the most productive laborers in the country are workers from the construction industry. In particular, the Philippines employs about 4.8 million construction workers.1 Due to the manual labor and nature of this industry, the workers are constantly exposed to dangerous working environments and are at high risks of musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). MSDs comprise of 30% of all recorded occupational injuries of construction workers in the country.2 Despite having standards to ensure worker safety, a high number of cases of injuries are still reported annually. Consequently, the injuries Philippine Statistics Authority. 2025 2 Bureau of Labor and Employment Statistics. (2011). PSIC F: CONSTRUCTION. Retrieved from http://www.bles.dole.gov.ph/PUBLICATIONS/Industry%20Yearbook/Part%20A%20- %20Occupational%20Injuries.html sustained by the construction workers remain heavily unreported.3 While the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) has supervised many legitimate construction agencies, it is imperative that construction workers and their families are not denied opportunities to adopt better safety protocols and accident and life insurance. When unfortunate circumstances like accidents happen, the construction workers and their families are often just paid a small amount of money by their employers that does not capture the sacrifices and dignity of labor. Many of these construction workers are denied better opportunities for livelihood because of days lost for being confined in hospitals or, worse, death due to work-related accidents. This bill seeks to ensure that construction workers and their families are justly compensated with dignity and respect for their sacrifices in nation- building. This legislation shall provide group personal accident insurance coverage for construction workers. label: HB 10804
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING THE FORMER PRISONER’S EMPLOYMENT PROGRAM AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Society is judged not only by how well it takes care of its outstanding citizens but by how it treats its prisoners, according to philosopher Fyodor Dostoevsky. When offenders are released from prison, they are assumed to have undergone the necessary rehabilitation to once again be integrated into society. However, offenders face a variety of challenges after they are released from prison - stigma from having been incarcerated and discrimination, often in employment due to deprivation in terms of education. Most of these challenges hinder their ability to become law-abiding citizens. When they fail to become law- abiding citizens because of these barriers, institutions need to take an active role in greater reforms and second chances. As such, prisons and correctional institutions ought to prepare offenders for social reintegration before release. That is the philosophy of a criminal justice system that aims to be more rehabilitative than punitive. This kind of perspective is geared towards comprehensive crime prevention, whereas the system must include effective measures to prevent the cycle of failed adaptation by repeat offenders. This bill seeks to provide support to ex-offenders and ensure that they establish productive and crime-free lives in the community through the creation of the Office of Employment Opportunities for Former Prisoners under the Department of Justice. The proposed office is directed to draft and implement provisions and policies for the training and employment of former prisoners. Furthermore, this bill seeks to provide incentives to private establishments that will hire former prisoners. To create a better community for everyone, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10805
title: AN ACT TO MODERNIZE THE DEVELOPMENT OF MSMEs BY AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6977, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE MAGNA CARTA FOR SMALL ENTERPRISES, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9501, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE MAGNA CARTA FOR MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are the backbone of the Philippine economy. They are the sari-sari stores in our communities, family-owned restaurants and shops, farmers and producers, online sellers, small manufacturers, and countless businesses that provide jobs and livelihood to Filipino families. According to the Department of Trade and Industry, MSMEs account for 99.63% of registered business establishments in the Philippines. Yet despite their importance, many continue to face difficulties in accessing affordable financing, technology, markets, government opportunities, and reliable business support. The Magna Carta for MSMEs, or Republic Act No. 6977, as amended by Republic Act No. 9501, was enacted to address these challenges. However, the business environment has changed significantly. Digitalization, e-commerce, new financing models, and global markets now play a much greater role in determining whether a small business can survive and grow. This measure therefore seeks to modernize the Magna Carta for MSMEs and make government support more responsive to the realities of today's Filipino entrepreneurs. First, the bill adopts a harmonized MSME classification system based on employment size and annual sales turnover, removing asset size as a determining factor. This will provide a clearer and more consistent basis for identifying MSMEs and delivering government assistance. Second, it establishes a National MSME Information System to consolidate government data on MSMEs. Better data will allow government to better understand the needs of entrepreneurs and design programs that reach the right businesses. Third, the bill promotes digital transformation and connectivity through a National Digital Skills Program and an MSME Digital Adoption Fund. Digitalization is no longer a luxury for small businesses. In 2025, the Philippine digital economy reached ₱2.74 trillion, or 9.8% of GDP, demonstrating the growing importance of digital tools and markets to our economy. Fourth, the bill strengthens access to finance by empowering the Small Business Corporation to develop innovative financing mechanisms, including risk-based and movable asset-based lending, and to expand credit guarantees for startups and underserved MSMEs. Fifth, the bill gives MSMEs greater access to the government procurement market by requiring procuring entities to set aside at least twenty percent (20%) of their procurement of goods and services for local MSMEs, while providing for simplified bidding procedures and prompt payment. Finally, the bill establishes an Expanded Global Market Access Program for MSMEs to help Filipino businesses move beyond local markets and compete internationally. The Program will provide export-readiness training, market intelligence, assistance in obtaining international certifications, participation in trade fairs and business missions, access to digital marketplaces, and linkages with foreign buyers and global value chains. The objective is simple: when a Filipino takes the risk of starting a business, government should help make that business capable of surviving, growing, creating jobs, and competing—not only in the Philippines, but in the global marketplace. By modernizing the Magna Carta for MSMEs, we invest in the entrepreneurs who keep our communities and our economy moving. We give Filipino MSMEs a fairer chance to access capital, technology, government opportunities, and international markets—and ultimately, a better chance to grow from small businesses into stronger and more competitive enterprises. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10806
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE FAIR USE OF SOCIAL MEDIA, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND INTERNET TECHNOLOGY IN ELECTIONS, REGULATING DIGITAL ELECTION PROPAGANDA AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many Filipinos today, the first place they encounter election news is no longer television, radio or newspapers. It is Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, X, messaging applications and other online platforms. The problem is that not everything that looks real online is real. This is no longer simply a matter of “fake news.” Artificial intelligence can now create convincing videos, photographs and audio recordings of people saying or doing things that never happened. Fake accounts and automated bots can make a political message appear more popular than it actually is. Political advertisements can be precisely targeted to particular groups using personal information. Paid influencers can promote political messages without making it clear that they are being compensated. Recent evidence shows that this is a serious concern among Filipinos. The Reuters Institute's Digital News Report 2025 reported that 67% of Filipinos expressed concern about online misinformation and disinformation, the highest level recorded in the Philippine data at that time. The report also noted that social media remain a major source of news for Filipinos amid an increasingly fragmented and politically polarized information environment. The problem is not limited to fabricated stories. In 2025, an investigation reported extensive use of fake social media accounts in Philippine political discourse, with researchers estimating that as much as 45% of election-related online discussion in a particular period was driven by inauthentic accounts. Such operations can create the illusion that a candidate or political position enjoys widespread public support when, in reality, much of the apparent engagement may have been artificially generated. At the same time, any law addressing online misinformation must be careful not to silence legitimate political speech. Filipinos have the right to criticize candidates, express political opinions, share commentary, make jokes, create satire and parody, and engage in political debate—even when others disagree with them. An honest mistake should not automatically become an election offense simply because it was posted online. This measure therefore draws an important line between ordinary political expression and deliberate digital manipulation. It distinguishes misinformation from disinformation and recognizes that satire, parody, opinion and legitimate editing are different from deliberately deceptive content. It specifically prohibits the use of deepfakes to impersonate candidates or election officials when intended to deceive voters. The bill likewise addresses the use of bots, fake accounts and coordinated inauthentic behavior designed to artificially influence electoral discourse. It regulates political microtargeting, particularly the use of sensitive personal information, while allowing legitimate digital campaigning. The measure also promotes transparency. Filipinos should be able to know who paid for a political advertisement and when a social media influencer is being paid or otherwise compensated to promote political content. Digital platforms are likewise required to maintain records of political advertising so that campaign spending and digital influence operations can be properly monitored. Digital campaign spending should not be invisible simply because it happens online. Payments for social media advertisements, digital influencers, online campaign services, content production and other digital activities should be properly reported as campaign expenditures. The bill also makes candidates and campaign organizations accountable when they knowingly authorize, finance or coordinate unlawful digital operations, while making clear that a candidate should not automatically be liable for every post, comment, share or reaction made independently by an ordinary supporter. Finally, the measure gives the Commission on Elections the authority to issue implementing rules and regulations, with consultation among technology platforms, media organizations, civil society, political parties, digital experts and other election stakeholders. The objective of this measure is simple: technology should help Filipinos make informed choices, not create an artificial picture of what Filipinos believe. The Internet has become an important part of Philippine democracy. This bill does not seek to take political discussion away from Filipinos. Instead, it seeks to make digital campaigning more transparent, accountable and fair—so that when Filipinos cast their votes, their choices are influenced by genuine political discourse and not by hidden digital manipulation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHARISSE ANNE C. label: HB 10808
title: AN ACT SUSPENDING FOR TWO (2) YEARS THE IMPLEMENTATION OF CERTAIN PROVISIONS OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12001, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “REAL PROPERTY VALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REFORM ACT,” PROVIDING FOR THE CONTINUED APPLICATION OF EXISTING SCHEDULES OF MARKET VALUES DURING THE PERIOD OF SUSPENSION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12001, otherwise known as the “Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act,” introduced far-reaching reforms intended to establish a uniform, transparent, and internationally aligned system for the valuation of real property in the Philippines. The objectives of the law remain laudable and necessary. However, reforms must also be responsive to the economic circumstances prevailing at the time of their implementation. What may constitute sound policy under normal conditions may impose unintended hardship when introduced during a period of extraordinary economic and natural disruption. The Philippine economy is presently confronting precisely such circumstances. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the Philippine economy grew by only 2.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026. This represents a significant slowdown from the rates of economic expansion to which the country had become accustomed in recent years. At the same time, Filipino households continue to contend with elevated prices. Headline inflation stood at 6.2 percent in July 2026, following 6.4 percent in June. These economic difficulties have been aggravated by circumstances that are, to a significant degree, beyond the control of the Philippine Government. The continuing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted global energy markets and contributed to elevated fuel prices and supply-side pressure which are external uncertainties weighing on the Philippine economy. _________ NOVFFFFFFF Our country has likewise suffered successive natural calamities. On June 8, 2026, a magnitude 7.8 earthquake struck off Sarangani, affecting communities across Mindanao and damaging homes, schools, bridges, and other infrastructure. And there were other strong earthquakes during the previous year as well, with the local governments, and constituents, still in the process of recovering from the effects of the natural disaster. The Government has responded—and continues to respond—to these challenges. Nevertheless, public policy must recognize that the burden of global conflict, natural disasters, elevated inflation, and slower economic growth ultimately falls upon ordinary Filipino households and businesses. This is therefore not the appropriate time to introduce another potential source of financial pressure upon them, hence the move to suspend the reform legislation for a period of two (2) years. Additionally, without the suspension, the effects extend beyond the real property taxes imposed by local government units. Under Republic Act No. 12001, the approved Schedule of Market Values may likewise affect local transfer taxes and other property- related taxes, fees, and charges. It may also be used in determining the tax base for internal revenue taxes involving real property transactions. Thus, an abrupt adjustment in government property valuations at this particular time may increase the cost of owning, transferring, inheriting, donating, developing, and conducting business upon real property precisely when households and enterprises are already adjusting to higher prices and weaker economic conditions. This measure proposes a two-year suspension of the implementation of the provisions of Republic Act No. 12001 relating to the adoption and use of new or updated Schedules of Market Values and the general revision of real property assessments based thereon. Fiscal reform and taxpayer protection are not incompatible. Republic Act No. 12001 can achieve its long-term objectives without requiring its full financial consequences to be imposed upon taxpayers at the height of extraordinary economic difficulties. A temporary suspension is therefore not an abandonment of reform. It is a measured and compassionate adjustment in its timing. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. FERDINAND L. HERNANDEZ ATTY. MIRO S. label: HB 10809
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING ANTI-LITTERING MEASURES IN PUBLIC AND PRIVATE PLACES, MANDATING AGGRAVATED PENALTIES FOR OBSTRUCTING DRAINAGE SYSTEMS, CANALS, AND SPILLWAYS, CREATING ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Flooding in urban and sub-urban areas in the Philippines has escalated from a seasonal inconvenience to a recurring humanitarian and economic crisis. While typhoons and heavy rainfall are natural phenomena, the severity and rapid onset of severe flooding are overwhelmingly man-made—driven largely by the unmitigated, habitual dumping of solid waste into streets, esteros, canals, and waterways. Every year, millions of tons of plastic waste, household trash, and commercial refuse clog city drainage systems, catch basins, pumping stations, and critical spillways. During typhoon season and heavy monsoons, this accumulated garbage forms dense impoundments that paralyze water conveyance systems, causing water levels to back up and submerge entire towns, highways, and residential communities within minutes. The result is billions of pesos in damaged infrastructure, loss of lives, destruction of property, and severe disruption to commerce. Existing laws and local ordinances against littering have proven insufficient to deter offenders. Soft fines and lax enforcement have fostered a culture of disregard for public sanitation and environmental responsibility. Throwing a single plastic wrapper or dumping a bag of waste into a gutter may seem minor to an individual, but collectively, it acts as a primary trigger for catastrophic urban inundation. This bill seeks to address this crisis by prohibiting all forms of littering in both public and private spaces, with aggravating penalties specifically targeting acts that obstruct, dump into, or contaminate drainage networks, waterways, and spillways. It elevates penalties from minor infractions to serious administrative and criminal offenses, mandating scaled monetary fines, compulsory community service centered on waterway rehabilitation, and imprisonment for repeat or high- impact offenders. By imposing stringent liability and reinforcing local enforcement mechanisms, this legislation aims to restore water infrastructure function, protect lives and livelihoods, and foster strict civic discipline regarding solid waste management. In view of the urgent need to protect public safety and mitigate flood disasters, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 10810
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE MUNICIPAL ROAD IN BRGY. TUMANA – MACAIBAN, BRGY. POBLACION IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, BULACAN INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the vibrant and rapidly growing Municipality of Santa Maria, local infrastructure serves as the essential pulse of everyday commerce and community life. Spanning approximately 1.60 kilometers, the Barangay Tumana – Macaiban Road in Barangay Poblacion is far more than a simple strip of concrete; it is a vital artery connecting fundamental residential, agricultural, and economic hubs within the town. Every single day, hundreds of motorists, public transport drivers, small business owners, and commuters traverse this thoroughfare. It bears a volume of heavy everyday traffic far beyond what a standard municipal road was ever originally designed to handle. Under our current decentralized framework, local government units bear the primary responsibility for municipal road maintenance. However, as Santa Maria continues its rapid urbanization, the toll on this 1.60-kilometer stretch has grown increasingly severe. Potholes, surface deterioration, and drainage limitations are frequent occurrences that demand continuous, capital-intensive intervention. While our Local Government Unit in Santa Maria works tirelessly to serve its constituents, municipal resources are finite. Every peso spent on emergency road repairs is a peso pulled away from other crucial frontline services—whether in public health, education, social welfare, or local disaster risk reduction. Passing the responsibility of this critical road to the national government through the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) is both a logical and necessary legislative step. By converting the Barangay Tumana – Macaiban Road into a National Road, it integrates the road's maintenance, rehabilitation, and long-term expansion directly into the annual General Appropriations Act (GAA). It ensures that road widening, flood mitigation systems, standard pavement markings, and structural reinforcements meet rigid national DPWH engineering standards. Our local communities cannot shoulder the weight of regional growth alone. It is our duty as legislators to provide the structural support our towns need to thrive. Converting this key municipal road into a national thoroughfare is a tangible, high-impact step toward ensuring the safety, convenience, and economic vitality of the residents of Santa Maria and the motorists plying this route. For these reasons, I earnestly ask for the passage of this bill. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 10813
title: AN ACT ASSISTING YOUNG ATHLETES BY PROVIDING PROGRAMS AND INCENTIVES FOR THEIR DEVELOPMENT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sports play a vital role in shaping national identity and unity. It promotes essential values such as discipline, sportsmanship, teamwork, perseverance, resilience, and leadership, while providing young Filipinos with opportunities to develop their skills, build confidence, and become active and productive members of society. The Philippines has a vast pool of young athletes participating in grassroots, school-based, local, provincial, regional, and national sports competitions. The Batang Pinoy National Championships and the Palarong Pambansa, among other national sports programs, provide thousands of young Filipinos with opportunities to compete, develop their athletic abilities, and pursue excellence in sports. These programs also serve as important avenues for identifying and developing athletes who may eventually represent the country in national and international competitions. Numerous Filipino Olympians, Southeast Asian Games medalists, and national champions, including Hidilyn Diaz, Carlos Yulo, and Nesthy Petecio, began their athletic careers through grassroots and school-based sports programs. Their achievements demonstrate the importance of providing young athletes with sustained opportunities, proper support, and an environment conducive to athletic development. Despite the talent and potential of Filipino young athletes, many face financial and structural barriers that prevent them from participating consistently and developing their abilities. The costs of training, membership and participation fees, equipment, uniforms, transportation, and access to suitable sports facilities can be beyond the means of many young athletes and their families. For local sports and recreation organizations, limited resources likewise constrain their ability to expand programs, accommodate more participants, and maintain or improve sports facilities. This measure seeks to address these barriers by establishing a state- supported grassroots sports program for young athletes through three complementary financial assistance initiatives to be administered by the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC). The "Get Started in Sports Fund" shall provide eligible young athletes with vouchers amounting to Three Thousand Pesos (₱3,000.00) to help defray membership, registration, participation, training, equipment, uniforms, and other reasonable sports-related expenses. The "Get Going Fund" shall provide Fifty Thousand Pesos (₱50,000.00) in assistance to qualified local sports and recreation organizations for projects that increase opportunities for young athletes to participate in organized sports and recreation programs. The "Get Playing Fund" shall provide up to Five Hundred Thousand Pesos (₱500,000.00) to qualified local sports and recreation organizations for the improvement, rehabilitation, upgrading, or development of sports facilities. To ensure the sustainability of these initiatives, an annual amount of Eighty Million Pesos (₱80,000,000.00) shall be made available for the implementation of the Act, subject to existing laws and the annual appropriations process. Through these measures, the State can reduce financial barriers to sports participation, strengthen grassroots sports programs, improve access to sports facilities, and provide young athletes with greater opportunities to develop their abilities. More importantly, the measure seeks to establish a sustained and accessible government support system that will help young Filipinos pursue excellence in sports while contributing to the development of a healthier, more disciplined, and productive citizenry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10814
title: AN ACT GRANTING TEN (10) DAYS BEREAVEMENT LEAVE WITH FULL PAY TO ALL EMPLOYEES IN THE PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The death of an immediate family member is one of the most difficult experiences an employee may face. Beyond the emotional and psychological pain of losing a loved one, bereaved employees are often required to attend to funeral arrangements, burial, family obligations, and other personal and legal matters at a time when they are least able to perform their regular duties. While existing laws provide various leave benefits to employees, there is presently no general statutory bereavement leave benefit applicable to employees in both the private and public sectors. Employees should not be compelled to choose between grieving and fulfilling their obligations at work during such a difficult period. This measure seeks to institutionalize a ten (10)-day bereavement leave with full pay for employees in the private and public sectors following the death of an immediate family member. The leave may be used consecutively or intermittently within thirty (30) days from the date of death, allowing employees reasonable flexibility to attend to their family and personal responsibilities. The measure likewise ensures that the availment of bereavement leave shall not result in discrimination, loss of employment, or other adverse employment action. It further provides that the proposed benefit shall not diminish or adversely affect existing leave benefits that are more favorable to employees. By recognizing the need of workers to grieve, care for their families, and attend to essential matters following the death of a loved one, this measure promotes worker welfare while affirming the importance of the Filipino family. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10815
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE INCLUSIVE DEVELOPMENT AND WELL-BEING OF CHILDREN WITH SPECIAL NEEDS, PROVIDING FOR COMPREHENSIVE SUPPORT SYSTEMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every child deserves the opportunity to develop to his or her fullest potential. Yet many Filipino children with special needs continue to face barriers in accessing timely identification, assessment, therapy, rehabilitation, education, and other essential support services. Families often bear significant financial and emotional burdens arising from the cost of therapy, rehabilitation, medical care, assistive devices, transportation, and specialized educational support. These challenges are particularly severe in underserved and geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas where specialized professionals and facilities are limited. While existing laws, including Republic Act No. 7277, as amended, and Republic Act No. 11650, provide important protection for persons with disabilities and promote inclusive education, gaps remain in the coordination, accessibility, and continuity of services for children with special needs and their families. This measure seeks to establish a comprehensive and coordinated support framework for children with special needs, covering early identification and intervention, therapeutic and rehabilitation services, inclusive education, financial assistance, community-based support, caregiver training, and workforce development. It strengthens coordination among the Department of Health, Department of Education, Department of Social Welfare and Development, PhilHealth, local government units, and other relevant agencies to ensure that children and their families can access appropriate services and benefits. The bill also establishes a CSN Support Grant and Assistance Program for qualified families and promotes the enhancement of existing PhilHealth benefit packages for medically necessary services. It strengthens community-based support systems, referral and case-management mechanisms, public awareness, and monitoring to ensure that services reach children, particularly those in underserved and geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. The measure is intended to complement, and not diminish or duplicate, existing laws and programs on disability rights, inclusive education, healthcare, rehabilitation, social protection, and child development. By strengthening the systems that identify, support, and include children with special needs, the State can help ensure that every child receives timely and appropriate support and is given the opportunity to reach his or her fullest potential. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10816
title: AN ACT PROVIDING DEATH, DISABILITY, AND ACCIDENT INSURANCE COVERAGE TO OTHER BARANGAY OFFICIALS, BARANGAY TANODS, BARANGAY HEALTH WORKERS, BARANGAY DAY CARE WORKERS AND MEMBERS OF THE LUPONG TAGAPAMAYAPA, AND INCREASING THE INSURANCE BENEFITS PROVIDED THEREIN, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6942 AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The barangay is the basic political unit of the country and serves as the primary venue for the delivery of government services and the implementation of programs at the community level. Barangay officials and other barangay frontliners are often the first to respond to emergencies, maintain peace and order, assist in disaster response, facilitate community programs, and address the immediate needs and concerns of their constituents. These responsibilities expose them to various risks, including death, permanent disability, and injuries arising from accidents in the course of performing their duties. While Republic Act No. 6942, otherwise known as the “Act Increasing the Insurance Benefits of Local Government Officials and Providing Funds Therefor,” provides insurance coverage to certain local officials, its coverage does not adequately extend to other barangay personnel who likewise perform essential frontline functions in their communities. The benefits provided under the law likewise require enhancement in view of present economic conditions and the increasing costs associated with death, disability, hospitalization, and medical care. This measure therefore seeks to expand the coverage of Republic Act No. 6942 to include barangay tanods, barangay health workers, barangay day care workers, and members of the Lupong Tagapamayapa, and to increase the death, disability, and accident insurance benefits available to covered personnel. The measure further provides for the corresponding payment of insurance premiums based on the actual number of covered personnel, subject to annual appropriations and periodic actuarial assessment by the Government Service Insurance System to ensure the sustainability and adequacy of the insurance program. Through this measure, the State recognizes the invaluable contribution of barangay officials and other barangay frontliners and seeks to provide them and their families with greater financial protection against the risks attendant to the performance of their public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10817
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING DISASTER-RESILIENT SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT, PROVIDING FOR THE CONTINUITY AND RAPID RESTORATION OF SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT SERVICES DURING AND AFTER DISASTERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the "Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000," established the country's comprehensive framework for the segregation, collection, transport, processing, recycling, recovery and disposal of solid waste and placed primary responsibility for solid waste management on local government units. Disasters, particularly typhoons and floods, can severely disrupt this waste disposal system. They can generate extraordinary volumes of household waste, spoiled food, fallen vegetation, damaged furniture and appliances, bulky materials, construction debris and other waste within a short period of time, while simultaneously limiting access to roads, collection facilities and disposal sites. When ordinary waste management capacity is overwhelmed, accumulated waste may obstruct roads and drainage systems, impede emergency response, aggravate flooding, create public health risks and contaminate waterways. Existing laws already provide mechanisms for disaster risk reduction, anticipatory action and emergency procurement. Republic Act No. 10121 provides the disaster risk reduction and management framework and the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund. Republic Act No. 12287 provides for anticipatory action before an imminent disaster. Republic Act No. 12009 provides appropriate procurement mechanisms for emergency situations. What is needed is to ensure that solid waste management is expressly integrated into these existing mechanisms. The measure likewise draws from international best practices in disaster waste management, urban drainage protection and flood resilience, adapting these approaches to the Philippine local government and solid waste management framework. This measure therefore strengthens Republic Act No. 9003 by requiring local government units to incorporate disaster-resilient solid waste management into their existing solid waste management plans. It requires LGUs to assess their waste surge capacity, identify temporary staging areas and alternative facilities, establish arrangements for additional collection and hauling capacity, and provide for the continuity and rapid restoration of waste- management services. The measure further clarifies that compatible, non-hazardous disaster- generated waste may be consolidated with ordinary municipal solid waste, thereby avoiding the unnecessary creation of a separate disaster-waste system. Waste requiring special handling, including hazardous waste, shall continue to be governed by applicable special laws. The bill further strengthens the enforcement of solid waste management rules by establishing a national ₱5,000 penalty for prohibited disposal of solid waste and a higher penalty for dumping into esteros, canals, waterways, drainage systems and flood-control facilities, with the maximum penalty applicable when the offense is committed during an officially declared disaster period. The measure also allows recovery of reasonable and documented government cleanup costs from the offender, without prejudice to liability under other environmental laws. At the same time, the measure recognizes that effective solid waste management should not rely solely on penalties. It therefore strengthens the existing incentive framework under Republic Act No. 9003 and links disaster- resilient solid waste management performance with the existing Seal of Good Local Governance under Republic Act No. 11292. LGUs and communities that demonstrate sustained compliance, effective waste diversion, protection of waterways and preparedness for disaster-generated waste may thereby be recognized and supported through existing government incentive mechanisms. The bill does not create a new national bureaucracy, a separate disaster fund or a new procurement exemption. It instead strengthens and integrates existing legal mechanisms. Through this measure, solid waste management becomes an integral component of disaster preparedness, response and recovery, helping ensure that a disaster does not result in a secondary crisis caused by unmanaged waste. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 10819
title: AN ACT REMOVING SYSTEMS LOSS AS A SEPARATE COMPONENT OF ELECTRICITY BILLS, LIMITING RECOVERY OF COSTS AND PROMOTING ACCOUNTABILITY OF DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Systems loss charge has been defined as the component of the distribution rate that represents the recovery of the cost of power due to technical and non-technical losses. Technical losses are those inherent in the physical delivery of electricity while non-technical losses refer to electricity lost due to pilferage, meter reading errors, meter tampering, and losses which are not related to the physical characteristics and function of the electric system. According to Republic Act No. 9136, the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) is empowered to determine caps on systems loss charge based on load density, sales mix, cost of service, delivery voltage, and other technical considerations it may promulgate. The ERC is also mandated to establish minimum efficiency performance standards for distribution utilities including systems losses, interruption frequency rates, and collection efficiency. While distribution utilities are allowed to pass on systems loss to consumers, this entitlement did not lead to distribution systems improvement to achieve efficiency. Eventually, as distribution systems remain the same, it is inevitable for systems losses to rise, burdening consumers with additional charges that do not redound to their benefit. Hence, this bill is filed to remove systems loss as a component of electricity bill and limit recovery costs that may be passed on to consumers. This bill likewise requires distribution utilities to improve efficiency of electricity distribution by modernizing facilities. Ultimately, this bill aims to alleviate consumers plight of high electricity rates and improve electricity distribution in the country. Thus, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 NICANOR M. label: HB 10820
title: AN ACT DECLARING A ONE-TIME AMNESTY ON ALL UNPAID INTERNAL REVENUE TAXES IMPOSED BY THE NATIONAL GOVERNMENT FOR TAXABLE YEAR 2025 AND PRIOR YEARS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In 2025, the Bureau of Treasury recorded a budget deficit of Php 1.58 trillion. This was driven by weaker revenue collections, temporary suspension of rice importation, and reduced tax collection from imports. Given this deficit, the government restrained expenditure to cushion its impact. For 2027, the national budget was proposed at Php 7.2 trillion, which is six percent (6%) higher than the 2026 budget. This budget aims to fund major programs for education, agriculture, health, social welfare, and developmental infrastructure that will boost economic activity across the country. In order to address the revenue shortfalls of the previous year given the higher budget proposal for 2027, this bill is thus introduced to provide tax amnesty covering all internal revenue collections for taxable year 2025 and prior years. This will allow a clean slate for delinquent taxpayers, encouraging more Filipinos to register with the Bureau of Internal Revenue. Likewise, it is hoped that this will expand tax base, increase tax collection, and reduce corruption. The previous tax amnesty law, Republic Act No. 11213, enacted in 2019, covered only estate tax and settlement of delinquent accounts. This law reportedly generated a preliminary estimate of Php 14.6 billion in additional collections for 2019 to 2021. The last general tax amnesty law, Republic Act No. 9480 in 2007, generated Php 5.902 billion from 20,629 taxpayers. This measure thus hopes to improve fiscal capacity of the country to ensure that national programs are adequately funded. Thus, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. NICANOR M. label: HB 10840
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT AND IMPLEMENTATION OF A NATIONAL BUDGET BLOCKCHAIN SYSTEM TO ENHANCE TRANSPARENCY, ACCOUNTABILITY, AND PUBLIC PARTICIPATION IN THE PHILIPPINE BUDGET PROCESS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution recognizes transparency and accountability as essential principles in the administration of public affairs and in the use of public funds. The national budget involves billions of pesos appropriated for programs, projects, and services intended to benefit the Filipino people. However, the complexity of government financial systems and the fragmentation of budget, procurement, disbursement, accounting, and auditing records can make it difficult for citizens and oversight institutions to independently and promptly trace the movement and utilization of public funds. The rapid development of digital technologies presents an opportunity to strengthen existing mechanisms for fiscal transparency and accountability. Blockchain technology, through its distributed, cryptographically secured, and tamper-resistant ledger, can provide a reliable means of recording and verifying transactions across the government budget cycle. When properly designed and implemented, such a system can create a continuous and auditable record from the appropriation of funds under the General Appropriations Act to their release, disbursement, utilization, and audit. This measure therefore seeks to establish the Philippine National Budget Blockchain, a blockchain-based budget system that will serve as a government-managed digital ledger for national budget records. The proposed system shall record budget-related transactions as Digital Public Assets (DPAs), providing immutable and verifiable records that can be independently examined by citizens, government agencies, oversight bodies, and other authorized stakeholders. Under the measure, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), in coordination with the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and the Commission on Audit (COA), shall establish and administer the blockchain-based budget system. The system shall cover the budget cycle from preparation and legislation to execution and audit. It shall also provide a public-facing portal through which citizens and oversight institutions may access and verify relevant budget information in a timely manner. The measure further recognizes the importance of integrating the proposed system with existing government financial and information systems. Government budgeting, accounting, disbursement, procurement, and reporting platforms shall therefore comply with interoperability standards and ensure that relevant financial data are anchored to the blockchain. This will prevent the proposed system from operating as an isolated platform and will instead allow it to complement and strengthen existing government processes. To promote accountability, the proposed system shall incorporate key features such as immutability, decentralization, traceability, security and resilience, and interoperability. These features are intended to preserve the integrity of budgetary records, prevent unauthorized alteration or manipulation, enable the tracking of public funds from appropriation to actual utilization, and ensure the continuity and security of the system. The measure also assigns specific responsibilities to concerned government agencies. DICT shall serve as the lead implementing agency and may engage qualified private-sector partners, technology providers, and academic institutions, subject to applicable procurement laws and regulations. DBM shall ensure the integration and timely submission of national budget data, while COA shall incorporate blockchain-based records into its audit systems and processes. All government agencies, bureaus, offices, commissions, and government-owned or controlled corporations shall likewise integrate their financial management systems into the blockchain- based budget system and submit the required budget, procurement, and expenditure information. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10842
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING MICROINSURANCE MUTUAL BENEFIT ASSOCIATIONS AS INSTRUMENTS OF SOCIAL PROTECTION, FINANCIAL INCLUSION, AND COMMUNITY-BASED RISK PROTECTION, RATIONALIZING THEIR TAX TREATMENT, EXPANDING THEIR AUTHORITY TO PROVIDE MICROINSURANCE AND MICRO-RISK PROTECTION PRODUCTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Microinsurance Mutual Benefit Associations, or Mi-MBAs, play a vital role in providing affordable, accessible, and community-based risk protection to low- income, vulnerable, underserved, and informal-sector Filipinos. They serve members who are often excluded from, or unable to afford, conventional insurance products, including microentrepreneurs, farmers, fisherfolk, workers, cooperative members, microfinance clients, and families dependent on small livelihood activities. Unlike ordinary commercial insurance providers, Mi-MBAs are member- based and non-profit in character. They operate on the principles of mutual aid, pooled contributions, democratic participation, and community-based risk sharing. Through small and affordable contributions, members are able to obtain basic protection against death, sickness, accident, calamity, fire, flood, crop loss, livestock loss, livelihood disruption, business interruption, and other risks that may severely affect low-income households. Despite their importance, Mi-MBAs continue to face legal, tax, and operational limitations that affect their ability to provide broader and more responsive protection to their members. There is a need to clarify the tax treatment of member contributions, premiums, dues, assessments, claims expense, benefit funds, guaranty funds, reserves, member equity value, investment income, revenue- generating activities, and related documents. There is likewise a need to rationalize the tax burden on non-life microinsurance products so that transaction costs do not unduly reduce the benefits intended for low-income members. The need for non-life microinsurance has become more urgent in light of the recurring risks faced by low-income communities. Many Mi- MBA members do not only need protection against death or life-related contingencies. They also need protection against re, typhoon, ood, earthquake, crop loss, livestock loss, damage to residential homes used for livelihood, loss of tools and equipment, business inventory loss, livelihood asset loss, and microenterprise interruption. These risks are often too small for ordinary insurance markets, but too devastating for poor households and microentrepreneurs to bear on their own. This bill therefore seeks to strengthen Mi-MBAs by allowing quali ed associations, subject to the approval and supervision of the Insurance Commission, to provide limited non-life microinsurance products to their members. The authority granted is not intended to convert Mi-MBAs into full commercial non-life insurance companies. Rather, it is limited to member-based, low-value, microinsurance-speci c products, subject to actuarial review, reserve requirements, separate accounting, risk management standards, reinsurance, catastrophe protection, and other safeguards prescribed by the Insurance Commission. The bill also recognizes that Mi-MBAs may not always be legally, technically, or nancially capable of developing or underwriting all products needed by their members. For this reason, it authorizes Mi-MBAs to facilitate access to Micro- Products and micro-risk protection products issued by duly licensed or regulated providers, such as commercial insurers, non-life insurers, pre-need companies, health maintenance organizations, takaful operators, and other authorized risk- protection providers. This authority is limited to facilitation, administration, servicing, collection, member education, and claims assistance, and does not authorize Mi-MBAs to act as underwriters or issuers of products beyond their license. This measure also supports the development of Micro-Products, including Microinsurance and Micro Takaful, as inclusive and affordable protection mechanisms for low-income and informal-sector members. These products are intended to expand access to basic protection while remaining subject to the rules and supervision of the Insurance Commission and other appropriate regulators. To ensure sustainability, the bill authorizes Mi-MBAs to engage in regulated investments and revenue-generating activities, provided that such activities are incidental, complementary, or supportive of their mutual bene t and microinsurance purposes. Any net income from these activities must be used exclusively for member-bene t purposes, including payment or enhancement of bene ts, reduction or stabilization of member contributions, strengthening of reserves and member equity value funds, improvement of claims processing, digitalization, nancial literacy, disaster preparedness, calamity assistance, educational scholarships, civil documentation assistance, and other member-support programs. The bill likewise promotes the digital transformation of Mi-MBAs. It encourages the adoption of secured, safe, accessible, and member-friendly digital fi fi fi fi fi fl fi fi fi systems for onboarding, know-your-customer procedures, contribution collection, certi cate issuance, claims ling and payment, member engagement, regulatory reporting, tracking of member equity value, and product monitoring. This will make Mi-MBA operations more ef cient, transparent, responsive, and accessible to members. At the same time, the bill strengthens member protection. It requires clear disclosure of bene ts, exclusions, fees, charges, claims requirements, and the identity of the actual issuer or underwriter in the case of facilitated products. It also requires timely claims processing, written explanation for denied claims, internal grievance mechanisms, annual or periodic reporting, internal audit, risk management, data privacy safeguards, and member education, consistent with the Bill of Rights of Policyholders and applicable issuances of the Insurance Commission. The bill does not remove or diminish the authority of the Insurance Commission. On the contrary, it reinforces the Commission’s supervisory, visitorial, regulatory, and enforcement powers over Mi-MBAs, their products, funds, investments, partnerships, facilitated products
