label: HB 10843
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MONTHLY DISABILITY SUPPORT ALLOWANCE FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES (PWDs), PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly mandates the State to prioritize the needs of the underprivileged, sick, elderly, disabled, women, and children. Specifically, Section 13 of Article XIII provides that the State shall establish a special agency for disabled persons for their rehabilitation, self-development, and self-reliance, and their integration into the mainstream of society. 21 While the passage of Republic Act No. 7277, otherwise known as the "Magna Carta for Persons with Disabilities," and its subsequent amendments have significantly advanced the rights of Persons with Disabilities (PWDs) through tax exemptions, mandatory discounts, and health coverage, substantial economic gaps remain. PWDs in the Philippines continually face a compounding cycle of poverty and vulnerability. 27 Living with a disability entails significant, unavoidable extra costs. Families and individuals must routinely absorb expenses for specialized medical care, rehabilitation, assistive devices, therapy, accessible transportation, and personal assistance. These "disability costs" run parallel to an severely restricted capacity to generate income, as PWDs encounter disproportionate barriers to formal employment and livelihood opportunities. 33 This bill seeks to address these systemic inequities by establishing a guaranteed, non- conditional Monthly Disability Support Allowance in the initial amount of Two Thousand Pesos (₱2,000.00) for all registered PWDs. 37 Crucially, to prevent this financial lifeline from being eroded by macroeconomic pressures, this measure introduces a mandatory Inflation Indexation mechanism. By legally tethering the monthly allowance to the annual Consumer Price Index (CPI) through the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the State ensures that the real purchasing power of the social safety net is shielded against inflation and rising utility and commodity costs. 43 To ensure long-term fiscal sustainability and accountability, the bill mandates that funding be directly and explicitly integrated into the annual General Appropriations Act (GAA). This allowance acts not as a handout, but as a crucial economic equalizer aimed at lowering poverty poverty rates, mitigating the financial shocks of living with a disability, and fostering authentic social inclusion. 49 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 51 52 53 HON. label: HB 10844
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A MAGNA CARTA FOR PRIVATE HEALTH WORKERS, PROVIDING FUNDS FOR ITS IMPLEMENTATION AND ENFORCEMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill aims to institutionalize a Magna Carta for Private Health Workers, extending to health personnel in the private sector protections comparable to those enjoyed by their counterparts in government service under Republic Act (RA) No. 7305, otherwise known as the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers. The measure finds constitutional anchor in Article II, Sections 15 and 18, which mandate the government to protect public health and uphold the welfare and rights of workers. Furthermore, Article XIII, Sections 3, 11, and 14 of the 1987 Constitution, which respectively mandate the State to afford full protection to labor, to ensure the delivery of quality and affordable health services, and to promote equal work opportunities regardless of sex, disability, or other status. The Philippine Government has continuously underscored the critical roles of health workers in carrying out health programs and projects. The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) issued DBM Budget Circular 2020-4 on July 17, 2020, which implemented the Supreme Court ruling to upgrade entry-level government nurses (Nurse I) from Salary Grade 11 to Salary Grade 1. Although this was a milestone for our public health workers, this has resulted in a disparity of benefits and privileges between public health workers and private health workers. The Magna Carta of Private Health Workers aims to level the playing field between public and private health workers, and seeks to afford them the benefits and safeguards they deserve. While it will substantially mirror the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers, this proposed measure seeks to implement a minimum wage rate for nurses and other health workers, subject to the increases deemed appropriate by a tripartite body. This proposed measure seeks to: a) Align its labor standards provisions (probationary employment, hours of work, overtime, holiday and rest-day pay, wage-fixing, legal interest, and due process) with the Labor Code of the Philippines, as renumbered by Department of Advisory No. 01-15, and with prevailing Supreme Court jurisprudence; b) Reconcile the proposed statutory minimum wage with the wage-fixing machinery under Republic Act No. 6727 (Wage Rationalization Act) by treating it as a national floor without prejudice to more favorable Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board (RTWPB) wage orders; c) Qualify the right to self-organization and to strike with the Secretary of Labor and Employment's power to assume jurisdiction over labor disputes in industries indispensable to the national interest under Article 278(g) of the Labor Code, and with the concomitant duty to maintain an unhampered skeletal workforce in hospitals and clinics, in order to safeguard patients' constitutional right to life and health; and d) Clarify that the funds to be appropriated under this Act are for the Department of Labor and Employment's administrative and enforcement functions, and not a government subsidy for private-sector wages and benefits, which remain the obligation of private employers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this legislative measure is earnestly sought. JC M. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION AND SAFETY OF PEDESTRIANS, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 4136, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE LAND TRANSPORTATION AND TRAFFIC CODE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 Initiatives to address the worsening transport crisis tend to dominate the public discourse and remedial measures proposed are primarily centered on alleviating the plight of motorists and commuters. Conveniently sidelined in the race to identify and propose solutions to the traffic problem are the pedestrians whose protection appear to be neglected and whose safety, when compromised on any road, are merely relegated as ordinary traffic incidents. 29 The root causes of road traffic deaths and injuries are often overshadowed by the growing conundrum of vehicular traffic. Measures to effectively address road traffic deaths and injuries have not been seriously considered and pushed with steadfastness. As a result, deaths and injuries associated with road traffic continue to rise and have reached alarming levels in recent years. 35 In its Global Status Report on Road Safety released in 2018. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that road traffic deaths continue to rise in the Philippines, with an estimated 12,690 deaths in 2016. About half of the number of road traffic deaths involved vulnerable road users such as motorcyclists, cyclists and pedestrians. 40 The WHO considers road traffic injuries as a major but neglected public health challenge. It underscores that unsafe road traffic systems are seriously harming global public health and development. It contends that the level of road traffic injury is unacceptable but it is largely avoidable. 45 Indeed, a serious effort to put in place an effective and sustainable prevention measure is now imperative. This effort can commence by enhancing our archaic traffic laws, according to paramount consideration to the protection and safety of pedestrians, penalizing any person who violates the traffic laws, and mandating the training of violators. 51 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 1 2 3 REP. label: HB 10846
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A MINIMUM AGE FOR SOCIAL MEDIA USE, PRESCRIBING OBLIGATIONS FOR SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS, PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Social media and digital platforms have become deeply embedded in the daily lives of Filipino children and young people. As of early 2025, the Philippines had approximately 97.5 million internet users, representing 83.8% of the country’s population, while social media user identities reached approximately 90.8 million or around 78% of the population. Filipinos also remain among the world’s heaviest internet users, spending an average of 8 hours and 52 minutes online daily. While digital platforms provide opportunities for education, communication, entrepreneurship, creativity, civic participation, and access to information, they also expose minors to increasingly serious online harms. International child protection organizations such as UNICEF have documented how cyberbullying, online harassment, harmful content exposure, manipulative online behavior, and compulsive platform use can negatively affect the emotional, psychological, and social well-being of children and adolescents. UNICEF has likewise emphasized that cyberbullying may lead to anxiety, emotional distress, social withdrawal, loss of motivation, and mental health consequences among children and young people. Today, digital platforms are no longer merely passive communication tools. Many social media systems are intentionally designed to maximize engagement through algorithmic amplification, personalized feeds, behavioral targeting, notifications, and continuous content exposure. These systems increasingly shape how children consume information, interact socially, and form opinions, often at ages where they may not yet possess sufficient maturity, discernment, or emotional resilience to safely navigate online risks. This proposed “Children’s Safety in Social Media Act” seeks to establish a minimum age requirement of sixteen (16) years for the use of age-restricted social media platforms and to impose enforceable obligations upon platform providers to adopt reasonable, effective, proportionate, and privacy-preserving safeguards against underage access and harmful online exposure. The measure adopts a rights-based and risk-based regulatory framework that balances child protection, constitutional freedoms, privacy rights, and access to information. Instead of placing the burden solely upon parents, guardians, or schools, the bill places primary responsibility upon covered social media platform providers to implement age assurance mechanisms and safety-by-design measures proportionate to the risks posed by their platforms. The bill further recognizes the importance of protecting privacy and preventing excessive data collection. Accordingly, it prohibits the mandatory use of government-issued identification as the sole method for age verification and requires compliance with Republic Act No. 10173, otherwise known as the “Data Privacy Act of 2012.” It likewise mandates data minimization, purpose limitation, and safeguards against the unauthorized use or retention of personal information collected for age assurance purposes. The measure also promotes digital citizenship, media literacy, and public awareness programs involving the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), Department of Education (DepEd), National Privacy Commission (NPC), National Telecommunications Commission (NTC), Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), Department of Justice (DOJ), Commission on Human Rights (CHR), and other relevant agencies. The bill recognizes that effective child online protection requires a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach involving families, schools, communities, regulators, and technology platforms themselves. The bill additionally establishes mechanisms for disabling underage accounts, reporting violations, implementing platform accountability measures, and enforcing administrative penalties for non-compliance. These provisions seek to ensure that online child safety obligations are enforceable, proportionate, and consistent with due process and constitutional protections. Globally, governments have increasingly moved toward stronger online child protection frameworks. Australia enacted legislation in 2024 restricting social media access for children below sixteen (16) years old, reflecting growing international concern regarding the impact of social media platforms upon minors. Similar global policy discussions continue in various jurisdictions concerning age assurance, child online safety, platform accountability, and digital well-being. This proposed measure likewise aligns with the constitutional duty of the State to defend the right of children to assistance, including proper care and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and conditions prejudicial to their development. It bears emphasizing that a substantially similar measure was already passed on Third Reading in the Senate during the 19th Congress through Senate Bill No. 1955 principally authored by Senator Loren Legarda. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 10847
title: AN ACT GRANTING A FINAL FIREARMS AMNESTY, STRENGTHENING ACCOUNTABILITY FOR LOOSE FIREARMS, PROSECUTING THE UNLAWFUL POSSESSION OF A LOOSE FIREARM AS A SEPARATE AND DISTINCT OFFENSE, ESTABLISHING GUN-FREE SCHOOL ZONES, IMPOSING SAFE STORAGE AND ADULT LIABILITY DUTIES, REGULATING PRIVATELY MADE AND UNTRACEABLE FIREARMS, AMENDING FOR THESE PURPOSES REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10591, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "COMPREHENSIVE FIREARMS AND AMMUNITION REGULATION ACT," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our schools should be the safest rooms in the Republic. In the span of fifty-seven days, two of them became crime scenes. On June 22, 2026, two students aged fourteen and fifteen opened fire inside San Jose National High School in Tacloban City, killing three of their classmates and wounding twenty. On August 18, 2026, a Grade 9 student walked into the Ateneo de Zamboanga University junior high school with a pistol and a rifle, killed a schoolmate, and then took his own life. In both tragedies, the guns came from the adult world around the children. In Tacloban, one weapon was the service pistol of a police officer, and the other a revolver registered to a security agency, and the strongest charge the State could bring against the firearm keeper was malversation. When a child dies, and the law can speak only of property, the law is insufficient. The numbers confirm what the tragedies revealed. The Philippine National Police estimates that around 1.7 million loose firearms circulate against about 4.12 million registered firearms, that more than 700,000 registrations have lapsed, and that almost all gun crimes are committed with loose firearms. Since 1980, the government has declared at least thirteen firearms amnesties. All of them failed, because each offered forgiveness without finality and without the consequence that must follow. This bill does what those amnesties did not. First, it grants one final, non- extendible amnesty of one hundred twenty days, with penalties and surcharges waived, fees reduced, registration brought by mobile teams to rural and island communities, and every firearm test-fired and screened against crime gun databases so that no weapon used against our people is ever laundered into legality. Second, it ends the rule that lets an offender who uses an unlicensed gun escape a separate charge for the gun itself: unlawful possession of a loose firearm becomes a separate and distinct offense. Third, it reserves the gravest, non-bailable penalty for the gravest conduct: using a loose firearm in a crime, trafficking in firearms, bringing a firearm into a school, and arming a minor. Fourth, it makes safe storage a legal duty, holds adults to account when their negligence places a gun in the hands of a child, and brings privately made and 3D- printed firearms under the law. The Constitution permits a non-bailable offense only where the penalty reaches reclusion perpetua, and it forbids cruel and disproportionate punishment. This measure honors both commands. The farmer with an inherited shotgun is given a door to legality. The trafficker, the smuggler, and the one who hands a gun to a child meet the full weight of the law. One last open door, then a locked gate. The approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL "JAVI" L. label: HB 10848
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE TRADE OF GOODS PRODUCED WHOLLY OR IN PART WITH FORCED LABOR AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On June 2, 2026, the Office of the United States Trade Representative found that the Philippines had failed to impose and effectively enforce an express prohibition on the importation of goods produced wholly or in part through forced labor. On July 23, 2026, the United States consequently imposed an additional tariff of twelve and one- half percent (12.5%) on products of the Philippines, subject to specified exemptions. The tariff took effect on July 24, 2026. The Executive Branch has issued a Joint Administrative Order establishing an inter-agency mechanism for investigating imported goods suspected of having been produced through forced labor. However, an administrative issuance is not a substitute for an unequivocal and permanent statutory prohibition. This bill expressly prohibits the importation of goods produced wholly or in part through forced labor, authorizes the Bureau of Customs to exclude and forfeit such goods, and provides corresponding penalties. It also requires permanent inter-agency coordination for its effective implementation. Its immediate enactment will protect workers and Filipino enterprises from unfair competition and provide a clear legal basis for seeking the modification or termination of the additional United States tariffs imposed on Philippine products. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. RAYMOND ADRIAN E. label: HB 10849
title: AN ACT FURTHER PROMOTING ENTREPRENEURSHIP BY STRENGTHENING, EMPOWERING, AND ENHANCING THE FINANCING AND OTHER SUPPORT PROGRAMS FOR MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6977, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "MAGNA CARTA FOR MICRO, SMALL AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMEs)"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) are a significant component of the Philippine economy, contributing substantially to employment generation, entrepreneurship, innovation, and economic growth. According to the Department of Trade and Industry’s 2024 Philippine MSME Statistics, MSMEs accounted for 99.63%, or 1,236,908, of the 1,241,476 registered business establishments in the country. Republic Act No. 6977, as amended, or the “Magna Carta for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs),”provides the existing framework for the promotion and development of MSMEs. However, changing economic conditions and emerging challenges call for stronger and more responsive government support. This proposed measure seeks to further strengthen the Magna Carta by improving access to financing, simplifying regulatory requirements, expanding market opportunities, supporting digitalization and innovation, and strengthening MSME assistance at the local level. Among its key reforms are the proposed 20% allocation of government procurement opportunities for eligible MSMEs, strengthened MSME financing, an Enterprise Rehabilitation Fund of up to ₱500 million for calamity-stricken MSMEs, and an increase in the authorized capital of the Small Business Corporation from ₱10 billion to ₱50 billion. The measure also promotes simplified loan requirements, cash-flow-based lending, alternative credit data, digital financial literacy, entrepreneurship education, and the creation of MSMED Councils in cities, municipalities, and barangays to ensure that MSME policies respond to local needs. Through these reforms, the bill seeks to create a more enabling environment where Filipino MSMEs can start, sustain, expand, and recover their businesses, contributing to inclusive and resilient economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10850
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE AND RESPONSIVE CIVIL REGISTRATION AND VITAL STATISTICS SYSTEM, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive, responsive, and modern Civil Registration and Vital Statistics (CRVS) system that will ensure the universal, timely, and secure registration of vital events involving Filipinos, whether in the country or abroad. It aims to address fragmented civil registration processes by creating an integrated framework that strengthens legal identity, improves public service delivery, and ensures the accuracy and reliability of civil registry records. The measure recognizes civil registration as an important component of protecting individual rights and facilitating access to essential government services. It seeks to ensure that the registration of births, deaths, marriages, and other civil status events remains free, accessible, and responsive, particularly for marginalized and vulnerable groups such as indigenous peoples, foundlings, children in need of special protection, persons with disabilities, and overseas Filipinos. The bill also supports the modernization and digitization of civil registration through the interconnection of existing systems and the development of a national database. It promotes closer coordination among the Philippine Statistics Authority, local government units, and other concerned government agencies to streamline processes, reduce delays, strengthen data management, and improve the integrity of civil registry information. Ultimately, the measure seeks to strengthen the country's civil registration system while upholding the principles of legal identity, data privacy, accessibility, and inclusive governance. By ensuring that every Filipino is properly registered and recognized before the law, the State can help provide individuals with more reliable access to public services, legal protections, and other opportunities that depend on official civil registry records. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10851
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING, INSTITUTIONALIZING A PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK FINANCING AND INSURANCE STRATEGY FOR PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE ASSETS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, disasters are not rare events, they are a constant reality. Typhoons, floods, earthquakes, and volcanic eruptions strike with such frequency that they have become part of the daily lives of our people. Each storm that destroys homes, each tremor that shakes our land, is a reminder that our nation sits at the center of one of the most dangerous regions in the world. The 2025 World Risk Index confirms a difficult reality: the Philippines remains the most disaster‑prone country in the world, holding this position for four consecutive years. This is not just a number on a report—it reflects the daily struggles of millions of Filipinos who live under constant threat from typhoons, earthquakes, floods, and other natural hazards that place lives, livelihoods, and communities at risk. This ranking is a reminder of the urgent need to strengthen disaster preparedness, improve infrastructure, and invest in climate resilience. At the same time, it highlights the courage and resilience of the Filipino people, who continue to rebuild and rise after each calamity. Their strength must be matched by decisive action from government, civil society, and international partners to protect communities, uphold dignity, and secure a safer future for generations to come. The Climate Change Commission estimates that disasters cost our economy around 200 billion pesos annually. Since 1990, more than 565 natural disasters have struck the Philippines, claiming nearly 70,000 lives and causing damages worth $23 billion. These numbers show the heavy burden disasters place on our people and our economy. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, marked a significant advancement in national policy. It redefined disaster management from a reactive framework to a proactive system centered on preparedness and risk reduction. Nevertheless, despite these institutional reforms, the economic consequences of disasters remain substantial and continue to challenge financial resilience. This proposed measure seeks to strengthen our resilience by creating a Disaster Risk Financing and Insurance Council. The Council will develop a framework to ensure quick, reliable, and well- coordinated financing for disaster-related repair, reconstruction, and rehabilitation of government- owned infrastructure. It will use both insurance and non-insurance mechanisms to guarantee that funds are available when urgently needed. The bill also establishes a National Public Asset Insurance Consortium, led by the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS) and composed of insurance and reinsurance companies offering public asset coverage. This Consortium will craft a national disaster risk insurance strategy, ensure faster claims processing, and support rapid recovery of damaged public assets. By protecting critical infrastructure and ensuring timely financial support, this measure will help communities recover faster, reduce economic losses, and limit the long-term impact of disasters on our people. It is a step toward building a stronger, safer, and more resilient Philippines. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10852
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE GRANT OF EMERGENCY LEAVE TO EMPLOYEES IN THE PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS DIRECTLY AFFECTED BY CALAMITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is no stranger to calamities. The country experiences an average of twenty (20) typhoons annually, in addition to recurring floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. Although Filipinos have demonstrated remarkable resilience in the face of these events, workers who are directly affected by calamities should be afforded sufficient time to attend to their safety, recover from damages and losses, and address urgent personal and family concerns without the added burden of reporting for work. Hence, this proposed bill seeks to institutionalize the grant of five (5) days of emergency leave to employees in both the public and private sectors who are directly affected by calamities. It aims to provide workers with a reasonable period within which to recover from the effects of a disaster, attend to their basic needs and restore their homes and livelihoods, without fear of losing their employment or suffering further financial hardship. It is also consistent with the existing government policies and issuances recognizing the need to protect employees affected by natural disasters and similar occurrences. These include Civil Service Commission Memorandum Circular No. 2, Series of 2012 entitled Special Emergency Leave to Government Employees Affected by Natural Disasters, Memorandum Circular No. 16, Series of 2012 or the Supplemental Guidelines in the Grant of Special Emergency Leave and Labor Advisory No. 17, Series of 2022 on the Suspension of Work in the Private Sector by reason of Weather Disturbances and Similar Occurrences issued by the Department of Labor and Employment. This legislative measure is likewise proposed in furtherance of the constitutional duty of the State to afford full protection to labor and promote their welfare. It is a positive stance to ensuring that Filipinos are able to recover from calamities despite continuing threats these pose to their livelihood, property, financial resources, and, in some cases, the lives of their loved ones. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. LAZATIN, JR. label: HB 10853
title: AN ACT REMOVING SYSTEMS LOSSES AS A SEPARATE COMPONENT OF ELECTRICITY BILLS, EMPOWERING THE ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION TO DETERMINE THE COSTS THAT MAY BE RECOVERED AS PART OF DISTRIBUTION SERVICE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an essential daily need for every Filipino family and a key driver of our local economy. However, for years, consumers have been forced to shoulder high electricity bills—partly because of "system loss charges." Electric companies are allowed to pass the cost of lost electricity straight to consumers, whether the loss is from aging power lines, poor equipment, administrative errors, or power theft. Given that the distribution utilities can easily pass these costs to the public, these companies have little reason to modernize their equipment, fix operational issues, or stop power theft. The burden falls entirely on the paying consumer. This bill, the "System Loss Charge Abolition Act" amends Republic Act No. 9136 (EPIRA) to fix this unfair arrangement. Under this measure the power companies can no longer list system loss as a separate pass-through fee on monthly bills, shall strictly direct the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) to strictly ban utilities from recovering costs caused by power theft, poor maintenance, inefficiency, or administrative mistakes and provides a transition period up to three years (3) years to give utilities time to fix their systems without disrupting power service. By forcing distribution utilities to take full responsibility for their own technical and operational losses, this bill will make power rates fair, hold power companies accountable, and shall give relief to everyday electricity consumers. For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 10854
title: AN ACT CREATING THE METROPOLITAN CEBU INTEGRATED WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT BOARD, PRESCRIBING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water scarcity in Metropolitan Cebu has reached critical levels, threatening public health, economic productivity, and long-term urban resilience. Rapid population growth, uneven infrastructure development, and fragmented resource management have strained the region’s ability to ensure safe, sufficient, and sustainable water access for its residents, leaving a governance gap in one of the country’s most densely populated and economically vital corridors. Despite various efforts at the national and local levels, the absence of a unified, science-based, and locally responsive governance framework has hindered the development of long-term solutions. Jurisdictional overlaps, limited coordination among stakeholders, and the lack of integrated planning mechanisms have contributed to inefficiencies in water resource management and infrastructure investment. This bill proposes the creation of the Metropolitan Cebu Integrated Water Resources Management Board. It is a multi-sectoral, inter-local body mandated to plan, coordinate, and implement strategic water resource initiatives across key cities and municipalities in the region. The Board shall be empowered to identify and harness viable water sources, promote conservation technologies, and facilitate infrastructure development through data-driven and climate-resilient approaches. By institutionalizing this Board, the measure aims to bridge existing governance gaps, foster collaboration among local governments and stakeholders, and ensure that water resource planning is aligned with the region’s development goals and climate adaptation needs. It affirms the constitutional right to water and reinforces the State’s duty to promote equitable, transparent, and sustainable resource management. For these reasons, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. REP. EDUARDO R. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With almost everything within reach of our fingertips because of the internet, several unsuspecting debtors became vulnerable to debt-shaming and harassment by debt collectors or debt collection agencies. As of August 2023, the Securities and Exchange Commission (“SEC”) has revoked the primary registration of 2,084 lending companies and ordered the closure of 81 online lending applications for their non-compliance with Republic Act 9474 or the Lending Company Regulation Act for using threats, obscene language, false representation and maliciously using personal information in their debt collection practices.1 The number of online lenders involved in this kind of debt collection practice is quite alarming, especially considering that there is a lack of a law that penalizes said practice. label: HB 10856
title: AN ACT PROVIDING ENHANCED PROTECTION, SECURITY, AND SAFETY BENEFITS FOR MEDIA PERSONNEL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Media personnel play an essential role in keeping the public informed and holding democratic institutions accountable. Despite this immense responsibility, journalists, newsroom staff, and field personnel often work under hazardous conditions, economic instability, and a lack of adequate social safety nets. The proposed bill, entitled the "Media Personnel Welfare Act," intends to address these systemic challenges by establishing clear social, economic, and safety protections for all media personnel in the private sector, including freelancers and regular employees. Specifically, the measure provides a guaranteed minimum compensation and benefits by enforcing compliance with standard labor laws, minimum wage rates, mandatory coverage under the SSS, Pag-IBIG, PhilHealth, and retirement benefits, mandates a minimum hazard pay of ₱500.00 per day for personnel assigned in dangerous, distressed, or emergency areas, alongside compulsory provision of basic protective gear such as bulletproof vests, helmets, and medical equipment. Further, entitles workers to compulsory coverage including ₱200,000 for death benefits, up to ₱200,000 for disability benefits, and up to ₱100,000 for medical insurance, grants automatic regular status to media personnel after six (6) months of service- whether continuous or cumulative—to curb unfair employment practices and finally, establishes the News Media Tripartite Council under the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to serve as a platform for policy alignment, dispute resolution, and stakeholder dialogue. 1 By improving working conditions and ensuring fair compensation, this legislation seeks to build a safer and more secure environment for a responsible and sustainable media. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 10857
title: AN ACT GRANTING POSTPARTUM DEPRESSION LEAVE TO QUALIFIED FEMALE WORKERS AND SUPPORT LEAVE TO THEIR QUALIFIED PARTNERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, female workers are entitled to one hundred five (105) days of paid maternity leave for childbirth, regardless of the manner of delivery, under Republic Act No. 11210, otherwise known as the “105-Day Expanded Maternity Leave Law.” A qualified solo mother is entitled to an additional fifteen (15) days of paid maternity leave, while a female worker may opt to extend her maternity leave for an additional thirty (30) days without pay, subject to the conditions provided by law. In cases of miscarriage or emergency termination of pregnancy, a female worker is entitled to sixty (60) days of paid maternity leave. Under R.A No. 8187, otherwise known as the “Paternity Leave Act of 1996,” a qualified married male employee is entitled to seven (7) days of paid paternity leave for the first four (4) deliveries of his legitimate spouse with whom he is cohabiting. Republic Act No. 11210 likewise permits a female worker to allocate up to seven (7) days of her maternity leave credits to the child’s father or, in the circumstances specified by law, to a qualified alternate caregiver. The allocated benefit is separate from and in addition to the benefit under Republic Act No. 8187. Although maternity leave provides a period of rest, recovery, and recuperation in connection with childbirth, Republic Act No. 11210 does not expressly establish a separate leave benefit specifically for female workers who are clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression. Postpartum depression is a serious mental-health condition that may affect a woman’s ability to care for herself and her child and may require professional treatment, counseling, medical monitoring, and family support. Its symptoms may arise after childbirth and may persist beyond the period ordinarily needed for physical recovery. According to an online medical article, postpartum conditions may include postpartum blues, also known as “baby blues”, postpartum depression, and postpartum psychosis.1 Postpartum blues are common and generally begin within the first few days of delivery, but their symptoms may subside within a week or two weeks. Postpartum depression is more intense and severe than the baby blues as it can start within one week of delivery and last several months. The article describes postpartum psychosis as an extremely severe form of postpartum depression that requires emergency medical attention. Its symptoms generally develop quickly and intensely, lasting for many weeks or months.2 This proposed legislation seeks to grant thirty (30) days of paid postpartum depression leave to qualified female workers who are clinically diagnosed with postpartum depression. It likewise seeks to grant seven (7) days of paid support leave to the child’s father or the female worker’s qualified partner so that the latter may provide care and support during the female worker’s treatment or recovery. The benefits under this bill shall be separate from and in addition to the maternity leave benefits under Republic Act No. 11210, the paternity leave benefit under Republic Act No. 8187, and any maternity leave credits allocated under Republic Act No. 11210. They shall not be deducted from the female worker’s existing maternity leave credits or from any other leave benefit to which the worker is entitled under law, a collective bargaining agreement, an employment contract, or an established company policy, when the latter is more beneficial. Postpartum depression is a serious concern that affects the behavior, livelihood, and well- being of women after birth, as well as that of their newborns and families. Granting a separate leave benefit will enable qualified female workers to obtain appropriate treatment and additional time for medically necessary recovery, while allowing their qualified partners to provide essential care and support. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CARMELO G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed General Appropriations Bill (GAB) for Fiscal Year (FY) 2027 translates the National Expenditure Program (NEP) into the annual spending authority of the National Government. It is anchored on the theme: "People-Centered Growth for an Inclusive and Resilient Future" Consistent with this theme, the proposed appropriations direct public resources toward expanding access to quality education and healthcare, strengthening social protection, creating quality employment and sustainable livelihoods, improving food and energy security, accelerating development of strategic and climate-resilient infrastructure, and reinforcing responsive, transparent and accountable public institutions. The measure carries forward the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 and Ambisyon Natin 2040 through investments in human capital, social protection, food and energy security, strategic infrastructure, digital transformation, climate resilience, peace and security, and capable institutions. The FY 2027 proposal was prepared amid slower economic growth, inflationary pressure, geopolitical conflict, volatile fuel prices, climate-related risks, and constrained fiscal space. These conditions require a budget that protects essential government services, sustains productive investment, responds to immediate vulnerabilities, and preserves the country's capacity to finance development over the medium term. Constitutional Mandate and the Power of the Purse The 1987 Constitution vests in Congress the power of the purse. Through appropriations legislation, Congress determines the purposes for which public funds may be spent, the amounts that may be made available, and the conditions governing their use. This authority is inseparable from legislative oversight and ensures that public money is applied only to lawful, necessary, efficient, and accountable ends. i Article VI, Section 24 provides: "All appropriation, revenue or tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills, shall originate exclusively in the House of Representatives, but the Senate may propose or concur with amendments." Article VI, Section 29(1) further declares: "No money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law." Article VII, Section 22 states: "The President shall submit to the Congress within thirty days from the opening of every regular session, as the basis of the general appropriations bill, a budget of expenditures and sources of financing, including receipts from existing and proposed revenue measures." Constitutional Timeline for the FY 2027 Budget On July 27, 2026, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. delivered his fifth State of the Nation Address, formally opening the Second Regular Session of the Twentieth Congress and setting the Administration's policy direction for FY 2027. On August 11, 2026, the President submitted the proposed FY 2027 National Budget to Congress, together with the President's Budget Message, the National Expenditure Program, and the Budget of Expenditures and Sources of Financing, in compliance with Article VII, Section 22 of the Constitution. The submission commenced the House review through the Committee on Appropriations, which examines agency requirements, performance, implementation capacity, policy coherence, and changes from the FY 2026 General Appropriations Act, and recommends the allocations and safeguards needed to address national and local priorities. Fiscal Context, Strategy, and Directions The FY 2027 budget seeks to support economic recovery and transformation while advancing fiscal consolidation. Under the macroeconomic assumptions adopted for the budget, real gross domestic product is projected to grow by 5.0 to 6.0 percent in 2027, following an adjusted growth outlook of 3.5 to 4.5 percent for 2026. The macroeconomic assumptions for FY 2027 include an inflation forecast of 4.0 to 5.0 percent, a foreign exchange rate of ₱60.00 to ₱62.00 per US dollar, and a Dubai crude oil price of US$70.00 to US$90.00 per barrel. Goods exports are projected to grow by 4.0 percent, while goods imports are projected to increase by 5.0 percent. Financing-related assumptions place the 364-day Treasury Bill Rate at 5.0 to 6.0 percent, and the six-month Secured Overnight Financing Rate at 3.0 to 4.0 percent. Collectively, these parameters provide general planning references for estimating revenues, financing requirements, operating costs, procurement requirements, and the resource needs of government programs and projects. label: HB 10862
title: AN ACT REMOVING SYSTEMS LOSS AS A SEPARATE COMPONENT OF ELECTRICITY BILLS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 25 AND 43 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It has been more than 25 years since the passage of Republic Act No. 9136 or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act (EPIRA). While this measure restructured the energy sector in the country to ensure reliable electric supply, crucial amendments thereto are said to be long overdue to be responsive to the realities faced by Filipino households. One of the main burdens of the Filipino Household is the rising electricity costs, with the Philippines recorded to have the highest electricity rates in Southeast Asia1. One of the significant factor to this burden is the practice of on system loss charges to end-users. Under Section 43(f) of EPIRA, distribution utilities (DUs) and electric cooperatives (ECs) are legally allowed to pass system loss charges directly onto end-users. While Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) enforces a recoverable system loss cap for private DUs at 5.5% to 6.5%, other ECs, particularly those operating across Mindanao and rural provinces, are permitted pass-through caps of up to 12.0% to 12.5%. This disparity places an unequal financial strain on households in rural areas and Mindanao, where consumers pay significantly higher bills to cover operational inefficiencies, technical line losses, and non-technical losses like power pilferage and theft. 1 Lelis, Brix. "DOE: Philippines power rates now highest in SEA." The Philippine Star, 21 Jul. 2026, https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/21/2543545/doe-philippines-power-rates-now-highest-sea. Accessed 16 Aug. 2026. Because these losses fall squarely within the operational control of distributors, current policy unfairly socializes business failures by shifting the cost onto captive consumers who receive no benefit from energy they never consumed. To address this, this measure seeks to reform the system loss pass-through framework to protect end-users and mandate true utility accountability. Through the removal of the system loss pass-through charges, we protect consumer interest and encouraging DUs and ECs to protecting the interest of the Filipino consumers by ensuring that they no longer pay for “ghost electricity” due to technical and non- technical system losses, and (2) encourage the DUs and ECs to improve operations through investment of modern infrastructures and efficient technologies to minimize or eliminate operational losses and inefficiencies. By requiring DUs and ECs to absorb operational inefficiencies rather than passing them on to end-users, this bill restores fairness to power pricing and safeguards the welfare of the Filipino households. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 10863
title: AN ACT EXCLUDING SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM VALUE-ADDED TAX ON ELECTRICITY, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The high cost of electricity remains one of the most pressing economic burdens on Filipino households. The imposition of the 12% Value-Added Tax (VAT) on the "system loss" component of electric bills is a major factor that adds to this monthly financial strain. Under the National Internal Revenue Code (NIRC), as amended, and existing Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) guidelines, the 12% VAT is computed on the gross bill, which is composed of generation, transmission, distribution, and system loss charges. System loss represents electricity lost during distribution due to technical line resistance or non-technical factors such as illegal hookups, theft, and metering errors. Consequently, consumers are not only paying for "ghost electricity" that they never consumed, but they are also paying a 12% VAT on top of those operational losses. The imposition of VAT on system loss fundamentally distorts the principle of Value-Added Tax, which is intended to tax actual consumption of goods or services. Paying VAT on power lost in transit or stolen by third parties forces end-users to shoulder a tax on an operational inefficiency. This tax, unfortunately, hits rural communities and Mindanao hardest. While private distribution utilities have ERC system loss caps between 5.5% and 6.5%, electric cooperatives operating in provinces and Mindanao carry caps of up to 12.0% to 12.5%. As a result, provincial households pay a disproportionately higher tax penalty simply because the system loss charge base in their electric bill is nearly double. To address this, this measure seeks to amend the NIRC and energy regulations to expressly exclude system loss charges from the computation of the 12% VAT on the sale of electricity. This ensures that the Filipino consumers only pay taxes on the actual electricity delivered to and consumed by their households. Together with the other proposed complementary legislative measures addressing system losses charges, this bill provides a direct and practical measure towards economic relief and tax fairness. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 10864
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Schools are meant to be one of the safest places for our children. This is where they learn, make friends, form their character, and develop skills they will need later in life. However, recent events in the country have shattered this expectation, turning our learning institutions into places of fear and anxiety. We do not have to look far for an example. Just last year, in the 2nd District of Parañaque, a Grade 8 student was fatally stabbed by a classmate inside Moonwalk National High School. Initial reports revealed that the conflict may have stemmed from a piece of makeup that was not lent by one student.1 Since the opening of School Year 2026-2027, there have already been multiple incidents of school-based violence, including two tragic school shootings in Tacloban– which killed 3 students and injured more than 202 – and Zamboanga–which killed 2 students including the perpetrator who took his own life.3 These incidents do not just 1 Macababbad, EJ; Tupas, Emmanuel. (2025). Grade 8 student killed by classmate over makeup kit. Philstar. Available at https://www.philstar.com/nation/2025/03/28/2431568/grade-8-student-killed-classmate-over-makeup- kit. 2 Gabieta, Joey. (2026). School shooting kills 3 students in Tacloban. Inquirer.net. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2250793/school-shooting-kills-3-students-in-tacloban. 3 Sigales, Jason; Agonoy, Leah. (2026). Ateneo de Zamboanga shooting: 2 students dead. Inquirer.net. Available at https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2287724/ateneo-de-zamboanga-shooting-2-students-dead. 1 affect our students. Last year, a teacher in Lanao del Sur was shot and killed by a student over a failing grade.4 These alarming incidents demonstrate the need for a comprehensive measure to ensure our children’s safety in school. This need is further supported by the findings of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), which noted that bullying and aggression often remain unreported because learners fear retaliation or do not know where or how to seek assistance5. Data from the Programme for International Student Assessment or PISA likewise show that bullying remains a significant concern among learners.6 To help address these incidents of school-based violence, this proposed measure seeks to establish, maintain, and periodically update a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework, which will prescribe the standards for school safety plans, school safety infrastructure and security measures, violence prevention and anti-bullying mechanisms, learner well-being and mental health promotion, and emergency preparedness. This measure also provides policies for a safe school culture, zero-tolerance against violence, and anti-bullying. This bill also specifies and clarifies the responsibilities of school heads, school counselors and counselor associates, learner formation officers, and school safety officers. In addition, it seeks to promote the meaningful participation of parents, guardians, and families in the improvement of school safety programs. It likewise prescribes safety infrastructure and equipment, such as CCTV cameras in strategic areas, appropriate screening equipment, visitor management systems, the presence of appropriate security personnel, and emergency equipment. Further, in recognition of the prevalence of technology in children’s lives, this measure also mandates schools to adopt policies and programs that promote safe, responsible and age-appropriate use of digital technologies, including measures to protect learners from cyberbullying. Finally, it requires schools to establish protocols for reporting, assessment, interventions, and immediate response to school safety concerns. No child should enter a classroom in fear. With this measure, we hope to ensure that our educational institutions are safe and remain conducive environments for learning. 4 Bravo, Drema. (2025). label: HB 10865
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE AGRICULTURE INFORMATION SYSTEM IN ALL CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, at its core, an agricultural economy, yet the persistent paradox of its farm sector is not scarcity, but supply mismatch. The bountiful harvests of our farmers often go to rot or are sold at a loss, while nearby markets face shortages and higher prices for the very same commodities. This chronic disruption is a traceable crisis that recurs due to failure of information and coordination between production and demand. As a country with agricultural yields, it is highly necessary that we bank on the strengths of our existing industries. It is also shown during times of emergency and crisis that there exists a gap in the information system involving our farming sectors. This pattern has repeated with striking regularity in recent years. In Benguet, in one instance, the country’s so-called “Salad Bowl” that supplies nearly 80% of the upland vegetables sold in Metro Manila, cabbage farmers have seen farmgate prices collapse to as low as P4 to P10 per kilo, forcing many to either sell at a loss or abandon their harvest altogether, even as prices in the end-market remain multiple times higher.1 Likewise, in Nueva Ecija and Rizal provinces, tomato farmers faced a similar collapse in early 2025, with farmgate prices falling to P4 to P5 per kilo, prompting Department of Science and Technology – Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic, and Natural Resources Research and Development (DOST- PCAARRD) and Sen. Kiko Pangilinan to launch multiple initiatives, such as “Operation Sagip-Kamatis-an” to rescue the unsold produce and calling on local government units to procure the excess for feeding programs.2 As one farmer- 1 Carby Rose Basina, “Benguet farmers struggle with low vegetable prices, oppose planned carrot imports,” GMA News Online, 25 May 2026, available at: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/988714/benguet- farmers-struggle-with-low-vegetable-prices-oppose-planned-carrot-imports/story/ 2 Clarizel Joy Jamille Gomez, “Tomato Price Volatility in Luzon: Challenges for Farmers, Consumers, and the Need for Market Stability,” DOST-PCAARD’s ISP-IS, 4 April 2025, available at: advocate group put it plainly: “There is actually market demand. It’s just not reaching it. So, it looks like overproduction.”3 The government has not been without initiatives to address this gap. The Department of Agriculture (DA) currently maintains several digital platforms, among them the Registry System for Basic Sectors in Agriculture (RSBSA), the e-Kadiwa e-commerce platform, and the Bantay-Presyo price-monitoring application. These are valuable, but largely function as centralized, top-down tools; none of them is mandated to operate as real-time, two-way local matching system at the city, municipal, and barangay level where oversupply and undersupply typically originate, and where the earliest, most actionable information exists. The gap that this bill seeks to address is precisely that last- mile layer, the absence of a legally mandated, LGU-anchored information system that captures hyperlocal production data as it is harvested, and connects, in real time, to buyers and to the national platforms/registries that already exist. It was recently shown that a lot of farming communities are forced to throw away their crops due to the supposed oversupply. However, upon careful investigation, it shows that there exists demand in several areas in the country which are not taken account of because of this information gap. Such gaps have become more urgent to close now that the National Government has significantly scaled up its investment in agricultural infrastructure. For example, the 2026 National Budget substantially increased funding for farm-to-market roads, precisely to move produce out of the farms and into markets faster. Roads without a matching information system to tell farmers where the demand is, and buyers where the supply is, will only get produce to market faster without ensuring that it goes to where it is needed. 4 Physical infrastructure and information infrastructure must be developed together. It is for these reasons that this bill seeks to reestablish, in an updated and strengthened form, the Agriculture Information System, built to interoperate with existing national platforms rather than duplicate them, while accessible to farmers who lack reliable internet access through SMS and community kiosks and not just a web application, and backed by a funding mechanism that does not leave under-resources municipalities, communities, and farmer groups to shoulder an unfunded mandate alone. label: HB 10866
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ENFORCEMENT OF MANDATORY SEGREGATION-AT-SOURCE OF SOLID WASTES AT THE BARANGAY LEVEL, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9003, or the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000,” already requires households and establishments to segregate solid waste at source under Section 21 of the law. More than two decades since its passage, however, segregation-at-source often remains the weakest-enforced link in the country’s solid waste management chain. Barangays, which are on the frontline of collection, generally have no clear, standardized mechanism to refuse uncollected, unsegregated waste, to inspect compliance, or to impose graduated, due-process-compliant penalties on repeat violators. This absence of a workable enforcement mechanism at the barangay level has allowed segregation-at-source to remain, in practice, optional in many communities, undermining the entire downstream chain of materials recovery, composting, and waste diversion that later legislation and local ordinances have tried to strengthen. This bill amends Republic Act No. 9003 by inserting a new section, Section 22, that gives barangays a clear, standardized, and due-process-compliant enforcement toolkit: (1) a designated Barangay Segregation Enforcement Team; (2) authority to refuse collection of unsegregated waste; (3) a graduated schedule of warnings and fines for households and establishments; (4) authority to conduct spot inspections; and (5) a self-sustaining Barangay Solid Waste Management Enforcement Fund sourced from the fines themselves, primarily for information campaigns and segregation materials rather than punitive revenue- raising. By giving barangays real, low-cost enforcement tools instead of merely repeating the mandate to segregate, this measure aims to close the compliance gap that has persisted since RA 9003 took effect. It is our view, that given the precarious situation in which the country finds itself in vis-à-vis solid waste and environmental waste-leakage, tackling segregation-at-source provides a solid step towards the right direction. It is high time that we move on from the old mantra of “tapat ko, linis ko,” and into a new adage: I will keep my community, and therefore the country, clean. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10867
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DISCLOSURE OF FOOD ALLERGENS IN PRODUCTS OFFERED BY FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State, under Article II, Section 15 of the Constitution, is mandated to protect and promote the right to health of the people. In line with this, the Department of Health issued Administrative Order No. 2014-0030 requiring prepackaged food products to list their ingredients, including allergens, to safeguard consumers. However, this protection remains incomplete, as food served in restaurants, cafeterias, and other establishments is not subject to the same mandatory disclosure, leaving millions of Filipinos vulnerable to accidental allergic reactions. Food allergies pose a serious and recurring public health concern. Even the smallest serving of an allergen can trigger severe reactions ranging from swollen tissues, vomiting, abdominal cramps, and painful blisters to difficulty breathing, coma, and even death. Studies in the Philippines confirm that food allergies affect a growing number of children and adults, with many cases going unreported due to limited awareness and lack of disclosure mechanisms. These risks are magnified in provinces and rural communities where access to emergency medical care is limited, making prevention through transparency all the more critical. This bill seeks to institutionalize the duty of food establishments to automatically disclose allergy-causing ingredients in their menu items. By complementing the existing requirement for prepackaged foods, this measure ensures that consumers are protected not only in grocery aisles but also in everyday dining settings. It recognizes that diligence must be shared: while customers have the responsibility to inquire, establishments must carry the equal responsibility to inform. This measure embodies humane regulation as it seeks to protect vulnerable groups like children, the elderly, and those in marginalized communities, by reducing preventable health risks. It also strengthens trust between consumers and establishments, fostering a safer and more inclusive dining culture across the country. The institutionalization of allergen disclosure is a simple yet powerful step toward health equity. It ensures that every Filipino, regardless of where they live or what they can afford to eat, enjoys a safer and more dignified dining experience. It is for these reasons that the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10868
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR COMPENSATION FOR STAY-AT-HOME SPOUSES AND HOMEMAKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under current conventions in economics, work that is not remunerated does not count as productive labor. Unfortunately, this category would include the work done by housewives, stay-at-home mothers, or homemakers who care for dependents, both young and elderly, in their household. Cooking breakfast, washing and preparing the clothes for the day, cleaning the home, balancing the household budget are only some of the many things our mothers, sisters, and many more do that require not only the fullest dedication, time, and a wide variety of skills. And yet, society in its current form, often dismisses or undervalues the labor of home- making. But imagine a tomorrow, where suddenly, housewives and homemakers cease to do the work they usually do. The most likely result would be that the lives of everyday Filipinos as we know it would become commensurately more difficult. Those considered in the productive economy would feel the extra burden of having to pick up the labor gap that ensues, becoming less productive in their professional jobs in the process. It is then worth considering, that if full-time housework is indeed inconsequential, how come that it would be impossible to maintain a productive economy without it? It is thus imperative upon the State to recognize the “invisible labor” done by stay-at-home women, mothers, wives, and homemakers as a valuable part of our economy. In line with the Constitutional imperatives to promote a just and dynamic social order, to value the dignity of every human person, and to recognize the role of women in nation-building, housewives and homemakers should be given the equivalent of a wage. With this, the State takes a step not only to provide a means for families with only one breadwinner to lift themselves out of poverty, but also take a step to recognize the vital role that women and homemakers perform from the onset of one’s life to the twilight of their years. It is for these foregoing premises that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10869
title: AN ACT PROVIDING MENSTRUAL HEALTH PRIVILEGE TO EMPLOYEES IN THE PUBLIC AND PRIVATE SECTORS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall recognize the role of women in nation-building1 and shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.2 Furthermore, the Constitution also provides that the State shall protect working women by providing safe and healthful working conditions, taking into account their maternal functions, and such facilities and opportunities that will enhance their welfare and enable them to realize their full potential in the service of the nation.3 Menstruation is the recurring discharge of blood and tissue from the inner lining of the uterus as part of the menstrual cycle. Menstruation is usually experienced by individuals with a uterus, including cisgender women and transgender men. Some individuals may experience pain and discomfort during menstruation due to dysmenorrhea, the severe and frequent cramps during the menstruation period. It was reported that more than half of women who menstruate have some pain for 1 to 2 days each month4, affecting between 45 and 95% of all women5. 1 1987 CONST. Art. II, Sec. 14. The State recognizes the role of women in nation-building, and shall ensure the fundamental equality before the law of women and men. 2 1987 CONST. Art. II, Sec. 15. The State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. 3 1987 CONST. Art. XIII, Sec. 14. 4 National Nutrition Council. (October 28, 2021). Why do women experience Dysmenorrhea?. URL: https://nnc.gov.ph/regional-offices/mindanao/region-ix-zamboanga-peninsula/6274-why-do- women-experience-dysmenorrhea 5 Stella Iacovides, Ingrid Avidon, Fiona C. Baker (September 07, 2015). What we know about primary dysmenorrhea today: a critical review. Available at: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26346058/ The pain during menstruation is normal, but for some individuals, the pain and discomfort may be severe enough to interfere with their normal activities.6 The pain may be due to hormonal activity during the menstrual cycle or may be an associated phenomenon of an underlying medical condition. In light of the constitutional mandate and the factual backdrop surrounding menstrual health, this bill proposes that a menstrual health privilege be made available to employees in the public and private sectors who experience pain and discomfort during menstruation. The menstrual health privilege shall be in the form of either a two-day paid leave or an option for a work-from-home arrangement during their menstruation period, if applicable to the nature of their duties and responsibilities. The option for a two-day paid leave, distinct and separate from the legally mandated sickness benefit under existing laws, is made available to allow the employee to recuperate in extreme and severe cases of painful menstruation. On the other hand, the option for a work-from-home arrangement is made available to allow the employee to maintain productivity in less-severe cases of painful menstruation. The menstrual health privilege aims to promote the general well-being of employees who suffer from painful and burdensome menstruation and alleviate the distress that they experience. The menstrual health privilege proposed by this bill should not be seen as a special treatment for a particular class of employees. Menstruation and its associated pain and discomfort are both health issues and medical concerns. It is high time that we recognize the plight of employees who experience these realities and give them our support as they go through this recurring struggle. Based on the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. DELOS SANTOS Representative, Ang Probinsyano Party-List 6 Ibid. label: HB 10870
title: AN ACT PRESCRIBING AN ACTIVE MONITORING AND URGENT RESPONSE MECHANISM BY THE GOVERNMENT TO PREVENT THE KILLING, RAPE, AND OTHER ABUSES COMMITTED AGAINST OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the height of tragedy when Overseas Filipino Workers travel to foreign lands in search of opportunities, seeking to help uplift the lives of their family and countrymen, just to be met with grisly, violent deaths in the hands of a stranger. Joanna Demafelis, Jeanelyn Villavende, and Constancia Dayag are just Filipinos whose lives were untimely snuffed out. More saddening is the fact that we are not at all helpless to provide our OFWs the necessary protections. We have had the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration (POEA), the Overseas Labor Office, Filipino Resource Center, and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA), most of which, exempting the OWWA, are now under the Department Of Migrant Workers (DMW), and all mandated to serve and protect our OFWs. With their combined wealth of experience, resources, and connections inaction is unacceptable. And yet there are cases, such that of Jeanelyn Villavende, where complaints from OFWs regarding their safety are not promptly acted upon. This is even more timely, as areas of the globe with high concentrations of OFWs continue to grapple with warfare, geopolitical tensions, and other such economic uncertainties, leading to the further precarious situations our OFWs sometime find themselves in. This is the gap that this bill seeks to address. It provides active monitoring and urgent response mechanism to address incidents and emergencies endangering the life, limb, and liberty of our OFWs and to instill that consciousness among our frontline government agencies and stakeholders, under pain of administrative and criminal penalty. This way, prevent future cases of OFWs being abused, raped or killed may be prevented. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10871
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT AND INTEGRATION OF SOLAR-POWERED COLD-CHAIN FACILITIES IN THE PHILIPPINE FISHERIES SECTOR, PROVIDING SUPPORT MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is one of the world’s top fish-producing countries, and the fisheries sector remains a primary source of food and livelihood for millions of Filipinos, particularly small-scale and municipal fisherfolk in coastal communities nationwide. Yet a significant share of the sector’s harvest never reaches the market at full value, this is mostly due to post-harvest losses, which include spoilage, quality degradation, and reduced shelf life, among others. Post- harvest losses remain a persistent problem, driven in large part by the absence of reliable and affordable cold-chain infrastructure at the point of landing, and throughout the seafood supply chain. Many municipal fishing communities are in areas that lack proper infrastructure or suffer from energy insecurity. As a result, fishers and fish processors in these areas often lack access to ice, chilling, or cold storage facilities capable of preserving the quality of their catch between capture and market. This translates directly into lost income for fisherfolk, reduced product value, lower exportability, and food that never reaches the consumers’ tables. At the same time, the falling cost of solar photovoltaic technology has made solar powered cold-chain equipment increasingly viable in remote, under-served, off-grid, or energy insecure areas, such as island communities and remote coastal towns. Solar-powered cold-chain facilities offer a practical, low-emission, and increasingly cost-competitive solution, one that does not require waiting for grid extension and that insulates fishing communities from fuel price volatility associated with diesel-powered generators commonly used for the same purpose today. This Act seeks to harness that opportunity by mandating the establishment and integration of solar-powered cold-chain facilities in priority fishing communities. This measure is expected to generate significant knock-on benefits, such as higher and more stable incomes for municipal fisherfolk, improved food security, greater climate and energy resilience in coastal communities, and the growth of a local industry centered around renewable energy and cold-chain equipment manufacturing, installation, and servicing. Through this Act, we aim to advance the country' s renewable energy goals, its fisheries development goals, and safeguard a way of life that has been thriving for generations. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10872
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE USE AND UTILIZATION OF SOLAR ENERGY IN NATIONAL HOSPITALS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNIT HOSPITALS, STATE AND UNIVERSITY HOSPITALS, AND OTHER GOVERNMENT-OWNED AND -CONTROLLED HOSPITALS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Reliable electricity is not a convenience for hospitals, it is a matter of life and death. Ventilators, incubators, blood banks, operating rooms, dialysis machines, and cold-chain storage for vaccines and medicines all depend on an uninterrupted power supply. Yet many of our public hospitals, particularly those in far-flung and off-grid areas, continue to grapple with unstable, intermittent, or altogether absent electricity service. During typhoons, earthquakes, and other calamities and public health emergencies, precisely when hospitals are needed most, power interruptions place patients' lives at risk and compromise the delivery of essential health services. At the same time, public hospitals that do enjoy stable grid access shoulder some of the highest and most continuous electricity demands among government facilities, placing a significant and recurring burden on public funds that could otherwise be channeled toward direct patient care, medical supplies, and health workforce needs. Solar energy offers a practical, sustainable, and increasingly cost-effective solution to both dependence on costly and often unreliable conventional electricity sources, lower long-term operating costs, and, when paired with appropriate energy storage, provide a critical layer of resilience that keeps essential hospital services running through outages, calamities, and emergencies. This is consistent with the policy already established under Republic Act No. 9513, or the "Renewable Energy Act of 2008," which promotes the development and utilization of renewable energy to strengthen the country's energy security and reduce its dependence on fossil fuels. This bill mandates the installation, integration, and maintenance of solar energy systems in national hospitals, local government unit hospitals, state and university hospitals, and other government-owned and controlled hospitals. To ensure that this mandate is achievable rather than aspirational, the bill provides for a phased implementation: covered hospitals are required to achieve solar energy generation capability equivalent to at least twenty percent (20%) of their annual electricity demand within one (1) year from the law's effectivity, and at least fifty percent (50%) within three (3) years, subject to standards and guidelines to be jointly established by the Department of Health (DOH) and the Department of Energy (DOE), in coordination with other relevant agencies. The bill likewise directs covered hospitals to integrate energy storage and backup capabilities where technically and financially feasible, so that critical hospital facilities and services remain powered during grid outages and emergencies. In recognition of the role of local industry in nation-building, the bill gives priority to local businesses in the contracting and purchase of solar energy systems from accredited solar photovoltaic installers, while ensuring that all procurement remains fully compliant with existing bidding and procurement laws and is conducted with transparency. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 10873
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING DISCRIMINATION OF TEACHERS WHO ARE UNWED MOTHERS, SINGLE PARENTS, AND/OR MEMBERS OF THE LGBT COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Teachers play a vital role in shaping the minds, character, and future of the Filipino people. Their competence and commitment to the teaching profession should be the standards by which their qualifications and performance are assessed, and not their civil status, family circumstances, gender identity, or sexual orientation. Despite the importance of their profession, teachers and applicants for teaching positions may face discrimination on the basis of being an unwed mother, a single parent, or a member of the LGBTQIA+ community, and other such non-heteronormative identifiers. Such discriminatory practices may deprive otherwise qualified individuals of employment opportunities, livelihood, salaries, and benefits solely because of circumstances that do not diminish their ability to perform their duties as educators. This measure seeks to uphold the right of teachers and applicants for teaching positions to equal employment opportunities by expressly prohibiting discrimination on these grounds. It likewise establishes appropriate penalties and institutional accountability to ensure that schools maintain fair, inclusive, and non-discriminatory workplaces. By protecting teachers from discrimination, this measure seeks to foster a more equitable educational system where professional competence, integrity, and dedication determine one's opportunity to serve as an educator, not personal circumstances or identity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C.
