label: HB 10982
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE ADVERTISING, PROMOTION, ENDORSEMENT, AND SPONSORSHIP OF ONLINE GAMBLING, REGULATING THE ADVERTISING, PROMOTION, ENDORSEMENT, AND SPONSORSHIP OF OTHER GAMBLING ACTIVITIES, STRENGTHENING AGE AND IDENTITY VERIFICATION REQUIREMENTS FOR ONLINE GAMBLING, ESTABLISHING JUDICIAL AND ADMINISTRATIVE ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS, PROVIDING FOR THE TREATMENT AND REHABILITATION OF PERSONS AFFECTED BY GAMBLING DISORDER, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Gambling in the Philippines was once a physically circumscribed activity, confined to licensed casinos, cockpits, and lottery outlets whose physical barriers naturally kept children and other vulnerable persons at bay. Mobile technology has since dissolved those barriers: every smartphone is now a potential twenty-four-hour casino. According to the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR), the industry’s gross gaming revenues reached approximately ₱396.14 billion in 2025, driven chiefly by electronic and online gaming, which grew by roughly 30 percent to ₱201.12 billion and, for the first time, overtook land-based casinos to account for 50.77 percent of total industry revenue.1 PAGCOR further estimates that approximately ten million Filipinos are active users of licensed online platforms — a figure that has expanded several-fold within two years, and that does not account for users of unlicensed offshore platforms operating beyond the reach of Philippine regulation. This is not merely an economic phenomenon but a matter of public health. The World Health Organization, in its 2024 fact sheet on gambling, characterized gambling disorder as a health- harming addictive behavior fueled by the industry’s commercialization and digitization, and called for banning gambling advertising, promotion, and sponsorship as a necessary first step toward reducing harm.2 The Lancet Public Health Commission on Gambling likewise found, in 2024, that an estimated 450 million people worldwide experience gambling-related harm, with about 80 million meeting the clinical threshold for gambling disorder, and identified online accessibility and sophisticated marketing, including targeted digital advertising and sports sponsorships, as principal drivers, with harm falling disproportionately on adolescents and lower-income communities. 3 This measure adopts a risk-proportionate structure. It prohibits outright the advertising, promotion, endorsement, and sponsorship of online gambling, whose defining characteristics such as continuous availability, high event frequency, the absence of any physical barrier to entry, and algorithmically personalized solicitation are precisely the characteristics the evidence associates most strongly with gambling-related harm. It does not prohibit, but instead regulates, 1 PAGCOR, Gross Gaming Revenue Report, Fiscal Year 2025. 2 World Health Organization, “Gambling,” Fact Sheet, 2 December 2024. 3 Lancet Public Health Commission on Gambling, The Lancet Public Health (2024). the advertising of gambling that is not conducted remotely: play within licensed gaming venues, the charity sweepstakes and lottery draws conducted by the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office, horse races, and cockfighting in licensed cockpits. For these, the Act requires a responsible gaming advisory, imposes content standards, and forbids placement directed at or likely to reach persons below the applicable minimum age. The distinction rests on the structure of the product, not on the identity of its operator. It therefore applies with equal force to the State’s own gambling operations and to those of private licensees, and it does not exempt any operator from the prohibition merely because the operator is a government instrumentality. Because operators of online platforms are frequently affiliated with land-based establishments sharing a common brand, Section 9 addresses the promotion of an online platform through the advertising of a related non-online activity or of other goods and services. Republic Act No. 9211 confronted the same problem in the tobacco context, and the provision follows that precedent. Without such a provision, a prohibition confined to online advertising would be defeated within weeks of its effectivity. Regulatory measures already undertaken have demonstrated both their worth and their limits. PAGCOR has ordered the removal of gambling billboards and other out-of-home advertising, entered into a memorandum of understanding with the Ad Standards Council subjecting gambling advertisements to pre-screening, restricted advertising during primetime broadcast hours, and, in June 2026, directed its licensees to replace gaming advertisements with materials promoting the newly launched twenty-four-hour National Problem Gambling Helpline. 4 These are regulatory issuances and voluntary industry undertakings. They bind licensees but not the advertising agencies, media entities, digital platforms, affiliate networks, and endorsers through whom the bulk of gambling marketing now flows; they may be revised or withdrawn by the very agency whose remittances depend upon the activity being advertised; and they carry no penal consequence. What is required is a statute. This is not the first instance in which the State has confronted a legal product whose promotion poses a disproportionate risk to public welfare. Republic Act No. 9211, the Tobacco Regulation Act of 2003, kept tobacco lawful for adults while imposing stringent restrictions on its advertising, promotion, and sponsorship. That was a legislative judgment consistent with the constitutional mandates that the State protect and promote the right to health of the people (Article II, Section 15) and promote and protect the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being of the youth (Article II, Section 13), and with the right of children to special protection from all conditions prejudicial to their development (Article XV, Section 3[2]). The measure has been calibrated to withstand constitutional scrutiny on four fronts. First, it proceeds from clear legislative rather than merely administrative authority. In Pharmaceutical and Health Care Association of the Philippines v. Duque III, the Supreme Court invalidated an administratively imposed absolute advertising ban because the enabling statute authorized regulation, not prohibition, expressly leaving to Congress the question of a legislated prohibition.5 S

label: HB 10983
title: AN ACT PROMOTING AWARENESS OF CHRONIC FATIGUE SYNDROME
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Myalgic encephalomyelitis or chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a complex, chronic illness characterized by debilitating fatigue, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulties, and other symptoms that substantially limit daily activities. No definitive diagnostic test or universally established cure currently exists, and prevalence estimates vary because of differences in diagnostic criteria.1 Management generally focuses on individualized medical care, symptom monitoring, sleep support, and energy management to prevent worsening after physical or mental activity. Patients may also experience stigma because the illness is often invisible and poorly understood, resulting in delayed diagnosis, inadequate treatment, and social isolation. 2 In the Philippines, research and official data specifically concerning myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) remain limited. The absence of reliable national prevalence data highlights the need for local epidemiological studies, clinical guidelines, health-worker training, and improved reporting and referral systems. International research describes ME/CFS as a disabling, multisystem illness characterized by persistent fatigue, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, and cognitive difficulties 1 https://www.cdc.gov/. May 30, 2024 2 Recommendations | Myalgic encephalomyelitis (or encephalopathy)/chronic fatigue syndrome: diagnosis and management | Guidance | NICE. October 21, 2021 The lack of Philippine-specific data should not be interpreted as evidence that the condition is uncommon. Limited recognition, the absence of a definitive diagnostic test, and the possibility of misdiagnosis may contribute to underreporting. Accordingly, this measure seeks to promote awareness, strengthen clinical recognition, reduce stigma, support research, and improve access to appropriate assessment, treatment, rehabilitation, mental-health support, and social services for persons with ME/CFS. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PARICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10984
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A HEALTH CARE PROGRAM FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face significant learning challenges. In the latest available PISA 2022 results, Filipino 15-year-old students ranked 76th out of 81 countries in reading, 75th in mathematics, and 79th in science. Only 24 percent reached the minimum reading proficiency level, while only 16 percent reached the minimum mathematics proficiency level and 23 percent reached the minimum science proficiency level.1 The World Bank’s 2024 Learning Poverty Brief likewise reported that 91 percent of Filipino children of late-primary age were not proficient in reading, adjusted for those out of school. Approximately 90 percent of students also failed to achieve minimum reading proficiency by the end of primary school. These results underscore the need to strengthen the capacity and well- being of public school teachers, who play a central role in improving student learning outcomes. While reforms on compensation, training, and professional development are important, ensuring that teachers have reliable access to quality health care is equally necessary. Although the Universal Health Care Act has expanded health-insurance coverage, gaps in access and implementation remain. This bill therefore seeks to provide public school teachers with Healthcare Maintenance Organization 1 Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. 2023 coverage to supplement existing government health benefits and reduce their out-of-pocket medical expenses. Investing in teachers’ physical and mental health will help promote teacher welfare, reduce work-related health burdens, and support a more effective and resilient public education system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10985
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A COMPREHENSIVE RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY (RRT) FOR PATIENTS WITH END STAGE RENAL DISEASE IN NATIONAL, REGIONAL, AND PROVINCIAL GOVERNMENT HOSPITALS, INCREASING THE PHILHEALTH PACKAGE RATE FOR RENAL REPLACEMENT THERAPY OF MEMBERS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Chronic kidney disease remains a major public-health concern in the Philippines and is consistently identified among the country’s leading causes of illness and death. Recent reports estimate that approximately 2.3 million Filipinos are living with chronic kidney disease, while the number of patients undergoing dialysis increased from 53,296 in 2023 to 64,845 in 2024, representing a 22-percent increase in one year.1 The latest data from the Philippine Renal Disease Registry, as of March 2025, indicate that hypertensive nephrosclerosis accounted for 33.07 percent of reported kidney-disease cases, followed by diabetic nephropathy at 30.04 percent and chronic glomerulonephritis at 12.20 percent. These figures demonstrate the continuing need for early detection, preventive care, timely treatment, and expanded access to renal replacement therapy. Dialysis remains financially burdensome for many Filipino families, particularly when patients must also pay for medicines, laboratory tests, transportation, vascular-access procedures, and other related medical expenses. Although the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation increased its hemodialysis benefit to ₱6,350 per session effective October 9, 2024, eligible 1 Philippine News Agency. 2025 patients with Chronic Kidney Disease Stage 5 may avail themselves of up to 156 sessions annually, equivalent to a maximum annual coverage of approximately ₱990,600.2 Despite this expansion, gaps in access and coverage remain, particularly for patients in underserved areas and those requiring comprehensive treatment beyond routine hemodialysis. The high and increasing number of dialysis patients also places substantial pressure on public hospitals, dialysis facilities, health professionals, PhilHealth, and the families of persons suffering from end-stage renal disease. This bill seeks to reduce the financial burden of patients with kidney failure by providing comprehensive and accessible renal replacement therapy in national, regional, and provincial government hospitals. It further seeks to strengthen government support for hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, kidney transplantation, related medicines and procedures, and other medically necessary services for qualified patients. The measure also aims to increase and regularly review the PhilHealth package rates for renal replacement therapy so that reimbursement remains responsive to actual treatment costs and does not result in unreasonable out- of-pocket expenses for patients and their families. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10986
title: AN ACT PROVIDING A STANDARD OF CARE FOR THE TREATMENT OF PERSONS WITH BLEEDING DISORDERS, ESTABLISHING TREATMENT CENTERS AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Bleeding disorders are a group of conditions where the blood cannot clot properly. People suffering from bleeding disorders experience longer bleeding and random bleeding in muscles, joints, and other areas of the human body.1 There is an estimated number of 10,000 Filipinos who have hemophilia, but only 1,500 have been registered under the Philippine Hemophilia Foundation. About one million Filipinos suffer from Von Willebrand disease (VWD), a genetic disorder caused by a missing or defective clotting protein known as the von Willebrand factor (VWF). This disease is known to affect both sexes, but women have higher chances of experiencing VWD due to menstrual periods, pregnancies, and post-childbirth. Unfortunately, only 20 individuals have been registered to have VWD in the Philippines. According to the Hemophilia Advocates Philippines, the majority of patients suffering from the disorder are living below the poverty line and experience limited to no access to medicines, facilities, and professional help, leaving them undiagnosed 1 . For some, this is also caused by the lack of awareness of the symptoms due to the lack of education. 1 www.hemophilia.ph/bleeding The minimal access to medical care for people with bleeding disorders is a grave concern, and the treatments for the disorders are expensive. A case of mild bleeding in the joints can cost around Php 30,000 to Php 50,000 per treatment. Treating severe cases would cost hundreds of thousands to millions of pesos. Furthermore, the lack of treatment facilities that cater to this disease forces patients from rural areas to travel to urban centers for aid. As it is the mandate of the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people (Article II) and prioritize the needs of the underprivileged sick, elderly, disabled, women, and children (Article XIII), there is an urgent need for the State to include hemophilia care in the national health agenda. This bill provides for the establishment of hemophilia treatment facilities in key cities and regions in the Philippines to provide more accessible and affordable medical care. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7719, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE NATIONAL BLOOD SERVICES ACT OF 1994, PROMOTING VOLUNTARY BLOOD DONATION, PROVIDING FOR AN ADEQUATE SUPPLY OF SAFE BLOOD, REGULATING BLOOD BANKS, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The National Blood Services Act of 1994 sought to promote voluntary blood donation and provide sufficient supply of safe blood and regulate blood banks. Blood transfusions in the Philippines reach more than 2,000 blood units in a day, with an estimated 1 million blood units needed every year to address victims of accidents, natural disasters, or other grave illnesses. Although the Philippines is at par with international standards in terms of blood services, there is a need to strengthen more important practices in ensuring the provision of adequate, safe, and equitable blood for the Filipinos. Blood services should not be used to make profits in exchange for saving a life. Charging minimal fees is acceptable as they help maintain and sustain blood bank facilities, but to use blood donation to take advantage and gain profit is highly unacceptable. This bill seeks to safeguard the significance of voluntary blood donation. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10988
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING THE MEDICAL RESERVE CORPS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine health system continues to face serious shortages and uneven distribution of medical and health-related personnel. Recent data indicate that the Philippines had approximately 21.2 health workers per 10,000 population, less than half of the 44.5 health workers per 10,000 population benchmark cited by the World Health Organization. The country reportedly needs approximately 290,000 additional health professionals, including projected shortages of about 94,000 doctors and 196,000 nurses. The shortage is also reflected in the country’s physician density. In 2023, there was approximately one doctor for every 25,280 Filipinos, or about 3.96 doctors per 10,000 population. Regional disparities remain significant: the National Capital Region had approximately one doctor for every 14,200 people, while the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao had approximately one doctor for every 49,400 people. These deficiencies highlight the vulnerability of the country’s health system during pandemics, disasters, epidemics, and other public-health emergencies. Health-worker shortages and the continuing migration of Filipino medical professionals make it more difficult to provide timely and adequate health services, particularly in geographically isolated, disadvantaged, and underserved communities. The World Health Organization has likewise recognized that health-worker shortages weaken national preparedness for pandemics and other health emergencies. This bill seeks to strengthen the country’s health-system capacity by promoting the participation of qualified medical and health-related personnel in public service, emergency response, and community health activities. It proposes the establishment of a Medical Reserve Corps composed of graduates in medicine, nursing, medical technology, and other health-related fields who have not yet obtained their professional licenses, as well as other qualified personnel as may be provided by law. Members may be mobilized, subject to appropriate supervision, training, and safeguards, to assist the national government and local government units in addressing public-health emergencies and the medical needs of underserved communities. The measure shall not authorize unlicensed persons to independently practice a regulated profession. Rather, members of the Medical Reserve Corps shall perform only such supportive, non-independent, and legally permissible functions as may be assigned under the supervision of duly licensed health professionals and in accordance with existing health and professional-regulation laws. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10989
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH TO ESTABLISH A RESEARCH CENTER ON OBESITY PREVENTION
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 2019 National Nutrition Survey of the Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI) reported that there are about 27 million Filipinos who are obese and overweight. Furthermore, the Philippines is said to have “very rapid growth” in adult obesity over the last two decades and is mostly attributed to poor diet and nutrition. Numerous studies have indicated that obesity increases risks in an individual’s health, thereby also reducing a person’s life expectancy. Potentially fatal conditions associated with obesity include Type 2 diabetes, coronary heart disease, cancers, and gall bladder disease. As a State policy “to protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them” (Article II, 1987 Philippine Constitution), this bill seeks to curb obesity in the country and protect Filipinos from this epidemic by establishing a research center on obesity prevention. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10990
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE HEALTHCARE SYSTEM IN CULTURAL AND INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES BY INSTITUTIONALIZING THE TRAINING AND EMPLOYMENT OF TRIBAL HEALTH WORKERS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Globally, indigenous cultural communities (ICCs) suffer from poorer health, are more likely to experience disability, and ultimately die younger than their non-indigenous counterparts. In the Philippines, evidence suggests that IPs are among the poorest, with low educational attainment and experience pervasive problems of undernutrition. They remain a marginalized sector of society, making them highly vulnerable to the same persistent nutritional and health problems non-IPs experience.1 While this is the case, it is important to note that many of the most widespread causes of mortality among indigenous people (e.g., malnutrition, diarrhea, parasitic infections, etc.) are preventable and treatable. The ICCs’ lack of access to adequate healthcare is due in part to the physical and geographical barriers of their locations, their economic challenges, and the cultural barriers that limit their understanding of the social and cultural factors deriving from the knowledge, attitudes, and practices in health of indigenous people. In addition, finding health workers who speak and understand indigenous languages is difficult. This leads to poor communication between the health providers and indigenous people, thereby compromising the latter’s access to healthcare. 1 Philippine Journal of Science, 2022 It is therefore crucial that there are culturally sensitive and appropriate interventions tailor-fit for the ICCs to improve their overall health and nutritional status in the country. To break all these barriers and improve the ICC’s access to quality healthcare, this bill seeks to establish and institutionalize the training of tribal health workers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10991
title: AN ACT GRANTING IMMEDIATE COMPENSATION BENEFITS FOR MENTAL HEALTH SERVICE USERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 5 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11036, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE MENTAL HEALTH ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The passage of Republic Act No. 11036, also known as the Mental Health Act, has paved the way for the Philippines to establish a mental health framework in terms of understanding the mental health struggles of Filipinos and delivering better mental health care to those in need. However, access to mental health services for the greater population remains limited due to economic constraints. Thus, the government must increase its efforts to enable service users to equitably access appropriate care when needed. This bill seeks to propose an amendment that ensures service users in need of mental healthcare receive adequate and immediate compensation benefits and/or any special financial assistance under existing laws should the service user sustain temporary or permanent mental disability while in the performance of duty or by reason of his or her office or position. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10992
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING PALLIATIVE AND HOSPICE CARE INTO THE PHILIPPINE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The World Health Organization estimates that about 40 million people worldwide need palliative and hospice care yearly. In the Philippines, the Department of Health declares the annual rise in the number of patients in need of end-of-life palliative care services. Palliative care is a healthcare approach that allows support for patients and their families who are facing life-threatening illness. Early delivery of palliative care reduces hospital admissions and thereby the use of health services. Although there are over a hundred hospice and palliative care services in the country, there is still a fragmented effort of various stakeholders in the implementation of palliative care. This bill therefore seeks to address these challenges through the integration of palliative and hospice care into the country’s health care system. Furthermore, it seeks to preserve human dignity and improve the quality of a patient’s last day of life by providing high -quality healthcare services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10993
title: AN ACT CREATING A DENTAL UNIT IN EVERY RURAL HEALTH UNIT UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AS PART OF THE PRIMARY APPROACH IN THE DELIVERY OF HEALTH SERVICES AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution mandates that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them (Article II, Section 15) and to undertake appropriate health, manpower development and research responsive to the country’s health needs and problems. (Article XIII, Section 12). In a report by the World Health Organization, dental care is among one of the most neglected health aspects of an individual that has affected one’s overall health, well-being, and quality life. The Department of Health’s National Monitoring and Evaluation Dental Survey states that about 83 million Filipinos suffer from tooth decay and that seven out of ten Filipinos have never sought the services of a dentist. With only less than 1% of Filipinos seeking treatment for dental care1, oral disease remains to be a serious public health problem in the country affecting the overall work performance, nutrition, social interactions, and self- esteem of the people. To address the gaps and to improve the oral care and hygiene of the Filipinos, this bill seeks to create a dental unit each of the rural health units (RHUS) listed under the Department of Health. 1 National Demographic and Health Survey 2017 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 10994
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A FRAMEWORK IN THE CARE AND TREATMENT OF DIABETES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mortality due to diabetes is a silent and persistent health concern in the Philippines. In recent years, the loss of lives due to the disease has increased dramatically, claiming an average of more than 30,000 lives annually1. With one in 14 adult Filipinos having diabetes2, the country ranks 5th among its Southeast Asian neighbors in terms of the prevalence of the disease. As it is the obligation of the State, under the Constitution, to promote and protect the right of the people to health by instilling health consciousness among the people, there is a need to undertake more health promotion and disease preventive measures, particularly with respect to diabetes. While the Department of Health already provides the Insulin Access Program for diabetes treatment, this bill proposes a systematic framework and collaborative effort among the various national and local government agencies as well as the private sector to better address the growing epidemic of diabetes in the country. 1 Philippine Statistics Authority (2020) 2 International Diabetes Federation (2019) By promoting a different approach in responding to this illness, this bill seeks to improve diabetes care and treatment for Filipinos in the hopes of enhancing the overall public health in the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 10996
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 150-B AND 288-A OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE AND CREATING A NEW SECTION, 150-C, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen public health measures against diet-related diseases while generating sustainable funding for critical national health and nutrition initiatives. The primary policy objective of this legislation is to curb the rising prevalence of lifestyle illnesses, such as diabetes and obesity, by using fiscal policy to encourage healthier consumer choices and incentivize manufacturers to reformulate their products with lower sugar content. To achieve this health deterrent, the measure updates tax rates on sweetened beverages, establishing higher rates for drinks containing high fructose corn syrup to disincentivize its widespread industrial use. The policy scope is also broadened to encompass commercial sweetened milk and coffee products, ensuring a comprehensive framework across the beverage market. At the same time, the bill safeguards essential public nutrition by strictly exempting staple items such as plain unsweetened milk, infant formula, and standard unflavored coffee products. Beyond deterrence, a core outcome of this legislation is establishing a dedicated legal mechanism for statutory revenue earmarking. The bill guarantees that revenues collected are funneled directly into essential public services. To address rooted health disparities, forty percent of revenues are ring-fenced specifically for local government support, focusing on targeted nutrition programs for pregnant mothers and children in their first five years of life, alongside vital water, sanitation, and hygiene infrastructure. Finally, the bill incorporates an annual tax indexation mechanism so that the health deterrent maintains its real value over time without being eroded by economic changes. Coupled with expanded legislative oversight to strictly track the distribution and use of funds at the local level, the ultimate outcome of this measure is a self-sustaining cycle where taxes collected from sugary beverage consumption are directly transformed into long-term investments in maternal care, child nutrition, and accessible healthcare for all Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 10997
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAM FOR GRADUATE STUDIES IN GUIDANCE AND COUNSELING, STRENGTHENING THE GUIDANCE AND COUNSELING WORKFORCE OF THE COUNTRY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SEC. 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “National Guidance and Counseling Scholarship Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is the policy of the State to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education and to the highest attainable standard of mental health, and to maintain a system of scholarship grants available to deserving students. Toward this end, the State shall build a sufficient, competent, and equitably distributed corps of Registered Guidance Counselors by financing graduate education in Guidance and Counseling, directing that investment to underserved regions, and securing a period of public service in return. SEC. 3. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: (a) Program refers to the Scholarship Program established under Section 4 of this Act; (b) Registered Guidance Counselor (RGC) refers to a person duly registered and licensed under Republic Act No. 9258, otherwise known as the “Guidance and Counseling Act of 2004”;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Programme for International Student Assessment recorded the Philippines as having the highest incidence of bullying among all participating countries in 2018, with 65% of Filipino learners reporting bullying at least a few times a month; in 2022, roughly 43% of girls and 53% of boys still reported repeated monthly incidents, against OECD averages of about 20% and 21%.1 DepEd itself has declared bullying a national concern rather than a school-level problem.2 Meanwhile, the National Center for Mental Health registered 7,189 suicide-related hotline calls from January to September 2025 mostly from individuals aged 18 to 30.3 These are the ordinary, daily conditions that a functioning guidance service exists to meet. Yet Filipino learners are in the middle of a mental health crisis that our schools are not staffed to answer. In the hearing of the Committee on Appropriations on 3 September 2025, the Department of Education (DepEd) confirmed that the country had only 4,069 licensed guidance counselors as against the more than 50,000 required to meet the recommended global ratio of one counselor for every 250 students.4 Roughly 79% of DepEd guidance counselor positions (4,460 positions) remain unfilled, with several regions posting vacancy rates above 80% and with single counselors covering multiple campuses.5 Higher education fares no better: data of the Philippine Guidance and Counseling Association (PGCA) show an 80% shortfall in higher education institutions (HEIs), where only 1,029 counselors serve against an ideal requirement of 5,315.6 1 EDCOM II, “High incidence of bullying in PH public schools alarming,” 13 June 2024, citing OECD, PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 results. 2 “Angara convenes the largest executive committee to combat bullying,” Department of Education, 15 April 2025. 3 “Mental health crisis hotline receives 7,189 suicide-related calls,” The Philippine Star, 2 November 2025, reporting National Center for Mental Health data for January to September 2025. 4 Statement of DepEd Secretary Juan Edgardo Angara before the House Committee on Appropriations, 3 September 2025, as reported in “Angara: Guidance counselor shortage worsens amid bullying surge in PH schools.” 5 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), Turning Point: A Decade of Necessary Reform (2026–2035), Final Report, Priority 10: Home and School Environment, Issue No. 3, p. 198. 6 Philippine Guidance and Counseling Association survey data, as cited in Villarin et al., “The State of Guidance Counseling in Philippine Education,” International Multidisciplinary Journal of Research for Innovation, Sustainability, and Excellence (IMJRISE), Vol. 1, Issue No. 5 (2024). The deficiency is not one of demand but of supply. Since 2008, only a little over 3,000 individuals have passed the licensure examination for guidance counselors.7 Against approximately 4,286 counselors needed and only about 339 graduates of master's programs in Guidance and Counseling produced each year, there are roughly seventeen (17) vacant posts for every graduate, and the system would require twelve (12) to fourteen (14) years to close the existing gap even on the heroic assumptions of zero attrition and zero enrollment growth.8 The bottleneck is the graduate degree itself: Republic Act No. 9258 requires both a master's degree and licensure,9 yet the cost of that degree is borne almost entirely by the individual, while entry-level compensation begins at Salary Grade 11 (PhP 31,705.00) and rises only to PhP 36,125.00 at Salary Grade 13 for the same qualification.10 This bill institutionalizes that investment as a permanent national program. A scholarship alone will not solve a problem this large, and this bill does not pretend otherwise. It does, however, address the single constraint that no amount of plantilla creation, campus security hardware, or emergency deployment can overcome: there are simply not enough licensed professionals to hire. Metal detectors screen for weapons; only a counselor can screen for despair. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 10998
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL VETERANS BURIAL ASSURANCE PROGRAM THROUGH THE ACQUISITION OF PERPETUAL INTERMENT RIGHTS IN ACCREDITED MEMORIAL PARKS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6948, AS AMENDED, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XVI, Section 7 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State “shall provide immediate and adequate care, benefits, and other forms of assistance to war veterans and veterans of military campaigns, their surviving spouses and orphans,” and directs that “[f]unds shall be provided therefor.”1 That obligation does not end at the veteran's death. A dignified place of interment is the last benefit the Republic can confer on those who bore its arms, and at present the Republic confers it unevenly. The Libingan ng mga Bayani in Taguig City remains the principal national resting place for Filipino military veterans. It is also, for most of them, unreachable. Republic Act No. 6948, as amended, furnishes a burial flag and burial assistance now fixed at Twenty Thousand Pesos (PhP 20,000.00).2 That sum defrays funeral expenses. It does not purchase a burial lot, which in most provinces now costs several times that amount, and it does not secure perpetual care. The result is a benefit structure that pays for the rites but not for the ground. This bill takes the other road. Rather than build, the State buys, acquiring through competitive public procurement and in consolidated volume perpetual interment rights in memorial parks that already exist, that are already developed, and that are already subject to regulation and contractual perpetual care obligations. The economic case is not that the arrangement is free. It is that a single, fixed, present payment extinguishes an open-ended future liability: the cost of upkeep is prepaid into a perpetual care fund held in escrow, the land is never bought, no civil works are undertaken, and a plot becomes available to a grieving family in days rather than in budget cycles. The proponent reports a developed lot in Nueva Vizcaya, inclusive of perpetual care, 1 CONST. (1987), art. XVI, sec. 7. 2 Rep. Act No. 6948 (1990), secs. 19–20, as amended by Rep. Act No. 7696 (1994), sec. 6, and Rep. Act No. 10649 (2014), which increased burial assistance from PhP 10,000.00 to PhP 20,000.00. at approximately PhP 89,000.00.3 Bulk acquisition should improve on that figure; the bill requires that any such advantage be captured through competitive bidding under the New Government Procurement Act rather than assumed.4 Three safeguards distinguish this measure from a simple purchase order, and the Committee's attention is respectfully invited to them. First, a memorial lot in this jurisdiction is ordinarily conveyed not as titled land but as a right of interment under contract.5 A statute that assumed the Republic would receive a certificate of title for each plot would fail in the registry. The bill therefore secures the State's interest as a perpetual, irrevocable, and registered encumbrance annotated on the certificate of title of the memorial park itself, so that the veteran's resting place survives the sale, foreclosure, or insolvency of the developer. Second, perpetual care funds must be held in escrow with a government financial institution and pass automatically to a successor administrator upon default, rather than remaining an unsecured promise. Third, every plot is inalienable, exempt from execution, and traceable in a national registry, and its commercial resale is penalized. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ATTY. TIMOTHY JOSEPH E. CAYTON, PhD. label: HB 11000
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE MINDANAO FUNCTIONAL LITERACY AND HUMAN CAPITAL DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM IN SUPPORT OF THE MINDANAO AGENDA 2023–2028, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Recent data from the Philippine Statistics Authority, particularly the 2024 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS), reveal that while basic literacy remains high, functional literacy in the Philippines stands at only about 70.8%, leaving a significant portion of the population unable to effectively comprehend and apply information in daily life. This challenge is more pronounced in Mindanao, particularly in disadvantaged and conflict- affected regions, where educational access, poverty, and historical inequalities continue to constrain human capital development. The Mindanao Agenda 2023–2028, spearheaded by the Mindanao Development Authority, identifies human capital development, inclusive growth, and peacebuilding as central pillars to sustain Mindanao’s economic gains and long-term stability. However, functional illiteracy remains a structural barrier to achieving these objectives. The 2024 Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS) revealed that all Mindanao regions posted functional literacy rates lower than the national average functional literacy rate of 70.8%, with Zamboanga Peninsula (59.3%), Northern Mindanao (70.0%), Davao Region (66.7%), SOCCSKSARGEN (65.8%), Caraga (63.1%), and BARMM (64.7%) reflecting the percentage of the population aged 10 to 64 years who can read, write, compute, and comprehend. Functional illiteracy undermines workforce readiness, weakens productivity, limits civic participation, and constrains the successful reintegration of conflict-affected populations. Without targeted intervention, it threatens to erode the gains envisioned under the Mindanao Agenda. This bill seeks to institutionalize a Mindanao-wide Functional Literacy and Human Capital Development Program, anchored on the strategic priorities of the Mindanao Agenda 2023– 2028, integrating education, workforce development, digital inclusion, and community-based learning systems. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11001
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 15, 19, 30, AND 31 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 12001, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “REAL PROPERTY VALUATION AND ASSESSMENT REFORM ACT”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 12001, otherwise known as the "Real Property Valuation and Assessment Reform Act" (RPVARA), was enacted to effectively establish a uniform, transparent, and equitable real property valuation system across the Philippines. This law centralizes valuation standards and implements a definitive framework for adopting the Schedule of Market Values (SMV). By doing so, it decisively eliminates arbitrary property assessments, strengthens local revenue generation, and guarantees a predictable environment for real property transactions. However, implementation since its passage has revealed structural gaps in specific procedural timelines, administrative coordination, and local governance adaptability. This amendatory bill addresses these practical hurdles by strengthening BLGF oversight, establishing clear fallback mechanisms for SMV approval, refining tax relief parameters, and providing a realistic transition period for capacity- constrained LGUs. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11002
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING CLIMATE LITERACY IN THE BASIC EDUCATION CURRICULUM, MANDATING TEACHER TRAINING THEREFOR, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines consistently ranks among the most climate-vulnerable countries in the world. As an archipelagic nation situated along the Pacific Typhoon Belt, the country bears the brunt of increasingly severe tropical cyclones, prolonged droughts, rising sea levels, and catastrophic flooding. While structural investments in climate adaptation and disaster risk management are critical, long-term resilience requires a fundamental shift in mindset—a transformation that must begin in the classroom. Section 16, Article II of the 1987 Philippine Constitution mandates that the State shall "protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature." Furthermore, Paragraph 2, Section 3, Article XIV dictates that educational institutions shall inculcate patriotism and nationalism, foster love of humanity, and teach the rights and duties of citizenship. While existing subjects in the K to 12 basic education curriculum incorporate environmental concepts in general science, climate change education remains fragmented, abstract, and unevenly integrated. Youth today are not merely passive victims of environmental degradation; they are pivotal agents of community resilience, innovation, and climate action. To prepare Filipino youth for the reality of climate disruption, climate literacy must be institutionalized as a distinct, age-appropriate, and practical subject across elementary and secondary levels. True climate literacy extends beyond fundamental climate science—it encompasses ecological ethics, community disaster preparedness, local ecosystem conservation, renewable energy, and climate justice. This proposed measure seeks to mandate the Department of Education (DepEd), in coordination with the Climate Change Commission (CCC) and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), to institutionalize a comprehensive Climate Literacy Subject in the basic education curriculum. In light of the urgent need to build a climate-resilient citizenry from the ground up, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11003
title: AN ACT RESTRUCTURING THE MOTOR VEHICLE USER’S CHARGE, PROVIDING FOR A MOTOR VEHICLE ROAD USER’S TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8794, ENTITLED “AN ACT IMPOSING A MOTOR VEHICLE USER’S CHARGE ON OWNERS OF ALL TYPES OF MOTOR VEHICLES AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to replace the Motor Vehicle User’s Charge (MVUC) established under Republic Act (RA) No. 8794 entitled “An Act Imposing a Motor Vehicle User’s Charge on Owners of All Types of Motor Vehicles and For Other Purposes”, as amended, and replace it with a Motor Vehicle Road User’s Tax (MVRUT). It aims to direct a portion of additional revenues toward public transportation and road safety. Since the enactment of RA No. 8794 in 2000, the number of motor vehicles has continued to increase and placed greater pressure on an already congested road network. Construction, maintenance, and rehabilitation costs have likewise increased, yet still the country continues to face persistent challenges in public transportation and road safety. Motor vehicles also vary in type, weight, capacity, use, and their impact on public roads likewise differs. Despite this, the existing rates do not provide a sufficiently responsive basis for determining the cost of road use. The proposed measure introduces a revised tax structure based on vehicle classification and gross vehicle weight, and shall cover registered private and government motor vehicles. It shall also provide a reduced rate for for-hire vehicles in recognition of their role in public transportation and commercial activity. It likewise recognizes that improving the country’s transportation system requires more than maintaining roads. Fifty percent (50%) of the incremental revenues will be directed to public utility vehicle modernization, programs for the prevention of road deaths, and assistance to road accident victims. This ensures that the additional tax placed on vehicle owners benefits not only them, but also the millions of Filipinos who depend on the country’s roads everyday. A road user tax should reflect the realities of road use today and contribute to addressing the transportation challenges that come with it. The modernization of the existing tax system for motor vehicle users provides a manageable transition and makes the country’s roads more sustainable, its public transportation more efficient and reliable, and its communities safer. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11004
title: AN ACT GRANTING RETIREMENT, HEALTH CARE AND MORTUARY BENEFITS TO PROFESSIONAL FILIPINO ATHLETES WHO WIN CHAMPIONSHIP TITLES IN INTERNATIONAL PROFESSIONAL SPORTS COMPETITIONS OR OTHER EQUALLY PRESTIGIOUS INTERNATIONAL GAMES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant retirement, health care, and death benefits to professional Filipino athletes who win championship titles in international professional sports competitions or other equally prestigious international sporting events. Professional Filipino athletes bring honor and international recognition to the Philippines through exceptional athletic achievement. However, many world champions face financial insecurity, limited access to health care, and inadequate social protection after retirement due to the absence of a dedicated welfare system. While Republic Act No. 10699, otherwise known as the “National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and Incentives Act,” provides incentives for amateur athletes, there is no comparable legal framework recognizing the long-term welfare needs of professional athletes who likewise achieve distinction for the country. This measure provides lifetime retirement pensions, PhilHealth coverage, hospitalization assistance, death benefits, and a Professional Filipino Athletes Welfare Development Trust Fund. It likewise authorizes the Games and Amusement Board to administer the program and ensure its long-term sustainability. The proposed measure recognizes the invaluable contributions of professional Filipino athletes and affirms the State’s commitment to safeguarding their welfare beyond their competitive careers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11005
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INSTALLATION OF SOLAR ENERGY SYSTEMS IN ALL PUBLIC SCHOOLS, ESTABLISHING THE SUSTAINABLE SCHOOLS PROGRAM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a Sustainable Schools Program which mandates the installation of solar energy systems in all public elementary and secondary schools. It promotes the use of renewable energy to improve learning environments, strengthen climate resilience, and reduce electricity costs in public schools. Many public schools continue to experience inadequate ventilation and rising indoor temperatures due to extreme heat, which adversely affect student health, concentration, and learning outcomes. At the same time, electricity costs consume a significant portion of school operating expenses, while schools in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas continue to face unreliable or limited access to electricity. The transition to renewable energy presents an opportunity to address these challenges while supporting the country’s clean energy and climate commitments. This measure institutionalizes a nationwide solarization program for public schools. It prioritizes schools with the highest heat indices, off-grid locations, and high student populations. The bill also establishes phased energy capacity targets, provides for maintenance funding and technical training, promotes net-metering for grid-connected schools, and ensures that procurement follows life-cycle cost and energy efficiency standards. These measures are intended to improve energy security, lower operating costs, and provide a more conducive environment for teaching and learning. Investing in renewable energy for public schools is an investment in both education and sustainable development. This bill promotes quality education while advancing energy security, environmental sustainability, and climate resilience. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11006
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE INCLUSION OF A PERSONAL FINANCIAL LITERACY COURSE IN THE TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL EDUCATION AND TRAINING CURRICULUM OF TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS AND TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY TRAINING CENTERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to include a Personal Financial Literacy Course (PFLC) as a mandatory component of the Technical-Vocational Education and Training (TVET) curriculum in all public and private Technical-Vocational Institutions (TVIs) and Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) training centers. It recognizes that preparing Filipinos for employment and entrepreneurship requires not only technical competence but also the ability to manage income and make sound financial decisions. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas recognizes financial capability as essential to meaningful financial inclusion, since access to financial services do not by itself enable individuals to make informed financial decisions1. While TVET equips learners with industry-relevant skills for employment and livelihood, it does not uniformly provide structured instruction on personal financial management. Republic Act (RA) No. 10922, otherwise known as the “Economic and Financial Literacy Act”, and RA No. 10679, otherwise known as the “Youth Entrepreneurship Act”, promote financial education but do not specifically require a dedicated financial literacy course across TVET programs. The proposed measure requires the PFLC as a stand-alone course for all TVET learners, regardless of their chosen program or qualification. The course will cover essential personal finance concepts, which includes but are not limited to budgeting, saving, debt management, investment, insurance, retirement, planning, credit, consumer protection, and digital financial services. It shall also introduce learners to the Philippine financial system and cybersecurity risks in digital transactions. The curriculum shall be periodically reviewed to remain responsive to developments in financial products, technology, and national financial inclusion priorities. Financial literacy empowers individuals long before wealth is accumulated. For many technical-vocational graduates, their first paycheck is the beginning of a family’s opportunity to move forward. Technical skills may open the door to 1 Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas. (n.d.). Financial Inclusion. Accessed from: https://www.bsp.gov.ph/SitePages/InclusiveFinance/InclusiveFinance.aspx. Accessed on July 20, 2026. employment, but financial knowledge helps ensure that the fruits of that work are not lost to avoidable debt, fraud, or poor financial decisions. This measure recognizes that preparing Filipinos for decent work also means preparing them to achieve lasting financial stability and economic independence. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11007
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE REGULATORY FRAMEWORK ON THE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the development, deployment, and use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Philippines. It adopts a risk-proportionate approach that sets standards for transparency, human oversight, accountability, and safety according to the potential impact of AI systems. Artificial intelligence has rapidly become an essential component of public administration, commerce, finance, education, healthcare, media, and critical infrastructure. In 2025, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO)1 reported that while the Philippines has legal frameworks on privacy and cybersecurity, it still lacks an AI-specific regulatory regime addressing transparency, accountability, algorithmic bias, deepfakes, and other emerging risks associated with advanced AI systems. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)2 likewise noted that the National AI Strategy Roadmap 2.0 recognizes gaps in AI governance, intellectual property, and synthetic media regulation and calls for an adaptive framework that balances innovation with public protection. The Philippine Institute for Development Studies also found that local government units remain only at low to moderate levels of AI readiness due to limited institutional capacity, digital infrastructure, and governance mechanisms, demonstrating that AI adoption is advancing more rapidly than the country’s regulatory capacity3. The measure establishes the Philippine AI Regulation Council (PARC) as the 1 United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization. (2025). UNESCO AI Readiness Assessment Report: Anchoring Ethics in AI Governance in the Philippines. Accessed from: https://www.unesco.org/en/articles/unesco-ai-readiness-assessment-report-anchoring-ethics-ai-governance-ph ilippines?hub=66941. Accessed on: July 25, 2026. 2 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development. (2026). National AI Strategy Roadmap 2.0 (NAISR 2.0). OECD AI Policy Observatory. Accessed from: https://oecd.ai/en/dashboards/policy-initiatives/national-ai-strategy-roadmap-20-naisr-20. Accessed on July 25, 2026. 3 Quimba, F. M. A., Caboverde, C. E. C., & Salazar, A. M. C. (2025). How ready are LGUs for AI adoption? Philippine Institute for Development Studies Discussion Paper No. 2025-48. Accessed from: https://www.pids.gov.ph/publication/discussion-papers/how-ready-are-lgus-for-ai-adoption. Accessed on July 25, 2026. central body for AI governance and requires a Mandatory Technical Compliance Code for key actors in the AI value chain. It sets rules for risk classification, technical audits, training data records, AI disclosures, opt-out mechanisms, bias assessments, incident reporting, and regulatory sandboxes, while limiting regulatory requirements for personal, academic, educational, and artistic uses. As artificial intelligence continues to reshape economic activity, public services, and social interaction, the country requires a modern legal framework that encourages technological advancement while protecting the rights, safety, and welfare of the Filipino people. The establishment of clear national standards for responsible AI governance shall strengthen regulatory certainty, improve investor confidence, safeguard innovation, and enable both government and industry to harness AI responsibly for inclusive and sustainable national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11008
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DISABILITY SUPPORT FUND FOR THE EMPOWERMENT, FULL PARTICIPATION, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES IN SOCIETY, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide regular financial assistance and strengthen disability support services for indigent persons with disabilities (PWDs). It establishes a Disability Support Fund that augments the rights and benefits guaranteed under Republic Act (RA) No. 7277, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Disabled Persons”, as amended by RA No. 9442 and RA No. 10754. PWDs incur out-of-pocket expenses for rehabilitation, maintenance medicines, and other health-related needs. Inaccessible facilities and limited support services drive up these costs, pushing indigent PWDs and their families deeper into poverty and exclusion. Existing discounts, privileges, and social protection programs do not sufficiently cover these recurring expenses. This measure institutionalizes the Disability Support Fund that shall provide an Individual Support Allowance initially set at Two thousand pesos (Php 2,000.00) to qualified indigent PWDs and support disability services managed by local government units. It also mandates the development of a Disability and Needs Assessment System and an integrated disability data management system to ensure that assistance reaches eligible beneficiaries efficiently and transparently. A nation demonstrates its strength not by how it serves the most privileged, but by how it protects those who face the greatest barriers every single day. For many PWDs, every journey to school, every trip to work, every medical consultation, and every attempt to live independently comes with costs that others never have to bear. Without meaningful government support, these barriers become lifelong obstacles that deny opportunities, dignity, and equal participation. This measure recognizes that genuine inclusion demands more than legal recognition, it requires sustained public investment that empowers persons with disabilities to live with dignity, independence, and hope. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11009
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES AND SOLO PARENTS FROM GOVERNMENT FEES AND CHARGES IN THE ISSUANCE OF BASIC DOCUMENTARY REQUIREMENTS FOR EMPLOYMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to exempt persons with disabilities (PWDs) and solo parents from government fees and charges for the issuance of basic documentary requirements for employment. It aims to eliminate financial barriers that may prevent qualified jobseekers from securing gainful work. The Philippine Statistics Authority’s 2025 Labor Force Survey1 recorded more than fifty-two (52) million individuals in the labor force, with more than two (2) million unemployed. When applying for jobs, applicants are often required to secure clearances and certificates, like barangay or police clearances, medical certificates, and academic and other government-issued records. Although individually modest, the hefty accumulative cost of these pre-employment requirements can burden PWDs and solo parents who may find themselves having to prioritize expenses related to the everyday sustenance of their families. The bill therefore waives government fees and charges for essential pre-employment documents issued by national government agencies and local government units (LGU). Qualified beneficiaries may avail themselves of the exemption upon presentation of the appropriate identification issued or recognized by the concerned LGU. Employment should be determined through a person’s competence, determination, and potential, not merely by their ability to pay for documentary requirements before getting their first paycheck. This measure promotes equal opportunities and strengthens the economic participation of PWDs and solo parents without lowering employment standards. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 Philippine Statistics Authority. (2025, July 8). Participation in the labor force in May 2025 increased to 52.32 million Filipinos aged 15 years and over. Accessed from: https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/labor-force-survey/node/1684077662. Accessed in July 5, 2026. label: HB 11010
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE PENALTIES FOR AND BANNING THOSE CONVICTED OF ANIMAL CRUELTY FROM OWNING ANIMALS, STRENGTHENING ANIMAL WELFARE PROTECTION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8485, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ANIMAL WELFARE ACT OF 1988, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to impose higher penalties for acts of animal cruelty, maltreatment, and neglect; permanently prohibit persons convicted of violations under Republic Act (RA) No. 8485, otherwise known as the “Animal Welfare Act of 1998”, as amended, from owning animals; and establish a National Animal Offender Registry under the Department of Agriculture. In February 2025, public outrage followed the discovery of a dead dog inside a government-run dog pound in Masbate, prompting renewed calls for stronger accountability and animal welfare protections1. In March 2025, the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) likewise called for stronger enforcement following the fatal stabbing of a dog in Subic, Zambales. These incidents shows the challenges in reporting and prosecuting animal cruelty cases, particularly due to weak enforcement and limited public awareness of legal remedies2. Highly publicized cases of animal cruelty shared on social media have further stressed the need for stronger safeguards. “Tiktok”, a dog from Negros Occidental, was shot multiple times with arrows, while “Axle”, an American Bully from Mountain Province, was brutally beaten and killed after allegedly urinating on the perpetrator3. These cases show the continuing need to strengthen the country’s legal framework on animal welfare and ensure that such acts of cruelty are met with penalties commensurate with their severity. While RA No. 8485, as amended, prescribes criminal penalties for acts of animal cruelty, its existing safeguards remain limited in preventing convicted offenders from gaining access to animals in the 1 Barcelonia, W. (2025, February 13). Poe slams alleged animal abuse in Masbate, sees need for stronger laws. Philippine News Agency. Accessed from: https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1243994. Accessed in June , 2026. 2 Serquiña, M. (2025, March 27). Animal cruelty is a crime, here’s what you should do to stop it. GMA News Online. Accessed from: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/940789/animal-cruelty-paws-tips/story/. Accessed in July 6, 2026. 3 Serquiña, M. (2025, December 18). Justice pursued: Rap filed for dog’s death in Mountain Province. GMA News Online. Accessed from: https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/regions/970080/charges-dog-death-mountain-province/story . Accessed in July 6, 2026. future. The proposed measure increases the penalties for animal cruelty to ensure that the punishment reflects the gravity of the offense and strengthens its deterrent effect. It also permanently prohibits convicted offenders from owning animals and establishes a National Animal Offender Registry to enable law enforcement agencies, regulatory authorities, animal shelters, breeders, rescue organizations, and other authorized stakeholders to verify a person’s history of animal welfare violations. A nation’s compassion is measured not only by how it treats its people, but also by the mercy it extends to those without a voice. Animals depend entirely on human conscience for their protection, and when the law allows convicted abusers to regain access to them without meaningful safeguards, innocent lives remain vulnerable to repeated cruelty. As stewards of the environment and of creatures that cannot protect themselves, we have a duty to ensure that cruelty has no place in a civilized society. Advocating for the welfare of animals is not merely an act of kindness, but is a reflection of our collective commitment to justice and humanity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11011
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A PUBLIC VETERINARY CLINIC IN EVERY CITY AND MUNICIPALITY IN THE COUNTRY, PROVIDING FOR THEIR OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Public Veterinary Clinic in every city and municipality in the country. It aims to provide preventive, diagnostic, curative, and emergency animal health services, strengthen disease surveillance and response, promote responsible pet ownership, support livestock and poultry raisers, and advance animal welfare as an essential component of public health and food security. Despite the passage of Republic Act (RA) No. 8485, otherwise known as the “Animal Welfare Act of 1988”, as amended; and RA No. 9482, otherwise known as the “Anti-Rabies Act of 2007”, access to veterinary services remains uneven across the country. Many municipalities still lack permanent veterinary offices, adequate facilities, and sufficient veterinary personnel, leaving pet owners, farmers, and livestock raisers with limited access to essential animal health services. The Department of Health reported two hundred and sixty (260) human rabies cases from January to September 2025, with ninety-five percent (95%) of infections involving animals that were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status1. Likewise, veterinary experts have emphasized that many municipalities continue to operate without permanent veterinarians, making sustained vaccination campaigns, disease surveillance, and animal health planning difficult to implement effectively2. The proposed measure establishes fully operational public veterinary clinics in every city and municipality to expand vaccination and sterilization programs, improve disease surveillance and emergency response, enhance animal rescue and welfare services, provide technical assistance to livestock and poultry producers, and institutionalize accessible veterinary care as a regular local government service. It also reinforces local preparedness against zoonotic diseases while promoting healthier communities and protecting agricultural productivity. 1 Montemayor, M. (2025, September 29). DOH pushes for responsible pet ownership as rabies cases in PH hit 260. Philippine News Agency. Accessed from: https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1259841. Accessed on July 6, 2026. 2 Varcas, M. (2026, March 5). Experts push for municipal veterinary offices bill to curb rabies cases. Philippine Star-Business World. Accessed from: https://bworldonline.com/health/2026/03/05/734549/. Accessed on July 6, 2026. Animals enrich families, sustain livelihoods, and contribute to the nation’s food security, yet countless Filipinos continue to struggle to obtain even the most basic veterinary care because these services remain unavailable or financially out of reach in many communities. Every missed vaccination, untreated illness, or delayed response to disease increases the risk to both animal and human lives and places greater economic burdens on households and local governments. Establishing public veterinary clinics throughout the country transforms animal healthcare into an essential public service that protects families, strengthens rural economies, safeguards the nation’s food supply, and promotes a more compassionate and healthier society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11012
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING PROVINCIAL SOIL LABORATORY FACILITIES IN ALL PROVINCES OF THE PHILIPPINES, STRENGTHENING SOIL HEALTH MANAGEMENT AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish at least one (1) Provincial Soil Laboratory Facility in every province of the Philippines under the Department of Agriculture (DA), through the Bureau of Soils and Water Management (BSWM). It aims to provide accessible, reliable, and comprehensive soil testing, analysis, and technical advisory services for farmers and local government units. The agricultural sector continues to grapple with declining soil fertility, inefficient fertilizer application, increasing production costs, and the growing impacts of climate change. Although the BSWM currently provides laboratory services, access remains limited, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged provinces. Many farmers rely on generalized fertilizer recommendations or basic field-based Soil Test Kits that cannot adequately determine nutrient deficiencies, soil organic matter, salinity, contamination, and other critical indicators necessary for precision agriculture. The DA1 launched the country’s first Mobile Soil Laboratory in December 2024 to bring advanced soil testing closer to farming communities, acknowledging that access to science-based soil analysis remains a challenge. The DA-BSWM’s National Soil Health Program identifies accessible and accurate soil testing as a cornerstone of sustainable agriculture and productivity. Additionally, the 2024 Status of the World’s Soils2 reported that thirty-three percent (33%) of the global soils are already moderately to highly degraded, threatening food production and environmental sustainability. These realities highlight the urgent need to establish permanent provincial laboratories capable of providing comprehensive diagnostics to support informed fertilizer use, higher yields, and long-term food security. 1 DA-AFID. (2024, December 10). DA Unveils Mobile Soil Lab. Department of Agriculture. Accessed from: https://www.da.gov.ph/gallery/da-unveils-mobile-soil-lab-december-6-2024/. Accessed on July 5, 2026. 2 Smith, P. et al., 2024. Status of the World’s Soils. Annual Review Environment and Resources. 49:73-104. https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-environ-030323-075629 This proposed measure ensures these facilities conduct macro- and micronutrient analysis, soil organic matter assessment, soil texture and structure evaluation, salinity and contamination testing, and other diagnostic procedures beyond conventional test kits. It integrates laboratory-generated data into fertilizer assistance programs, agricultural extension services, and provincial development planning through a mandatory Site-Specific Nutrient Management framework. The bill also ensures affordable access to soil testing, prioritizes smallholder farmers, promotes partnerships with state universities and research institutions, and establishes a nationwide soil health monitoring system that will enable evidence-based policymaking. Farmers have long carried the responsibility of feeding millions despite facing declining soil quality and escalating production costs. Every harvest lost to poor soil management weakens rural livelihoods, drives food prices upward, and threatens national food security. Investing in provincial soil laboratories is an investment in every farming family and Filipino household. Providing farmers with accurate soil information empowers them to make better decisions, improve productivity, reduce unnecessary expenses, and preserve the country’s most valuable agricultural resource for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G.
