label: HB 11013
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE ALTERNATIVE CLASSROOM LEARNING EXPERIENCE PROGRAM TO ALL SECONDARY AND TERTIARY EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS THROUGHOUT THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize the Alternative Classroom Learning Experience (ACLE) Program in all public and private secondary and tertiary educational institutions throughout the Philippines. It complements formal classroom instruction through student-led academic, civic, and experiential learning activities that cultivate critical thinking, democratic participation, leadership, and social responsibility. The country continues to confront a learning crisis that extends beyond academic performance, but also to the development of critical thinking, civic engagement, and leadership among learners. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II)1 described the state of Philippine education as a matter of “national survival” and emphasized that ninety one percent (91%) of Filipino ten-year-old learners are unable to read and understand age-appropriate texts, while persistent weaknesses in analytical reasoning, communication, and problem-solving continue to undermine the country’s human capital. The report further stressed that learning recovery cannot rely solely on traditional classroom instruction and called for transformative reforms that develop learners’ higher-order thinking, collaboration, and real-world competencies. Likewise, the Department of Education’s Quality Basic Education Development Plan (Q-BEDP) 2025–20352 recognizes that improving education quality requires learner-centered, experiential, and innovative approaches that prepare students for rapid technological change, artificial intelligence, and the Fourth Industrial Revolution. Internationally, UNICEF Philippines3 continues to warn that the country’s learning crisis threatens its demographic dividend, noting 1 Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). (2025,January). Fixing the Foundations: A Matter of National Survival (Year Two Report). Accessed from: https://edcom2.gov.ph/media/2025/01/EDCOM-2-Year-2-Report-Fixing-the-Foundations-2025.pdf. Accessed on July 4, 2026. 2 Department of Education. (2025). Quality Basic Education Development Plan (Q-BEDP) 2025–2035. 2025. Accessed from: https://planipolis.iiep.unesco.org/en/2025/quality-basic-education-development-plan-2025-2035. Accessed on July 4, 2026. 3 Piojo, L. M. (2024, Updated2025). Education: The Learning Crisis. UNICEF Philippines. Accessed from: https://www.unicef.org/philippines/education. Accessed on July 4, 2026. that without quality and inclusive education, the Philippines risks producing a generation that is inadequately prepared for employment, civic participation, and sustainable national development. Despite these realities, opportunities for structured, student-led academic discussions, community immersion, interdisciplinary learning, and civic engagement remain largely dependent on the initiatives of individual schools rather than on a consistent national policy. This measure institutionalizes the Alternative Classroom Learning Experience (ACLE) Program as a mandatory activity to be conducted at least once every semester or academic term in all secondary and tertiary educational institutions. It empowers student councils and student governments to organize educational discussions, policy fora, workshops, community integration activities, lectures, symposia, fieldwork, film screenings, and other experiential learning initiatives with the support of school administrations. It transforms these activities into an integral component of the educational experience, guaranteeing that learners develop not only academic competence but also leadership, civic consciousness, social awareness, innovation, and the capacity to engage constructively with diverse ideas and contemporary national issues. The bill reinforces the policy objectives of Republic Act (RA) No. 9155, otherwise known as the “Governance of Basic Education Act of 2001”; RA No. 7722, otherwise known as the “Higher Education Act of 1994”; RA No. 8292, otherwise known as the “Higher Education Modernization Act of 1997”; and RA No. 9500, otherwise known as the “University of the Philippines Charter of 2008”, all of which uphold quality education, academic freedom, institutional autonomy, and the holistic development of Filipino learners. Education must do more than produce graduates who can pass examinations; it must nurture citizens who can question, innovate, lead, and serve. Every learner deserves opportunities to experience education beyond the confines of textbooks and classrooms, where ideas are challenged, perspectives are broadened, and meaningful engagement with society begins. As the nation strives to recover from years of learning loss while preparing its youth for an increasingly complex and interconnected world, investing in programs that cultivate critical thinkers and responsible leaders has become an urgent national imperative. Institutionalizing the Alternative Classroom Learning Experience Program will help ensure that Filipino students are not merely equipped to earn a diploma, but are empowered to shape communities, strengthen democratic institutions, and lead the country's future with competence, integrity, and purpose. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. title: AN ACT PROVIDING A LEGAL FRAMEWORK FOR TRANSACTIONS AND OTHER LEGALLY RELEVANT ACTS PERFORMED THROUGH ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AGENTS, ESTABLISHING A VOLUNTARY DIGITAL AUTHORITY CREDENTIAL FRAMEWORK, PRESERVING ACCOUNTABILITY AND GOOD-FAITH RELIANCE, PROTECTING LAWFUL DIGITAL ASSET OWNERSHIP, SELF-CUSTODY, PEER-TO- PEER AND OPEN-SOURCE TECHNOLOGIES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial intelligence is rapidly evolving from a technology that merely generates recommendations or content into one capable of acting on behalf of people and businesses. AI agents can increasingly negotiate terms, communicate with counterparties, execute electronic documents, initiate payments, and interact with automated systems without requiring a human to approve every individual step. Philippine law already recognizes electronic transactions and automated information systems. The next policy challenge is to provide greater legal certainty when increasingly autonomous AI agents perform legally consequential acts: when should an act be attributed to the person who authorized the agent, when may a third party reasonably rely upon that authority, and how should accountability be preserved without granting legal personhood to software? This measure adopts an enabling rather than prohibitory approach. It recognizes AI agents as technological instruments through which natural and juridical persons may act, while ensuring that an identifiable Principal remains accountable. It establishes a primarily voluntary Digital Authority Credential framework so that persons and businesses that need greater certainty may make delegated authority verifiable to counterparties. Mandatory registration is reserved for narrowly designated high-risk autonomous transactions where existing regulation is inadequate. The measure is also founded on technological neutrality. AI agents may interact with conventional payment systems, application programming interfaces, blockchain networks, smart contracts, digital assets, self-custodial wallets, and future technologies, subject to laws independently applicable to the person or transaction. The Act does not create a new license for digital assets, does not require the registration of wallets or blockchain addresses, does not require disclosure of private keys or seed phrases, and does not prohibit lawful self- custody or peer-to-peer transactions. The bill likewise protects open-source and non-custodial innovation by providing that developers and infrastructure participants are not treated as Principals or financial intermediaries merely because they publish or maintain software without controlling users' assets or transactions. The objective is simple: to give Filipinos and Philippine businesses a clear legal framework for using AI agents to transact, while preserving accountability, consumer and third- party protection, privacy, cybersecurity, innovation, competition, and technological freedom. 1 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL CONTINUOUS VEGETABLE PLANTING INTENTIONS SURVEY AND MODERNIZING AGRICULTURAL STATISTICAL FORECASTING THROUGH REAL-TIME DATA AND GEOSPATIAL TECHNOLOGIES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide timely and forward-looking information on vegetable production, supply, demand, and market conditions. It aims to strengthen production planning and enable the government and agricultural stakeholders to identify emerging imbalances and respond before these translate into significant losses for farmers and disruptions in the market. In April 2026, cabbage farmers in Atok, Benguet reportedly received as little as Four pesos (Php 4.00) to Eight pesos (Php 8.00) per kilogram, while some opted not to harvest as prices fell below production and harvesting costs1. At the La Trinidad Vegetable Trading Post, adequate supply coincided with weaker demand, fewer buyers, and high transport costs, leaving some produce unsold2. Farmers and traders subsequently sought temporary floor prices for selected vegetables after cabbage prices fell to about Five pesos (Php 5.00) per kilogram against production costs of approximately Twenty pesos (Php 20.00) per kilogram3. These show the need for reliable information on what farmers intend to plant, where production will occur, and when harvests are expected, so that potential supply and market imbalances can be identified earlier. The proposed measure institutionalizes the National Vegetable Planting Intentions Survey under the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), which shall regularly collect information on intended crops, planting areas, locations, production schedules, expected output, and intended markets. Planting-intentions data will be integrated with production and administrative records, market and demand indicators, weather and climate information, and geospatial data. Digital reporting platforms, Geographic Information Systems, remote sensing, and statistical and econometric models may be used to generate geographically disaggregated forecasts and assess planting intentions against actual planting, harvested area, production, and market outcomes. For vegetable farmers, timely information can mean the difference between a profitable harvest and a crop that is left to rot. When vegetables are sold below production cost or abandoned in the fields, farmers lose not only their expected income but also the capital, labor, and months of work invested in every planting season. These losses also affect consumers, traders, transporters, and the broader agricultural economy. The State should not wait for farmgate prices to collapse, trading posts to be filled with unsold produce, or crops to spoil before responding. Farmers deserve a government that can see emerging risks, act ahead of market disruptions, and use public resources where they can have the greatest impact. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the Philippines’ most important natural assets. Stretching from Cagayan in the north to Quezon in the south, it forms a vast interconnected landscape of forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems. Its ecological functions extend far beyond the mountain range itself, providing essential services that sustain communities, agriculture, water systems, infrastructure, livelihoods, and economic activities in both upland and downstream areas. The Sierra Madre likewise serves as a critical natural defense against typhoons, flooding, landslides, storm surges, drought, and other climate-related hazards. Its forests, watersheds, wetlands, riparian areas, ecological corridors, and coastal ecosystems regulate water flows, store and sequester carbon, support biodiversity, and contribute to the resilience of communities and critical infrastructure. The protection and restoration of the Sierra Madre are therefore not merely matters of environmental conservation, but matters of national development, public safety, water security, climate resilience, and national security. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre remains vulnerable to continuing degradation arising from illegal logging, destructive extraction, incompatible land conversion, habitat fragmentation, biodiversity loss, and other activities that undermine ecological integrity. Existing governmental mandates and management arrangements, while important, operate through different agencies, jurisdictions, plans, and regulatory systems. Such fragmentation makes it difficult to manage the Sierra Madre as one 1 interconnected ecological system and to consistently account for impacts that cross administrative boundaries. This proposed measure seeks to address this institutional and ecological gap by establishing the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA) as a government-owned or -controlled corporation with an original charter, attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination and administrative supervision. The Authority is envisioned as the lead policy, planning, coordinating, and regulatory body for range-wide ecological governance, while preserving the lawful mandates of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), local government units, Protected Area Management Boards, the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, and other competent institutions. At the center of the proposed framework is the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, geospatially explicit, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. The measure adopts a landscape-scale and ridge-to-reef approach to conservation. Rather than treating forests, watersheds, rivers, biodiversity areas, and coastal ecosystems as isolated units, the proposed framework recognizes their ecological and hydrological interdependence. It provides for the identification and protection of ecological corridors, riparian buffers, critical habitats, key biodiversity areas, and other connectivity systems necessary to maintain biodiversity and ecosystem resilience. The bill further advances a Nature-Based Solutions-First policy. Government interventions addressing flooding, landslides, erosion, watershed degradation, water insecurity, coastal hazards, and climate risks will be required to consider the feasibility of nature-based, green, or green-gray solutions before relying solely on conventional infrastructure. The proposed approach recognizes natural ecosystems as functional infrastructure capable of providing long-term disaster-risk reduction, water-security, and climate-adaptation benefits. Recognizing that conservation cannot be sustained without viable communities and economic incentives, the proposed measure promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples, upland communities, and lawful tenure holders to participate in conservation and restoration activities and benefit from verified ecological outcomes. A significant innovation of the measure is the establishment of a Sierra Madre Nature Credit System. The system is intended to create a transparent and independently verified mechanism through which measurable protection, restoration, biodiversity, watershed, water-security, and climate-resilience outcomes may be recognized and financed. Covered enterprises that materially depend upon Sierra Madre ecosystem services may be required to satisfy Nature Credit Purchase Obligations, thereby 2 helping align economic activity with the ecological services upon which such activity depends. The system expressly does not authorize prohibited activities or substitute for environmental, tenure, protected-area, or Indigenous Peoples safeguards. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, certain environmental charges, penalties and restoration recoveries when legally assignable, grants and technical assistance, and other lawful sources. The Fund is limited to the Authority’s statutory public-good and market-governance functions and is subject to government accounting, procurement, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. label: HB 11018
title: AN ACT CREATING THE BICOL RIVER BASIN MANAGEMENT OFFICE (BRBMO), DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bicol River Basin is one of the most significant river systems in the Philippines, serving as a vital source of water for agriculture, domestic use, fisheries, and ecological sustainability in the Bicol Region. It plays a critical role in supporting food security, livelihoods, and regional economic development. However, the basin continues to face persistent and complex challenges, including recurrent flooding, watershed degradation, sedimentation, climate change impacts, and fragmented governance mechanisms. Despite the existence of various national and local initiatives, the management of the Bicol River Basin remains institutionally fragmented, with multiple agencies exercising overlapping mandates over water resources, irrigation, flood control, environmental protection, and land use. This has resulted in inefficiencies, lack of coordination, and suboptimal outcomes in addressing both environmental and socio-economic concerns. The Constitution mandates the State to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology (Article II, Section 16), and to ensure the rational utilization and conservation of natural resources. In line with this, there is a compelling need to adopt an integrated river basin management (IRBM) approach, which recognizes the interdependence of land, water, ecosystems, and human communities within a river basin. While prior executive issuances, such as Presidential Decree No. 926 and Executive Order No. 359, have established project-level and programmatic mechanisms for the Bicol River Basin, these measures remain limited in scope, continuity, and institutional authority. Moreover, existing structures under the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), including the River Basin Control Office, primarily provide policy direction at the national level and are not designed to function as dedicated, basin-specific coordinating bodies with sustained operational capacity. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps through the creation of the Bicol River Basin Management Office (BRBMO), which shall serve as a central coordinating and integrative body for all programs, projects, and policies affecting the Bicol River Basin. The BRBMO is designed not to duplicate or supplant existing agencies, but to harmonize their efforts, facilitate inter-agency collaboration, and ensure a coherent and science-based approach to river basin management. Consistent with the principle of local autonomy under the Local Government Code of 1991, the proposed Office shall work in close coordination with local government units, ensuring that local development plans are aligned with basin-wide strategies while respecting the powers and functions of LGUs. Furthermore, the measure institutionalizes multi-stakeholder participation, recognizing that sustainable river basin management requires the active involvement of communities, farmers, fisherfolk, indigenous peoples, civil society, and the private sector. By establishing a dedicated institutional mechanism anchored on integrated, participatory, and science-driven management, this bill aims to enhance the resilience, sustainability, and productivity of the Bicol River Basin, thereby contributing to national priorities on environmental protection, disaster risk reduction, food security, and inclusive development. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11019
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING CHARACTER EDUCATION IN THE PHILIPPINE BASIC EDUCATION SYSTEM THROUGH A HOLISTIC AND VALUES-BASED APPROACH INSPIRED BY INTERNATIONAL BEST PRACTICES, INCLUDING JAPAN’S EDUCATIONAL MODEL, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The strength of a nation lies not only in the intelligence of its people, but in their character, discipline, and sense of responsibility to others. In recent years, concerns have been raised regarding declining discipline, lack of civic consciousness, and weakening social responsibility among the youth. While the Philippine education system has made significant strides in expanding access and improving academic outcomes, there remains a pressing need to reinforce character formation as a central pillar of education. Japan’s educational system offers a compelling model in this regard. It is globally recognized not only for academic excellence but for its deep-rooted emphasis on discipline, respect, responsibility, and collective accountability. Students are taught early on the value of hard work, cleanliness, cooperation, and respect for others, not merely through classroom instruction, but through daily school practices and community engagement. This proposed measure seeks to adapt these best practices to the Philippine context, strengthening the existing K to 12 curriculum by institutionalizing a more structured, experiential, and community-based approach to character education. It aims to produce learners who are not only academically competent but also morally grounded, socially responsible, and committed to nation-building. The bill is firmly anchored on Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution, which mandates the State to promote quality education and develop moral character. It complements existing laws such as Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013 by reinforcing the holistic development of learners. Importantly, this measure respects academic freedom, cultural diversity, and inclusivity, ensuring that character education remains secular, values- based, and responsive to the needs of Filipino communities. At a time when the nation faces complex social and economic challenges, it is imperative to invest not only in knowledge, but in the values and character of future generations. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11020
title: AN ACT REQUIRING ALL SHIPPING LINES OPERATING IN THE PHILIPPINES TO ADOPT ELECTRONIC TICKETING (E-TICKETING) AND CASHLESS PAYMENT SYSTEMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The maritime transport sector remains a critical backbone of inter-island connectivity in the Philippines, particularly in regions such as Bicol where mobility, trade, tourism, and access to essential services rely heavily on domestic shipping. Despite its importance, many shipping operations in the country continue to rely on manual ticketing systems and cash-based transactions, which are prone to inefficiencies, long queues, revenue leakages, and limited transparency. The continued reliance on manual and cash-based systems also poses challenges to passenger convenience, financial inclusion, and public safety, especially in the context of increasing demand for contactless and technology- driven services. Moreover, the absence of standardized digital systems limits the ability of government agencies to maintain accurate passenger manifests, monitor compliance, and implement data-driven policies in the maritime sector. The proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by requiring all domestic shipping lines and maritime passenger carriers to adopt electronic ticketing (e-ticketing) systems and cashless payment options. This initiative is aligned with the State policy to promote the development of information and communications technology, digital innovation, and efficient delivery of public services, consistent with Article II of the 1987 Constitution. This measure complements existing laws such as the E-Commerce Act of 2000 (Republic Act No. 8792), which recognizes the legal validity of electronic transactions, and the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173), which ensures the protection of personal data in digital systems. It likewise aligns with the national government’s thrust toward digital transformation and financial inclusion, as supported by the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas and the Department of Information and Communications Technology. Importantly, the bill does not eliminate cash transactions entirely but instead requires the availability of cashless alternatives, thereby ensuring inclusivity for passengers in areas with limited digital access while gradually transitioning the sector toward modernization. The measure also strengthens inter-agency coordination by designating the Department of Transportation, the Maritime Industry Authority, the Philippine Ports Authority, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and the Department of Information and Communications Technology as implementing agencies. This ensures that existing mandates are respected and harmonized, thereby avoiding duplication of functions and potential conflicts in authority. For the Bicol Region, the adoption of e-ticketing and cashless systems is expected to significantly improve port efficiency, passenger experience, tourism flow, and regional economic activity, while enhancing transparency and accountability in maritime operations. By institutionalizing digital ticketing and payment systems in the maritime sector, this bill aims to promote a modern, efficient, and inclusive transportation system that is consistent with national development goals and the evolving needs of the Filipino people. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11021
title: AN ACT ADOPTING A NATIONAL FLOOD CONTROL BENCHMARK BASED ON INTERNATIONAL BEST PRACTICES, INCLUDING JAPAN’S FLOOD MANAGEMENT STANDARDS, STRENGTHENING INTEGRATED RIVER BASIN MANAGEMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Flooding remains one of the most persistent and destructive natural hazards in the Philippines, causing significant loss of life, displacement of communities, and damage to infrastructure and the economy. The increasing intensity of rainfall due to climate change, combined with rapid urbanization and environmental degradation, has further heightened the country’s vulnerability to flooding. Despite substantial investments in flood control infrastructure, many existing systems remain fragmented, reactive, and insufficiently coordinated, often focusing on isolated structural interventions rather than comprehensive, basin-wide solutions. Japan is widely recognized as a global leader in flood management, having developed highly advanced systems that integrate engineering excellence, river basin management, land use planning, early warning systems, and community preparedness.1 Its approach is characterized by a multi-layered flood control strategy, combining structural and non-structural measures and grounded in long-term planning and scientific data. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a National Flood Control Benchmark Framework, drawing from Japan’s proven practices while adapting them to Philippine conditions. The objective is not merely to replicate foreign models, but to establish a unified, science-based standard for flood control across the country, ensuring consistency, efficiency, and resilience. 1 Tsukasa Nakamura, Deloitte, “How Japan is turning climate and ﬂood risk into economic growth through infrastructure innovations,” World Economic Forum, 10 August 2026, available at: https://www.weforum.org/stories/climate-action/japan-climate-ﬂood-resilience-infrastructure/ The measure is anchored on the State’s constitutional duty to protect the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology (Article II, Section 16) and to promote the general welfare. It also complements existing laws such as the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010 and the Climate Change Act of 2009, by strengthening the integration of infrastructure, environmental management, and disaster preparedness. Importantly, the bill respects the mandates of existing agencies and the autonomy of local government units, positioning the national framework as a coordinating and standard-setting mechanism rather than a centralizing authority. By adopting international best practices and institutionalizing integrated flood control standards, this measure aims to enhance the country’s capacity to prevent, mitigate, and respond to flooding, ultimately safeguarding lives, protecting property, and promoting sustainable development. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11022
title: AN ACT ENSURING GENDER-RESPONSIVENESS IN NATIONALITY LAWS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE COMMONWEALTH ACT NO. 473, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE REVISED NATURALIZATION LAW, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9139, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ADMINISTRATIVE NATURALIZATION LAW
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution enshrines the role of women in nation-building and the responsibility of the State to ensure the fundamental equality of women and men before the law (Article II, Section 14). Republic Act No. 9710, otherwise known as the Magna Carta of Women, and the UN Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (UN CEDAW), of which the Philippines is a State Party, underscores the equal rights of men and women to acquire, change, or retain their nationality (Section 19; Article 9, respectively). Further, both emphasize that neither marriage to an alien nor change of nationality by the husband during marriage shall automatically change the nationality of the wife, render her stateless, or force upon her the nationality of the husband (Section 19(g); Article 9). Despite these frameworks, the Philippines has been identified as one of fifty (50) States that continue to have distinctions in terms of conferral and acquisition/retainment of citizenship1. These are embodied in the country’s 1 Reference: https://equalnationalityrights.org/the-issue/the-problem Page 1 of 14 naturalization laws which are governed by Commonwealth Act No. 473, otherwise known as the Revised Naturalization Law, and Republic Act 9139 No. or the Administrative Naturalization Law. Article 15 of the Revised Naturalization Law denies a married woman the right to choose her nationality following the naturalization of her husband. Furthermore, Section 12 of the Administrative Naturalization Law prevents married women that have been granted Philippine citizenship through naturalization, from conferring her nationality to her husband. Not only do these provisions violate the principles and commitments of the Philippines under international2 and national laws, but it also inhibits inclusive sustainable development as citizenship serves as the gateway to access other rights and services3. Hence, this bill seeks to (1) harmonize existing laws4, (2) amend the current Administrative and Judicial Naturalization Laws, especially, the automatic conferment of derivative naturalization in Section 15 of Commonwealth Act No. 473, and the differential effect of naturalization on non-national spouses as indicated in Sections 11, 12, and 13 of Republic Act No. 9139, and (3) ensure safeguards to prevent statelessness in line with the General Recommendation No. 32 of the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women5 and the recently ratified 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. This proposed measure is also in line with efforts to remove gender discrimination in nationality laws under Action Point 3 of the National Action Plan to End Statelessness by 2024. It contributes to the fulfillment of the Philippines’ pledge to enhance its “policy, legal, and operational framework” during the 2011 Ministerial Inter-Governmental Event on Refugees and Stateless Persons6 and 2019 High-Level Segment on Statelessness7. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 The right to nationality is also enshrined in several international and regional human rights instruments. The list of which could be found in pages 26-28 of 2020 Guidelines on Statelessness on Loss and Deprivation of Nationality under Articles 5-9 of the 1961 Convention. 3 Reference: https://equalnationalityrights.org/the-issue/the-problem 4 Harmonization of naturalization laws with the Republic Act 9710 and the UN CEDAW would also contribute to the fulfillment of the recommendation of the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination of Women in its Concluding Observations on the Combined 7th and 8th Reports of the Philippines. 5 Specifically, paragraph 63 (b, e, i) of the General Recommendation No. 32 of the Gender-related Dimensions of Refugee Status, Asylum, Nationality and Statelessness of Women. 6 Information on the 2011 Ministerial Inter-Governmental Event on Refugees and Stateless Persons as well as the pledges manifested by the Philippines can be accessed through: https://www.unhcr.org/4ff55a319.pdf 7 Pledges manifested by the Philippines during the 2019 High-Level Segment on Statelessness can be accessed through: https://www.unhcr.org/ibelong/results-of-the-high-level-segment-on-statelessness/ Page 2 of 14 REP. label: HB 11023
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FIFTEEN THOUSAND PESOS (PHP 15,000) ACROSS THE BOARD INCREASE IN THE BASIC MONTHLY SALARY OF TEACHERS AND EMPLOYEES IN THE PUBLIC BASIC EDUCATION AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is the foundation of a strong, progressive, and inclusive nation. At the heart of our public education system are the teachers and employees who dedicate their knowledge, skills, time, and energy to shaping the future of our children and strengthening the human capital of our country. Every day, public school teachers and education personnel perform responsibilities that go far beyond the traditional boundaries of their jobs. Teachers prepare lessons, assess learners, provide individualized support, address learning gaps, manage classrooms, and respond to the diverse needs of students. Non- teaching personnel, meanwhile, provide essential administrative, technical, and support services that ensure the continuous and effective delivery of basic education. Despite the vital nature of their work, many public school teachers and employees continue to face increasing financial pressures brought about by the rising cost of food, transportation, housing, utilities, healthcare, and other basic necessities. The demands of the profession have likewise continued to grow, with education personnel being called upon to perform increasingly complex responsibilities in an evolving educational environment. The State recognizes the invaluable contribution of teachers and education personnel to national development. The 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall assign the highest budgetary priority to education and shall ensure that teaching will attract and retain its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration and other means of job satisfaction and fulfillment. Providing adequate and competitive compensation is not merely an issue of employee welfare. It is an investment in the quality and stability of our public education system. Fair and meaningful increases in salaries can help improve the economic well- being of education personnel, strengthen employee morale, promote retention, and encourage qualified and competent individuals to remain in or enter the public education service. In recognition of their indispensable contribution to the Filipino people, this measure seeks to grant an across-the-board increase of Fifteen Thousand Pesos (₱15,000.00) in the basic monthly salary of teachers and employees in public basic education. To ensure fiscal sustainability and facilitate the orderly implementation of the measure, the proposed increase shall be implemented in three tranches: ₱6,000.00 in the first year, ₱5,000.00 in the second year, and ₱4,000.00 in the third year. The proposed salary increase shall be granted in addition to existing salary adjustments under applicable salary standardization laws and shall not prejudice any succeeding salary increases that may be granted to government employees pursuant to law. The measure further recognizes that the welfare of teachers and education personnel is directly connected to the quality of education that our children receive. By providing them with better compensation and stronger economic security, the government can help create a more motivated, committed, and resilient public education workforce capable of responding to the changing needs of Filipino learners. Our teachers and education personnel are not merely government employees. They are builders of communities, shapers of minds, and partners in nation-building. Their work creates opportunities, transforms lives, and lays the foundation for the country's future. It is therefore imperative that the State provide them with compensation commensurate with the importance of their work and the responsibilities they carry. This measure seeks to reaffirm our commitment to the men and women who serve at the frontlines of public education and to ensure that their dedication and sacrifices are met with meaningful support from the government. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11024
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING STANDARDS FOR RELATED LEARNING EXPERIENCES (RLE) IN NURSING EDUCATION, PROHIBITING THE COLLECTION OF RLE FEES FROM NURSING STUDENTS IN STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES (SUCs) AND LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES (LUCs), AND PROVIDING FUNDING SUPPORT THROUGH THE COMMISSION ON HIGHER EDUCATION (CHED)
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) Memorandum Order No. 14, Series of 2009, students of the Bachelor of Science in Nursing (BSN) program are mandated to complete at least 46 units or 2,346 hours of Related Learning Experiences (RLE), which may be extended until expected competencies are satisfactorily achieved. RLE are integral to nursing education as teaching-learning opportunities designed to develop the competencies of nursing students utilizing the nursing process in varying health situations. Through RLE, Filipino nursing students are provided with hands-on clinical training and essential exposure to real-world healthcare settings. However, despite the existence of Republic Act No. 10931, otherwise known as the Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act (UAQTE), that provides for free tuition and institutional fees in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) and Local Universities and Colleges (LUCs) and Tertiary Education Subsidies (TES) in private higher education institutions (HEIs), RLE impose substantial financial burdens on nursing students through various fees, including affiliation charges, hospital training fees, transportation expenses, and allowances for clinical instructors. These RLE fees and related expenses, which are mostly shouldered by the nursing students themselves, range from P20,000 to P80,000 per year,1 thus creating significant barriers and placing underprivileged nursing students at a disadvantage. 1 Bonzo, L.T. (26 May 2026). CHED rolls out financial aid for 19,000 healthcare students. GMA News. Retrieved from https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/989023/ched-rolls-out-financial- aid-for-19-000-healthcare-students/story/. 1 In recognition of the noble contribution and significant role of nurses to the country’s healthcare sector, and in fulfilling the State’s mandate to make quality education accessible to all citizens, this bill seeks to institutionalize the non-collection of RLE fees from students in SUCs and LUCs. Under this bill, all RLE-related expenses shall be considered part of the tuition or institutional costs charged to the government through the Unified Student Financial Assistance System for Tertiary Education (UniFAST). As such, this bill mandates that all SUCs and LUCs offering nursing programs submit projected RLE expenses to CHED for funding through the UniFAST or other designated CHED mechanisms. For nursing students enrolled in accredited private HEIs, this bill also expands eligibility for the TES program to cover RLE fees. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Walfredo “Arman” Dimaguila, Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, Antolin Oreta III, and Javier Benitez in the House of Representatives, and Senator Bam Aquino in the Senate. This bill fully adopts Senator Bam Aquino’s Senate Bill No. 123. In view of the foregoing, early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. label: HB 11025
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING JOB PLACEMENT OFFICES IN ALL PUBLIC SENIOR HIGH SCHOOLS, STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND CREATING A NATIONAL INDUSTRY-ACADEME COUNCIL AND LOCAL INDUSTRY-ACADEME COUNCILS TO ADDRESS JOBS- SKILLS MISMATCH AND PROMOTE DECENT EMPLOYMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution provides for the State’s commitment to promoting full employment and a rising standard of living. This is further affirmed by Article XIII, Section 3 which declares the State’s mandate to promote full employment and equality of employment of all. Additionally, Article XIV, Section 2(1) provides that, “[t]he State shall [e]stablish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” In recent years, the State has taken significant steps towards ensuring equal access to quality education at all levels, including tertiary education, through the enactment of landmark legislation such as Republic Act No. 10931, or the “Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education (UAQTE) Act,” and the continuous filings of, and deliberations on amendatory measures to strengthen existing laws. However, despite these efforts, unemployment and underemployment remain persistent problems facing Filipino graduates after completing their senior high school or college education. According to CHED Chairperson Shirley Agrupis, the June 2025 Labor Force Survey by the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) showed a 2.6% increase in the number of unemployed college graduates from 35.6% in December 2024.1 1 Cariaso, B. (15 August 2025). ‘Rising number of unemployed grads troubling.’ PhilStar. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2025/08/15/2465562/rising-number-unemployed-grads- troubling. 1 Additionally, “even when job opportunities exist, there is a persistent mismatch between available jobs and graduates’ skills.”2 In the January 2025 nationwide job fairs held by DOLE, only 3,364 out of 25,876 job seekers were hired and the majority were placed in “low-skilled roles that do not require a college degree.”3 Based on a recent study, an estimated 40% of Filipinos face educational-employment mismatches, where over 1 out of 3 Filipinos have an educational attainment way beyond their job requirements.4 This job mismatch problem underscores allocative inefficiency, given the greater public investment in education, and more importantly, the “wage penalties” that millions of Filipino workers suffer instead of reaping the full benefits that tertiary education promised. This bill seeks to establish Job Placement Offices (JPOs) in all public senior high schools, state universities and colleges (SUCs), and local universities and colleges (LUCs) to provide greater access for students transitioning from education to employment. A Tripartite National Industry-Academe Council (NIAC) shall be created to strengthen collaboration and coordination between the government, education, and industry sectors. Local Industry-Academe Councils (LIACs) shall be institutionalized in every province and highly urbanized city to guide local institutions and the JPOs. The Philippine Labor Market Information System (PhilLMIS) shall be established within the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) to harmonize labor market data and guide policy. Lastly, the Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF) shall be reinforced as the national reference for classifying qualifications and formalizes the Philippine Skills Framework (PSF) as the tool for defining job-specific competencies. In strengthening the linkages between the government, education, and industry sectors, providing greater access to career guidance for students transitioning from education to employment, and establishing a system of harmonizing labor market data, qualifications, and competencies, this bill does not merely intend to create new instrumentalities, but to establish the steps in bridging the current education- employment gap. This is essential for the Filipino people, especially the youth, to attain an educational system where every Filipino has an opportunity to fully use their skills to maximize their income and professional potential. label: HB 11026
title: AN ACT FURTHER STRENGTHENING THE INCENTIVES FOR PRIVATE SECTOR PARTICIPATION IN PUBLIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8525, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ADOPT-A- SCHOOL ACT OF 1998”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Constitution provides that “[t]he State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Almost three (3) decades ago, Republic Act No. 8525, otherwise known as the “Adopt-a-School Act of 1998,” was enacted as a step towards achieving accessible quality education by facilitating the participation of the private sector in the country’s education sector. Under the law, tax incentives are given to private entities supporting public schools. However, recent data reflect the need for the law to be amended to better respond to current challenges, such as bureaucratic red tape and administrative complexity that prevent private entities from receiving their mandated tax incentives.1 Amidst the education crisis, exacerbated by inadequate learning facilities and classroom shortages, limited digital connectivity, and insufficient teaching resources, Filipino children and students increasingly struggle with access to quality education.2 These gaps accumulate and become barriers hindering the Filipino youth from enjoying their freedoms and rights to education, to self-development and self- actualization, and to social mobility. This bill amends Republic Act No. 8525 to allow private sector donors to support a wider range of educational programs, including early childhood care, technical- 1 Second Congressional Commission on Education (2025). Fixing the Foundations: A matter of national survival, EDCOM II year two report. Congress of the Philippines. 2 Cariaso, B. (28 May 2025). Classroom shortage still at 165,000 – DepEd. The Philippine Star. https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2025/05/28/2446283/classroom-shortage-still-165000-deped. 1 vocational education and training (TVET), and alternative-learning system (ALS). The bill also restructures the tax incentives to include clear and enhanced deductions, payroll tax credits for employing senior high school graduates, and exemptions for imported donations. This bill recognizes that addressing the education crisis requires not only sustained government investment and action, but also participation from the private sector, communities, and civil society. This bill affirms the principle that the equal opportunity for a better life through quality education cannot and should not be achieved by the government alone, but also through institutions that empower citizens, communities, and the private sector to participate in the endeavor of nation-building. In the 20th Congress, similar bills were filed by Representatives Jaime Fresnedi, Crispin Diego Remulla, Ryan Recto, Kenneth Gatchalian, Walfredo Dimaguila, Roman Romulo, Agatha Paula Cruz, Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo, David Suarez, Eric Go Yap, and Antonio Legarda in the House of Representatives, and Senators Win Gatchalian, Bam Aquino, Pia Cayetano, Loren Legarda, and Joel Villanueva. This bill adopts Senator Bam Aquino’s Senate Bill No. 129. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. LEILA M. title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE CLASSIFICATION OF DISTRICT OFFICE OF THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) IN LUCENA, QUEZON FROM CLASS "C"TO CLASS "A" DISTRICT OFFICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Land Transportation Ofice (LTO) District Office in Lucena City serves as the primary transportation regulatory and enforcement hub for Lucena City and the entire Second District of Quezon Province. However, operating under a restrictive Class "C" designation has created severe operational bottlenecks, resulting in long client waiting times due to an insufficient personnel complement, limited physical space, and inadequate IT workstations. LTO Lucena's actual workload and financial performance have far outgrown its current Class "C" classification. Under LTO Memorandum Circular No. 2020-2200, office reclassifications are evaluated based on annual transaction volume weighted at seventy percent and total revenue collection weighted at thirty percent. From CY 2023 to CY 2025, LTO Lucena handled an average of 114,794.67 total transactions annually, surpassing the 111,001 national threshold required for a maximum transaction score. Over the same three-year period, the office generated an average annual revenue ofP160,467,548.06, wellabove the P67.77 Million benchmark needed for a maximum revenue score. Official evaluation data from LTO Region IV-A confirms that LTO Lucena fully qualifies for classification as a Class "A" District Office. Upgrading its status wil formally expand its permanent staffing, improve its facility and IT capacity, shorten turnaround times, andstrengthen road safety and enforcement across the province. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sOught. label: HB 11035
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 33 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990," TO EXPAND THE COVERAGE OF BACCALAUREATE DEGREES ELIGIBLE FOR LATERAL ENTRY IN THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 33 of Republic Act No. 6975, or the “Department of the Interior and Local Government Act of 1990,” provides for the Lateral Entry Program of the Philippine National Police (PNP), allowing qualified professionals with specialized skills and expertise to enter the police service as commissioned officers. Since the law was enacted in 1990, however, the nature of crime and policing has significantly changed. The PNP now faces increasingly complex challenges, including cybercrime, financial fraud, digital threats, disaster response, and issues involving mental health and community safety. These challenges require a wider range of professional expertise beyond those specifically identified in the existing law. While Section 33 recognizes professions such as medicine, law, engineering, nursing, dentistry, optometry, chaplaincy, and criminology, it does not adequately cover emerging fields that are now essential to modern policing. These include Cybersecurity, Information Technology, Data Science, Accountancy, Finance, Psychology, Behavioral Sciences, Public Administration, and Disaster Risk Management, among others. This bill seeks to amend Section 33 of R.A. 6975 by expanding the qualifications for lateral entry and giving the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM), in coordination with the PNP, the flexibility to recognize additional baccalaureate and postgraduate degrees based on the evolving needs of the police organization. By opening the PNP to a broader pool of qualified professionals, the measure will strengthen the organization's capacity to respond to emerging threats, improve police operations, and provide more effective and specialized public safety services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP REP. ANTONIO T. label: HB 11036
title: AN ACT MANDATING LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS TO USE BODY-WORN CAMERAS DURING LAW ENFORCEMENT OPERATIONS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article III, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, while Section 2 secures the fundamental right of the people against unreasonable searches and seizures. In recent years, public demand for greater transparency, accountability, and protection of human rights during police and law enforcement operations has escalated significantly. Although the Supreme Court, through A.M. No. 21-06-08-SC, requires the use of body-worn cameras (BWCs) during the execution of search and arrest warrants, no comprehensive law yet mandates their use in all law enforcement operations, including buy-bust operations, checkpoints, and warrantless arrests. This bill seeks to institutionalize the mandatory use of BWCs and authorized recording devices during police and field operations to promote transparency, accountability, and protection for both civilians and law enforcement officers. It also provides penalties for deliberate non-use, tampering, or unauthorized disclosure of recordings, while ensuring data privacy and due process and providing funding for equipment, training, and implementation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP REP. ANTONIO T. label: HB 11037
title: AN ACT CONFERRING UPON THE CADETS OF THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY THE STATUS OF GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES, GRANTING SALARIES, BENEFITS, AND PRIVILEGES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine National Police Academy (PNPA) serves as the country's premier institution for educating and training future public safety leaders. Its cadets undergo intensive academic, military, and police training in preparation for their future service in the Philippine National Police (PNP), Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP), and Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP). Despite the demanding nature of their training and the discipline expected of them, PNPA cadets currently do not enjoy the same status and benefits as cadets of the Philippine Military Academy (PMA). Their allowances and benefits remain limited and inconsistent, even though they are under full-time government supervision and are being prepared for careers in public service. This bill seeks to recognize PNPA cadets as government employees during their training. This recognition will entitle them to appropriate salaries and government benefits, including medical and disability coverage, life insurance, and other protections provided by law. Beyond providing financial security, this measure recognizes the commitment, sacrifices, and service of PNPA cadets and helps ease the financial burden on their families. It also promotes fairness by bringing their benefits closer to those enjoyed by cadets of other government service academies. By giving PNPA cadets the support and recognition they deserve, the State invests in the welfare and professional development of the men and women who will one day lead our country's police, fire, and jail services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. ELISA T. KHO, M.D., FPCCP REP. ANTONIO T. label: HB 11038
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE MARITIME INDUSTRY AUTHORITY SATELLITE OFFICE IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SOGOD, PROVINCE OF SOUTHERN LEYTE, INTO AN EXTENSION OFFICE AND TRANSFERRING ITS LOCATION TO THE MUNICIPALITY OF LILOAN, PROVINCE OF SOUTHERN LEYTE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Second Legislative District of Southern Leyte consists of coastal municipalities that have a long history of ishing, maritime trade, and participation in the country’s Overseas Employment Program. It is known as the “Gateway to Mindanao,” since both Liloan Ferry Terminal and San Ricardo Port provide passenger and cargo transport to Lipata, Surigao City. The easing of domestic and international travel restrictions has increased inter-island transport and maritime activity. This development has underscored the need to bring government maritime services closer to the public, vessel owners and operators, maritime education and training institutions, and Filipino seafarers. The Maritime Industry Authority (MARINA) is the government agency responsible for the regulation, promotion, and development of the Philippine maritime industry. Its functions include the registration and licensing of vessels and the implementation of applicable laws, rules, and standards relating to maritime safety, maritime education and training, and the certi ication of seafarers. MARINA’s regulatory powers and functions have been strengthened by existing law, including the transfer to MARINA of powers relating to the issuance, validation, veri ication, correction, revocation, or 1|Page cancellation of certi icates and other documentary evidence required of seafarers under the applicable provisions of Republic Act No. 10635. At present, MARINA maintains an extension of ice in Maasin City and a satellite of ice in the Municipality of Sogod, Province of Southern Leyte. This bill seeks to convert the Sogod satellite of ice into an extension of ice and transfer its location to the Municipality of Liloan. Liloan is strategically located within the Second Legislative District of Southern Leyte. It is home to the Liloan Ferry Terminal, which connects the Luzon-Visayas segment of the Pan-Philippine Highway with Mindanao. It is also in proximity to the Port of San Ricardo and the Port of Sogod and is accessible to the municipalities of Silago, Hinunangan, Hinundayan, Anahawan, San Juan, and Saint Bernard. The transfer and conversion of the of ice will improve access to vessel registration, licensing, inspection, maritime safety, seafarer certi ication, and related MARINA services. It will also enable the Authority to more effectively monitor maritime transport operations and maritime education and training activities within its area of responsibility. The measure is consistent with the policy of strengthening MARINA’s regional and local presence. Similar legislation has converted MARINA satellite of ices into extension of ices in Maasin City, Southern Leyte, and Calbayog City, Samar. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. title: AN ACT TO FURTHER DEVELOP CAPABILITY AND ESTABLISH EXPEDITIOUS TRANSFORMATION OF THE DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENSE AND ITS BUREAUS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A comprehensive national defense plan that addresses both conventional and non- conventional threats to national security in the present and the future goes beyond merely modernizing our military capabilities; it necessitates the modi ication of antiquated policies, starting with the Commonwealth Act No. 1, the National Defense Act of 1935. Crafted in an era when the Philippines was still under American control and protection, our ninety-year-old primary law on national defense is now obsolete and needs a major overhaul to keep up with the times. This proposal will modernize national security-related policies, principles, and concepts while institutionalizing reforms to the Armed Forces of the Philippines and the entire Department of National Defense which are introduced via executive or administrative iat. Key features of this measure include the: (1) Addition of the Secretary of Defense in the Chain of Command; the provision of maximum tenure for rank of icers; 1|Page (2) Establishment of the Warrant Of icers – highly technical experts, including combat leaders and trainers; (3) Provision of free legal assistance to military personnel charged with service- related offenses; (4) Establishment of the Government Arsenal tasked with the manufacture and/or supply of arms and ammunition to the Armed Forces and law enforcement; (5) Organization of the National Defense College into the National Defense University; (6) Integration of the Technical and Administrative Services and the Women’s Auxiliary Corps in the Component Services. With the growing geopolitical tension near our borders, the time to revisit our National Defense Act is now. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many people struggling with substance use, the hardest part of recovery is not only overcoming addiction but also overcoming the judgment of others. Negative labels and stereotypes can lead to discrimination, shame, and rejection, making it harder for recovering individuals to seek help and rebuild their lives. While accountability remains important, recovery should also give people a chance to change. A person who has completed rehabilitation should not be de ined forever by his or her past. Recovery does not end after rehabilitation. For many recovering individuals, the next challenge is inding a job, earning a living, and becoming productive and independent members of society. Without skills, livelihood opportunities, and support, they may struggle to rebuild their lives and become vulnerable to returning to harmful circumstances. The State must therefore provide them with a real opportunity to start again. This measure seeks to institutionalize Technical-Vocational Education and Training (TVET) and livelihood programs speci ically for rehabilitated drug dependents. These programs will help them gain practical skills, improve their chances of inding decent employment, and pursue small businesses or other livelihood opportunities. By 1|Page investing in their skills and self-reliance, we give recovering individuals not only a second chance, but also the means to make that second chance last. A similar measure was iled during the 19th Congress. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. label: HB 11041
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING AND EXPANDING THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT GOVERNMENT INTERNSHIP PROGRAM, PROVIDING INTERNSHIP OPPORTUNITIES IN NATIONAL GOVERNMENT AGENCIES, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND OTHER GOVERNMENT INSTRUMENTALITIES, GRANTING A STIPEND TIED TO THE PREVAILING REGIONAL MINIMUM WAGE, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The lack of work experience remains one of the biggest barriers faced by Filipinos seeking employment. While the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) Government Internship Program (GIP) gives people a chance to gain skills and practical experience, its regular age requirement of 18 to 30 years old leaves many capable Filipinos behind. Not everyone gets their irst opportunity while they are young. For many, the need for a irst job comes later in life. This measure seeks to expand the GIP to Filipinos aged 18 years old and above who have no substantial prior work experience. This recognizes that irst-time jobseekers are not limited to young people. Adults who have never had stable employment, displaced workers, persons returning to the workforce, and older Filipinos who still want to work deserve a fair chance to learn, gain con idence, and become employable. The bill keeps the internship temporary and focused on training and skills development. It does not create a permanent position in government, guarantee employment, or allow interns to replace regular government employees. Instead, it gives participants meaningful exposure to actual workplaces in national government 1|Page agencies, local government units, and other government instrumentalities, while helping them develop skills that can open doors to future employment. To make the opportunity meaningful and accessible, interns shall receive a daily stipend equivalent to the highest prevailing regional minimum wage in their region of assignment. The measure also provides for government-funded accident insurance, proper supervision and training, fair and transparent selection, protection from discrimination and abuse, and employment facilitation after the internship. These safeguards ensure that interns are not merely given work but are given a genuine opportunity to grow. Every Filipino who wants to work deserves a chance to prove what they can do, regardless of when that opportunity comes in their life. Age should not be a barrier for a quali ied person who is willing to learn, work, and build a better future. By expanding the GIP, the government can give more Filipinos the experience, skills, and con idence they need to enter the workforce. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 11042
title: AN ACT PROTECTING THE RIGHTS OF INTERNALLY DISPLACED PERSONS AND PENALIZING THE ACTS OF ARBITRARY INTERNAL DISPLACEMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has long faced disasters and armed con licts that force families to leave their homes and communities. Behind every evacuation is a family that has lost its home, livelihood, and sense of security. From Typhoon Yolanda to the Marawi Siege, millions of Filipinos have experienced the pain and uncertainty of being displaced. Yet, despite these recurring crises, our country still lacks a comprehensive law that clearly protects the rights of internally displaced persons (IDPs). Displacement does not end when people are brought to evacuation centers or temporary shelters. Many IDPs continue to struggle with access to safe housing, food, clean water, healthcare, education, livelihood, and other basic needs. Local governments and irst responders also face dif iculties in coordinating assistance and protecting the rights of displaced families. There is therefore an urgent need for a clear and uni ied framework that tells government what to do and, more importantly, reminds us of what displaced Filipinos are entitled to. This measure, which was previously iled during the 19th Congress, recognizes the rights and unique needs of IDPs, especially women, children, older persons, and other vulnerable groups. It strengthens coordination among national agencies, local governments, and other organizations, while ensuring access to adequate shelter, healthcare, education, livelihood, and other essential services. It also promotes durable solutions, including safe and voluntary return, relocation when necessary, 1|Page and meaningful reintegration into communities. Most importantly, it seeks to prevent arbitrary displacement and hold accountable those who unlawfully force people from their homes. As climate change, natural disasters, and armed con licts continue to threaten communities, displacement may become an even greater challenge in the years ahead. The government must be prepared not only to respond to emergencies, but also to protect the dignity, safety, and future of every displaced Filipino. No family should be left without protection simply because they were forced to lee their home. The immediate passage of this bill is therefore earnestly sought to build a safer, more compassionate, and more resilient Philippines. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 11043
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE TECHNICAL-VOCATIONAL-LIVELIHOOD CURRICULUM IN SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL, INSTITUTIONALIZING INDUSTRY-RESPONSIVE TRAINING AND CERTIFICATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine economy needs workers who have not only academic knowledge, but also practical and industry-recognized skills. The Technical-Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) track in senior high school was created to help students prepare for work, entrepreneurship, or further education. However, outdated equipment, limited access to quali ied trainers, and weak links with industries can prevent students from gaining the skills employers need. We must make sure that every TVL student is given a real chance to succeed after graduation. This measure strengthens the TVL track by bringing government, schools, local governments, and industries together. It creates a TVL Coordinating Council to ensure that training remains relevant to actual jobs and industry needs, while improving access to competency assessment and certi ication. DepEd will continue to oversee the academic curriculum, while TESDA will remain responsible for technical skills, assessment, and certi ication. DOLE and DTI will help connect schools and learners with labor-market information, employers, work immersion, and entrepreneurship opportunities. The bill also encourages stronger partnerships with industries through work immersion, mentoring, teacher and trainer exposure, equipment support, job fairs, 1|Page and employment facilitation. These partnerships will help students learn skills that are actually used in the workplace, while ensuring that work-based learning is safe, supervised, educational, and free from exploitation. It also promotes support for quali ied donations and existing tax incentives allowed under the National Internal Revenue Code, helping schools gain access to needed resources without creating new tax exemptions. Education should open doors, not leave young Filipinos wondering what comes next after graduation. A strong TVL program can give students practical skills, con idence, and a pathway to decent and productive work even without a college degree. By making TVL more accessible, industry-responsive, and trusted by employers, we invest not only in our students but also in the future workforce and economy of the Philippines. In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. CHRISTOPHERSON “COCO” M. label: HB 11044
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PARTICIPATION OF THE YOUTH SECTOR IN ALL DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT COUNCILS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10121, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE PHILIPPINE DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2010
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to harness their power and ensure the participation and entry of the youth sector, especially those who are no longer members of the Sangguniang Kabataan, in the country’s disaster risk reduction and management system. Considering the country’s vulnerability to natural disasters, especially with the impacts of climate change, it is important that all sectors, especially the majority of the population who are at the prime of their lives and technologically aware, are reminded and legally mandated to participate in and play an important role in disaster risk reduction. Speci ically, the bill mandates the inclusion of the Chairperson of the National Youth Commission as member of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC). Individuals and Youth organizations are likewise mandated to be included in all organizational levels of the disaster risk reduction and management system, in order to afford them a venue to participate and engage with government of icials and community leaders in formulating, planning and programming activities. 1|Page In view of the foregoing, ug sa ngalan sa SERBISYONG TINUORAY, the undersigned respectfully requests the immediate passage of this measure. label: HB 11049
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Guidance and Counseling Act of 2004 (RA 9258) was passed more than two decades ago, but until now, the need for guidance counselors still remains a problem in schools. In a feature article from 2018,1 the story of a “guidance teacher” was shown where a licensed teacher had to practice guidance and counseling due to the lack of registered guidance counselors in the public school system. This and many similar incidents happening in the country shows that it is almost impossible for the State to enforce RA 9258 at present and in the near future because the number of registered guidance counselors fall too short compared with the number of institutions and schools which are supposed to retain their services. While we are thankful for the teachers who are willingly undertaking to do this task, it is imperative that we do something to actually address the problem and not rely on band-aid solutions. We need to attract and retain guidance counselors. We need to make sure that students will see the profession of guidance and counseling as lucrative and fulfilling so that more will be encouraged to undertake the rigorous studies and training to become registered guidance counselors. We need to make sure that the young generation will have qualified persons who can help them in times of emotional distress so we can prevent incidents of dropping out from school, bullying, self-harm, and even death. Thus, this representation drafted the Magna Carta for Public Counselors and their Practice in response to the growing need for better access to counseling and psychological aid. It is our bounden duty to ensure that the youth are safe, secure, and holistically healthy, and we can only help them by making sure that the resources and people that they need are within 1 Lack of registered guidance counselors forces schools to keep unlicensed ones (Part 1), https://news.abs- cbn.com/focus/01/14/18/lack-of-registered-guidance-counselors-forces-schools-to-keep-unlicensed-ones- part-1, retrieved on February 19, 2020. their reach. As the sad events in the past months have shown us2, prioritizing counselors in schools is not only imperative, but necessary. Hence, this bill seeks to improve the current entry level salary for guidance counselors in order to attract more applicants to move into public service, and to create an enhanced guidance and counseling program, through the aid of concerned government agencies and organizations, that will target the needs of school children and teenagers. It is hoped that through this legislative policy, the state of guidance and counseling practice in the Philippines will improve not for us, but for our children. ALFRED C. label: HB 11050
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL METEOROLOGY SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAM AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall give priority to education and science and technology to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development.1 The Constitution also states that science and technology are essential for national development and progress.2 Furthermore, the Constitution also provides that the State shall establish and maintain a system of scholarship grants, student loan programs, subsidies, and other incentives which shall be available to deserving students in both public and private schools, especially to the underprivileged.3 The country is visited by an average of twenty (20) typhoons annually. Typhoons naturally have destructive capabilities as a result of the strong winds they generate, the intense rainfall they bring, and the major floodings that they can produce. The effects range from structural damages both to man-made and natural structures in the surroundings as well as economic impacts on human life and livelihood. Especially now, as the globe grapples with the undeniable effects of climate change, the poly-crisis it brings, and its awe-inspiring negative impact on ways- of-life, livelihoods, safety, and societal peace overall, the country must increase its capacity to mitigate such negative effects by training professionals in the meteorological sciences. In order to mitigate the consequences brought by typhoons, it is important that government will continue to strengthen its weather forecasting and 1 1987 CONST., Art. II, Sec. 17. 2 1987 CONST., Art. XIV, Sec. 10. 3 1987 CONST., Art. XIV, Sec. 2 (3). monitoring efforts. To this end, it is imperative that the government ensure a capable and competent human resource trained in the field of meteorology and its allied sciences. In light of the foregoing, this bill proposes establishing a National Meteorology Scholarship Program to encourage the youth to pursue and gain expertise in the field of Meteorology. These deserving students who will benefit from the proposed scholarship program will be great assets to the country in the government's efforts in providing information to the public and organizations during typhoons, protecting life and property during weather disturbances, reducing weather-related economic losses, and promoting national safety and prosperity. Based on the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C.
