label: HB 11085
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF THE OUT-OF-SCHOOL YOUTH
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State values the dignity of every human person and guarantees full respect for human rights. Consistent with this mandate, the State must ensure that out-of-school youth are not left behind in the country’s education, employment, and social protection systems. Out-of-school youth face intersecting barriers that limit their full participation in society. Many are unable to complete formal education due to poverty, family responsibilities, early pregnancy, lack of access to schools, displacement, abuse, disability, conflict with the law, or other difficult circumstances. Without adequate intervention, they are placed at greater risk of unemployment, exploitation, violence, trafficking, and long-term poverty. While existing programs such as the Alternative Learning System, technical-vocational education, livelihood assistance, youth development programs, and social welfare services provide important support, these interventions remain dispersed across different agencies and local government units. There is a need for a comprehensive rights-based framework that will clearly define the rights of out-of-school youth, harmonize government programs, and ensure coordinated delivery of education, employment, health, social protection, and reintegration services. This bill seeks to provide a Magna Carta for Out-of-School Youth by recognizing, protecting, and promoting their rights and by mandating government agencies to provide targeted assistance and support. It strengthens access to formal, non-formal, informal, and technical-vocational education; promotes decent work and livelihood opportunities; ensures health, psychosocial, and social welfare interventions; and provides special protection for those in especially difficult circumstances. The measure further mandates the creation of an updated database and profiling system for out-of-school youth, strengthens the role of the National Youth Commission, local government units, Sangguniang Kabataan, Local Youth Development Councils, and concerned agencies, and encourages partnership with the private sector and non-government organizations. Through these mechanisms, programs for out-of-school youth may be better coordinated, monitored, and made more responsive to their actual needs. Ultimately, this measure recognizes out-of-school youth not as liabilities, but as rights-holders and partners in nation-building. By providing them with meaningful access to education, skills training, employment, social services, and protection, the State invests in their potential and strengthens inclusive national development. This measure has been filed since the 16th Congress. During the 19th Congress, it was approved on the third and final reading. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11086
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF AGRICULTURAL DEVELOPMENT WORKERS, STRENGTHENING THEIR WELFARE, LABOR PROTECTION, AND PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 18, Article II of the 1987 Constitution recognizes labor as a primary social economic force and mandates the State to protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. Section 3, Article XIII further guarantees the rights of all workers to just and humane conditions of work, security of tenure, and a living wage, and promotes full employment and equality of employment opportunities. Complementarily, Section 5, Article XIII directs the State to provide support to agriculture through appropriate technology and research, and adequate financial, production, marketing, and other support services. These provisions underscore the State’s duty not only to strengthen the agricultural sector but also to protect and develop the workforce that sustains it. Agricultural development workers, who include agriculturists, engineers, technicians, extension workers, and support personnel, serve as the backbone of agricultural productivity, extension services, and rural transformation. While farmers and fisherfolk remain at the forefront of food production, agricultural development workers play an equally critical role in sustaining and strengthening the sector by providing the technical expertise, research support, extension services, and institutional capacity necessary for modern, efficient, and climate- resilient agriculture. They are indispensable in translating policies into practice, supporting communities on the ground, and ensuring that agricultural programs are effectively implemented across the country. Despite their indispensable role, agricultural development workers continue to face structural challenges, including inadequate compensation, limited career advancement opportunities, unsafe working conditions, and inconsistent labor protection across institutions and local government units. The devolution of agricultural services under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the “Local Government Code of 1991,” has resulted in uneven capacity and disparities in the delivery of agricultural services across local government units. This situation has been further shaped by the landmark ruling in Mandanas v. Ochoa,1 which expanded the fiscal resources of local governments by increasing their share in national taxes. While this development enhances the capacity of LGUs to deliver devolved services, it likewise underscores the need to strengthen institutional systems, standardize staffing, and ensure adequate protection and professionalization of agricultural development workers at the local level. While Republic Act No. 12215, otherwise known as the “Philippine Agriculturists Act,” and other professional laws regulate licensure and professional standards, there remains a significant policy gap in addressing the employment conditions, welfare, labor rights, and occupational safety of agricultural development workers across the public and private sectors. This proposed Magna Carta seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a comprehensive framework that ensures just compensation, wage protection, security of tenure, safe and humane working conditions, and occupational safety and health protection, while strengthening the professionalization of agricultural services, particularly at the local government level. The measure further integrates labor standards, human resource development mechanisms, and inter-agency coordination, recognizing that the effectiveness of agricultural programs depends not only on policy and funding but also on the competence, protection, and motivation of the workforce. Ultimately, this bill aims to strengthen the foundation of agricultural development by investing in the people who drive it. By protecting and 1 Mandanas v. Executive Secretary (G.R. No. 199802, July 3, 2018; affirmed April 10, 2019) 2 empowering agricultural development workers, the State advances food security, improves rural livelihoods, and supports long-term agricultural modernization. Similar bills have been filed since the 10th Congress, but have remained pending with the Committee on Agriculture and Food. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11087
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF MUNICIPAL SMALL- SCALE AND SUBSISTENCE FISHERFOLK, STRENGTHENING THEIR RIGHTS, PROTECTION, AND ACCESS TO SUPPORT SERVICES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 7, Article XIII of the 1987 Constitution guarantees the protection of the rights of subsistence fishermen, especially of local communities, to the preferential use of local marine and fishing resources, both inland and offshore. It further mandates the State to provide support through appropriate technology and research, adequate financial, production, and marketing assistance, and other services; to protect, develop, and conserve such resources; to safeguard offshore fishing grounds against foreign intrusion; and, to ensure that fishworkers receive a just share from their labor in the utilization of marine and fishing resources. Complementing this mandate, Section 5, Article XIII of the Constitution directs the State to provide support to agriculture and fisheries, while Section 16, Article II guarantees the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology, and Section 18, Article II affirms the State’s duty to protect the rights of workers and promote their welfare. Taken together, these provisions establish the State’s obligation not only to secure the dignity, welfare, and economic resilience of fisherfolk, but also to ensure the sustainability of fisheries resources. Municipal small-scale and subsistence fisherfolk remain among the most economically vulnerable sectors in the country, despite their indispensable role in ensuring food security, sustaining coastal communities, and supporting local economies. Their contributions extend beyond food production, as they also serve as frontline stewards of marine and coastal ecosystems. However, structural challenges continue to limit their full participation in economic growth and development. While Republic Act No. 8550, otherwise known as the Philippine Fisheries Code of 1998, as amended, recognizes their preferential rights in municipal waters and provides the legal framework for fisheries management, many fisherfolk continue to face persistent and overlapping challenges. These include limited access to markets, inadequate post-harvest and cold storage facilities, exposure to exploitative trading practices, vulnerability to climate change and natural disasters, and increasing operational costs, particularly due to fuel price fluctuations. Existing government interventions, such as fuel subsidy programs, credit and insurance facilities, and livelihood assistance, have provided some relief. However, these initiatives remain fragmented, unevenly implemented, and often insufficient to address the long-term and systemic needs of the sector. Moreover, the growing role of digital technologies in governance and market systems highlights the need to improve the fisherfolk’s access to information, services, and economic opportunities through more integrated and accessible platforms. This proposed Magna Carta seeks to address these gaps by establishing a comprehensive and integrated policy framework for municipal small-scale and subsistence fisherfolk. It consolidates and reinforces their rights, strengthens access to fisheries support services, promotes fair and equitable market participation, and institutionalizes social protection mechanisms, particularly during emergencies such as natural disasters, fuel price shocks, and other disruptions affecting fisheries operations. The measure further promotes the adoption and use of digital systems to enhance access to government services, improve data-driven policy implementation, and ensure more efficient delivery of programs. It also strengthens inter-agency coordination and the targeting of beneficiaries through the integration of existing registry systems. By reinforcing existing laws and addressing implementation gaps, this measure aims to uplift the welfare of fisherfolk, enhance their resilience to economic and environmental shocks, and ensure the sustainable use of marine 2 resources. Ultimately, it contributes to long-term food security, inclusive economic growth, and the protection of coastal and marine ecosystems. Similar measures have been filed since the 8th Congress but have remained pending with the Committee on Agriculture and Food, underscoring the continuing need for a comprehensive and responsive policy framework for the sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11088
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR FREE PUBLIC ACCESS TO INTERNATIONAL AND MAJOR LOCAL SPORTING EVENTS INVOLVING FILIPINO ATHLETES AND PARA-ATHLETES THROUGH STATE-RUN BROADCAST AND DIGITAL PLATFORMS, PROMOTING MEDIA PARTNERSHIPS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the vital role of sports in fostering national unity, pride, and identity. Filipino athletes and para-athletes who compete in international and local sporting events serve as symbols of discipline, perseverance, and excellence, inspiring millions of Filipinos across the country. Pursuant to Section 19, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions, to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence for developing a healthy and alert citizenry. Complementarily, Section 24, Article II mandates the State to recognize the vital role of communication and information in nation- building. Ensuring accessible platforms for the dissemination of sports content aligns with this constitutional directive by enabling broader public engagement in national events. Despite widespread public interest, access to coverage of international competitions such as the Olympic Games, Asian Games, Southeast Asian Games, and Asian Beach Games remains limited, as broadcast rights are often held by private entities and made available primarily through subscription-based platforms. This restricts the ability of a significant portion of the Filipino public to readily watch and support national athletes and para-athletes in real time, resulting in limited lawful and accessible viewing opportunities and reducing broader public engagement in national sporting events. More critically, coverage of major local sporting events remains even more limited and, in many instances, inaccessible. Competitions that serve as training grounds, qualifiers, and talent-identification platforms for future national representatives are rarely televised or livestreamed, resulting in limited public awareness and engagement. This lack of visibility weakens the pipeline of support for emerging athletes and undermines efforts to build a sustained and inclusive sports culture. At the same time, media consumption patterns in the Philippines have increasingly shifted toward digital and mobile-based platforms, with a substantial number of Filipinos accessing audiovisual content through freely accessible online applications and social media platforms. Leveraging these technologies presents a strategic opportunity for the State to democratize access to sports content and ensure that Filipino representation in sporting events, whether at the elite, grassroots, or developmental level, becomes more visible and accessible to the public. In anticipation of the Philippines’ participation in the upcoming Southeast Asian Games, there is a timely need to ensure that Filipinos are able to follow and support their athletes and para-athletes through accessible and inclusive platforms. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by providing for free public access to sporting events involving Filipino athletes and para-athletes in both international and major local competitions through state-run television and official digital platforms, while respecting existing broadcast rights. It further promotes partnerships with media entities to expand coverage, improve reach, and ensure sustainability. 2 By making sporting events involving Filipino athletes and para-athletes more accessible to the public, the State affirms its commitment to inclusive recognition, sustained public engagement, and the continued development of Philippine sports. This measure seeks not only to expand access to sports content, but also to strengthen national pride, encourage broader support for Filipino athletes and para-athletes, and foster a culture that values participation, representation, discipline, and excellence. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11089
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE MENTAL HEALTH AND PSYCHOSOCIAL SUPPORT SYSTEM FOR FILIPINO ATHLETES AND PARA-ATHLETES, PROMOTING SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SPORTS ENVIRONMENTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the importance of promoting the mental health and well-being of Filipino athletes and para-athletes as an integral component of sports development. Athletes at all levels, from grassroots and school-based participants to elite national representatives, face unique psychological pressures arising from training demands, performance expectations, injuries, and even career uncertainties. These challenges, if left unaddressed, may adversely affect not only the athletic performance but also the long-term personal development of the athletes. Pursuant to Section 19, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions. Complementarily, Section 15, Article II provides that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people, including mental health, while Section 13, Article II recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation- building. While existing laws such as Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” establish a general framework for mental health services, and Republic Act No. 12080, otherwise known as the “Basic Education Mental Health and Well-Being Promotion Act,” institutionalizes mental health programs in basic education, there remains a gap in the delivery of specialized and accessible mental health services tailored to the unique needs of athletes. Moreover, Republic Act No. 10699, otherwise known as the “National Athletes and Coaches Benefits and Incentives Act,” provides health-related benefits for national athletes but does not sufficiently address the systematic provision of mental health and psychosocial support within sports systems. At present, mental health services in sports remain fragmented, unevenly accessible, and often reactive rather than preventive. Grassroots and school-based athletes, in particular, have limited access to structured mental health support, despite being at a critical stage of development. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by institutionalizing a comprehensive mental health and psychosocial support system for athletes and para-athletes across all levels of participation. It provides for increased access to mental health services, integration of mental health mechanisms in sports programs, capacity-building for stakeholders, and strengthened inter-agency coordination, while ensuring confidentiality and data privacy. By prioritizing mental health as a core component of athlete development, the State affirms its commitment to fostering resilience, sustaining performance, and promoting the overall well-being of Filipino athletes and para-athletes. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11090
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL DIGITAL SPORTS ARCHIVE FOR THE SYSTEMATIC COLLECTION, PRESERVATION, AND PUBLIC DISSEMINATION OF SPORTS RECORDS AND DATA INVOLVING FILIPINO ATHLETES AND PARA-ATHLETES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes the importance of preserving and promoting the achievements of Filipino athletes and para-athletes as part of the nation’s cultural, historical, and sporting heritage. Sporting events, whether at the international or local level, document the journey, performance, and progress of athletes and serve as valuable resources for public engagement, education, and future development. Pursuant to Section 15, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution, the State shall conserve, promote, and popularize the nation’s historical and cultural heritage and resources. Complementarily, Section 24, Article II recognizes the vital role of communication and information in nation-building, underscoring the need for accessible platforms for the dissemination and preservation of information. Despite the increasing participation of Filipino athletes and para-athletes in both international and local competitions, there is currently no centralized and accessible repository of sports records, game footage, athlete profiles, and related data. Existing materials are often fragmented across various platforms, inconsistently documented, or entirely unavailable to the public. This results in the loss of valuable historical records and limits opportunities for analysis, recognition, and sustained engagement. Moreover, the absence of a unified digital archive, supported by standardized records management and archival practices, hinders the ability of coaches, researchers, policymakers, and aspiring athletes to access reliable data for performance analysis, training development, and evidence-based decision- making. This proposed measure seeks to establish a National Digital Sports Archive that will serve as a centralized, publicly accessible platform for the systematic collection, preservation, and dissemination of Philippine sports data and audiovisual materials, in coordination with relevant agencies, including the National Archives of the Philippines, to ensure proper records management and long-term preservation. By institutionalizing a digital archive, the State affirms its commitment to preserving the nation’s sporting heritage, promoting transparency and accessibility, and strengthening the overall sports ecosystem. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. FERDINAND MARTIN G. ROMUALDEZ YEDDA MARIE K. ROMUALDEZ ANDREW JULIAN K. ROMUALDEZ JUDE A. label: HB 11108
title: AN ACT DISQUALIFYING RELATIVES OF PUBLIC OFFICIALS WITHIN THE FOURTH CIVIL DEGREE OF CONSANGUINITY OR AFFINITY FROM PARTICIPATING IN GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Delicadeza is a Spanish word which means “delicateness, fineness or tact, or showing regard for the feelings of others, or sensitive in action or operation.” However, in Filipino culture, it is the character of holding oneself into a higher moral and ethical standard which is a burden of a public office. For the longest time in Philippine politics, delicadeza is no longer the standard. Rather, it is considered as a nuisance, an unwanted word word shall be kept out of the spotlight. Delicadeza should not only extend to public officials but also to their relatives. The past couple of months highlighted the outrageous luxury that these contractors possess. If they are so comfortable at public flaunting their wealth, then they must also be held accountable over how they made these luxuries. They shall be held into the same moral and ethical standards which public officials are being held to account. Under Section 79 of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, no person shall be appointed in the career service of the local government if he or she is related to the appointing authority within the fourth civil degree of consanguinity or affinity. The proposed bill barring relatives within the 4th civil degree in from participating in government contracts is consistent with the policy against nepotism already recognized under Local Government Code. If the existing law prohibits an appointing authority from favoring a relative within the fourth civil degree in public employment, then there is a similar, if not stronger, reason to prohibit public officials from participating in, approving, recommending, or awarding government contracts where the contractor, supplier, beneficial owner, incorporator, officer, or controlling stockholder is related to them within the same prohibited degree. No longer shall relatives of public officials make money out of government contract. This bill seeks to disqualify them from making money out of the hard-earned tax money of Filipinos. label: HB 11109
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PROVISION OF EXCLUSIVE PARKING SPACE FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES AND PENALIZING THE UNAUTHORIZED USE THEREOF, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE ACCESSIBILITY LAW
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State recognizes persons with disabilities and their remarkable contributions to our development as a nation. In line with this, the country has enacted Batas Pambansa (B.P.) Blg. 344, otherwise known as the “Accessibility Law” in 1983. This piece of legislation has initially facilitated the inclusion of persons with disabilities into the mainstream of Philippine society. However, after almost 40 years of its enactment, it has been observed that the Accessibility Law does not fully cater to the accessibility needs of persons with disabilities. For one, B.P. 344 does not provide for sanctions for the unauthorized use and obstruction of parking spaces reserved for persons with disabilities. As such, these parking spaces are frequently used by persons without disabilities, thereby preventing persons with disabilities from being able to access essential services. Similarly, Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, simply states, in Section 25 thereof, that the State “shall ensure the attainment of a barrier-free environment for disabled persons in accordance with the Accessibility Law.” With the absence of clear penalties for the unauthorized use and obstruction of such designated spaces, persons with disabilities are further robbed of opportunities and spaces that ought to be for them. Thus, there remains a need to improve our existing laws for the welfare of Filipino persons with disabilities. This bill seeks to address this limitation of the Accessibility Law by mandating the provision of exclusive parking for persons with disabilities, defining the prohibited acts, and providing the penalties in cases of violation. It is the hope of this measure to strengthen the Accessibility Law and complement existing laws that protect and uphold the rights of persons with disabilities to attain an inclusive and barrier-free environment In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11110
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FREE EDUCATION TO SENIOR CITIZENS AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The role of senior citizens in the Filipino family and in nation-building is valuable and is recognized by the State, with laws such as the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2003 and 2010 among others. Similarly, quality education for all is fervently valued by the State as well. Sec. 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall promote the “right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all,” calling for the establishment of a “complete, adequate and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” This bill seeks to affirm our recognition of the invaluable contributions of senior citizens and support those who have yet to gain access to education or are interested in continuing their academic journey. It is the hope of this measure to support the dreams of every Filipino, regardless of age, for quality education. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11111
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE PRIVILEGES FOR SENIOR CITIZENS TO INCLUDE FREE PARKING IN ALL ESTABLISHMENTS AND EXEMPTION FROM THE NUMBER CODING SCHEME, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7432, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9994, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE EXPANDED SENIOR CITIZENS ACT OF 2010
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9994, or the Expanded Senior Citizens Act of 2010, defines ‘senior citizens’ as individuals aged 60 years old and above. Senior citizens make up 10.2 percent of the total population, or 11.2 million Filipinos, as of the latest census of the Philippine Statistics Authority in 2024. The Philippine government recognizes the role of the elderly in nation- building and their continued contributions to society and development. As such, legislation that encourages mobility, growth, and protection for our dear elderly is of importance. In line with the State’s policy to promote the welfare of senior citizens, this legislation seeks to create opportunities for their continued participation in social and economic life, while ensuring that their rights and well-being are protected. It reflects the government’s continuing commitment to reduce the burdens faced by senior citizens and to support their meaningful contribution to national development. This bill seeks to provide additional benefits and privileges to the Filipino elderly. This proposed legislation exempts them from paying parking fees in all establishments and from the Unified Vehicular Volume Reduction Program or the number coding scheme implemented by the Government. Through this initiative, we are providing our senior citizens simple economic benefits that would reward their great contributions to our country’s development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11112
title: AN ACT CREATING THE PHILIPPINE CENTER FOR DISEASE CONTROL AND PREVENTION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) has taken most of the world by surprise, infecting more than five million persons and taking the lives of at least three hundred thousand persons worldwide. It has become a pandemic that threatens countries without strong public health care systems and facilities for control and prevention of communicable and infectious diseases. Our lack of institutional capacity to implement comprehensive public health management programs, especially in public health protection, shows the harsh reality that our country needs to modernize and upgrade our public health systems to decisively address the risks of communicable diseases. From sudden cases of polio-related diseases, to human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related infections, to tuberculosis and dengue outbreaks, there is a need for an institution to focus and create scientifically accurate and research- backed solutions to combat infectious and emerging diseases. While the Department of Health has been effective to some degree in the delivery of health services amid the pandemic, we must strengthen its absorptive capacity and framework in dealing with difficult communicable diseases. This bill seeks to establish a Philippine National Center for Disease Control and Prevention, which shall serve as the principal health protection agency of the Philippines aimed at preventing, protecting, and managing the spread of communicable and infectious diseases and other health emergencies in the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The COVID-19 pandemic remains one of the most significant public health crises in recent history. Although the World Health Organization ended the Public Health Emergency of International Concern in May 2023, COVID- 19 continues to circulate globally, with WHO reporting over 779 million confirmed cases and more than seven million confirmed deaths as of mid- 2026, and the global risk still assessed as moderate1. The pandemic exposed gaps in health systems worldwide, especially in countries with limited infrastructure, workforce, and emergency coordination capacity. It also underscored the need for stronger preparedness mechanisms that can respond quickly to future outbreaks while preserving essential health services and minimizing social and economic disruption.2 To reduce the impact of future pandemics and similar public health emergencies, there is a need to strengthen the country’s emergency preparedness architecture. label: HB 11115
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL DAM SAFETY PROGRAM, ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL DAM SAFETY AUTHORITY, PENALIZING VIOLATIONS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Dams are critical infrastructure that support water supply, irrigation, flood control, and power generation, but their operation also carries significant risks to communities located downstream, particularly during typhoons, extreme rainfall, earthquakes, and other hazards, making dam safety an essential component of national disaster risk reduction and public safety. The need for a dedicated and comprehensive national framework is underscored by the country’s multi-hazard environment. A recent national study on dam safety drawing on the assessments of 348 qualified National Irrigation Administration engineers noted that Philippine dams face limitations in monitoring capacity.1 At the same time, the urgency of strengthening such systems is heightened by climate variability and changing water conditions: in May 2026, the Climate Change Commission reported that major Luzon dams had recorded declining water levels amid prolonged dry conditions and high heat indices, with Angat Dam, Metro Manila’s primary water source, falling to 177.41 meters from its 210-meter normal water level.2 These changing conditions 1 Department of Science and Technology–National Research Council of the Philippines (DOST- NRCP), Multi-Criterion Evaluation of Dam Safety Using Analytic Hierarchy Process: A Case Study of Philippine Dams. 2 Climate Change Commission, reported by the Philippine Information Agency, “CCC: Local Climate Change Action Plans key to water security amid declining dam levels,” May 22, 2026. demonstrate that dam safety must address not only structural integrity but also the management of water levels, extreme weather, operational decisions, and timely communication with communities. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) already operates a Flood Forecasting and Warning System for Dam Operation covering five major dams in Luzon: Angat, Pantabangan, Magat, Binga, and Ambuklao. This system uses real-time rainfall and water-level monitoring, forecasting, warning dissemination, and inter- agency information sharing to help ensure safe reservoir operations and warn downstream communities of impending water releases.3 Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, already recognizes the importance of national risk mapping, monitoring, and comprehensive early warning and emergency alert systems, including the provision of timely information to national and local emergency organizations and the general public.4 This proposed measure builds upon that policy by establishing a dedicated National Dam Safety Authority tasked with coordinating the management and operation of dams, developing a comprehensive National Dam Safety Plan, ensuring safe construction and maintenance, and strengthening early warning, consultation, and public information mechanisms. The bill likewise requires consultation and disclosure of relevant dam information during calamities, typhoons, and other disasters, recognizing that a warning is effective only when communities receive timely, understandable, and actionable information. By institutionalizing a unified dam safety program and clearly assigning responsibility for prevention, monitoring, emergency coordination, and public disclosure, the measure seeks to shift the country from a reactive approach to dam-related emergencies toward one based on prevention, preparedness, accountability, and protection of human life. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11116
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR SOLO PARENTS PROGRAM (FASPP) OF THE DEPARTMENT OF SOCIAL WELFARE AND DEVELOPMENT (DSWD) AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Solo parents carry the responsibility of raising and providing for their children without the full and regular support of another parent, making access to reliable social protection particularly important for families with limited resources. The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) estimates that there are approximately 14 million solo parents in the Philippines, and the agency recognizes solo parents as a sector requiring social protection and government assistance under the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act, or Republic Act No. 11861.1 The scale of this sector underscores the need for government programs that not only recognize solo parents' rights in law but also provide practical assistance when families face immediate financial difficulty. The need for responsive assistance is particularly evident among low- income households facing rising costs of basic necessities. In June 2026, food inflation among the bottom 30% of income households reached 8.2 percent, while the cost of housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels increased by 8.7 percent and transport costs increased by 15.6 percent year-on-year.2 These 1 Department of Social Welfare and Development, Provision of Assistance to Solo Parents, citing National Statistics Office data on approximately 14 million solo parents and discussing the implementation of Republic Act No. 11861, the Expanded Solo Parents Welfare Act. 2 Philippine Statistics Authority, Summary Inflation Report Consumer Price Index for the Bottom 30% Income Households (2018=100): June 2026. pressures are especially significant for solo parents, who must stretch a single household income across food, utilities, transportation, health care, education, and other expenses for themselves and their dependents. The DSWD's experience with its Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program likewise demonstrates the continuing demand for government safety-net assistance: more than 8.2 million Filipinos in crisis received assistance from AICS from January to November 2025, exceeding the program's target for the year.3 While existing government programs provide important support, there is a need to institutionalize a dedicated and predictable mechanism through which qualified solo parents can receive assistance for essential needs. The proposed Financial Assistance for Solo Parents Program (FASPP) Act responds to this need by establishing a statutory framework for assistance that may cover food, medical expenses, education, livelihood, and cash relief, while allowing complementary assistance through LGUs in the form of rice assistance. The Bill also provides safeguards through eligibility requirements, social-worker assessment, documentary requirements, and penalties for fraudulent or improper claims, while ensuring that assistance may complement support from LGUs, other government agencies, and non-government organizations. By institutionalizing the FASPP and providing for its continuing appropriation, the measure seeks to make government assistance more accessible, coordinated, and responsive to the actual needs of solo parents and their dependents. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11117
title: AN ACT PROVIDING CASH ASSISTANCE TO KASAMBAHAY PARENTS, INCLUDING OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKER (OFW) HOUSEHOLD SERVICE WORKERS, WITH THE OPTION TO CONVERT SUCH ASSISTANCE INTO SOCIAL SECURITY SYSTEM (SSS) CONTRIBUTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Sa araw-araw, milyon-milyong mga Pilipino ang nililisan ang kanilang tahanan bago magbukang-liwayway, iniiwan ang kanilang pamilya at kadalasan maging ang ating bansa upang mamasukan at mag-alaga ng hindi nila anak at ng ibang pamilya. Likas na mapagmahal ang mga Pilipino. Madali nating makapalagayan ng loob ang mga taong nakasasalamuha natin, lalo na kung palagi natin silang kapiling. Ngunit masakit para sa isang magulang na higit na maalagaan ang mga anak na hindi niya kadugo kaysa sa sarili niyang anak. Filipino kasambahay prepare another family’s meals, comfort another family’s children when they cry, and stay awake when someone else’s child is sick, while their own children wait for them, often under the care of a grandmother, an older sibling, or a neighbor, for months or even years at a time. This is the quiet burden carried by the Filipino kasambahay: those who give the best of their care to households that are not their own, often at the cost of the time and presence they wish they could give their own children. Based on a recent joint survey of the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), there are approximately 1.4 million kasambahay in the Philippines1. Of this number, the majority are on a live-out arrangement, leaving their own households each day to care for another family's home and children. The same survey found that 83 per cent of kasambahay have no social security coverage at all, leaving them and their families exposed in the event of illness, disability, or 1 https://nwpc.dole.gov.ph/dole-and-psa-survey-1-4-million-kasambahays-in-the-country- 72-on-live-out-arrangement-2/ old age, on top of the earnings they have spent by being away from their own children for most of the day2. For those who leave the country to work as domestic helpers, the burden is even heavier. The PSA reported that the number of overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) rose to 2.19 million in 2024, from 2.16 million in 2023, with women comprising 57.2 per cent, or 1.25 million, of this workforce3. Approximately four (4) out of every ten (10) OFWs are in elementary occupations, which include domestic and household work. Moreover, Filipina household service workers are heavily concentrated in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, and Hong Kong4. Estimates from the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) place domestic workers at 20 to 30 per cent of all OFWs deployed each year. These figures demonstrate that household service work is one of the most common forms of overseas employment for Filipino women. Hindi lamang ito basta mga numero… sa likod ng bawat datos na ito ay ang mga anak na naiiwan ng kanilang mga magulang na naghahanapbuhay. Researchers estimate that at least 1.5 million Filipino children are growing up with one or both parents working overseas. A study published in The Lancet Regional Health – Western Pacific linked prolonged parental separation to loneliness, emotional strain, and health and developmental concerns among left-behind children, even as the remittances sent by their parents help support their education5. This is the irony this bill seeks to address: the very people entrusted with the care of other people's children often cannot afford the time, presence, or financial security to properly care for their own. Albeit existing laws such as Republic Act (RA) No. 10361, otherwise known as “Batas Kasambahay Act” and RA No. 8042, as amended by RA No. 10022 or the “Migrant Workers and Overseas Filipinos Act”, protect the kasambahay as a worker, there remains no law that directly assists them in their role as parents. The Kasambahay Parents Support Act aims to fill this gap. It provides monthly cash assistance to Kasambahay Parents, whether locally employed or deployed overseas, for the benefit of their qualified children left at home. This measure also addresses the concern that 83 per cent of kasambahay currently have no social security coverage. 2 https://dole.gov.ph/news/dole-psa-1-4m-hsws-72-on-liveout/ 3 philstar.com/business/2025/12/19/2495253/ofws-rise-219-million-2024-psa 4 https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/1758590/sws-survey-says-7-of-filipino-households-have- an-ofw 5 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9391573/ 1 The bill gives beneficiaries the option to apply the cash assistance toward their Social Security System (SSS) contributions, thereby enabling them to build long-term social protection for themselves and their families. Kasambahay devote their care, patience, and time to families that are not their own. It is only just that the State, in turn, help them care for the families waiting for them at home. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JC M. label: HB 11130
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR AN AUTOMATIC TOLL RELIEF MECHANISM DURING MAJOR TOLL FACILITY DISRUPTIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Toll facilities are established to ensure the safe, efficient, and reliable movement of motorists and vehicles. However, natural disasters, accidents, fires, landslides, infrastructure failures, and other emergencies may substantially disrupt their normal operation, resulting in prolonged delays, severe congestion, and significant hardship to motorists and passengers. The recent flooding along the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX), particularly in the Tulaoc area and San Simon, Pampanga, underscores the need for a clear and predictable mechanism to address such disruptions. The flooding rendered portions of the expressway impassable, severely restricted traffic flow, and resulted in motorists being stranded for extended periods. The incident also demonstrated the difficulties faced by passengers who may require food, water, sanitation, medical attention, or other forms of assistance while trapped in prolonged traffic. In response to the situation, government authorities directed the provision of assistance to affected motorists and subsequently implemented toll-free passage along the San Fernando–Pulilan stretch of NLEX. The Department of Transportation and Toll Regulatory Board has also directed the NLEX Corporation to provide toll relief to assist motorists affected by the flooding and resulting traffic congestion, with the measure remaining in effect until normal conditions return, including the provision of food and drinking water and the setup of portable toilets for stranded motorists. While such measures provide necessary relief, the circumstances also highlight the need for a standing mechanism that does not rely solely on ad hoc decisions after a major disruption has already occurred. Motorists should not have to wait for separate directives before knowing whether they are entitled to toll relief when objectively verifiable conditions have substantially impaired their use of a toll facility. This measure therefore seeks to establish an Automatic Toll Relief Mechanism that will provide appropriate temporary suspension, waiver, reduction, credit, refund, or other adjustment of toll fees when defined conditions constituting a major toll facility disruption are met. The mechanism will provide uniform standards for determining when toll relief shall commence, the extent of relief to be provided, and when regular toll collection may resume. It likewise recognizes that the effects of major disruptions extend beyond traffic congestion and toll charges. Motorists and passengers may be exposed to prolonged periods of confinement, limited access to food, water, sanitation, medical assistance, and safe areas. Accordingly, toll operators shall be required to provide appropriate roadside and emergency assistance, facilitate access to safe locations when practicable, and give priority response to senior citizens, persons with disabilities, children, pregnant women, persons requiring medical attention, and others requiring immediate assistance. It also promotes timely and adequate public information during major disruptions so that motorists can make informed decisions regarding their routes and travel. Clear information on affected areas, available routes, emergency assistance, and applicable toll relief can help prevent motorists from entering severely affected portions of a toll facility and further aggravating congestion. The recent experience in San Simon, Pampanga demonstrates that major toll facility disruptions can occur with little warning and can affect thousands of motorists and passengers. Establishing an automatic and uniform mechanism before the next emergency will enable the government and toll operators to respond more efficiently, provide appropriate relief, and better protect the public. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RODOLFO “OMPONG” M. label: HB 11131
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE UNDERPRIVILEGED AND HOMELESS FROM THE, REQUIRED PAYMENT OF SUPERSEDEAS BOND TO PERFECT AN APPEAL IN RELATION TO EJECTMENT CASES FILED AGAINST THEM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7279 OR THE "URBAN DEVELOPMENT HOUSING ACT OF 1992"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE More than three decades after the enactment of Republic Act (R.A.) No. 7279, or the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992, housing insecurity remains one of the pressing issues that the government seeks to address and end. Related to this, the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) reported that 238,747 informal settler families, of whom only 57,134, or 23.93 percent, had been relocated as of August 2025, leaving more than 181,000 identified families still awaiting resettlement.1 The vulnerability of these families is aggravated when housing disputes and cases are filed before the courts. In May 2025, for instance, residents of a Tondo community resisted the implementation of a court-ordered demolition, with affected families expressing that they had nowhere else to go. The dispute had already undergone approximately four years of litigation before the final demolition order was issued.2 Similar disputes underscore the realities for indigent families that ejectment cases are not simply a question of possession but determines whether a family continues to have a roof over its head. Under Rule 70 of the Rules of Court, judgments against defendants in ejectment cases are immediately executory. To stay or put on hold the execution pending appeal, the defendant must, among others, file a sufficient supersedeas bond and continue making the required deposits for the use and occupation of the property. 1 INQUIRER.net (2025, August 15). 57,134 informal settler families relocated from Manila Bay — DILG. Accessed last 11 August 2026 from: https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2096123/57134-informal-settler-families-relocated-from-manila-bay-dilg 2 Locus, S. (2025, May 26). Tension grips demolition in Tondo residential area. Accessed last 11 August from:https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/metro/947366/tension-grips-demolition-in-tondo-residential-area/story/ 1 The Supreme Court has consistently held that failure to comply with these requirements may result in the immediate execution of the judgment. For underprivileged and homeless citizens, however, the very financial incapacity that places them at risk of homelessness may also prevent them from securing the temporary protection necessary to meaningfully pursue their appeal. This measure seeks to amend Section 28 of R.A. No. 7279 by clarifying the treatment of court-ordered eviction and demolition and by exempting qualified underprivileged and homeless citizens from the supersedeas bond requirement, subject to appropriate proof of indigency. It does not extinguish the property rights of lawful owners, nor does it prevent courts from ultimately enforcing valid judgments. Rather, it ensures that the ability to seek appellate relief and temporarily stay displacement will not depend solely on one's ability to pay. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure, which is a counterpart measure of Senate Bill no. 70, is earnestly sought. HON. BERNADETTE “DETTE” G. label: HB 11132
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE JUDICIAL HAZARD COMPENSATION FOR ALL MEMBERS OF THE JUDICIARY IN THE FIRST AND SECOND-LEVEL COURTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The strength of our democratic institutions rests upon the bedrock of a judiciary that is not only competent but, more importantly, insulated from the chilling effects of external pressures, physical threats, and other occupational hazards. Under Section 1, Article VIII of the 1987 Constitution, judicial power is vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as may be established by law. To ensure the effective exercise of this power, the 1987 Constitution provides several safeguards to maintain the independence of the members of the Bench. Section 3, Article VIII also guarantees the fiscal autonomy of the Judiciary, ensuring that appropriations may not be reduced by the legislature below the amount appropriated for the previous year, and shall be automatically and regularly released. Furthermore, Section 10, Article VIII protects the stability of the Bench by mandating that the salary of the Chief Justice and the Associate Justices of the Supreme Court, and of judges of lower courts, shall be fixed by law and shall not be decreased during their incumbency in office. In light of these constitutional protections, the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (CJCA) adopted by the Supreme Court of the Philippines was implemented to ensure that judicial independence is upheld as a precondition to the rule of law. The CJCA demands that judges stay resolute and fearless of threats, as Canon I of the CJCA requires that a judge must pursue their actions independently, resisting and rejecting any form of undue influence, intimidation, or pressure from whatever source. Despite the Herculean efforts of the members of the Bench, the grim reality on the ground presents a bleak outlook for achieving these ideals. In recent decades, the Philippine legal community, and the judges in particular, have faced an unprecedented surge in violence, with at least 61 lawyers, judges, and prosecutors having been killed since 2016. From 2004 to 2021, public reports indicate that only seven (7) cases have resulted in charges filed in court. As of 2022, documented attacks on legal professionals reached 271. These targeted assaults have continued into 2025 and 2026. Such violence constitutes a direct assault on the judiciary and threatens to diminish the public’s trust in the administration of justice. Tragically, the physical and psychological threats are not confined to the courtroom. Judges frequently risk their lives in transit to remote court stations, navigating land, air, and sea to serve as Acting Presiding Judges in areas lacking permanent appointees. For these magistrates, the journey itself is as hazardous as the high-stakes cases they adjudicate. In fact, there were noted incidents of death by accidents while judges were in transit, an ominous fact staring the members of the Bench in the face. Moreover, it is worth emphasizing that the adoption of Republic Act No. 11576, or the Act expanding the jurisdiction of first-level courts, has significantly increased the workload of first-level court judges, who are now tasked with adjudicating the heavier, more complex civil cases once reserved for second-level courts. The shift in the jurisdictional threshold, however, has not created a distinction in safety. Current threat assessments reveal that judges in both first and second-level courts face the same level of professional risks and physical threats. Accordingly, while their legal duties are differentiated, the danger to their personal security remains a shared and equally urgent reality across both tiers. Complementing the preventive approach of Republic Act No. 11691, or the “Judiciary Marshals Act,” a monumental step toward securing the physical safety of the Bench, with a measure that aims both to recognize the devotion to duty of magistrates and to augment their financial resources for security, is vital to maintaining the judiciary as a public institution and a workplace. The persistent threat of retaliation, the necessity of living under constant surveillance, and the hazards inherent in the judicial robe remain occupational risks that even the Judiciary Marshals Act itself recognizes by granting hazard compensation to the Marshals themselves. If such compensation is mandated for those sworn to protect, it is only fair and just that it be equally mandated for the judges who are the primary targets of those very threats. This would effectively place judges on a similar footing with public health workers,1 public social workers,2 and scientists (and science and technology personnel),3 among others, whose indispensable presence on the ground define the fulfilment of the service-oriented purposes of their organizations. Finally, this bill provides a long-overdue legislative response to the Supreme Court’s call for protection. By instituting tax-exempt hazard compensation, the State recognizes that while the judge is responsible for upholding ethical and legal standards, the State is accountable for safeguarding the judge’s physical and economic security. 1 Republic Act No. 7305 2 Republic Act No. 9433 3 Republic Act No. 8439 In view of the foregoing, the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11133
title: AN ACT AMENDING THE PROBATION LAW INCREASING THE AMOUNT OF FINE FROM ONE THOUSAND PESOS (P1,000.00) TO FORTY THOUSAND PESOS (P40,000.00) IN VIEW OF THE PASSAGE OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10951
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Probation Law was enacted to afford convicted persons the opportunity for rehabilitation outside the confines of penal institutions, taking into consideration the nature and gravity of the offense committed. It is founded on the recognition that qualified offenders may be better reformed to become productive members of society if given the chance for reintegration rather than immediate incarceration. While the law principally seeks to promote the welfare and protection of society through the reformation of offenders, it likewise extends humanitarian consideration to deserving individuals by giving them the opportunity to avoid the harmful effects and social stigma of imprisonment. To preserve the integrity of the probation system and harmonize probation with the recognized ends of criminal justice, limitations are set on those who may avail themselves of alternative judicial relief by identifying disqualified offenders and offenses. However, with the enactment of Republic Act No. 10951, entitled “An Act Adjusting the Amount or the Value of Property and Damage on Which a Penalty is Based, and the Fines Imposed Under the Revised Penal Code,” the fines imposed for several offenses were substantially increased. As a consequence, certain offenses that were previously probationable effectively became excluded from the coverage of the Probation Law, thereby narrowing its application and depriving some accused persons of a remedy previously available to them under existing law. It bears stressing that the law favors interpretations and enactments that are beneficial to the accused. Rights and benefits already granted by law, and to which an accused has become entitled, should not be withdrawn absent a clear and compelling justification. Our legal system provides safeguards to uphold this principle. Section 22, Article III of the 1987 Constitution prohibits the passage of ex post facto laws, including laws that deprive an accused person of lawful protections or benefits already available at the time of the commission of the offense. Accordingly, this bill seeks to address the unintended consequences brought about by the enactment of Republic Act No. 10951 by restoring and clarifying the availability of probation in appropriate cases. In doing so, it upholds the rehabilitative and restorative objectives of the Probation Law, remains faithful to the constitutional policy of according favorable treatment to the accused where warranted, and reinforces the State’s commitment to justice tempered with compassion and social reintegration. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. FERDINAND L. label: HB 11134
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE COVERAGE OF QUALIFIED BENEFICIARIES UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9946, TO INCLUDE OTHER QUALIFIED DEPENDENTS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The passage of Republic Act No. 910, as amended by Republic Act No. 9946, otherwise known as “An Act Granting Additional Retirement, Survivorship, and Other Benefits to Members of the Judiciary,” has long been recognized as a significant measure acknowledging the invaluable contributions of judges and justices to the administration of justice. By granting retirement, survivorship, and related benefits, the law not only provides financial security to members of the Judiciary and their families, but also reinforces judicial independence by ensuring that judges and justices are accorded proper protection even after their service. These benefits likewise encourage competent and distinguished members of the Bar to join the Judiciary despite the financial sacrifices and opportunity costs associated with leaving private practice. However, the present provisions of the law on survivorship benefits require reconsideration and expansion in light of evolving family structures and the realities faced by members of the Judiciary today. At present, the law primarily limits survivorship benefits to the surviving legitimate spouse and heirs or those who are entitled to succeed in the estate of the deceased Judge or Justice under the law on succession. Such limitation fails to account for situations where a judge or justice, although unmarried at the time of death, leaves behind dependents who relied upon them for support and who would otherwise qualify as their lawful heirs. In modern society, the concept of “heirs” and “dependents” has become more nuanced and should not be confined to a restrictive interpretation. The law must recognize that members of the Judiciary may have other qualified dependents, who remain financially and emotionally dependent upon them regardless of marital status. Extending survivorship benefits to these dependents promotes fairness and ensures that judges and justices who are differently situated in life are not unjustly excluded from the full protection intended by the law. Such an expansion is neither novel nor unprecedented. Section 1 of Republic Act No. 11643, otherwise known as “An Act Granting Survivorship Benefits to the Surviving Legitimate Spouse and Dependent Children of a Deceased Retired Member of the National Prosecution Service,” adopts a broader and more inclusive definition of dependents. Under the said law, dependents include legitimate, illegitimate, or legally adopted children who are chiefly dependent upon the deceased member of the National Prosecution Service, provided they are unmarried, not gainfully employed, and not more than twenty-one (21) years of age, or regardless of age if incapable of self-support due to mental or physical incapacity. Under similar considerations, this Bill seeks to expand the coverage of heirs and dependents entitled to survivorship benefits under Republic Act No. 910, as amended, in order to reflect the present realities faced by members of the Judiciary and their families. By doing so, the proposed measure strengthens the State’s continuing recognition of the sacrifices and service rendered by judges and justices, while ensuring equal and compassionate treatment regardless of their civil status or family circumstances. In view of the foregoing, , the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. FERDINAND L. label: HB 11135
title: AN ACT DECLARING SEPTEMBER 3 OF EVERY YEAR A SPECIAL NONWORKING HOLIDAY IN THE CITY OF IRIGA, PROVINCE OF CAMARINES SUR, IN COMMEMORATION OF ITS CHARTER DAY ANNIVERSARY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The City of Iriga traces its roots to the Spanish colonial period, when it was established as a pueblo and later developed into a municipality that became a center of commerce, culture, education, and governance in the Rinconada District of Camarines Sur. With the enactment of Republic Act No. 5261 on June 15, 1968, the Municipality of Iriga was converted into a component city, granting it greater autonomy and strengthening its capacity for local governance and development. On September 3, 1968, the formal inauguration of the City of Iriga was held, marking a defining milestone in the history and identity of the Irigueño people. Since then, September 3 has been observed as an important occasion to commemorate Iriga's cityhood, celebrate its heritage, and recognize its continuing progress. The annual Charter Day provides an opportunity to honor the contributions of past and present generations while fostering civic pride, community unity, cultural appreciation, tourism, and economic development. Several cities across the country have similarly been granted special non- working holidays through national legislation to commemorate their charter anniversaries and cityhood. Consistent with this practice, declaring September 3 as a Special Non-Working Holiday in the City of Iriga would allow its residents to meaningfully participate in civic, historical, cultural, educational, religious, and community activities celebrating its cityhood and development. Recognizing Iriga's cityhood likewise affirms its distinct identity and acknowledges the significant contributions of the Irigueño people to the social, cultural, and economic life of Camarines Sur and the Bicol Region. 1 In view of the foregoing, it is fitting and proper to declare September 3 of every year as a Special Non-Working Holiday in the City of Iriga. The measure will provide the people of Iriga with an opportunity to celebrate their shared history and heritage, strengthen community solidarity, and honor the city's continuing growth and development. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LEILA M. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN INTEGRATED SCHOOL IN CIUDAD KAUNLARAN, BARANGAY MOLINO 2, CITY OF BACOOR, PROVINCE OF CAVITE TO BE KNOWN AS THE CIUDAD KAUNLARAN INTEGRATED SCHOOL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish an integrated school in Ciudad Kaunlaran, Barangay Molino 2, City of Bacoor, Province of Cavite to be known as Ciudad Kaunlaran Integrated School. Ciudad Kaunlaran is an in-city vertical socialized housing project of the National Housing Authority (NHA) located in Molino 2, City of Bacoor, Cavite built on 52,718 square meters of land. It has a total of 1,860 units allocated for informal settler families (ISFs) residing along the coastal barangays of Bacoor Bay, subject of Manila Bay continuing mandamus of the Supreme Court. The CKIS will be responsible for educating the school-aged children from the 1,860 families in Ciudad Kaunlaran, which is in compliance to Section 21 of Republic Act No. 7279 or the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992 which required the provision of basic services. As an integrated school, CKIS will offer complete basic education from Kindergarten to Grade 12 with a unified instructional program as defined under DepEd Order No. 40, series of 2014 ad Republic Act No. 10533 or the K to 12 Law. Considering that there are already residents in Ciudad Kaunlaran, immediate approval of this bill is hereby sought. REP. label: HB 11137
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL REGULATORY FRAMEWORK FOR THE DEVELOPMENT, DEPLOYMENT, AND USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS IN THE PHILIPPINES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE REGULATORY AUTHORITY AND THE NATIONAL AI MULTI-STAKEHOLDER ADVISORY COUNCIL, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Artificial Intelligence (AI) has moved from the margins of Philippine economic and civic life to its center. Independent industry research cited in recent House deliberations found that more than nine in ten surveyed Philippine organizations have already adopted AI in some form, with more than half using generative AI tools for over a year. AI already assists in hiring and firing decisions, credit and loan approvals, medical triage, classroom instruction, government frontline services, and the content millions of Filipinos see on their screens every day. This proliferation of AI across the economy and daily life can no longer be treated as a future concern to be legislated once the technology matures. It is a present reality, and a national regulatory framework must be set in place now, before gaps in oversight translate into irreversible harm to workers, consumers, and vulnerable groups. Despite this reality, the Philippines has no single law that defines or regulates AI as such. Existing statutes like the Data Privacy Act of 2012, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012, and the recently enacted E-Governance Act each cover only a slice of the problem, while the executive branch's National AI Strategy for the Philippines (NAIS-PH), approved in May 2025, and the Department of Science and Technology's National Artificial Intelligence Center for Research and Innovation (NAICRI), activated in February 2026, provide policy direction and research infrastructure but carry no binding regulatory force on their own. Congress has not been silent on this gap. Both chambers of the 19th and 20th Congresses have seen a steady stream of measures responding to different facets of AI governance. The Department of Information and Communications Technology has consistently urged that AI regulation be "principle-based and flexible" and calibrated to actual risk, cautioning that heavy-handed rules could stifle innovation and discourage the investment the country needs to remain competitive; industry and startup groups have echoed concerns that blanket registration or documentation requirements could be disproportionately burdensome for micro, small, and medium enterprises. At the same time, labor advocates pointing to the Department of Labor and Employment's own acknowledgment that Filipino workers are already losing jobs to automation have pressed for enforceable protections: advance notice before AI-driven displacement, access to retraining, and an assurance that no worker will be dismissed by an algorithm alone. Civil society and academic voices behind the AI Bill of Rights language found in earlier bills have emphasized transparency, protection from discriminatory profiling, a right to human review of consequential decisions, and safeguards for children and other vulnerable groups. Data privacy regulators and legal commentators, for their part, have stressed that any new AI framework must remain harmonized with, rather than duplicate or contradict, the Data Privacy Act of 2012. Community concerns have also emerged around the energy and water footprint of the AI data centers now concentrating around Metro Manila and Cebu. This bill seeks to reconcile these positions in a single, risk-based, and workable framework. It does not impose uniform, one-size-fits-all obligations on every AI system regardless of its actual risk profile. Instead it: (i) affirms a Bill of Rights in Artificial Intelligence covering notice, explanation, human review, data control, and protection from discrimination; (ii) creates the National Artificial Intelligence Regulatory Authority (NAIRA) under the Department of Information and Communications Technology, supported by a National AI Multi-Stakeholder Advisory Council representing government, labor, industry, academe, and civil society; (iii) classifies AI systems by risk prohibiting unacceptable uses outright, subjecting only high-risk systems to registration and pre-deployment review, requiring basic transparency for limited-risk systems, and leaving minimal-risk innovation largely unencumbered; (iv) guarantees that no Filipino worker may be dismissed, demoted, or have compensation reduced on the sole basis of an automated decision, and requires at least sixty (60) days' advance notice and access to retraining before AI-driven displacement; (v) establishes a regulatory sandbox to keep the door open for startups, researchers, and MSMEs; and (vi) provides proportionate administrative, civil, and criminal remedies for violations. Innovation and regulation are not opposing goals. A clear, predictable, and appropriately calibrated legal framework is the foundation on which sustained public trust and, with it, sustained AI adoption and investment will be built. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly requested. REP. ALEXANDER T. label: HB 11138
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE PERPETUAL EXISTENCE OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION (PITC), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 2 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1071, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE REVISED CHARTER OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine International Trading Corporation (PITC) was created through Presidential Decree No. 252, and its charter was subsequently revised by Presidential Decree No. 1071, otherwise known as the “Revised Charter of the Philippine International Trading Corporation.” Under Section 2 of Presidential Decree No. 1071, the Corporation is authorized to exist for a period of fifty (50) years, with its present corporate term set to expire on 25 January 2027. For several decades, PITC has served as a government corporate vehicle in pursuing the State’s objectives in international trade. Consistent with its charter, the Corporation has undertaken trade-related activities and provided services intended to facilitate international trade, promote Philippine products and enterprises, and support the Government in its foreign procurement and marketing activities. As the expiration of PITC’s corporate term approaches, there is a need to ensure the continuity of its juridical personality, operations, and existing commitments. The expiration of its corporate term without an appropriate legislative measure may create uncertainty regarding the Corporation’s authority to continue performing its lawful functions, administering its assets and liabilities, honoring its contractual commitments, and undertaking transactions necessary for the fulfillment of its mandate. The proposed measure seeks to address this concern by providing for the continued corporate existence of PITC, while ensuring that such continued existence remains subject to appropriate government oversight and accountability. The measure provides for the perpetual term of existence of the Corporation, unless otherwise provided by law, while recognizing the authority of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or -Controlled Corporations (GCG) to evaluate the Corporation in accordance with Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. The proposed framework recognizes that the continued existence of a government- owned or -controlled corporation must be accompanied by mechanisms for periodic assessment of its relevance, efficiency, financial viability, performance, and consistency with national development policies and priorities. Accordingly, the GCG may conduct periodic performance evaluation and oversight of PITC, taking into account, among others, its financial performance, operational efficiency, governance and risk management systems, delivery of services, and contribution to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. The measure further recognizes that perpetual corporate existence does not exempt PITC from continuing government evaluation, oversight, and accountability. The Corporation shall remain subject to the evaluation, monitoring, and other appropriate actions authorized under Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. Where warranted by such evaluation and consistent with applicable law, the appropriate government authorities may undertake or recommend such lawful measures as may be necessary to ensure that the Corporation remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. The grant of perpetual existence is not intended to constitute a determination that the Corporation shall operate indefinitely regardless of its continued relevance, performance, or economic viability. Rather, PITC shall remain subject to the performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight mechanisms applicable to government-owned or -controlled corporations under Republic Act No. 10149 and other applicable laws. At the same time, the proposed measure does not seek to expand the substantive powers and functions of PITC under Presidential Decree No. 1071. Rather, it seeks to ensure the continuity of the Corporation’s juridical personality and operations while strengthening accountability and providing for continuing evaluation by the appropriate government authorities. The proposed perpetual corporate term will also eliminate the need for periodic legislative action solely for the purpose of extending the Corporation’s corporate existence, while preserving the authority of Congress to amend, repeal, or otherwise modify the Corporation’s charter or corporate existence through subsequent legislation. This approach provides greater institutional stability and continuity while maintaining the necessary safeguards to ensure that PITC remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. Perpetual corporate existence does not preclude the State from undertaking performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight of the Corporation's relevance, performance, efficiency, and financial viability, nor does it prevent the appropriate government authorities from recommending or undertaking such lawful measures as may be warranted by the results of such evaluation. The continued corporate existence of PITC is therefore intended to prevent disruption in its legal existence and operations and to ensure the orderly continuity of its contracts, obligations, assets, liabilities, and other lawful commitments. It will likewise enable the Corporation to continue performing its existing mandate and contributing, within the scope of its charter, to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this measure is earnestly sought. ATTY. ROY M.
