label: HB 11140
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SCHOOL-BASED SPORTS DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMS AND VARSITY TEAMS IN BASIC EDUCATION, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR STUDENT-ATHLETES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to promote physical education, sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, and requires educational institutions to undertake regular sports activities. Republic Act No. 5708, or the Schools Physical Education and Sports Development Act of 1969, likewise provides for an integrated physical education and sports development program in schools. Consistent with these mandates, the Department of Education has adopted policies supporting the organization of junior and senior varsity teams and the gradual expansion of school sports programs. Despite these existing frameworks, implementation remains uneven. Many schools, particularly those that are small, geographically isolated, or economically disadvantaged, continue to face limitations in qualified coaches, facilities, equipment, training opportunities, competition, and medical and safety support. Some schools also lack the resources to maintain independent varsity teams or participate regularly in organized competitions. This measure seeks to strengthen and institutionalize school-based sports development by establishing a clear and sustainable framework for varsity teams in elementary and secondary schools. Its implementation shall be phased and responsive to the resources, facilities, student population, and sports interests of each school or school cluster. The proposed Act shall provide standards for the identification and development of student-athletes, training and recognition of coaches, provision of equipment, organization of training and competitions, maintenance of athlete records, and coordination among schools, local government units, the Philippine Sports Commission, national sports associations, and other stakeholders. It shall also promote equitable access to sports, including traditional and indigenous games, while protecting the health, safety, academic welfare, and rights of student-athletes. School sports contribute not only to athlete development but also to the physical, social, and personal growth of learners by fostering fitness, discipline, teamwork, leadership, resilience, and mental well-being. A properly supported varsity system can provide a structured pathway for grassroots talent development while ensuring that sports opportunities are accessible, safe, and inclusive. The measure therefore seeks to complement and strengthen existing constitutional, legislative, and DepEd policies by providing statutory support for the sustainable and equitable implementation of school sports programs throughout the country. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11141
title: AN ACT INCORPORATING SCAM PREVENTION EDUCATION IN THE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL CURRICULA, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Over the years, fraudsters and scammers have become more dangerous and have proliferated even in the digital space, especially during the pandemic. Various scams and economic fraud have threatened not only wealthy businesses but also individual citizens. Those who do not have access to education or enough information on their existing modus operandi are vulnerable to these crimes. The continued expansion of digital services in the Philippines has been accompanied by persistent cyber-enabled fraud, phishing, identity theft, and other online scams. Enforcement activities and advisories from the Philippine National Police Anti-Cybercrime Group, the Anti-Money Laundering Council, the Department of Information and Communications Technology, the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas, and telecommunications providers demonstrate the continuing need for stronger prevention, reporting, investigation, and victim-support mechanisms. Globe Telecom, for example, reported blocking 71 million spam and phishing messages and deactivating 5,670 confirmed spam and phishing numbers in 2021, illustrating the scale of fraudulent communications directed at mobile users. Children and adolescents are likewise increasingly exposed to online risks through smartphones, social-media platforms, online games, messaging applications, digital-payment services, and e-learning platforms. Their limited experience in recognizing phishing, impersonation, fraudulent offers, and improper requests for personal information may make them particularly vulnerable to scams and identity theft. There is therefore a need to strengthen digital-safety education and preventive measures for school- aged children, while promoting cooperation among schools, families, government agencies, telecommunications providers, financial institutions, and online platforms to protect minors and assist victims of cyber-enabled offenses. While scams typically target adults, the recent increased exposure and access of school-aged children to the internet have also made them prey to fraudulent schemes. The growing threat of fraud in society not only stresses the need to protect young people from scams. It also points to the alarming fact that students are exposed to the dangers these fraudsters create. It is therefore vital for schools to promote anti-scam awareness throughout society as well as equip students with the knowledge so that they can report cases once they encounter an incident of potential fraud or scam. This bill seeks the protection of students against fraud through the integration of scam prevention education in the school curriculum of senior high schools. It is the hope of this measure to empower the next generation of Filipinos with the critical thinking skills to be able to protect themselves and their families from exploitative scammers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11142
title: AN ACT CREATING THE HEALTH EMERGENCY AUXILIARY REINFORCEMENT TEAM UNDER THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure seeks to establish the Health Emergency Auxiliary Reinforcement Team (HEART) under the Department of Health as a pool of trained and qualified health professionals, allied health workers, students, retirees, and other volunteers who may be mobilized to assist government health facilities during disasters, disease outbreaks, pandemics, and other public health emergencies. The proposed HEART complements, rather than replaces, the regular health workforce by providing surge capacity whenever existing personnel become insufficient. The proposal is firmly anchored on the Constitution, which mandates the State to protect and promote the people's right to health and adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development.1 It likewise supports the objectives of Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act, which recognizes the importance of strengthening the health workforce as an essential building block of an effective healthcare system.2 Furthermore, the bill aligns with Republic Act No. 11332 by enhancing the government's capacity to respond 1 1987 Philippine Constitution, Article II, Section 15, and Article XIII, Section 11. 2 Republic Act No. 11223 (Universal Health Care Act), particularly provisions on strengthening the National Health Workforce Support System and the National Health Workforce Registry. to notifiable diseases and public health events of national and international concern.3 Beyond domestic law, the measure advances the Philippines' commitment under the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being), which calls on States to strengthen health systems and improve preparedness for health risks and emergencies.4 By institutionalizing a trained reserve force and establishing clear mechanisms for recruitment, training, mobilization, protection, and coordination, the bill ensures that the country is better prepared to respond swiftly and effectively to future health crises while fostering the Filipino spirit of Bayanihan through organized public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT GIVING PRIORITY TO RETIRED TEACHERS IN THE AVAILMENT OF GOVERNMENT SERVICES AND PUBLIC UTILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Teaching is considered the noblest profession because of the selfless sacrifices of our teachers and educators in the delivery of quality education and ensuring that each student has the necessary knowledge to succeed in their chosen careers. It then follows that retired teachers, having spent the majority of their lives in this noble profession, have contributed greatly in nation-building. In recognition of their sacrifices and dedication in the field of providing quality education, our teachers deserve to be granted certain benefits for the many years they have spent serving the nation. This bill seeks to recognize the important role of our retired teachers in nation-building and providing quality education in the country by providing priority in the availment of government services and public utilities. label: HB 11144
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE REVITALIZATION AND ADVANCEMENT OF ORIGINAL FILIPINO MUSIC AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino musicians and artists are world-class. Our country has produced countless artists to sing and perform abroad. Our kababayans have dominated the stage overseas, and we have seen the likes of Lea Salonga, Arnel Pineda, Apl.De.Ap., and Freddie Aguilar, whose song “Anak” became an international hit and was translated into 26 languages. It is undeniable that the Philippines is teeming with top-notch talent. However, many radio and television stations allot more of their airtime to foreign music rather than their local counterparts. Presently, Executive Order No. 225, which was issued on 25 July 1987, mandates all radio stations to “broadcast a minimum of four (4) original Filipino musical compositions in every clock hour of a program with a musical format.” However, the said law lacks strength as it merely imposes a fine in the amount of Php100.00 per violation. This bill seeks to mandate all radio stations and TV stations devoted to broadcasting music within the country to allot a sizeable amount of airtime for Original Pilipino Music or OPM. Through this, we are providing our OPM artists a wider platform, giving them the opportunity to showcase and offer their gifts to their countrymen and eventually, the world. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11145
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE SALARY SCALES OR LEVELS OF PUBLIC DENTISTS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Dental health experts often say that the mouth is the gateway to our overall health. Taking care of our dental health can protect our bodies from a variety of health problems. However, the public’s awareness of the importance of dental health care and services remains low, in part due to the scarcity of dentists working in the public sector. The country’s dentists-to-patients ratio is currently at 1:53,000, and only very few licensed dentists intend to work in the government due to its meager salary and benefits compared to private dental practitioners. To encourage more dentists to render public service in government and mainstream the importance of dental health care and services, this bill seeks to upgrade the salary grades of all public dentists in recognition of their essential role in maintaining and promoting the oral health of the people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11146
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE INCENTIVIZED SOLID WASTE REDEMPTION AND RECOVERY SYSTEMS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, provides for an ecological solid waste management program and a framework that creates necessary institutional mechanisms and incentives, declaring certain acts prohibited and providing penalties therefor. Under the law, local government units (LGUs) are also mandated to be primarily responsible for the implementation and enforcement of the provisions of the Solid Waste Management Act within their respective jurisdictions. However, rewards and incentives have limitations and must be innovated to adapt to the needs of the “new normal”. The social and economic climate brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic has presented challenges to food security and environmental protection. The multitude of consumption in the pandemic has increased solid waste production, thus bringing up the need to properly organize solid waste management and segregation at the level of the household. In its efforts to aid its citizens economically amid the pandemic while also promoting efforts to save the environment, the Quezon City government has launched a point system program on waste management entitled the “Trash to Cashback” Program. Under the “Trash to Cashback” Program, residents can trade their recyclable materials for environmental points which can be exchanged for basic commodities such as rice, eggs, vegetables, and other essential grocery items. This bill seeks to institutionalize innovative efforts to incentivize solid waste management and recycling through the exchange or rewarding of basic commodities such as rice, eggs, vegetables, canned goods, basic household consumer items, other essential grocery items, or even cash. This legislation further provides that the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the Department of Agriculture (DA), and the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) shall determine the reasonable and compliance-inducing exchange values for graduated weights or volumes of solid waste provided. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COHERENT FRAMEWORK BY ALIGNING THE QUALITY ASSURANCE SYSTEMS OF THE COMMISSION ON HIGHER EDUCATION, THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, AND THE DEPARTMENT OF LABOR AND EMPLOYMENT WITH LABOR MARKET NEEDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes education as a fundamental instrument of national development and directs the State to establish and maintain an educational system that is responsive to the needs of the people and society. In an increasingly technology-driven and rapidly changing economy, this responsibility extends beyond expanding access to education. It also requires ensuring that the knowledge, skills, and competencies acquired by Filipinos remain relevant to the changing demands of work and enable them to obtain productive, decent, and sustainable livelihoods. The Philippines has made significant gains in educational access and attainment. Nevertheless, persistent unemployment, underemployment, skills shortages, and education-to-employment mismatches continue to challenge the country's human capital development. These conditions suggest that the issue is not simply whether Filipinos have access to education, but whether education and training are sufficiently connected to labor-market opportunities and the evolving requirements of the economy. Data from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) underscore the continuing challenge. In January 2026, the unemployment rate stood at 5.8 percent, equivalent to approximately 2.96 million unemployed Filipinos. In May 2026, approximately 2.50 million Filipinos remained unemployed, while the underemployment rate stood at 12.2 percent. These figures demonstrate that the challenge extends beyond creating jobs; it also involves improving the quality of employment and ensuring that workers are able to find jobs that appropriately utilize their skills and provide opportunities for advancement.1. 2 The concern is particularly significant as the Philippine economy undergoes technological and structural transformation. The World Bank's Philippines Country Growth and Jobs Report 2025 identified skills scarcity as one of the constraints affecting technology adoption and productivity among Philippine firms. It emphasized the need to address skills mismatches and strengthen human capital to support the creation of better and more productive jobs.3 Earlier World Bank research likewise found that Philippine employers experienced difficulty finding workers with the technical and socioemotional competencies required in the workplace, including communication, interpersonal skills, work ethic, adaptability, and other capabilities necessary for effective https://psa.gov.ph/content/number-unemployed-persons-january-2026-increased-296-million-filipinos-aged-15- years-and 2 https://psa.gov.ph/content/underemployment-rate-declined-122-percent-may-2026 3 https://www.worldbank.org/en/country/philippines/publication/philippines-growth-and-jobs-report-2025 participation in changing work environments.4 These findings demonstrate that employability cannot be measured solely by the possession of a degree, diploma, or technical certificate. Workers increasingly require a combination of technical, cognitive, interpersonal, and adaptive competencies that can be continuously developed throughout their careers. The education-employment mismatch has also been recognized by Philippine stakeholders. The Philippine Business for Education has consistently called attention to the gap between the competencies developed through education and the requirements of employers and has supported initiatives involving stronger industry participation and skills-based approaches to workforce development. The Philippine Institute for Development Studies has likewise identified skills mismatch as an issue affecting Philippine economic growth and the efficient utilization of human capital.5 The challenge, therefore, is not necessarily the absence of programs or institutions. Rather, it is the need for stronger coherence among the country's education, technical-vocational training, labor-market information, and employment systems. A stronger education-to-employment framework can help ensure that labor-market information is meaningfully considered in curriculum development, program review, quality assurance, skills training, career guidance, and workforce planning. Reliable information concerning occupational demand, skills shortages, vacancies, wages, emerging occupations, and regional labor-market conditions can enable educational and training institutions to make better-informed decisions while allowing government to identify areas requiring intervention. However, should not reduce education to a short-term response to employer vacancies. Educational institutions serve broader purposes, including intellectual development, professional formation, research, citizenship, creativity, and lifelong learning. Accordingly, labor-market information should be treated as an important source of evidence for continuous improvement, not as the sole or mechanical determinant of academic decisions. Academic freedom, institutional autonomy, diverse educational missions, and learner choice must remain protected. The transition from education to employment likewise requires greater attention. Possession of a qualification does not automatically guarantee successful entry into the workforce. Students and graduates may encounter barriers involving insufficient workplace experience, limited access to career information and professional networks, geographic constraints, or differences between classroom instruction and actual workplace requirements. Strengthening work-integrated learning, apprenticeships, internships, enterprise-based training, career guidance, job placement, and recognition of prior learning can help address these barriers. The proposed Comprehensive Education-to-Employment Alignment Act seeks to respond to these challenges by strengthening coherence among the existing education, training, and labor- market systems. label: HB 11181
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE INTERNATIONALIZATION CAPACITY OF PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, ESTABLISHING A HIGHER EDUCATION, CREATING AN INTERNATIONALIZATION SUPPORT FUND, PROVIDING FOR INTER-AGENCY COORDINATION ON EDUCATION EXPORT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has strong potential to become a competitive destination for international higher education. Its widespread use of English, cultural diversity, and relatively affordable tuition make its higher education sector attractive to foreign students and academic partners. Yet, despite these advantages, the country remains a modest participant in global academic mobility. Foreign student enrollment increased from 14,132 in 2017 to 22,247 in 2022, but still trails behind neighboring countries such as Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. This gap reflects persistent institutional barriers, including complex regulatory processes, limited opportunities for foreign faculty, inadequate funding, weak international partnerships, and insufficient campus facilities. While existing laws, including Republic Act No. 7722 and Republic Act No. 11448, provide a foundation for higher education development and transnational education, they do not establish a comprehensive and sustained national strategy for internationalization. This measure seeks to address these gaps by establishing a National Internationalization Framework for Higher Education, supported by institutional internationalization plans and an Internationalization Support Fund. The framework will support student and faculty mobility, international research partnerships, joint academic programs, and Internationalization at Home, allowing students to gain global competencies even without studying abroad.The measure also strengthens coordination among CHED, the Department of Trade and Industry, and the Department of Foreign Affairs to promote Philippine higher education internationally. Internationalization should not be pursued solely as a means of competing with other countries. It should strengthen the quality of Philippine higher education, expand opportunities for Filipino learners, and connect institutions across the country to the global academic community. Through a coordinated and inclusive national policy, the Philippines can move from having the potential to internationalize to actually becoming an active participant in global higher education. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11183
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE HIGHER PARTNERSHIP FRAMEWORK, CREATING THE HIGHER EDUCATION-INDUSTRY COORDINATION COUNCIL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFORE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face a persistent mismatch between higher education outcomes and the needs of the labor market. Many college graduates remain underemployed or work in positions that do not require a college degree, while employers continue to report difficulty finding workers with the skills needed in key sectors. This reflects a deeper disconnect between what higher education produces and what the economy demands. One major cause is the fragmentation of labor market information. Relevant data are collected separately by government agencies, making it difficult for higher education institutions (HEIs), policymakers, training providers, and employers to work from a common and updated understanding of emerging skills needs. At the same time, partnerships between HEIs and industry remain largely informal and inconsistent, limiting opportunities to align curricula, internships, research, and training with actual workforce demand. This measure therefore a Higher Education-Industry Partnership Framework to establish sustained cooperation between HEIs and industry stakeholders. The bill creates a Higher Education-Industry Coordination Council to consolidate labor market and skills information and produce a National Skills Gap Inventory and an Annual National Skills and Labor Market Intelligence Report. It also establishes Regional Industry-Higher Education Advisory Boards to ensure that regional industries, local employment conditions, and the needs of state universities and colleges are reflected in higher education planning. By connecting education planning with reliable labor market intelligence and meaningful industry participation, this measure seeks to ensure that Filipino graduates are equipped not only with degrees, but with competencies relevant to the changing needs of the economy. It provides a more coordinated and responsive approach to reducing skills gaps, improving graduate employability, and strengthening the contribution of higher education to national and regional development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11184
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE RECOGNITION, QUALITY ASSURANCE, STACKABILITY, AND PORTABILITY OF MICROCREDENTIALS AND SHORT COURSES, STRENGTHENING WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT, PROVIDING FLEXIBLE LEARNING PATHWAYS AND PROTECTIONS FOR LEARNERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face a growing mismatch between the skills possessed by its workforce and those required by a rapidly changing economy. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II), in its Year Two Report, found that skills mismatches persist across all levels of education. Around one-third of employed Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) graduates are working in positions that do not fully utilize their qualifications, while senior high school graduates record the highest unemployment rate among educational cohorts. Moreover, from 2021 to 2022, approximately 35% of the labor force was engaged in the informal sector, many of whom have limited access to portable and recognized credentials that can be readily accepted by employers, educational institutions, and government programs. Despite these challenges, the country still lacks a unified legal framework governing microcredentials and short courses. The Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF), established under Executive Order No. 83 in 2012 and institutionalized through Republic Act No. 10968 in 2018, was intended to provide a national system for recognizing and building upon qualifications acquired through various learning pathways. However, EDCOM II reported that little substantial progress has been made in implementing the PQF since its establishment. The National Coordinating Council became nonfunctional in 2017 due to staffing and funding limitations, while the framework continued to lack a permanent secretariat, coordinated financing, and a comprehensive strategic plan at the time of the Year Two Report. As a result, skills and competencies gained through short courses, workplace-based training, and other forms of non-formal learning remain difficult to recognize, accumulate toward higher qualifications, or transfer across employers and educational institutions. EDCOM II likewise identified the lack of a clear national framework for the equivalency and recognition of non-formal and informal learning as a major barrier to lifelong learning and workforce development. Workers who acquire new skills through industry training, online learning platforms, or community-based learning programs often have no reliable mechanism through which these competencies can be converted into academic credit or formal certification. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by formally integrating microcredentials and short courses into the Philippine education and training system and aligning them with the PQF. It establishes minimum quality standards and requires the accreditation of qualified providers by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and the Department of Education (DepEd). It also provides for the creation of a Digital Credential Registry to facilitate the verification, portability, and interoperability of credentials. The proposed measure further safeguards learner rights, provides protections for employed individuals pursuing additional education or training, and institutionalizes access to Recognition of Prior Learning. An Inter-Agency Coordination Committee composed of CHED, TESDA, DepEd, and the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) will be established to harmonize national standards. Its work will be complemented by an Industry Advisory Council and mechanisms for scholarships, training vouchers, and employer tax incentives. Through these reforms, the measure seeks to establish a unified and coherent national system for flexible learning that recognizes diverse forms of education and training and enables Filipinos to acquire, build upon, and carry their skills throughout their education and careers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11185
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE AND SUSTAINABLE FRAMEWORK FOR FACULTY DEVELOPMENT AND RESEARCH IN PHILIPPINE HIGHER EDUCATION, CREATING THE FACULTY DEVELOPMENT AND RESEARCH FUND, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The quality and competitiveness of Philippine higher education are closely tied to the qualifications, research capabilities, and continuous professional development of its faculty. However, available data indicate that these areas remain significantly underdeveloped. In Academic Year (AY) 2018–2019, only 54.2% of faculty members in Philippine higher education institutions (HEIs) possessed advanced degrees, an improvement from 32.8% in AY 1997–1998. Of this figure, only 16.6% held doctoral degrees. These levels remain below international standards for tertiary education and demonstrate that progress in faculty development has been gradual rather than transformative. The implications go beyond the quality of instruction. Research productivity among Philippine HEIs continues to lag behind other ASEAN countries. Based on Scopus-indexed publications, the Philippines ranks below Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam and remains considerably below the ASEAN average. This disparity is projected to persist and potentially widen. Moreover, the country has only 172.01 researchers per million people, compared with the World Bank benchmark of 322.51 researchers per million for lower-middle-income countries in 2021. This limited research capacity weakens the ability of higher education institutions to contribute meaningfully to the country's science, technology, and innovation ecosystem. Existing government mechanisms have not generated the level of improvement necessary to address these persistent gaps. The Higher Education Development Fund, established under Republic Act No. 7722 to support the development of higher education, saw the share of its resources allocated for developmental functions decline from 86.63% in 2016 to only 11.43% in 2022. Increasingly, resources have been directed toward regulatory functions instead of long-term capacity-building. Faculty development initiatives have likewise lacked a unified, adequately funded, and institutionally sustained national framework. Consequently, support remains fragmented, unevenly distributed across regions, and insufficient to establish a continuous pipeline for faculty scholarship and research advancement. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) National Education Plan 2026–2035 recognizes the need for substantial investment in faculty development. It sets a target of increasing the proportion of HEI faculty with at least a graduate degree from 58.2% in AY 2023– 2024 to 88.1% by 2035. Meeting this target requires sustained and systematic investment in professional development and research capacity. Legislative intervention is therefore necessary, as administrative initiatives alone have not been sufficient to ensure the funding, coordination, and accountability required for nationwide and long-term reform. This proposed measure seeks to address these gaps by establishing a permanent and comprehensive national framework for faculty development and research across all HEIs. It provides for the creation of a Faculty Development and Research Fund supported by multiple funding sources; institutionalizes competitive scholarships and research grants responsive to national priorities; and establishes equity-based funding mechanisms for underserved and geographically isolated institutions. It further mandates the establishment of a national research repository and creates within the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) a Faculty Development and Research Service to serve as the principal coordinating and oversight body. The bill also introduces a Professors of Practice program to bring industry and professional expertise into higher education classrooms and strengthen the relevance of academic instruction. Taken together, these measures seek to improve faculty qualifications, expand the country's research capacity, promote greater equity among higher education institutions, and strengthen the role of Philippine higher education in advancing national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. . ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11186
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE PERPETUAL EXISTENCE OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION (PITC), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 2 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 1071, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE REVISED CHARTER OF THE PHILIPPINE INTERNATIONAL TRADING CORPORATION”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine International Trading Corporation (PITC) was created through Presidential Decree No. 252, and its charter was subsequently revised by Presidential Decree No. 1071, otherwise known as the “Revised Charter of the Philippine International Trading Corporation.” Under Section 2 of Presidential Decree No. 1071, the Corporation is authorized to exist for a period of fifty (50) years, with its present corporate term set to expire on 25 January 2027. For several decades, PITC has served as a government corporate vehicle in pursuing the State’s objectives in international trade. Consistent with its charter, the Corporation has undertaken trade-related activities and provided services intended to facilitate international trade, promote Philippine products and enterprises, and support the Government in its foreign procurement and marketing activities. As the expiration of PITC’s corporate term approaches, there is a need to ensure the continuity of its juridical personality, operations, and existing commitments. The expiration of its corporate term without an appropriate legislative measure may create uncertainty regarding the Corporation’s authority to continue performing its lawful functions, administering its assets and liabilities, honoring its contractual commitments, and undertaking transactions necessary for the fulfillment of its mandate. The proposed measure seeks to address this concern by providing for the continued corporate existence of PITC, while ensuring that such continued existence remains subject to appropriate government oversight and accountability. The measure provides for the perpetual term of existence of the Corporation, unless otherwise provided by law, while recognizing the authority of the Governance Commission for Government-Owned or - Controlled Corporations (GCG) to evaluate the Corporation in accordance with Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. The proposed framework recognizes that the continued existence of a government-owned or -controlled corporation must be accompanied by mechanisms for periodic assessment of its relevance, efficiency, financial viability, performance, and consistency with national development policies and priorities. Accordingly, the GCG may conduct periodic performance evaluation and oversight of PITC, taking into account, among others, its financial performance, operational efficiency, governance and risk management systems, delivery of services, and contribution to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. The measure further recognizes that perpetual corporate existence does not exempt PITC from continuing government evaluation, oversight, and accountability. The Corporation shall remain subject to the evaluation, monitoring, and other appropriate actions authorized under Republic Act No. 10149, otherwise known as the “GOCC Governance Act of 2011,” and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. Where warranted by such evaluation and consistent with applicable law, the appropriate government authorities may undertake or recommend such lawful measures as may be necessary to ensure that the Corporation remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. The grant of perpetual existence is not intended to constitute a determination that the Corporation shall operate indefinitely regardless of its continued relevance, performance, or economic viability. Rather, PITC shall remain subject to the performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight mechanisms applicable to government-owned or -controlled corporations under Republic Act No. 10149 and other applicable laws. At the same time, the proposed measure does not seek to expand the substantive powers and functions of PITC under Presidential Decree No. 1071. Rather, it seeks to ensure the continuity of the Corporation’s juridical personality and operations while strengthening accountability and providing for continuing evaluation by the appropriate government authorities. The proposed perpetual corporate term will also eliminate the need for periodic legislative action solely for the purpose of extending the Corporation’s corporate existence, while preserving the authority of Congress to amend, repeal, or otherwise modify the Corporation’s charter or corporate existence through subsequent legislation. This approach provides greater institutional stability and continuity while maintaining the necessary safeguards to ensure that PITC remains relevant, efficient, financially viable, and responsive to the national interest. Perpetual corporate existence does not preclude the State from undertaking performance evaluation, monitoring, and oversight of the Corporation's relevance, performance, efficiency, and financial viability, nor does it prevent the appropriate government authorities from recommending or undertaking such lawful measures as may be warranted by the results of such evaluation. The continued corporate existence of PITC is therefore intended to prevent disruption in its legal existence and operations and to ensure the orderly continuity of its contracts, obligations, assets, liabilities, and other lawful commitments. It will likewise enable the Corporation to continue performing its existing mandate and contributing, within the scope of its charter, to the promotion and development of Philippine international trade. In view of the foregoing, the immediate enactment of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11187
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES TO APPOINT DISTINGUISHED FOREIGN NATIONALS TO TEACHING AND RESEARCH POSITIONS AND GRANT THEM ACADEMIC TENURE UNDER EXCEPTIONAL CONDITIONS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed bill seeks to strengthen the quality and global competitiveness of Philippine public higher education while preserving the State’s fundamental commitment to the development of Filipino scholars, researchers, and academic leaders. State Universities and Colleges (SUCs) play a vital role in advancing national development through education, research, innovation, and the formation of highly skilled professionals. As the demands of science, technology, and emerging academic disciplines continue to evolve, there may be instances when institutions require expertise that is highly specialized, newly developing, or not yet sufficiently available within the country. In such circumstances, carefully structured engagement with distinguished foreign academics may provide opportunities for collaboration, knowledge exchange, research advancement, and exposure to international standards and practices. The measure is therefore anchored on the principle that the participation of foreign academic experts should be exceptional, complementary, and directed toward strengthening Philippine academic capacity. It does not seek to diminish the role of Filipino faculty. Rather, it recognizes that international academic collaboration can serve as a strategic means of accelerating the development of Filipino scholars and researchers, particularly in fields where expertise is rapidly advancing or where domestic capacity remains in the process of being established. At the same time, the proposed legislation recognizes the constitutional and institutional importance of Filipino participation in government service and public higher education. The engagement of foreign nationals in the academic sector must consequently remain consistent with national sovereignty, public accountability, and the primacy of Filipino academic development. The measure adopts this approach by treating foreign academic expertise not as a substitute for Filipino talent, but as a potential catalyst for building stronger and more sustainable domestic capabilities. The proposed framework is also intended to promote a culture of academic excellence and internationalization within SUCs. Greater interaction with internationally recognized scholars can facilitate meaningful research partnerships, strengthen academic programs, expand opportunities for Filipino faculty and students, and contribute to the development of globally competitive institutions. Such engagement may likewise help Philippine public universities participate more effectively in international research networks and respond to emerging areas of knowledge that are increasingly important to national development. Ultimately, the measure seeks to establish a balanced policy: one that welcomes exceptional international academic expertise when genuinely beneficial to the country, while ensuring that the long-term objective remains the cultivation of world-class Filipino faculty, researchers, and academic leaders. The State’s investment in Filipino higher education must remain central, and any international engagement should contribute to, rather than compete with, that national priority. The proposed Act thus represents an effort to reconcile the constitutional character of public service with the realities of an increasingly interconnected global academic community. By creating a principled framework for exceptional international academic participation, the measure aims to enhance the capacity of Philippine public higher education to generate knowledge, foster innovation, develop Filipino talent, and ultimately contribute to the country's social, scientific, and economic progress. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11188
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL MEDICINE SECURITY FRAMEWORK, STRENGTHENING LOCAL PHARMACEUTICAL MANUFACTURING AS A STRATEGIC INVESTMENT, ENSURING THE QUALITY, SAFETY, AND AFFORDABILITY OF MEDICINES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The COVID-19 pandemic exposed the vulnerability of the Philippine healthcare system to disruptions in global pharmaceutical supply chains. During the initial wave of the pandemic, border closures, export restrictions, and logistical bottlenecks significantly constrained the country’s ability to import essential medicines, placing public health at risk. While existing laws promote access to affordable medicines (e.g. Cheaper Medicines Act), the current regulatory framework relies heavily on administrative issuances of the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to safeguard medicine quality and ensure supply continuity. At the same time, domestic pharmaceutical manufacturers incur substantial fixed costs to comply with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, while import-dependent products may enter the market with uneven quality oversight. This imbalance undermines medicine security, public trust, and long-term industrial resilience. Local pharmaceutical manufacturing occupies a distinct and strategic role in the national health system. Unlike purely distribution-based or import-based models, local manufacturing directly supports medicine security by maintaining domestic production capacity, enabling closer regulatory oversight, sustaining technical and skilled employment, and strengthening the country’s ability to respond to public health emergencies and external supply disruptions. For this reason, local pharmaceutical manufacturing should be recognized not merely as an ordinary commercial activity, but as a strategic capability necessary to safeguard public health and national resilience. This bill seeks to establish a statutory medicine security Framework that balances access, availability, affordability, safety, and quality, while strengthening local pharmaceutical manufacturing as a strategic component of national health security. It does not prohibit imports nor confer automatic incentives. The bill also does not discriminate between multinational and local industry players in the market. Instead, it ensures that all medicines, whether locally produced or imported, are subject to equivalent, science-based quality standards. The measure aligns fully with the CREATE Act, the CREATE MORE Act, and the Strategic Investment Priority Plan by recognizing pharmaceutical manufacturing as a strategic investment activity subject to existing incentive regimes. It further strengthens regulatory enforcement through statutory FDA-BOC coordination, risk-based traceability, and enhanced oversight of online pharmaceutical sales. Ultimately, this bill aims to protect Filipino patients, promote fair competition, and ensure that the availability of affordable medicines is never achieved at the expense of quality, safety, and national resilience. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. label: HB 11189
title: AN ACT EXPRESSLY INCLUDING BAMBOO AS A HIGH-VALUE CROP, RECOGNIZING IT AS AN INDUSTRIAL CROP, AND STRENGTHENING THE IMPLEMENTATION OF THE HIGH- VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT ACT BY INSTITUTIONALIZING THE NATIONAL HIGH- VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT AND BIOECONOMY OFFICE AND THE NATIONAL HIGH-VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT AND BIOECONOMY PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7900, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “HIGH- VALUE CROPS DEVELOPMENT ACT OF 1995”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7900, or the High-Value Crops Development Act of 1995, established the national framework for the production, processing, marketing and distribution of high-value crops. Three decades later, climate change, biotechnology, plant-variety innovation, stricter product standards, supply-chain disruptions and growing demand for renewable and bio- based materials require a more integrated, science-based, market-oriented and institutionally sustained approach. This bill expressly includes bamboo as a high-value crop and recognizes it as a strategic industrial crop. Bamboo can provide food, fiber, biomass, engineered and construction materials, furniture, packaging, bioenergy, biochar, biomaterials and other value- added products. Developed through appropriate agroforestry and multi-storey farming systems, it can diversify rural livelihoods and support climate, soil, water and ecosystem objectives, subject to environmental, biodiversity, land-use, agrarian reform and ancestral- domain laws. The measure establishes within the Department of Agriculture the Office of the Undersecretary for High-Value Crops Development, Innovation and Bioeconomy. The Office shall provide policy guidelines on technology management and innovation, exercise direct oversight over the National High-Value Crops and Bioeconomy Development Program, and supervise the functional roles, mandates and performance of its component offices. Two Assistant Secretaries shall support the Undersecretary. The Assistant Secretary for High-Value Crops Program Management shall coordinate implementation, technical services, farming systems, bamboo and industrial-crop development, agribusiness, processing, standards, investment and markets. The Assistant Secretary for High-Value Crops Knowledge and Agricultural Statistics shall lead the National High-Value Crops Information System, agricultural statistics and data science, knowledge management, market intelligence, geospatial services, monitoring, evaluation and results reporting. The bill further integrates research, innovation, biotechnology, genetic resources, plant-variety development, quality planting materials, climate-resilient production, integrated development areas, processing, enterprise development, financing, standards, trade and agricultural bioeconomy applications. It strengthens the High-Value Crops Development Fund and permits the Department to propose an indicative initial program envelope of Five Hundred Million Pesos for strategic industrial bamboo development, subject to the regular budget process and without creating an automatic appropriation. The proposed structure is designed as an integrating and coordinating mechanism. It preserves the statutory mandates of the Philippine Statistics Authority and other competent regulatory, research, standards, environmental and local-government institutions, while requiring compliance with government-optimization, civil service, position-classification, budgeting, accounting and auditing laws. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this measure is earnestly requested. RUFUS B. RODRIGUEZ MAXIMO B. RODRIGUEZ, JR. label: HB 11190
title: AN ACT CREATING A CONGRESSIONAL COMMISSION ON MOBILITY TO REVIEW, ASSESS, AND EVALUATE THE STATE OF MOBILITY IN THE PHILIPPINES AND RECOMMEND INNOVATIVE AND TARGETED POLICY REFORMS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A country's mobility system is highly indicative of a State's treatment of every citizen's right to experience an improved quality of life and to participate meaningfully in society. The barriers each citizen faces just to get from one place to another reveal not only issues with the transportation system, but also issues concerning public health, economic opportunity, environmental sustainability, and the rights of more vulnerable persons. This is evident in the Philippines’ mobility system, which has been characterized as a "carmageddon" for being extremely congested and almost dehumanizing to the common Filipino.1 Metro Manila, for example, ranked as the most congested metropolitan area in the world in 2023, causing immense economic losses estimated at PHP 3.5 billion per day.2 This crisis is attributed, among others, to a highly car-centric system. Government agencies measure success by the number of roads they widen and the expressways they build. A 2015 technical report of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) showed that 88 percent (88%) of households in Metro 1 Gatarin, G. R., & Andal, A. G. T. (2024). Towards just transitions in cities of the Global South: Civil society and street experiments against the Carmageddon in Metro Manila, Philippines. Journal of Urban Mobility. Retrieved from https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2667091724000050. 2 Romero, A. (5 April 2024). Marcos Jr. wants holistic plan to solve Metro Manila traffic woes. The Philippine Star. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2024/04/05/2345483/marcos-jr-wants-holistic-plan-solve- metro-manila-traffic-woes 1 Manila and the rest of the Greater Manila Area do not own cars, while the remaining 12 percent own at least one. Despite these numbers, infrastructure design and even government funds disproportionately favor this minority. In fact, from 2010 to 2021, road-based public transport and active transport programs received a meager 1% (PHP 40 billion) as opposed to the country's PHP 2.8 trillion road-infrastructure budget.3 What seems to be forgotten is that the vast majority of Filipinos actually rely on public transportation, accounting for approximately 70% of daily trips.4 For them, each day they go to work is marked by a grueling and undignified ordeal consisting of systemic shortages in public transport supply, endless terminal queues, and highly unpredictable travel times. Urgent priority must therefore be given to addressing the myriad issues underlying the country's mobility system. This bill seeks to do exactly this by mandating the creation of the Congressional Commission on Mobility ("MobiComm"), a ten- member bicameral body co-chaired by the Chairpersons of the Senate Committee on Public Services and the House Committee on Transportation. The MobiComm will also establish specialized standing committees to engage resource persons in addressing issues concerning active mobility, public transport, road safety, and universal accessibility. The MobiComm is structured to exist until 2031, with a mandate to submit a mid-term report in 2028 and a final, comprehensive roadmap with key performance indicators at the end of its term to guide future reforms. To ensure that its policy recommendations are evidence-based and community-informed, the bill also creates a Technical Secretariat led by an Executive Director and designates the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) as its primary research arm. Lastly, a ten-member Mobility, Legislation and Policy Advisory Council, which consists of experts from academe, transport cooperatives, LGUs, and civil society, is also created to provide written inputs before any final report can be adopted. Ultimately, this bill is but a first step, albeit a necessary one, to address the longstanding issues that have been plaguing the country's mobility system for decades. label: HB 11192
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING AND REGULATING EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING AND OFF-CAMPUS ACTIVITIES IN BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, ESTABLISHING PROPORTIONATE STANDARDS FOR THEIR APPROVAL, PREPARATION, IMPLEMENTATION AND ASSESSMENT, REGULATING THE COLLECTION OF FEES, PRESCRIBING STANDARDS FOR EDUCATIONAL DESTINATIONS AND SERVICE PROVIDERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education does not take place only inside the classroom. Learners understand history differently when they encounter the places where it happened. Science becomes more concrete when they see it applied. Communities, workplaces, museums, cultural institutions, government offices, farms, laboratories, and other learning environments can help connect classroom instruction with real life. Experiential learning, however, takes many forms. A nearby museum visit is different from a multi-day educational tour. A community immersion is different from participation in a national competition. Senior High School work immersion has purposes and requirements distinct from a commercial tour package. Regulation should recognize these differences. This measure therefore adopts a proportionate approach. Educational field trips and tours involving substantial travel, organized itineraries, tour operators, significant fees, or overnight stays are subject to stricter permit, financial, destination, and safety requirements. Site-based experiential learning activities are subject to a simplified approval process, unless their cost, distance, duration, or risk warrants higher review. Competitions and work exposure or immersion remain principally governed by their respective program rules, while being subject to the minimum learner-protection standards of this Act. At the heart of every activity must be a genuine educational purpose. An activity should begin with clear learning objectives, be implemented with proper supervision and safeguards, and end with reflection and assessment. An educational tour should not simply be a recreational trip given an educational label. The measure likewise allows schools to collect reasonable fees for approved activities, while requiring transparency, affordability, proper accounting, and protection against commissions, markups, and other personal benefit. For public schools, approved expenses may also be supported from the Special Education Fund, subject to the approval of the Local School Board and applicable budgeting and auditing rules. Finally, the bill establishes clear standards for destinations and service providers. Commercial tourism enterprises must possess the appropriate government accreditation, while historical, cultural, scientific, environmental, workplace, and similar learning sites must be duly recognized, licensed, or authorized by the competent government agency. Theme parks, amusement parks, water parks, resorts primarily intended for recreation, gaming establishments, and similar entertainment venues are expressly excluded as educational destinations. 2 Experiential learning should open the world to the learner. But every activity undertaken in the name of education must remain, first and foremost, educational, safe, accessible, and worthy of the trust placed in our schools. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 11193
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE COVERAGE AND STRENGTHENING THE ENFORCEMENT OF THE PROHIBITION AGAINST THE “NO PERMIT, NO EXAM” POLICY IN ALL EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11984, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “NO PERMIT, NO EXAM PROHIBITION ACT,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution provides that "The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all." A student who is turned away from an examination hall because of an unpaid balance has been denied that access at the very moment it matters most. The country took an important first step with the enactment of Republic Act No. 11984, the “No Permit, No Exam Prohibition Act,” on 11 March 2024. That law mandates public and private educational institutions to allow a student to sit the scheduled periodic and final examinations without a permit despite unpaid tuition and other school fees. Its passage settled the principle. What remains is to make the remedy reach the students who need it. Republic Act No. 11984, as presently written, protects only a “Disadvantaged Student,” and conditions that protection on a certification issued by a local or regional social welfare and development officer on the ground of calamities, emergencies, force majeure, and other valid or justifiable reasons. This bill amends Republic Act No. 11984 to close the gaps within RA 11984. It makes the right to sit an examination universal and unconditional, so that no certification of any kind is required to claim it. It prohibits the examination permit requirement outright. It extends coverage to every technical-vocational program regardless of duration. It caps the down payment that may be required upon enrollment at thirty percent (30%) of total fees. It prohibits the public disclosure or posting of a student’s unpaid account. It replaces the denial of re-enrollment with a structured payment agreement. It guarantees the release of records and credentials where these are needed for employment, for a licensure or civil service examination, or for transfer. And it provides graduated administrative sanctions together with a complaint mechanism that carries fixed periods for action, including provisional relief allowing a student to sit the examination while a complaint is pending. The legitimate interest of educational institutions in collecting what is due them is fully preserved, and in one respect improved. Schools may still require a promissory note or a structured payment agreement, still withhold the release of grades, records, and credentials subject to the narrow exceptions this Act provides, and still pursue every legal and administrative remedy for collection. What they may no longer do is interrupt a student’s education as a collection device. Students who are refused admission to their examinations are exposed to public humiliation before their classmates and are placed at markedly higher risk of dropping out altogether. The burden falls hardest on those least able to bear it. This is a harm the State can end at no cost to the public treasury and at no real cost to the schools. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11194
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN ONLINE NATIONAL REGISTRY OF SKILLED WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The role of labor as a primary social force is affirmed by the State in no less than the 1987 Constitution. In the same article, the State commits itself to the protection of workers and protection of their welfare.1 Article XIII, Section 3 also imposes on the State the duty to afford full protection to labor, local and overseas, organized and unorganized, and promote full employment and equality of employment opportunities for all. This bill seeks to link skilled workers with employers by establishing an online national registry of skilled workers. The online registry shall be made available to prospective employers and shall contain all relevant details to allow the employer to contact the skilled workers but shall be subjected to safeguard measures to protect the privacy of the skilled workers as well. Under Article XIII, Section 2 of the 1987 Constitution, the State’s policy in the promotion of social justice shall include the commitment to create economic opportunities based on freedom of initiative and self-reliance. This measure is envisioned to promote the employment of skilled workers in furtherance of the State’s efforts to reduce property and improve the lives of Filipinos. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11195
title: AN ACT MANDATING ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE PRIMARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS TO INCLUDE MEDIA AND INFORMATION EDUCATION, INCLUDING THE RESPONSIBLE USE OF THE INTERNET, IN THEIR CURRICULUM, FOR OTHER PURPOSES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The State, under Article II, Section 24 of the 1987 Constitution, “recognizes the vital role of communication and information in nation- building.” Meanwhile, under Section 17 of the same Article, the State vows to prioritize education and science and technology, “to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development.” Connecting these two provisions is Article XIII, Section 2(1), under which the State is mandated to “[e]stablish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” One application of this is the attention given to deepening our understanding of the different types of literacy that we have to help our students develop. Per Literacy Statistics, Functional Literacy, Education and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS) of 2024, 90.0 percent of Filipinos were literate,1 a decrease from 96.5 percent in the same survey conducted in 2013. 2 In an era of rapid technological change and mediated communication, and where Filipinos have wholeheartedly embraced such technologies, we must also be cognizant of the risks and dangers such technologies present. Enter the establishment of Media and Information Education as a necessary component of our primary and secondary curricula:3 1 Philippine Statistics Authority, “Basic and Functional Literacy Rates were Higher among those Who Reached at Least High School Level Education,” 27 May 2025, available at: https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/education-mass-media/node/1684076282 2 PIA, “Literacy in the age of social media,” October 10, 2018, available at https://pia.gov.ph/news/articles/1013738. 3 Center for Media Freedom and Responsibility, “Why Media Literacy?,” available at https://cmfr-phil.org/media-literacy/what-is-media- literacy/?__cf_chl_jschl_tk__=135143fb5a99b5473da3e051c737775f9e1e7cc2-1600011205- 0-AQHnaiCBz9CKk5PbXnuCzwQstadSbf03EzCL-praC3mNK2ePLQIJPp1oxjBipp- TSOErI2doeYCkh_A56D6kvf8HixUyPhrEornySS8vsUL8eRQp7Ntb6UkDmU0lXeBJwsCu1gQ Media literacy, declares the National Association for Media Literacy Education (NAMLE), “represents a necessary, inevitable, and realistic response (underscoring ours) to the complex, ever- changing” electronic and communication environment that has become part of the lives of millions all over the planet. Responsible citizenship requires citizens in a democracy not only to access but also to understand and to be critical of the billions of words, bytes and images—the totality of information—that the media disseminate daily through print, broadcast, moving pictures, and the Internet. The interactivity made possible by the new electronic media has made this an even more crucial imperative not only for responsible citizenship and responsible communication, but also for the development of every human being in society. “Today’s information and entertainment technologies,” continues NAMLE, “communicate to us through a powerful combination of words, images, and sounds. As such, we need to develop a wider set of literacy skills helping us to both comprehend the messages we receive and effectively utilize these tools to design and distribute our own messages.” Being media literate thus “requires critical thinking skills that empower us as we make decisions, whether in the classroom, the living room, the workplace, the boardroom, or the voting booth.” However, media literacy enables the individual not only to be critical of the media but also to create messages appropriate to each medium. In the Philippine context, media literacy is also a long-term solution to the many problems and issues that afflict the Philippine media, in that a media literate public aware of the role, values and standards of the media can demand that the media adhere to their own standards as a necessary condition to improving their capacity to provide the public the information it needs. These standards the media themselves disseminate through codes of ethics and professional guidelines with which media organizations encourage compliance. These standards are meant to assure that media practitioners—who today include ordinary citizens who access the Internet and its various platforms of expression to make their views known on various matters XR58YGghZcbtGW4- RmJ3hedgwdZe62MKnBlBaDe4CjFsgUGoNQRgltyVOjFDFUyUtAHSUEhgBLthMcVHEBNhJy hRPcPGIr-jbcWd5MJ7c6F1dVaZb628UI-E7HoY7LQAI1CyiRq2oQbP2g01sC- rlOQJqxb79PlMsnfsnSe3YS2uk3OsCNqS4isMcPQ. including issues and events of public concern—are able to provide accurate, relevant, and fair reports, analysis and opinion to the billions of individuals who read newspapers, listen to the radio, view television and motion pictures, and access the Internet. This bill is offered as a way to give students a responsive and structured way to hone their Media and Information Literacy. This Bill aims to ensure that all students in Grades 1 to 12 shall receive sufficient instruction in this field, to equip them with the skills and understanding that they will need to (1) protect themselves, their community, and by extension, the nation, from fake news and (2) contribute to the enrichment of knowledgeable/informed discussion online, especially on national issues, as responsible citizens. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11196
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE EMPLOYMENT OF NATIONAL ATHLETES AND COACHES AS REGULAR EMPLOYEES OF THE GOVERNMENT THEREBY SECURING THEIR SALARIES AND BENEFITS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The country's national athletes are our modern-day heroes. They dedicate years of blood, sweat, and tears in honing their craft and skills. They bring honor, glory, and prestige every time they represent the country in international competitions. Excellence in sports requires not only physical aptitude but more importantly, mental, and emotional fortitude. But how can we expect our national athletes to focus on their training if they still must worry if they will be able to financially sustain themselves and their families? The 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall give priority to education, science and technology, arts, culture, and sports to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development.1 It further provides that the State shall promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports, including training for international competitions, to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence for the development of a healthy and alert citizenry.2 The government tries its best to perform its mandate under the Constitution, encouraging participation in sports through the provision of support and assistance to our national athletes. Although the current system has provided them with allowance, this mechanism is still not sufficient and is haunted by uncertainties. In one such instance, the allowances of national athletes were reduced to half for a period of time during the onset of the COVID- 19 Pandemic because of a lack of available funds.3 Many athletes rely on the allowance to support not only themselves but also their families. After all, their training demands time and effort and they can no longer have a separate full- 1 1987 CONST. Art. II, Sec. 17. 2 1987 CONST. Art. XIV, Sec. 19 (1). 3 Pigeon Lobien. “Cordillera athletes tighten belt as allowance cut to half”. Philippine News Agency. (June 9, 2020). https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1105327 time occupation. Their sport is their profession. The better supported they are, the better they can excell at their chosen sport. To respond to these realities, this bill is proposed to provide an opportunity for national athletes and coaches to be regularized employees of the government thereby securing their benefits and remuneration. Their dedication to fight for the flag and the country is their service to our nation. In exchange for their services, this bill proposes the following: 1. Regularization of National Athletes and Coaches. – subject to certain qualifications, national athletes and coaches shall have the option to be employed as regular employees by the government. They shall receive all benefits entitled to regular employees in the civil service. To this extent, they will have the security of their benefits since the funding will be a regular part of the general appropriations of the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) and will no longer depend on the revenue from the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (PAGCOR). The proposed salary grades for the positions of national athletes and coaches are determined ensuring that mandatory deductions for contributions will not reduce their net income to less than the current allowance that they are receiving. 2. Membership in the Government Service Insurance System (GSIS). – Being employees of the government, national athletes and coaches will be eligible to become members of the GSIS. This will allow them to receive a higher pension upon their retirement. 3. Priority Athlete Benefit. – National athletes employed as regular employees who garnered medals during international competitions shall be entitled to an additional allowance of three thousand pesos (Php 20,000.00) per month for a period of twelve (12) months. This measure aims to dignify our national athletes and coaches. This is to inform them that their dedication and services to our country are always deeply appreciated. This bill is also named in honor of “Asia's fastest woman of the 1980s”, Lydia De Vega, who has brought glory and prestige to our country in the sport of track and field. She succumbed in her battle against cancer on August 10, 2022. We commemorate her memory and legacy in the hopes that she will inspire the younger generation to strive for excellence. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11202
title: AN ACT ENHANCING THE PROTECTION AND DEVELOPMENT OF THE SIERRA MADRE RANGE IN THE ISLAND OF LUZON, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE SIERRA MADRE CONSERVATION AND DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Sierra Madre Mountain Range, known as the "Backbone of Luzon," rising to 6,283 feet and spanning over 540 kilometers, serves as the country’s longest mountain range and a natural shield against typhoons entering the Pacific side. Aside from its role as a natural typhoon barrier, the Sierra Madre Mountain Range is home to around 40 percent of the Philippines’ forest cover and supports rich biodiversity, including approximately 3,500 plant species, 58 percent of which are endemic and serves as a crucial carbon sink, with forested areas covering approximately 1.4 million hectares. 1 Despite its ecological importance, the Sierra Madre Mountain Range is threatened by illegal logging, mining, unregulated land conversion, and deforestation. Existing conservation efforts remain disconnected due to jurisdictional overlaps among local government units (LGUs) and various national agencies. This bill seeks to create the Sierra Madre Conservation and Development Authority (SMCDA) to establish a unified, centralized, and dedicated governing body tasked with the holistic management, protection, restoration, and sustainable development of the Sierra Madre region. Specifically, the creation of the Sierra Madre Conservation and Development Authority (SMCDA), an administrative body, shall formulate, coordinate, and execute a comprehensive conservation 1 Climate Change Commission. September 26.2024. Sierra Madre: Mountain Range for Resilience. https://www.climate.gov.ph/news/934 1 and master development plan for the Sierra Madre region, covering the Sierra Madre Range and its surrounding areas encompassing the provinces of Cagayan, Isabela, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Nueva Ecija, Aurora, Bulacan, Rizal, Laguna, and Quezon. Also, the SMCDA shall be mandated to conduct intensive forest protection, ecosystem restoration, and engagement in agricultural, industrial, or other activities contributing directly to the socio-economic development of the Region. Furthermore, it shall require the cities and municipalities in the Region to pass appropriate zoning ordinances and other regulatory measures necessary to carry out the Authority’s objectives. In view of the urgent necessity to protect and preserve our primary natural shield against climate disasters, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 11203
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING SAFETY STANDARDS AND REGULATORY MEASURES FOR CHILDREN’S USE OF SOCIAL MEDIA AND PROMOTING RESPONSIBLE DIGITAL ENGAGEMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Social media has become an important part of children's daily lives. While it provides opportunities for communication, learning, and self- expression, children may also be exposed to harmful content, unsafe interactions, exploitation, and excessive or unhealthy use. Children need stronger protection in the digital environment. The State must ensure that social media platforms adopt safeguards appropriate to a child's age and development, while respecting children's rights to privacy, access to information, and freedom of expression. This measure establishes clear standards for children's access to social media. It prohibits children below thirteen (13) years of age from creating or maintaining social media accounts and requires parental or guardian consent and supervision for users aged thirteen (13) to below eighteen (18). It likewise requires platforms to implement age verification, privacy and safety measures, parental controls, content safeguards, and accessible reporting mechanisms. The measure also promotes transparency in the use of algorithms, strengthens protection against harmful and misleading content, and provides for digital literacy and responsible social media use in schools. It further encourages communities to provide meaningful activities that promote healthy interaction beyond the digital environment. Protecting children online is a shared responsibility. label: HB 11204
title: AN ACT REQUIRING FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS TO SERVE HALF-CUP RICE SERVINGS, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATION THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Rice is a staple in the Filipino diet and an important component of daily meals. However, unnecessary rice wastage remains a concern, particularly when consumers are served portions that exceed their needs. One practical way to address this concern is to give consumers greater flexibility in the amount of rice they purchase and consume. This measure seeks to require food establishments to offer half-cup rice servings as an option, allowing consumers to choose a portion that better corresponds to their needs and reducing the likelihood of excess rice being left uneaten. By promoting appropriate portion sizes and responsible consumption, this measure seeks to reduce avoidable rice wastage, conserve valuable food resources, and encourage more sustainable consumption practices. It likewise provides consumers with a more affordable option when a full cup of rice is more than they require. In light of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T.
