label: HB 11209
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE MINIMUM SALARIES OF PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS TO P50,000 AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The amendments to the Salary Standardization Law in 2020 and 2024 were meant to uplift government workers, but the truth is that public school teachers still live on salaries that cannot sustain a decent life for their families. The imbalance between the pay of rank-and-file employees and that of top officials is stark and unjust. A Teacher I, earning ₱30,024 monthly, falls short of the family living wage of ₱36,510 for a household of five. This is not just about figures—it is about the daily reality of teachers who, despite years of training and professional qualifications, struggle to provide food, shelter, and education for their own children. Meanwhile, officials in the highest salary grades earn hundreds of thousands of pesos monthly, and uniformed personnel have already benefited from substantial increases, leaving teachers behind despite their equally vital role in nation-building. According to the Department of Budget and Management and the Department of Education (2022 Manpower Information System), about 803,272 teachers occupy positions from Teacher I to Teacher III. These educators, who carry the weight of the country’s education system, continue to earn salaries that are insufficient to meet the rising cost of living. In contrast, top officials in Salary Grades 31 to 33 earn between ₱293,191 and ₱438,844 monthly. Even after the last tranche of SSL V and the 2025 installment of SSL VI, teachers remain disadvantaged compared to military and uniformed personnel whose salaries were doubled under the Duterte administration. Teachers, despite their higher qualifications, were granted increases of only 4.95% to 5.6%—a small adjustment that is quickly consumed by inflation, excise taxes under the TRAIN Law, and income taxes that reduce their take-home pay. The economic pressures faced by teachers are severe. Inflation steadily widens the gap between their salaries and the family living wage, while the COVID-19 pandemic and the international oil crisis have worsened their financial struggles. The Philippine Statistics Authority reported that in May 2025, the consumer price index in the National Capital Region reached 123.9. This means that what ₱100 could buy in 2018 now costs ₱123.90. In real terms, a basket of goods that once filled a household pantry seven years ago now barely covers half of it. For teachers earning ₱30,024 monthly, the rising costs of fuel and basic commodities make it nearly impossible to sustain their families. It is no surprise that many choose to work abroad, where they can earn three to eight times more than their current salaries, despite the risks and hardships. This bill seeks to provide substantial salary increases for public school teachers to bridge the gap between their current pay and the actual cost of living. It also mandates annual adjustments to ensure that salaries keep pace with inflation and addresses the distortion created by the disproportionate increases granted to military and uniformed personnel. The Department of Budget and Management, in consultation with public sector unions, will be tasked to recommend to Congress the appropriation of the necessary funds. Passing this measure transcends the issue of wages; it is a matter of fairness, dignity, and justice. Teachers constitute the backbone of our education system, and their invaluable service must be recognized not merely through rhetoric but through decisive action. Any delay in the enactment of this measure is tantamount to denying them the dignity they rightfully deserve and to undermining the very foundation of our nation’s future. Educators have long expressed apprehension that the final adjustment under the Salary Standardization Law will once again replicate the inequitable pattern of past amendments—granting meager increases to rank-and-file employees while leaving them behind for extended periods without meaningful adjustments. This proposed legislation seeks to break that cycle and to ensure that teachers, together with other government employees, are accorded just and equitable compensation, thereby affirming their indispensable role in nation-building. For the foregoing reasons, the passage of this bill is sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11210
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Personnel Economic Relief Allowance (PERA) was first granted in 1991 at ₱500 per month. In 2009, through Joint Resolution No. 4 of the Senate and the House of Representatives, the ₱1,500 Additional Compensation and the ₱500 PERA were consolidated into a fixed monthly allowance of ₱2,000 for all government employees. Since then, no further increase has been legislated. For more than sixteen years, this allowance has remained stagnant despite the undeniable rise in the cost of living. PERA was intended to provide modest relief to public servants against inflation and the increasing prices of basic goods and services. However, its current level has long ceased to fulfill its purpose. The erosion of purchasing power has left government employees—particularly those in the lower and middle income brackets—struggling to meet the daily needs of their families. The situation has grown heavier because of the lasting effects of the COVID-19 pandemic, the unstable rise and fall of fuel and petroleum prices, the pressure brought by tax reforms like the TRAIN Law, and the unrest in West Asia. Together, these forces have placed a greater burden on ordinary families, including those of our civil servants, making daily life harder and more uncertain. It is a fundamental duty of the State to ensure that the men and women who keep the machinery of government running are afforded fair and reasonable compensation. Public service requires sacrifice, but it should not demand that our employees endure economic hardship without adequate support. By increasing the PERA to ₱5,000 per month, this measure seeks to restore fairness, provide genuine relief, and recognize the indispensable role of government employees in nation-building For the foregoing reasons, the passage of this bill is sought. label: HB 11211
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SUPPORT MECHANISMS FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL IN MATTERS OF STUDENT DISCIPLINE AND MECHANISMS FOR CLASSROOM MANAGEMENT AND PROVIDING FOR THEIR PROTECTION IN CASES RELATED THERETO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 2(1) of the 1987 Philippine Constitution affirms the State’s duty to “establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” This constitutional mandate recognizes education not merely as the transmission of knowledge, but as a fundamental institution in the development of responsible and productive citizens. For a substantial part of their formative years, children are immersed in the school environment under the care, supervision, and guidance of teachers and other school personnel. The experiences they gain, the lessons they learn, and the values they develop during their time in school significantly contribute to shaping their future. Schools consequently serve as an extension of the home, providing an environment where students are guided toward becoming responsible, capable, and socially conscious members of the community. Teachers and other school personnel who interact directly with students assume responsibilities that go beyond academic instruction. In many respects, they serve in the capacity of second parents by helping students develop not only the knowledge and skills necessary for their future endeavors, but also the discipline, values, and character needed to become responsible Filipino citizens. Such responsibility necessarily includes the proper management of student behavior. As partners of parents and guardians in raising children, school personnel cannot be expected to remain passive when students engage in misconduct or violate established school rules. Teachers, in particular, have the dual responsibility of educating students and preparing them to become respectful, responsible, and law-abiding members of society. This includes the authority, subject to applicable laws and regulations, to impose appropriate disciplinary measures when students violate school policies or exhibit improper conduct. Disciplinary interventions are intended not merely as punishment, but as opportunities for students to understand the consequences of their actions, correct inappropriate behavior, and develop respect for others. This is particularly important in instances involving disrespect toward teachers, school personnel, visitors, or fellow students. The ability of teachers to effectively manage their classrooms and address misconduct is therefore an essential component of maintaining a safe, orderly, and productive learning environment. The legal foundation for this responsibility may be found in the doctrine of in loco parentis. Article 218 of the Family Code recognizes the special parental authority and responsibility of schools, administrators, teachers, and other institutions engaged in child care over minors while they are under their supervision, instruction, or custody. Similarly, Article 349 of the Civil Code recognizes teachers and professors among those who exercise substitute parental authority. These provisions demonstrate that the law recognizes the legitimate role of educators in supervising students and promoting proper conduct within the school environment and during school-sanctioned activities. The law likewise imposes responsibilities upon school personnel. Article 2180 of the Civil Code provides for liability in certain circumstances for damages caused by pupils, students, or apprentices while under the custody of teachers or educational institutions. In light of these responsibilities, teachers and school personnel must also be afforded reasonable protection when they exercise their lawful authority and perform their duties in good faith. They should not be placed in a situation where fear of unfounded complaints or punitive consequences prevents them from addressing student misconduct appropriately. The rapid growth of technology and social media has further complicated this concern. Allegations involving teachers and school personnel can now be disseminated to a wide audience almost instantaneously, often before the facts have been properly established. False, malicious, or misleading accusations can subject educators to public humiliation, online harassment, and reputational damage. Even when an allegation is subsequently proven unfounded, the damage to an educator’s professional standing and personal reputation may already be difficult to reverse. These circumstances highlight the need for safeguards that protect both the rights of students and the legitimate authority of educators. Teachers should be able to perform their responsibilities as educators and persons exercising special parental authority without being unduly exposed to malicious attacks simply for carrying out their lawful duties. At the same time, mechanisms must remain in place to ensure that legitimate complaints involving abuse, misconduct, or violations of students’ rights are properly investigated and resolved. This measure therefore seeks to provide appropriate protection to teachers and other school personnel against demonstrably false and malicious accusations that may undermine the teaching process, disrupt the learning environment, and cause lasting harm to their professional reputation. An allegation, even when eventually disproven, may continue to circulate online and remain accessible long after the person concerned has been cleared. Such circumstances can have consequences that extend beyond the resolution of the complaint itself, including damage to one’s career, credibility, and standing in the community. The protection of children and the preservation of their rights must remain paramount. However, such protection should be balanced with the equally important right of teachers and school personnel to due process and protection from malicious or demonstrably false imputations. label: HB 11212
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING JOB PLACEMENT OFFICES IN ALL PUBLIC SENIOR HIGH SCHOOLS, STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND LOCAL UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES, AND CREATING A NATIONAL INDUSTRY-ACADEME COUNCIL AND LOCAL INDUSTRY-ACADEME COUNCILS TO ADDRESS JOB-SKILLS MISMATCH AND PROMOTE DECENT EMPLOYMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The enactment of the law guaranteeing universal access to quality tertiary education represented a significant step toward making higher education more accessible to every Filipino. However, expanding access to colleges and universities is only part of the challenge. For many graduates, the transition from education to stable and meaningful employment remains difficult and uncertain. Each year, thousands of Filipinos enter the workforce with academic qualifications but encounter difficulty securing jobs that correspond to their education and training. Meanwhile, industries continue to face challenges in finding workers who possess the competencies required by available positions. This continuing disconnect between what education provides and what the labor market demands diminishes the value of our investments in human capital and limits the economic opportunities available to our young people. The Education-to-Employment Pathways Act of 2025 seeks to address this gap by strengthening the link between education and employment. It advances a system in which learners are provided with the information, guidance, skills, and institutional support necessary to move from the classroom into decent, productive, and sustainable work. To achieve this objective, the measure establishes key mechanisms that will strengthen the education-to-employment pathway: 1. Establishment of Job Placement Offices (JPOs). - Job Placement Offices shall be established in all public senior high schools, state universities and colleges (SUCs), and local universities and colleges (LUCs). These offices shall assist learners in making informed career decisions and transitioning into the workforce through career guidance, job matching, employer linkages, soft skills development, and entrepreneurship support. 2. Creation of the Philippine Labor Market Information System (PhilLMIS). - A comprehensive and integrated labor market information system shall be established under the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE). The PhilLMIS shall function as the government's central platform for labor market intelligence, occupational forecasting, skills mapping, and evidence-based policy development. Its information shall support decision- making in education, workforce development, employment, and economic planning. 3. Strengthening of the Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF) and institutionalization of the Philippine Skills Framework (PSF). - The bill reinforces the PQF as the national reference for classifying and recognizing qualifications while formalizing the PSF as a framework for identifying job-specific competencies. Together, these frameworks shall support curriculum alignment, certification, skills recognition, and more effective job matching. They shall be digitally integrated, regularly maintained in coordination with industry stakeholders, and promoted for nationwide adoption. Taken as a whole, these measures seek to ensure that education does not end with the attainment of a diploma but leads to concrete opportunities for employment, professional growth, dignity, and economic mobility. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11213
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE PROFESSIONAL STANDARDS AND QUALITY ASSURANCE SYSTEM
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education is the great equalizer of our nation. It is the promise that every Filipino child, regardless of background, can rise to a life of dignity and opportunity. Yet for too long, this promise has been weakened by a fragmented system where the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and the Professional Regulation Commission (PRC) operate in silos, with overlapping mandates and misaligned standards. The result has been confusion for learners, inefficiency for institutions, and lost opportunities for workers and professionals who strive to compete in an increasingly globalized world. This measure, the Philippine Professional Standards and Quality Assurance System Act of 2025, seeks to transform that reality. By establishing the Board of Curriculum Standards and the Skills and Standards Harmonization Councils, the Act envisions a unified system where education, training, and professional regulation are seamlessly integrated. It is a vision of a country where every student’s effort, every worker’s skill, and every professional’s qualification is recognized, valued, and aligned with both national priorities and international benchmarks. Through this Philippine Professional Standards and Quality Assurance System, CHED shall be empowered to harmonize higher education programs with the needs of industry and the standards of professional practice. TESDA shall continue to strengthen technical-vocational training, opening pathways for lifelong learning and workforce mobility. Together, these institutions will no longer work in isolation, but in unity, building bridges instead of barriers for Filipino learners and professionals. This proposed measure to strengthen the foundations upon which parents may entrust their children’s future, workers may claim dignity in their labor, and professionals may uphold excellence and integrity in the global arena. This proposed measure affirms that the State must not only provide access to learning, but must also guarantee that such access leads to empowerment, productivity, and progress for every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11214
title: AN ACT MODERNIZING THE TECHNICAL EDUCATION AND SKILLS DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY (TESDA), AMENDING AND REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7796, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "TESDA ACT OF 1994," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) plays a critical role in preparing Filipinos for employment, entrepreneurship, and lifelong learning by providing opportunities to acquire practical and industry-relevant skills. As the Philippine economy continues to evolve, however, the nature of work, the technologies used in various industries, and the competencies required of workers are likewise changing at an unprecedented pace. These developments call for a modern, responsive, and forward-looking technical education and skills development system capable of keeping pace with the needs of both Filipino workers and the industries that employ them. The TESDA Modernization Act of 2026 is therefore necessary to strengthen the country's technical education and skills development framework and ensure that it remains relevant to the realities of a rapidly changing labor market. While the Philippines has made significant progress in expanding access to technical-vocational education and training, continuing challenges remain in ensuring that training programs are sufficiently responsive to emerging industries, technological change, regional labor market needs, and the evolving expectations of employers. There is a need to move beyond simply increasing access to training and to place greater emphasis on quality, relevance, employability, mobility, and lifelong skills development. A modern technical education system must be closely connected to the actual world of work. Employers and industries are not merely beneficiaries of a skilled workforce; they are essential partners in identifying the competencies that workers need, shaping training standards, and providing meaningful opportunities for practical learning. Strengthening collaboration among government, industry, labor, educational institutions, and local governments will help ensure that skills development is driven by actual economic and employment opportunities rather than by training supply alone. The proposed measure also recognizes that Filipinos acquire knowledge and skills through different pathways. Formal education is only one avenue for learning. Work experience, apprenticeships, community-based training, enterprise-based learning, and other forms of skills development can likewise produce valuable competencies. A more flexible and integrated system can provide workers and learners with opportunities to have their skills recognized, upgraded, and further developed, while allowing them to move more easily between technical-vocational education and higher education. Equally important is the need to make skills development more accessible and responsive to communities and regions. The country's labor market is diverse, with different localities having distinct economic activities, industries, and workforce requirements. A strengthened partnership with local governments and private-sector institutions can bring training opportunities closer to communities and allow skills development programs to respond more effectively to local needs, including those of marginalized and underserved learners. Modernization must likewise be supported by stronger institutional capacity, effective quality assurance, adequate investment, research and innovation, competent trainers, and sustainable financing. TESDA must be equipped to anticipate future workforce requirements, continuously improve training systems, and support the development of internationally competitive Filipino workers. At the same time, mechanisms for accountability and periodic assessment are essential to ensure that reforms remain responsive to national development priorities. Ultimately, the proposed TESDA Modernization Act of 2026 seeks to ensure that technical education and skills development remains a powerful instrument for inclusive economic growth, decent employment, productivity, and national competitiveness. By strengthening the country's capacity to develop a quality-assured and future-ready workforce, the measure will help Filipino workers adapt to changing opportunities, enable industries to access the skills they require, and contribute to a more resilient and competitive Philippine economy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11215
title: AN ACT FURTHER STRENGTHENING THE INCENTIVES FOR PRIVATE SECTOR PARTICIPATION IN PUBLIC EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS BY AMENDING CERTAIN PROVISIONS IN REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8525, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "ADOPT-A-SCHOOL ACT OF 1998"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education plays an important role in preparing Filipino learners for further education, employment, and participation in society. While the government continues to provide the necessary support for public education, partnerships with the private sector can provide additional resources, expertise, and opportunities that complement existing government efforts. Republic Act No. 8525, otherwise known as the “Adopt-a-School Act of 1998,” established a framework for such partnerships. With the changing needs of learners and educational institutions, there is an opportunity to further strengthen and update the program. The continuing demand for additional educational resources highlights the value of sustained cooperation between the public and private sectors. As of June 2026, the Department of Education reported an estimated nationwide classroom backlog of 143,543 classrooms, underscoring the continuing need to expand and improve learning spaces. 1At the same time, recent assessments by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) found that approximately one in two learners from Grades 1 to 10 remained below grade-level reading proficiency by the end of School Year 2025–2026.2 These conditions highlight opportunities for additional partnerships in areas such as school facilities, learning resources, teacher development, and learner support. This measure seeks to enhance the Adopt-a-School Program by expanding the forms of assistance that private individuals and entities may provide to educational institutions. These may include teacher and personnel development, scholarships, school facilities, learning materials and technologies, technical-vocational equipment, health and nutrition support, and assistive learning devices for learners with disabilities. The expanded areas of assistance are intended to give participating institutions greater flexibility in addressing their particular educational needs. The measure also recognizes the importance of strengthening the connection between education and employment. The National Education and Workforce Development Plan 2026–2035 reports baseline employment rates of 60% among higher education graduates and 70% among TVET graduates.3 The Plan also notes that approximately 20% of Senior High School graduates entered the labor force in 2025, while more than 70% proceeded to further education.³ These figures 1 https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/07/26/2544741/classroom-shortage-down-143543-deped 2 Improvements seen, but half of learners still below grade level in literacy - EDCOM 2 3 https://edcom2.gov.ph/media/2026/01/EDCOM-II_Y03_National-Education-Plan.pdf demonstrate the value of closer cooperation between educational institutions and industries in providing learners with relevant training, certifications, and opportunities as they transition from school to employment or further education. The measure further provides incentives for qualified expenses related to scholarships, training, and other forms of assistance under the Adopt-a-School Program. It also provides appropriate exemptions from customs duties, taxes, and other fees for qualified donations. These measures are intended to encourage sustained participation while ensuring that assistance is directed toward legitimate educational purposes. The bill also strengthens coordination among the Department of Education, Commission on Higher Education, Technical Education and Skills Development Authority, Department of Trade and Industry, Department of Labor and Employment, and other relevant agencies. Through closer coordination, the implementation of the program can be better aligned with the needs of educational institutions, learners, and participating private-sector partners. Overall, this measure seeks to build on the existing framework of the Adopt-a-School Program by encouraging more meaningful and sustained partnerships in education. By bringing together the resources, expertise, and opportunities of the public and private sectors, the program can provide additional support to educational institutions, strengthen learning and training opportunities, and help learners gain access to the facilities, skills, and employment opportunities they need to pursue their goals. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. . ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11216
title: AN ACT CREATING AN INDEPENDENT PEOPLE'S COMMISSION TO INVESTIGATE ANOMALIES IN ALL GOVERNMENT INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine higher education system has expanded significantly, yet persistent challenges remain in access, quality, institutional capacity, and the alignment of graduates' competencies with the needs of the labor market. The Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II) reported that only 34.89% of Filipinos participate in higher education, below the ASEAN average of 41.10%. It likewise identified continuing concerns on graduate underemployment and skills mismatch, including the finding that approximately 24% of specialized graduates work in industries unrelated to their field of study. 1 These challenges demonstrate the need to strengthen higher education not only as a pathway to employment, but also as a driver of research, innovation, and national development. As industries and technologies continue to change, higher education institutions must be given greater capacity to develop programs responsive to emerging skills and regional development needs. The Philippine Statistics Authority's Jobs and Skills Survey similarly recognizes the need to better understand skills gaps, technological changes, and emerging labor market requirements.2 The proposed measure also strengthens pathways between higher education and technical-vocational education and training through ladderized education, micro-credentials, associate degrees, diplomas, and other flexible learning pathways. These mechanisms can provide learners and workers with alternative routes toward employment, further education, and professional advancement while supporting the implementation of the Philippine Qualifications Framework. Ultimately, this aims to ensure that higher education institutions are not merely producers of credentials, but active contributors to a skilled workforce, a stronger research ecosystem, and inclusive national development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11217
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS MANDATE, POWERS, AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine education system stands at a critical juncture. Despite significant investments and continuing efforts by the government, persistent challenges in learning outcomes, teacher development, workforce preparation, access, and the transition of learners across different levels of education continue to affect the country’s capacity to develop a highly capable and productive citizenry. These challenges are complex and interconnected, requiring not only reforms within individual agencies but also stronger and more sustained coordination across the entire education and workforce development system. At present, education and workforce development concerns are addressed by several government institutions, each with distinct mandates, programs, priorities, and resources. While such specialization is necessary, the absence of a permanent, high-level mechanism that can consistently bring these efforts together may result in fragmented policies, overlapping initiatives, gaps in implementation, and difficulties in sustaining reforms. Changes in administration may likewise affect the continuity of priorities and programs, making it more difficult to pursue long- term reforms whose benefits may only become evident over many years. The passage of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) Act is therefore necessary to establish a durable institutional mechanism for coordination, policy coherence, and accountability in the education and workforce development sector. The proposed measure recognizes that improving education outcomes cannot be achieved through isolated interventions. It requires a whole-of-government approach in which agencies work toward common goals, share information, align resources, and collectively address problems that extend across basic education, higher education, technical and vocational education, employment, science and technology, and national development planning. The proposed Council is intended to strengthen the continuity and coherence of education reforms by providing a permanent platform for collaboration at the highest levels of government. This is particularly important in addressing the learning crisis and ensuring that reforms are not dependent solely on the priorities or organizational arrangements of a particular administration. Institutionalizing coordination can help ensure that important reforms are sustained, evaluated, improved, and carried forward over time. The measure is likewise important because education outcomes are closely connected with the country’s economic and workforce needs. Students must be equipped not only with foundational knowledge but also with skills relevant to a changing labor market. Stronger coordination between education institutions and agencies responsible for employment, economic planning, science and technology, and public resources can help bridge the gap between what the education system provides and what society and the economy require. Equally important is the need for greater accountability in the implementation of education reforms. A coordinated national mechanism can provide clearer lines of responsibility, strengthen monitoring of outcomes, and promote evidence-based decision-making. It can also facilitate the use of reliable and integrated information in determining priorities and allocating public resources, thereby helping ensure that government investments in education produce meaningful and measurable results. The proposed legislation also complements ongoing efforts to improve the Philippine education system, including reform initiatives arising from the work of the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM II). Rather than allowing recommendations and reforms to remain isolated within individual institutions, there is a need for an institutional structure capable of translating national priorities into coordinated and sustained government action. Ultimately, education is a long-term national investment. The quality of today’s education system will shape the country’s workforce, productivity, competitiveness, social mobility, and capacity for inclusive development in the years ahead. Addressing the country’s education challenges therefore requires more than additional programs; it requires stronger institutional coordination and a sustained commitment to common national objectives. The passage of the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE) Act will provide the government with a permanent framework through which education and workforce development reforms can be coordinated, sustained, and held accountable. By strengthening the unity of purpose among government institutions, the measure seeks to ensure that education remains a consistent and enduring national priority, regardless of changes in administration. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11218
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING PERMANENT SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICER POSITIONS IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE, PROVIDING FOR A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY AND SECURITY PROGRAM FOR SCHOOLS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE No learner’s right to education should be curtailed by a lack of security, yet Philippine public schools continue to send children into classrooms that the Department of Education (DepEd) itself admits it cannot adequately protect. This bill seeks to establish a Comprehensive School Safety and Security Program covering all public and private basic education institutions. It creates permanent civil service plantilla positions for School Security Officers (SSOs) in every public school, mandates a dedicated Emergency Hotline System with prioritized routing to the Philippine National Police (PNP) and local medical services, directs DepEd to fund metal detectors, CCTV systems, and fortified perimeter fencing, and institutes mandatory safety training for teachers and learners. Over the past year, campus violence in the Philippines has escalated from isolated incidents into a recurring national concern. A gun attack at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City in June 2026 left three (3) students dead and twenty (20) others wounded, barely two (2) months before a second fatal shooting struck the Ateneo de Zamboanga University Junior High School campus.1 Investigations on these tragedies have likewise flagged a string of earlier firearm-related incidents, including a student who accidentally shot himself after bringing a gun to school and another who fired a .45-caliber pistol inside a Batangas classroom, alongside stabbing incidents recorded within the same weeks.2 These episodes show that Philippine schools now face threats that existing child protection issuances were never designed to repel. Underlying these tragedies is a chronic shortage of trained security personnel. DepEd currently fields only around two thousand two hundred (2,200) permanent 1 Chi, C. (2026, August 21). Accessed via https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/08/21/2550825/deped-sets-nationwide-school-safety -drill-campus-threats-august-25. Accessed on 27 August 2026. 2 Sinaking, E. P., & Bacon, P. Accessed on 27 August 2026. security guard positions across more than forty-eight thousand (48,000) public schools nationwide—roughly one (1) guard for every twenty (20) campuses—after a prior rationalization program stripped away most security plantilla items.3 DepEd has admitted that several campuses, particularly those enrolling more than a thousand learners, need more than a single guard, and that the department must request fresh funding from the Department of Budget and Management year after year rather than rely on a standing legal mandate. Without permanent, civil-service-protected SSO positions fixed in law, school security remains contingent on administrative discretion and annual budget negotiations instead of a guaranteed minimum standard. Beyond firearms, the PNP Women and Children Protection Center recorded one thousand, two hundred seventy-five (1,275) school-related incidents involving children in conflict with the law from 2022 to 2025, highlighting that violence, bullying, and other safety concerns extend beyond isolated shootings. While DepEd has responded through a nationwide School Safety Campaign, bag inspections, and proposed 2027 funding for guards, counselors, CCTV systems, fences, and metal detectors, these measures remain subject to administrative changes and budget priorities. This bill institutionalizes such safeguards by establishing permanent staffing, equipment, emergency hotline, and compliance requirements, ensuring that learner safety remains protected regardless of changes in administration or funding priorities. Parents send their children to school trusting that classrooms will nurture them, not endanger them. Every week without a permanent, funded, and legally mandated school safety framework is a week in which the State falls short of its constitutional promise of safe and accessible quality education. This Representation therefore pushes to accord this measure its immediate approval, so that no Filipino family has to bury a child because protection arrived too late. label: HB 11219
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE REHABILITATION AND SUPERVISION OF CHILDREN EXEMPT FROM CRIMINAL RESPONSIBILITY WHO COMMIT SERIOUS CRIMES, ESTABLISHING REGIONAL REHABILITATION CENTERS FOR YOUTH, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9344, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUVENILE JUSTICE AND WELFARE ACT OF 2006”, AS AMENDED, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A child exempt from criminal responsibility who commits a serious crime deserves secure, government-run rehabilitation rather than confinement in an overcrowded facility that local governments were never funded to build. This bill amends Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No. 10630, otherwise known as the “Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006,” to strengthen the rehabilitation and supervision of children exempt from criminal responsibility who commit serious crimes. It establishes a Regional Rehabilitation Center for Youth (RRCY) in every region of the country, to be established, funded, administered, and operated directly by the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD). After nearly a decade of decline, cases involving children in conflict with the law have begun climbing again: reported cases reached 5,698 by June 2025 alone, already surpassing the total recorded for the whole of 2024.1 The June 2026 shooting at San Jose National High School in Tacloban City exposed how unprepared the existing system is to respond. Tacloban, a highly urbanized city required by law to operate a Bahay Pag-asa, has none, thereby forcing authorities to place the accused minors in a regional youth facility in Tanauan, Leyte, while the nearest Bahay Pag-asa, in Biliran, was already operating beyond capacity.2 Nationwide, only 30 of 83 provinces and 28 of 33 highly urbanized cities have established a Bahay Pag-asa despite the mandate under Republic Act No. 10630, and only 28 of the existing facilities have secured DSWD accreditation more than a decade after that law took effect.2 Even where facilities exist, oversight has repeatedly fallen short. The Commission on Human Rights has documented congestion, understaffing, and subhumane conditions in several Bahay Pag-asa facilities nationwide, along with 1 Baclig, C. E. (2026, April 16). After decade of gains, juvenile offenses show signs of reversing. Inquirer. Retrieved from https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2213322/after-decade-of-gains-juvenile-offenses-show- signs-of-reversing. Accessed on 1 September 2026. 2 Ronquillo, A. & Mateo, J. (2026, July 6). Lack of facilities shows gaps in juvenile justice system. The Philippine Star. Accessed on 1 September 2026. allegations of abuse and mistreatment of the children placed in their care.4 Because these facilities remain locally built, funded, and managed, their quality varies sharply from one local government unit to the next, and children who commit the most serious offenses are sometimes held in the same under-resourced spaces as those facing minor infractions, without the specialized, secure treatment their cases demand.3 The national government has recognized the shortfall. label: HB 11220
title: AN ACT DECLARING QUEZON CITY AS THE “FILM AND TELEVISION ARTS CAPITAL OF THE PHILIPPINES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Quezon City has already earned international recognition as the heart of Philippine cinema and television, and it is time national law caught up with what the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the industry, and generations of Filipino filmmakers have long known to be true. This bill declares Quezon City as the “Film and Television Arts Capital of the Philippines” in recognition of its status as home to the country’s largest film and television production companies and institutions. It directs the Department of Tourism (DOT), in consultation with the Quezon City government, to incorporate this official designation into its national tourism programs, and further directs the DOT to develop, together with the Quezon City government and local film and television institutions, tourism events and destinations that showcase the country’s film and television history and heritage. Quezon City is already the undisputed center of Philippine broadcast and film production. It hosts an estimated sixty to sixty-five percent (60-65%) of the country’s television transmission facilities and forty percent (40%) of its post-production capacity, anchored by the headquarters of GMA Network in Diliman, the ABS-CBN Complex nearby, and the Araneta City studios in Cubao that host forty-five percent (45%) of Metro Manila’s major concert and live event productions.1 This industry weight has already drawn international recognition: in October 2025, Quezon City became one of the first cities in Southeast Asia to be designated a UNESCO Creative City of Film, a title tracing back through the golden era of Sampaguita Pictures and the legacies of Lino Brocka, Dolphy, Nora Aunor, and Fernando Poe Jr.2 1 Quezon City Government. (2024, October 2). Quezon City unveils bid to become UNESCO Creative City of Film. Accessed via https://quezoncity.gov.ph/quezon-city-is-now-a-unesco-creative-city-of-film/. Accessed on 3 September 2026. 2 Quezon City Government. (2025, October 31). Quezon City is now a UNESCO Creative City of Film. Quezon City Government. Accessed via https://quezoncity.gov.ph/quezon-city-is-now-a-unesco- creative-city-of-film/. Accessed on 3 September 2026. The Quezon City government has already moved to institutionalize this identity at the local level. In May 2025, the city established the Quezon City Screen Commission through a City Council ordinance, tasked with harmonizing film-related policies, streamlining permits through a dedicated Film Permits Office, and coordinating training and industry programs down to the barangay level.3 Building on its UNESCO designation, the Commission is now developing the QC Screen Academy, the Global Producers Exchange, and the Southeast Asia Film Summit to further cement the city’s role as a regional hub for film production and worker welfare. What remains missing is the corresponding recognition and support at the national level: without a law declaring Quezon City’s status and directing national tourism agencies to build around it, these local gains remain vulnerable to being under-promoted nationally and unsupported by the country’s tourism infrastructure. The scale of what is at stake is considerable. Quezon City’s media and creative production sector is estimated at forty-two and a half (42.5) billion and growing at six point two percent (6.2%) annually, generating thousands of jobs in production, post-production, and animation, with the city’s universities producing roughly fifteen thousand (15,000) communication and film graduates every year.4 A formal national declaration, implemented with a DOT-led tourism program built around the city’s film and television heritage, would not only affirm an identity Quezon City has already earned locally and internationally, but would also open new avenues for tourism revenue, structured industry promotion, and pride of place for the workers, artists, and institutions that have sustained the country’s film and television industry for generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. JEFFREY SORIANO 3 Ecosio, J. (2025, May 1). label: HB 11221
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING COMPREHENSIVE POLICIES TO PREVENT AND ADDRESS ACTS OF BULLYING, HARASSMENT, AND OTHER FORMS OF VIOLENCE IN THE WORKPLACE, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE No worker should have to endure daily humiliation, intimidation, or exclusion simply to keep a paycheck. This bill institutes comprehensive policies to prevent and address workplace bullying, harassment, and other forms of violence. It covers physical, verbal, psychological, social, cyber, and gender-based bullying, as well as abuse of authority and management by threat or intimidation. It requires all government and private offices to adopt written anti-bullying policies and report compliance to the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) or the Civil Service Commission (CSC), as applicable. A nationwide poll by the Lloyd’s Register Foundation and Gallup found that twenty-two percent (22%) of Filipino women and eighteen percent (18%) of men have experienced violence or harassment at work, with psychological harassment the most commonly reported form and sixty percent (60%) of victims saying it happened three (3) or more times.1 Yet, a majority of victims never report the abuse: forty-seven percent (47%) of women and sixty percent (60%) of men who experienced it stayed silent, largely out of fear of repercussions, or the belief that nothing would come of speaking up.1 This silence poses no surprise given how thin the country’s legal protections remain outside of the school setting. The Philippines currently has no standalone law against workplace bullying. Republic Act (RA) No. 10627, otherwise known as the “Anti-Bullying Act”, applies only to schools, leaving working adults to rely on a patchwork of statutes never designed to address bullying directly, including RA No. 11058, otherwise known as the “Occupational Safety and Health Standards Act”, RA No. 11313, otherwise known as the “Safe Spaces Act”, RA No. 7877, otherwise known as the “Anti-Sexual Harassment Act”, and general Labor Code due process rules, none of which squarely 1 Philstar. (2023, January 31). Around a Fifth of Filipino Employees Have Experienced Workplace Harassment — Poll. Philstar.com. Retrieved from https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2023/01/31 /2241812/around-fifth-filipino-employees-have-experienced-workplace-harassment-poll. Accessed on 7 September 2026. define or penalize workplace bullying as such. This problem persists even after the Philippines ratified International Labour Organization Convention No. 190 in February 2024, becoming the first country in Asia to commit to eliminating violence and harassment in the world of work.2 In the absence of a unified statute, employers are left to assemble their own policies from overlapping and sometimes inconsistent frameworks, with no clear, government-wide standard for investigation timelines, reporting channels, or penalties.3 This bill creates a single and enforceable statute, defining workplace bullying in all its forms and applying uniformly across government and private establishments. It fixes concrete investigation timelines, in place of the vague standards that currently leave complainants uncertain of when their case will be resolved, and extends coverage to remote work and third parties such as clients and vendors, consistent with how modern workplaces actually operate. It also introduces a graduated schedule of administrative fines, rather than leaving penalties entirely to future rules, and expressly harmonizes this Act with the Safe Spaces Act, the Anti-Sexual Harassment Act, the Occupational Safety and Health Standards Act, and the Mental Health Act, so that victims of gender-based or sexual misconduct continue to receive the specific protections those laws provide, without being caught between overlapping and potentially conflicting processes. A worker who is bullied into silence loses more than comfort at work. They lose their health, productivity, and often their zest for life. This Representation therefore urges the immediate approval of this measure, so that Filipino workers finally have a clear, enforceable law that treats their dignity at work as a right, not a privilege left to the goodwill of their employer. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. JEFFREY SORIANO 2 International Labour Organization. (2024, February 22). Workplace Anti-Bullying Laws in the Philippines. Respicio & Co. Retrieved from https://www.respicio.ph/commentaries/workplace-anti-bullying-laws-in-the- philippines. Accessed on 7 September 2026. label: HB 11222
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF BARANGAY DRUGSTORES, TO BE CALLED AS “BOTIKA NG BARANGAY”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A barangay drugstore that runs out of medicine or funding is failing to serve its community. This bill institutionalizes the Department of Health’s (DOH) Botika ng Barangay (BNB) program, directing the establishment of barangay drugstores in every barangay within a three-year period, with priority given to economically depressed and underserved communities. More than two decades after it was first established under DOH Administrative Order No. 70, the BNB program remains hampered by the very problems the bill seeks to resolve. A government review found that while the number of BNBs expanded rapidly, not all of them received sufficient financial and management support to remain sustainable. This prompted the DOH to institute a moratorium on further BNB expansion until problems in restocking and financing could be addressed.1 Field research in Cebu Province similarly found that the top complaints among BNB clients were the availability of stocks, inconsistent operating hours, and limited variety of medicines sold, even as households that did have reliable access to a BNB saved significantly on health-related expenses compared to commercial drugstore prices.2 Part of the problem is that the program’s funding and supply mechanisms have relied on a patchwork of administrative issuances rather than a permanent statutory framework. DOH Administrative Order No. 70 provided the original licensing framework in 2002, DOH Administrative Order No. 64 in 2003 tapped Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office funds and Philippine International Trading Corporation procurement support to sustain BNB operations, and DOH 1 Picazo, O. F. (2012, September 12). Review of the Cheaper Medicines Program of the Philippines: Botika ng Barangay, Botika ng Bayan, P100 Treatment Pack, and the Role of PITC Pharma, Inc. in Government Drug Procurement. Discussion Paper Series No. 2012-13. Philippine Institute for Development Studies. doi.org/10.62986/dp2012.13. 2 Palompon, D. R., et. al. (2010, December 2). Community Drugstore (Botika ng Barangay): Its Contribution to Family Living Standards. Liceo Journal of Higher Education Research (Vol. 6 No. 2 (ISSN: 2094-1064). doi.org/10.7828/ljher.v6i2.69. Administrative Order No. 159 in October 2022 introduced financial assistance mechanisms through accredited Pharmaceutical Distribution Networks. These measures have kept the program alive, but each remains an executive issuance that can be revised or discontinued at any time, leaving BNBs without the guaranteed, continuous funding a program of this scale requires. This bill mandates the DOH to establish a standardized inventory monitoring and quarterly replenishment system to prevent the stockouts that have long undermined community confidence in the BNB program. It creates a revolving fund from BNB medicine sales, directs local government units to draw on their share of national taxes under the Mandanas-Garcia ruling and the Special Health Fund under the Universal Health Care Act, and allows continued access to Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office assistance. It further sets minimum operating-hour standards and provides for a Botika ng Barangay Aide honorarium, and adds an explicit appropriations clause so that funding for the program is guaranteed year after year rather than left to chance. A Botika ng Barangay that families cannot rely on to be open, stocked, or staffed defeats the very purpose for which it was built. It must be a dependable source of affordable medicine for the Filipino families who need it most. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. label: HB 11223
title: AN ACT OFFICIALLY CREATING BARANGAY SANTA CRUZ IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF TAMPAKAN, PROVINCE OF SOUTH COTABATO, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This Bill seeks the official statutory creation and recognition of Barangay Santa Cruz in the Municipality of Tampakan, Province of South Cotabato, so that it may receive its lawful share in the National Tax Allotment, formerly referred to as the Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA). Similar measures were filed in previous Congresses. Barangay Santa Cruz came into existence through Sangguniang Bayan Resolution No. 122, Series of 2001, and succeeding Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution Nos. 13 and 170, both Series of 2001. Its creation was subsequently ratified in a plebiscite conducted by the Commission on Elections on 30 June 2003. Since its creation, Barangay Santa Cruz has functioned as a regular local government unit, serving its constituents, electing its officials, implementing public service projects and programs, and administering its assets and facilities. Because Barangay Santa Cruz was created by a local government unit after the effectivity of the Local Government Code of 1991 and was not created by statute, its financial requirements have historically been borne by the local government units concerned pursuant to the final proviso of Section 285 of Republic Act No. 7160. Its official recognition by Congress will allow Barangay Santa Cruz to receive its just share of national revenues and strengthen its ability to finance essential services and development programs. Fiscal autonomy at the barangay level translates directly into better and more responsive services for the people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. ________________________________ FERDINAND L. title: AN ACT CREATING A BARANGAY TO BE KNOWN AS BARANGAY JUAN- LORETO TAMAYO IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF TUPI, PROVINCE OF SOUTH COTABATO, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This proposed measure seeks the statutory recognition and creation of Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo in the Municipality of Tupi, Province of South Cotabato, and to ensure that it is entitled to its lawful share in the National Tax Allotment, formerly referred to as the Internal Revenue Allotment (IRA). Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo was created pursuant to Sangguniang Panlalawigan Resolution No. 158, Series of 2023, which enacted Provincial Ordinance No. 14, Series of 2023. Its creation was ratified in a plebiscite conducted by the Commission on Elections on 13 July 2024. Section 285 of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, provides that the financial requirements of barangays created by local government units after the effectivity of the Code shall be the responsibility of the local government unit concerned. Statutory recognition is therefore necessary to place Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo on the same fiscal footing as other barangays and to enable it to receive its corresponding share from national taxes. Barangays are the basic political units through which essential public services are delivered directly to communities. Providing Barangay Juan-Loreto Tamayo with a regular and predictable share in national revenues will strengthen its capacity to finance basic services, local development programs, public infrastructure, disaster preparedness, and other responsibilities entrusted to barangay governments. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this Bill is earnestly sought. ________________________________________ FERDINAND L. label: HB 11227
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION OF PATIENTS AGAINST HOSPITAL DETENTION ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES AND PROVIDING STIFFER PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT 9439 TITLED “AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DETENTION OF PATIENTS IN HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL CLINICS ON GROUNDS OF NONPAYMENT OF HOSPITAL BILLS OR MEDICAL EXPENSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Carry each other’s burdens, and in this way, you will fulfill the law of Christ.” — Galatians 6:2 “Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in the power of your hand to do so.” – Proverbs 3:27 Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution explicitly establishes that the protection and promotion of health, and access to health care is fundamentally a human right, to wit: “[T]he State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them.” In the same vein, Article III, Section 20 stipulates that "[N]o person shall be imprisoned for debt or non-payment of a poll tax.” These key Constitutional provisions are the guiding principles on the enactment of Republic Act No. 9439, otherwise known as the Anti-Hospital Detention Law, which prohibits the unlawful detention of patients on account of unpaid medical obligations. However, gaps in the coverage and enforcement mechanisms of the law continue to leave patients and their families vulnerable, particularly those who are financially incapacitated and those confronted with the release of medical documents, personal belongings, or the remains of a deceased loved one. This measure seeks to strengthen the protections under Republic Act No. 9439 by expressly covering hospitals, medical clinics, and other similar healthcare facilities, and by prohibiting the detention not only of patients but also of their relatives, representatives, caregivers, and, in appropriate cases, newborn children. It further provides a clearer definition of detention to include acts that effectively prevent discharge or release, such as withholding documents necessary for discharge, benefit claims, or interment, refusing the medically appropriate removal of medical devices, withholding personal belongings, or refusing to release the remains of a deceased patient on account of unpaid obligations. The bill also establishes safeguards for patients who are financially incapable of settling their obligations. While allowing the execution of secured promissory notes 1 where appropriate, it provides alternative mechanisms such as guarantees from government agencies and assignments of benefits or proceeds. Indigent patients endorsed through the hospital's medical social services may be exempted from the requirement of a promissory note upon submission of an appropriate guarantee from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) or the Department of Health (DOH). These mechanisms seek to balance the legitimate financial interests of healthcare facilities with the patient's right to timely discharge and access to essential documents and benefits. Recognizing that vulnerable patients may require assistance beyond the immediate prohibition against detention, the measure mandates DOH to facilitate access to government medical assistance programs and establish a grievance and redress mechanism for unlawful detention. It likewise requires healthcare facilities to adopt standard discharge protocols, provide transparency in healthcare costs and billing, prominently post patients' rights, and refer indigent or financially incapacitated patients to medical social service offices. These provisions strengthen accountability and ensure that the prohibition against hospital detention is translated into an accessible and enforceable patient protection system. To ensure meaningful enforcement, the bill imposes higher penalties when unlawful detention is committed pursuant to an established institutional policy or management instruction. Repeated violations under such policy may likewise result in the revocation of the health facility's license to operate. The measure further provides a tax deduction for certain unpaid balances guaranteed to facilitate the discharge of financially incapacitated patients, thereby helping mitigate the financial burden on healthcare facilities while preserving the patient's right to timely release. By amending and strengthening Republic Act No. 9439, this measure seeks to ensure that financial hardship does not become a barrier to a patient's liberty, dignity, or access to necessary medical and legal documents. It establishes clearer responsibilities for healthcare institutions and government agencies while providing practical mechanisms for the recovery or settlement of legitimate medical obligations without resorting to the detention of patients or their families. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. EDUARDO “BRO. EDDIE” C. label: HB 11231
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE UNIVERSITY OF ANTIQUE, EXPANDING ITS CURRICULAR OFFERINGS AND THE COMPOSITION OF THE GOVERNING BOARD, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The University of Antique (UA), established under Republic Act No. 9746, has long served as a principal institution of higher learning in the Province of Antique and a key contributor to human resource development, research, extension services, and socio-economic progress in Western Visayas. As the demands of higher education continue to evolve, there is a need to strengthen the University’s institutional framework and expand its capacity to respond to emerging academic, technological, and development priorities. This bill seeks to revise the Charter of the University of Antique by broadening its academic mandate, strengthening its governance and administrative structures, enhancing institutional autonomy, and improving access to quality higher education throughout the province. The measure expands the University’s curricular offerings to include undergraduate and graduate programs, advanced professional and technical instruction, and training in fields such as law, medicine, nursing, maritime education, engineering, information and communications technology, and other disciplines responsive to the needs of Antique and Western Visayas. It likewise strengthens UA’s functions in research, extension, innovation, technology transfer, and entrepreneurship. The bill also strengthens UA as a multi-campus state university. It recognizes its existing regular campuses in Sibalom, Tibiao, and Hamtic; converts the extension campuses in Caluya and Libertad into regular campuses; and mandates the creation of new regular campuses in Bugasong, Tobias Fornier, and San Remigio. It further authorizes the establishment of additional 1 branches or extension campuses as may be necessary to improve access to quality education and advance the University’s research and academic capabilities. Taken together, these reforms will provide the University of Antique with a stronger and more responsive institutional framework to deliver accessible, relevant, and globally competitive higher education, while further advancing research, innovation, public service, and sustainable regional development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. FELIMON M. title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF PUBLIC SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT WORKERS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the "Magna Carta of Public Solid Waste Management Workers Act." SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — It is hereby declared the policy of the State to recognize the indispensable role of public solid waste management workers in safeguarding public health, protecting the environment, promoting ecological balance, and ensuring the effective implementation of ecological solid waste management programs. The State shall protect and promote the rights and welfare of public solid waste management workers by ensuring humane working conditions, just and equitable compensation, occupational safety and health, adequate social protection, opportunities for training and capacity development, and protection against discrimination, harassment, exploitation, and unsafe working conditions. Towards this end, the State shall adopt measures that enhance their dignity, improve their quality of life, and strengthen the delivery of public solid waste management services. SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: a. Public Solid Waste Management Workers refer to all personnel employed by national government, local government units (LGUs), government owned
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public solid waste management workers perform one of the most essential yet often overlooked public services. Every day, they collect, transport, process, and dispose of solid waste, ensuring the cleanliness of communities, protecting public health, and safeguarding the environment. Their work is indispensable to the effective implementation of ecological solid waste management programs and the promotion of sustainable urban and rural development. Despite the hazardous nature of their duties, public solid waste management workers continue to face numerous challenges, including prolonged exposure to harmful substances, infectious waste, toxic chemicals, extreme weather conditions, and occupational accidents. Many of them also endure inadequate compensation, limited access to healthcare and insurance, and the absence of comprehensive legal framework that recognizes and protects their rights and welfare. While existing laws, such as Republic Act No. 9003 or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, provide the policy framework for solid waste management, they do not comprehensively address the employment conditions, occupational safety, benefits, and professional development of the workers who carry out these vital functions. It is therefore imperative to establish a Magna Carta that institutionalize their rights, promote their welfare, ensure safe and humane working conditions, and recognize their invaluable contribution to society. This proposed measure seeks to provide public solid waste management workers with just compensation, hazard pay, appropriate personal protective equipment, health benefits, opportunities for training and capacity development, and protection against discrimination and unjust labor practices, among others. It likewise mandates the adoption of occupational safety standards and appropriates the necessary funds to ensure the effective implementation of these benefits. By recognizing the dignity of their profession and investing in their welfare, the State affirms its commitment to protecting workers who perform vital environmental and public health services while strengthening the country’s solid waste management system. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MAURICIO G. label: HB 11233
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA FOR PUBLIC DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKERS, INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PUBLIC DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKFORCE CREATING THE DISASTER RISK REDUCTION AND MANAGEMENT WORKERS SUPPORT FUND, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 12 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10121, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10121, the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, built a system. It did not build the workforce that the system runs on. Section 12 of that law requires every province, city, and municipality to establish a Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office headed by a DRRM Officer and assisted by three staff for administration and training, research and planning, and operations and warning. Where the offices exist, a large share of the people staffing them hold job order or contract of service engagements, renewed every six months, without security of tenure, without leave credits, without insurance, and without any legal claim to the hazard pay that the danger of their work plainly warrants. This is the workforce that clears the road before the convoy, that reads the rain gauge at two in the morning, that carries the body bags, and that signs the damage assessment on which every peso of relief depends. Several measures on this subject are pending before this Chamber, and this bill seeks to expand from all of them. It departs from them in three respects. First, on hazard pay. The pending measures set the hazard allowance at a rate "not exceeding twenty-five percent (25%)" of daily basic salary. The provision they are modeled on, Section 21 of Republic Act No. 7305, the Magna Carta of Public Health Workers, reads "at least twenty-five percent (25%)." A ceiling has been substituted for a floor, and under a ceiling a local government unit that grants one percent is fully compliant. This bill restores the floor and adds a fifteen-day release deadline, so that an earned benefit does not become a receivable. Second, on who pays. The pending measures charge the cost to local funds "subject to Personal Service Limitations pursuant to Section 325 of Republic Act No. 7160." For the fourth to sixth class local government units where DRRM staffing is thinnest and hazard exposure highest, that proviso is a legal bar on compliance: the unit cannot grant the benefit without breaching the Local Government Code. This bill excludes risk-related DRRM benefits from the personal services limitation and creates a Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Workers Support Fund so that the poorest municipalities are not asked to fund a national mandate out of a budget they do not have. It likewise bars the Local Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Fund from being converted into a payroll account, so that the workers are not funded by defunding the preparedness work they are hired to do. Third, on integrity. No pending measure protects a DRRM worker who refuses to sign a false damage assessment, refuses to certify a project that does not exist, or reports the misuse of disaster funds. The events of the past year have made the cost of that omission plain. A DRRM officer's signature is a control on public money, and a control is worth nothing if the person exercising it can be removed for exercising it. This bill protects that refusal and makes retaliation for it a punishable act. Beyond these, it amends Section 12 of Republic Act No. 10121 to require that the positions the law has demanded since 2010 are actually created, funded, and filled, on a deadline and against hazard-weighted staffing standards. It creates no new profession, no new board, and no new bureaucracy. It fills positions that existing law already requires, pays for exposure that already occurs, and protects people who are already doing the work. A Magna Carta for our DRRM workers is long overdue. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C.
