label: HB 11236
title: AN ACT GRANTING AN AMNESTY ON UNPAID INTERNAL REVENUE TAXES IMPOSED BY THE NATIONAL GOVERNMENT FOR TAXABLE YEAR 2026 AND PRIOR YEARS WITH RESPECT TO ESTATE TAX, OTHER INTERNAL REVENUE TAXES, AND TAX ON DELINQUENCIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipino families, workers, entrepreneurs, and businesses are presently confronting an unusually difficult economic environment. The continuing effects of elevated prices, higher energy and transportation costs, disruptions in international trade and fuel markets, and slower economic growth have placed considerable pressure on household finances and business activity. Headline inflation remained elevated at 6.2 percent in July 2026, while economic growth slowed to 2.3 percent in the second quarter of 2026. These conditions are felt not merely in economic statistics, but in the everyday cost of food, electricity, transportation, housing, education, and the operation of small and medium enterprises. Government policy must therefore strike a careful balance. Revenue must continue to be raised for essential public services and national development, but taxation should not become an obstacle to the recovery and continued economic participation of otherwise productive citizens and enterprises. This policy direction was expressly articulated by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. during his 2026 State of the Nation Address. Recognizing the burden borne not only by low-income families but also by workers, the middle class, and small businesses, the President called upon Congress to pursue tax relief measures that promote economic growth, generate revenue, and advance equity. More particularly, 1 the President expressly called for an amnesty covering unpaid taxes, including income tax, estate tax, donor's tax, value-added tax, and the penalties attached thereto. This bill is modeled upon previous tax amnesty laws, but updated with additional safeguards against fraud and abuse in order to better attain the policy objectives of the current administration. Among the concerns raised were the following: the continued restrictions imposed by bank secrecy laws in cases of suspected fraud, the absence of an adequate framework for the automatic exchange of tax information, and insufficient mechanisms to verify the truthfulness of declarations of assets and net worth. Certain provisions involving the previous attempts for different versions of Estate Tax Amnesty were likewise changed. In particular, the issue over allowing several successive unsettled estates to be discharged through a single tax computation based only upon the last decedent, notwithstanding that estate tax attaches at each taxable transfer. Additionally, provisions regarding conclusive presumption of correctness, originally granted to Estate Tax Amnesty Returns, has been balanced with a safeguard in order to prevent a situation wherein the Government is deprived of a reasonable opportunity to verify ownership, valuation, succession, and other material information. Congress subsequently enacted Republic Act Nos. 11569 and 11956, progressively extending and simplifying the Estate Tax Amnesty. These amendments recognized that an effective amnesty must be accessible to ordinary taxpayers. They allowed easier filing, reduced documentary barriers, separated payment of estate taxes from the later process of transferring property, and permitted installment payments. This bill builds upon all of these legislative developments. First, it expands the coverage of the Estate Tax Amnesty to estates of decedents who died on or before December 31, 2026, and grants taxpayers two (2) years from the effectivity of the implementing rules and regulations within which to avail themselves of the program. Second, it reinstates the General Tax Amnesty originally contemplated under Republic Act No. 11213 and updates its coverage to taxable year 2026 and all prior years. Taxpayers are likewise granted two (2) years from the effectivity of the implementing rules and regulations within which to avail themselves of the amnesty. To encourage taxpayers to come forward promptly, the bill preserves the principle of the original early-availment incentive. A taxpayer who avails during the first six months receives a twenty percent reduction in the amnesty tax; those availing during the succeeding six months receive a fifteen percent reduction; those availing during the third six-month period receive a ten percent reduction; and those availing during the final six months may still obtain the amnesty but without an additional reduction. 2 Third, the bill directly addresses the objections that prevented the General Tax Amnesty from taking effect in 2019. Tax Amnesty Returns and declarations of assets and net worth will no longer become conclusively and immediately unassailable upon filing. Instead, honest taxpayers will enjoy a prima facie presumption of correctness, while the Bureau of Internal Revenue is afforded a three-year period within which to conduct ordinary verification. After this period, the amnesty becomes final and irrevocable, subject to the taxpayer’s continuing liability for the full payment of the correct tax due if the declarations are subsequently determined to contain an inaccuracy affecting the tax due. Fraud, willful concealment, or material misrepresentation receives no protection and may additionally give rise to revocation, civil penalties, and criminal liability even if discovered beyond the three-year verification period. Where the amnesty itself was obtained through fraud, willful concealment, or material misrepresentation, the special protection of the amnesty may be revoked. Consistent with the long-established principle under the National Internal Revenue Code applicable to fraudulent returns, the Government is given ten (10) years from the discovery of the fraud within which to pursue the appropriate action. This distinction is essential. The bill forgives tax violations committed during the periods covered by the amnesty; otherwise there would be no amnesty at all. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Philippine Entrepreneurs Academy Act.” 30 SEC. 2. Establishment. – There is hereby established a learning institution, under the supervision of the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), to be known as the “Philippine Entrepreneurs Academy”, hereinafter referred to as the Academy. 34 SEC. 3. General Mandate. – The Academy shall provide undergraduate and graduate degree programs, short-term technical-vocational nondegree courses and modular trainings that will enhance the core competencies of individuals on entrepreneurship. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 A stronger Philippine economy begins with Filipinos who have the knowledge and opportunity to build businesses. 24 Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are undeniably the backbone of the Philippine economy. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) 2023 List of Establishments, MSMEs account for 99.6 percent of all business establishments and 67.0 percent of total employment in the country. They also contribute an estimated 25 percent of total export revenue and 40 percent of the country's GDP. 30 These figures only show that when Filipino entrepreneurs succeed, the Philippine economy grows with them. 33 However, starting and sustaining a business remains a challenge for many Filipinos. Access to proper training, business knowledge, technology, mentoring, financing, and markets remains uneven, while government programs for entrepreneurship are spread across different agencies and institutions. The market is here, and the audience is very much alive. 39 Hence, there is a need for a dedicated institution that brings these efforts together and makes entrepreneurship education more accessible and practical. 42 The proposed measure which establishes the Philippine Entrepreneurs Academy seeks to address this need by establishing a national institution dedicated to entrepreneurship education, training, research, and industry development. This will offer degree programs, technical-vocational courses, short-term training, and research while working with TESDA, DTI, DOST, the private sector, and other stakeholders. 48 The Academy will bridge the gap between learning how to start a business and actually building one. Through industry partnerships and practical training fit for the selected industry, it will equip aspiring and current entrepreneurs with the exact skills needed to establish, sustain, and grow their businesses. 5 By helping more Filipinos turn ideas into sustainable and profitable enterprises, the Academy can help create businesses that last, jobs that remain, and communities that grow. 9 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 11 12 13 REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 A bamboo pole sold cheaply at the farm gate can become furniture, a construction material, a household product, or an export commodity. 25 The Department of Science and Technology estimates that the Philippines has approximately 39,000 to 53,000 hectares of bamboo stands. Yet these resources remain largely scattered across backyards, forests, and even private properties, with relatively few established as commercial plantations. At the same time, DOST- PCAARRD has recognized that existing bamboo resources have struggled to meet the industry's demand for quality and quantity of raw materials. 32 This is a missed economic opportunity. 34 In 2023, Philippine bamboo production was reported at approximately 1.8 million poles, while recorded exports stood at around 2,000 kilograms. These figures might be commendable but somehow, it reveals a striking gap between the country's natural resource base and its ability to convert bamboo into a globally competitive industry. 39 The problem, therefore, is not the absence of bamboo’s economic potential. Despite the country's substantial bamboo resources, farmers and entrepreneurs continue to face barriers in plantation development, access to technology and financing, processing, and market access. 44 Without addressing these gaps, much of the economic value of bamboo will remain unrealized. Hence, this proposed measure seeks to transform bamboo from an underutilized natural resource into a sustainable engine of rural livelihood, domestic manufacturing, employment, and economic growth. 4 The proposed measure seeks to establish a national framework for the development of the Philippine bamboo industry. It strengthens the Philippine Bamboo Industry Development Council and creates a Bamboo Industry Research and Development Center to coordinate programs on plantation development, research, technology, training, processing, and market access. It also provides incentives to encourage bamboo plantations and bamboo based enterprises. 11 By developing the bamboo value chain from production to processing and commercialization, the measure aims to create rural jobs and livelihood, support Filipino businesses, strengthen local manufacturing, and expand Philippine bamboo products in domestic and international markets. It seeks to turn bamboo into a sustainable source of income and economic growth for Filipinos. 17 The Philippines already has the bamboo. This Act shall be known as the “Integration of the National Building Code to the Engineering and Architecture Curriculum and Professional Licensure Examination Act”. 37 SEC. 2. It is the policy of the State to promote the principles of sound environmental management and control consistent with its Constitutional mandate to safeguard life, health, property and public welfare. To this end, the State shall ensure that those who are authorized to practice the engineering and architecture professions receive the necessary formal instructions on building design, construction, occupancy and maintenance, are sufficiently trained in ensuring the safety and integrity of building and non-building structures, and given adequate instruction and training on the latest regulations, know-how, and building technologies.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 When a building fails, the consequences are measured not only in pesos, but in lives. 23 In June 2026, a building collapse in Angeles City, Pampanga resulted in a government investigation that found violations of occupational safety and health standards and led to more than ₱11.7 million in liabilities and administrative fines. The incident is a painful reminder that the safety of a building begins long before people enter it. 28 In short, the safety of a building begins with the knowledge, judgment, and professional responsibility of those who design and build it. 31 Thus, a professional entrusted with the design and construction of a building must first be equipped with the knowledge necessary to make that building safe. 34 Hence, this measure is as simple as it can be. 36 This measure now requires that the National Building Code should be taught in engineering and architecture programs and included in their licensure examinations. This way, it ensures that future professionals responsible for designing and building our structures know the rules that keep people safe. 41 We cannot afford to learn the value of building safety only after a tragedy. This measure ensures that safety begins where every profession begins: in education and in actual training. 44 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 46 47 48 REP. label: HB 11243
title: AN ACT FURTHER AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITY,” AS AMENDED, TO PROVIDE FOR THE LIFETIME VALIDITY OF IDENTIFICATION CARDS ISSUED TO PERSONS WITH PERMANENT DISABILITY”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Persons with disabilities should not be required to repeatedly renew their identification cards when their disabilities are permanent and irreversible. The periodic renewal of PWD identification cards creates unnecessary inconvenience, administrative burdens, and expenses for persons who are already living with permanent conditions. This measure seeks to amend Republic Act No. 7277, as amended, otherwise known as the “Magna Carta for Persons with Disability,” by providing for the lifetime validity of PWD identification cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities. Under the proposed measure, permanent disability shall be medically certified and appropriately verified, while the PWD identification card shall remain valid for the lifetime of the cardholder. Replacement shall remain available in cases of loss, damage, change in material information, or when the card becomes unusable, without requiring automatic re-certification of the permanent disability. The measure likewise provides that existing PWD identification cards issued to persons with permanent disabilities shall be deemed lifetime-valid, subject to the applicable rules on replacement and verification. By eliminating unnecessary periodic renewal while maintaining appropriate verification and registration safeguards, this measure seeks to make government services more accessible, efficient, and responsive to the needs of persons with permanent disabilities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11244
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A COMPREHENSIVE HOUSING PROGRAM FOR PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS, PROVIDING FOR GOVERNMENT- BUILT HOUSING, SUBSIDIZED HOUSING FINANCING, RENT- TO-OWN AND OTHER HOUSING ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS, CREATING A PUBLIC SCHOOL TEACHERS' HOUSING FUND, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public school teachers play a vital role in educating the Filipino youth and advancing national development. Many teachers, however, continue to face difficulties in securing decent, safe, affordable, and accessible housing, particularly those assigned to remote, underserved, and geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas. This measure seeks to establish a Public School Teachers’ Housing Program that will provide qualified teachers with access to government-built and near-site housing, subsidized housing loans, rent-to-own arrangements, down-payment and rental assistance, housing construction financing, and other appropriate housing assistance. The bill also creates a Public School Teachers’ Housing Fund and a Public School Teachers’ Housing Program Council to ensure coordinated implementation, sustainable financing, transparent beneficiary selection, and proper monitoring of the Program. By providing teachers with affordable and secure housing, the State can strengthen their economic security and welfare while helping ensure that they remain able to serve effectively in schools and communities throughout the country. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11245
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE PASS-THROUGH AND RECOVERY OF SYSTEM LOSS CHARGES FROM ELECTRICITY CONSUMERS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ELECTRIC POWER INDUSTRY REFORM ACT OF 2001,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Electricity is an essential commodity that directly affects the daily lives of Filipino households, businesses, and industries. Ensuring that electricity rates remain fair, reasonable, and affordable is therefore a vital concern of the State. Under the existing framework, system losses incurred in the distribution of electricity may be reflected in the rates charged to consumers. These losses may result from technical inefficiencies, inadequate infrastructure, pilferage, and other conditions within the distribution system. Consumers, however, have no control over the operation, maintenance, efficiency, or security of the distribution system and should not be made to bear the cost of such losses. This measure seeks to prohibit distribution utilities and electric cooperatives from passing on or recovering system loss charges from electricity consumers, directly or indirectly. It likewise directs the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC), in coordination with the Department of Energy (DOE) and other stakeholders concerned, to establish the necessary mechanisms to implement the prohibition and ensure that such charges are excluded from consumer billing. The measure aims to strengthen consumer protection, promote accountability and efficiency among distribution utilities, and ensure that consumers pay only for the electricity they actually consume. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11246
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THREATENING, HARASSING, COERCIVE, AND ABUSIVE DEBT COLLECTION PRACTICES BY ONLINE LENDING APPLICATIONS, DIGITAL CREDIT PROVIDERS, FINANCING COMPANIES, LENDING COMPANIES, AND OTHER SIMILAR ENTITIES, PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid growth of digital financial services has expanded access to loans and credit facilities, but has likewise given rise to abusive debt collection practices through text messages, social media, mobile applications, and other digital platforms. Reports of threats, intimidation, public shaming, unauthorized disclosure of personal information, and coercive communications have caused serious harm to the dignity, privacy, and security of borrowers. While existing laws and regulations provide remedies against certain unlawful collection practices, there remains a need for a clear and comprehensive framework specifically addressing threatening, harassing, coercive, and abusive debt collection conducted through digital and electronic means. This measure seeks to establish fair and lawful standards for digital debt collection, prohibit specified abusive practices, protect borrowers from harassment and misuse of personal information, strengthen compliance and regulatory oversight, and provide appropriate administrative, civil, and criminal remedies, without prejudice to liabilities and penalties under other applicable laws. The immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11247
title: AN ACT PROVIDING INCENTIVES AND FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR THE MODERNIZATION OF PUBLIC UTILITY JEEPNEYS AND TRICYCLES, ENSURING THE PROTECTION OF DRIVERS AND SMALL TRANSPORT OPERATORS DURING THE TRANSITION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The continuing modernization of public transportation is necessary to provide the riding public with a safer, more reliable, accessible, and efficient transport system. The transition, however, also presents significant financial and livelihood challenges to small public utility jeepney and tricycle operators and drivers who may not have the resources to immediately comply with modernization requirements. This measure seeks to ensure that modernization is inclusive and does not unnecessarily displace small transport operators and drivers. It provides a special low- interest financing window, with an interest rate not exceeding four percent (4%) per annum and a repayment period of at least seven (7) years, together with reasonable transition assistance for qualified small transport operators. It likewise provides a minimum five-year transition period for small transport operators owning three (3) units or fewer and protects them from being compelled to consolidate with corporate operators solely to participate in the modernization program or access assistance under the Act. To protect affected drivers, the measure provides for priority consideration for employment in modernized fleets, free retraining through TESDA, and transitional livelihood assistance for up to three (3) months, subject to eligibility requirements and availability of appropriations. Through these measures, the bill seeks to make public transport modernization a just, gradual, and inclusive transition—modernizing the system while protecting the livelihood of those who have long provided this essential public service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11248
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES OF STATE UNIVERSITIES AND COLLEGES AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mental health is an integral component of overall health and well-being and has become an increasingly pressing concern among young people, particularly students in higher education. College and university students face academic, financial, social, and personal pressures during a stage of life when mental health conditions may first emerge or become more pronounced. The World Health Organization (WHO) reports that one in seven persons aged ten (10) to nineteen (19) years experiences a mental disorder, with depression and anxiety among the leading causes of illness in this age group. Suicide is likewise the third leading cause of death globally among persons aged fifteen (15) to twenty-nine (29) years, an age group that includes a significant portion of the college and university population. In the Philippines, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported a suicide mortality rate of 2.7 deaths per 100,000 population in 2024. At the same time, access to mental health services remains limited. The Department of Health’s National Objectives for Health 2023–2028 reports only seventy- five (75) mental health facilities nationwide and three hundred sixty-two (362) Mental Health Management and Assistance Program (MH-MAP) access sites, which the government seeks to expand to five hundred fifteen (515). The WHO Mental Health Atlas 2024 Country Profile for the Philippines further reflects gaps in available human resources, reporting only 3.9 mental health workers per 100,000 population, including 0.2 psychiatrists and 0.3 psychologists per 100,000 population. The same profile also reported no functioning school-based mental health program under WHO reporting criteria, underscoring the need to strengthen accessible mental health services in educational settings. This need is particularly relevant to State Universities and Colleges (SUCs). Data from the Commission on Higher Education (CHED) show that, as of June 26, 2025, there were one hundred thirteen (113) SUC main campuses and four hundred forty-two (442) satellite campuses nationwide. Their broad reach places SUCs in a strategic position to provide mental health promotion, early intervention, counseling, crisis response, and referral services to students, faculty, and personnel. Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act,” established the national policy for the promotion and protection of mental health and the delivery of integrated mental health services. Consistent with this policy and the Philippine Council for Mental Health Strategic Framework 2024– 2028, there is a need to strengthen institutional mechanisms for mental health services within SUCs. Thus, this bill seeks to institutionalize Mental Health Offices in SUC campuses and ensure the hiring, training, deployment, and professional development of qualified mental health personnel. Through accessible campus-based services, appropriate referral mechanisms, suicide prevention programs, and timely crisis intervention, SUCs can better support the mental health and well-being of their academic communities. During the 19th Congress, a similar measure, which this representation co-authored, was approved on Third Reading by the House of Representatives. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 12 The right to travel is a fundamental liberty guaranteed by the Constitution. Article III, Section 6 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the right to travel shall not be impaired except in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health, as may be provided by law. 16 The issuance of a Philippine passport facilitates the exercise of this constitutional right by enabling Filipino citizens to travel internationally for lawful purposes, including employment, education, business, family reunification, and tourism. Under the New Philippine Passport Act (2024), the State shall protect the people’s constitutional right to travel, prescribe only minimum requirements, and ensure expeditious action on applications for and the issuance of passports and other travel documents.1 23 Further, the DFA may provide mobile passport services and consular outreach missions to Filipinos in areas outside its offices to make passport services accessible.2 This is particularly relevant given the continuing volume of Filipinos travelling abroad. 27 According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) 2025 Philippine Statistical Yearbook, there were 3,890,671 outbound Philippine residents in 2023 and 6,853,204 in 2024, representing a 76.14 percent increase.3 In addition, the DFA reported that it issued 2,615,953 passports in 2024. Of this number, 1,474,317 passports were issued through Regional Consular Offices, while 161,384 passports were issued through Temporary Offsite Passport Services (TOPS).4 These growing figures demonstrate the growing importance of establishing timely and accessible passport services. 35 1 Republic of the Philippines, Republic Act No. 11983: An Act Providing for a New Passport Law, Repealing for the Purpose Republic Act No. 8239, Otherwise Known as the “Philippine Passport Act of 1996,” as Amended, and Providing Funds Therefor. 2 Ibid. 3 Philippine Statistics Authority, 2025 Philippine Statistical Yearbook (Quezon City: Philippine Statistics Authority, 2025), chap. 8, “Tourism,” https://psa.gov.ph/system/files/psy/2025%20PSY%20Final_signed.pdf. 4 Department of Foreign Affairs, 2024 DFA Accomplishment Report (Manila: Department of Foreign Affairs, 2025), 84, https://dfa.gov.ph/images/2024/transparency/2024_Annual_Accomplishment_Report.pdf. label: HB 11252
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE SAFE SPORTS CENTER, INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL ATHLETE SAFEGUARDING SYSTEM, PREVENTING AND ADDRESSING ABUSE, HARASSMENT, EXPLOITATION, NEGLECT, RETALIATION, UNSAFE PRACTICES, AND SERIOUS SAFETY FAILURES IN SPORTS, PRESCRIBING THE DUTIES OF COVERED ENTITIES, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR GRASSROOTS SPORTS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On June 8, 2026, Ateneo de Manila University men’s basketball players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili died by drowning during a team-building activity in Dipaculao, Aurora. The Philippine Sports Commission subsequently formed a multi- stakeholder panel, while the National Bureau of Investigation and the Philippine National Police initiated separate investigative action. As these investigations remain pending, this measure makes no finding regarding fault, negligence, or liability. The tragedy presents a broader legislative concern: the responsibility of a sports organization does not end when formal training or competition ends. Camps, retreats, travel, billeting, swimming, recreation, and team-building activities conducted under institutional authority remain part of the sporting environment. These activities require proper risk assessment, competent supervision, emergency action plans, medical readiness, communication protocols, and clear accountability. Drowning remains a major public-health concern. The World Health Organization reported that more than 300,000 people died from drowning worldwide in 2021. Children and young people accounted for fifty-seven percent of these deaths, while approximately ninety-two percent occurred in low- and middle-income countries. More than half of global drowning deaths occurred in the Western Pacific and South- East Asia regions. The Constitution recognizes sports as an instrument of national development. Article II, Section 17 directs the State to give priority to sports, while Article XIV, Section 19 directs the State to promote physical education and sports programs to foster self-discipline, teamwork, excellence, and the development of a healthy and alert citizenry. These constitutional purposes cannot be achieved when athletes are exposed to abuse, harassment, exploitation, retaliation, unsafe training practices, inadequate supervision, preventable hazards, or deficient emergency response. Athletic excellence and athlete safety are not competing objectives. Safety is a necessary condition for sustainable participation and responsible sports development. Republic Act No. 6847 created the Philippine Sports Commission as the policy- making and coordinating body for amateur sports development. Philippine sports, however, is administered through a dispersed structure involving the PSC, National Sports Associations, schools, local governments, leagues, clubs, coaches, volunteers, and private organizers. This structure permits valuable autonomy but may also produce different safeguarding standards, reporting mechanisms, investigative procedures, and emergency protocols among organizations. Existing laws already address particular forms of abuse and misconduct. Republic Act No. 7610 protects children against abuse, neglect, cruelty, exploitation, and discrimination. Republic Act No. 11313 penalizes gender-based sexual harassment in workplaces, educational institutions, training institutions, public spaces, and online settings. The Anti-Hazing Act, Anti-Bullying Act, Mental Health Act, criminal laws, civil laws, and child-protection statutes likewise provide applicable rights and remedies. These laws do not yet create a unified sports-specific system for safeguarding education, risk assessment, emergency action planning, background screening, confidential reporting, interim protective measures, independent investigation, and recognition of sports-related sanctions across organizations. The proposed Philippine Safe Sports Act addresses this institutional gap by creating the Philippine Safe Sports Center. The Center shall establish a National Safe Sports Code, receive and investigate serious safeguarding complaints, issue minimum safety standards, conduct education and certification, maintain appropriate records of sanctioned persons, and coordinate with law-enforcement and child-protection agencies. The bill covers not only sexual, physical, psychological, and emotional abuse, but also serious safety failures and unsafe practices. Covered entities must prepare written risk assessments and emergency action plans for training, competitions, camps, travel, billeting, team-building, swimming, open-water activities, and other high-risk undertakings. Independent investigation is necessary where a sports organization may otherwise be required to investigate its own coaches, officials, employees, or programs. Independence protects athletes, complainants, witnesses, respondents, and the integrity of the institution itself. At the same time, the bill preserves the proper autonomy of sports organizations. Team selection, playing time, technical coaching decisions, competition results, and ordinary game-related discipline remain with the appropriate sports bodies unless an identifiable safeguarding violation is involved. The measure incorporates due-process safeguards. Respondents are entitled to notice, an opportunity to be heard, access to relevant evidence subject to confidentiality rules, representation, and appeal. Provisional measures may be imposed when necessary to protect athletes or witnesses, but they do not constitute a final finding of liability. The United States Center for SafeSport illustrates both the need for an independent safeguarding institution and the importance of adequate resources and clear procedures. The Center reported receiving nearly 8,100 reports in 2024 and more than 32,000 reports since its establishment. Reports increased by more than 2,780 percent from 2017, demonstrating the substantial administrative demands placed on a national sports-safeguarding system. The proposed Philippine system therefore requires precise jurisdiction, reasonable case timelines, periodic review of provisional measures, confidentiality protections, an appeals process, phased implementation, and proportionate compliance requirements for schools, National Sports Associations, local leagues, barangay teams, and grassroots organizations. label: HB 11253
title: AN ACT PROMOTING URBAN FLOOD RESILIENCE AND RAINWATER HARVESTING THROUGH THE ADOPTION OF A NATIONAL URBAN DRAINAGE AND RUNOFF MANAGEMENT CODE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Urban flooding has become one of the most pressing public safety, economic, and environmental concerns in the Philippines. Typhoons, monsoon rains, and localized thunderstorms regularly overwhelm drainage systems, causing property damage, business disruptions, displacement of families, and loss of life. In Metro Manila alone, flood-related incidents cause an estimated ₱5 billion in annual economic losses. The situation is aggravated by rapid urbanization, which has replaced natural ground cover with impermeable surfaces such as concrete and asphalt. These changes increase surface runoff while reducing natural infiltration, overwhelming outdated drainage networks—many of which were designed for rainfall patterns that no longer reflect current climate conditions. Improper solid waste disposal further clogs waterways, reducing flow capacity. Current legal provisions addressing drainage and water management are scattered across various statutes, such as the Local Government Code, the Water Code of the Philippines, and certain environmental regulations. However, there is no single, binding national standard for urban runoff management that integrates both flood mitigation and water conservation. The proposed Urban Flood Resilience and Rainwater Harvesting Act seeks to fill this gap by mandating the creation of a National Urban Drainage and Runoff Management Code, to be developed by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in coordination with the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD), and other agencies. The measure requires the installation of on-site detention and retention systems, permeable paving, and rainwater catchment facilities in all new developments above a certain threshold, while promoting retrofitting in older districts. Rainwater harvesting will serve the dual purpose of reducing peak runoff and conserving water for non-potable uses such as irrigation, fire suppression, cooling, and cleaning. Through uniform technical standards, strict compliance timelines for LGUs, and capacity-building programs, this measure will provide a clear national framework to address urban flooding while also promoting water sustainability. Incentives will be available for LGUs and private developers that go beyond compliance through innovative, climate-resilient solutions. By passing this bill, Congress will directly address urban flood risks, protect lives and livelihoods, and help achieve the country’s climate adaptation and sustainable development goals. In view of the urgent need to institutionalize a coherent and enforceable framework for stormwater and rainwater management in urban areas nationwide, the swift passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11254
title: AN ACT DECLARING IT A POLICY OF THE STATE TO PROVIDE UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO RELIABLE, AFFORDABLE, AND ENVIRONMENTALLY SUSTAINABLE ELECTRICITY, ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE PROGRAM FOR THE SOLAR ELECTRIFICATION OF BARANGAYS THAT REMAIN OFF-GRID, PROVIDING A PACKAGE OF FISCAL AND NON-FISCAL INCENTIVES TO ENCOURAGE THE ACTIVE PARTICIPATION OF THE PRIVATE SECTOR, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Energy insecurity in the Philippines is no longer a distant or abstract risk—it is a present and pressing reality that directly affects the daily lives of millions of Filipinos. While significant progress has been made in electrification, a number of barangays, particularly those in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, remain without access to reliable and affordable electricity. For these communities, development is not merely delayed—it is effectively denied. The urgency of this measure is further magnified by recent economic conditions. The country remains heavily dependent on imported petroleum, exposing it to global price volatility. The recent surge in international oil prices, driven by geopolitical tensions, has resulted in consecutive increases in domestic fuel prices. At the same time, the depreciation of the Philippine peso has amplified the cost of imported fuel, compounding the burden on power generation, transportation, and basic goods. These factors are now feeding directly into inflation, eroding purchasing power and placing additional strain on Filipino households. Nowhere is this more acutely felt than in off-grid communities. In these areas, electricity is often generated using diesel, making power costs highly sensitive to fuel price movements and currency fluctuations. As global oil prices rise and the peso weakens, electricity becomes more expensive, less reliable, and increasingly inaccessible. This creates a cycle of disadvantage—where the most vulnerable communities pay the highest price for the least reliable service. This proposed measure responds to this urgent reality by advancing a decisive and forward-looking solution: the accelerated electrification of off-grid barangays through solar energy. Solar power offers a stable, indigenous, and sustainable alternative to imported fuel. It insulates communities from global oil shocks, reduces long-term electricity costs, and provides a reliable foundation for economic activity, education, healthcare, and local enterprise. Through the establishment of a comprehensive Solar Barangay Electrification Program, this bill sets a clear national target of achieving full electrification of all off- grid barangays within ten (10) years. It recognizes that government alone cannot carry this burden and therefore mobilizes private sector participation through well-structured incentives, streamlined processes, and viable public-private partnership models. In doing so, it unlocks capital, innovation, and efficiency at a scale necessary to meet this national objective. This measure is not merely about electrification—it is about equity. It is about ensuring that no Filipino is left behind simply because of geography. It is about transforming energy from a barrier into a bridge for development. And most importantly, it is about asserting that in the face of rising global uncertainty, the Philippines must invest in solutions that are resilient, sustainable, and within our control. In a time when fuel prices are volatile, the peso is under pressure, and inflation threatens the stability of every household, the shift toward renewable, decentralized energy is not optional — it is imperative. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11255
title: AN ACT RECOGNIZING MOTORCYCLES AS PUBLIC UTILITY VEHICLES, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 4136, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LAND TRANSPORTATION AND TRAFFIC CODE,” AS AMENDED, AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991,” AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 4136 does not currently recognize two-wheeled motorcycles as public utility vehicles (PUVs). The Local Government Code authorizes cities and municipalities to regulate tricycles under Sections 447(3)(vi) and 458(3)(vi), but it is silent on motorcycles-for-hire. The result is a regulatory gap: motorcycles are the country’s most accessible two-wheeled mode for short trips and first/last-mile connectivity, yet their carriage of passengers remains governed only by scattered issuances, local ordinances, and a time-bound pilot program. This bill closes that gap by expressly classifying motorcycles-for-hire as PUVs in the Land Transportation and Traffic Code and by aligning LGU franchising powers under the Local Government Code. It is a counterpart measure to Senator Imee R. Marcos’ Senate Bill No. 751. Urban congestion underscores the need for safe, regulated two-wheel public transport. The 2024 TomTom Traffic Index places Davao City, Manila, and Caloocan among the world’s slowest city centers, with average travel times per 10 kilometers of about 32:59, 32:10, and 30:44, respectively, and Davao ranked in the global top ten for worst traffic in 2024. These figures reflect substantial annual hours lost in rush hour for commuters in all three Philippine cities, based on TomTom’s floating-car-data methodology. Policy and regulatory context also point to the need for a clear statute. Republic Act No. 4136 (Land Transportation and Traffic Code) pre-dates platform-mediated transport and contains no category for motorcycles-for-hire; conversely, Republic Act No. 7160 (Local Government Code) explicitly empowers sanggunians to regulate and franchise tricycles but does not address motorcycles-for-hire. The counterpart bill amends Section 3 and Section 7 of RA 4136 to define and classify “motorcycle-for- hire,” and aligns Sections 447(3)(vi) and 458(3)(vi) of RA 7160 so LGUs can franchise motorcycles-for-hire operating strictly within their jurisdictions, subject to LTFRB guidelines. The measure also harmonizes with established safety law. It preserves the helmet mandate and standards under the Motorcycle Helmet Act (RA 10054) and directs LTO to enforce roadworthiness through type-specific inspections, permitted accessories, and speed-limiting/monitoring devices. It further declares motorcycles- for-hire to be common carriers for purposes of Civil Code diligence and liability—an approach consistent with jurisprudence that defines common carriers by the nature of the transport business rather than by vehicle type. Finally, the bill provides institutional clarity between national and local regulation. LTFRB remains the public service franchising authority for route and service standards, while LGUs can set place-specific operating rules (e.g., terminals, lanes, parking) within their territory, consistent with DPWH right-of-way and traffic management standards. This is responsive to the transition from the Department of Transportation’s motorcycle-taxi pilot to a permanent legal framework, following official statements in 2025 acknowledging the 2024 end of the pilot and the urgency of legislation that protects commuters and livelihoods alike. By codifying a national standard for motorcycles-for-hire — including classifications, licensing, insurance, safety equipment, roadworthiness, and clear LGU coordination — Congress will replace ad-hoc, uneven regulation with a uniform, rights- and safety-based framework that matches how Filipinos actually move through their cities. The measure is straightforward: legal recognition in RA 4136, aligned LGU powers in RA 7160, explicit safety and insurance requirements, and Civil Code-based accountability. In a country where city-center trips routinely take half an hour or more per 10 kilometers, lawful, well-regulated motorcycles-for-hire are not a loophole; they are part of the solution. This is a counterpart bill of the Senate Bill No. 751 filed by Sen. Imee Marcos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE DIRECT OR INDIRECT RECOVERY FROM WATER CONSUMERS OF COSTS ATTRIBUTABLE TO NON-REVENUE WATER, REQUIRING WATER SERVICE PROVIDERS TO REDUCE AND PUBLICLY DISCLOSE WATER LOSSES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 63 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 198, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Water is indispensable to life, health, sanitation, commerce, and the daily functioning of every Filipino household. How water is measured and billed is therefore not a mere matter of utility accounting; it is a question of consumer protection and responsible stewardship of a vital natural resource. The scale of the need is stark. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority's preliminary 2024 Annual Poverty Indicators Survey, only 53.1 percent of Filipino families had access to safely managed drinking water service. When water is this scarce and this essential, not a single drop lost to leaks, faulty meters, or mismanagement should be quietly charged to the very families struggling to obtain it. Yet that is precisely what happens. Non-revenue water—the gap between water entering a system and water actually billed—captures both real losses from leaking pipes, reservoirs, and connections, and apparent losses from inaccurate meters, unauthorized use, and billing errors. Authorized public uses such as firefighting and disaster relief are treated separately when properly documented. The Philippine Water Supply and Sanitation Master Plan 2019–2030 records the National Water Resources Board's mandate that non-revenue water should not exceed 25.0 percent. That ceiling exists precisely because water loss is a manageable operating condition — not an unlimited cost to be dumped onto consumers. This measure is the water counterpart to the reform now sweeping the power sector. Just as Congress and the Executive move to stop electric utilities from passing their system losses to consumers by amending Republic Act No. 7832, this bill stops water providers from passing their water losses down the line. The principle is identical across both utilities: the burden of losses belongs to those who control the infrastructure, not to the households at the end of the pipe. The Fair Water Billing Act is the companion measure to system-loss reform in electricity — one Congress, two utilities, a single standard of fairness. The Constitution supplies a firm foundation. Article II, Sections 15 and 16 direct the State to protect the rights to health and to a balanced and healthful ecology. Article XII, Section 2 vests ownership and full control of the nation's waters in the State. Presidential Decree No. 198 authorizes water districts to set cost-recovering rates, but nowhere establishes the nationwide, progressively declining framework this bill provides. Executive Order No. 22 (2023) recognized the sector's fragmentation and created the Water Resources Management Office to harmonize it. The gap this bill fills is therefore real and unaddressed by existing law. The Fair Water Billing Act delivers these principal reforms: 1. Consumers do not pay for inefficiency. During the transition, Sec. 5 bars recovery of non-revenue-water costs exceeding the efficiency benchmark. Even costs within it are recoverable only after audit, public hearing, and specific regulatory findings. 2. The benchmark must keep falling. Sec. 6 caps the initial benchmark at 25 percent of system input (or any lower binding benchmark) and drives it to zero by the end of the fifth year after the implementing rules take effect. 3. The transition is temporary, not a permanent allowance. On expiration, all recovery of non-revenue-water costs is prohibited. 4. The rule covers the whole sector. Sec. 3 reaches water districts, LGU waterworks, MWSS and its concessionaires, private utilities, cooperatives, community and subdivision systems, bulk suppliers, and operators under concessions, joint ventures, and similar arrangements. 5. Hidden recovery is barred. Secs. 7, 9, and 10 prevent prohibited costs from being buried in base rates, fixed charges, tariff adjustments, bulk- water contracts, affiliate transactions, management fees, or renamed billing lines. 6. Loss-reducing investment stays recoverable—under safeguards. Sec. 7 permits prudent pipeline rehabilitation, leak detection, district metering, pressure management, and meter replacement where necessary, cost-effective, transparently procured, independently verified, and protected against double recovery. 7. Consumers gain enforceable rights. Annual performance scorecards, disclosure of beneficial ownership and related-party transactions, public hearings, independent audits, refunds with legal interest, personal accountability for knowing violations, and whistleblower protection. The bill accounts for real differences among providers. A one-time extension of not more than two years may be granted only to a qualified financially distressed public, cooperative, community, or nonprofit provider, and only upon public hearing, an independently audited rehabilitation plan, definite targets, quarterly reporting, and a finding that its distress arose from neither fraud, gross negligence, fund diversion, prohibited related-party dealings, nor willful neglect. A Water Loss Reduction and Modernization Program further assists qualified public and community systems, with assistance walled off from dividends, bonuses, management fees, refunds, and any cost traceable to fraud or gross negligence. The principle is simple and fair: Ang tubig na hindi umabot sa gripo ay hindi dapat umabot sa bayarin. Responsibility must rest with those who control the pipelines, meters, reservoirs, billing systems, and investment decisions. By pairing a defined transition, declining benchmarks, public scrutiny, and eventual zero recovery, the Fair Water Billing Act protects consumers while preserving lawful and prudent utility operations — completing, on the water side, the same promise of fairness now being written into the nation's power bills. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 11257
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS PENSION FUND TO PROVIDE PENSION TO OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The constitutional foundation is clear: the State affirms labor as a primary social and economic force and shall protect workers and promote their welfare. A permanent OFW pension responds to a measurable need in a sector that sustains national income and household consumption. Official statistics show the scale and persistence of overseas employment: the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) estimates 2.16 million OFWs worked abroad from April to September 2023, up 9.8 percent from 2022. This is not an abstract constituency but a large, continuing labor cohort whose earnings drive remittance flows and anchor macroeconomic stability. Remittances remain a pillar of external accounts. The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas reports bank-coursed cash remittances reached US$34.49 billion in 2024, three percent higher than 2023, with monthly inflows approaching US$3.0 billion by August 2025. The reliability of these inflows is precisely why social protection for the workers who generate them merits statutory support. Institutional readiness also exists. The Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), created under Republic Act No. 11641, is mandated to protect OFWs throughout the migration cycle, including reintegration. Assigning the DMW to design, administer, and regulate the OFW pension mechanism aligns with its legal mandate and consolidates accountability in a single implementing agency with sector expertise, existing field networks, and regulatory reach. The policy substance of this measure is straightforward and implementable. First, it establishes an OFW Pension Fund and a DMW-administered pension plan that guarantees not less than ₱5,000 per month to eligible retirees, separate from SSS or GSIS benefits, thereby avoiding overlap and preserving the integrity of existing social insurance systems. Second, it defines clear eligibility grounded in verifiable employment history and registration records, minimizing administrative discretion and enabling credible targeting. Third, it mandates inter-agency coordination among DMW, DOF, OWWA, POEA’s successor offices, and DFA to ensure sound fund governance, accurate data matching, and international servicing through posts and welfare offices. These features mirror institutional arrangements already used for OFW services and can be implemented with existing registries and remittance data, reducing transaction costs and leakage risk. The economic and social rationale is compelling: One, the OFW population skews toward occupations with physical strain and irregular income continuity; a predictable pension offsets late-life income volatility and reduces old-age poverty risk in households historically sustained by remittances. Two, remittance-dependent localities benefit when returning workers have stable purchasing power, supporting local enterprise and mitigating negative demand shocks. Three, the program codifies the State’s recognition of a group whose foreign earnings cushion the current account and stabilize consumption during domestic downturns, strengthening social cohesion and trust in public institutions. Each of these impacts is anchored in the documented size of the OFW workforce and the volume and stability of remittance inflows cited above. This bill is a counterpart measure to Senate Bill No. 252, “OFW Pension Act of 2025,” filed by Sen. Erwin Tulfo, which seeks to establish a dedicated pension fund for Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs) to provide a minimum monthly pension upon retirement. In view of the magnitude of the sector, the proven role of remittances in the economy, and the DMW’s statutory mandate to protect and reintegrate OFWs, the immediate passage of this counterpart measure is respectfully sought. label: HB 11258
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING GOVERNMENT SUPPORT FOR THE DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION OF MICRO, SMALL, AND MEDIUM ENTERPRISES (MSMEs) THROUGH E‑COMMERCE AND RESPONSIBLE USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Micro, small, and medium enterprises constitute 99.63 percent of the Philippines’ 1.24 million business establishments and generate 6.35 million jobs—roughly two-thirds of total employment nationwide. Yet only 15,998 of these firms were actively transacting online in 2023, a fraction of the sector’s potential market reach. This participation gap persists even as the digital economy contributed ₱2.25 trillion, or about 8.5 percent of gross domestic product, in 2024. Household connectivity barriers are receding: the Women and ICT Development Index survey recorded a surge in home internet access from 17.7 percent in 2019 to 76.9 percent in 2022, confirming that physical access is no longer the primary hurdle to online commerce. Instead, MSMEs cite cost, skills shortages, logistics frictions, and mounting cyber-risks. Fortinet’s 2024 threat-landscape report found that six in ten Philippine companies experienced a three-fold increase in cyber-attacks in 2023. At the same time, the Philippines climbed nine places to 56th out of 188 economies in Oxford Insights’ 2024 Government AI Readiness Index, evidence of growing institutional capacity to deploy artificial intelligence responsibly. Harnessing these twin trends — rapid connectivity gains and improving AI readiness — demands a coherent policy response that lowers the cost of digital entry, embeds cybersecurity, and accelerates skills formation for the country’s smallest firms. The MSME E-Commerce Support Act delivers that response. First, it creates a Digital and AI Transformation Grant that defrays the costs of web storefronts, AI-enabled marketing tools, smart-logistics interfaces, and mandatory data-protection safeguards. Second, it mandates a nationwide capacity-building programme — jointly implemented by DTI, DICT, TESDA, and CHED — to upskill entrepreneurs and employees in e-commerce operations, AI fundamentals, and cybersecurity compliance. Third, it institutionalises a logistics-access scheme that links MSMEs to affordable warehousing and last-mile delivery services, especially in underserved regions. Fourth, it establishes voluntary AI sandboxes where firms can pilot emerging technologies under regulatory guidance from the DICT and National Privacy Commission. Fifth, the bill directs the MSME Development Council to publish open-data dashboards tracking digital-adoption rates, sales growth, and risk-reduction outcomes, ensuring transparency and evidence-based course correction. The measure aligns squarely with Article XII, Section 1 of the Constitution, which obliges the State to promote industrialization and full employment. By lowering the threshold for digital participation, the bill empowers the sector that already provides the majority of jobs to reach new domestic and export markets, strengthens consumer protection through mandatory cybersecurity upgrades, and positions Philippine enterprises to capitalize on responsible artificial-intelligence tools. Enactment will not only modernize commerce but also deepen economic resilience and broaden the tax base—benefits that accrue to workers, consumers, and the national treasury alike. Passage of this bill is therefore earnestly sought. label: HB 11259
title: AN ACT PROMOTING THE WIDESPREAD USE OF SOLAR POWER AMONG FILIPINOS, PROVIDING INCENTIVES FOR SOLAR ENERGY ADOPTION, ESTABLISHING THE SOLAR POWER ACCESS PROGRAM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines, as an archipelago situated in the tropical Pacific, is among the most solar-rich countries in the world, receiving an average solar irradiance of approximately 4.5 to 5.5 kilowatt-hours per square meter per day. Despite this immense natural endowment, solar energy remains significantly underutilized, with millions of Filipinos — particularly those in rural, remote, and island communities — still lacking access to reliable and affordable electricity. According to the Department of Energy, the Philippines' total installed solar capacity stands at approximately 3,600 megawatts, a fraction of the country's enormous solar potential estimated at over 150,000 megawatts. The Philippine Development Plan and the National Renewable Energy Program have set ambitious targets for renewable energy, yet the pace of solar adoption — especially at the household and community levels — remains far too slow to meet these goals. The high upfront cost of solar power systems remains the single greatest barrier to adoption for ordinary Filipino families. A basic residential rooftop solar installation costs between Php 150,000 to Php 400,000 — far beyond the reach of most households, particularly the estimated 22 million Filipinos living below the poverty line. Compounding this is the lack of accessible financing options, insufficient consumer protection, and the absence of a comprehensive national framework targeting solar adoption among ordinary citizens. Meanwhile, the country continues to suffer from high electricity rates, among the highest in Southeast Asia, which disproportionately burden low-income families and undermine the competitiveness of Filipino businesses. Frequent power outages, dependence on imported fossil fuels, and the devastating impacts of climate change — to which the Philippines is acutely vulnerable as one of the world's most disaster- prone nations — underscore the urgency of accelerating the transition to solar energy. The enactment of Republic Act No. 9513 or the Renewable Energy Act of 2008 and subsequent Net Metering Rules were significant milestones. However, these laws have largely benefited middle- and upper-income consumers and businesses, leaving behind the very Filipinos who stand to gain the most from cheaper, cleaner electricity. There is presently no dedicated law that comprehensively addresses the barriers to solar adoption for low-income households, geographically isolated communities, and small enterprises. In response to this urgent need, this bill — the Solar Power Access and Adoption Act of the Philippines or the SolarPH Act — seeks to establish a comprehensive legal and institutional framework for the widespread adoption of solar energy among all Filipinos. Specifically, the bill aims to: First, establish the Solar Power Access Program (SolarPH Program) — a government-led initiative that will provide subsidized and affordable solar power systems to low-income households, fund community solar installations in public schools and health centers, and ensure the full electrification of geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas (GIDAs) through off-grid solar solutions; Second, provide a robust package of fiscal incentives — including a 25% income tax credit, VAT exemptions, customs duty exemptions, and low-interest concessional loans — to make solar power genuinely affordable for ordinary Filipino households and small businesses; Third, strengthen and expand the Net Metering Program to enable more Filipino solar prosumers to sell excess electricity back to the grid, transforming households from passive consumers into active participants in the energy market; Fourth, mandate local government units to play an active role in promoting solar energy adoption within their jurisdictions, streamlining permitting processes, and funding community solar projects; Fifth, promote the development of a local solar industry through domestic manufacturing incentives, a TESDA certification program for solar technicians, and government-funded research and development; and Sixth, establish strong consumer protection mechanisms, including mandatory product standards, warranty requirements, and a licensing system for solar installers, to safeguard Filipino consumers. The Philippines cannot afford to delay its solar transition. Every year without comprehensive solar policy is a year of continued dependence on expensive imported oil, continued exposure to fuel price volatility, continued carbon emissions, and continued energy poverty for millions of our countrymen. The sun shines generously on every Philippine island — this bill ensures that its light and warmth reach every Filipino home. In view of the foregoing, the swift passage of this measure is earnestly sought. label: HB 11260
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO PUBLIC ATTORNEYS EXPOSED TO HAZARDOUS SITUATIONS AND PERFORMING HAZARDOUS DUTIES RELATED TO THEIR OFFICIAL FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Republic Act No. 9406, the Public Attorney’s Office (PAO) is mandated to independently provide legal representation, assistance, and counseling to indigent persons in criminal, civil, labor, administrative, and other quasi-judicial cases. In the performance of this mandate, public attorneys are often required to handle cases involving serious and violent offenses and to represent persons who may be associated with dangerous criminal organizations, drug syndicates, or armed groups. They may likewise be assigned to remote, isolated, or conflict-affected areas, where they are exposed to threats of violence, retaliation, infectious diseases, and other substantial risks arising from the nature and circumstances of their duties. Republic Act No. 9406 and its Implementing Rules and Regulations provide for special allowances funded from a Special Trust Fund consisting principally of success fees collected after successful litigation. Those special allowances, however, are distinct from hazard pay because they are not specifically tied to the actual performance of dangerous assignments or exposure to hazardous conditions. The proposed measure seeks to grant a monthly hazard pay of Five Thousand Pesos ((₱5,000.00) to public attorneys who, by reason of the nature, location, or circumstances of their assignments, are exposed to substantial risks to their safety, health, or security. The measure recognizes that the hazards faced by public attorneys are not merely incidental to the practice of law but may arise 1 directly from their duty to provide legal assistance to indigent persons, particularly in criminal and other high-risk cases. In view of the foregoing, the passage of the bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 11261
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO PUBLIC PROSECUTORS EXPOSED TO HAZARDOUS SITUATIONS AND PERFORMING HAZARDOUS DUTIES RELATED TO ASSIGNED CASES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Public prosecutors are the State’s principal litigators. They are responsible for enforcing the law, protecting the public, and ensuring that justice is served. In the discharge of their duties, they handle sensitive and high-risk cases involving drug syndicates, terrorist groups, organized crime, corrupt officials, and other dangerous criminal elements. The nature of their work exposes prosecutors to threats, harassment, intimidation, and violence, with some even losing their lives in the line of duty. Records from 2013 to 2024 show that at least 14 prosecutors have been killed in connection with their official duties. These incidents demonstrate the serious risks associated with prosecutorial work and the need for the State to provide adequate protection and support to those who perform these vital functions. Despite the risks inherent in their work, public prosecutors do not currently receive hazard pay or a similar risk allowance under existing laws. This is in contrast to other frontline government workers, such as health personnel, disaster responders, and law enforcement officers, who are granted additional compensation for performing hazardous duties. Extending a similar benefit to public prosecutors is a recognition of the risks they face in the performance of their official functions. This measure seeks to address this disparity by granting a monthly hazard pay of Five Thousand Pesos (₱5,000.00) to qualified public prosecutors who are involved in the investigation or prosecution of cases involving crimes against national security, illegal drugs, graft and corruption, money laundering, terrorism, and other analogous offenses. The hazard pay shall be granted in 1 addition to their basic salary and other existing allowances and shall not be subject to reduction or diminution. This measure recognizes the hazardous nature of prosecutorial work and the personal risks undertaken by public prosecutors in the pursuit of justice. It seeks to provide appropriate compensation for such risks and affirm the State’s support for those who uphold the rule of law. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. EDUARDO R. label: HB 11262
title: AN ACT CREATING FIVE (5) ADDITIONAL BRANCHES OF THE REGIONAL TRIAL COURT IN THE CITY OF CEBU, PROVINCE OF CEBU, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 129, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUDICIARY REORGANIZATION ACT OF 1980”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Cebu City is the most populous highly urbanized city in Central Visayas. It serves as a principal center for commerce, education, health care, and government services in the region and consequently receives a substantial volume of litigation arising from its dense population and extensive economic activity. The existing Regional Trial Court (RTC) branches in Cebu City are required to handle a broad range of cases, including criminal prosecutions, civil actions, commercial disputes, special proceedings, and other matters assigned by law. Evidently, the increasing volume of cases place significant burden on the existing courts, judges, and court personnel. When judicial dockets become congested, hearings may be scheduled farther apart, resulting in delays in the resolution of cases and litigants incurring additional expenses in pursuing or defending their claims. The creation of additional RTC branches will allow for a more equitable distribution of cases, improved calendar management, and closer attention to the requirements of each docket. It will also help promote the constitutional guarantee of a speedy disposition of cases and enhance public access to justice. Thus, enactment of this measure will help reduce docket congestion, improve the timely disposition of cases, lower the costs of litigation, and strengthen the delivery of judicial services in Cebu City. 1 It is therefore earnestly urged that this bill be given favorable consideration and immediate approval. label: HB 11265
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING CHILDREN BELOW TWELVE (12) YEARS OF AGE FROM CREATING OR MAINTAINING PERSONAL SOCIAL-MEDIA ACCOUNTS, PROVIDING FOR CHILD-SAFETY MECHANISMS, PLATFORM ACCOUNTABILITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward.” — Psalm 127:3 (KJV) “The State shall defend the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation and other conditions prejudicial to their development.” — Article XV, Section 3(2), 1987 Constitution The Holy Writ warns of a generation that “curseth their father,” is “pure in their own eyes,” has “lofty” eyes, and whose words are like “swords” and “knives” that harm the poor and needy (Proverbs 30:11–14, KJV). In today’s digital age, social media can amplify and normalize the disrespect, self-righteousness, pride, cruelty, and harmful behavior described in these passages. Young children, whose judgment and character are still developing, are particularly vulnerable to absorbing, imitating, or becoming victims of such influences. The State must therefore establish reasonable safeguards to protect them from premature exposure to online environment they may not yet be equipped to navigate safely and responsibly. Against this moral and constitutional backdrop, children increasingly encounter digital technologies at home and through social-media services. While digital technologies may provide communication and access to information, social- media platforms may also expose young children to grooming, luring, online sexual abuse or exploitation, cyberbullying, harmful content, privacy violations, fraudulent schemes, excessive screen use, and manipulative design. Page 1 of 14 Young children below twelve (12) years of age require heightened protection because of their developing capacity to assess risks, understand privacy consequences, identify manipulation, and protect themselves from online abuse and exploitation. This bill therefore prohibits children below twelve (12) years of age from creating, registering, operating, or maintaining personal social-media accounts, but does not prohibit them from accessing the internet generally, viewing publicly available lawful content, or using an account controlled by a parent, guardian, government agency, or institution for a lawful non-personal purpose. Under the bill, covered platforms are mandated to take reasonable and proportionate measures to prevent children below twelve (12) years of age from creating or maintaining personal social-media accounts. They shall apply child-safety safeguards, provide child-friendly reporting mechanisms, restrict unlawful and seriously harmful content, and refrain from using age-assurance information for targeted advertising or behavioral profiling. The bill likewise requires privacy-preserving age assurance and prohibits the routine collection of government-issued identification documents and biometric information. It also requires covered platforms to maintain child-safety programs, designate responsible officers, establish reporting and appeals mechanisms, and cooperate with competent government authorities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. BIENVENIDO M. ABANTE, JR.
