label: HB 11266
title: AN ACT CREATING THE PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD COMMISSION AS AN INDEPENDENT PERSONNEL GOVERNANCE AND OVERSIGHT BODY FOR THE PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING FOR ITS HARMONIZATION WITH THE REVISED PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD LAW, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9993, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "PHILIPPINE COAST GUARD LAW OF 2009," APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 16 Article II, Section 3 of the 1987 Constitution declares that civilian authority is, at all times, supreme over the military. Article XVI, Section 6 thereof mandates the State to establish and maintain one police force, national in scope and civilian in character, to be administered and controlled by a national police commission. Both provisions proceed from a common constitutional premise: that an armed and uniformed service of the Republic must remain accountable to an institutional authority beyond its own chain of command. 23 The Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), notwithstanding its character as an armed and uniformed service, has never been accorded such an institutional mechanism. 26 Originally constituted as a major unit of the Philippine Navy under Republic Act No. 5173 in 1967, transferred to the then Department of Transportation and Communications in 1998, and subsequently established as an armed and uniformed service under Republic Act No. 9993 in 2010, the PCG has expanded from a force of approximately three thousand (3,000) personnel into one of the largest maritime law enforcement agencies in the region. It now comprises tens of thousands of officers and non-officers, maintains a fleet of ocean-going vessels and aircraft, and performs a frontline role in the assertion of the country's sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the West Philippine Sea. Its personnel bear arms, exercise powers of arrest, search, and seizure, board and detain vessels, and operate in contested waters where the decision of a single officer may carry consequences of national significance. 37 The institutional governance of the PCG, however, has not kept pace with the growth of its organization and mandate. Under existing law, the command of the service and the administration of its personnel are vested in a single office. The Commandant directs operations and, at the same time, determines matters of promotion, assignment to major commands, and discipline. Unlike the Philippine National Police, whose administration and control are vested in the National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM) under Republic Act No. 6975, as amended by Republic Act No. 8551, the PCG has no specialized statutory body that reviews these matters independently of the chain of command. 46 This deficiency is most pronounced at the highest ranks. Under Article VII, Section 16 of the Constitution, as construed by the Supreme Court in Manalo v. Sistoza (G.R. No. 107369, 11 August 1999), only officers of the armed forces from the rank of colonel or naval captain require confirmation by the Commission on Appointments. Flag officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines are thus subject to legislative scrutiny, while senior officers of the Philippine National Police are subject to the screening and endorsement of the NAPOLCOM. Flag officers of the PCG are subject to neither. No professional body evaluates their qualifications prior to appointment, nor reviews the exercise of their authority thereafter. 6 This measure is introduced while Congress undertakes a comprehensive revision of the statutory framework of the PCG. On 11 August 2026, the Senate approved on third and final reading Senate Bill No. 2116, or the proposed Revised Philippine Coast Guard Law, which reorganizes the PCG into functional, support, and technical commands, prescribes clearer rules on ranks, appointments, and promotions, and strengthens internal accountability through a Coast Guard Internal Affairs Service. In the House of Representatives, the Committee on Transportation is deliberating on a Substitute Bill to House Bills Nos. 426, 1120, 3390, 4693, 4758, 5127, 5131, 5471, 5552, 5758, 6104, 6173, 6244, 6386, 8027, and 9204, which seeks to strengthen the PCG through policy and organizational reforms. 16 Mindful of these parallel efforts, this bill is crafted to complement, and not to duplicate, the Revised Philippine Coast Guard Law. It does not establish a separate organizational, personnel, promotion, disciplinary, or career-management system. It contains an express harmonization clause and rule of construction; it requires that professional standards and career progression criteria conform to the functional organization adopted under the Revised Philippine Coast Guard Law; it relies upon the Internal Affairs Service for investigation and fact-finding, in lieu of creating a competing investigative body; and it limits any transfer of functions to those expressly vested in the Commission by law. 25 Neither does this bill place the Commission within, or above, the chain of command of the PCG. The Commission is constituted as an independent personnel governance and oversight body, not as an administrative superior of the Commandant, and is expressly denied any authority over the operations, budget, finances, procurement, and assets of the service. Its powers are confined to those enumerated by law, namely: the promulgation of governance standards and the review of compliance therewith; the validation of the promotion of senior officers; the validation of the assignment of flag officers to major unit commands; the professional screening of nominees for Commandant for the consideration of the President; and the exercise of appellate and review authority in administrative disciplinary cases. 35 The distinction between command and governance is deliberate. Command, being the direction of personnel, vessels, aircraft, and resources in the accomplishment of the mission, is vested in, and shall remain with, the Commandant. The PCG shall continue to administer its personnel system, including recruitment, training, assignment, career management, and personnel records, while the Commission shall safeguard the integrity of that system. The Commandant recommends; the Commission independently validates; and the President appoints or promotes where so required by the Constitution or by law. In no instance may the Commission substitute its own choice for the recommendatio

label: HB 11273
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A NATIONAL EYE HEALTH PROGRAM FOR SENIOR CITIZENS WITH FUNCTIONAL VISUAL IMPAIRMENTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to provide accessible and comprehensive eye care services for senior citizens with functional visual impairments. It establishes a National Eye Health Program for Senior Citizens which aims to improve early detection, treatment, rehabilitation, and vision support services to help older Filipinos maintain their independence and quality of life. Visual impairment is one of the leading causes of disability among older persons and is often caused by preventable or treatable conditions such as cataracts, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, and age-related macular degeneration. According to the World Health Organization, at least 2.2 billion people worldwide have a vision impairment, and over one (1) billion cases could have been prevented or have yet to be addressed.1 In the Philippines, the growing senior citizen population underscores the need to strengthen accessible eye care services to prevent avoidable blindness and vision loss.2 Despite existing public health programs, many elderly Filipinos continue to experience barriers to eye care due to financial constraints, limited access to specialists, and inadequate community-based vision services. This measure addresses these gaps by institutionalizing a dedicated national program under the Department of Health to deliver essential eye services and improve the functional capacity and overall well-being of older persons. Protecting the eyesight of senior citizens enables them to remain active, productive, and independent members of society while reducing preventable disability and improving their quality of life. Jakarta, Indonesia: Economic Research Institute for ASEAN and East Asia. national eye health program is a timely investment in healthy aging and dignified elderly care. label: HB 11274
title: AN ACT TO PROHIBIT SECONDARY AND HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS FROM CONDUCTING MANDATORY IMMERSIONS, INTERNSHIP PROGRAMS, OR ON-THE-JOB TRAINING PROGRAMS OUTSIDE THE PROVINCE WHERE THE CAMPUS IS LOCATED OR ABROAD, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to prohibit secondary schools and higher education institutions from requiring students to complete work immersion, internship, or on-the-job training (OJT) programs abroad or outside the province where the institution is located as a mandatory requirement for graduation. It ensures that participation in such programs remains voluntary and subject to the informed consent of students and their parents or guardians. Experiential learning programs play a vital role in preparing students for the workforce. However, when these programs are conducted outside the student's home province or abroad and are made compulsory, they often impose significant financial burdens on students and their families. Transportation, accommodation, meals, and other incidental expenses can become prohibitive, particularly for learners from low-income households, forcing some students to incur debt, delay completion of their academic requirements, or forego educational opportunities altogether. Education shall be accessible to all, and existing laws recognize the duty of the State to remove barriers that prevent students from completing their education. This measure ensures that educational institutions cannot compel students to participate in costly off-site immersion or internship programs as a condition for graduation. At the same time, it preserves opportunities for students who voluntarily wish to participate in such programs and strengthens accountability through mandatory reporting and regulatory oversight. No student should be denied the opportunity to graduate simply because they cannot afford the additional expenses associated with mandatory out-of-province or overseas training. This measure upholds fairness, protects the right to accessible education, and ensures that experiential learning remains an opportunity rather than a financial obstacle. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11275
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL COORDINATING COUNCIL FOR EDUCATION, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish the National Coordinating Council for Education (NCCE), a body under the Office of the President, which shall harmonize policies, plans, and investments across the Philippine education sector. It shall strengthen coordination among the Department of Education (DepEd), the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), and other key agencies to ensure that education reforms are aligned with national development priorities and labor market demands. The Philippine education system continues to face fragmented governance, resulting in weak coordination and policy consistencies. The Second Congressional Commission on Education pointed out that the historical “trifocalization” of the Philippine education system, which split DepEd, CHED, and TESDA has led to fragmented planning and a lack of accountability. This resulting absence of a central coordinating mechanism has contributed to persistent learning gaps, skills mismatch, and inefficiencies in education planning and resource allocation.1 This measure establishes the NCCE as the government’s principal coordinating body for education and workforce development. It integrates aligning curricula with labor market needs, strengthening data-driven policymaking national education policies and aligns curricula with labor market needs. Education is the cornerstone of national development. Ensuring effective coordination across all levels of the education sector is indispensable to producing globally competitive, highly skilled, and future-ready Filipinos. Second Congressional Commission on Education. measure will help build a more responsive, efficient, and resilient education system capable of meeting the country's long-term development goals. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11276
title: AN ACT CREATING A SUSTAINABLE FISCAL FRAMEWORK FOR THE PENSION SYSTEM OF THE MILITARY AND UNIFORMED PERSONNEL, PROVIDING MECHANISMS FOR THE DISPOSITION OF GOVERNMENT ASSETS FOR THE PURPOSE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a sustainable and fiscally responsible pension system for Military and Uniformed Personnel (MUP). It creates a comprehensive funding framework, institutionalizes dedicated trust funds, and safeguards the welfare of both current and future personnel. The country’s military and uniformed personnel perform indispensable roles in defending national sovereignty, maintaining peace and order, enforcing the law, responding to disasters, and ensuring public safety. In recognition of the unique risks and sacrifices inherent in their profession, the State has long provided retirement and pension benefits that serve as a vital form of social protection. However, the current pension system has become increasingly vulnerable to fiscal pressures due to its non-contributory structure, automatic indexation, rising life expectancy, and the growing number of retirees. These factors have significantly increased the financial burden on the National Government, raising concerns over the long-term sustainability of pension obligations. The measure introduces a contributory pension scheme for new entrants while preserving the vested rights of existing personnel. It likewise strengthens fiscal risk management, harmonizes retirement and disability benefits, provides assistance to indigent pensioners, and institutionalizes mechanisms that ensure transparency, accountability, and actuarial soundness in the administration of pension funds. This vital piece of legislation promotes a pension system that is equitable, sustainable, and responsive to future generations. It strengthens public confidence that those who dedicate their lives to protecting the nation will continue to receive secure retirement benefits without compromising the country's long-term financial stability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11277
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL AFFORDABLE STUDENT LOAN PROGRAM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a National Affordable Student Loan Program, which offers a sustainable, low-interest student financing system for Filipino learners. It provides affordable education loans with a fixed interest rate, flexible repayment terms, and borrower protection mechanisms to complement existing government scholarship and financial assistance programs. While the government has expanded access to free tertiary education through Republic Act No. 10931, otherwise known as the “Universal Access to Quality Tertiary Education Act”, many Filipino students continue to struggle with expenses that remain beyond the coverage of free tuition, including books, transportation, accommodation, digital learning tools, internship costs, review classes, and other education-related expenses. These financial burdens continue to prevent many students, particularly those from low-income families, from completing their education or pursuing graduate and professional studies. This measure institutionalizes the National Affordable Student Loan Program administered by government financial institutions, providing accessible financing at a fixed two percent (2%) annual interest rate. It likewise introduces a reasonable grace period, collateral-free borrowing, borrower protection measures, and transparent lending standards to ensure that financial assistance remains affordable, sustainable, and responsive to the needs of Filipino learners. Investing in education is an investment in the country's future. In making educational financing more accessible and equitable, the State continues to empower more Filipinos to acquire knowledge and skills that will strengthen the nation's workforce, improve social mobility, and promote inclusive economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11278
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE ACCESS OF UNQUALIFIED INDIVIDUALS TO ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to restrict the purchase, sale, possession, and provision of alcoholic beverages to persons below twenty-one (21) years of age and other individuals who, because of a physical or mental disability or condition, are unable to adequately protect themselves from abuse or exploitation. It also holds adults and establishments accountable for selling and providing alcohol to these individuals. The World Health Organization1, has identified alcohol as a psychoactive and dependence-producing substance associated with more than two hundred (200) diseases, injuries, and health conditions. Starting to drink at an early age may also increase the risk of developing harmful drinking habits later in life. Preventing access to alcohol among young people is therefore an important measure to protect their health and well-being. The Philippines currently does not have a law which prohibits underage access to alcoholic beverages, and that sets the guidelines for enforcing such prohibition. As a result, protection and enforcement may vary across communities. This proposed measure clearly defines the prohibited acts, allocates responsibilities among establishments, parents, local government units, and government agencies in enforcing the law. It also recognizes that young and vulnerable individuals should receive guidance rather than be subjected immediately to criminal penalties, therefore adopting interventions that emphasize rehabilitation over punishment for young offenders. The consequences of underage drinking extend far beyond a single act of alcohol consumption. label: HB 11279
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING THE PAYMENT OF REVIEW FEES FOR BOARD AND BAR EXAMINATIONS FOR QUALIFIED INDIGENTS ON THEIR FIRST TAKE
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to exempt qualified indigent Filipino graduates from paying review fees for their first board or bar examination. It helps remove what may prevent academically qualified graduates from obtaining the review preparation necessary to ace the exams. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (2026)1, eight hundred and eighty-one (881) out of one thousand six hundred eleven (1,611) cities and municipalities recorded poverty incidence levels of twenty percent (20%) or lower in 2023, while seven hundred and twenty two (722) localities continued to register poverty incidence above twenty percent (20%), including areas classified under higher poverty levels. Fresh graduates invest for review courses and examination materials after completing their degrees. For indigent graduates from economically disadvantaged backgrounds, these costs may delay their first attempt at the board or bar examination, thus limiting professional opportunities that their education would otherwise provide. The proposed measure provides assistance to indigent graduates who are first-time license exam takers who have demonstrated academic excellence. It shall cover review courses and related preparatory materials for board and bar examinations. Expanding opportunities for qualified indigent graduates to obtain professional licenses strengthens the country’s human capital and allows more Filipinos to contribute their knowledge and expertise to national development. label: HB 11280
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE OWNERSHIP AND OPERATION OF DRONES BY PRIVATE PERSONS AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to regulate the ownership and use of drones by private individuals. It authorizes the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) to regulate drone registration and operation and addresses public safety concerns arising from the increasing use of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). While the CAAP has adopted regulations governing drone registration, certification, and flight limitations, these remain administrative in nature and do not cover private ownership, accountability of registered owners, and enforcement of violations. The institutionalization of such regulations is necessary to provide a more stable and enforceable basis for regulating private drone ownership and use. The proposed measure requires all privately owned drones to register with the CAAP and subjects commercial operations to a permit-to-operate requirement. It also provides CAAP with authority to establish no-drone zones, prescribe operational standards, and impose measures responsive to developments in drone technology. It likewise provides penalties for violations of safety regulations and imposes responsibility for damage, injury, or loss which shall result from its negligent, reckless, or unlawful operation. Drones have become valuable tools in various industries and activities, but their increasing accessibility requires corresponding safeguards to protect public safety and individual rights. A single irresponsible operation can compromise airspace security and infringe upon personal privacy. The establishment of clear rules for drone ownership and use shall build public confidence in the safe adoption of emerging technologies. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11281
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SCHOOL-BASED MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES FOR THE YOUTH, PROVIDING FOR THE DEPLOYMENT OF MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS AND STRENGTHENING EARLY INTERVENTION MECHANISMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to improve the delivery of mental health services for the Filipino youth in basic education institutions, secondary schools, and State Universities and Colleges (SUCs). It mandates the deployment of at least one (1) licensed mental health professional in each institution and strengthens early intervention efforts for the students. Mental health disorders among children and adolescents have become a growing public health concern, with excessive screentime seen as a contributing factor to it. It has also exposed young people to addictive platform designs, which adversely affects their mental health, and impedes their emotional development and academic performance1. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the “Mental Health Act”, access to mental health services in schools remains limited, and many educational institutions lack adequate personnel and structured intervention programs. This bill offers annual mental health screening, counseling services, and teacher training on mental health and psychosocial support. It likewise mandates the deployment of licensed mental health professionals, establishes an annual Digital Detox Week, and requires the publication of a national report on youth mental health and digital behavior. These steps are taken to strengthen prevention, facilitate early intervention, and improve coordination among the education, health, and digital governance sectors. Promoting the mental health and digital wellbeing of Filipino learners is essential to improving educational outcomes and developing a healthy, resilient, and productive generation. Institutionalizing these interventions will enable the government to provide sustained and evidence-based support to young Filipinos. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 World Health Organization (2x026). Mental health of adolescents. World Health Organization. Accessed via https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/adolescent-mental-health. Accessed on 8 July 2026. label: HB 11282
title: AN ACT PENALIZING THE ACT OF WAGE THEFT, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE ARTICLES 87 AND 116 OF PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 442, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “LABOR CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to amend Articles 87 and 116 of Presidential Decree No. 442, otherwise known as the “Labor Code of the Philippines”, and penalize the act of wage theft. It expands the prohibition against the unlawful withholding of wages and employment benefits, and imposes criminal and administrative penalties on employers who violate workers’ rights. Incidents of unpaid wages, underpayment, delayed compensation, non-payment of overtime pay, and withholding of employment benefits continue to undermine labor standards and workers’ right to just compensation. It affects low-income workers who rely on timely payment of wages to meet their daily needs, and that of the daily sustenance of their families. This bill expands existing prohibitions to cover unpaid wages, overtime pay, bonuses, tips, reimbursements, and other legally due benefits. It likewise penalizes discriminatory practices in the allocation of overtime work, imposes criminal liability on responsible employers and corporate officers, and authorizes the suspension or cancellation of business permits for repeated violations. These shall strengthen workers’ rights while promoting compliance with labor standards. The payment of lawful wages is not merely a contractual obligation but a matter of social justice. Legislation must uphold the dignity of labor and ensure that every worker receives the compensation rightfully earned. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11283
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PARTICIPATION OF CIVIL SOCIETY ORGANIZATIONS IN THE PREPARATION AND AUTHORIZATION PROCESS OF THE ANNUAL NATIONAL BUDGET, PROVIDING EFFECTIVE MECHANISMS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize the participation of civil society organizations (CSOs) in the preparation and authorization of the annual national budget. It establishes mechanisms for accreditation, consultation, and access to budget information. Meaningful public participation is a fundamental component of transparent, accountable, and responsive governance. While citizen participation in local governance exists, providing for its institutionalization ensures the systematic involvement of CSOs throughout the national budget process. This promotes transparency, enhances public trust in government institutions, and improves the allocation of public resources. This bill requires national government agencies and government-owned or -controlled corporations to adopt participatory mechanisms, grants accredited CSOs access to key budget documents and deliberations, and institutionalizes structured engagement during budget preparation and congressional authorization. It likewise promotes transparency by requiring the timely disclosure of budget information and safeguards the integrity of CSO participation through accreditation and conflict-of-interest provisions. The proposed measure reinforces the constitutional principles of transparency, accountability, and public participation in governance. Further, it ensures that the national budget more accurately reflects the needs and priorities of the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11284
title: AN ACT MAINSTREAMING CLIMATE ACTION ACROSS NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE A CLIMATE FINANCE UNIT UNDER THE CLIMATE CHANGE COMMISSION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Climate Finance Unit (CFU) under the Climate Change Commission. This institutionalizes a comprehensive national climate finance framework and enhances access to multilateral climate financing mechanisms and public-private partnerships. The Philippines remains among the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change. Increasingly frequent and severe typhoons, floods, droughts, sea level rise, and extreme heat continue to threaten lives, livelihoods, infrastructure, food security, and economic development. While the country has adopted key climate policies, access to and coordination of climate finance remain fragmented across government agencies and local government units, limiting the timely implementation of climate adaptation and mitigation initiatives. The proposed measure likewise integrates climate finance into national and local development planning, promotes innovative financing instruments, and strengthens monitoring and reporting systems to ensure that public investments generate measurable climate resilience and sustainable development outcomes. Establishing a centralized climate finance mechanism shall improve resource mobilization, strengthen fiscal accountability, and accelerate the implementation of climate-resilient programs nationwide. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11285
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR AN ADVANCED NURSING EDUCATION PROGRAM, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9173, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE NURSING ACT OF 2002”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to institutionalize a more comprehensive nursing education framework that formally recognizes both basic and advanced nursing education programs. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9173, otherwise known as the “Philippine Nursing Act of 2002”, and integrates master’s and doctoral degree pathways into the nursing education system. It enhances faculty qualification standards and aligns the preparation of Filipino nurses with the evolving demands of healthcare delivery and higher education. The Philippine healthcare system continues to face increasing demand for highly trained nursing professionals capable of assuming advanced clinical, research, academic, and leadership roles. According to the World Health Organization1, nurses constitute the largest segment of the global health workforce. Yet, many countries continue to experience shortages of highly skilled nursing professionals capable of delivering specialized care and strengthening health systems. Nursing students are presented with limited opportunities for structured career progression and constrains the country’s capacity to expand nursing research, improve evidence-based practice, and strengthen healthcare leadership. The proposed measure establishes a legal framework for advanced nursing programs that cultivate expertise in clinical practice, research, health policy, leadership, and nursing education, while raising qualification standards for faculty engaged in graduate instruction. It likewise institutionalizes community-oriented learning and research that respond to the healthcare needs of underserved and vulnerable populations. These reforms require legislative action because they redefine the structure of nursing education under Republic Act No. 9173 and establish enduring national standards that cannot be achieved through administrative issuances alone. Filipino nurses have long carried the country’s reputation for excellence in 1 World Health Organization. (2025). State of the world's nursing 2025: Investing in education, jobs, leadership and service delivery. World Health Organization. Accessed from: https://www.who.int/publications/b/78362. Accessed on July 25, 2026. healthcare through their competence and dedication to patients both locally and around the world. Providing them with opportunities for advanced professional education will develop a new generation of nurse leaders, researchers, educators, and healthcare innovators who can strengthen patient care, contribute to evidence-based health policies, and respond effectively to emerging public health challenges. More importantly, the measure creates pathways for highly skilled nurses to further their careers within the country, allowing their expertise and experience to directly benefit Filipino communities, particularly those who remain underserved. Supporting advanced nursing education is therefore not only an investment in the nursing profession but also a commitment to building a stronger, more resilient, and more responsive healthcare system for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11286
title: AN ACT DEFINING GOOD CONDUCT AND PROVIDING CONDITIONS FOR THE GRANT OF GOOD CONDUCT TIME ALLOWANCE, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE ARTICLE 97 OF ACT NO. 3815, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “REVISED PENAL CODE”, AS AMENDED BY REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10592
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish clear and objective conditions for the grant of Good Conduct Time Allowance (GCTA). It further amends Article 97 of Act No. 3815, otherwise known as the “Revised Penal Code”, as amended by Republic Act (RA) No. 10592, to strengthen the administration of sentence credits while preserving GCTA as an incentive for genuine rehabilitation. RA 10592 recognizes good conduct as a basis for reducing the period of imprisonment and encourages persons deprived of liberty to reform while serving their sentences. However, the lack of uniform standards to determine whether an inmate has earned sentence credits often lead to inconsistent assessments, which undermines the confidence in the fair and accountable administration of the GCTA. The proposed measure establishes the standard for determining good conduct based on an inmate’s demonstrated conduct and participation in rehabilitation, productive activities, restorative efforts, and institutional discipline. It recognizes that sentence reduction must be administered with due regard to the gravity of the offense, public safety, and the interests of victims and their families. Thus, it retains the GCTA for offenders who demonstrate meaningful compliance toward rehabilitation; and excludes persons convicted of heinous crimes. A credible correctional system must encourage reform without weakening accountability. This vital piece of legislation shall ensure that sentence credits are granted on the basis of demonstrable conduct rather than inconsistent standards. It therefore reinforces the integrity of the correctional system, recognizes genuine rehabilitation, and protects public confidence in the administration of criminal justice. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11287
title: AN ACT CREATING FLIGHT STANDARDS INSPECTORATE CENTERS UNDER THE CIVIL AVIATION AUTHORITY OF THE PHILIPPINES IN VISAYAS AND IN MINDANAO, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9497, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “CIVIL AVIATION AUTHORITY ACT OF 2008”, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish at least one (1) Flight Standards Inspectorate Centers (FSIC) each in Visayas and Mindanao under the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP). It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9497, otherwise known as the “Civil Aviation Authority Act of 2008”, and strengthens CAAP’s capacity to implement and enforce civil aviation safety standards. CAAP is mandated to regulate, supervise, and oversee civil aviation activities in the country. The concentration of a single FSIC in just one (1) region constrains the timely conduct of surveillance, certification, licensing, and other regulatory processes in distant areas. Thus, establishing additional FSICs shall provide extension services for these functions in Visayas and Mindanao. The proposed measure establishes FSICs which shall abide by International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices. They shall also certify commercial air transport and general aviation operators, approve training and maintenance organizations, and issue airmen licenses to qualified applicants within Visayas and Mindanao. This improves regulatory accessibility, strengthens monitoring capability, and allows the CAAP to deliver aviation safety services more efficiently. For an archipelagic nation where distance and geography often determine access to services and opportunities, the State must continue to improve the capacity of its aviation institutions to deliver timely and effective regulatory oversight. This vital piece of legislation brings aviation safety functions closer to the people and industries that depend on them. It strengthens the foundation of public trust in air transportation, supports balanced regional development, and safeguards the continued growth of Philippine civil aviation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 9497, otherwise known as the “Civil Aviation Authority Act of 2008”, and strengthens CAAP’s capacity to implement and enforce civil aviation safety standards. CAAP is mandated to regulate, supervise, and oversee civil aviation activities in the country. The concentration of a single FSIC in just one (1) region constrains the timely conduct of surveillance, certification, licensing, and other regulatory processes in distant areas. Thus, establishing additional FSICs shall provide extension services for these functions in Visayas and Mindanao. The proposed measure establishes FSICs which shall abide by International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Standards and Recommended Practices. They shall also certify commercial air transport and general aviation operators, approve training and maintenance organizations, and issue airmen licenses to qualified applicants within Visayas and Mindanao. This improves regulatory accessibility, strengthens monitoring capability, and allows the CAAP to deliver aviation safety services more efficiently

label: HB 11288
title: AN ACT CREATING ADDITIONAL DIVISIONS IN THE COURT OF APPEALS, INCREASING THE NUMBER OF COURT OF APPEALS JUSTICES FROM SIXTY-NINE (69) TO SEVENTY-EIGHT (78), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE BATAS PAMBANSA BLG. 129, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “JUDICIARY REORGANIZATION ACT OF 1980”, AS AMENDED, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to increase the number of Associate Justices from sixty-nine (69) to seventy-eight (78). It amends Batas Pambansa Blg. 129, otherwise known as the “Judiciary Reorganization Act of 1980”, and improves the accessibility, efficiency, and responsiveness of the justice system. According to the Supreme Court of the Philippines (2024)1, the judiciary continues to experience substantial appellate caseloads that require sustained institutional strengthening to preserve the constitutional right to the speedy disposition of cases. The concentration of appellate divisions in Metro Manila also imposes additional logistical burdens on litigants, lawyers, witnesses, and government agencies coming from far-flung regions. This often results in higher litigation costs and delays in the administration of justice. This proposed measure decentralizes appellate services in the country and establishes permanent regional stations in Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Every unresolved appeal represents individuals, families, businesses, and communities waiting for justice to take its course. Delayed appellate review prolongs uncertainty and burdens those who seek the protection of the law. Strengthening the Court of Appeals through expanded judicial capacity and broader regional accessibility shall bring the administration of justice closer to the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. YAP 1 Supreme Court of the Philippines. (2024). 2024 Supreme Court Annual Report. label: HB 11289
title: AN ACT TO INCLUDE OTHER BACCALAUREATE DEGREES TO THE LATERAL ENTRY PROGRAM FOR LINE AND TECHNICAL OFFICERS, AMENDING FOR THIS PURPOSE SECTION 33 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6975, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT OF 1990”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to strengthen the lateral entry program of the Philippine National Police (PNP). It amends Section 33 of Republic Act (RA) No. 6975, otherwise known as the “Department of the Interior and Local Government Act of 1990”, and expands the professional qualifications eligible for appointment to line and technical services, and establishes appropriate entry ranks. RA No. 6975 only identifies certain professions for lateral entry into the PNP technical services despite the growing operational requirements of a modern police organization. This bill includes professionals in fields such as physical and sports therapy, psychology, nutrition and dietetics, and other technical professions. It also recognizes qualified PNP personnel and creates a more structured pathway for career advancement and organizational development. A modern police organization requires more than traditional law enforcement capabilities. It demands specialized knowledge and diverse expertise to effectively respond to emerging threats and increasingly complex public safety concerns. A broader and more clearly defined lateral entry system shall enable the PNP to draw from a wider pool of qualified professionals. This shall maximize the expertise of its existing personnel and strengthens its capacity to provide an avenue for professional development within the service. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11290
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR INCENTIVES TO MEMBERS OF THE LEGAL PROFESSION ENGAGED IN THE DEFENSE OF THE RIGHTS OF INDIGENT INDIGENOUS PEOPLES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8371, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS “THE INDIGENOUS PEOPLES’ RIGHTS ACTS OF 1997”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to ensure that Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) have immediate access to legal assistance. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 8371, otherwise known as the Indigenous Peoples' Rights Act of 1997, and provides tax incentives to lawyers who render pro bono legal services to ICC/IPs. Although RA No. 8371 recognizes and protects the rights of ICCs/IPs, other members of these communities do not have immediate access to legal representation when the situation calls for it. Mainly due to poverty, geographic isolation, and the complexity of legal proceedings involving ancestral domains, it prevents them from effectively asserting and protecting their rights guaranteed under the Philippine constitution. This bill empowers the National Commission on Indigenous People (NCIP) to appoint counsels de oficio for indigent ICC/IPs with pending cases. It also encourages lawyers to provide pro bono services through tax incentives. The call for justice for one of the country’s most vulnerable sectors is of utmost importance and thus shall be prioritized. This measure reinforces the State’s constitutional duty to recognize, protect, and promote the rights of indigenous people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11291
title: AN ACT RESTORING THE REGULATORY AND STABILIZATION FUNCTIONS OF THE NATIONAL FOOD AUTHORITY, STRENGTHENING DIRECT FARMER SUBSIDIES, AND ENSURING THE ACTIVE PARTICIPATION OF CIVIL SOCIETY AND PEOPLE’S ORGANIZATIONS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8178, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “AGRICULTURAL TARIFFICATION ACT”, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to restore the National Food Authority’s (NFA) authority to perform market regulation and price stabilization functions. It amends Republic Act (RA) No. 8178, otherwise known as the “Agricultural Tariffication Act”, and authorizes the NFA to procure palay directly from local farmers at competitive support prices and regulate rice warehouses and grain business operators to deter hoarding, price manipulation, and the circulation of smuggled rice. Agriculture remains a vital pillar of the Philippine economy, yet Filipino rice farmers continue to face depressed farmgate prices, rising production costs, and increasing competition from imported rice. While RA No. 11203, otherwise known as the “Rice Tariffication Law”, liberalized rice importation to stabilize consumer prices, its implementation has also diminished the regulatory functions of the NFA. Consequently, many small-scale farmers remain vulnerable to market volatility, while consumers continue to experience fluctuations in rice prices. The bill expands direct input subsidies under the Rice Competitiveness Enhancement Fund, supports crop insurance and community-based post-harvest facilities, and ensures the meaningful participation of farmers’ organizations and civil society organizations in the formulation of rice industry policies. It further authorizes the Department of Agriculture to suspend the issuance of rice import clearances during peak harvest periods, following mandatory consultation with farmer representatives, to prevent the artificial depression of farmgate prices. Restoring the NFA’s regulatory mandate and expanding direct support to farmers shall contribute to a more resilient, competitive, and sustainable rice industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ERIC G. label: HB 11294
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MAGNA CARTA OF BARANGAY HEALTH WORKERS, PROFESSIONALIZING AND STRENGTHENING THE BARANGAY HEALTH WORKFORCE, PROVIDING FOR THEIR REGULAR EMPLOYMENT, JUST COMPENSATION, BENEFITS, RIGHTS, AND SECURITY OF TENURE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay health workers (BHWs) are the first and often the most accessible link between Filipino families and the public health system. They assist in maternal and child care, immunization, disease prevention and surveillance, health education, patient navigation, community mobilization, and the maintenance of local health information. Their work is indispensable to a primary care-led health system and to the effective implementation of universal health care. Yet many BHWs continue to serve under uncertain volunteer arrangements, receive widely varying honoraria, and remain vulnerable to displacement whenever local political leadership changes. This situation undervalues essential community health work, much of which is performed by women, and weakens continuity of care at the barangay level. This measure combines professionalization with a comprehensive framework for the rights, welfare, development, and organization of BHWs. It provides for standardized registration and competency certification, continuing education, a national information 1 system, progressive creation of regular plantilla positions, a minimum Salary Grade 1 entry level for employed BHWs, security of tenure, minimum benefits for volunteer BHWs during the transition, and national assistance to local governments with limited fiscal capacity. The bill also protects BHWs against discrimination and political interference, recognizes their right to organize and participate in health policy discussions, and establishes clear grievance and appeal mechanisms. By investing in the people who sustain health care at the community level, the State strengthens both the dignity of BHWs and the reliability of public health services for every family. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11295
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE PROTECTION OF THE ENVIRONMENTAL RIGHTS OF CHILDREN, PROVIDING ENABLING MECHANISMS FOR ITS IMPLEMENTATION, MONITORING, ENFORCEMENT, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES [ Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Title. This Act shall be known as the “Protection of Environmental Rights of Children Act.” SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared the policy of the State: (a) To recognize, uphold, and protect the inherent dignity and worth of children and their fundamental right to a clean, healthy, safe, and sustainable environment; (b) To ensure that children’s rights are taken into account in environmental decision- making processes at all times and in all State instrumentalities, including situational analysis, environmental planning, implementation of interventions, and evaluation of impacts; (c) To implement programs, projects, and activities that promote sustainable development and environmental stewardship aligned with the environmental rights and well-being of children; (d) To hold relevant government instrumentalities, corporations, and citizens accountable for actions and decisions that adversely affect children’s environmental rights;
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Philippine Constitution recognizes the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature. Children, however, experience environmental harm in a distinct, disproportionate, and often irreversible manner due to their physical, mental, and developmental vulnerabilities. Environmental degradation, climate change, pollution, unsafe water, hazardous living conditions, and disasters directly impair children’s rights to life, survival, development, health, education, and dignity. These harms also undermine the ability of future generations to enjoy a safe and sustainable environment. The Philippines is a State Party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), which obliges States to ensure the best interests of the child, the right to survival and development, non-discrimination, and the right of children to be heard in matters affecting them. Recent international standards further recognize the right of the child to a clean, healthy, and sustainable environment as essential to the full enjoyment of all other rights. This measure seeks to operationalize these commitments by recognizing the environmental rights of children as enforceable legal rights, consistent with the proposed Protection of Environmental Rights of Children Act. It defines the substantive and procedural environmental rights of children, clarifies the obligations of State and non- State actors, institutionalizes child participation, strengthens child protection in environmental emergencies, and establishes accountability mechanisms with aggravated penalties when violations affect children. 1 By adopting a child-centered, rights-based, and intergenerational approach to environmental governance, this bill ensures that environmental protection becomes an instrument for safeguarding the present and future of Filipino children. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11296
title: AN ACT PROMOTING “SARILING KURYENTE” BY RECOGNIZING AND EMPOWERING HOUSEHOLDS, COMMUNITIES, FARMS, ENTERPRISES, ECONOMIC-ZONE LOCATORS, LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND OTHER END-USERS TO GENERATE, STORE, AND USE ELECTRICITY FROM RENEWABLE ENERGY SOURCES PRIMARILY FOR SELF-CONSUMPTION; ESTABLISHING SIMPLIFIED PERMITTING, INTERCONNECTION, NET-METERING, FINANCING, WORKFORCE-DEVELOPMENT, CONSUMER-PROTECTION, AND GRID- INTEGRATION MECHANISMS; AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines continues to face high and volatile electricity costs. Households, farms, businesses, industries, and local communities remain exposed to imported-fuel price shocks, supply disruptions, natural disasters, and constraints in centralized power systems. Renewable energy technologies—particularly rooftop and on-site solar, battery storage, micro-hydro, biomass, and small wind systems—now allow electricity consumers to produce a substantial part of their own requirements. Yet many willing end-users are still discouraged by fragmented permits, uncertain interconnection rules, duplicative product requirements, limited financing, and delay in the approval and installation of net-metering facilities. Republic Act No. 9513, or the Renewable Energy Act of 2008, established net metering and other mechanisms for renewable energy development. Republic Act No. 9136, or the Electric Power Industry Reform Act of 2001, likewise recognizes the need for reliable, secure, and affordable electricity. The next step is to make distributed renewable energy practical and accessible not only for households and small businesses, but also for farms, cooperatives, communities, large enterprises, and economic-zone locators that seek to generate electricity primarily for their own use. This bill establishes a coherent national framework for “Sariling Kuryente.” It recognizes the right of qualified end-users to install and operate renewable energy systems for self- consumption, while preserving legitimate requirements for electrical safety, structural integrity, environmental protection, and grid reliability. The measure replaces an obsolete one-size-fits-all capacity approach with a connected-load framework: up to two hundred percent (200%) of verified connected load for systems without qualifying storage, and up to four hundred percent (400%) for systems with adequate energy storage, subject to technical standards. 1 The measure also provides a fairer net-metering design. Electricity exported within a billing period offsets an equivalent amount of electricity imported on a one-kilowatt-hour-to-one- kilowatt-hour basis. Exports beyond the consumer’s imports are credited at the applicable blended generation charge. Clear billing, carryover, and limited transfer rules are required, while the Energy Regulatory Commission retains authority to prevent double recovery and protect non- participating consumers. Permitting is simplified through a nationally uniform Unified Solar Permit, a single checklist, consolidated notices of deficiency, time-bound action, and a review pathway when a local office fails to act. The bill recognizes accredited domestic and international product certifications, discourages duplicative testing, establishes stronger post-market surveillance and warranty enforcement, and directs the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority to build a certified renewable-energy workforce. These safeguards are intended to expand deployment without tolerating unsafe equipment or unqualified installers. The bill further clarifies ownership of renewable energy certificates, creates financing windows subject to applicable fiduciary and public-finance laws, supports solarization of public facilities, and directs distribution utilities and system operators to plan for progressively higher renewable-energy hosting capacity. Ordinary network upgrades needed to meet approved hosting- capacity obligations are treated as utility system investments subject to ERC review, while purely applicant-specific facilities are governed by transparent and uniform cost-allocation rules. Distribution utilities may not use unsupported claims of grid saturation to defeat an application. Finally, the measure strengthens accountability. It prohibits unjustified delay, discriminatory requirements, unauthorized charges, falsified records, deceptive sales practices, and interference with lawful renewable-energy systems. Affected consumers may claim compensation for demonstrable loss of use caused by delay beyond prescribed periods, subject to fair exceptions and procedures. An inter-agency coordinating council, assisted by consumer, industry, labor, and technical representatives, will address implementation problems and report to Congress. By allowing Filipinos to produce more of the electricity they use, the State can lower exposure to volatile power prices, improve resilience, encourage domestic investment, create skilled green jobs, and reduce pressure on the national grid. Sariling Kuryente is therefore both a consumer-protection measure and a practical national energy-security strategy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11298
title: AN ACT REGULATING ADVERTISEMENTS ON GAMBLING-RELATED ACTIVITIES, PROVIDING LIMITATIONS AND SAFEGUARDS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Gambling has become increasingly accessible and visible to the public due to the rapid expansion of digital platforms, online gaming services, social media, and other forms of electronic communication. While gambling activities may be subject to existing laws and regulations, the manner and extent to which gambling-related activities are advertised and promoted present emerging concerns that warrant appropriate legislative action. In the Philippines, gambling has long been part of the country's entertainment landscape. However, the rapid growth of online gambling, coupled with the widespread use of smartphones, social media, streaming services, and other digital platforms, has transformed the way gambling is promoted and accessed. Gambling-related advertisements can now reach Filipinos directly and repeatedly through the digital content they consume, including content viewed by minors. The increasing prevalence of gambling advertisements may contribute to the normalization of gambling as an ordinary form of entertainment or, more concerningly, as a means of earning money or addressing financial difficulties. This is particularly troubling for Filipino families and individuals who may be financially vulnerable and more susceptible to advertisements portraying gambling as a quick or easy path to financial gain. The use of celebrities, athletes, influencers, content creators, and other public personalities in gambling promotions may further enhance the appeal and perceived legitimacy of gambling, particularly among younger audiences. Similarly, gambling promotions integrated into sporting events, entertainment programs, social media content, and other popular forms of media can substantially increase public exposure to gambling-related messages. Of particular concern are advertisements that downplay the risks of gambling or create misleading impressions regarding the likelihood of winning. Representations that gambling can provide a reliable source of income, achieve financial security, or solve financial problems may encourage irresponsible gambling. Promotional offers, bonuses, and rewards may likewise be misleading when material terms and risks are not clearly disclosed. The State therefore has a legitimate interest in ensuring that gambling-related advertisements are truthful, transparent, and responsibly presented, while protecting minors and vulnerable persons from exploitative or deceptive marketing practices. Regulation of gambling advertising does not seek to prohibit lawful gambling activities, but to ensure that their promotion is consistent with consumer protection and the public welfare. This measure seeks to establish clear and comprehensive standards for gambling-related advertising and promotion in both traditional and digital media. It covers advertisements, sponsorships, endorsements, influencer and affiliate marketing, branded content, and other analogous commercial communications. It likewise provides for appropriate age-assurance measures, responsible gambling messages, restrictions on advertising directed toward minors, and safeguards against misleading claims concerning winnings, financial returns, bonuses, and promotional offers. The bill further promotes a whole-of-society approach to responsible gambling by providing for continuing public awareness and education on the risks of excessive, compulsive, and irresponsible gambling and on available counseling, treatment, rehabilitation, and support services. Ultimately, this measure seeks to foster a safer and more responsible advertising environment in the Philippines, balancing legitimate commercial interests with the State's responsibility to protect Filipino consumers, families, minors, and other vulnerable persons from harmful, deceptive, and irresponsible gambling promotion. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ERNESTO “ERNIX” M. DIONISIO, JR. label: HB 11300
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE PHILIPPINE SPORTS COMMISSION TO RECOGNIZE E- SPORTS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Video games as an industry and an activity have progressed alongside our society’s technological capabilities. From classic pixel games such as Pong and Tetris, to today’s triple A (AAA) titles such as the franchises of Resident Evil and Assassin’s Creed. The quality of today’s video games has indeed come a long way. Parallel to our technological progress is the number of people who play these games. With computers more accessible than ever, a large number of individuals across age brackets have turned to video games as one form of recreational activity, and in some instances, into full-time, professional, and culturally- relevant professions. Recently, the term E-Sports has been ingrained into the mainstream consciousness. What was seen as merely a recreation became a global phenomenon with the advent of games such as League of Legends, DOTA 2, Overwatch, and the like. For these games, several global tournaments are now held annually, with viewerships reaching millions, and pot sizes running into the millions of US Dollars. Indeed, the E-Sports scene had grown so large and prevalent that prize pools for events such as The International reach upwards of millions and millions of pesos, when converted. The rise of competitive video games has also caught on with major sporting events. In fact, the Southeast Asian Games now features video game titles as medal events. In a globally competitive sport that tests reflexes, spatial awareness, and technological access, amongst others, Filipinos must not fall behind. Philippine teams show the potential to go up the rankings in the worldwide E-Sports scene. That is why the State should offer its support towards this up-and-coming sporting events so we can proudly show the world just what the Filipino is capable of. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11301
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING THE INDISCRIMINATE DISPOSAL OF ELECTRONIC WASTE AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE With the onset and rapid development of technology, it follows that e-waste have also been increasing. E-waste are widely understood as various forms of electric and electronic equipment that have ceased to be of value to their users or no longer satisfy their original purpose.1 Electronic waste (e-waste) products have exhausted their utility value through either redundancy, replacement, or breakage and include both “white goods” such as refrigerators, washing machines, and microwaves and “brown goods” such as televisions, radios, computers, and cell phones. Every year, companies are releasing new electronic equipment which results into the ever-increasing waste. Given that the information and technology revolution has exponentially increased the use of new electronic equipment, it has also produced growing volumes of obsolete products; e-waste is one of the fastest-growing waste streams. Although e-waste contains complex combinations of highly toxic substances that pose a danger to health and the environment, many of the products also contain recoverable precious materials, making it a different kind of waste compared with traditional municipal waste. According to the WHO, e-waste constitutes one of the fastest form of solid waste streams in the world.2 This is a heavier burden in developing countries, such as ours, where informal and hazardous setups for the extraction and sale of metals are common. This leads to improper handling which may greatly affect human health of our people. In addition, manufacturing, reprocessing, and disposal of these products. The emission of fumes, gases, and particulate matter into the air, the discharge 1 World Health Organization. Available at: https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/electronic-waste- (e-waste) 2 Ibid. of liquid waste into water and drainage systems, and the disposal of hazardous wastes contribute to environmental degradation. Thus, it is necessary that the disposal of e-waste be regulated. It is then for these reasons that this bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11302
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE MULTI-HAZARD EARLY WARNING NETWORK, MANDATING A COMMON ALERTING STANDARD, PRESCRIBING AUTOMATIC AND LOCALIZED RULES ON THE SUSPENSION OF CLASSES AND WORK, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10639, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Amidst a changing climate and worsening natural disasters, early warning may sometimes spell the difference between safety, disaster, and even death. In the Philippines’ case, where typhoons after typhoons batter communities and send local economies to a halt, a warning system that advises early and in logical anticipation of impending disruption may allow for proper reaction in the part of citizens, institutions, schools, and the private sector, among others. Additionally, the poly-crises we are facing due to climate change and global warming, present a complex tapestry of natural disruptions that have found our disaster-response lacking. We are always playing catch-up. And we are still stuck with post-disaster action rather than pre-disaster preparedness. The poly-crises comes in multiple forms. It can be drought in one area, torrential rain in another. It can also be haze in some parts of the country, and unhealthy temperatures in others. What we need now, is to revamp and modernize our disaster warning systems so that we can plan, mitigate damage and loss, ease the burden of adaptation put on the individual, and overall, help with how the individual Filipino deals with a changing environment. Ours is an archipelago that is varied, storied, rich, and diverse. All the more reason to prepare and preserve our islands through more rigorous systems, innovative approaches, and maximizing the institutions that already exist. It is high time to consolidate and deliver early warning systems. It is high time we adapt before it is too late. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11303
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE OPERATION OF PRIVATELY-OWNED PARKING SPACES AND FACILITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Republic Act No. 3262 or the Consumer Act of the Philippines, it is a declared policy of the State “to protect the interests of the consumer, promote his general welfare and to establish standards of conduct for business and industry.” To achieve the foregoing policy, the State endeavors to enact measures for the “protection against deceptive, unfair and unconscionable sales acts and practices. In line with the abovementioned policy and its commitment to enact the necessary measures, the State, through this Bill, will be able to properly regulate the operators of parking spaces and facilities which have been functioning without any form of regulation or standards of operation. As part of the various measures to be proposed, this Bill aims to impose a standardized grace period wherein vehicle users shall be under no obligation to pay for parking provided that they remain within the period prescribed. This particular measure effectively renders illegal the unconscionable practice of imposing a flat rate which is payable upon entry. Furthermore, this Bill aims to impose a standardized ceiling rate for all operators of parking spaces and facilities in order to control the imposition of unreasonably high and exorbitant fees. It must be noted that these measures are not proposed to dissuade the operators of parking spaces and facilities. These measures are imposed primarily under an ethical consideration in favor of the users or customers of the parking spaces and facilities. It is for the foregoing premises that the approval of this Bill is earnestly sought. ALFRED C. label: HB 11304
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SYSTEM OF NATIVE FLOWER PARKS, CREATING FOR THIS PURPOSE THE NATIONAL NATIVE FLOWER PARKS COUNCIL AND THE NATIVE FLOWER PARKS DEVELOPMENT FUND, PROMOTING THE CONSERVATION, PROPAGATION, AND PUBLIC APPRECIATION OF PHILIPPINE NATIVE AND ENDEMIC FLOWERING PLANTS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every Filipino child knows the sampaguita. We string it into garlands. We give it to our mothers, to our teachers, and to the Santo Niño. We call it our national flower. Here is something most of us were never told: the sampaguita did not originally come from the Philippines. It was brought in from across the sea. Meanwhile, in our own forests and mountains, there are multiple species of jasmine that grow nowhere else in the world, and only few are aware of their names. Our country is home to more than nine thousand two hundred fifty (9,250) native plants.1 At least one out of every three is found only here, and nowhere else on Earth. Of our one thousand (1,000) orchid species, roughly seven out of ten grow only in these islands.2 By any honest measure, we are one of the most flower-rich countries on the planet. And yet most are not aware of this wonderous flora diversity. Our children grow up admiring the tulips of Holland, the cherry blossoms of Japan, and the lavender fields of France, places far from the realities and ecosystems of our own islands, while the waling-waling, the tayabak, and the Rafflesia bloom quietly in our own provinces, unvisited, unphotographed, and underappreciated. Recently, the Senate passed a measure declaring the waling-waling our national orchid.3 The harder truth is that the waling-waling is vanishing from the wild. We are naming our flowers faster than we are saving them. A title on 1 Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund, “Philippines – Species,” available at: https://www.cepf.net/our-work/biodiversity-hotspots/philippines/species 2 Henrylito D. Tacio, “Philippines' national orchid waling-waling faces extinction, conservation efforts urged,” Manila Bulletin, 06 July 2026, available at: https://mb.com.ph/2026/07/06/philippines-national-orchid-waling-waling-faces-extinction- conservation-efforts-urged 3 Ibid. paper does not water a plant. And where are these flowers? Not in Manila. They are in the Cordillera and in Apayao. In Samar and Palawan. In Davao, Bukidnon, and the Zamboanga Peninsula. They are in the provinces, in the same towns our people leave because there is no work, in the same barangays that wait longest for a road, in the same provinces handed the smallest sliver of our tourism money. The wealth is already there. It has been there for millions of years. The probinsya has been sitting on a treasure while being told it has nothing. This bill establishes a national system of Native Flower Parks, at least one in every region of the country, built in partnership with our local government units, people's organizations, the academe, and our indigenous communities. The Flower Parks will become pride you can touch. Pride you can smell. Pride that you can show off. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is urgently sought. ALFRED C. title: AN ACT AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7925, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PUBLIC TELECOMMUNICATIONS POLICY ACT OF THE PHILIPPINES”, BY REQUIRING PUBLIC TELECOMMUNICATIONS ENTITIES AND INTERNET SERVICE PROVIDERS TO INSTITUTE A REFUND MECHANISM FOR SERVICE OUTAGES AND DISRUPTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Reliable internet and telecommunications are vital to daily commerce, education, and public communication. However, subscribers frequently face prolonged service interruptions without receiving compensation or bill adjustments. This bill amends Republic Act No. 7925 to protect consumers by mandating automatic billing adjustments and refunds for significant network downtime. Key Provisions include automatic pro-rated refunds, enforcement and penalties, and revocation and consumer relief. To ensure fair business practices, hold telecom providers accountable, and safeguard consumer rights, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. Approved, RAMIL L. label: HB 11312
title: AN ACT GRANTING PHILIPPINE CITIZENSHIP TO DAVID LORAN SISSON
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant Philippine citizenship to Mr. David Loran Sisson, an American national who has spent most of his life in the Philippines and has established deep and enduring ties to the country and the Filipino people. Mr. Sisson was born on September 24, 1991 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, United States of America. At the age of four, he moved with his family to General Santos City, Philippines, where his parents served as missionaries. He and his three siblings grew up in General Santos City and became immersed in Filipino culture and community life. In May 1998, his father established a church in General Santos City as part of the family's missionary work. From modest beginnings, their ministry expanded to reach thousands of children through weekly classes and developed various programs serving children, young people, persons with disabilities, widows, pastors, and members of the community. Their activities likewise included values formation programs involving police trainees and personnel, youth camps, pastors' conferences, a television ministry, a Bible institute, and a four-year Bible college. Having grown up in the Philippines, Mr. Sisson learned to communicate in Cebuano and Tagalog and developed strong personal and cultural ties with Filipinos. He pursued his college education at West Coast Baptist College in California from 2011 to 2015 and thereafter returned to a life closely connected with the Philippines. In 2015, Mr. Sisson became a full-time personal assistant to Filipino boxing champion and former Senator Manny Pacquiao. In 2016, he married Ruthie Alonzo Sisson, whose family is of Filipino descent, and the couple thereafter made the Philippines their home. They now have three children. For nearly three decades, Mr. Sisson's life has been closely intertwined with the Philippines. He spent his formative years in General Santos City, has participated in religious and community activities serving Filipinos, has established his family here, and has chosen the Philippines as the country where he intends to permanently reside and raise his children. His desire to become a Filipino citizen is therefore not merely incidental to his residence in the country, but is consistent with his longstanding attachment to the Philippines, his integration into Filipino society, and his commitment to continue living in and serving the country he considers his home. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JAVIER MIGUEL L. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE RULES ON SYSTEM LOSS CAP OF ELECTRIC DISTRIBUTION UTILITIES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7832 AND REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9136
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE At every stage of the electric system—from generation power plants to substations of distribution utilities (DUs) up to household outlets—there are bound to be energy losses. System losses are inherent when electricity is transported from one place to another due to several reasons such as heat, noise, pilferage, and technical losses. The only way to zero-out system loss in the power system is to turn the power off. In a Senate Committee on Energy hearing conducted last 2017, a number of DUs presented simulations if reduction of technical losses to 5% will be required from them. Using 2017 financial parameters, Angeles Electric Corp. will need to spend P892 million, Cagayan Electric Power and Light Company will be needing P1.84 billion, and Meralco would have to spend P65.53 billion. Repeated simulations showed that the costs that the utilities will incur in investing on infrastructure will significantly outweigh any possible decrease in the system loss charge. Capital Expenditure (CAPEX) is a pass on charge to the consumers, hence it will eventually lead to electricity rate increases to customers. Since it is scientifically and technically impossible to eliminate system losses completely, governments and electric regulators around the world allow electric DUs to recover minimal system loss rates as part of their regulated charges. In the Philippines, the Congress enacted the Anti-Electricity Pilferage Act of 1994, which set an initial cap on losses that was gradually reduced over time. In 2017, the ERC issued a resolution further reducing the cap to its present level of 5.50 percent for private DUs and 12 to 8.25 percent for electric cooperatives. Recognizing the urgent need to mitigate the rapid increase of electricity rates while also taking into account the viability of distribution operations, this bill seeks to regulate and reduce system losses by institutionalizing a set of rules on the allowable systems loss cap of electric distribution utilities. As such, this measure is ultimately aimed at enhancing the efficiency and competitiveness of DUs in their delivery of electric service to the public. More importantly, this bill is envisioned to cushion the impact of electricity bill spikes to Filipino consumers as well as inflation and impending surges in fuel costs and other commodities. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly and sincerely sought. REP. SERGIO C. DAGOOC APEC Party-List REP. PRESLEY C.
