label: HB 11412
title: AN ACT IMPOSING EXCISE TAXES ON HIGH-SODIUM AND HIGH-SUGAR FOOD AND SWEETENED BEVERAGES, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 150-B AND 288-A, CREATING A NEW SECTION 150-C, OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE A healthy population is indispensable to national productivity and inclusive growth. The excessive intake of sodium and added sugars are dietary risk factors that drive the country’s most burdensome noncommunicable diseases such as hypertension, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, all of which further contribute to chronic kidney disease (“CKD”). Diabetes and hypertension has been recognized as the two leading drivers of CKD, which was reported to contribute 50.62% and 23.26% to CKD worldwide, respectively.1 The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has found that approximately one- third of adults with diabetes have CKD, while approximately one-fifth of adults with hypertension have CKD.2 Diabetes and hypertension are major risk factors for cardiovascular disease. Since the cardiovascular system and kidneys are deeply interconnected, when one of these systems develops problems, it can lead to problems in the other. A UK Biobank study showed that about 5.6% of people with cardiovascular disease developed CKD within 10 years.3 1 Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Hepatitis C Work Group, "KDIGO 2018 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Prevention, Diagnosis, Evaluation, and Treatment of Hepatitis C in Chronic Kidney Disease," Kidney International, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2018.03.018. 2 Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, "Risk Factors for Chronic Kidney Disease," U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, May 15, 2024, https://www.cdc.gov/kidney-disease/risk-factors/index.html. 3 Sophie Claudel et al., "Abstract 40: Risk of Incident Chronic Kidney Disease Among Subtypes of Prevalent and Incident Cardiovascular Disease: UK Biobank”, March 24, 2026, accessed at https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/cir.153.suppl_1.40. 1 Fiscal measures can reduce consumption of products that contain excessive levels of nutrients of concern while giving manufacturers a direct incentive to reformulate. A well- designed excise tax should therefore be objective, measurable, administratively workable, and structured so that a product can avoid or reduce the tax when its sodium or added-sugar content is lowered. This bill adopts that approach. For sweetened beverages already covered by Section 150-B of the National Internal Revenue Code, the bill retains the existing excise-tax framework but shifts calorically sweetened beverages toward sugar-concentration tiers. This aligns the tax more closely with the public- health objective by imposing a higher tax on beverages with more added sugar while preserving the existing treatment of beverages that use non-caloric sweeteners. Products already taxed under Section 150-B are not again taxed for sugar under the new Section 150-C. For prepackaged processed foods, it uses uniform nutrient concentrations per one hundred (100) grams and applies tiered specific excise taxes per kilogram of product. The use of a uniform one-hundred-gram basis avoids manipulation through artificially small serving sizes and creates a clear reformulation target. The tax is based on the highest applicable nutrient tier so that a single product is not subjected to cumulative sodium and sugar excises under the same section. Fresh and unprocessed basic foods, food prepared and sold for immediate consumption on-site, infant formula, and food for special medical purposes are excluded. The bill does not exempt particular high-sodium processed products merely because they are inexpensive. Instead, every manufacturer is given the same path to lower tax liability: reduce the sodium or added- sugar content below the statutory threshold. The measure also provides for inflation indexation of specific tax rates, objective rules for determining nutrient content, manufacturer and importer declarations subject to verification, a reasonable transition period for reformulation and compliance, and periodic review by Congress based on revenue, health, consumer, and industry effects. The revenues from the new food excise are dedicated to Universal Health Care, medical assistance and health facilities, and nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions. In this manner, the tax both discourages excessive consumption and helps finance the public health programs needed to address the diseases associated with unhealthy diets. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. _____________________________________ REP. HENRY “INDY” F. OAMINAL JR. label: HB 11413
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTION 15 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 6770, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "OMBUDSMAN ACT OF 1989", GRANTING ANTI-CORRUPTION LAW ENFORCEMENT POWER TO THE OFFICE OF THE OMBUDSMAN
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 12, Article XI of the 1987 Constitution declares the Ombudsman and his Deputies as protectors of the people and directs them to act promptly on complaints against public officials and employees of the government. This constitutional mandate is further operationalized under Republic Act No. 6770, otherwise known as the “Ombudsman Act of 1989,” which vests the Office of the Ombudsman with broad powers to investigate and act upon acts or omissions of public officers and employees. The effective discharge of this mandate requires not only investigative and prosecutorial authority, but also an institutional capability to secure evidence, protect witnesses, enforce lawful orders, and undertake necessary law enforcement operations. Strengthening these capabilities will enable the Office of the Ombudsman to respond more effectively to acts of corruption, abuse, inefficiency, and other forms of misconduct in government. For this purpose, this measure seeks to establish an Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Service within the Office of the Ombudsman, to be known as the Ombudsman Marshal Service. The proposed Service is intended to provide the Office with a dedicated law enforcement arm capable of conducting proactive inspections, inquiries, investigations, arrests, detention, searches, seizures, and other lawful measures necessary for the effective implementation of the Ombudsman’s mandate. The bill likewise provides for the appropriate organization of the Office of the Ombudsman, including the Office of the Special Prosecutor and the Ombudsman Marshal Service, and defines their respective roles and authority under the supervision and control of the Ombudsman. It further provides for the necessary rank, salary, benefits, retirement privileges, staffing, and operational support for personnel performing these functions. Recognizing the importance of protecting witnesses, whistleblowers, detainees under investigation, and other persons placed in the custody of the proposed Service, the measure likewise provides for adequate facilities and appropriate safeguards. It also ensures that the implementation of the Service is supported by regular appropriations of the Office of the Ombudsman, with such augmentation as may be necessary for the sustained performance of its mandate. By strengthening the enforcement and institutional mechanisms available to the Office of the Ombudsman, this measure seeks to ensure that investigations are conducted effectively, lawful orders are carried out, evidence is secured, and cases involving corruption and other irregularities in government are pursued with greater efficiency and consistency. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. ATTY. GERVILLE “JINKY BITRICS” R. label: HB 11419
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE TECHNICAL, VOCATIONAL AND LIVELIHOOD CURRICULUM FOR THE SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 25 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 28 Section 1. Short Title. — This Act shall be known as the “TVL Curriculum Act.” 30 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. — The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. The right to education shall be promoted with the end goal of producing graduates who are prepared to become civically active and economically productive members of society.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 After graduating from senior high school under the Technical, Vocational and Livelihood (TVL) track, a young Filipino applies for a job as an automotive technician. He has learned the fundamentals in school and has a senior high school diploma in hand. During the application, however, he is asked for a National Certificate and specific competencies required by the employer. He realizes that although he completed the TVL track, he does not have all the certifications and skills that the industry expects. 28 This situation reflects a gap that the TVL curriculum must address. For many students, choosing the technical and vocational education track is a deliberate choice to gain practical skills that can help them find work to support themselves and their families after graduation. They place their hopes in the skills they learn in school, trusting that these skills will open the door to a decent livelihood. Their education should therefore be closely connected to the realities of the workplace, giving them recognized certifications that employers value and significantly consider in employing them. 36 This proposed measure seeks to make sure that TVL graduates leave school with skills and National Certificates that can help them find work. They should not have to discover after graduation that the skills they learned are not enough for the job they want. 40 By bringing schools and industries closer together, and by specifically addressing what employers want, the measure seeks to give TVL graduates a fair chance to be hired, earn decent wages, and build a better life for themselves and their families. 44 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 46 47 REP. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE SPECIAL PROGRAM IN CREATIVE ARTS FOR JUNIOR AND SENIOR HIGH SCHOOL, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 24 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 27 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Special Program in the Creative Arts Act”. 30 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – The State recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Moreover, the government is committed to fulfill its constitutional mandate to foster the preservation, enrichment, and dynamic evolution of a Filipino national culture based on the principle of unity in diversity in a climate of free artistic and intellectual expression and to place arts, design and other intellectual creative creation under the patronage of the State. 38 To this end, the State shall promote creative arts education, encourage arts programs, support national art competitions, and strengthen education for the development of creative industries. The State shall provide adequate training for students with artistic abilities, with the end in view of producing world-class artists with firm academic foundation and strong patriotic ideals. 44 SEC. 3. Objective. – The Special Program in the Creative Arts (SPCA) is hereby strengthened to provide a continuing source of artists of excellence and leaders in the preservation and promotion of culture, arts, and the creative industry in the Philippines. Admitted students shall be trained under a special curriculum oriented in the fields of architecture and allied arts, cinema, dance, dramatic arts, literary arts, music, visual arts, design, digital fabrication and new media, along with financial literacy, entrepreneurship skills, and basic knowledge on intellectual property rights, with the end in view of providing quality education to students while giving way to opportunities for a sustainable profession.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 22 A young Filipino student discovers that she has a gift for music. Another finds joy in painting, while another dreams of becoming a filmmaker, dancer, writer, or designer. They have the talent and the passion, but for many of them, the path to building a career from it is uncertain, if not expensive. Without proper training, guidance, and opportunities, many young artists eventually set aside their dreams and choose a different path simply because they don’t know where to start or where to better fluorish their talents. 29 Now, this proposed measure seeks to strengthen the Special Program in the Creative Arts by giving students specialized training in their chosen fields, access to experienced artists who can mentor them, and information on scholarships, college programs, and employment opportunities. Unlike similar existing programs, students will also learn how to manage their finances, start and manage a creative business, and protect their work through basic knowledge of intellectual property rights. Through these opportunities, students can graduate with stronger artistic skills, and a clearer path toward further education or a sustainable career in the arts. 37 The measure also seeks to strengthen the support given to SPCA schools by encouraging partnerships with the private sector and providing appropriate tax incentives for donations and the importation of equipment and materials needed for the training of students. 41 A young Filipino should not have to give up a talent simply because there is no clear sustainable path to pursue it. 44 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 46 47 48 REP. label: HB 11424
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE CLIMATE DUE DILIGENCE, TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY OF THE STATE, ESTABLISHING THE PHILIPPINE GREENHOUSE GAS INVENTORY AND ACCOUNTING SYSTEM AND THE CLIMATE ADVISORY COUNCIL, PROVIDING FOR THE PREPARATION, PUBLICATION AND REVIEW OF NATIONAL CLIMATE COMMITMENTS AND PLANS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE On 23 July 2025, the International Court of Justice delivered its Advisory Opinion on the Obligations of States in respect of Climate Change, rendered upon the request of the General Assembly. The Court held that the obligations of States in this field arise not only from the climate treaties but from customary international law; that limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius is the primary temperature goal of the Paris Agreement; that a State must exercise stringent due diligence and employ all means at its disposal, according to its capabilities and national circumstances, to prevent significant harm to the climate system; that the discretion of a State in preparing its nationally determined contribution is limited, and that such contribution must be capable of making an adequate contribution to the temperature goal and must reflect the highest possible ambition; that a State may incur responsibility where it fails to regulate the emissions of private actors within its jurisdiction; that climate effects, including downstream emissions, must be assessed in environmental impact assessment; and that the efforts of a State in this field may not be presented as entirely voluntary and exempt from scrutiny. The Court likewise affirmed that the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities is a core guiding principle, that the standard of conduct required is measured against the capabilities and circumstances of each State, and that breach of the obligations identified engages the ordinary consequences of State responsibility, including cessation, guarantees of non- repetition and full reparation. The year before, in its Advisory Opinion of 21 May 2024, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea held that anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions constitute pollution of the marine environment within the meaning of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that States Parties owe a stringent obligation of due diligence to prevent, reduce and control it. The Philippines is an archipelagic State and a Party to that Convention. Under Section 2, Article II of the Constitution, the Philippines adopts the generally accepted principles of international law as part of the law of the land. The customary obligations articulated by the Court are therefore already part of Philippine law. What is absent is the domestic machinery through which they are performed, recorded and made answerable. Republic Act No. 9729, as amended by Republic Act No. 10174, establishes a planning framework and a Commission, but it was enacted before the Paris Agreement and contains no duty to prepare a nationally determined contribution, no duty to maintain a greenhouse gas inventory, no duty to reconcile the national energy and development plans with the climate commitments the country has made, and no duty to report to Congress on whether those commitments are being met. The consequence is that the most consequential climate decisions of the State rest upon executive issuances that may be withdrawn without notice. The national greenhouse gas inventory system exists by Executive Order No. 174, series of 2014. The nationally determined contribution exists only as a submission to a treaty body. The National Adaptation Plan 2023-2050 has no statutory foundation at all. Climate change expenditure tagging rests upon a joint memorandum circular. A framework of this importance cannot rest upon instruments of this fragility. This bill supplies the machinery. It is important to state at the outset what it does not do. It does not establish a national emissions cap. It does not set a net-zero date. It does not create carbon budgets, and it does not convert the conditional component of the Philippine nationally determined contribution into a domestic legal obligation. Those omissions are deliberate and are matters of national interest, not of timidity. The Philippines accounts for less than one-half of one percent of global greenhouse gas emissions. Our nationally determined contribution is expressly structured so that the greater part of our ambition is conditional upon the finance, technology and capacity-building that the instruments of the climate regime require developed country Parties to provide. That structure is the country’s position and its leverage. A statute which silently converted the conditional component into a domestic duty would surrender, for nothing, the very distinction upon which our claim to support rests, and would sit uneasily with the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities which the Court has now affirmed. Section 7 of this Act therefore preserves the distinction expressly: the unconditional component is a duty of the State enforceable under this Act, and the conditional component is and remains contingent upon the means of implementation being actually provided. What the bill does establish is the conduct that the Court has held to be obligatory, and the record by which that conduct may be judged. It places the national greenhouse gas inventory on a statutory footing, with independent verification, mandatory submission of data by sectoral agencies and by large emitting establishments, and a particular requirement that the land use, land-use change and forestry account state its uncertainties, this being the account upon which our present contribution most heavily relies. It imposes a duty to prepare, publish and submit a nationally determined contribution and, for the first time, a long- term low greenhouse gas emission development strategy, which the Philippines has never adopted. It gives the National Adaptation Plan a statutory basis, adaptation having been recognized by the Court as a legal obligation and not a matter of policy preference alone. label: HB 11425
title: AN ACT REQUIRING CLIMATE AND DISASTER RISK SCREENING OF RESILIENCE PROJECTS, INSTITUTIONALIZING CLIMATE AND RESILIENCE EXPENDITURE TAGGING AND DISCLOSURE, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines does not lack laws on climate change and disaster risk reduction. It lacks any law that requires the money appropriated for climate and disaster resilience to actually reduce risk. Republic Act No. 9729, as amended by Republic Act No. 10174, establishes a planning framework. Republic Act No. 10121 establishes a disaster management system. Neither imposes on any agency or local government a duty to achieve a resilience outcome with the funds it receives, and neither provides a remedy when the funds are spent on works that do not reduce the hazard they were appropriated to address. The consequences of that gap are now a matter of public record. Flood control appropriations rose from roughly Seventy-Nine Billion Pesos (P79,000,000,000.00) in 2016 to more than Two Hundred Billion Pesos (P200,000,000,000.00) annually by 2021, without any corresponding change in how projects are selected, sited, disclosed or audited. What followed were ghost projects, substandard works, and structures built where they could not reduce risk or which displaced flooding onto communities downstream. Hazard information is not the missing element. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration, modernized under Republic Act No. 10692, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology, the National Mapping and Resource Information Authority and the Mines and Geosciences Bureau produce the data. What is missing is any legal duty to consult it before a resilience project is designed, sited, funded, procured or built. A flood control structure may today be designed for historical rainfall, sited in a hazard zone, and built where it worsens flooding downstream, without any law being broken. This measure supplies the missing duty, and does so in the narrowest way that will work. It requires every resilience project to undergo climate and disaster risk screening and to obtain a Resilience Screening Certificate. The certificate states the hazard the project is meant to address, the hazard conditions projected over the design life of the project, the alternatives considered, the expected reduction in risk, and the effect of the project upon adjacent, upstream and downstream communities. The certificate is issued by a Resilience Screening Technical Panel composed of the agencies that already hold the hazard data, and not by the agency that proposes to build the project. An implementing agency cannot be permitted to certify to itself that its own project is well-sited and adequate to the hazard; that is the precise failure this measure is directed against. The Panel may issue the certificate, deny it, or issue it subject to conditions, and its action is appealable. The head of the implementing agency remains personally accountable for the truth and completeness of the application and for implementing the project in accordance with the certificate issued. The bill is deliberately modest in where it applies pressure. It contains no provision addressed to the contents of the National Expenditure Program or of the General Appropriations Act. Screening is required of the implementing agency as part of project development, before a project enters its pipeline and before detailed engineering design is commissioned. The certificate then operates as a condition precedent to the release of funds, to procurement and to award, all of which are matters of budget execution. Appropriations for items that remain uncertified are declared not to constitute savings, so that the requirement cannot be evaded by realignment. The bill creates no new department, bureau or office. The screening panel is composed of agencies that already exist and already produce the data on which it will act. The bill further institutionalizes in statute the climate and resilience expenditure tagging that has until now rested only upon a joint memorandum circular, requires an annual Climate and Resilience Budget Statement showing the certification status of every resilience item, mandates publication in machine- readable form within a fixed period, and requires the geotagging, as-built documentation and public marking of every resilience project. Compliance is secured by the nullity of any release or award made without a certificate, by the personal liability of the officers responsible, by the audit powers the Commission on Audit already possesses, by the right of any citizen to sue, and by the penalties provided in this Act. The question of a permanent body to conduct technical and engineering audits of public infrastructure is a substantial one, and it is reserved for separate legislation so that it may receive the deliberation it deserves without delaying the requirement established here. The right to a balanced and healthful ecology under Section 16, Article II of the Constitution, and the mandate that public office is a public trust under Section 1, Article XI, are not vindicated by appropriating larger sums for resilience. They are vindicated by ensuring that what is appropriated is spent on the right projects, at the right cost, at the right quality, by the right people, and delivered on time. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA. title: AN ACT MANDATING COASTAL CITIES AND MUNICIPALITIES TO PROVIDE FREE EMERGENCY COMMUNICATION AND SAFETY GEAR TO MUNICIPAL FISHERFOLK, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL MARITIME SAFETY NETWORK, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Municipal fisherfolk constitute a vital productive force in the national economy, anchoring rural livelihoods and national food security while facing severe structural vulnerabilities, maritime risks, and a persistent lack of basic safety infrastructure within municipal waters. While the 1987 Constitution explicitly mandates the State to protect marginal fishers and advance social justice, small-scale producers remain exposed to sudden weather shifts, engine failures, and collision hazards without direct access to emergency response networks monitored by maritime authorities. The “Fisherfolk Safety at Sea Act” translates this constitutional obligation into a concrete operational framework by mandating coastal local government units to equip registered municipal fisherfolk with free waterproof two-way emergency radios, life vests, and emergency SOS distress beacons. Designed to respect the operational independence and daily realities of small-scale fishing without imposing restrictive bureaucracy, the bill mandates permanent equipment custody under Property Acknowledgement Receipts, eliminates burdensome clearance fees, guarantees automatic qualification through the Municipal Fisherfolk Registry, and secures direct funding through local disaster risk reduction resources supported by civil society collaboration. By strengthening local search-and-rescue capabilities and safeguarding the working conditions of small producers at sea, this measure advances a practical, rights-based policy that protects both the lives and the economic viability of our coastal communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MA. label: HB 11427
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A REAL-TIME MECHANISM FOR THE MONITORING OF FUEL PRICE MOVEMENTS AND THE AUTOMATIC GRANT OF EMERGENCY FUEL SUBSIDIES, CREATING FOR THE PURPOSE THE NATIONAL FUEL PRICE VIGILANCE AND RAPID SUBSIDY COUNCIL, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE AHENSYA NG GABAY AT ALERTO SA PETROLYO OR AGAP UNDER THE OFFICE OF THE PRESIDENT, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Fuel price volatility constitutes one of the most immediate and disruptive economic shocks besetting the ordinary Filipino household. Every fluctuation in global crude oil benchmarks, or every depreciation of the peso vis-à-vis the United States dollar, is almost invariably and swiftly transmitted to pump prices, thereby imposing an undue burden upon public utility vehicle (PUV) drivers, tillers of the soil, fisherfolk, and low-income families who possess no adequate buffer against abrupt increases in the cost of living. Under the prevailing regulatory framework, the response of government to fuel price hikes remains largely reactive, ad hoc, and bereft of institutional permanence. While the Department of Energy (DOE) regularly monitors and publishes weekly pump prices, the grant of fuel subsidies — when extended at all — is customarily the product of piecemeal legislation or executive issuance, the formulation, funding, and implementation of which consume weeks, if not months. By the time relief is finally extended, the gravest impact of the price shock shall have already been absorbed by the sectors least equipped to bear it. It is in this regard that this Act serves as remedy to this deficiency. The proposed measure establishes the National Fuel Price Vigilance and Rapid Subsidy Council, otherwise known as the Ahensya ng Gabay at Alerto sa Petrolyo, or AGAP, under the Office of the President, and vests the same with the continuing mandate to monitor, in real time, domestic and international fuel price movements, and, upon the breach of a clearly defined price-hike threshold, to cause the automatic and immediate release of targeted fuel subsidies, without necessity of a new law or executive issuance for each such occurrence and in view of a prompt assistance to the country’s most vulnerable sectors during such tremors, which has become frequent these days. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. DUTERTE HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 11428
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The recent school shootings in Tacloban City, Zamboanga City, and Banga, South Cotabato, have resulted in the loss of young lives and injuries to learners. These incidents have brought renewed urgency to the duty to protect children while they are in school. They also underscore the need for schools nationwide to be prepared to identify threats, respond promptly to emergencies, and support affected learners and personnel. School safety requires more than a response to an incident after it occurs. Schools must have clear preventive measures, accessible reporting channels, trained personnel, emergency protocols, and reliable referral systems. Learners and school personnel affected by violence must also receive appropriate care and assistance in returning safely to school. This bill seeks to institutionalize a National Comprehensive School Safety Framework for all public and private basic education institutions. It requires each school to adopt a School Safety Plan suited to its circumstances and establishes standards for learner protection, violence prevention, physical and digital safety, mental health support, incident response, and recovery. It further strengthens coordination among the Department of Education, other government agencies, local government units, families, and communities. The State has a duty to ensure that schools remain places where learners can pursue their education without fear and where school personnel can discharge their responsibilities in safety. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 11435
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY FRAMEWORK, ENSURING THE SAFETY AND WELL-BEING OF LEARNERS AND SCHOOL PERSONNEL, AND PROMOTING A SAFE AND SUPPORTIVE SCHOOL COMMUNITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Article XIV, Section 1 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution explicitly mandates that the State "shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all." Furthermore, Article II, Section 13 underscores that the State "recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation- building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being." Implicit in these constitutional mandates is the obligation of the State to maintain learning environments where students, educators, and school workers can exercise their constitutional right to education free from physical harm, fear, and violence. However, our educational institutions—long revered as safe sanctuaries for learning and development—are increasingly being shattered by an unprecedented surge of violence. In recent months, a terrifying pattern of physical attacks, knife stabbings, and deadly shootings inside and immediately around school premises across the country has laid bare severe gaps in campus security, child protection, and early intervention mechanisms:  June 16, 2026 (General Trias, Cavite): A Grade 8 student armed with a kitchen knife entered a Grade 5 classroom at Bethel Academy and attacked seven young pupils without provocation, leaving two needing emergency surgery.  June 19, 2026 (Cavite City): A Senior High School student was repeatedly stabbed in the arm and back during a violent altercation inside Cavite National High School.  June 22, 2026 (Tacloban City): Two minors armed with firearms opened fire at San Jose National High School, killing three students and injuring 20 others.  June 23, 2026 (San Carlos City, Negros Occidental): A 17-year-old Grade 10 student was stabbed outside Julio Ledesma National High School due to a personal grudge.  July 1, 2026 (Zamboanga City & Bacolod City): Stabbing incidents erupted involving students at Cabaluay National High School in Zamboanga and near Sum- ag National High School in Bacolod.  July 31, 2026 (Las Piñas City): A 13-year-old Grade 9 student was fatally stabbed in the chest by a 14-year-old classmate right outside a classroom during recess at Las Piñas National High School.  August 18, 2026 (Zamboanga City): A tragic shooting incident inside the Junior High School premises of Ateneo de Zamboanga University left two dead.  September 18, 2026 (Banga, South Cotabato): A horrific campus shooting at Banga National High School claimed 3 lives and wounded 8 others. Between June and September 2026 alone, at least eight major violent incidents involving bladed weapons and firearms have resulted in 9 fatalities and over 40 injuries among learners. This alarming wave of campus violence—compounded by bullying, mental health crises, and the exposure of vulnerable youth to online radicalization and extremism— demands an immediate, structured, and comprehensive legislative intervention. This bill seeks to institutionalize a Comprehensive School Safety Framework. By adopting a whole-of-society and all-hazards approach, the measure strengthens institutional response mechanisms across prevention, preparedness, and recovery. Furthermore, it mandates seamless coordination among the Department of Education (DepEd), local government units (LGUs), law enforcement agencies, and community stakeholders to enforce strict access controls, mental health support, and child protection policies. In light of the constitutional duty to safeguard the youth and preserve the right to a secure, quality education, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 63 64 65 HON. label: HB 11436
title: AN ACT GRANTING HAZARD PAY TO LOCAL GOVERNMENT ENVIRONMENT AND NATURAL RESOURCES PERSONNEL EXPOSED TO OCCUPATIONAL HAZARDS IN THE PERFORMANCE OF THEIR DUTIES, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Local government environment and natural resources personnel serve at the frontlines of environmental protection, conservation, solid waste management, pollution control, forest and watershed protection, environmental enforcement, and other environmental programs of local government units. The nature of their work regularly exposes some of these personnel to occupational hazards, including extreme weather, contaminated waste, polluted environments, dangerous terrain, poisonous plants, venomous animals, and other conditions that may endanger their health and safety. Recognizing these risks, the Philippine League of Local Environment and Natural Resources Officers, Inc. (PLLENRO-SOC), South Cotabato Chapter, through Resolution No. 01, Series of 2026, approved on July 26, 2026, requested the Representatives of the Province of South Cotabato to sponsor legislation granting hazard pay to qualified environmental workers regularly exposed to occupational hazards in the performance of their official duties. While existing government compensation rules provide hazard duty pay under particular circumstances, there is a need for a specific statutory benefit for local environmental personnel who are actually exposed to occupational hazards in the performance of their duties. This measure therefore seeks to recognize the risks borne by local environmental personnel by granting hazard pay when they are actually exposed to occupational hazards in the performance of their official duties. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. __________________________________ FERDINAND L. label: HB 11437
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 19 The Sierra Madre Mountain Range is one of the country’s most important natural sources. Stretching for more than 500 kilometers, it runs north-to-south along the entire eastern coast of Luzon, from Cagayan down to Quezon province.1 It is home to diverse wildlife, rivers, and a critical sanctuary for thousands of unique species. It is relevant not only to those areas near this mountain range, but also to the entirety of Luzon. 25 Perhaps the Sierra Madre's most well-known role is its function as a natural barrier and the country’s first line of defense against destructive tropical cyclones coming from the Pacific Ocean.2 As storms approach, the mountain range helps slow down and weaken their winds before they reach inland areas. This natural shield helps reduce the destructive effects of typhoons, protecting lives, infrastructure, ecosystems, and livelihoods. It also helps regulate water that supports communities and agricultural areas across the region.3 32 However, the “Backbone of Luzon” is in urgent need of protection. Despite its importance, the Sierra Madre continues to face severe environmental degradation. Every year, the mountain range reportedly loses roughly 9,000 hectares of forest cover due to human activities, including illegal logging, agricultural expansion, mining, and other forms of 1 Climate Change Commission. (2024). Sierra Madre: Mountain range for resilience. Available at https://climate.gov.ph/news/934 2 Ibid. 3 Department of Environment and Natural Resources. (2026). DENR assists House committee in aerial inspection for proposed Sierra Madre Authority. Available at https://calabarzon.denr.gov.ph/news-events/denr-assists-house- committee-in-aerial-inspection-for-proposed-sierra-madre-authority/ 1 development.4 When the Sierra Madre loses its forest cover, its ability to absorb rainfall, regulate water flow, and reduce the impact of strong winds is also diminished. As forest degradation continues, communities in Central Luzon and Metro Manila may face greater risks of flooding and landslides. This proposed measure therefore seeks to establish the Sierra Madre Mountain Range Authority (SMMRA), which will lead the formulation and implementation of a comprehensive and long-term plan for the conservation, protection, and sustainable development of the Sierra Madre Mountain Range. It will also coordinate the efforts of concerned national government agencies and local government units to ensure a unified and sustained approach to the protection and development of the mountain range. The bill also proposes the creation of the Sierra Madre Ecological Integrity and Sustainable Development Master Plan, a comprehensive, science-based, 25-year plan that will establish ecological limits, management zones, no-go areas, permitted and prohibited uses, restoration priorities, measurable outcomes, investment requirements, and implementation responsibilities. The Master Plan will provide a common framework for harmonizing national, regional, local, ancestral-domain, and sectoral plans affecting the Sierra Madre. This measure also promotes sustainable livelihoods, including agroforestry, ecotourism, and sustainable non-timber forest products. It also provides avenues for Indigenous Peoples to participate in conservation and restoration activities. To support the long-term implementation of the law, the bill establishes a Sierra Madre Fund and provides for lawful and transparent financing mechanisms, including national government appropriations, environmental charges, and grants and technical assistance. The Fund is limited to the SMMRA’s statutory functions and is subject to government accounting, auditing, transparency, and disclosure requirements. The measure also strengthens accountability by establishing ecological standards, monitoring systems, environmental liability mechanisms, and stronger prohibitions against destructive activities. It prohibits, among others, unauthorized land conversion, destructive extractive activities, introduction of invasive species, unauthorized commencement of covered works, and the use of false compliance documents. The proposed legislation therefore seeks to move Sierra Madre governance from fragmented management toward an integrated, science-based, and investment-oriented system. It recognizes that protecting the Sierra Madre is an investment in the country’s overall well-being, which include food and water security, biodiversity, climate resilience, and disaster-risk reduction. 36 4 Sierra Madre losing 9,000 hectares of forest cover each year — Haribon. label: HB 11438
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING FOOD WASTE REDUCTION AND PREVENTION EDUCATION IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, PROMOTING RESPONSIBLE FOOD CONSUMPTION AMONG LEARNERS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Food waste is a major socio-economic and environmental issue that impacts national food security, economic efficiency, and environmental sustainability. According to estimates from the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) Philippines and the Department of Agriculture, thousands of tons of edible food are wasted daily in the country, even as millions of Filipino families experience involuntary hunger and nutritional deficits. While supply chain inefficiencies and retail practices contribute significantly to food loss, consumer behavior—particularly wasteful consumption patterns—plays a critical role in generating preventable food waste. Establishing lifelong habits of mindful consumption, respect for food resources, and awareness of nutritional value must begin at an early age. Schools serve as the primary institutional setting for shaping the values, social consciousness, and daily behaviors of young citizens. By integrating comprehensive, age-appropriate food waste reduction, zero-waste principles, and responsible consumption education into the basic education curriculum, the State can foster a culture of sustainability among future generations. This bill seeks to institutionalize food waste reduction and prevention education across all public and private basic education institutions in the Philippines. It mandates the Department of Education (DepEd), in coordination with relevant agencies, to incorporate practical food management skills, zero-waste concepts, and agricultural literacy into existing curricular frameworks. Furthermore, it encourages schools to establish zero-waste canteen management guidelines, composting initiatives, and school garden programs. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11439
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DISPLAY OF NUTRITIONAL INFORMATION ON THE MENUS AND MENU BOARDS OF FOOD ESTABLISHMENTS AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution guarantees the protection and promotion of the right to health of the people and the instillment of health consciousness among them (Article II, Section 15). The Philippines has faced a rising burden of non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and obesity. According to data from the Department of Health (DOH) and the Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI), lifestyle-related conditions account for a significant portion of mortality in the country. A contributing factor to this trend is the shift in dietary habits, marked by an increased consumption of food prepared outside the home, which often contains high levels of sodium, saturated fats, added sugars, and total calories. While consumers are increasingly conscious of their health choices, they are often hindered by a lack of accessible and clear information regarding the nutritional value of the food they purchase in chain restaurants, fast-food outlets, and other commercial food establishments. Providing point-of-decision nutritional information empowers individuals to make informed, healthy dietary choices for themselves and their families. Similar policies implemented in other jurisdictions have encouraged food service operators to reformulate recipes to offer healthier alternatives, thereby fostering a culture of health responsibility across the food industry. This bill seeks to mandate standard food service establishments with five (5) or more branches to prominently display total calorie counts and core nutritional values on their menus, menu boards, and drive-thru displays. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11440
title: AN ACT MANDATING AND INSTITUTIONALIZING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A PEOPLE'S COUNCIL IN EVERY CITY AND MUNICIPALITY IN THE PHILIPPINES, DEFINING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, PROVIDING MECHANISMS FOR CITIZEN PARTICIPATION IN LOCAL GOVERNANCE, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Section 16, Article XIII of the 1987 Philippine Constitution guarantees the right of the people and their organizations to effective and reasonable participation at all levels of social, political, and economic decision-making. Furthermore, Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, directs local government units (LGUs) to promote the establishment and operation of people's and non-governmental organizations to become active partners in the pursuit of local autonomy. Despite these constitutional and statutory mandates, civil society participation in many local government units remains consultative, informal, or merely symbolic. Citizens and sectoral organizations often lack a formal, institutionalized mechanism to directly participate in policy formulation, budget deliberation, program monitoring, and local governance. This bill seeks to mandate and institutionalize the establishment of a People's Council in every city and municipality across the Philippines. Inspired by successful local participatory models, such as the Naga City People's Council, this measure empowers accredited civil society organizations (CSOs), non- governmental organizations (NGOs), and sectoral groups to sit in local special bodies, attend legislative sessions, propose local measures, and participate directly in local decision-making processes. By providing a structured framework for civil society engagement, this legislation aims to deepen local democracy, ensure transparency, foster accountability, and guarantee that public policies genuinely reflect the needs of the community. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11441
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES IN ALL PUBLIC AND PRIVATE ELEMENTARY AND HIGH SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE, CREATING THE POSITIONS OF SCHOOL MENTAL HEALTH PROFESSIONALS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Mental health is a fundamental component of overall well-being, directly influencing a child’s capacity to learn, build healthy relationships, and navigate life’s challenges. In recent years, the urgency of addressing mental health issues among Filipino youth has escalated significantly. Rates of anxiety, depression, and self-harm among primary and secondary school students have reached alarming levels, further exacerbated by modern social pressures, economic difficulties, and the aftermath of global disruptions. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 11036, otherwise known as the "Philippine Mental Health Act," and Republic Act No. 11206, or the "Career Guidance and Counseling Act," a severe gap remains in the actual delivery of mental health services within the basic education system. Currently, the public school system faces a catastrophic shortage of registered guidance counselors (RGCs), primarily due to low salary grades and non-competitive compensation structures. Consequently, thousands of elementary and high schools across the country operate without a single mental health professional on site. This bill seeks to address these critical vulnerabilities by establishing a comprehensive Mental Health Program in all public and private elementary and high schools nationwide and creating a dedicated mental health personnel positions with competitive compensation packages (adjusting salary grades for Guidance Counselors and creating Mental Health Associate positions) to recruit and retain qualified professionals. Prioritizing the mental health of our learners is an urgent social imperative. By building a resilient, supportive, and accessible mental health infrastructure within our schools, we safeguard the future of our nation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11442
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING A NATIONAL CHILD RIGHTS AND RULE OF LAW EDUCATION PROGRAM, STRENGTHENING THE IMPLEMENTATION OF GOOD MANNERS AND RIGHT CONDUCT AND VALUES EDUCATION UNDER REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11476, PROVIDING FOR THEIR HARMONIZED INTEGRATION IN EDUCATIONAL AND YOUTH DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution recognizes the vital role of our youth in nation-building and directs the State to promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. It likewise mandates the right of children to assistance and to special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. As a result, the Republic has enacted an extensive body of laws protecting children and learners from violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation, trafficking, bullying, discrimination, child marriage, online sexual abuse or exploitation, child sexual abuse or exploitation materials, and other threats to their safety and development. These include Republic Act No. 7610, as amended; Republic Act No. 9344, as amended by Republic Act No. 10630; Republic Act Nos. 10173, 11476, 11510, 11596, 11650, 11930, 12080, and 12199; and other child-protection, education, mental- health, disability, and data-privacy laws. These laws provide important substantive protections. Yet a legal right cannot fully protect a child who does not know, in an age-appropriate manner, that such right exists, how to recognize a situation requiring protection, whom to approach, and how to obtain lawful assistance. Child protection must therefore include not only response and enforcement, but also prevention through practical, inclusive, and developmentally appropriate education. Children need not be of legal age to understand their rights, recognize danger, seek assistance, respect the rights of others, and appreciate the responsibilities of citizenship. Legal literacy enables children and young people to understand the protections available to them, recognize situations requiring assistance, use lawful reporting and referral mechanisms, and appreciate the responsibilities that accompany the exercise of rights. This measure draws, among other sources, upon the policy proposal advanced by Atty. Robie P. Quiño in the legal research paper entitled “Not of Legal Age, but of Legal Mind.” It is likewise anchored on Articles 29 and 42 of the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the 1 Child, which relate education to respect for human rights and require the principles and provisions of the Convention to be made widely known to adults and children alike. Republic Act No. 11476 already institutionalizes Good Manners and Right Conduct (GMRC) as a separate subject from Grades 1 to 6, integrates GMRC into kindergarten learning activities, and establishes Values Education for the higher grade levels. Its full promise, however, depends upon faithful classroom implementation, trained teachers, adequate and relevant learning resources, meaningful character-building activities, school-family-community partnership, and continuing review of actual learner outcomes. This measure therefore strengthens, rather than duplicates or displaces, the GMRC and Values Education framework. It integrates age-appropriate child-rights and rule-of-law competencies with the formation of human dignity, respect, honesty, self-discipline, responsibility, peaceful conflict resolution, obedience to law, and concern for others, while preserving the separate-subject requirements and time allotments mandated under Republic Act No. 11476. The proposed National Child Rights and Rule-of-Law Education Program does not create an additional stand-alone academic subject where existing curricula and learning areas can adequately deliver the required competencies. Instead, it establishes a national framework through which existing education, child-protection, GMRC, values-education, mental-health, digital- safety, juvenile-justice, alternative-learning, technical-vocational, higher-education, and youth- development programs may be mapped, harmonized, strengthened, and connected. This integration shall not diminish the teaching of GMRC and Values Education as separate subjects where required by Republic Act No. 11476. The Program is age-progressive. For young children, it emphasizes dignity, personal safety, respectful relationships, personal boundaries, trusted adults, safe and unsafe situations, and help- seeking. For older learners, it progressively introduces children’s rights and responsibilities, digital citizenship, privacy, crime prevention, due process, restorative justice, civic participation, the functions of public institutions, and lawful mechanisms for obtaining protection and assistance. The measure also protects learners from retraumatization, compelled disclosure, stigma, retaliation, and misuse of personal information. Teachers and other education personnel are trained to recognize concerns, secure immediate safety, comply with applicable reporting duties, and make appropriate referrals, but they are not converted into investigators, forensic interviewers, social workers, counselors, prosecutors, or lawyers. Nothing in the measure creates a new criminal offense, increases criminal liability, or lowers the minimum age of criminal responsibility. The bill further provides measurable implementation standards, accessible and legally accurate learning resources, local referral directories, inter-agency coordination within existing mandates, phased implementation, administrative accountability through existing lawful mechanisms, monitoring, periodic review, and reporting to Congress. 2 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11443
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE SEAL OF GOOD LOCAL GOVERNANCE BY REQUIRING DISTINCT, MEASURABLE, INCLUSIVE, AND OUTCOME-BASED LOCAL SPORTS DEVELOPMENT INDICATOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 7(E) OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11292, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “SEAL OF GOOD LOCAL GOVERNANCE ACT OF 2019,” AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to promote physical education and encourage sports programs, league competitions, and amateur sports to foster self-discipline, teamwork, and excellence and to develop a healthy and alert citizenry. Local government units, as the public institutions closest to their communities, are uniquely positioned to translate this policy into sustained and accessible opportunities for participation in sports and physical activity. Republic Act No. 11292, otherwise known as the “Seal of Good Local Governance Act of 2019,” already recognizes the fostering of sports development under Programs for Sustainable Education. It likewise empowers the Council of Good Local Governance to develop and revise outcome-based performance indicators while taking into account that local government units are not similarly situated. The law, however, does not expressly require at least one distinct and measurable sports-development indicator among the statutory examples under this assessment area. This measure closes that limited gap. It requires a durable, outcome-based indicator covering both school-based and community-based sports programs undertaken or supported by the local government unit, whether through the Local School Board, local sports development council, local youth development office, barangays, or other lawful local bodies. It directs the assessment to consider program continuity, participation, inclusion, qualified coaching, safe and accessible facilities, athlete health and welfare, safeguarding, sustained local support, and measurable community benefits. The measure deliberately avoids reducing good local governance to infrastructure spending, isolated tournaments, or medal counts. Verified competitive achievements may support an assessment, but they should demonstrate the results of a functioning local sports-development system rather than serve as the sole or controlling measure. Standards must also remain proportionate to the category, population, geography, fiscal capacity, and other circumstances of each province, city, or municipality. To integrate the reform into the existing SGLG system, the Council and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) are directed to revise the existing implementing rules, performance indicators, assessment tools, and technical notes in coordination with the Department of Education (DepEd) and the Philippine Sports Commission (PSC) and after consultation with the leagues of local government units, local sports development councils, organizations representing persons with disabilities, and recognized sports, athlete-welfare, and safeguarding stakeholders. By making local sports development mandatory, measurable, inclusive, and durable across assessment cycles, this measure will encourage local governments to build healthier communities, widen access to sports, protect athlete welfare, and invest consistently in grassroots development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. RICHARD I. label: HB 11446
title: AN ACT GRANTING EDUCATIONAL ASSISTANCE TO THE CHILDREN AND DEPENDENTS OF FARMERS AND FISHERFOLKS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our farmers and ﬁsherfolk remain to be among those with the highest poverty incidence in the country. It is unfortunate that despite their sacriﬁce and hard work, they struggle to meet the basic needs of their families. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the ﬁsherfolk sector recorded a poverty incidence of 27.4%, while farmers recorded a poverty incidence at 27%. Their livelihoods are highly susceptible to the adverse eﬀects of climate change, natural disasters, and ﬂuctuating market prices. In the face of these hardships, education serves as the great equalizer and the most sustainable pathway out of poverty. Under Article XIV of the 1987 Constitution, the State is mandated to protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, ensuring it is accessible to all. It is our moral and social obligation to make true of this commitment to our agricultural workers. Through extending targeted educational assistance to their children and dependents, we ensure that the youth are not deprived of a brighter future simply due to ﬁnancial constraints. To this end, this bill seeks to provide a comprehensive educational assistance, speciﬁcally for the children and dependents of farmers and ﬁsherfolk. The proposed measure will cover all all the necessary expenses for primary, secondary and tertiary education, which includes tuition fees, miscellaneous fees, learning materials, board and lodging, transportation expenses, clothing allowance, and other similar expenses. By covering these miscellaneous expenses, our farmers and ﬁsherfolk will not be forced to make a diﬃcult choice between ﬁnancing the next harvest and sending their children to school. In addition, the bill proposes to establish a special fund to sustain this government assistance. Through this dedicated fund, we can guarantee the program’s continuity and wider reach across the country. This, in turn, will empower the next generation of our agricultural sector to break free from the vicious cycle of poverty. Let us honor the blood, sweat, and tears of our agricultural workers by giving their sons and daughters the ﬁghting chance they deserve. Through this measure, we are saying investing in a brighter and more digniﬁed future for the families who feed our entire nation. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11447
title: AN ACT EXEMPTING MICRO AND SMALL ENTERPRISES FROM THE IMPOSITION OF MINIMUM CORPORATE INCOME TAX, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 27 OF THE NATIONAL INTERNAL REVENUE CODE OF 1997, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Local entrepreneurs, particularly micro and small enterprises, remain the backbone of the Philippine economy as they are estimated to form 99.5% of the businesses in the country. Considering the successive crises that the Philippine economy has suffered, it is undeniable that the livelihood of these micro and small enterprises was adversely affected. It is also undeniable that these businesses are responsible for employing millions of Filipino workers. The Philippine Chamber of Commerce and Industry (PCCI) recently warned that escalating fuel prices place the heaviest burden on micro and small enterprises, as they operate on notoriously thin margins. Maintaining a punitive tax on gross revenue forces small businesses to pay taxes out of their capital rather than their profits. Currently, the National Internal Revenue Code provides for the imposition of the 2% Minimum Corporate Income Tax (MCIT) on the gross income of Domestic Corporations. Without any distinction on the size of the corporation, this necessarily includes those corporations categorized as micro and/or small enterprises. Under current regulations, this means vulnerable enterprises are forced to pay income tax based on gross revenues, even when operating at a loss. When the 1987 Constitution speaks of equitable taxation, it pertains to the fairness of a tax levy in consideration of the totality of the circumstances of the concerned taxpayers. Applying a blanket MCIT goes against this principle by ignoring a small business’s actual ability to pay, most especially during times of high inflation and external shocks. This bill seeks to provide relief to Micro and Small enterprises by exempting them from the imposition of the 2% Minimum Corporate Income Tax. By doing so, we are giving them a direct relief which also translates to indirect economic benefits. Shielding these vulnerable businesses allows them to preserve local jobs, hire new workers, and confidently reinvest capital to stabilize their operations. This proposed exemption creates a win-win scenario for both the public and private sectors. In this manner, businesses are given the breathing room they need to survive periods of loss or unprofitability, while the government builds and cultivates a stronger, more resilient tax base that promises to yield higher regular corporate income taxes once these enterprises grow and become profitable. We should stop taxing the mere survival of our smallest businesses and start investing in the prosperity of our entire nation. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROTECTION AGAINST BULLYING IN SCHOOLS, DEFINING AND PENALIZING THE CRIME OF BULLYING
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 10627 or the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013 was the glimmer of hope for countless learners suﬀering in silence. Yet, the sad and painful reality is that the law has not served as a suﬃcient deterrent against bullies, nor has it oﬀered a strong shield for the victims. We can no longer stay complacent while our children are subjected to all sorts of acts or words that instill fear, humiliation, and life-threatening harm in spaces meant to be safe for learning and growth. The undeniable need to fortify our laws and impose penalties has never been clearer. According to the updated 2022 report of the Program for International Student Assessment (PISA), 1 out of 3 Filipino students reported being bullied in schools. Just recently, there was an 8-year-old student in Davao City who died from a traumatic brain injury after being mercilessly struck by a classmate, 1 and two 16-year-old students in Zamboanga City who were stabbed during a violent altercation fueled by bullying.2 The Department of Education (DepEd) has aWempted to stem the tide through internal administrative frameworks. Under DepEd Order No. 55, s. 2013, the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) for the Anti-Bullying Act required schools to form Child Protection CommiWees and adopt local intervention programs. Acknowledging the escalating severity of school violence, DepEd recently issued DepEd Order No. 006, s. 2026, or the Guidelines on Ensuring a Safe and Motivating 1 Kristoﬀer Lou Ataylar, Rojean Grace G. Patumbon, and David Ezra M. Francisquete, "Alleged Bullied Child Dies of Brain Injury," SunStar, July 24, 2026, hNps://www.sunstar.com.ph/davao/alleged-bullied-child-dies-of-brain-injury. 2 Leah D. Agonoy, "2 Students Wounded in Zamboanga City School Stabbing Incident," INQUIRER.net, July 1, 2026, hNps://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2256219/2-students-wounded-in-zamboanga-city-school-stabbing-incident. Learning Environment (ESMLE). This urgent policy enforces a progressive disciplinary framework where high-risk bullying oﬀenses can result in preventive suspension, non-readmission, permanent exclusion, and immediate turnover to law enforcement. However, administrative department orders alone are not enough to dismantle this systemic issue. While DepEd policies outline vital procedures for intervention and school-level discipline, the statutory law itself must evolve to mandate harsher penalties and broader institutional accountability. To address the gap, this bill seeks to strengthen the protection aﬀorded to the learners by clearly deﬁning what constitutes “bullying” and outline corresponding penalties for such acts. This aims to aﬀord protection to all the student population, particularly those who are disproportionately targeted, including students suﬀering from mental and/or physical disabilities, members of the LGBTQ Community, and all other vulnerable individuals who suﬀer silently in the hands of bullies. We should aim to create a society where bullying does not exist. Only when this culture of intimidation stops can we expect our students to thrive and excel, and our communities to remain peaceful. Thus, the swift passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11449
title: AN ACT FURTHER EXTENDING THE ESTATE TAX AMNESTY UNTIL JUNE 30, 2028, THEREBY AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11213, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE When an individual dies and leaves behind assets or properties, there arises an obligation to se4le the corresponding estate tax, among other tax implications. This process undoubtedly burdens the grieving families both emotionally and ﬁnancially. Without the se4lement of the estate and the payment of the estate tax, the property of the deceased become dormant, encumbered by legal impediment that hinder the heirs from developing and/or transferring them. The Estate Tax Amnesty by the government provides an opportunity for the family members or heirs to se4le the obligations a4ached to the decedent assets. This grants them the liberty to ﬁnally decide how to utilize the properties left behind by their loved ones, free from the paralyzing burden of compounded penalties and surcharges. This bill seeks to extend the Estate Tax Amnesty until June 30, 2028. It also proposes to expand the coverage of the amnesty to include the estates of those decedents who died on or before May 31, 2024. Through this, we are aﬀording this privilege to more Filipinos. Further, this bill will serve as a strategic economic measure. It will signiﬁcantly improve overall tax collection despite the waiver of penalties that would have been otherwise imposed on the estates. Families who were previously deterred from se4ling their obligations out of fear of exorbitant ﬁnes and penalties will now be encouraged to ﬁnally se4le the estates of their decedents and pay the estate tax. Through the removal of legal impediments a4ached to unse4led estates, families are empowered to legally act on the assets they stand to inherit, whether to transfer, sell, or develop their inheritance. This, in turn, will maximize the use of idle assets and boost productivity as dormant "dead capital" is brought back into the active market, broadly stimulating the Philippine economy. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11451
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE USE AND MAINTENANCE OF SIDEWALKS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE It is the policy of the State to safeguard life, health, property, and public welfare, consistent with the principles of environmental management and control. However, the Philippine streets and sidewalks are still among the world’s most dangerous for pedestrians.1 Our sidewalks remain to be unpassable due to poor conditions and obstructions at the expense of our citizens. Reports show that motorcycles and jeepneys passing through the sidewalks has been a common practice in some areas in the country. In one instance, this has led to a student acquiring phobia in an accident with a motorcycle while crossing the sidewalk.2 Unfortunately, this is just one of the pervasive cases caused by sidewalk obstruction. Illegally parked vehicles, store extension, signages, construction of pens or cages of animals among others, also pose threat to the welfare of our citizens. The Department of Transportation even observed the danger of the current state of our sidewalks, thus, the need to remove obstructions to give importance to our pedestrians.3 Efforts have been made to curb this prevalent dilemma through issuances of DILG Memorandum Circulars 019-121, 2020-027, 2020-145, and 2022-085. However, despite these national directives in place, proper implementation to clear out our sidewalks remains to be a challenge. Mobility is public service. Mobility is a right. 1 https://opinion.inquirer.net/178416/unsafe-roads 2 https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/849537/pedestrians-lament-being-eased-out-of-sidewalks-by-vehicles/story/ 3 https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/2152758/edsa-sidewalk-repairs-to-begin-in-early-2026-dotr-dpwh With the passage of this bill, a stronger legal mechanism will be strongly enforced to ensure that we return the sidewalk to our People. In the best interest of our Pedestrians, the immediate passage of this bill is urgently sought. JANICE V. label: HB 11452
title: AN ACT EXPANDING FRONTLINE SERVICE HOURS INCLUDING WEEKEND COVERAGE FOR VOICE AND NON-VOICE INQUIRIES AND IN-PERSON TRANSACTIONS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE In the Philippines, both private employees and government offices essentially follow the same weekday work schedule. This presents a fundamental difficulty for working Filipinos who must process official transactions during business hours such as license applications, loan and benefits facilitation, or payment of taxes and fees. They are often left with an impossible choice: postpone essential transactions, use their vacation leaves or absent themselves from work at the cost of their daily wage. This burden falls heaviest upon our daily wage earners and frontline workers. Through the years, technology has been integrated into government services to assist citizens who cannot personally visit government offices. Various agencies such as the Social Security Service (SSS), Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth), and Home Development Mutual Fund (PAG-IBIG) have adopted digital solutions, including mobile applications, chat support services, and online portals. However, these advancements remain insufficient. Certain transactions inherently demand face-to-face processing and personal review, particularly those involving frontline services that require physical presence, identity verification, or the submission of original documents. This bill seeks to institutionalize accessible government service. Frontline services shall operate on extended working hours, including Saturdays or even Sundays if deemed necessary, with 24/7 availability for digital platforms, hotline, inquiries, appointments, and document submissions. By mandating extended operating hours across all covered agencies, we ensure that Filipinos can complete essential matters including urgent and emergency transactions without sacrificing their time and wages. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. JANICE V. label: HB 11455
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A PHILIPPINE PSYCHOLOGY PROFESSIONALIZATION ACT, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10029, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “PHILIPPINE PSYCHOLOGY ACT OF 2009”, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 Section 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the "Philippine Psychology Professionalization Act". ARTICLE Il STATEMENT OF POLICY SEC. 2. Statement of Policy. The State recognizes that psychologists have an important role in nation-building and development. It also acknowledges the diverse specializations of psychologists and the distinct functions specific to the varied specializations, including those that do not involve the professional practice of psychology or the delivery of psychological services. It further acknowledges the need to protect the public by preventing unqualified individuals from engaging in psychological practice or offering psychological services. Hence, it shall nurture competent, upright, and diligent registered professional psychologists whose standards of practice and service shall be excellent and globally competitive through the administration of inviolable, effective, and credible licensure examinations and the imposition and promotion of regulatory measures, programs, and activities that enhance their professional growth and well-being.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 When a Filipino seeks psychological help, the person should be able to find a professional who is properly trained for the kind of help that is needed. This need becomes more pressing in light of the limited number of mental health professionals in the country. The World Health Organization's Mental Health Atlas 2024 reports only 0.3 psychologists per 100,000 population, or approximately 3 psychologists for every 1,000,000 Filipinos. 28 With so few professionals available, it becomes even more important that the psychology profession is properly structured and that available professionals are able to perform the functions for which they are trained. 32 Republic Act No. 10029, or the Philippine Psychology Act of 2009, established the regulation of psychologists and psychometricians. Now, this proposed measure seeks to update this framework by replacing the psychometrician classification with the Registered Psychology Associate, giving it a broader and clearly defined scope of practice, while reserving specialized clinical assessment and intervention for Registered Psychologists. 39 The proposed measure also recognizes that psychology professionals should have a rightful place in the institutions where their services are needed. It mandates the creation of plantilla positions for Registered Psychologists and Registered Psychology Associates in local government units, hospitals, educational institutions, and workplaces, with appropriate job descriptions, ranks, and salary grades that reflect the training, responsibilities, and value of their work. 46 A stronger psychology profession means better protection for the people who need help and better support for those who provide it. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 2 3 4 REP. JERNIE JETT V.
