label: HB 11518
title: AN ACT DECLARING JULY 2 AS A SPECIAL NONWORKING HOLIDAY IN THE FIFTH DISTRICT OF QUEZON CITY TO BE KNOWN AS THE “ARAW NG NOVALICHES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Fifth District of Quezon City, or the Novaliches District, is one of the fastest developing areas in Quezon City. It has a size of 5,246.72 hectares, comprises 14 barangays, and its population has already reached the half- million mark. Located at the northernmost part of the city, Novaliches serves as the gateway to the metropolis of the big province of Bulacan and is also the geographical center of Quezon City, San Jose, and Caloocan City. The District also houses the La Mesa Dam Watershed, which supplies water to over 20 million residents of Metro Manila, and the La Mesa Eco-Park, an ecological nature reserve site that has become a favorite destination of city dwellers. Apart from its development potential, the Novaliches District has also been a witness to the Philippines’ rich history. The District is the home of the Katipunan Tree, which was a staging area of the Katipuneros during the Philippine Revolution. Under this old duhat tree, the Katipuneros held meetings and treated their wounded1. Additionally, it is in one of the barangays in Novaliches where Melchora Aquino, more popularly known as Tandang Sora, last stood her ground and was eventually arrested by the Guardia Civil on August 29, 1896, prior to her 1 Philippine News Agency. 2018. “Significance of the Katipunan Tree in Novaliches cited.” https://www.pna.gov.ph/articles/1038015 (Accessed Online 9 September 2022) exile to Guam. On July 2, 2012, a separate legislative district of Novaliches was reapportioned and created in Quezon City by virtue of Republic Act No. 10170. It is on this day that the newly established Fifth District of Quezon City was founded and continued to flourish and thrive with Hon. Alfred Vargas as its first-ever district representative in the Philippine Congress. This bill seeks to commemorate this historic event and declare July 2 of every year as “Araw ng Novaliches”, a special nonworking holiday in the Fifth District of Quezon City. It is the hope of this measure to instill a sense of pride and consciousness in all Novaleños. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. label: HB 11519
title: AN ACT REQUIRING THE PROVISION OF INFANT-FRIENDLY FACILITIES IN GOVERNMENT AGENCIES AND MAJOR ESTABLISHMENTS IN THE PHILIPPINES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Under Article XV of the 1987 Constitution, “the State recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation,” and shall defend “the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition.” Consistent with this mandate, the State is duty-bound to create an enabling environment that supports parents and guardians in fulfilling their caregiving responsibilities. Recent national data underscore the urgency of this measure. The 2023 National Nutrition Survey (NNS) on Infant and Young Child Feeding shows that only about 50.4% of infants under six months are exclusively breastfed, while more than one-third (36%) of infants under six months are fed infant formula. Although the Philippines has made gains—exclusive breastfeeding rose from 35.9% in 2008 to 60.1% in 2021, and the 2023 NNS reports 50.4%— significant gaps remain in ensuring that caregivers can feed, change, and attend to infants safely and comfortably in public spaces. Existing laws already recognize the need for infant- and mother-friendly facilities. Republic Act No. 10028 (the “Expanded Breastfeeding Promotion Act of 2009”) mandates lactation stations in workplaces and public places, and Republic Act No. 11311 (the “Safe Mobility Act of 2019”) requires, among others, exclusive spaces for diaper-changing in land transport terminals. However, compliance remains uneven, and many government offices, commercial establishments, and food service venues still lack basic infant- friendly amenities—particularly diaper-changing stations accessible to both mothers and fathers, and child-friendly seating in dining areas. This bill, titled the “Infant-Friendly Facilities Act,” seeks to close these gaps by: • Requiring all government agencies and major establishments to provide at least one safe, sanitary, and convenient diaper-changing station on each floor, located in restrooms or in a common area accessible to both men and women; and • Mandating all food service establishments to provide child-friendly seats for their customers. The measure explicitly recognizes the growing role of Filipino fathers in childcare. Observations on the ground indicate that where diaper-changing tables exist, they are often installed only in women’s restrooms, effectively excluding fathers and other male caregivers. By ensuring gender-inclusive access, this bill promotes shared parental responsibility and removes practical barriers to family participation in public life. Through this simple but high-impact initiative, the State affirms the value of family quality time, supports optimal infant feeding and hygiene practices, and helps parents and guardians rear children in conditions conducive to health, dignity, and civic efficiency. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM’ D. label: HB 11520
title: AN ACT PRESCRIBING SCHOOL BUS SAFETY STANDARDS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The World Health Organization published those deaths due to traffic accidents in the Philippines has reached more than 13,000 in 2020. In Metro Manila alone, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) reported that there are 227 accidents per day that have put the lives of Filipino citizens in danger. Among the highly susceptible age groups to road accidents are children, who, with full-time face-to-face classes, now travel from their homes to their schools and back daily. As the State seeks to improve road safety and to protect pedestrians and motorists alike, this bill empowers the Department of Transportation to prescribe safety standards for school buses, set proficiency measures for school bus drivers, require the installation and use of seatbelts in school buses, and determine the practicability and feasibility of certain safety and access requirements for school buses. In ensuring that our students are safe from vehicular accidents, we are safeguarding the future development of our nation. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11522
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF CULTURE, ARTS, TOURISM AND HERITAGE COUNCILS IN EVERY PROVINCE OF THE COUNTRY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Nations that fail to learn from the past are bound to repeat their mistakes. For this reason, civilizations have long valued their art, heritage, and traditions. Our culture—expressed through our languages, cuisines, music, handicrafts, museums, and literature—shapes the shared identity of Filipinos today. When we enrich and celebrate our nation’s culture, we do more than honor those who came before us; we also equip and inspire the next generations of Filipinos to build a stronger future. The National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA) was created primarily for the purpose of developing, enhancing, and institutionalizing arts and culture programs in the country. However, it remains limited by its organizational nature – an agency based in the country’s capital with no bureaucratic network to expand its programs, projects, and activities up to the grassroots level. At best, it could only enter into memoranda of agreement with local government units to fund particular programs or projects with an arts and culture component. Animating the citizenry with the love and passion for their culture, arts, tourism, and heritage should be a shared responsibility of both the national and the local government units. Cultural programs at the provincial and city level must be complemented with the support of national agencies like the NCCA, the National Museum, the National Historic Commission of the Philippines, and stakeholders from the private sector. While a number of local government units have taken the initiative of organizing their own arts, culture, tourism, and heritage councils, a vast number of our provinces, which have rich untapped potential, remain in need of such support. In order to strengthen and institutionalize this necessary collaboration, this bill seeks to establish Culture, Arts, Tourism, and Heritage Councils in every province of the country. These opportunities to preserve, enhance, and develop local arts, culture, tourism, and heritage shall be a fitting gift for the next generation to appreciate and enjoy. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11523
title: AN ACT GRANTING A SPECIAL LEAVE OF ABSENCE OF FIFTEEN (15) DAYS A YEAR WITH FULL PAY TO ALL LEGITIMATE SPOUSES OF OVERSEAS WORKERS IN THE PRIVATE AND PUBLIC SECTORS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines ranks as one of the major labor-sending countries worldwide.1 With most Filipino migrants being parents, many children need to live away from their OFW parents for an extended period. With the proliferation of transnational families, studies have shown impacts on the mental and emotional health of children due to prolonged parent-child separations and the overall transnational living arrangements. 2 As the State recognizes the sanctity of family life, it strives to protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. In this endeavor, it shall also protect the well-being of left-behind families, especially children who are significant predictors of the development of a nation. With the limited number of days of leave for employees in the country, many OFWS whose spouses are employed in the Philippines do not get to spend a hundred percent of their vacation time with their family. 1 “Number of OWFs nearly fell nearly a fifth to 1.8M in 2020”. 2020 https://www.bworldonline.com/top-stories/2022/03/09/434745/number-of-ofws-fell-nearly-a-fifth- to-1-8m-in-2020/ Accessed Online on September 6, 2022 2 Graham, E and LP Jordan, 2011” Migrant Parents and the Psychological Well-being of Left-behind Children in Southeast Asia”. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3229683/ Accessed Online on 19, 2022 To ensure that OFWs’ rare vacations are well spent with their loved ones and to reinforce their familial ties, this bill aims to give every legitimate spouse of an OFW in the private and public sectors an additional special leave credit of fifteen (15) days a year with full pay, subject to certain qualifications. While the bill recognizes that mere additional days in the OFWs’ vacations would not compensate for the number of days that they are away from the family, the bill hopes that by providing the left-behind spouses additional days of leave, every transnational family will choose to strengthen the bond of their families, and be as involved as possible in their homes, as basic structures of the institution. It further hopes that the bill can help address the rising number of marriage dissolutions among transnational couples. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11524
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE ESTABLISHMENT OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY AFFAIRS OFFICES (PDAOs) IN ALL LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AMENDING REPUBLIC ACT NO. 10070, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS AN ACT ESTABLISHING INSTITUTIONAL MECHANISM TO ENSURE THE IMPLEMENTATION OF PROGRAMS AND SERVICES FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES IN EVERY PROVINCE, CITY, AND MUNICIPALITY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The objective of Republic Act No. 10070, which establishes an institutional mechanism to ensure the implementation of programs and services for Persons with Disabilities in every province, city, and municipality, is to ensure that relevant and sustainable programs for Persons with Disabilities are implemented at the local level. Under this law, specific roles ascribed to Local Government Units (LGUs) are initially delineated and coordinated within the operational framework of the Persons with Disability Affairs Office (PDAO). For provinces, cities, and 1st to 3rd class municipalities, PDAO shall be established through a Local Ordinance. In 4th to 6th class municipalities, a Focal Person (FP) performs the functions of PDAO, which is mandated through an Executive Order. However, thirteen years after RA No. 10070 was passed, over 50% of LGUs still have yet to establish their respective PDAO. Based on the recent record of the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA), there are 739 PDAOs, or 43% compliance, as of February 2022. One of the primary reasons for non-compliance is funding constraints. Since the establishment of an office is subject to the availability of funds, it leaves discretion to LGUs to create their respective PDAO. Not to mention that the success of data gathering, a comprehensive database, further capacity building, information dissemination, and public awareness campaigns all remain to be seen. In addition, there is still a lack of updated and reliable official data on the actual number of people in the disability sector, which has a strong correlation to delays in policy implementation. Due to a lack of capacity and funding sources, many LGUs do not have a properly maintained database. This highlights the pressing need to capacitate and establish PDAOs in all LGUs tasked with having a uniform and standardized local database linked to a national Philippine Registry for Persons with Disability (PRPWD) system. In light of the implementation of the Mandanas ruling and in the continuous and overdue quest for improving local service delivery for the disability sector, the need to insist on the mandatory nature of the creation of PDAOs and appropriate funding source for the establishment and operations of PDAOs is timely and imperative. This measure proposes to amend RA No. 10070 specifically to: (1) ensure the mandatory creation and operation of PDAOs in all Local Government Units (LGUs); (2) provide a clear budget allocation for their establishment; (3) further strengthen their functions; (4) include a uniform and standardized local database linked to a national PRPWD system; (5) ensure mechanisms for data management, capacity building, and information dissemination about PDAOs; and (6) refine its fragmented institutional framework. After more than a decade since the enactment of RA No. 10070, policy interventions should be made to fully strengthen the implementation of RA No. 7277 and to ensure relevant and sustainable programs as well as active participation and empowerment of the disability sector in various undertakings and projects of LGUs. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 There are moments in a young person's life that mark the beginning of something new. Graduation is one of them. It is the day a student closes one chapter of life and begins to build a future of his or her own. 25 But while graduation marks the beginning of a new chapter for the student, it should also mark the beginning of something new for the country. 28 This proposed Graduation Legacy for Reforestation Act seeks to make tree planting a meaningful part of a student’s life. By requiring every graduating senior high school and college student to plant two trees, graduation becomes not only the beginning of a new chapter in a student's life, but also the beginning of a new life in the form of a tree. Years from now, the graduate may no longer remember the exact details of the ceremony, but the tree can remain as a living reminder of the day he or she began a new journey. 35 More than a graduation requirement, this measure seeks to give every graduating Filipino an opportunity to leave a living legacy. 38 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 40 41 42 REP. title: AN ACT PROVIDING STRONGER MEASURES FOR THE CONSERVATION AND PROTECTION OF WILDLIFE RESOURCES AND THEIR HABITATS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9147 OR THE “WILDLIFE RESOURCES CONSERVATION AND PROTECTION ACT” 26 27 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 30 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Revised Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act”. 33 SECTION. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It shall be the policy of the State to conserve and protect the country's wildlife resources and their habitats for sustainability and to promote ecological balance, enhance biological diversity, and ensure the provision of ecosystem services. In the pursuit of this policy, this Act shall have the following objectives: 39 (a) Regulate the collection, possession, use, and trade of wildlife, wildlife by- products and derivatives; 42 (b) Pursue, with due regard to the national interest, Philippine commitments to international conventions, treaties, and agreements on the protection of wildlife and their habitats, and on the fair and equitable sharing of the benefits from the lawful utilization of wildlife genetic resources; 47 (c) Initiate or support scientific studies on the conservation of biological diversity and sustainable utilization of wildlife resources. 50 (d) Promote full awareness and widest dissemination of policies on wildlife conservation and protection; and
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 The Philippines is a home to many unique and threatened wildlife species. However, wildlife continues to be threatened by illegal hunting, collection, transport, trade, and destruction of their habitats. While Republic Act No. 9147, or the Wildlife Resources Conservation and Protection Act, already provides the current basic law for the protection and conservation of wildlife, the changing nature and increasing scale of wildlife crimes require stronger penalties and better enforcement measures. 28 Hence, this proposed measure now seeks to strengthen and update the existing wildlife protection law, particularly by providing clearer and heavier penalties for serious violations. The bill also adds important enforcement measures, including presumptions in certain wildlife cases, stronger administrative powers to confiscate and forfeit wildlife and equipment used in violations, Wildlife Enforcement Agents, Wildlife Traffic Monitoring Units, and a wildlife law enforcement information system. 35 Through these measures, the bill seeks to provide stronger penalties, better enforcement, and greater government support for the protection and conservation of Philippine wildlife. 39 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 41 42 43 REP. label: HB 11528
title: AN ACT PROVIDING THE REGULATORY FRAMEWORK TO CONSERVE, PROTECT, RESTORE, AND SUSTAINABLY MANAGE PEATLANDS AND THEIR RESOURCES TO ENHANCE THE COUNTRY’S RESILIENCE TO CLIMATE CHANGE 25 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 28 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Peatland Conservation Act”. 31 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. - It is the policy of the State to promote the conservation, restoration, and sustainable development of the country’s peatland and peatland resources; enhance the resilience of the Filipino people towards climate change adaptation and mitigation, disaster risk reduction and management (DRRM) consistent with the principles of sustainable and inclusive economic development, poverty reduction, and biodiversity conservation, while advancing the right to a balanced and healthful ecology in harmony and rhythm of nature. 39 SEC. 3. Scope and Coverage. — This Act shall apply to all peatland and peatland resources nationwide within public and private lands. 42 SEC. 4. Definition of Terms. — As used in this Act: 44 (a) Adaptation refers to the adjustment in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climatic stimuli or their effects, which moderates harm or exploits beneficial opportunities. 48 (b) Climate change refers to a change of climate which is attributed directly or indirectly to human activity that alters the composition of the global atmosphere and which is in addition to natural climate variability observed over comparable time periods. (c) Carbon sink refers to carbon reservoirs and conditions that take in and store more carbon than they release.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 The country’s peatlands are more than ecosystems to be protected. In July 2025, a peatland fire in the Agusan Marsh affected approximately 152 hectares. In 2026, another peatland fire burned for nearly two weeks, although the exact area affected had yet to be determined. These incidents show the continuing vulnerability of peatlands to fire, drainage, land conversion, and other human activities. 27 Despite their importance, peatlands have received less attention in environmental and climate policies compared with other ecosystems. Their value as carbon sinks, water regulators, and habitats for biodiversity is often overlooked. This measure aims to address this gap by providing specific rules for the protection, restoration, and proper management of peatlands. It provides for the mapping and monitoring of peatlands, the prevention and control of peatland fires, the restoration of damaged areas, and the regulation of activities such as drainage, conversion, reclamation, and peat extraction. 35 By protecting our peatlands, we protect one of nature’s most important stores of carbon. 37 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 39 40 41 REP. label: HB 11529
title: AN ACT ADOPTING INTEGRATED COASTAL MANAGEMENT AS A NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR THE HOLISTIC AND SUSTAINABLE MANAGEMENT OF COASTAL AND RELATED ECOSYSTEMS AND THE RESOURCES THEREIN FROM RIDGE-TO-REEF, ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL COASTAL GREENBELT ACTION PLAN, OTHER SUPPORTING MECHANISMS FOR IMPLEMENTATION, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR 28 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 31 CHAPTER I GENERAL PROVISIONS 34 35 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “Integrated Coastal Management Act.” 38 SEC. 2. Policy Statement. – It shall be the policy of the State to ensure the sustainable management of the country’s coastal and marine environment and resources by looking at the interconnectivity of ecosystems from the watersheds to the coastal and marine areas. Towards this end, it shall adopt Integrated Coastal Management as a framework in regulating different human activities, restoring or rehabilitating ecosystems, and ensuring a multi-stakeholder participation and ridge-to- reef approach to ecosystem management, with due consideration to ecological connectivity and their impact on social and ecological systems. The framework shall support the country’s achievement of sustainable development, promotion of blue economy, food security, just transition to sustainable livelihood, poverty alleviation and its resilience and risk reduction, from sea-level rise and other coastal stresses, while respecting the traditional resource rights of indigenous peoples and gender equality. 52
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 The Philippines is, by geography and by livelihood, a nation deeply connected to the sea. With a coastline stretching approximately 36,289 kilometers, and more than 70 million Filipinos living in coastal areas, the health of our seas and coastlines is inseparable from the welfare of our people. 26 Our coastal ecosystems are likewise among the country's most valuable natural assets. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), as of 2025, the Philippines had approximately 2.15 million hectares of coastal resources, consisting of 1.34 million hectares of coral reefs (or at least 62.3%) 496,560 hectares of seagrass (or at least 23%) and seaweed areas, and 318,160 hectares of mangrove forests (or at least 14.8%) 33 Likewise, the PSA, in 2024, reported that the country's ocean-based industries generated ₱943.05 billion in 2023, contributing 3.9% to the country's Gross Domestic Product, with the ocean economy growing by 9.9% from the previous year. Ocean fishing alone accounted for 28.6% of the total ocean economy. 38 However, undeniably, these resources and industries face increasing, if not constant, pressures from development, pollution, climate change, habitat degradation, and poorly coordinated activities across political boundaries. 42 Hence, this proposed measure establishes Integrated Coastal Management (ICM) as a national strategy to coordinate national agencies, LGUs, communities, and other stakeholders in protecting and managing coastal resources. Aside from the creation of a National Coordinating Committee on ICM to lead this initiative, it also creates a National Coastal Greenbelt Action Plan to identify and restore vulnerable coastal areas, revert abandoned, undeveloped, and underutilized fishponds to mangroves, and remove illegal structures in protected areas. 3 In short, the proposed measure combines coordinated governance, science-based planning, and ecosystem restoration—including penalties for unauthorized structures and other violations within designated coastal greenbelts. By institutionalizing integrated coastal management, the measure aims to ensure that the Philippines' coastal resources remain productive and capable of sustaining communities and the economy for generations to come. 10 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 12 13 14 REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The absence of a cybersecurity law leaves a big gap in our legal framework, considering its importance in terms of national security and economic stability. Without a robust cybersecurity law, the country’s digital infrastructure remains highly vulnerable to increasingly sophisticated cyber threats. Earlier in 2024, the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) reported 282 cyberattacks against government organizations, 90% of which were resolved. In other cases, only about 76% of the early-stage hacking attempts were detected and neutralized by the agency’s National Security Operations Center.’ The absence of legislation on the identification, management, and regulation of Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) creates a discernible blind spot. We cannot protect what we have not formally identified. This lack of a clear framework, combined with the poor coordination among CII and government agencies, means our most essential digital assets are at a high risk from uncoordinated and fragmented defense strategies. Further, the lack of mandatory disclosure of cybersecurity incidents hinders our ability to build a comprehensive national threat intelligence picture. Without a clear understanding of the attacks that are happening, we cannot effectively prepare for future ones. label: HB 11532
title: AN ACT AMENDING SECTIONS 4 AND 12 OF THE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9514, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "FIRE CODE OF THE PHILIPPINES OF 2008”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 9514, also known as the Fire Code of the Philippines of 2008, stands as a cornerstone of the nation's commitment to public safety, economic development, and the professionalization of the fire service. Since its enactment, the Code has provided a comprehensive framework for fire prevention, suppression, and the enforcement of safety standards across the country. However, with the rapid pace of urbanization, came the emergence of new economic and industrial zones, technological advancements, and the increasing complexity of fire hazards that have exposed regulatory gaps and operational challenges within the jurisdiction of the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) that must be inevitably addressed. This proposed measure seeks to update and strengthen the Fire Code to ensure its continued relevance and effectiveness in safeguarding lives, property, and critical infrastructure. The bill expands the applicability of the law to encompass all persons, buildings, facilities, and structures-including those situated within economic zones, information technology parks, tourism zones, and other special entities, as well as vehicles, ships, petroleum installations, airports, and other high-risk areas. By closing existing regulatory gaps, the measure ensures that all sectors, particularly those with heightened fire risks, are subject to uniform and robust fire safety standards. Recognizing the need for adequate fiscal resources to fulfill its mandate, the bill likewise modernizes the funding mechanisms of the BFP by introducing new sources of income, including fees for the issuance of clearances assessed based on floor area and hazard level. These mechanisms are intended to support the continuous upgrading of the BFP's manpower, infrastructure, and equipment, enabling it to respond effectively to the evolving landscape of fire risks that BFP are currently facing. Given the wider scope that this measure seeks to achieve, this measure will invariably address the concerns on regulatory gaps in jurisdiction as well as to give the BFP sufficient autonomy to carry out its mandate independently and effectively. During the Spanish occupation, the Spanish Crown had issued several contradictory laws regarding language, where the missionaries were urged to learn the local vernaculars, but were subsequently required to teach Spanish. ' Due to the several foreign rule that governed the country, the traditional way of writing had been threatened with extinction in that the foreign language was more often used to communicate rather than using the traditional methods. It is thus imperative that we preserve our culture and the native languages endemic only to the areas where they are spoken. This proposed measure aims to implement joint efforts by differen: agencies in their respective duties in order to ensure the preservation and proliferation of the indigenous and traditional writing systems by promoting. developing and integrating the use thereof in educational systems. Moreover. the proposed bill mandates the treatment of indigenous and traditional texts as important cultural properties which should be preserved to be taught. exhibited and showcased for learning by the Filipino people, lest a part of the Filipino cultural identity be lost to the annals of time. In light of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ' Rodriguez, Rebeca Fernandez. “Early Writing and Printing in the Philippines.” 9 July 2013. label: HB 11534
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A SEGREGATED SHARP AH-COMPLIANT PROVIDENT SAVINGS AND HOUSING FINANCE WINDOW WITHIN THE HOME DEVELOPMENT MUTUAL FUND, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9679, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “HOME DEVELOPMENT MUTUAL FUND LAW OF 2009”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a segregated Shari’ah-compliant provident savings and housing finance window under the Pag-IBIG Fund, amending for the purpose Republic Act (RA) No. 9679, otherwise known as the “Home Development Mutual Fund Law of 2009.” While the 1987 Constitution guarantees access to decent, affordable housing and promotes broad-based economic participation, structural gaps in the existing financial framework continue to limit access to provident savings and housing finance for members who adhere to non-interest-based financial principles. Under RA No. 9679, Pag-IBIG’s existing savings and financing mechanisms are principally structured around conventional, interest- bearing arrangements. Providing an alternative mechanism within the country’s principal public provident savings and housing finance institution can help address this gap and broaden financial inclusion. Republic Act No. 11439, or the “Islamic Banking Act,” recognizes Islamic banking and establishes a policy of tax neutrality between Islamic banking transactions and _ their conventional equivalents. However, RA No. 11439 principally governs banks and Islamic banking units, while Pag-IBIG is a government provident fund and housing finance institution. Express authority under RA No. 9679 is therefore necessary for the Fund to establish and sustainably operate a Shari ‘ah-compliant window suited to its mandate. To bridge this gap, this measure establishes a segregated operational and accounting window within Pag-IBIG. It authorizes the use of recognized, non-interest-based and asset- backed structures such as Mudarabah (profit-sharing), Murabahah (cost-plus sale), [jarah Muntahiyah bi al-Tamlik (lease-to-own), Musharakah Mutanagqisah (diminishing partnership), and Istisna (construction financing). The Window will be available to all qualified Pag-IBIG members on a voluntary basis, regardless of religion, while existing conventional savings and housing programs remain available and unaffected. Because certain Shari’ah-compliant structures may require the Fund to acquire, hold, lease, co-own, sell, or transfer property, the measure provides the incidental authority necessary to implement such transactions. It likewise requires appropriate segregation of assets, liabilities, income, and expenses, prudent standards for investment, liquidity, reserves, risk management, valuation, accounting, and internal controls, and policies that facilitate access by lower-income members while preserving the actuarial soundness and solvency of the Fund. To ensure Shari’ah compliance and protect members, the bill establishes a Shari’ah Advisory Committee to certify products, contracts, operational policies, and investments and to conduct compliance reviews. It also provides for appropriate disclosures, transparent pricing, fair treatment in matters such as default and early settlement, and accessible complaints mechanisms. The implementing rules will provide the detailed procedures for enrollment, participation, fund management, accounting, standard contracts. disclosures, compliance, and other operational matters. The measure likewise adopts the principle of tax neutrality so that additional transfers or documents required solely by an approved Shari ’ah-compliant financing structure do not result in more burdensome tax treatment than a functionally equivalent conventional transaction. This is intended to prevent structural double taxation while preserving existing tax laws and exemptions applicable to the Fund. By modernizing Pag-IBIG’s framework to accommodate voluntary, inclusive financing options, this bill expands member choice, strengthens financial inclusion and savings mobilization, and makes state-backed housing programs more accessible while safeguarding the provident character, financial stability, and public accountability of the Fund. For these reasons, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. o~ USTADZ YUSOP T. label: HB 11538
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE FULL ACCOUNTING OF ALL DISASTER-RELIEF AID OR DONATIONS RECEIVED BY THE PHILIPPINE GOVERNMENT FOR NATURAL AND HUMAN-INDUCED CALAMITIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is among the countries with the highest number of calamities annually due to its geographic location along the Pacific Ring of Fire and the typhoon belt. The country is highly vulnerable to earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, typhoons, and severe flooding, which result in significant economic and humanitarian challenges each year. The Department of Science and Technology (DOST) reports that an average of 20 storms and typhoons enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility annually, while the country also experiences between 100 and 150 earthquakes of varying magnitudes. These recurring disasters necessitate robust mechanisms, including immediate relief efforts and long-term recovery programs. Over the years, the resilience of the Filipinos in facing these disasters has been strengthened by both local and international humanitarian aid. Donations in the form of cash and in-kind assistance from foreign governments, multilateral organizations, private institutions, and individuals have played a crucial role in the disaster relief and recovery efforts. However, concerns regarding the transparency, accountability, and proper utilization of these donations have persisted, raising questions about their efficient deployment to affected communities. The proposed Donation Transparency Act seeks to establish a legal framework for the full disclosure and accounting of all disaster-related aid received by the Philippine government. The measure aims to ensure that every donation- whether from foreign entities or domestic sources-is properly documented, tracked, and utilized strictly for its intended purposes. The bill is designed to enhance public trust in disaster-relief efforts by eliminating opportunities for mismanagement and corruption in the handling of donations. By ensuring that all aid is appropriately accounted for and disclosed, the measure promotes good governance, transparency, and efficient disaster response and recovery. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11539
title: AN ACT ENSURING CHILD SUPPORT AND PENALIZING PARENTAL REFUSAL OR NEGLECT THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE As indicated in the 1987 Philippine Constitution, it is the duty of the State to defend a child’s right to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. This is further enshrined in several laws, including the Presidential Decree No.603 or the Child and Youth Welfare Code, the Republic Act No. 7610 or the Special Protection of Children against Child Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act, and the Republic Act No.9262 or the Anti-Violence against Women and Children Act. Every child, whether legitimate or illegitimate, has the right to receive support from their parents. Support, as defined in Section 194 of the Family Code of the Philippines, comprises everything indispensable for sustenance, dwelling, clothing, medical attendance, education, and transportation, in keeping with the financial capacity of the family. On February 18, 2022, the Philippines signed the Convention on the International Recovery of Child Support and Other Forms of Family Maintenance (known as the Child Support Convention), which was negotiated under the authority of the Hague Conference on Private International Law. This convention is but one of the affirmations of the country’s commitment to protecting children’s rights by ensuring child support. While the State has enacted and implemented several laws that protect a child’s right to support, these laws do not penalize parents who willfully fail to provide child support. This bill seeks to penalize any person who willfully fails to pay child support for at least one year or has an outstanding amount due of Fifty Thousand Pesos (Php 50,000.00) or more. It is the hope of this measure to protect children’s rights and ensure child support as they grow up by penalizing parental refusal or neglect of child support. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11540
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE REGULATORY POWERS OF THE NATIONAL FOOD AUTHORITY TO SUPPORT THE RICE INDUSTRY AND ENSURE CONSUMER PROTECTION THROUGH ADEQUATE SUPPLY AND STABLE PRICE OF RICE, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8178, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “AGRICULTURAL TARIFFICATION ACT”, AS AMENDED
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Rice is a staple food of Filipino households and remains central to the country’s food security, agricultural economy, and household welfare. Republic Act No. 8178, as amended by Republic Act No. 11203, liberalized rice importation and shifted the National Food Authority (NFA) away from its previous regulatory and commercial functions toward maintaining an emergency rice buffer stock.1 While rice tariffication was intended to improve market efficiency and provide consumers access to competitively priced rice, subsequent experience has underscored the continuing need for effective government capacity to monitor the rice market, protect consumers from unreasonable price movements, and safeguard the interests of domestic rice producers. The proposed measure therefore seeks to strengthen the regulatory powers of the 1 Republic Act No. 8178, Agricultural Tariffication Act, § 2, as amended by Republic Act No. 11203, Rice Tariffication Law (2019), Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines. Department of Agriculture (DA), through the NFA, and improve the government’s ability to respond to supply disruptions and market abuses.2 The measure recognizes that food security requires more than simply ensuring the availability of imports. The proposed amendments strengthen the government’s ability to register and inspect grain warehouses and other facilities, collect and analyze market data, and respond to cornering, hoarding, profiteering, artificial scarcity, and unwarranted increases in rice prices.3 These powers are intended to give the government the tools necessary to identify and address conduct that can undermine the normal operation of the rice market and adversely affect consumers. The bill also provides for greater coordination among the DA, NFA, Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), Bureau of Customs (BOC), local government units, and law-enforcement agencies, recognizing that effective rice-market regulation requires timely information and coordinated enforcement. At the same time, the bill seeks to strengthen the role of the government in maintaining a reliable rice buffer stock and supporting domestic farmers. It requires the NFA to source its buffer stock primarily from local farmers, farmer cooperatives, and farmers’ associations, while allowing procurement in milled- rice form when necessary and providing an order of preference that gives priority to local agricultural institutions and facilities. The measure also establishes more flexible mechanisms for the disposition of buffer stocks, including sales through accredited retailers, government entities, KADIWA outlets, farmers and farmer cooperatives, and public auction, subject to requirements of transparency, competitiveness, accountability, and public monitoring. These provisions are designed both to improve stock management and to ensure that government procurement can provide a dependable market for local farmers while preventing the unnecessary aging and wastage of public rice stocks. Finally, the measure seeks to provide farmers with greater protection against excessively low palay prices while balancing this objective with consumer welfare. It authorizes the DA to establish reasonable and flexible floor prices for palay at the national, regional, and provincial levels, taking into account production costs, prevailing market prices, reasonable farmer margins, and the welfare of both farmers and consumers. This approach recognizes that a resilient rice industry must protect both ends of the food-supply chain: consumers must 2 Republic Act No. 11203, An Act Liberalizing the Importation, Exportation and Trading of Rice, Lifting for the Purpose the Quantitative Import Restriction on Rice, and for Other Purposes, §§ 2, 5 and 6 (2019), Official Gazette of the Republic of the Philippines. 3 Republic Act No. 8178, as amended, § 5 have access to adequate and reasonably priced rice, while farmers must receive prices that make rice production economically sustainable. By restoring stronger regulatory capacity, improving buffer-stock management, strengthening enforcement against market abuses, and providing mechanisms for more reasonable farmgate prices, the proposed RICE Act seeks to build a rice sector that is more secure, responsive, and capable of serving the long-term interests of Filipino consumers and farmers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11541
title: AN ACT GRANTING FULL TAX BENEFITS TO GOVERNMENT PURCHASES DURING A STATE OF CALAMITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines remains among the countries most exposed and vulnerable to natural and climate-related hazards. Its location along the Pacific Ring of Fire, archipelagic geography, extensive coastline, and exposure to tropical cyclones, flooding, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, droughts, and other extreme-weather events make the country particularly susceptible to recurrent disasters. In the 2025 World Risk Index, the Philippines ranked first among 193 countries, with a “very high” disaster-risk score of 46.56, underscoring the continuing urgency of strengthening the country’s disaster preparedness, response, and recovery systems. The country’s experience with the COVID-19 pandemic further demonstrated that large-scale public emergencies may arise not only from natural hazards but also from public-health threats. The pandemic disrupted livelihoods, overwhelmed health systems, and required the immediate mobilization of public resources for medicines, vaccines, personal protective equipment, testing supplies, food assistance, emergency shelters, and other essential goods and services. To address the perennial challenge of the country, the State has enacted Republic Act No. 10121, otherwise known as the “Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010,” which institutionalized a comprehensive, all-hazards, and multi-sectoral approach to disaster risk reduction and management. Republic Act No. 10821, or the “Children’s Emergency Relief and Protection Act,” likewise requires special protection and emergency relief for children affected by disasters and other emergency situations. More recently, Republic Act No. 12009, or the “New Government Procurement Act,” authorizes negotiated procurement in emergency cases, including when there is imminent danger to life or property during a state of calamity, when time is of the essence due to natural or human-induced calamities, or when immediate action is necessary to prevent loss of life or property and restore essential public services. While this mechanism expedites government procurement, government agencies may still incur value-added tax, excise tax, customs duties, and other applicable taxes in the purchase or importation of urgently needed goods and services, thereby reducing the quantity of life-saving assistance that limited emergency funds can procure. This bill seeks to grant full tax benefits to qualified government purchases made during a duly declared state of calamity. By exempting such purchases from applicable taxes, duties, fees, and charges, the measure will enable the government to obtain more relief goods, medicines, medical equipment, emergency shelter materials, food, water, fuel, rescue equipment, and other critical supplies using the same appropriated funds. The proposed measure complements existing disaster-risk-reduction and emergency-procurement laws by strengthening the government’s fiscal capacity to respond immediately and effectively to calamities. It ensures that public resources are directed principally toward the urgent needs of disaster-affected individuals, families, and communities, while promoting accessible, equitable, and timely delivery of emergency assistance and essential public services. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAEL “PM” D. label: HB 11542
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL SCIENCE HIGH SCHOOL IN BARANGAY SALVACION, CITY OF IRIGA, PROVINCE OF CAMARINES SUR, TO BE KNOWN AS THE IRIGA CITY NATIONAL SCIENCE HIGH SCHOOL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIV, Section 1, of the 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all. Further, Section 10 states that science and technology are essential for national development and progress. Pursuant to this constitutional mandate, the Iriga City Science High School was granted authority by the Department of Education to offer Junior High School specializing in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) beginning School Year 2024– 2025. Since then, the school has demonstrated academic excellence and has earned recognition through its outstanding performances in national and international academic competitions. This bill seeks to provide the school with a statutory basis for its continued operation and development. It likewise seeks to strengthen the school's institutional mandate and facilitate its access to appropriate national government support, thereby ensuring the continuity and sustainability of the quality science-oriented education it provides. Various stakeholders, including the Local School Board of the City of Iriga, concerned local government officials, and the DepEd Region V, have expressed their support for this measure. The establishment of the Iriga City National Science High School will expand access to specialized science and STEM education for academically capable learners in the district and neighboring municipalities, particularly those who may not have the financial means to pursue similar programs outside the Rinconada area. In the long run, it will contribute to the development of a pool of future scientists, engineers, and other professionals in Rinconada by providing learners with a specialized educational environment that nurtures their aptitude in STEM. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MIGUEL LUIS R. label: HB 11543
title: AN ACT CREATING PERMANENT SCHOOL SECURITY OFFICER POSITIONS IN ALL PUBLIC ELEMENTARY AND HIGH SCHOOLS NATIONWIDE AND ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE SCHOOL SAFETY AND SECURITY PROGRAM, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 13 of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that the State recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation-building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Furthermore, Article XV, Section 3 guarantees the right of children to assistance, including proper care and nutrition, and special protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. Schools are meant to be safe havens where young learners acquire knowledge, foster friendships, and build the foundation for their futures. However, public schools across the Philippines face growing vulnerabilities to security threats, unauthorized intrusions, theft of government equipment, vandalism, and physical violence. Elementary and high school students, owing to their tender age, are particularly vulnerable and require proactive protection. At present, many public schools lack dedicated, regular security personnel due to budgetary constraints or reliance on short-term contractual hiring and voluntary community assistance. This leaves basic educational facilities unprotected, placing both students and educators at risk. This bill seeks to address this critical gap by creating permanent, regular position titles for School Security Officers (SSOs) across all public schools nationwide. By establishing plantilla positions under the Department of Education (DepEd), the government ensures professionalized, well- trained, and stable security coverage in our basic education system. Additionally, this legislation mandates a Comprehensive School Safety and Security Program applicable to both public and private elementary schools. This program includes physical security enhancements, compulsory emergency drills, mandatory visitor screening protocols, anti-bullying initiatives, and close coordination with local law enforcement and disaster risk management units. In view of the paramount importance of safeguarding our children and ensuring a conducive learning environment, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11544
title: AN ACT REQUIRING MAJOR SOCIAL MEDIA PLATFORMS AND DIGITAL CONTENT NETWORKS TO SECURE A CONGRESSIONAL FRANCHISE TO OPERATE IN THE PHILIPPINES, PROVIDING FOR REGULATORY COMPLIANCE, AND PRESCRIBING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled:
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Digital social media platforms have evolved far beyond basic communication networks; they are now the primary infrastructure for public discourse, commerce, news dissemination, and social interaction in the Philippines. As of recent estimates, over 90 million Filipinos—roughly 78 percent of the national population—utilize social media networks such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube, and X daily. Despite generating billions of pesos in advertising revenues from local businesses and content creators, major foreign technology conglomerates operate within Philippine digital borders without a physical corporate footprint, local regulatory oversight, or proper operational accountability. This lack of local jurisdiction creates significant public policy challenges. Platform operators frequently fail to act swiftly on takedown requests involving dangerous content, online scams, cyberbullying, hate speech, deepfakes, and illegal acts targeting Filipino minors. Further, these operators generate massive revenue streams locally while evading equivalent domestic corporate taxes, regulatory fees, and compliance burdens imposed on traditional broadcast and telecommunication entities. Under Commonwealth Act No. 146 (the Public Service Act), as amended, entities operating services of significant public consequence must be subject to state regulation to safeguard the public welfare. Just as traditional television, radio, and telecommunications networks require legislative franchises to access public airwaves and infrastructure, social media platforms operating at scale utilize public digital space and national telecommunications networks to reach citizens. This bill mandates that major social media platforms and digital content networks reaching a defined active user threshold must secure a Congressional Franchise to operate legally within the Republic of the Philippines. This requirement ensures that multinational technology companies establish a registered physical office, appoint local corporate officers subject to Philippine jurisdiction, comply with strict content safety protocols, and contribute fairly to the nation's tax base. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11545
title: AN ACT PROMOTING GREENING, FORESTLAND REHABILITATION, AND PROTECTION AT THE BARANGAY LEVEL, SPURRING LOCAL CLIMATE CHANGE ACTION, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is recognized as one of the countries most vulnerable to the adverse impacts of climate change. Severe weather events, accelerated deforestation, watershed degradation, and loss of biodiversity threaten rural livelihoods, compromise food and water security, and trigger catastrophic disasters like flash floods and landslides. While national environmental frameworks such as the Revised Forestry Code (P.D. 705), the Climate Change Act of 2009 (R.A. 9729), and the National Greening Program (NGP) exist, their implementation often lacks localized, community-anchored execution and sustainable follow-through. The Barangay is the primary planning and implementing unit of government policies, plans, programs, projects, and activities in the community. It stands at the frontline of disaster risk reduction and environmental management. However, many barangays lack both explicit mandates and dedicated, localized financial support to sustain forestland rehabilitation, seedling propagation, and continuous protection activities within their territorial jurisdictions. This bill seeks to institutionalize community-driven climate action by mandating a nationwide Community-Based Greening and Forest Rehabilitation Program at the barangay level. Specifically, this measure mandates every barangay with degraded forestlands to establish community nurseries, initiate localized reforestation, and conduct regular maintenance and protection activities. By decentralizing reforestation and empowering local communities as primary stewards of their natural environment, we build climate-resilient barangays and safeguard our ecosystems for future generations. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11546
title: AN ACT PROHIBITING HOSPITALS AND MEDICAL FACILITIES FROM IMPOSING ROOM, BOARD, AND DAILY ADMINISTRATIVE CHARGES ON PATIENTS CLEARED FOR DISCHARGE BUT REMAIN CONFINED DUE TO ADMINISTRATIVE REASONS BEYOND THEIR CONTROL, AND PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Constitution explicitly guarantees the right of the people to health and mandates the State to make essential goods, health, and other social services available to all at an affordable cost. However, a recurring issue in healthcare facilities across the country involves patients who, despite having been medically cleared for discharge, remain confined due to administrative delays and institutional processes beyond their control. These administrative delays include, but are not limited to, protracted discharge clearance workflows, delayed medical coding and billing preparation, unverified health insurance or PhilHealth coverage claims, delayed processing of government financial assistance (such as Malasakit Centers or DSWD medical aid), and system or software downtime. Under current practices, patients are frequently billed for extra days of room stay, nursing services, and administrative room fees accrued during these forced waiting periods. It is inherently unjust to financially penalize patients and their families for delays caused solely by institutional inefficiency, system failures, or third-party administrative processing. This bill seeks to address this injustice by prohibiting hospitals and medical facilities from imposing any room, board, nursing, or daily administrative charges on medically cleared patients whose physical discharge is delayed solely due to administrative reasons beyond their control. By enacting this measure, healthcare institutions will be incentivized to streamline their discharge protocols, ensuring fair treatment for patients while protecting families from unconscionable medical expenses. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11547
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE DIGITALIZATION OF STUDENT ACADEMIC RECORDS IN ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY SCHOOLS, ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL DIGITAL STUDENT RECORDS SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Over twenty-three million students are enrolled in basic education, from elementary to senior high schools, in the Philippines‘. This translates to vast amounts of academic and learner information across thousands of schools nationwide. Yet, many schools, particularly public schools, rely on paper-based records, resulting in significant administrative work for teachers and school personnel in the preparation, filing, retrieval, verification, and transfer of student records. Given the delays and additional administrative work associated with these processes, there is a need to maximize the use of technology in the education system. The digitalization of academic records presents an opportunity to modernize and streamline these processes. As we reduce the administrative workload of school personnel, we also provide students more time to focus on learning. This measure seeks to modernize the management of academic records through the establishment of a National Digital Student Records System (NDSRS). Through this system, the government can reduce administrative burdens, improve the efficiency and accuracy of record management, and facilitate the timely retrieval and transfer of learner information. 1 https://newsinfo.inquirer.net/19697 1 7/sy-2024-2025-sees-over-23-million -enrollees-in-elementary- high-school This proposed measure likewise recognizes the importance of interoperability across the broader basic education sector. While the digitalization of records in public elementary and secondary schools shall be mandated, private basic education institutions shall be allowed to voluntarily participate in the NDSRS. Their inclusion can promote greater continuity and efficiency in the movement and verification of learner records across public and private educational institutions. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. ETH T. label: HB 11548
title: AN ACT GRANTING UNRECOGNIZED ILLEGITIMATE CHILDREN THE RIGHT TO HAVE AND USE A MIDDLE NAME AND SURNAME
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to grant unrecognized illegitimate children the right to have and use a middle name and the surname of either parent. Article 176 of the Family Code of the Philippines originally provided that illegitimate children shall use the surname of their mother and be under her sole parental authority. However, on February 24, 2004, Republic Act No. 9255 was enacted amending the said article to allow the illegitimate children, upon recognition by the father, to use the father’s surname. As a result, the recognized illegitimate child may now use the surname of the mother as middle name and the father’s surname as the last name. However, illegitimate children whose parentage has not been formally acknowledged or recognized may be deprived of the opportunity to have and use a middle name. The absence of a middle name often serves as a visible marker of illegitimacy, which unfortunately perpetuates social stigma, invites discrimination, and undermines the inherent dignity of the child. This proposed measure allows an illegitimate child whose father has not acknowledged or recognized the child to use the mother’s middle name as the child’s middle name, followed by the mother’s surname. The mother may exercise this right by executing a Sworn Affidavit formally manifesting her choice of naming convention, subject to existing laws, civil registry rules, and the best interests of the child. Conversely, in cases where the mother has not acknowledged or recognized the child, the father may likewise exercise such right through a Sworn Affidavit, allowing the child to use the father’s middle name as the child’s middle name, followed by the father’s surname. The requirement of a Sworn Affidavit provides a formal mechanism through which the mother or father may manifest their choice of naming convention on behalf of the child. This mechanism is intended to provide the civil registry authorities with a clear documentary basis for the registration or annotation of the child’s middle name and surname, while ensuring that such exercise remains subject to existing laws, civil registry rules, and the best interests of the child. This approach is analogous in principle to the legal mechanism under Republic Act No. 9255, wherein an illegitimate father may execute the appropriate affidavit to allow the child to use his surname. In the same spirit, the mother should likewise be permitted to formally establish the child’s middie name and surname through a Sworn Affidavit, particularly in cases where the father has not acknowledged or recognized the child. The Supreme Court explained in re: Petition for Change of Name of Julian Lin Carulasan Wang, G.R. No. 159966, 30 March 2005, middle names identify maternal lineage and help distinguish individuals who may share the same given and family names. The absence or restriction of a middle name, therefore, has direct consequences on a child’s recognized identity, lineage, and dignity. This proposed measure ensures that unrecognized illegitimate children are legally acknowledged and given equal protection under the law. By allowing the use of the mother’s middle name or the father’s middle name as the child’s middle name, the proposed measure affirms the child’s right to identity, familial heritage, and legal recognition, thereby mitigating stigma and reinforcing the dignity of every child. More importantly, the measure is pro-poor and promotes equal access to justice. It provides a practical and accessible means for children to obtain legal recognition without requiring families, particularly those who lack financial means, to undergo costly and protracted court proceedings merely to secure a right that should be available to them by law. By removing this financial and procedural barrier, the measure ensures that legal recognition is not a privilege available only to those who can afford litigation, but a right accessible to every child regardless of economic status. In this way, the proposed measure advances not only the child’s right to identity and family affiliation, but also the State’s fundamental commitment to equality, social justice, and the protection of the dignity and welfare of every child. In view of the foregoing, an immediate apprgval is earnestly sought. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE DEVELOPMENTAL-BEHAVIORAL PEDIATRICS FELLOWSHIP SPONSORSHIP PROGRAM, PROVIDING GOVERNMENT SUPPORT FOR PEDIATRICIANS PURSUING SUBSPECIALTY TRAINING IN DEVELOPMENTAL-BEHAVIORAL PEDIATRICS, REQUIRING RETURN SERVICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE One in every five children, or roughly fifteen to twenty percent of the world’s population is neurodivergent. This encompasses conditions like Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), ADHD, dyslexia, and dyspraxia, among others. In the Philippines, the population of neurodivergent is_ still undetermined due to underreporting, misdiagnosis, and limited screening. Nevertheless, albeit fragmented, available local health data and advocacy suggest that ASD affects 1 in every 100, which translates to 1.2 million Filipinos; ADHD affects up to 80% of adolescents; and specific learning disabilities such as dyslexia affect about 10% of the population. It remains a challenge for children and families to seek proper assessment and care for neurodivergent individuals due to the limited pool of developmental pediatricians in the country. Nationwide, there are only about 80-100 actively practicing developmental and behavioral pediatricians, fifty percent of whom are concentrated in Metro Manila, while others are spread mostly across major cities like Cebu and Davao!. Aside from the high cost of professional fees, parents find it hard to secure consultation schedules from developmental and behavioral pediatricians - that is, if they find one nearby. To bridge this gap and encourage more Filipino pediatricians to take the path of becoming a full-fledged developmental and_ behavioral pediatrician, this bill establishes the Developmental-Behavioral Pediatrics t httos://onlinelibrary. wiley.com/doi/10.1111/pc.16055 Fellowship Sponsorship (DPFS) Program. This program shall provide financial and institutional support to qualified pediatricians pursuing accredited fellowship training in Developmental and Behavioral Pediatrics, with the aim of increasing the number of specialists serving neurodivergent Filipino children. Through this, early detection and intervention for neurodivergent children is more plausible, providing the public with more accessible, affordable, and responsive health care. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KE TH T. label: HB 11550
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE WELFARE, SOCIAL PROTECTION, TRAINING, AND OTHER SUPPORT MECHANISMS FOR CAREGIVERS OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES (PWDs), AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE There are over 2.5 million Filipinos living with disabilities. While the country has programs and projects for PWDs, that is not enough to fully care for PWDs. They would need assistive care in their homes and their daily activities. Across the country, parents, spouses, siblings, relatives, and other family members devote countless hours each day to providing physical assistance, medical care, rehabilitation, supervision, and advocacy for their loved ones with disabilities. Their work is indispensable, yet it remains largely unpaid, unrecognized, and unsupported. While Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Disabled Persons, affirms the rights and welfare of persons with disabilities, there remains no comprehensive law that recognizes and supports the equally vital role of their caregivers. Many caregivers are compelled to reduce their working hours, forego employment opportunities, or leave the workforce altogether to provide full-time care. Consequently, they experience financial hardship, physical exhaustion, emotional stress, social isolation, and increased vulnerability to mental health concerns. Amidst these, caregivers provide unpaid work 24 hours a day, seven days a week. While initiatives such as the Department of Social Welfare and Development's Therapy for Fee (TheraFee) Project, which provided cash-for- work assistance to family and community care workers who support persons with disabilities, represent a significant step forward, there remains a need for a comprehensive and sustainable framework that addresses the broader needs of caregivers of persons with disabilities. Financial assistance alone is not sufficient. This proposed measure seeks to institutionalize a comprehensive support system for caregivers of persons with disabilities. It provides qualified primary caregivers with a monthly caregiver assistance allowance, free skills training and certification, access to livelihood and employment support, mental health and wellness services, respite care, and priority consideration in appropriate government programs. Empowering caregivers is likewise an investment in persons with disabilities. When caregivers are adequately supported, they are better equipped to provide consistent and quality care, facilitate rehabilitation and development, promote independence, and help persons with disabilities participate more fully in society. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KE TH T. label: HB 11551
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A TEXTBOOK ASSISTANCE VOUCHER PROGRAM FOR STUDENTS ENROLLED IN PRIVATE BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Education remains one of the most effective means of promoting social mobility, strengthening human capital, and ensuring national development. While the State recognizes the complementary role of private educational institutions in the delivery of quality basic education, many Filipino families continue to struggle with the increasing cost of educational materials, particularly textbooks and learning resources. Although tuition and miscellaneous expenses are often the primary focus of educational assistance programs, the recurring cost of textbooks and instructional materials imposes a significant financial burden on parents and guardians, especially those belonging to low-income and middle-income households. In many cases, students rely on outdated, borrowed, or insufficient learning materials, adversely affecting learning outcomes and academic performance. This measure seeks to establish a Textbook Assistance Voucher Program that will provide qualified students enrolled in private elementary and secondary schools with targeted financial support for the acquisition of textbooks, workbooks, and other Department of Education-approved learning materials. The proposed voucher mechanism aims to promote equitable access to educational resources while supporting parental choice and the continued participation of private schools in the national education system. 1 The bill likewise ensures accountability and transparency through accreditation standards, digital tracking systems, and coordination with private schools, publishers, and authorized educational suppliers. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11552
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE, INTEGRATED, AND SUSTAINABLE REINTEGRATION PROGRAM FOR OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Overseas Filipino Worker (OFW) is an integral part of Filipino society and a significant contributor to our nation’s development. Yet, after years of working abroad and being separated from their families, many OFWs face another challenge upon returning home: rebuilding their livelihoods and reintegrating into their communities. This measure seeks to establish a comprehensive, integrated, and sustainable reintegration program for OFWs covering the entire migration cycle—from pre-departure, to on-site support, and upon return. It adopts a whole-of-government approach to provide returning OFWs with access to employment, entrepreneurship, education and skills development, financial literacy, psychosocial support, and other social protection services. The measure likewise seeks to strengthen coordination among government agencies and private sector partners, improve job matching and skills recognition, and ensure that undocumented OFWs are not excluded from reintegration assistance. It recognizes that effective reintegration requires not only financial assistance, but sustained support that enables OFWs to achieve economic self-sufficiency, social stability, and psychosocial well-being upon their return. 1 We owe it to our OFWs and their families to ensure that, when they return home, they are provided meaningful opportunities to rebuild their lives and contribute once again to the country’s development. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11553
title: AN ACT LOWERING THE OPTIONAL RETIREMENT AGE OF GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES FROM SIXTY (60) YEARS TO FIFTY-SIX (56) YEARS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 13-A OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8291, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE GOVERNMENT SERVICE INSURANCE SYSTEM ACT OF 1997
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Principle 3 of the 1991 United Nations Principles for Older Persons recognizes the right of older persons to participate in determining when and at what pace they withdraw from the labor force. Consistent with this principle, this measure seeks to lower the optional retirement age of government employees from sixty (60) years to fifty-six (56) years. Lowering the optional retirement age will allow government employees to enjoy their retirement benefits after years of dedicated public service and pursue other opportunities where their skills and experience may continue to contribute to the economy. At the same time, vacancies created by retirement will open opportunities for younger workers, bringing fresh skills and greater familiarity with emerging technologies into government service. This measure seeks to promote a more dynamic and responsive public service while expanding employment opportunities and supporting the financial independence of retiring government employees. Hence, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. Gatchalian EXPLANATORY NOTE Principle 3 of the 1991 United Nations Principles for Older Persons recognizes the right of older persons to participate in determining when and at what pace they withdraw from the labor force. Consistent with this principle, this measure seeks to lower the optional retirement age of government employees from sixty (60) years to fifty-six (56) years. Lowering the optional retirement age will allow government employees to enjoy their retirement benefits after years of dedicated public service and pursue other opportunities where their skills and experience may continue to contribute to the economy. At the same time, vacancies created by retirement will open opportunities for younger workers, bringing fresh skills and greater familiarity with emerging technologies into government service. This measure seeks to promote a more dynamic and responsive public service while expanding employment opportunities and supporting the financial independence of retiring government employees. Hence, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. KENNETH T. label: HB 11554
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE RIGHTS OF INFORMAL AMBULANT VENDORS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Every day, informal ambulant vendors earn a living by selling food, goods, and other products, or by offering services, in streets, parks, terminals, and other public spaces. They are part of the daily life of our communities and contribute to our local economies. Yet, despite their important role, many of them remain outside the reach of government programs and social protection because they are not formally registered or recognized by the local government units where they operate. Being part of the informal economy should not mean being invisible to government. Informal ambulant vendors face unique challenges. They often have no permanent place of business, limited access to social protection, and little security in their livelihood. At the same time, their operations must also be balanced with the legitimate concerns of consumers, communities, and local governments, particularly on public safety, sanitation, traffic, and the proper use of public spaces. This bill seeks to address these concerns by recognizing informal ambulant vendors as legitimate participants in our local economy and by providing a clear and simplified framework for their registration and protection. 1 The proposed Magna Carta of Informal Ambulant Vendors seeks to protect and promote their rights to just and humane working conditions, social protection, access to justice, and workplace security. It likewise provides for a simplified registration process at the local level so that informal ambulant vendors can be properly identified and connected to government programs and services without being burdened by complicated procedures and unnecessary fees. By formalizing the informal ambulant vending sector, this measure seeks to ensure that these workers are no longer overlooked, but are instead recognized as part of our communities and included in the social protection and economic opportunities that government provides. In light of the foregoing, the passage of this measure is earnestly sought. KENNETH T.
