label: HB 11556
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article 25 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the right to housing is a recognized fundamental human right ensuring that every person has access to a safe, secure, and affordable place to live. Adequate shelter means much more than just a roof and four walls. In keeping with international law, Article XIII, Section 9 of the Philippine Constitution mandates the State to undertake a continuing program of urban land reform and housing for the underprivileged and homeless in line with the policy of the State to promote a just and dynamic social order as enshrined in Section 9, Article II of our fundamental law. Despite the government's continuing efforts, however, millions of Filipinos remain without affordable, adequate, and secure shelter. This predicament is particularly significant among low-income families, informal settlers, and other vulnerable sectors who are unable to acquire or sustain homeownership due to the high cost of land, construction, and financing for housing. This bill seeks to establish a national policy providing qualified beneficiaries with free access to government-owned housing through usufruct. Under this arrangement, beneficiaries are granted the right to use and enjoy a government housing property for a specific period without transferring ownership of the property to the beneficiary. This approach allows the government to make productive use of its housing assets while providing qualified families with decent shelter. This bill proposes to accord underprivileged and homeless Filipino citizens who do not own any real property anywhere in the country. It shall also be extended to government employees under the auspices of Local Government units (LGUs) and other government agencies provided that the beneficiary does not own any real property within the territorial jurisdiction of the LGU where the employee is assigned or employed. This provision may help government institutions attract and retain personnel, particularly those assigned to areas where housing costs are beyond their means. To ensure that government housing resources remain available to future beneficiaries, the grant of usufruct shall not constitute a transfer of ownership and shall be subject to reasonable conditions on occupancy, maintenance, use, and termination. Beneficiaries are expected to use the property as their principal residence and to comply with the terms of the usufruct agreement. These safeguards will promote responsible stewardship of public housing assets and protect government property from unauthorized sale, transfer, or commercial use. The proposed policy is also intended to complement, rather than replace, existing national and local government housing programs. By introducing usufruct as an additional mechanism for providing secure housing, the government can expand access to shelter while maximizing the use of available public land and housing properties. It may likewise provide LGUs and government agencies with greater flexibility in addressing the housing needs of vulnerable communities and their qualified personnel. The urgency of this measure is underscored by the country's continuing housing deficit. Government estimates indicate that, without sustained intervention, the national housing backlog could reach approximately 22 million units by 2040. Addressing this gap requires not only the construction of additional housing units but also innovative approaches that make existing government resources more accessible to families who need them most. Free housing through usufruct offers a practical means of advancing the constitutional right to decent shelter while preserving public ownership of government housing assets. It places the State's existing land and housing resources at the service of Filipino families who have no adequate home of their own, while ensuring that these resources remain available for public benefit over the long term. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. ANTOLIN “LENLEN” A. label: HB 11557
title: AN ACT UPGRADING THE CLASSIFICATION OF TABACO DISTRICT OFFICE OF THE LAND TRANSPORTATION OFFICE (LTO) IN TABACO CITY, PROVINCE OF ALBAY FROM CLASS “D” TO CLASS “B” DISTRICT OFFICE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Province of Albay, where the world famous Mayon Volcano majestically sits, is the second most populous province in the Bicol region. The total population of the province stands at 1,379,398 distributed across 277,127 households (PSA Population Census 2024). Albay is accessible to tourists and other travelers via land, air or sea. A developing road network connects tourist destinations to urban centers and the countryside through public utility vehicles, i.e., buses, jeepneys, tricycles, padyaks (pedicabs) and privately owned motorcycles, cars and other conveyances. Expectedly, the rising vehicle density greatly contributes to traffic congestion – one of the critically urgent challenges to land transportation management. Albay is divided into three (3) Congressional Districts composed of fifteen (15) municipalities and three (3) cities. One of these three is Tabaco City, which together with the five (5) municipalities of Bacacay, Malilipot, Malinao, Sto. Domingo and Tiwi constitute the First District covering a population of approximately 433,349 (PSA Population Census 2024). The Land Transportation Office (LTO) Tabaco District Office hobbled by a meager workforce of only eight (8) plantilla positions as it is under the Class “D” category, provides the necessary major services. These include Licensing, Registration, Adjudication and Law Enforcement to a fast-growing population of road users. Despite human resource constraint, the LTO Tabaco District Office, although not without difficulty, has exhibited a commendable operational performance particularly for the period 2021-2025. An evidence-based analysis of the LTO Tabaco District Office’s overall performance for this five- year period reveals robust accomplishments in the delivery of the following services: • Motor Vehicle (MV) Registration: A total of 417,890 MV transactions were handled over the five-year period with an annual average of 83,578 transactions. Transactions increased significantly from 2021 to 1 2023, then declined in 2024 with a slight increase in 2025. This reduction may be attributed to the 2023 LTO policy extending the validity of initial registration for motorcycles to three (3) years, thereby decreasing the volume of annual renewal transactions in the succeeding years. • License and Permits: The office processed a total of 176,277 transactions, with an annual average of 35,255. The number of licenses and permits handled steadily rose from 2021 to 2024, before declining in 2025. The decrease may be partly due to the long- standing effect of the 10-year validity of driver’s licenses, which reduces the frequency of renewal activities, although overall figures remain higher compared to earlier years. • Apprehension Cases: A total of 4,367 apprehension cases were recorded over the five-year period, with an average of 873 cases per year. Cases gradually declined from 2021 to 2023, reflecting improved compliance with land transportation regulations. In 2024, apprehensions rose due to intensified enforcement operations; however, in 2025, the number decreased as motorists continued to adhere to traffic rules, demonstrating the positive impact of sustained enforcement and compliance efforts. • Revenue collection: The LTO Tabaco District Office generated a total revenue of P307,381,319.74, with an average annual collection of approximately P61.48 million. Despite the decline in some transaction volumes, revenue collection consistently increased from 2021 to 2023 and remained steady at a high level in 2024 and 2025, demonstrating sustained financial performance and efficiency in revenue-generating services. (Records of the Operations Division, LTO V) Needless to stress, the upgrade of the LTO Tabaco District Office from Class “D” to Class “B” is imperative. Hence, this proposed measure that seeks to implement the upgrade hopefully forthwith. The recommended upgrade shall necessarily increase the plantilla positions of the LTO Tabaco District Office to twenty (20), thereby creating an additional twelve (12) positions to its current eight (8) personnel complement. The change in classification and the consequent accompanying addition of personnel will indubitably benefit the patrons and clients from Tabaco City and nearby municipalities primarily through enhanced services and expedited transactions. These timely and much-needed reforms will trigger and promote higher revenue collection which in turn is expected to further expand and optimize provision of transport and allied public welfare services. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this bill is earnestly sought. CIELO KRISEL B. label: HB 11558
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE BED CAPACITY OF THE DRUG ABUSE TREATMENT AND REHABILITATION CENTER IN THE CITY OF LAS PINAS FROM ITS CURRENT CAPACITY TO ONE THOUSAND (1000) BEDS, UPGRADING ITS FACILITIES AND PROFESSIONAL HEALTHCARE SERVICES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development which shall endeavor to make essential goods, health and other social services available to all the people at affordable cost. The highly urbanized City of Las Pifias has seen continuous population growth and urban density, which brings a corresponding surge in demand for public health and social protection services, particularly in substance abuse treatment, mental health support, and community rehabilitation. While local health initiatives and outpatient drug treatment facilities exist in the city, the current physical capacity, medical infrastructure, and specialized personnel remain insufficient to meet the volume of individuals seeking residential rehabilitation and long-term recovery support. This measure seeks to expand and modernize the existing drug treatment and rehabilitation infrastructure in the City of Las Pifias by converting the existing locai facility into a high-capacity center named the Las Pifias City Drug Treatment and Rehabilitation Center. The bill explicitly mandates an increase in bed capacity to at least one thousand (1,000) beds, upgrades existing clinical, psychiatric, and vocational facilities to guarantee that the government provides adequate support to the city’s health sector. By enhancing the facility's bed capacity and integrating comprehensive medical, psychological, and vocational services, this Act ensures that residents of Las Pifias and neighboring localities in southern Metro Manila receive accessible, humane, and evidence-based rehabilitation without being displaced from their support systems. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARK ANTHONY G. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill institutionalizes a national drug education and life skills program across public and private basic education institutions, as well as the Alternative Learning System, covering learners from Grade 4 through Grade 12. Despite the existing statutory mandates under Republic Act No. 9165 and administrative initiatives like the Department of Education's Preventive Drug Education Program, drug prevention instruction in schools remains fragmented and vulnerable to administrative transition. By establishing a clear legislative framework to strengthen current laws and national programs, this measure ensures sustained, age-appropriate prevention education that equips young learners with critical life skills and capabilities to curb drug use and addiction at an early age. Despite the decline in drug prevalence observed by the Dangerous Drugs Board (DDB), purely punitive measures have proven insufficient in protecting the youth, necessitating a proactive, school-based approach anchored on health, education, and social development. title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE LOCAL HOUSING LAND BANK SYSTEM, MANDATING THE SUITABILITY ASSESSMENT AND PRIORITY RESERVATION OF TAX-DELINQUENT REAL PROPERTIES FOR SOCIALIZED HOUSING, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 264 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7160, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991," AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article XIII, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution mandates the State to undertake, in cooperation with the public sector, a continuing program of urban land reform and housing that will make available affordable and decent housing and basic services to underprivileged and homeless citizens. Yet in many highly urbanized cities, one of the greatest obstacles to providing affordable housing is not merely the cost of construction, but the extreme scarcity and high market cost of available land. At the same time, local government units periodically acquire real properties as a consequence of unpaid real property taxes. Under Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, real properties may, after compliance with the required notice, levy, and public auction procedures, be acquired by the local government when there is no qualified bidder or when the highest bid is insufficient to satisfy the taxes and related charges due. The law likewise preserves the property owner's statutory right of redemption before ownership finally vests in the local government unit. Once ownership has lawfully and finally vested in the local government, however, existing law generally allows the property to be subsequently disposed of through public auction. This measure seeks to introduce a more socially productive alternative. Before an LGU-owned property acquired through tax delinquency proceedings is resold, the property should first be evaluated to determine whether it can be utilized for socialized or public housing. Properties that are safe, accessible, appropriately located, and economically feasible for housing development may be placed in a Local Housing Land Bank rather than immediately returned to the private real estate market. This policy complements Republic Act No. 7279, otherwise known as the Urban Development and Housing Act of 1992, which recognizes land banking as a mode of acquiring land for socialized housing and accords priority to government-owned, abandoned, and idle lands. The proposed Local Housing Land Bank will provide LGUs with an VX YS Zz additional mechanism to address their housing requirements, particularly in highly urbanized areas where land prices frequently make in-city relocation difficult. The measure expressly protects property owners. Mere tax delinquency shall never be sufficient to place privately owned property in the Local Housing Land Bank. No property may be included until all procedures required by law have been completed and the owner's statutory right of redemption has fully expired. The measure further promotes in-city and on-site development whenever practicable so that families receiving government housing are not unnecessarily displaced far from their employment, schools, health facilities, transportation, and established communities. Housing should not merely provide a roof over a family's head. It should provide security of tenure while keeping families connected to their livelihoods and communities. label: HB 11564
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A COMPREHENSIVE NATIONAL HEALTH PROGRAM FOR THE PREVENTION, EARLY DETECTION, DIAGNOSIS, TREATMENT, AND MANAGEMENT OF SYSTEMIC LUPUS ERYTHEMATOSUS (SLE), PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR PERSONS LIVING WITH LUPUS AND THEIR FAMILIES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Lupus is a serious and lifelong illness that affects many Filipinos, yet it remains poorly understood by the general public. Its symptoms can differ from one person to another and may resemble those of other illnesses. As a result, some patients spend considerable time and resources seeking medical attention before their condition is properly identified. For an ordinary Filipino family, this delay has real consequences. Repeated consultations, laboratory tests, medicines, and continuing treatment can become a significant financial burden. More importantly, when the disease is not detected and properly managed early, the patient's condition may worsen and affect his or her ability to study, work, earn a living, and care for a family. Government intervention should therefore focus on a simple objective: help Filipinos recognize lupus earlier and make proper care more accessible and affordable. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive national program for lupus under the Department of Health. It provides for greater public awareness, early detection and proper referral, training of health workers, improved access to appropriate treatment and medicines, patient and family support, and the collection of reliable information necessary for government planning and research. The measure also recognizes that detecting an illness is only the beginning. A person diagnosed with lupus may require continuing care and regular monitoring. Thus, the bill directs the 1 Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) to provide appropriate coverage for lupus screening and early detection and to develop and periodically review an appropriate benefit package for medically necessary diagnostic procedures, laboratory monitoring, treatment, and other health services for persons living with lupus. Access to proper care should likewise not depend on where a Filipino lives or how much a family earns. The bill therefore strengthens the referral system among primary care facilities, government hospitals, specialists, and other health facilities, while giving particular attention to indigent and financially incapacitated patients and those living in underserved communities. No Filipino suffering from lupus should have to endure years of uncertainty before receiving proper care, nor should a family be left to face the financial and emotional burden of the disease on its own. Through greater awareness, earlier detection, accessible treatment, and continuing support, government can help persons living with lupus lead healthier and more productive lives. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. R. label: HB 11565
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL PLAN OF ACTION FOR THE CARE, SUPPORT, DEVELOPMENT, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, PROVIDING SUPPORT FOR THEIR FAMILIES AND CAREGIVERS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Filipinos with autism and their families face challenges that extend far beyond obtaining a diagnosis. Many families struggle to find affordable assessment, therapy, education, health services, and other forms of support. These difficulties become even greater for families with limited financial resources or those who do not have ready access to specialists and appropriate facilities. For parents and caregivers, raising and supporting a person with autism can be a lifelong responsibility. During childhood, families must navigate health care, education, therapy. and social services. As the child grows older, new concerns arise, including further education, skills development, employment, independent living, and continued care and support. Government assistance should therefore not end with diagnosis or childhood intervention. This bill seeks to establish a comprehensive National Plan of Action for the Care, Support. and Inclusion of Persons with Autism Spectrum Disorder. It brings together the programs and responsibilities of government agencies involved in health, education, social welfare, employment, skills development, and local government services so that persons with autism and their families can receive more coordinated support. The measure promotes early identification and appropriate intervention, accessible health and rehabilitation services, inclusive education, skills development and employment opportunities, support for parents and caregivers, and greater public awareness and acceptance. It likewise 1 strengthens referral systems so that families can more easily determine where and how to obtain appropriate government services. More importantly, the measure recognizes that persons with autism have different needs at different stages of their lives. Government programs must therefore provide continuity of support from childhood and education to adulthood, employment, community participation, and, when necessary, continuing care. Persons with autism are members of our families and communities who deserve the same opportunities to learn, work, participate, and live with dignity. A more inclusive society requires not only awareness and acceptance, but also accessible services and concrete opportunities that allow every Filipino to reach his or her potential. label: HB 11567
title: AN ACT DECLARING AUGUST 25 OF EVERY YEAR AS ILOILO CITY CHARTER DAY AND DECLARING THE SAME AS A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE CITY OF ILOILO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 The City of Iloilo is one of the oldest and most historically significant urban centers in the Philippines and has played an important role in the political, economic, cultural, and social development of the country. The legal foundation for the establishment and organization of the City of Iloilo is found in Commonwealth Act No. 57, otherwise known as the Charter of the City of Iloilo, as subsequently amended by Commonwealth Act No. 158 and other amendatory laws. Commonwealth Act No. 158, approved on November 9, 1936, amended the Charter and provided for the organization and administration of the City of Iloilo. The inauguration of the city was originally scheduled by the President for July 16, 1937. On January 23, 1937, President Manuel L. Quezon issued Proclamation No. 133, entitled “Setting Aside July 16, 1937, as a Day for the Inauguration of the City of Iloilo, and Declaring It a Special Public Holiday for the Province of Iloilo.” The inauguration date was subsequently changed. On August 20, 1937, President Quezon issued Proclamation No. 172, expressly amending Proclamation No. 133 and setting aside August 25, 1937 as the day for the inauguration of the City of Iloilo. The same proclamation declared August 25, 1937 a special public holiday for the Province of Iloilo. Project - Proclamations Series of Thus, August 25, 1937 represents the date officially designated by the national government for the formal inauguration of the City of Iloilo. The date consequently acquired historical significance as the city's Charter Day. The establishment of the City of Iloilo was likewise part of the transformation of several historic communities into a unified urban political jurisdiction. The Charter was subsequently amended to further define the territorial jurisdiction of the city. Among these later developments, Commonwealth Act No. 604, approved on August 22, 1940, provided for the inclusion of the territory of the municipality of Jaro into the City of Iloilo. The national government has, on various occasions, continued to recognize August 25 as a significant date for the City of Iloilo through presidential proclamations declaring the date a special non-working day in the city. A permanent declaration by Congress will ensure that the historical significance of August 25 is recognized every year and will provide the people of Iloilo City with an opportunity to commemorate the city's beginnings, celebrate its heritage, and reflect upon its continuing contribution to the development of Western Visayas and the Philippines. 48 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 50 51 52 53 54 HON. label: HB 11568
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING AN ELECTRIC VEHICLE FIRE SAFETY AND EMERGENCY RESPONSE SUPPORT PROGRAM, REQUIRING MANUFACTURERS, ASSEMBLERS, IMPORTERS AND, WHERE APPLICABLE, DISTRIBUTORS OF ELECTRIC VEHICLES TO PROVIDE THE BUREAU OF FIRE PROTECTION WITH ELECTRIC VEHICLE FIRE RESPONSE SAFETY EQUIPMENT FOR EVERY TEN (10) COVERED ELECTRIC VEHICLES INTRODUCED INTO THE PHILIPPINE MARKET, STRENGTHENING FIREFIGHTER TRAINING AND INDUSTRY COOPERATION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 15 Republic Act No. 11697, otherwise known as the “Electric Vehicle Industry Development Act” (EVIDA), established the national policy for the development and adoption of electric vehicles in the Philippines. 19 As electric mobility expands, the emergency-response capability of government must develop alongside it. 22 Electric vehicles equipped with rechargeable traction batteries present emergency-response considerations different from those encountered in conventional vehicle fires. Battery thermal runaway may involve extreme heat, hazardous gases, prolonged incident management, and the possibility of reignition even after visible flames have been controlled. 27 Republic Act No. 9514, otherwise known as the “Revised Fire Code of the Philippines of 2008”, mandates the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) to prevent and suppress destructive fires and enforce appropriate fire-safety standards. 31 Republic Act No. 11589, otherwise known as the “Bureau of Fire Protection Modernization Act”, further strengthens the capabilities of the BFP through the acquisition of modern fire suppression, rescue, hazardous-materials, specialized equipment, training, research and other resources necessary for effective emergency response. 36 There is therefore a need to ensure that the continuing growth of the electric vehicle industry is accompanied by a corresponding strengthening of the capability of the BFP to respond to electric vehicle fires and battery-related emergencies. 40 This measure establishes a statutory public-safety responsibility requiring manufacturers, assemblers, importers and, where applicable, distributors that first introduce covered electric vehicles into the Philippine market to provide the BFP with one (1) approved Electric Vehicle Fire Response Safety Set (EVFRSS) for every ten (10) covered electric vehicles introduced into the Philippine market. 46 Each EVFRSS shall include an appropriate BFP-approved Electric Vehicle Fire Containment Device (EVFCD) and such complementary equipment as may be required by the BFP. 50 The measure adopts technology-neutral terminology and does not mandate any particular brand, design or proprietary product. Technical requirements shall be determined and periodically reviewed by the BFP, in coordination with concerned government agencies, based on prevailing fire science, applicable safety standards and technological developments. 56 The measure likewise provides safeguards against double counting, establishes reporting and accountability mechanisms, requires proper government inventory and accounting of equipment received, mandates technical cooperation and firefighter training, and provides administrative due process. 61 As the number of electric vehicles on Philippine roads increases, the country’s capacity to safely respond to electric vehicle emergencies must increase with it. 64 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. 66 67 68 69 70 HON. label: HB 11569
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH (DOH) TO SET AND APPROVE THE BED CAPACITY AND SERVICE CAPABILITY OF ALL DOH HOSPITALS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution mandates the State to protect and promote the right to health of the people (Article II, Section 15) and to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development that makes essential health services available to all at affordable cost (Article XIII, Section 11). Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act, builds on this mandate by requiring a responsive network of public health facilities guided by a national facility development plan. Hospitals under the Department of Health (DOH) form the backbone of this public network, particularly for patients who cannot afford private care. Yet the authorized bed capacity and service capability of most DOH hospitals are fixed by statute, so any increase or change, however urgent, must pass through the full legislative process. As a result, Congress each term considers numerous local bills seeking to raise the bed capacity of individual hospitals. The process takes time, and in the interim hospitals operate beyond their authorized capacity, patients are placed in hallways and shared beds, and the plantilla positions, budget, and equipment that should accompany expansion lag behind actual demand. This bill proposes a more responsive arrangement. It authorizes the DOH, through an administrative issuance, to adjust and approve the bed capacities and corresponding service capabilities of hospitals under its supervision and control. Such decisions must be grounded on objective considerations, namely each hospital’s development plan, catchment population, burden of disease, available human resources, and health care provider networks, together with other standards the DOH may set. The DOH is directed to continue updating and implementing the Philippine Health Facility Development Plan (PHFDP) to 1 guide the modernization of government health facilities, and to include in its programs the funding requirements for each approved adjustment. Importantly, the measure preserves the constitutional power of the purse. Funding for bed capacity adjustments remains subject to the regular budget process and must be included in the annual General Appropriations Act. The DOH is likewise required to submit an annual report to the Committee on Health of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Health and Demography of the Senate on hospitals with approved bed capacities and the corresponding funding requirements, ensuring that Congress retains effective oversight. This measure adopts as its reference Senate Bill No. 1508, entitled “An Act Authorizing the Department of Health (DOH) to Set and Approve the Bed Capacity and Service Capability of All DOH Hospitals,” the substitute bill recommended for approval of the Senate of the Twentieth Congress. Filing a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives is intended to facilitate the timely enactment of this legislation and its harmonization with the Senate version. For communities such as Marikina and its neighboring localities, which rely on DOH hospitals like the Amang Rodriguez Memorial Medical Center, the ability of the health system to expand capacity promptly where the need is greatest is not an administrative detail but a matter of timely and dignified care. Rationalizing how DOH hospital capacity is set will allow resources to follow patients, rather than wait for a separate law for every hospital. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11570
title: AN ACT INSTITUTING A NATIONAL PLAN OF ACTION FOR THE CARE, SUPPORT, AND INCLUSION OF PERSONS WITH AUTISM SPECTRUM DISORDER, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution directs the State to adopt an integrated and comprehensive approach to health development and to give priority to the needs of, among others, the disabled and children (Article XIII, Section 11). It further mandates the establishment of a special agency for persons with disability for their rehabilitation, self-development, and self- reliance, and their integration into the mainstream of society (Article XIII, Section 13). The Philippines, as a State Party to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, has likewise committed to ensure the full and equal enjoyment of all human rights by persons with disability. Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a lifelong neurodevelopmental condition that affects how a person communicates, interacts with others, and experiences the world. Advocacy groups such as the Autism Society Philippines have long estimated that more than a million Filipinos may be on the autism spectrum, yet the country still lacks a dedicated national framework to guide how government responds to their needs. Families commonly face late or costly diagnosis, a shortage of developmental specialists outside major urban centers, expensive and hard-to-access therapies, limited inclusive learning environments, and few pathways to meaningful work once formal schooling ends. Existing laws provide important but general protections. Republic Act No. 7277, or the Magna Carta for Persons with Disability, as amended, sets out the rights and privileges of persons with disability; Republic Act No. 11228 provides for mandatory PhilHealth coverage of all persons with disability; and Republic Act No. 11650 institutes a policy of inclusion and services for learners with disabilities. None of these, however, establishes a single, coordinated plan that ties together screening, intervention, education, employment, and social protection specifically for persons with ASD across the life course. This bill seeks to close that gap. It mandates the formulation of a National Plan of Action for Autism Spectrum Disorder, to be led by the National Council on Disability Affairs (NCDA) through existing inter-agency mechanisms and in consultation with local government units, civil society, autism self-advocates, and parents’ groups. It assigns clear responsibilities: the Department of Health for integrating ASD screening, referral, and diagnostic protocols into primary and maternal and child health care; the Department of Health and PhilHealth for the progressive availability of evidence-based interventions in 1 public facilities; the Department of Education, the Commission on Higher Education, and the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority for inclusive education and transition pathways; the Department of Labor and Employment and the Civil Service Commission for equal and supported employment; and the Department of Social Welfare and Development and local government units for social protection and community-based support. The bill also declares discrimination against persons with ASD unlawful, requires sustained public awareness campaigns, and provides for funding through the General Appropriations Act. This measure adopts as its reference Senate Bill No. 1822, entitled “An Act Instituting a National Plan of Action for the Care, Support and Inclusion of Persons with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Appropriating Funds Therefor,” the substitute bill recommended for approval of the Senate of the Twentieth Congress. Filing a counterpart measure in the House of Representatives is intended to facilitate the timely enactment of this legislation and its harmonization with the Senate version. Local government units are often the first point of contact for families of children with ASD, whether through barangay health centers, child development programs, or local social welfare offices. A national plan that equips and connects these frontline services with national agencies will allow every Filipino with ASD, wherever he or she lives, to receive timely support and to take part in community life with dignity. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11571
title: AN ACT EXPANDING DEPOSIT INSURANCE COVERAGE AND STRENGTHENING THE INDEPENDENCE, MANDATES, AUTHORITIES AND FINANCIAL CAPABILITY OF THE PHILIPPINE DEPOSIT INSURANCE CORPORATION AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 3591, AS AMENDED, AND OTHER RELATED LAWS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine Deposit Insurance Corporation (PDIC) was created under Republic Act No. 3591 in 1963 to insure bank deposits and help maintain a sound and stable financial system. Since then, its Charter has been amended only twice in over sixty years — through Republic Act No. 9302 in 2004 and Republic Act No. 9576 in 2009 — even as the Philippine financial system has grown substantially more complex, more digital, and more interconnected with non-bank deposit-taking channels. This bill seeks to enact the Responsive Deposit Insurance Act (ReDI) to modernize and strengthen the country’s deposit insurance framework. It expands deposit insurance coverage beyond traditional banks to include other deposit-taking institutions, subject to appropriate regulatory safeguards, thereby extending protection to a broader segment of the depositing public. The measure also empowers the PDIC to adopt a more responsive insurance system by allowing periodic adjustments in deposit insurance coverage based on economic conditions, implementing risk-based premium assessments, and enhancing its capacity to monitor and manage risks to the Deposit Insurance Fund. It further institutionalizes mechanisms to address systemic risks and ensure the sustainability of the deposit insurance system. To improve operational efficiency and financial resilience, the bill strengthens the PDIC’s fiscal and administrative autonomy, enhances its governance structure, expands its investment and resolution authorities, and authorizes the creation of a subsidiary to manage and dispose of assets acquired from closed banks. These reforms are intended to maximize asset recovery, reduce resolution costs, and improve the Corporation’s overall effectiveness. Ultimately, this measure aligns the Philippines’ deposit insurance regime with evolving financial sector realities and international best practices. By enhancing depositor protection, strengthening financial safety nets, and promoting confidence in the financial system, the proposed legislation will contribute to a more stable, resilient, and inclusive financial sector. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought REP. MARCELINO “MARCY” R. label: HB 11572
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING THE FILIPINO FAMILY MAINSTREAMING FRAMEWORK, ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR THE FILIPINO FAMILY (NCFF), MANDATING FAMILY IMPACT ASSESSMENTS IN PUBLIC POLICYMAKING AND GOVERNANCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution gives the Filipino family a place of special constitutional protection. Article II, Section 12 recognizes the sanctity of family life and directs the State to protect and strengthen the family as a basic autonomous social institution. Article XV further recognizes the Filipino family as the foundation of the nation and mandates the State to strengthen its solidarity and actively promote its total development. This constitutional command is now confronted by measurable social and demographic realities. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) reported that registered marriages decreased from 414,213 in 2023 to 371,825 in 2024, while the crude marriage rate declined from 3.7 to 3.3 marriages per thousand population. The 2025 National Demographic and Health Survey reported a total fertility rate of 1.7 children per woman aged 15 to 49 for the three-year period preceding the survey, down from 1.9 in 2022 and below the replacement fertility level of 2.1 children per woman. PSA likewise recorded 1,358,989 registered live births in 2024, 6.2 percent fewer than the 1,448,522 registered in 2023. Of the 2024 registered live births, 808,965, or 59.5 percent, were non-marital births. This last figure does not, by itself, establish poor family functioning; rather, it underscores the range of family circumstances in which government must support children, parents, and caregivers. These demographic figures describe changing patterns of marriage, fertility, and childbearing; they do not, standing alone, measure family functioning or parental care. The case for family mainstreaming rests on the fact that child welfare and family resilience are shaped across multiple policy domains. A child’s welfare is affected by health, education, housing, labor, digital safety, local government capacity, and household economic resilience. A parent’s ability to raise and protect a child is likewise affected by employment conditions, childcare support, public safety, social protection, transport systems, housing affordability, and access to reliable services. The condition of the Filipino family is therefore a governance issue that cuts across agencies and sectors. The risks facing Filipino children further demonstrate the need for a coordinated family policy framework. UNICEF Philippines, citing the 2022 Disrupting Harm study conducted by UNICEF Office of Research, INTERPOL, and ECPAT International, reported that two in ten, or around two million, internet-using children aged 12 to 17 in the Philippines had experienced online sexual abuse and exploitation in the preceding year, while fewer than three percent reported such incidents to authorities. This study- based estimate highlights the need for stronger coordination among family support, child protection, law enforcement, education, digital safety, and community-based intervention systems. The proposed Filipino Family Mainstreaming Act responds to these realities by making family well-being a deliberate and measurable consideration in governance. It does not create a new large bureaucracy. Instead, it establishes the National Commission for the Filipino Family (NCFF), attached to the Office of the President for policy coordination, with the Department of Social Welfare and Development serving as Secretariat. It requires agencies to designate existing senior officials as Family Mainstreaming Focal Points, thereby avoiding unnecessary creation of new plantilla positions. It also integrates family mainstreaming into existing planning, budgeting, monitoring, and performance systems. The measure also introduces Family Impact Assessments (FIAs) as a policy discipline. Under Section 11, an FIA is mandatory for covered Executive department and agency measures, including nationally significant executive issuances, development plans, regulations, and major government programs reasonably expected to have substantial effects on Filipino families. For proposed legislation, however, the NCFF is directed to develop and make available an FIA methodology and technical assistance which either House of Congress, its committees, or legislative offices may use in accordance with their respective rules. FIAs are not another permit or clearance; they are intended to help decision-makers assess effects on child welfare, parental responsibilities, caregiving, household resilience, work- family balance, vulnerable family sectors, implementation costs, measurable outcomes, and less adverse policy alternatives. The proposal also addresses a recurring weakness of social legislation: the absence of measurable outcomes. It directs the National Commission for the Filipino Family, in coordination with the Philippine Statistics Authority and concerned agencies, to adopt National Family Well-being Indicators covering child development, educational participation and completion, family economic resilience, health and nutrition, housing conditions, caregiving, child protection, violence affecting family members, and work-life balance. These indicators will allow Congress, the Executive, local governments, researchers, and the public to evaluate family policy on the basis of evidence and measurable results. The bill also contains targeted obligations intended to give practical effect to the mainstreaming framework. In basic education, it requires advance curriculum transparency for defined Sensitive Topics, parental opt-out procedures, and specified parental consent and notification rules. In government procurement, it disqualifies natural or juridical entities with final administrative, civil, or judicial convictions for violations of specified laws protecting life, women, children, and family welfare, consistent with Republic Act No. 12009 or the New Government Procurement Act. label: HB 11573
title: AN ACT DECLARING OCTOBER 5 OF EVERY YEAR AS NATIONAL TEACHERS’ DAY, A NON-WORKING HOLIDAY FOR ALL TEACHERS
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our teachers play a big role in shaping our children into a responsible citizens and preparing the next generation to lead and contribute in the development of our country. The global celebration of "World Teachers' Day" during the month of October is dedicated to honoring the important role of teachers in transforming education. More importantly, it raises awareness about the systemic support they need to fully realize their potential as educators. Recent headlines in the Philippines have heavily underscored this need. While Republic Act No. 10743 already legally recognizes the ﬁfth day of October as National Teachers' Day, it currently designates it only as a special working holiday. Teachers cannot fully receive the appreciation of their students and communities if they are still required to report for their regular school responsibilities. Therefore, this bill seeks to declare October 5 of each year as a non-working holiday exclusively for all our teachers. This bill seeks to declare the ﬁfth day of October each year as the National Teachers’ Day, which will be a non-working holiday for all our teachers. Let us give our teachers the genuine recognition they truly deserve. They have tirelessness and selﬂessly dedicated their time and talents to imparting valuable lessons and even life skills to our children. They are indeed the unsung heroes of our society as that are often easily taken for granted. Giving them a dedicated, non-working day of rest is a small but meaningful token of gratitude. After all, it is the least we can do to honor the very people who spend their lives building the foundation of our country's future. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. CHEENO MIGUEL D. label: HB 11574
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON THE PAYMENT OF LOANS, MORTGAGES, AND OTHER CREDIT OBLIGATIONS DURING A DECLARED STATE OF CALAMITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is frequently affected by typhoons, floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, pandemics, and other natural or human-induced hazards. These calamities may result in the loss of lives and property, displacement of families, interruption of livelihoods, and temporary closure of businesses. For many individuals and households, the resulting loss of income significantly affects their ability to meet existing loan and credit obligations. During a declared state of calamity, affected borrowers may be compelled to prioritize food, shelter, medical needs, relocation, and the repair or reconstruction of damaged property. Requiring the immediate payment of loans during this period may further aggravate their financial hardship and expose them to penalties, additional interest, collection efforts, and possible legal action. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, recognizes the need for a comprehensive and coordinated system of disaster prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. Consistent with this policy, the State must adopt measures that protect affected communities and enable them to recover without being placed under additional and avoidable financial distress. mi ” * This bill seeks to establish a temporary moratorium on the payment and enforcement of loan and other credit obligations of natural persons residing in areas under a declared state of calamity. The proposed moratorium shall apply for a period not exceeding one hundred twenty (120) days from the declaration of the state of calamity, or until the declaration is lifted, whichever occurs earlier. The measure does not condone or extinguish the borrower’s obligation. Instead, it temporarily defers payment and allows the accumulated liability to be settled through not less than six (6) equal monthly installments without penalties or interest arising from the deferment. Borrowers who are able and willing to continue making payments may voluntarily do so during the moratorium period. By providing temporary financial relief during calamities, this measure will help affected individuals and families preserve their limited resources for essential needs, prevent the further deterioration of household finances, and support their recovery and rehabilitation. It will also promote fairness and social protection while preserving the underlying creditor-borrower relationship. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MICHAE “pM” D. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING CAMPUS SECURITY IN EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS THROUGH THE INSTALLATION OF CLOSED-CIRCUIT TELEVISION (CCTV) SYSTEMS IN STRATEGIC AREAS AND THE ADOPTION OF CAMPUS SECURITY PLANS, PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The proposed measure seeks to strengthen campus security in educational institutions through the installation of Closed-Circuit Television (CCTV) systems in strategic areas and the adoption of Campus Security Plans. Schools must provide safe and secure environments for students, teachers, non-teaching personnel, and visitors. However, violence, bullying, and other security incidents continue to threaten the safety and well-being of members of the school community. The 2024 Philippines Global School-based Student Health Survey found that 35.3 percent of students aged 13 to 17 had been involved in a physical fight during the preceding twelve months, while 30.2 percent reported having been bullied on school property.! Recent incidents of violence in schools further underscore the need to reinforce preventive security measures, prompt reporting, effective emergency response, and coordination with appropriate authorities. CCTV systems in strategic areas may help deter wrongdoing, monitor security risks, preserve 2 Global School-based Student Health Survey. 2024, m Z DATE October 5, 2026 ~ evidence, assist investigations, and support the timely response of school authorities and law-enforcement agencies.” The bill requires educational institutions to adopt Campus Security Plans that identify security risks and prescribe measures for access control, visitor management, incident reporting, emergency response, and coordination with relevant government agencies. It also requires the installation of CCTV systems only in strategic areas, while prohibiting their installation in toilets, washrooms, changing rooms, clinics, counseling rooms, sleeping quarters, and other areas where persons have a reasonable expectation of privacy. To protect the rights of students, personnel, and visitors, the bill mandates compliance with Republic Act No. 10173, or the “Data Privacy Act of 2012,” and relevant issuances of the National Privacy Commission governing the collection, use, storage, access, disclosure, retention, and disposal of CCTV footage. label: HB 11576
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A MORATORIUM ON RENTAL PAYMENT AND EVICTION DURING DISASTERS AND OTHER EMERGENCIES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is highly vulnerable to natural hazards and other emergencies that may result in the loss of livelihoods, interruption of economic activities, damage to homes, and displacement of families. For low-income households, informal workers, and other vulnerable sectors, these disruptions may immediately affect their ability to pay rent and maintain stable housing. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 2010, establishes a comprehensive framework for disaster prevention, preparedness, response, and recovery. However, existing laws, including Republic Act No. 9653, or the Rent Control Act of 2009, do not provide a uniform and automatic mechanism for temporarily protecting tenants from rental enforcement and eviction during declared disasters and emergencies. This bill seeks to establish a time-bound moratorium on the enforcement of rental payments and eviction proceedings involving covered residential units during a declared state of calamity or emergency, including a reasonable period after its termination. The measure does not condone the cancellation of rental obligations; rather, it provides temporary relief by allowing deferred payments to be settled through a reasonable installment arrangement without penalties or interest arising from the covered period. mi = DATE October 5, 2026 Subject to appropriate rules and eligibility requirements, similar relief may be extended to qualified micro, small, and medium enterprises affected by the closure or interruption of business operations. The bill likewise preserves safeguards for lessors and property owners by allowing mutually agreed payment arrangements and recognizing exceptions involving criminal acts or conduct that threatens life, safety, or property. By providing temporary housing and rental-payment security during disasters and emergencies, this measure will help prevent displacement, protect vulnerable households, support affected enterprises, and strengthen the country’s disaster risk reduction and management framework. Jac view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRIC Cc “pM” D. label: HB 11577
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR A TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON THE PAYMENT OF UTILITY CHARGES DURING A DECLARED STATE OF CALAMITY, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is frequently affected by typhoons, floods, earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and other calamities that may damage homes, disrupt livelihoods, reduce household income, and interrupt access to essential services. During such emergencies, affected families may find it difficult to pay electricity, water, telecommunications, and other utility charges while attending to their basic needs and recovery. Access to these services is essential to public health, safety, communication, disaster response, and community recovery. Republic Act No. 10121, or the Philippine Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act of 20 10, recognizes the need to strengthen community resilience and provide coordinated assistance during disasters. This bill seeks to establish a temporary moratorium on utility payments for residential customers in areas under a declared state of calamity. It prohibits the enforcement of covered utility charges, disconnection solely for nonpayment, and the imposition of penalties, surcharges, or interest arising from the deferment during the moratorium period. The deferred charges shall not be extinguished and shall be paid in at least six (6) equal monthly installments without penalties, surcharges, resulting from the moratorium. The measure may likewise extend to qualified micro, small, and medium enterprises affected by the calamity, subject to applicable rules and eligibility requirements. or interest The bill preserves exceptions involvin meter tampering, and other ground g fraud, unauthorized connections, intentional damage, public safety concerns, emergency repairs, S unrelated to nonpayment. By providing temporary relief from utility payments and disconnection, this measure will protect vulnerable consumers, preserve access to essential services, and support the recovery of disaster-affected communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICK MIC L “PM” D. label: HB 11578
title: AN ACT REGULATING AND MODERNIZING THE PRACTICE OF OPTOMETRY, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8050, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "REVISED OPTOMETRY LAW OF 1995"
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act (RA) No. 8050, otherwise known as the "Revised Optometry Law of 1995," has served as the principal legal framework governing the regulation and practice of optometry in the Philippines for more than three decades. Since its enactment, significant advances in eye care, diagnostic technology, clinical education, pharmaceutical science, digital health, and healthcare delivery have transformed the practice of optometry both locally and internationally. These developments underscore the need to modernize the law to ensure that Filipino optometrists are equipped to meet the evolving eye health needs of the public while maintaining the highest standards of professional competence, ethics, and patient safety. The proposed measure seeks to comprehensively update RA 8050 by strengthening the legal and regulatory framework governing the profession. It expands the clinical scope of optometric practice to reflect current standards of evidence-based eye care; enhances educational, licensure, and continuing professional development requirements; reinforces professional accountability and public protection; and recognizes the appropriate integration of technological innovations into the delivery of optometric services. Consistent with the State's policy under Section 15, Article II of the 1987 Constitution to protect and promote the right to health of the people, and in support of RA 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act,” this measure recognizes optometry as an integral component of the country's primary health care system. It likewise promotes greater access to quality eye care services, particularly in geographically isolated and disadvantaged areas, through the responsible use of digital health technologies and tele-optometry, subject to appropriate safeguards prescribed by law. The bill also strengthens professional education and competency by updating academic standards for the Doctor of Optometry program, reinforcing clinical training requirements, and introducing mechanisms to ensure that applicants for licensure possess the practical knowledge and clinical skills necessary for safe and effective professional practice. It likewise enhances the authority of the Professional Regulatory Board of Optometry to promote continuing competence, ethical practice, transparency, and effective regulation of the profession. Recognizing the rapid advancement of diagnostic technologies and pharmaceutical developments in eye care, the proposed measure provides a legal framework for the regulated use of authorized diagnostic pharmaceutical agents and other emerging technologies by duly qualified optometrists, subject to the supervision of the Professional Regulation Commission, the Department of Health, the Food and Drug Administration, and other appropriate government agencies. The bill likewise strengthens safeguards against the unauthorized practice of optometry, unlawful corporate interference with professional judgment, and other practices detrimental to public welfare. Furthermore, this measure harmonizes RA 8050 with existing national policies embodied in RA 10173 (Data Privacy Act of 2012), RA 8792 (Electronic Commerce Act of 2000), RA 10175 (Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012), and other applicable laws governing public health, digital governance, and professional regulation. By integrating these legal frameworks, the measure promotes innovation while ensuring accountability, patient confidentiality, cybersecurity, and responsible professional practice. Ultimately, this proposed legislation seeks not merely to update an existing law but to establish a modern, responsive, and internationally competitive legal framework that will enable the optometry profession to contribute more effectively to the promotion of public health, prevention of avoidable blindness and visual impairment, advancement of clinical excellence, and realization of universal access to quality eye care services for every Filipino. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. PATRICIA C. label: HB 11580
title: AN ACT INCREASING THE ALLOWANCES OF BARANGAY OFFICIALS, GRANTING HONORARIA AND OTHER BENEFITS TO THE BARANGAY WORKERS, GRANTING A LUMP SUMP RETIREMENT PAY, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT CODE OF 1991
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Barangay oﬃcials and members serve as the primary frontliners of our government. They are the ﬁrst responders in times of crisis, the primary implementers of national and local policies, and the closest and immediate representatives of the government at the grassroots level. Despite their round-the-clock duties and heavy responsibilities, they do not receive a regular salary per se, but are instead compensated merely through honoraria and allowances. Currently, the Local Government Code of 1991 mandates a minimum honorarium of only One Thousand Pesos (P1,000.00) per month for the Punong Barangay, and Six Hundred Pesos (P600.00) for the Sangguniang Barangay members, Barangay Treasurer, and Barangay Secretary. While local ordinances may increase these ﬁgures, many lower-income barangays are unable to provide living wages to their oﬃcials. In view of the continuous rising cost of living and the severe economic challenges that we all face today, these statutory minimums set over three decades ago are no longer just or realistic. This bill seeks to amend Section 393 of Republic Act No. 7160, or the Local Government Code of 1991, to provide the long-overdue ﬁnancial upgrade for our barangay oﬃcials. This measure proposes to increase the minimum honoraria to Ten Thousand Pesos (P10,000.00) for the Punong Barangay, Eight Thousand Pesos (P8,000.00) for the Sangguniang Barangay members, Treasurer, and Secretary, and Five Thousand Pesos (P5,000.00) for Barangay Tanods and members of the Lupon ng Tagapamayapa. Further, it increases their Christmas bonus to Five Thousand Pesos (P5,000.00) and grants a lump sum retirement gratuity pay for their dedicated years of service. Through this, we empower our barangay oﬃcials to serve their constituents with greater eﬃciency, dignity, and dedication. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11581
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR COMPASSIONATE EARLY RELEASE TO QUALIFIED PERSONS DEPRIVED OF LIBERTY
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE ‘In health, there is freedom. Health is the first of all liberties,” said Swiss philosopher Henri Frédéric Amiel. It is a woeful reality for some persons deprived of liberty (PDLs) that they are shackled not only by their being offenders serving sentence or as detainees awaiting trial for an offense they may not have at all committed, but also doubly restrained by severe health condition. This bill seeks to legislate Compassionate Early Release (CER) to afford PDLs with life-limiting illness, significant functional impairment, complex medical care needs that cannot be effectively addressed by the penitentiary or correctional institution particularly the elderly, women and juveniles a chance to return to their family and community and live productive and meaningful lives or spend their remaining days with dignity in the company of their loved ones. CER is imperative as it is a measure of compassion consistent not only with the constitutionally declared policy on the value of dignity and full respect for human rights but also with the Universal Health Care Act that seeks to improve access to appropriate, affordable and quality health care services for every Filipino. The law does not discriminate against institutionalized populations including PDLs who are more vulnerable to health service deprivation due to inherent security and legal barriers. No hapless Filipino rendered helpless by severe health and medical status deserves to languish in jail. Significantly as well is the fact that CER would contribute to solving the critical problem of congestion in jails and correctional institutions. Overcrowding has long hounded the country’s penitentiary system. The average congestion rate of all correctional facilities stands at 321% of the facilities’ capacity or more than three (3) times their budgeted capacity. There is only one (1) correctional officer to twenty-four (24) PDLs in the Bureau of Corrections. The already meagre health care budget is further constrained by the huge number of PDLs. Congestion necessarily restricts mobility and productivity which negatively impacts the mental health and overall well-being of PDLs. The dire situation likewise escalates the infection risk for communicable diseases and heightens the risk of exacerbation of disease for those with non-communicable diseases due to the poor living conditions and lack of access to regular health care. This multiplies mortality or morbidity of PDLs that can be thirty (30) times higher than that of the non-PDL population. Verily, decongesting places of deprivation of liberty through CER is beneficial to both the released PDLs and those who remain in the penal or correctional facility. Reducing the inordinately large number of PDLs would help government cut costs on food, water, health and medical care and allied services, and expend the freed funds to improve the living condition of the PDLs left behind. Highlighting the value of CER, former Justice Secretary Jesus Crispin Remulla posits that the mechanism “...reaffims our commitment to justice, human dignity and rehabilitation...” Mr. Remulla’s message brings to light the distinction between CER and medical parole. The two processes, although both mostly based on health and medical grounds, are not identical. The proposed CER which is heavily anchored on human rights and dignity, is based solely on the PDLs current health and medical condition as well as the corresponding prognosis regardless of the status of serving sentence or length of detention or deprivation of liberty. Whereas parole is the conditional release of a PDL before the full completion of a sentence on the undertaking of good behavior or non- commission of a crime after the release. In the case of a PDL on CER, they are unlikely to return to lawbreaking as they have been effectively or fully rehabilitated or too ill to have the capacity or energy to reoffend. The proposed law underscores appropriate, holistic, and inclusive rehabilitation of PDLs as it is guided by studies’ findings that inmates who undergo rehabilitation programs are less likely to recommit crimes and go back to prison compared to those who do not participate in the program. Congress should not temporize in actualizing deliverance of deserving PDLs through CER. Early approval of this measure is earnestly sought. ~~ Sua [I~ ISEL B. LAGMAN LEILA M. DE LIMA - KAKA J. label: HB 11582
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL MICROPLASTICS RESEARCH PROGRAM, PROMOTING RESEARCH ON THE PRESENCE OF MICROPLASTICS IN THE HUMAN BODY, FOOD, DRINKING WATER, AND THE ENVIRONMENT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Article II, Section 15 of the 1987 Constitution declares that the State shall protect and promote the right to health of the people and instill health consciousness among them. Likewise, Article XIII, Section 12 mandates the State to undertake appropriate health manpower development and research responsive to the country's health needs and problems. In recent years, microplastics have emerged as one of the most critical public health concerns in the world due to the worldwide increase in consumption of plastic-based products. Scientific research conducted in different countries have detected the presence of these microplastics in food packaging material, salt, drinking water, contaminated seafood, agricultural products, and even infiltrating our bodies, such as in our blood, lungs, placentas, breast milk, and even brain tissue. While research is still ongoing, evidence suggests that prolonged exposure to these microplastics may have implications for human health, including inflammation, endocrine disruption, reproductive health concerns, and the potential to act as carriers of pathogens and toxins, among others. |? The Philippines, being one of the world's largest users and contributors of plastic waste leakage into the marine environment’, faces heightened risks of human exposure to microplastics through food, water, and air. Despite this, there remains very limited local scientific research on microplastic prevalence in tissues and organs. The precise entry points of microplastics are unknown, and their possible health consequences are yet unclear in the Philippine context. Due to this research gap, government agencies currently lack sufficient data to formulate specific evidence-based policies. This proposed measure seeks to establish a National Microplastics Research Program to coordinate scientific studies on microplastics in the environment, food systems, drinking water, and the human body. It does not impose regulatory burdens on any sector. Rather, it is solely a research initiative anchored on the principle that effective policy must first be grounded on sound science. By investing in research today, the government can better protect public health, strengthen environmental management, and ensure that future decisions concerning plastic pollution are informed by credible and locally generated evidence. In view of the foregoing, the approval of this measure is earnestly sought. CRISPI “PING” D. label: HB 11583
title: AN ACT REDUCING THE FINANCIAL BURDEN OF MANDATORY CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL EDUCATION, TRAINING, CERTIFICATION, AND PERIODIC COMPETENCY REQUIREMENTS UPON FILIPINO PROFESSIONALS AND WORKERS, PROVIDING FOR A FIFTY PERCENT (50%) DISCOUNT ON QUALIFIED MANDATORY TRAINING FEES, ESTABLISHING SUBSIDIES AND OTHER FORMS OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE, PROVIDING ADDITIONAL PROTECTION FOR QUALIFIED GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Professional competence is not static. Physicians and nurses must remain abreast of developments affecting patient care. Engineers, architects, accountants, teachers, and other regulated professionals must continuously update their knowledge and skills. Filipino seafarers undergo recurrent training and certification to maintain competencies demanded by domestic regulation and international maritime standards. Many other occupations likewise require periodic training as a condition for continued employment or professional practice. These requirements serve legitimate and important public purposes. The State is justified in requiring persons engaged in professions and occupations affecting public health, safety, welfare, and national development to maintain appropriate standards of competence. Yet mandatory training carries a corresponding economic consequence. When the State makes completion of a particular course, training program, continuing professional development activity, competency assessment, or certification a prerequisite for the continued exercise of one's profession or livelihood, the professional or worker effectively has no option but to incur the corresponding expense. For many Filipino workers and professionals, the burden is cumulative. Training fees may be accompanied by transportation, accommodation, meals, lost working days, certification expenses, examination fees, renewal fees, and other incidental costs. The financial burden is particularly significant for entry-level professionals, government employees, healthcare workers, seafarers between contracts, and workers supporting their families. Republic Act No. 10912, or the Continuing Professional Development Act of 2016, recognizes the importance of continuously improving the competence of Filipino professionals. The objective of continuing professional development is unquestionably important. The accessibility and affordability of compliance must, however, form an equally important component of the State's professional development policy. Congress has already recognized this principle in the maritime sector. Republic Act No. 12021, or the Magna Carta of Filipino Seafarers, expressly declares that seafarers shall have access to educational advancement and training at reasonable and affordable costs. The law further authorizes the regulation of fees charged by accredited maritime training institutions for mandatory training required under the STCW Convention. There is compelling reason to extend the underlying principle to other similarly situated Filipino professionals and workers. The Constitution provides ample basis for such legislative intervention. Article II, Section 9 directs the State to promote a just and dynamic social order and free the people from poverty through policies providing adequate social services, promoting full employment, a rising standard of living, and improved quality of life. Article II, Section 18 affirms labor as a primary social economic force and directs the State to protect workers and promote their welfare. Article XII, Section 6 further declares that the use of property bears a social function, that all economic agents shall contribute to the common good, and that private economic enterprise remains subject to the duty of the State to promote distributive justice and intervene when the common good so demands. Article XIII, Section 1 commands Congress to give the highest priority to measures that protect and enhance human dignity and reduce social and economic inequalities. Article XIII, Section 3 likewise commands the State to afford full protection to labor, local and overseas. The proposed measure is also consistent with established principles concerning the police power of the State. In Carlos Superdrug Corporation v. Department of Social Welfare and Development, the Supreme Court sustained legislation requiring private establishments to provide statutory discounts as a legitimate exercise of police power. The Court recognized that the State, in advancing the welfare of a class requiring legislative assistance, may validly require private establishments to participate in carrying out a public welfare program. This doctrine was subsequently reiterated in Manila Memorial Park, Inc. v. Secretary of Social Welfare and Development and subsequent cases involving statutory discounts. These decisions recognize the broad authority of Congress to regulate economic activity in furtherance of the general welfare, while preserving the constitutional limitation that regulation must not become arbitrary, oppressive, or confiscatory. This bill takes these constitutional considerations into account. It does not simply compel training institutions to absorb the entire cost of a public program. It provides a tax mechanism for discounts granted, authorizes subsidies and fiscal assistance, directs regulators to establish reasonable fee frameworks, and requires government to progressively expand affordable public and online training alternatives. The classification of lower-salaried government employees for additional assistance is likewise founded upon substantial distinctions directly related to the purpose of the measure. The Supreme Court has consistently held that equal protection does not prohibit reasonable classification. A classification is constitutionally permissible when it: (1) rests upon substantial distinctions; (2) is germane to the purpose of the law; (3) is not confined to existing conditions; and (4) applies equally to all members of the class. Lower-salaried government employees required to personally finance continuing professional requirements occupy a materially different economic position from employees possessing greater capacity to absorb recurrent professional expenses. label: HB 11584
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOL IN BARANGAY MATALAPITAP, MUNICIPALITY OF PANIQUI, PROVINCE OF TARLAC TO BE KNOWN AS MATALAPITAP PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOL AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a public elementary school in Barangay Matalapitap, Municipality of Paniqui, Province of Tarlac. As provided in Resolution No. 093-s2026 of the Sangguniang Bayan of the Municipality of Paniqui, statistics show that the local government of Paniqui, Tarlac is experiencing a steady increase in population - leading to a rise in the number of school-aged children and students within Barangay Matalapitap, Municipality of Paniqui, Province of Tarlac. Moreover, the nearest existing public elementary school in the same municipality is located approximately one (1) kilometer away from Barangay Matalapitap which exposes the students of tender age to safety hazards as they travel to the existing public elementary school. Section 1, Article XIV of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provides that “The State shall protect and promote the right of all citizens to quality education at all levels, and shall take appropriate steps to make such education accessible to all.” Furthermore, paragraph 2, Section 2 of the same article mandates the State to “Establish, maintain, and support a complete, adequate, and integrated system of education relevant to the needs of the people and society.” Establishing and constructing a dedicated public school within Barangay Matalapitap will significantly alleviate classroom congestion in neighboring schools, reduce the financial burden on local families, and ensure a safer and more conducive learning environment for the youth of the Province of Tarlac. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. JAIME EDUARDO MARC D.
