title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PHILIPPINE HEALTHCARE SYSTEM TO ACHIEVE EFFICIENCY AND EQUITY, AND TO IMPROVE PUBLIC HEALTH EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 11223, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE "UNIVERSAL HEALTH CARE ACT” 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 SECTION 1. Section 4 of Republic Act No. 11223, otherwise known as the “Universal Health Care Act” is hereby amended to read as follows: 32 “SEC. 4. Definition of Terms. – As used in this Act: 34 (a) Abuse of authority - xxx; 36 (b) Amenities - xxx; 38 (c) Basic or ward accommodation - xxx; 40 (d) Co-insurance - xxx; 42 (e) Co-payment - xxx; 44 (F) DEPENDENTS OF A MEMBER REFER TO: 46 1) THE LEGITIMATE SPOUSE WHO IS NOT A MEMBER; 48 2) THE TWENTY-THREE (23) YEARS OF AGE AND BELOW WHO ARE UNMARRIED AND UNEMPLOYED, LEGITIMATE, LEGITIMATED, ILLEGITIMATE, ACKNOWLEDGED CHILDREN AS APPEARING IN THE BIRTH CERTIFICATE, LEGALLY ADOPTED, OR STEPCHILDREN, OR CHILDREN OF SOLO AND FOSTER PARENTS.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 There are moments when the promise of universal healthcare becomes most meaningful. 24 It is when a Filipino can seek medical care without having to choose between treatment and the family’s daily needs, when contributions to the health system translate into substantial benefits that address not only the most serious illnesses but also the broader healthcare needs, and when public health resources are managed with the highest degree of efficiency that actually translates to concrete benefits that will bring smiles to families. 31 Republic Act No. 11223, or the Universal Health Care Act, established the framework for providing every Filipino with comprehensive and affordable healthcare. However, aside from the debatable claim that healthcare under the law is truly “affordable,”, recent developments have shown that the implementation of this framework still requires clearer safeguards and stronger mechanisms. The Supreme Court's 2025 ruling on the transfer of PhilHealth funds underscored the need to protect the Corporation's reserves and ensure that excess funds are used consistently with the purposes expressly provided under the UHC Act. Concerns raised during the 2026 budget deliberations likewise highlighted questions surrounding the adequacy, release, and proper use of government funds intended for PhilHealth and universal healthcare. 42 Hence, this proposed measure seeks to translate these reforms into concrete benefits for Filipino patients and PhilHealth members. Excess PhilHealth reserves would be directed toward expanding benefits and reducing premium contribution rates, while future contribution rates would be based on updated actuarial assessments and subjected to legislative review. For migrant workers, the bill provides a clearer and more equitable arrangement for premium contributions and protects them from having unpaid contributions become a barrier upon their return to the country. 3 This proposed measure likewise seeks to make every peso contributed to PhilHealth work harder by allowing cost-effective public, private, and public-private arrangements for benefit delivery, while strengthening the Special Health Fund so that PhilHealth reimbursements can be used to improve local health facilities. 8 Moreover, this measure strengthens the systems that support universal healthcare. A national UHC Coordinating Council would bring together the agencies responsible for health, finance, labor, social welfare, education, technology, and local governance; independent external audits would supplement existing government oversight; and specific penalties would apply to the misuse of funds intended for healthcare. 14 In practical terms, these reforms seek to ensure that the money contributed by Filipinos and the resources appropriated for healthcare do not merely remain as funds on paper, but are ultimately converted into better coverage, more responsive health services, stronger local facilities, and greater financial protection for patients and their families. 19 With this, the promise of universal healthcare can become more tangible in the everyday lives of Filipinos. Under the current system, ordinary Filipinos like Juan and Maria may still find themselves forced to choose between paying a hospital bill and keeping the savings they need for their children’s education, daily necessities, and their family’s future, despite paying high contributions. 25 However, under this stronger healthcare system envisioned by this measure, Juan and Maria can face that moment differently. Their PhilHealth contributions can be kept at a level that is actuarially justified and corresponds to the realities of increasing costs of living, while ensuring that those contributions translate into more substantial benefits when illness strikes. Moreover, PhilHealth can now cover a greater share of their hospital expenses, leaving them with a smaller balance to pay and reducing the need to exhaust the savings they had set aside for their children’s education, a better home, or simply a more secure and comfortable life. 34 For families like Juan and Maria’s, this is what universal healthcare should ultimately feel like, that is, contributing fairly and receiving meaningful protection in return, knowing that when illness comes, they can receive the care they need without having to sacrifice the future they have worked so hard to build. 39 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 41 42 43 REP. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "People Empowerment Act.” 34 SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared a policy of the State to ensure participation of citizens in all avenues of local governance. Likewise, the State acknowledges the value of creating a mechanism where its citizens' views and opinions in different areas of governance may be heard and considered. Furthermore, pursuant to Article II, Section 23 of the Constitution, the State recognizes the value of non- government, community-based, or sectoral organizations in nation building and in creating an avenue to ensure their growth and development. The State also recognizes that the partnership with people's organizations (POs) and civil society organizations (CSOs) will spur development in local communities as envisioned by the Local Government Code of 1991. 45 SEC. 3. Definition of Terms. – As used in this Act: 47 (a) Civil society organization refers to any organized citizens' group including POs and non-government organizations such as community groups, labor unions, indigenous groups, charitable organizations, faith-based organizations, professional associations, and foundations; 52 (b) Local sanggunian refers to the local legislative body specifically the
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Meaningful participation of citizens and civil society organizations in local governance is essential to responsive, transparent, and accountable government. While existing laws recognize the role of civil society in local development, there remains a need for a clearer and more consistent mechanism through which organized citizens can participate in local decision-making and work with local governments. 27 Hence, this bill seeks to address this need by establishing a People’s Council in every local government unit and providing a clear framework for the accreditation, organization, recognition, and participation of civil society organizations in local governance. 32 The measure provides People’s Councils with a formal role in local planning, policy- making, program implementation and evaluation, as well as representation in local boards, councils, committees, task forces, and other similar bodies. The objective of this measure is clear – that is, to ensure that local policies and programs reflect the lived experiences of the communities they serve. 38 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 40 41 42 REP. title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE PROCEDURE FOR REGISTRATION OF VOTERS AND ADOPTING A SYSTEM OF ONLINE REGISTRATION, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTIONS 2, 3, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 22, 23, 24, 29, 32, 33 AND 45 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8189, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “VOTER’S REGISTRATION ACT OF 1996” 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 SECTION 1. Short Title. – Section 2 of Republic Act No. 8189, otherwise known as “The Voter’s Registration Act of 1996”, is hereby amended to read as follows: 32 “SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. - It is the policy of the State to [systematize the present method of registration in order to establish a clean, complete, permanent, and updated list of voters] ESTABLISH A SYSTEM OF REGISTRATION THAT ENSURES AND GUARANTEES A CLEAN, COMPLETE, PERMANENT, AND UPDATED LIST OF VOTERS. TO ENCOURAGE AND ENSURE A CONTINUING SYSTEM OF VOTER REGISTRATION, THE STATE SHALL ADOPT AND MAKE USE OF TECHNOLOGIES THAT SHALL FACILITATE AND ALLOW THE AUTOMATED AND ONLINE REGISTRATION OF VOTERS AS AN OPTION, TAKING INTO ACCOUNT THE INTEGRITY, COMPLETENESS, AND ACCURACY OF THE LIST OF VOTERS.” 44 SECTION 2. Section 3 of the same Act is hereby amended to read as follows: 46 “SEC. 3. Definition of Terms. – As used in is Act: 48 (a) Registration refers to the act of accomplishing and filing of a sworn application for registration by a qualified voter ONLINE OR before the election officer of the city or municipality wherein [he] THE APPLICANT resides and including the same in the book of registered voters upon approval by the
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 Voter registration remains largely a manual and paper-based process, despite the availability of technology that could make registration more accessible, efficient, and convenient for the public. 25 During the voter registration period that ran from October 20, 2025 to May 18, 2026, the Commission on Elections (COMELEC) processed 5,470,889 applications nationwide, including applications for new registration, transfer of registration, reactivation, and correction of entries. 30 This figure alone represents an overwhelming burden not only on our hardworking COMELEC personnel, but also raises a more important concern. Behind these millions of applications may be qualified Filipinos who remain unregistered because the existing manual process is difficult, time-consuming, or otherwise inaccessible to them. 35 The existing framework under Republic Act No. 8189, otherwise known as the “Voter’s Registration Act of 1996,” was established at a time when electronic registration, digital records, and secure online transactions were not yet part of ordinary government services. The law therefore needs to be updated to respond to the realities of modern voter registration. 41 Hence, this proposed measure seeks to modernize the voter registration system without compromising the integrity and accuracy of the voters’ list. 44 First, the bill allows online voter registration through the official website of the COMELEC as another option based the manual one. Second, the bill addresses a practical difficulty faced by voters who may be qualified to register but lack conventional documents proving their residence. It now allows alternative forms of proof of residence, including utility bills, certifications from landlords or lessors, and affidavits of qualified disinterested witnesses. These are more practical, yet the bill also proposes safeguards against fraudulent registration. 4 Further, the bill strengthens coordination between the COMELEC and the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) for the identification and cancellation of the registration records of deceased voters. This is intended to help prevent outdated records from remaining in the voters’ list. 9 This proposed bill recognizes that voter registration should not be made unnecessarily difficult by outdated procedures, nor should modernization come at the expense of electoral integrity. The objective is to modernize the voter registration system and make the exercise of the right to vote a little less burdensome to qualified Filipinos, so that more citizens are encouraged and able to register and participate in elections. 15 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 17 18 19 REP. title: AN ACT RENAMING THE LITERACY COORDINATING COUNCIL TO NATIONAL LITERACY COUNCIL, STRENGTHENING ITS POWERS AND FUNCTIONS, EXPANDING ITS MEMBERSHIP STRUCTURE AND SUPPORT MECHANISMS, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7165, AS AMENDED 26 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: 29 SECTION 1. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the “National Literacy Council Act”. 32 SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – Pursuant to Article II, Section 17 of the Constitution, it is the declared policy of the State to give priority to education to foster patriotism and nationalism, accelerate social progress, and promote total human liberation and development. 37 Article XIV, Section 2(4) of the Constitution likewise mandates the State to encourage non-formal, informal, and indigenous learning systems, as well as self- learning, independent, and out-of-school study programs particularly those that respond to community needs. To this end, the State shall give priority to the adoption of measures for the universalization of literacy. 43 SECTION 3. Renaming of the Literacy Coordinating Council. – The nomenclature of the Literacy Coordinating Council, established pursuant to Republic Act No. 7165, as amended, entitled “An Act Creating the Literacy Coordinating Council, Defining Its Powers and Functions, Appropriating Funds Therefor, and for Other Purposes”, is hereby changed to National Literacy Council, hereinafter referred to in this Act as the “Council”. 50 The Council shall serve as the lead inter-agency coordinating and advisory body to the various agencies of the national government, the local government units (LGUs), and the private sector, on matters pertaining to the formulation of policies
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 While the Philippines has a high basic literacy rate, functional literacy remains an area of worry. Functional literacy refers to the ability to read, write, compute, and understand and apply information in everyday life. The 2024 FLEMMS reported that 93.1% of Filipinos aged 10 to 64 had basic literacy, but only 70.8% had functional literacy. In other words, many Filipinos who can read, write, and compute still have difficulty understanding and applying information. 27 This concern is even more relevant today, when people are constantly exposed to fake news, misleading information, and other unreliable content. In today’s world, literacy must therefore go beyond the ability to read and write. 31 Hence, the proposed measure therefore seeks to strengthen the Literacy Coordinating Council as the country’s lead coordinating and advisory body on literacy. The Council will be given more specific functions to identify literacy needs, support marginalized and vulnerable groups, promote research and evidence-based policies, engage the private sector and other stakeholders, and strengthen coordination with the Bureau of Alternative Education (BAE) and the LGUs. It also establishes Local Literacy Councils to bring literacy efforts closer to communities and provides support for effective literacy programs and outstanding literacy workers and ALS mobile teachers. 40 Through these provisions and updates, the measure aims to ensure that literacy programs do not merely teach people to read and write, but help them understand, evaluate, and use information effectively in everyday life. 44 In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 46 47 48 REP. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE 21 The Philippines has a substantial and growing demand for motor vehicles, but this demand does not automatically translate into a strong domestic manufacturing base. The country needs to further develop its capacity to manufacture vehicles and automotive components, create skilled jobs, attract investments, and participate more meaningfully in global automotive value chains. 27 The proposed Philippine Motor Vehicle Manufacturing Industry Act establishes a national framework to strengthen this industry. label: HB 11625
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A NATIONAL HEALTH SERVICE OUTREACH PROGRAM FOR SENIOR CITIZENS AND INDIGENT PERSONS WITH FUNCTIONAL DISABILITIES, PROVIDING FOR INTER-AGENCY AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT COORDINATION, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE For many senior citizens and indigent Filipinos with disabilities, access to health care remains difficult even when government health services are available. Age, illness, disability, limited mobility, transportation costs, and financial hardship can prevent a person from regularly visiting a health center or hospital. This is particularly difficult for senior citizens who live alone, persons who are bedridden or have difficulty walking, and families who cannot afford repeated transportation and other expenses associated with seeking medical attention. In these situations, government health services should not always require the patient to come to government. Where circumstances require, government must also be capable of bringing basic health services closer to the patient. This bill seeks to establish a Health Outreach for Seniors and Indigents Program that will provide appropriate health services to qualified senior citizens and indigent persons with functional disabilities through coordinated national and local health outreach. The Program shall strengthen home and community-based health services, including basic health assessment, monitoring, appropriate medical consultation, access to medicines and basic diagnostic services, referral to hospitals and specialists when necessary, and health education for patients and their families. It shall likewise provide qualified beneficiaries with appropriate assistive devices and basic hygiene and oral-care supplies according to their individual needs. 1 The measure also recognizes the important role of local government units, barangay health workers, public health facilities, and other frontline health workers. By strengthening coordination among these existing institutions, government can identify persons who have difficulty accessing health facilities and connect them with the services they need without unnecessarily creating another layer of bureaucracy. A person's age, disability, inability to travel, or lack of financial resources should not become a barrier to receiving basic health care. Bringing appropriate health services closer to those who need them most is a practical way of making our health care system more accessible, responsive, and humane. label: HB 11626
title: AN ACT PROTECTING THE REMITTANCES OF OVERSEAS FILIPINO WORKERS, PROMOTING FAIR, TRANSPARENT, SECURE, AND AFFORDABLE REMITTANCE SERVICES, STRENGTHENING CONSUMER PROTECTION, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Millions of Filipino families depend on money sent home by overseas Filipino workers for their daily needs, education, medical expenses, housing, and other essential expenses. Every peso deducted from these remittances through excessive charges, unfavorable exchange rates, or undisclosed fees reduces the amount that ultimately reaches an OF W's family. OFWs already make significant sacrifices to earn their income abroad. Sending their hard- earned money home should therefore be safe, transparent, affordable, and convenient. This bill seeks to strengthen the protection of OF W remittances by promoting reasonable remittance costs and requiring greater transparency in fees, charges, and foreign exchange rates. Before completing a transaction, an OFW should be clearly informed of how much the transaction will cost and, as far as practicable, the actual amount that the intended beneficiary will receive. The measure likewise recognizes that remittances are increasingly being sent through digital platforms and electronic financial services. Consumer protection must therefore apply regardless of whether money is sent through a traditional bank or remittance center or through an authorized digital or electronic remittance service. The bill also strengthens mechanisms for addressing unauthorized transactions, fraud, erroneous transfers, unreasonable delays, and other problems encountered by OF Ws and their beneficiaries. Financial institutions and remittance service providers must maintain accessible channels through which complaints can be promptly addressed. At the same time, OF Ws and their families should be provided with clear information that allows them to compare remittance costs and make informed financial decisions. The money sent home by an OFW represents hours of work and years of sacrifice away from family. Government must ensure that this money reaches its intended beneficiaries through a financial system that is fair, transparent, secure, and accountable. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. 24 District, Caloocan City WN num 10 11 12 13 14 Republic of the Philippines House of Representatives Quezon City, Metro Manila TWENTIETH CONGRESS Second Regular Session HOUSE BILL No. 11626 Introduced by Representative EDGAR R. label: HB 11627
title: AN ACT AUTHORIZING THE DEPARTMENT OF HEALTH TO DETERMINE AND APPROVE THE BED CAPACITY AND SERVICE CAPABILITY OF HOSPITALS UNDER ITS DIRECT SUPERVISION AND CONTROL, PROVIDING STANDARDS AND SAFEGUARDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Government hospitals must be able to respond to the actual health needs of the communities they serve. As populations grow and demand for medical services increases, some Department of Health hospitals find themselves operating beyond their authorized bed capacity or requiring additional services, personnel, and facilities. At present, increasing the authorized bed capacity of a government hospital generally requires legislation. While congressional oversight remains important, requiring a separate law every time a DOH hospital needs to adjust its bed capacity can delay improvements that are already justified by actual patient demand. Hospital capacity should be able to respond more efficiently to changing conditions. This bill seeks to authorize the Department of Health to determine and approve the bed capacity and service capability of hospitals under its direct supervision and control. Such decisions shall be based on objective considerations, including actual hospital utilization, population and health needs of the area served, availability of other health facilities, demand for specialized services, and the capacity of the hospital to safely provide additional services. The measure also recognizes that increasing the number of authorized beds alone does not necessarily improve health care. Additional beds must be supported by sufficient doctors, nurses and other health personnel, as well as the necessary equipment, facilities, medicines, and operating resources. Any expansion in hospital capacity must therefore be accompanied by corresponding improvements in staffing and service capability. 1 By allowing the DOH to make evidence-based adjustments while retaining appropriate safeguards and congressional oversight, government hospitals can respond more quickly to increasing patient demand without sacrificing the quality and safety of health services. Ultimately, hospital capacity should reflect the number of Filipinos who actually need care rather than remain limited by figures that may no longer reflect present conditions. title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NATIONAL VEHICLE HISTORY AND SAFETY REGISTRY, INSTITUTIONALIZING ROADWORTHINESS INSPECTION AS A REQUIREMENT FOR THE REGISTRATION OF MOTOR VEHICLES, REQUIRING THE REPORTING OF MAINTENANCE, REPAIR, INSPECTION, AND ACCIDENT RECORDS OF MOTOR VEHICLES, MANDATING DISCLOSURE IN THE SALE OF USED MOTOR VEHICLES, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The 1987 Constitution provides that the State shall protect life and property, promote the general welfare and the right to health, protect consumers from substandard or hazardous products, and recognize the right of the people to information on matters of public concern. Congress has already exercised this power over motor vehicles through multiple statutory enactments which allow the LTO to inspect motor vehicles and to refuse registration to those found unsafe, set forth conditions for registration in an emission test, and prohibits deceptive sales acts and practices. According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), 13,125 persons died in land transport accidents in the Philippines in 2023. This was the highest number in more than a decade and 7.2 percent more than the 12,240 deaths recorded in 2022. Many of these deaths involved a defective vehicle which is unknown because the condition of vehicles is barely recorded. According to the Metro Manila Accident Reporting and Analysis System Annual Report 2020 of the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA), 63,741 of the 65,032 road crashes reported in Metro Manila in 2020, or 98 percent, were logged without any cause. Only six were attributed to brake malfunction and nine to mechanical defect. The registration process does not fill this gap. Republic Act No. 8749, or the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999, makes an emission test a condition for registration, but the law does not expressly require a test of the brakes, tires, steering, or lights. According to the Land Transportation Office (LTO), as reported by the Philippine Daily Inquirer on October 21, 2021, mandatory roadworthiness inspection has been suspended since August 2021. An owner may instead renew registration through a private emission testing center, which tests emissions only, together with a visual inspection by LTO personnel. According to the same 1 LTO statement, 80 percent of renewals take this route. A vehicle can thus be registered year after year without its brakes ever being tested. The same gap harms buyers of used vehicles. No official record shows whether a vehicle was regularly serviced, was flooded or wrecked, or has had its odometer altered. Republic Act No. 10642, or the Philippine Lemon Law, covers only brand-new vehicles. The proposed measure therefore seeks to establish a National Vehicle History and Safety Registry under the LTO that records the maintenance, repairs, inspections, odometer readings, accidents, and safety recalls of every motor vehicle; require a roadworthiness inspection, in addition to the emission test, before a motor vehicle is registered or its registration is renewed; and penalize odometer tampering, false entries, and the concealment of a vehicle's history. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly sought. HON. OMAR VINCENT S. DUTERTE HON. PAOLO Z. label: HB 11630
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A STANDARD ONE-STOP SERVICE CENTER IN EVERY BARANGAY IN THE PHILIPPINES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The barangay is the basic political unit in the Philippines. It is the primary planning and implementing unit of government policies, plans, programs, andprojects in the community. As the most immediate and accessible political unit, it is often the very first point of contact for citizens seeking public services, redress, or clarity about government programs. Despite this critical role, millions of Filipinos still face significant friction when processing government transactions. Residents often endure the financial and temporal burden of traveling to municipal or city halls—or even regional national agency offices—to secure basic documents, process registrations, or seek employment assistance. While Republic Act No. 11032, otherwise known as the "Ease of Doing Business and Efficient Government Service Delivery Act of 2018," successfully mandated the creation of one-stop business facilitation services at the city and municipal levels, the grassroots barangay level has largely been left to rely on fragmented, manual, and localized administrative systems. This bill seeks to bridge that gap by establishing a standard Barangay One-Stop Service Center (BOSSC) in every barangay nationwide. The BOSSC will serve as a unified, digitized frontline desk within the barangay hall. It will consolidate the issuance of all barangay-level documents (clearances, certificates of residency and indigency) and act as a digital conduit for national and municipal services. Furthermore, it will streamline the implementation of special mandates, such as the free issuance of pre-employment records under the First Time Jobseekers Assistance Act. By equipping these centers with standardized technology in partnership with the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) and the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), we empower barangays to serve not just as political boundaries, but as highly efficient service hubs. To ensure that no Filipino is left behind by bureaucratic red tape, and to bring the government directly to the doorsteps of the people, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11631
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING A COMPREHENSIVE LOCAL FLOOD AND DRAINAGE MANAGEMENT SYSTEM, MANDATING THE FORMULATION OF LOCAL FLOOD MASTER PLANS, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines is geographically situated in the Pacific Ring of Fire and the Pacific Typhoon Belt, making it one of the most vulnerable countries in the world to natural disasters, particularly typhoons and torrential monsoon rains. An average of twenty (20) tropical cyclones enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) annually, bringing massive rainfall that frequently results in devastating floods. While the national government, through the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the Metro Manila Development Authority (MMDA), implements macro-level flood control projects, these efforts are often undermined by inadequate, poorly maintained, or entirely absent drainage networks at the local and barangay levels. Rapid urbanization, improper solid waste disposal, informal settlements along waterways, and the effects of climate change have further exacerbated urban and rural flooding. Currently, flood management is highly fragmented. Local Government Units (LGUs) often lack the technical expertise, dedicated personnel, and financial resources to develop and maintain a scientifically sound local drainage master plan. This bill seeks to address this critical gap by institutionalizing a Comprehensive Local Flood and Drainage Management System. It mandates the creation of a Local Flood and Drainage Management Office (LFDMO) within every city and municipality, tasked specifically with the formulation, implementation, and maintenance of a 10-year Local Flood and Drainage Master Plan. Furthermore, it establishes a funding mechanism and ensures strict coordination with the DPWH, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) to ensure that local drainage systems seamlessly connect to national flood control infrastructures. By empowering LGUs and institutionalizing accountability in local drainage management, we can mitigate the devastating impacts of flooding on lives, properties, and the local economy. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11632
title: AN ACT MANDATING THE HIRING OF SCHOOL-BASED LICENSED GUIDANCE COUNSELORS, PSYCHOLOGISTS, AND OTHER MENTAL HEALTH PERSONNEL IN ALL PUBLIC BASIC EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS, UPGRADING THEIR SALARY GRADES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The psychological well-being and mental health of our youth are foundational to their overall development and academic success. In recent years, educational institutions have witnessed an alarming surge in mental health issues among students, including anxiety, depression, and self-harm. These challenges have been exacerbated by the long-term impacts of the pandemic, cyberbullying, and academic pressure. While the State has enacted milestone legislations such as Republic Act No. 11036 (The Mental Health Act) and Republic Act No. 11206 (Secondary School Career Guidance and Counseling Act), the effective delivery of mental health services in schools remains severely crippled by a critical shortage of licensed professionals. Currently, the public school system suffers from a disproportionate counselor-to-student ratio, sometimes reaching one counselor for every tens of thousands of students. A primary driver of this shortage is the uncompetitive compensation framework. Under the current system, highly qualified professionals with master’s degrees and board licenses are often offered entry-level positions at Salary Grade 11. Consequently, many licensed guidance counselors and psychologists opt for private practice or corporate roles, leaving our schools understaffed and our students vulnerable. This proposed measure seeks to address this crisis by mandating the Department of Education (DepEd) to hire and deploy school-based licensed guidance counselors, psychologists, and allied mental health personnel (such as psychometricians and clinical social workers) in all public basic education institutions. Furthermore, to attract and retain these vital professionals, this bill proposes the upgrading of their entry-level salary grades to match the rigorous educational and licensure requirements of their professions. By institutionalizing a standard student-to-mental-health-personnel ratio and providing competitive remuneration, we can ensure that every school becomes a safe, nurturing, and psychologically supportive environment for the Filipino youth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11633
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE HEALTHCARE SYSTEM IN CULTURAL AND INDIGENOUS COMMUNITIES BY INSTITUTIONALIZING THE TRAINING AND ENGAGEMENT OF INDIGENOUS COMMUNITY HEALTH WORKERS AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This measure seeks to institutionalize the training, recognition, and engagement of Indigenous Community Health Workers (ICHWs) who are members of the communities they serve. They will serve as a vital link between Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples (ICCs/IPs) communities and the formal health system by promoting health education, disease prevention, sanitation, nutrition, maternal and child health, immunization, basic health monitoring, first aid within the limits of their training, referral, and assistance in accessing appropriate health facilities. The measure likewise recognizes the value of traditional health practices of ICCs/IPs while ensuring that their use and promotion remain consistent with applicable laws, public health standards, and regulations governing traditional and herbal medicines. Community herbal gardens may also be supported as appropriate, subject to relevant health, environmental, biodiversity, and traditional knowledge protection requirements. The selection of ICHWs shall respect the customs, traditions, and customary decision-making processes of the concerned ICC/IP community, while their training and recognition shall be subject to standards established by the Department of Health. The measure also provides for continuing training, health insurance and hospitalization assistance, educational assistance, legal assistance, and appropriate honoraria and other incentives, subject to existing laws and the availability of funds. The proposed program shall complement, and not diminish, existing programs for Barangay Health Workers under Republic Act No. 7883. It shall likewise be implemented in coordination with the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples, local government units, and other concerned government agencies. Through this measure, the State can strengthen community-based primary health care, improve access to essential health services, and promote a more responsive and culturally appropriate healthcare system for Indigenous Cultural Communities/Indigenous Peoples. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11634
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE MODERNIZATION AND CAPABILITY ENHANCEMENT OF THE PHILIPPINE NATIONAL POLICE AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine National Police (PNP), as the country’s primary law enforcement agency, must be equipped with the infrastructure, technology, mobility assets, communications systems, investigative capabilities, and other resources necessary to effectively perform its mandate and respond to evolving public safety and security challenges. While the PNP has undertaken various capability enhancement initiatives, modernization efforts remain dependent on periodic appropriations and individual procurement programs. A comprehensive and sustained framework is therefore necessary to ensure that capability development is systematic, responsive to operational needs, and supported by appropriate procurement and institutional mechanisms. This measure seeks to institutionalize a PNP Modernization and Capability Enhancement Program covering infrastructure and facilities development, equipment acquisition and upgrading, information and communications technology, investigative and forensic capabilities, and institutional and professional development. It likewise provides for appropriate procurement strategies, supply-chain security, technology transfer, coordination with relevant government agencies, and a defined implementation period and funding framework. Through this measure, the PNP shall be better positioned to strengthen its operational capabilities, uphold human rights and professional standards, adopt modern technologies, and deliver more effective and responsive police services to the Filipino people. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11635
title: AN ACT PROVIDING MEASURES TO PREVENT MINORS FROM PURCHASING PRODUCTS THAT ARE HARMFUL OR MAY INCITE VIOLENCE, INCLUDING REALISTIC TOY WEAPONS, MANDATING SCHOOL AWARENESS PROGRAMS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The alarming rise of violence in schools involving minors calls for strengthened measures to protect children and promote safe learning environments. Recent incidents involving violence in schools, including shootings, knife attacks, and the confiscation of weapons from minors, underscore the need to address children's access to dangerous products and realistic toy weapons that may create safety risks in schools and communities. The 1987 Constitution provides the foundation for this measure. Article II, Section 13 declares that the State recognizes the vital role of the youth in nation- building and shall promote and protect their physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social well-being. Article XV, Section 3(2) further mandates the State to defend the right of children to assistance, including proper care and protection from all forms of neglect, abuse, cruelty, exploitation, and other conditions prejudicial to their development. This bill builds upon existing laws and policies, including: 1) Republic Act No. 7610, otherwise known as the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act, which provides special protection to children from abuse, exploitation, and discrimination; 2) Republic Act No. 10627, otherwise known as the Anti-Bullying Act of 2013, which provides measures to prevent and address bullying and violence in schools; 3) Republic Act No. 11934, otherwise known as the SIM Card Registration Act, insofar as applicable to measures promoting accountability in digital transactions; and 4) Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the Local Government Code of 1991, which provides the framework for local government action and community-based programs. Research on children's exposure to weapon-related toys and violent stimuli has identified potential short-term associations with aggressive cognition or behavior, although such exposure alone has not been established as a predictor of later criminality. These findings underscore the importance of age-appropriate safeguards, responsible supervision, and preventive education in school and community environments. This bill therefore seeks to: a) Prohibit the sale, distribution, or provision of specified harmful products and realistic toy weapons to minors; b) Establish reasonable age-verification requirements for transactions involving restricted products, including online transactions, while respecting applicable data privacy laws; c) Mandate school awareness and prevention programs to promote peace, conflict resolution, responsible behavior, and child safety; d) Strengthen coordination among national government agencies, local government units, schools, parents, and community organizations; and e) Provide appropriate mechanisms for monitoring, reporting, and enforcement while ensuring that children who may come into possession of prohibited products are treated primarily as children requiring protection and appropriate intervention. This measure is not merely about restricting toy guns, knives, or other products. It seeks to strengthen the State's preventive approach to child protection by addressing children's access to products that may endanger their safety, while promoting education, responsible behavior, and a culture of peace in schools and communities. The immediate passage of this bill is, therefore, earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11636
title: AN ACT REGULATING THE POSSESSION AND OPERATION OF UNMANNED SYSTEMS, PROVIDING PENALTIES FOR VIOLATIONS THEREOF, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Unmanned systems, commonly known as drones, have become increasingly accessible and are now widely used for recreational, commercial, agricultural, scientific, media, disaster response, and government purposes. Their continued development has contributed to innovation, improved efficiency, and economic development across various sectors. The proliferation of unmanned systems, however, has also raised concerns relating to public safety, national security, privacy, aviation safety, and the protection of critical infrastructure. Unauthorized operations near airports, military installations, government facilities, densely populated areas, and public events demonstrate the need for a clear and comprehensive legal framework governing the registration, possession, operation, and accountability of unmanned systems. At present, regulations issued by the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines (CAAP) principally govern unmanned aircraft operations. There remains a need for legislation establishing a broader and coordinated framework covering unmanned systems operating in the air, on land, and in maritime environments, while recognizing the respective mandates of concerned government agencies. This proposed measure seeks to establish a comprehensive regulatory framework governing the possession and operation of unmanned systems. It provides for appropriate registration and licensing requirements, operational standards, prohibited acts, privacy safeguards, enforcement mechanisms, and penalties, while recognizing legitimate uses of unmanned systems for commercial, educational, research, agricultural, humanitarian, disaster response, and other lawful purposes. The measure likewise establishes an inter-agency mechanism to promote coordination among concerned government agencies and to ensure that regulation keeps pace with technological developments. It recognizes the need to balance public safety and national security with innovation, research, economic activity, and the responsible development of the unmanned systems industry. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. ERIC L. label: HB 11637
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE STRATEGIC BITCOIN RESERVE OF THE PHILIPPINES, APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to establish a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve for the Republic of the Philippines as a proactive measure to safeguard national economic sovereignty and diversify our foreign reserves away from excessive dependence on the US Dollar. The Philippines faces a structural dilemma rooted in its heavy reliance on the US Dollar. More than 80 percent of our international trade settlements, overseas Filipino worker (OFW) remittances (which contribute roughly 9- 10 percent of GDP annually), and foreign exchange reserves are denominated in USD. While the dollar has historically served as the global reserve currency, the United States’ monetary and fiscal policies have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to print money out of thin air through successive rounds of quantitative easing, massive deficit spending, and unchecked expansion of the Federal Reserve’s balance sheet. This practice has fueled persistent global inflation, eroded the real purchasing power of the dollar, and exported monetary instability to dollar-dependent economies like ours. Every time the US prints trillions to finance its domestic priorities, the value of our hard-earned dollar reserves declines in real terms. This translates into higher costs for imported fuel, food, and raw materials, reduced purchasing power for OFW families, and diminished returns on the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas’ (BSP) reserve holdings. The Philippines is essentially subsidizing American fiscal profligacy while bearing the inflationary consequences without any say in US policy decisions. Bitcoin, by contrast, is the only major asset with a verifiably fixed supply of 21 million coins — a monetary policy enforced by unbreakable code Page 1 of 4 rather than political discretion. Its decentralized nature removes any single government’s ability to debase it. Establishing a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve will allow the Philippines to hedge against dollar depreciation, capture long-term appreciation potential, and position the country as a forward-looking digital-economy leader in Southeast Asia. The proposed reserve will be managed transparently by the BSP under strict custodial, security, and reporting standards. Initial funding will come from a modest reallocation of BSP profits and future appropriations, ensuring no immediate burden on the national budget. This is not speculation; it is strategic national insurance against the known risks of fiat-currency dependency. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this bill is earnestly requested. label: HB 11638
title: AN ACT
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The rapid growth of social media has fundamentally changed the way children communicate, learn, obtain information, and interact with others. While social media platforms provide valuable opportunities for education, expression, creativity, and social connection, children are increasingly exposed to online risks, including cyberbullying, exploitation, grooming, harmful or age-inappropriate content, privacy violations, excessive and compulsive use, manipulation through algorithms, and artificially generated or altered content. Children, by reason of their age and evolving capacities, require a level of protection that is different from that afforded to adults in the digital environment. The State has the responsibility to promote and protect the physical, moral, spiritual, intellectual, emotional, and social well-being of children and to ensure that their best interests remain paramount in all actions concerning them. For this reason, there is a need to establish a clear and comprehensive age-based regulatory framework for children's access to social media. This measure recognizes that children of different ages possess different levels of maturity, understanding, and capacity to identify and respond to online risks. Accordingly, the proposed Act adopts three distinct levels of protection. Beyond restriction and enforcement, the bill promotes digital literacy and responsible digital engagement among children, parents, guardians, and educators. It seeks to equip children with the knowledge and skills necessary to critically evaluate online information, recognize algorithmic influence, protect personal information, report harmful conduct, manage screen time, and engage responsibly in digital spaces. It likewise encourages local government units to provide community-based recreational, educational, cultural, civic, and device-free activities that support children's healthy development. Ultimately, this measure seeks to strike a careful balance between protecting children from the risks of the digital environment and respecting their rights to privacy, access to information, education, communication, and freedom of expression consistent with their age and evolving capacities. It does not seek to prevent children from participating in the digital world; rather, it seeks to ensure that such participation takes place in an environment that is safer, more responsible, age-appropriate, and respectful of their rights. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11639
title: AN ACT DECLARING JULY 16 OF EVERY YEAR A SPECIAL NON-WORKING HOLIDAY IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CARRASCAL, PROVINCE OF SURIGAO DEL SUR, IN CELEBRATION OF ITS ANNUAL TOWN FIESTA AND THE PAHINUNGOD FESTIVAL
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Carrascal, Province of Surigao del Sur, celebrates its annual town fiesta in honor of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, with the Pahinungod Festival serving as a distinctive cultural and religious celebration of the municipality. The Provincial Government of Surigao del Sur identifies the Pahinungod Festival as a major event of Carrascal, with festival activities traditionally held in July and centered on devotion, community participation, cultural expression, and thanksgiving. Declaring July 16 of every year a special non-working holiday in Carrascal will enable residents, visitors, workers, and families to participate meaningfully in the celebration and will help preserve and strengthen the municipality's cultural and religious heritage. This measure likewise recognizes the responsibility of the Local Government Unit of Carrascal to plan and support the orderly conduct of the Pahinungod Festival. For this purpose, the Municipality may appropriate funds in its annual budget, or utilize available and legally authorized local appropriations, subject to existing budgeting, accounting, auditing, procurement, and other applicable laws, rules, and regulations. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Cagwait, Province of Surigao del Sur, was created into an independent municipality on January 20, 1953 by virtue of Executive Order No. 559, Series of 1953, issued by then President Elpidio Quirino, organizing a portion of the Municipality of Tago, Province of Surigao, into a new independent municipality named Cagwait. January 20 is annually observed by the Municipality of Cagwait as its Foundation Day, or “Adlaw Nan Cagwait,” which commemorates its establishment and highlights the municipality's historical significance while strengthening the people's sense of identity, pride, and belongingness. Declaring January 20 of every year as a special non-working holiday in Cagwait will provide the residents, government personnel, schools, businesses, and other sectors of the community an opportunity to participate fully in the activities commemorating the municipality's founding anniversary. This measure seeks to institutionalize the annual observance of the founding anniversary of Cagwait and recognize its importance to the cultural and historical life of the municipality. in view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought. label: HB 11643
title: AN ACT EXPANDING THE PRIVILEGES OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITY TO INCLUDE FREE PARKING IN ALL ESTABLISHMENTS AND EXEMPTION FROM THE NUMBER CODING SCHEME, FURTHER AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE SECTION 32 OF REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7277, AS AMENDED, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “MAGNA CARTA FOR PERSONS WITH DISABILITY”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Bible reminds us in Proverbs 31:8–9: "Speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, for the rights of all who are destitute. Speak up and judge fairly; defend the rights of the poor and needy." This is a call to stand beside those whom society too often leaves behind, so that persons with disabilities may live with dignity, independence, and equal opportunity to take part in the life of the nation. The 2020 Census of Population and Housing found that about 8.47 million Filipinos aged five and over have difficulty in at least one functional domain, which the PSA reported as 8.7 percent of the household population. Among them, 1,895,026 have difficulty walking or climbing steps. For these Filipinos, the distance from the parking space to the door is only part of the journey. Over 135,000 have severe difficulty walking, and over 288,000 have moderate difficulty.1 For many persons with physical disabilities, walking to a destination or using available public transportation may not be feasible, making travel by private vehicle a necessity. Accessibility therefore extends beyond the distance from a parking space to the door: it also depends on whether they can afford the journey itself. Every trip may require careful planning, and even modest parking fees can add to the financial burden of reaching medical appointments, workplaces, and other essential destinations. 1 Philippine Statistics Authority (2020). Functional Difficulty in the Philippines: For Household Population Five Years Old and Over (2020 Census of Population and Housing) Retrieved from: https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/population-and-housing/node/168274 on October 5, 2026 Batas Pambansa Blg. 344 recognizes the right of persons with disabilities to access physically accessible parking facilities. However, the provision of a reserved parking space offers limited benefit when parking fees impose an additional financial burden on households already managing the costs of medicines, therapy, and assistive devices. Similarly, such accessibility measures lose their practical value when vehicle-number schemes compel persons with disabilities to postpone or cancel medical appointments, work obligations, or family engagements. These circumstances should not be regarded as mere inconveniences. Rather, they constitute recurring barriers that, over time, can significantly restrict a person’s mobility, independence, and ability to participate fully in community life. Some local governments have chosen to act. Taguig City maintains a dedicated PWD Affairs Office, provides free rehabilitation and therapy services, and delivers assistive devices to people's homes.2 Pasig City exempts vehicles carrying PWDs from its number-coding scheme3, and Marilao exempts PWDs from parking fees in business establishments and similar places.4 Their example demonstrates that genuine inclusion extends beyond the recognition of rights on paper. It requires ensuring that essential services and support are accessible, affordable, and within reach of those who need them most. The proposed "Free Parking and Coding Exemption for Persons with Disability Act" carries this compassion into national policy. It seeks to: 1. Grant free parking in commercial establishments and government facilities that charge parking fees; and 2. Exempt vehicles carrying or driven by a person with disability from the Unified Vehicular Volume Reduction Program, or number coding scheme. No Filipino should have to choose between a necessary trip and the cost or restriction that comes with it. By removing these barriers, the State affirms that persons with disabilities have an equal right to move freely, to work, to heal, to worship, and to be with their loved ones. In view of the foregoing, the early approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JORGE DANIEL S. BOCOBO 2 City of Taguig Website (n.d.). Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Public Higher Education Faculty Salary Upgrading and Progression Act." SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is the policy of the State to attract and retain competent faculty in public higher education through competitive pay and a fair, merit-based, regular, and adequately funded system of advancement in rank, while respecting institutional academic freedom. SECTION 3. Coverage. – This Act shall apply to all faculty members holding permanent plantilla positions in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs): Provided, That the University of the Philippines and Mindanao State University Systems shall retain their own promotion systems: Provided, further, That a local university or college may adopt this system by ordinance, subject to Section 325 of Republic Act No. 7160, otherwise known as the "Local Government Code of 1991." SECTION 4. Upgrading of Faculty Salary Grades. – The salary grades of faculty positions in SUCs are hereby upgraded, as follows: Faculty Rank Sub-Rank Present SG Upgraded SG I 12 14 Instructor II 13 15 III 14 16 I 15 17 Assistant Professor II 16 18 III 17 19 IV 18 20 Associate Professor I 19 21 II 20 22
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Our Constitution requires that teaching "attract and retain its rightful share of the best available talents through adequate remuneration."1 For faculty in State Universities and Colleges (SUCs), higher pay comes mainly through reclassification, from Instructor I (SG 12, PhP 33,947 monthly) to College/University Professor (SG 30, PhP 210,718).2 Since 1998 this system has rested only on executive circulars, now DBM-CHED Joint Circular No. 3, s. 2022, as enhanced by Joint Circular No. 01, s. 2026.3 No law requires cycles to be held, limits processing time, or funds to adjust benefit amounts to account for normative cost of teaching, inflation, changing educational cost, regional variations and other considerations., which each SUC must now certify from its own resources.4 Work done from August 2023 reaches the DBM only by June 2027.5 No institution can demand academic excellence while offering systemic precarity. Short Title. – This Act shall be known as the "Tulay sa Hanapbuhay Act." SECTION 2. Declaration of Policy. – It is hereby declared the policy of the State to promote the welfare of the youth and equality of employment opportunities for all. Toward this end, the State shall ease the transition of young Filipinos from education to employment by defraying the initial costs of seeking work, with preference for the poor and marginalized when resources are limited. SECTION 3. Definition of Terms. – As used in this Act: (a) Fresh Filipino Graduate refers to a Filipino citizen who has completed a bachelor's or associate degree program in a higher education institution recognized by the Commission on Higher Education (CHED), or a program registered with the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) leading to a National Certificate or its equivalent; (b) Combined Annual Gross Family Income refers to the total gross income of the applicant's parents or legal guardians in the preceding year or, for a self-supporting applicant, the applicant's own gross income; and (c) Special Equity Group refers to Indigenous Peoples under Republic Act No. 8371; persons with disabilities under Republic Act No. 7277, as amended; solo parents and their dependents under Republic Act No. 8972, as

label: HB 11648
title: AN ACT ESTABLISHING THE NCR POLYTECHNIC INSTITUTE THROUGH THE INTEGRATION OF THE TESDA TECHNOLOGY INSTITUTIONS (TTIs) IN THE NATIONAL CAPITAL REGION INTO A UNIFIED POLYTECHNIC SYSTEM, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The NCR Polytechnic Institute Act establishes a modern, unified polytechnic system in the National Capital Region to strengthen Technical Vocational Education and Training (TVET) as a strategic driver of national competitiveness, industrial transformation, innovation, and inclusive growth. Operating under the supervision of TESDA NCR, the measure integrates and transforms the TESDA NCR Regional Training Center (NCR RTC) and six (6) District Training Centers into a single institutional framework. This consolidation rationalizes existing TESDA technology institutions into an integrated polytechnic system to achieve stronger governance, operational efficiency, enhanced institutional performance, and academic excellence across the region. As the lead regional institution for higher-level and technology-driven TVET, the Institute is mandated to deliver Technical Diploma programs and specialized workforce courses designed in accordance with the Philippine Qualifications Framework (PQF). The academic framework promotes lifelong learning through stackable microcredentials, flexible learning pathways, and articulation agreements with higher education institutions to enable credit recognition and ladderization toward related bachelor's degree programs. Furthermore, the legislation establishes Regional TVET Innovation Centers to serve as regional hubs for applied research, technology demonstration, prototyping, entrepreneurship, and emerging technology training. Governance is structured around a centralized "One System" framework featuring One Governing Board, One Executive Management System, One Support Services System, and One Academic Delivery System. The multi- sectoral Governing Board includes representatives from TESDA, DOST, DOLE, DTI, LGUs, industry sectors, employers, workers, educational institutions, civil society, and students. Crucially, the legislation safeguards existing workforce rights by transferring all assets, personnel, and records without impairing the positions, rights, or security of tenure of faculty and staff. Initial implementation will be funded through current TESDA appropriations, with subsequent operations supported by the annual General Appropriations Act and local government contributions. In view of the foregoing, approval of this bill is earnestly requested. JUDE A. label: HB 11650
title: AN ACT INSTITUTIONALIZING SAFEGUARDS IN THE APPROPRIATION, RELEASE, UTILIZATION, REPORTING, AND AUDIT OF CONFIDENTIAL FUNDS OF LOCAL GOVERNMENT UNITS, AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES Be it enacted by the Senate and the House of Representatives of the Philippines in Congress assembled: SECTION 1. Short Title. This Act shall be known as the “Local Government Confidential Funds Accountability Act.” SEC. 2. Declaration of Policy. It is hereby declared the policy of the State to uphold local autonomy while ensuring fiscal responsibility, transparency, and accountability in the use of public funds. The State recognizes that certain legitimate peace and order and public safety activities may require confidentiality. However, confidentiality shall be the exception and shall be justified only by operational necessity. It shall not exempt any expenditure of public funds from lawful appropriation, accounting, audit, and appropriate government oversight. Accordingly, confidential funds shall be resorted to only when the intended public purpose cannot reasonably and effectively be accomplished through regular appropriations and ordinary government procedures without compromising a lawful confidential activity. SEC. 3. Coverage. This Act shall apply to confidential funds appropriated by provinces, cities, and municipalities for lawful peace and order and public safety purposes.
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Confidential funds serve a legitimate purpose where peace and order operations require secrecy. Yet the same secrecy that protects sensitive operations also makes these funds particularly vulnerable to abuse and misuse, with fewer opportunities for public scrutiny. For this reason, confidential funds must be treated as an exception justified by actual necessity, rather than as an ordinary component of local government spending. The experience of local government units exhibits that the amount spent in confidential funds does not necessarily determine the quality of peace and order. Davao City reported ₱530 million in confidential expenses in 2023, after spending ₱460 million annually from 2019 to 2022. Cagayan de Oro City allocated ₱200 million in 2023 and ₱250 million in 2024, while Cavite Province proposed ₱193.5 million for confidential expenses in 2024, following approximately ₱183 million in 2023. By contrast, in 2024, eight Metro Manila cities— Las Piñas, Navotas, Makati, Pasig, Taguig, Mandaluyong, Malabon and Valenzuela—reported no confidential-fund expenditures at all. Quezon City LGU likewise reduced its confidential funds from ₱100 million in 2023 to ₱75 million in 2024, even as its index crimes declined from 2,359 to 1,958 over the same period. Other LGUs have likewise chosen to rely less on confidential spending. Naga City announced the total removal of confidential funds from its budget, while the LGU of Capas, Tarlac chose to forego its ₱8-million confidential fund for 2026, with the amount instead intended for programs benefiting senior citizens and public school students. This measure seeks to institutionalize safeguards requiring LGU confidential funds to be supported by necessity, proportionate to legitimate peace and order requirements, and subject to audit, reporting, and safeguards against misuse. This is not intended to diminish or unduly restrict confidential funds where genuinely necessary. Rather, it seeks to ensure that such funds are used only when justified by actual peace and order requirements and subject to transparency and accountability. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this measure is earnestly sought. REP. ADRIAN MICHAEL A. title: AN ACT GRANTING THE ORIENTAL MINDORO- ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. (QRMECO) A FRANCHISE TO CONSTRUCT, INSTALL, ESTABLISH, OPERATE, OWN, MANAGE AND MAINTAIN DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS FOR THE CONVEYANCE OF ELECTRIC POWER TO THE END-USERS IN THE CITY OF CALAPAN AND MUNICIPALITIES OF BACO, BANSUD, BONGABONG, BULALACAO, GLORIA, MANSALAY, NAUJAN, PINAMALAYAN, POLA, PUERTO GALERA, ROXAS, SAN TEODORO, SOCORRO, AND VICTORIA IN THE PROVINCE OF ORIENTAL MINDORO
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Oriental Mindoro Electric Cooperative, Inc. (ORMECO) plays a critical role in the electrification, economic development and public welfare of the Province of Oriental Mindoro. As a distribution utility operating within a defined franchise area, it is imbued with public interest consistent with Article XII, Section 11 of the 1987 Constitution, which requires that public utilities operate under a legislative franchise subject to regulation by the State. This proposed measure grants ORMECO a franchise to construct, install, establish, operate, own, manage and maintain a distribution system for the conveyance of electric power to end- users within the City of Calapan and the municipalities comprising the Province of Oriental Mindoro. The bill aligns the operations of the Grantee with the regulatory framework established under Republic Act No. 9136 (EPIRA), ensuring continued oversight by the Energy Regulatory Commission, and with Republic Act No. 10531, strengthening the supervisory role of the National Electrification Administration. Recognizing the State policy to accelerate the exploration and development of renewable energy resources, the measure incorporates provisions consistent with Republic Act No. 9513. It mandates facilitation of renewable energy integration, compliance with Renewable Portfolio Standards, and implementation of net-metering mechanisms to enable households and private end-users to generate electricity from renewable sources and supply excess power to the distribution system under lawful and regulated conditions. To safeguard the independence of the cooperative and prevent undue political influence over a public utility, the bill includes a governance provision prohibiting members of the Board of Directors and the General Manager from having a relationship by consanguinity or affinity up to the third civil degree with incumbent elective officials within the franchise area. This measure promotes institutional integrity, policy independence, and public trust in the management of an essential public service. The bill likewise strengthens consumer protection, ensures transparency in rate-setting, preserves regulatory jurisdiction, provides procedural due process in franchise revocation, and harmonizes the franchise with existing statutory framework. In view of the foregoing, the immediate approval of this measure ig earnestly sought. AN C. label: HB 11652
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ADMINISTRATIVE CANCELLATION OF BIRTH CERTIFICATES REGISTERED THROUGH FRAUDULENT MEANS BY FOREIGN NATIONALS, CREATING A SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON CANCELLATION OF BIRTH CERTIFICATES, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Civil registry documents, particularly Certificates of Live Birth, are fundamental because it serves as the primary legal proof of an individual’s name, parentage, date of birth, and citizenship. However, the integrity of the Philippine civil registry is currently threatened by foreign nationals exploiting the system through the fraudulent registration of births, with an estimated 50,000 spurious records currently suspected in the database of the Philippine Statistic Office (PSA) (Cruz, 2026). Because birth certificates are the foundational document establishing citizenship, these fraudulent registrations grant illicit access to exclusive national rights, privileges, and government services reserved to legitimate citizens. The core of this systemic failure is the absence of an administrative remedy to address such fraudulent entries resulting in protracted proceedings thereby the continued existence of spurious records in official databases. With some government officials allegedly involved in this scheme (Casilao, 2026), a comprehensive, immediate, and effective intervention is imperative. The 1987 Constitution mandates the government to serve and protect the people, promote general welfare, and maintain honesty and integrity in public service. Likewise, the State remains the ultimate authority over matters of citizenship. Inherent to these Constitutional principles is the duty of the State to preserve the sanctity and reliability of its civil registry, particularly documents establishing birth and citizenship. This measure seeks to directly address these civil registry gaps by establishing an administrative mechanism for the cancellation of birth certificates fraudulently obtained by foreign nationals. Central to this proposed measure is the creation of a Special Committee on Cancellation of Birth Certificates, composed of representatives from key agencies authorized to resolve such matters with finality. This introduces a streamlined procedure that ensures due process while preventing undue delay. The proposed measure, which was previously introduced during the 19 th Congress, strengthens accountability by authorizing the Special Committee to recommend the institution of appropriate criminal, civil, administrative, and deportation proceedings against foreign nationals and any individuals, whether private or public officers, who participated in or facilitated the fraudulent registration. Through this bill, erroneous records are corrected while deterring future abuses of our civil registry system. Additionally, this version of the bill recognizes evidentiary realities by providing that the absence of any primary and secondary civil registry records, duly certified by local civil registrars after diligent and exhaustive search, shall constitute prima facie evidence of fraudulent registration. In such cases, this bill allows for the expeditious cancellation of the birth certificate by the Special Committee. Finally, the enactment of this measure affirms the State’s commitment to uphold the integrity of its legal identity systems, protect the rights and privileges of lawful citizens, and reinforce public trust and confidence in government records and procedures. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. BRYAN B. REVILLA 2nd District of Cavite AGIMAT Partylist REP. label: HB 11653
title: AN ACT PROVIDING FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF COMPOSTING FACILITIES IN ALL BARANGAYS, PROMOTING RESIDENTIAL COMPOSTING, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 9003, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “ECOLOGICAL SOLID WASTE MANAGEMENT ACT OF 2000,” AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Global waste generated in 2022 reached 2.56 billion tons, an amount originally projected for 2030. Without intervention, global waste is estimated to grow by fifty percent (50%) by 2050, or a total of 3.86 billion tons (Cook et al., 2026). Driven by urbanization, population growth, and rising consumption patterns, the Philippines ranked 27th globally in municipal solid waste production, at 15 million tons annually (Dela Peña, 2025). The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) reported that 52 to 58 percent of the country’s waste is biodegradable. With proper segregation, biodegradable waste is recovered and composted, diverting usable trash away from our dumpsites (Teves, 2021). Without segregation, a significant portion of biodegradable waste is disposed of in landfills or open dumpsites, contributing to environmental degradation, methane emissions, and public health risks. Despite the enactment of Republic Act No. 9003, otherwise known as the “Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000,” full compliance at the local level remains uneven and inconsistent, particularly in the segregation and processing of organic waste. A major gap in the solid waste management system is the limited support mechanisms for solid waste disposal, recycling, and recovery, including technologies, facilities, and systems at the barangay level (Rebullida & Taguibao, 2020). While Materials Recovery Facilities (MRFs) are mandated under existing law, many lack the capacity, coverage, and functionality for composting, resulting in the continued disposal of organic waste in landfills (Andaya, 2025). Decomposing biodegradable waste in landfills generates methane, a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming and climate change. Conversely, composting transforms organic waste into soil amendments that support agriculture, landscaping, and ecological restoration. In recognition of this challenge, grounded on Article II, Section 16 of the 1987 Constitution guaranteeing “the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology in accord with the rhythm and harmony of nature,” there is a need to strengthen the implementation of ecological solid waste management by shifting toward localized, decentralized, and resource-oriented approaches. This includes empowering barangays as primary units of implementation, institutionalizing composting infrastructure, and promoting household and community participation in organic waste diversion. To address these gaps, this bill seeks to amend the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000 by providing for the establishment, operationalization, and integration of Barangay Composting Facilities (BCFs) within existing solid waste management systems. By requiring all barangays to develop composting capacity, the measure ensures that biodegradable waste is processed at or near the source, thereby reducing dependence on landfills. Further, this measure strengthens community-level participation by institutionalizing the Residential Composting Support Desk (RCSD) in every barangay. The RCSD is designed to provide material and technical assistance to households, homeowners’ associations (HOAs), and condominium corporations, including the distribution of composting starter kits, training programs, and access to scaled composting equipment for larger residential developments. This approach lowers the barriers to entry for composting and promotes sustained behavioral change at the household level. To ensure coverage, subdivisions and condominium projects are required to divert organic waste either through on-site composting facilities or by utilizing their barangay’s BCF. Registered participants retain the right to the finished compost they produce, including personal use, public greening programs, agricultural use, and community distribution, with provisions allowing surplus compost to be sold commercially or directly to the government. This mechanism transforms organic waste from a disposal burden into an economic opportunity and environmental resource. Furthermore, while the Barangays are primarily responsible in organic waste diversion, this bill mobilizes key national agencies, including the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Department of Agriculture (DA), Department of Science and Technology (DOST), Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD), and the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), to ensure coordinated implementation, technical standard- setting, and regulatory oversight. Ultimately, this measure advances a circular approach to solid waste management by institutionalizing composting as a core component of environmental governance. By reducing landfill dependence, lowering greenhouse gas emissions, promoting resource recovery, and strengthening community participation, the bill contributes to building sustainable, climate-resilient, and environmentally responsible communities. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA, MSLG, DM (hc) REP. RAMON JOLO REVILLA III REP. BRYAN B.
