label: HB 11654
title: AN ACT PREVENTING AND PENALIZING FOREIGN INTERFERENCE IN THE PHILIPPINES, STRENGTHENING MECHANISMS TO DETECT AND COUNTER FOREIGN INTERFERENCE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Foreign interference in domestic and governmental processes has emerged as a significant and evolving threat to democratic states, including the Philippines. Global trends reveal how foreign actors utilized coordinated disinformation campaigns during elections, covert funding of political groups, and cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure to influence public opinion and policy outcomes. The European Commission, through its Action Plan Against Disinformation, documented the exploitation of online platforms to manipulate democratic discourse by polarizing communities and inciting antagonism in the society. 1 The North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) warns that information threats can cause real- world harm, directly endangering national security.2 Similarly, the Koffi Annan Foundation observed that new digital platforms and internet culture contributed to the scale, nature, and reach of foreign interference operations. 3 In the Philippine context, the absence of a comprehensive and unified legal framework specifically addressing foreign interference leaves critical gaps, as existing laws on espionage, cybercrime, and election offenses remain fragmented and insufficient to address the full scope of these modern threats. This measure is anchored on the constitutional principle of national sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national interest, while guaranteeing the protection of civil liberties under the Bill of Rights. It complements existing statutes such as the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2001 and the Anti-Wiretapping Law, the Foreign Agents Act of 1979, which promotes transparency in foreign-linked political activities. 1 European Commission. Retrieved from h7ps://www.koﬁannanfounda=on.org/news/foreign- interference-in-elections-how-to-deﬁne-it/ The proposed Foreign Interference Prevention Act establishes a comprehensive framework by clearly defining and penalizing foreign interference, including disinformation, covert influence operations, and support to foreign intelligence services; requiring the registration of foreign agents engaged in political or advocacy activities; addressing digital threats through access blocking; enabling financial investigation; strengthening inter-agency coordination; while explicitly safeguarding civil liberties, ensuring that speech, journalistic, and academic freedoms are respected and protected. The enactment of this measure is expected to strengthen national sovereignty and security by deterring foreign interference, protect the integrity of our election and democratic processes, enhance transparency and accountability in foreign- linked activities, improve the State’s capacity to respond to hybrid and cyber threats, and align the Philippines with international standards in countering foreign interference. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. BRYAN B. REVILLA 2nd District of Cavite AGIMAT Partylist REP. label: HB 11655
title: AN ACT CREATING THE NATIONAL NUTRITION COMMISSION, REPEALING FOR THE PURPOSE PRESIDENTIAL DECREE NO. 491, ENTITLED “CREATING A NATIONAL NUTRITION COUNCIL AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippines has an obligation to protect and promote the right to nutrition and adequate food under relevant domestic and international laws: 1987 Philippine Constitution; Universal Declaration of Human Rights; International Covenant on Economic, Social, and Cultural Rights; Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women; Convention on the Rights of the Child, as well as the United Nations 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. In line with this, several offices of government have taken on the task of directly or indirectly protecting and promoting the right to nutrition and adequate food, namely: The National Nutrition Council, created through Presidential Decree (PD) No. 491, s. 1974; National Food Authority, established through PD No. 4, s. 1972; Anti-Hunger Task Force, created through Executive Order (EO) No. 616, s. 2007; Inter-Agency Task Force on Hunger, established through EO No. 101, s. 2020; Presidential Assistant for Food Security and Agricultural Modernization under the Office of the President, established through Memorandum Order No. 70, s. 2014; Food and Nutrition Research Institute, which is one of the research and development institutes of the Department of Science and Technology; and, Department of Agriculture, specifically through its Food Staples Sufficiency Program. While the government has committed to AmBisyon Natin 2040, which promises a strongly rooted, comfortable, and secure life for every Filipino, where “no one is poor, no one is ever hungry,” undernutrition and malnutrition remain as perennial problems besetting the country. In fact, the Philippines missed its Millennium Development Goal of lowering the undernutrition and malnutrition rate to 15% by 2015, and the problem appears to be getting worse. The World Bank reports 1 that as of 2019, one in every three Filipino children younger than five years old suffer from stunting, resulting in the country being ranked fifth among countries in the East Asia and Pacific Region with the highest number of stunted children. The effect of COVID 19 on the economy has made hunger, undernutrition and malnutrition even worse in the country. The Social Weather Stations reported an alarming 31% of families experiencing hunger, and 9% suffering severe hunger in September 2020, seven months after the enforcement community quarantine—in both cases, the highest levels recorded in more than 20 years. In this regard, this Bill seeks to create a National Nutrition Commission to serve as the overarching agency responsible for establishing a unified policy direction and a comprehensive approach towards food accessibility and security, improved nutrition and overall health development of the Filipino people. This shall replace the existing National Nutrition Council, as well as streamline the nutrition functions rendered by other offices of government. Furthermore, nutrition programs at sub-national levels shall be guaranteed with manpower complement, as a way of improving nutrition performance. Immediate passage of this bill is hereby earnestly sought. REP. LANI MERCADO-REVILLA REP. label: HB 11656
title: AN ACT INTEGRATING TRADITIONAL AND COMPLEMENTARY MEDICINE INTO THE NATIONAL HEALTH CARE SYSTEM, REORGANIZING THE PHILIPPINE INSTITUTE OF TRADITIONAL AND ALTERNATIVE HEALTH CARE (PITAHC), AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 8423, OTHERWISE KNOWN AS THE “TRADITIONAL AND ALTERNATIVE MEDICINE ACT OF 1997,” AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Philippine health care system continues to face persistent challenges in ensuring accessible, affordable, and culturally responsive health services for all Filipinos. Despite advances in modern medicine, a significant portion of the population continues to rely on traditional and complementary medicine as part of their health care practices. Globally, the World Health Organization (WHO) reports that 88% of the population adopts traditional medicine for preventive, curative, or rehabilitative purposes (Agoot, 2023). In the Philippines, 43% of adult Filipinos have sought complementary and alternative medicine, particularly the services of manghihilot or bone setter and partera and albularyo or herbalist (Ladia, et al., 2018). These figures highlight the continuing relevance and demand for traditional and complementary health modalities. Republic Act No. 8423, otherwise known as the “Traditional and Alternative Medicine Act of 1997,” was enacted to promote and advocate the use of traditional and alternative health care. However, nearly three decades since its passage, significant gaps remain in terms of regulatory capacity, integration into the broader health system, and alignment with current health frameworks such as the Universal Health Care (UHC) Act. With growing preference on herbal formulations over synthetic medicine underscores the necessity to introduce regulation of herbal medicines to ensure quality, safety, and efficacy (Sachan, Vishnoi, & Kumar, 2016). The lack of standardized regulation and clinical validation mechanisms for traditional and complementary medicine may results in inconsistent quality, safety concerns, and limited integration into formal health systems. Moreover, under the Global Survey on Traditional Medicine conducted by the WHO, member States are assisted to research, integrate, and regulate traditional medicine in their national health systems (Zhao & Terry, 2023). This bill seeks to address gaps in the traditional and complementary medicine in the country by reorganizing the Philippine Institute of Traditional and Alternative Health Care (PITAHC) into the Traditional, Complementary, and Integrative Medicine Administration (TRACIMA), strengthening its mandate as the lead policy, regulatory, and research body. To achieve these objectives, TRACIMA shall be responsible to conduct research and development, validation, integration, regulation, consumer protection, and protection of indigenous knowledge systems of traditional and complementary health care practices. Through this measure, TRACIMA can establish the minimum standard of health care based on validated medical data. Finally, the bill strengthens inter-agency coordination and health technology assessment (HTA) mechanisms to ensure that only safe, effective, and cost-efficient practices are adopted within the national health system allowing coverage and inclusion in the health packages of the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) under the UHC. In view of the foregoing, the passage of this bill is earnestly sought to modernize the country’s approach to traditional and complementary medicine, ensure public safety, and fully harness its potential as a complementary pillar of a responsive and inclusive health care system. label: HB 11658
title: AN ACT STRENGTHENING THE ACADEMIC AND INSTITUTIONAL CAPABILITIES OF THE CAMIGUIN POLYTECHNIC STATE COLLEGE, EXPANDING ITS CURRICULAR OFFERINGS, AND PROVIDING FUNDS THEREFOR, AMENDING FOR THE PURPOSE REPUBLIC ACT NO. 7923, ENTITLED “AN ACT CONVERTING THE CENTRAL MINDANAO UNIVERSITY CAMPUS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF CATARMAN, THE MINDANAO POLYTECHNIC STATE COLLEGE CAMPUS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF MAMBAJAO, AND THE CAMIGUIN SCHOOL OF ARTS AND TRADES, ALL IN THE PROVINCE OF CAMIGUIN, INTO A STATE COLLEGE TO BE KNOWN AS THE CAMIGUIN POLYTECHNIC STATE COLLEGE, AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR”
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE Republic Act No. 7923, approved in 1995, consolidated three public postsecondary institutions in Camiguin into the Camiguin Polytechnic State College and gave the College a mandate centered on the educational and development conditions prevailing at that time. More than three decades later, CPSC serves a substantially changed province and higher-education environment. New professions, technologies, regulatory standards, modes of instruction, research needs, and workforce requirements have emerged, while the College has developed academic institutes, programs, extension activities, and institutional responsibilities that were not contemplated in detail by the original charter. CPSC remains the principal public higher-education institution based in the island province. Its present offerings provide important pathways in teacher education, engineering and computer studies, industrial technology, agriculture, business and public administration, tourism, marine biology, and graduate education. These programs have enabled generations of students to obtain an affordable public education close to their families. The statutory authority of the College, however, has not kept pace with the breadth of present and anticipated demand. Many qualified students seek programs that CPSC does not presently offer, particularly in nursing and allied health sciences, medicine and public health, emerging technologies, specialized engineering, environmental and marine-resource management, and other fields required by the province and the region. When a needed program is unavailable locally, a student may be compelled to leave Camiguin, assume additional transportation and living expenses, postpone higher education, or pursue a course that does not match the student’s aptitude or intended profession. These burdens fall most heavily on low-income families and may prevent the province from developing and retaining the professionals it needs. The proposed amendment is therefore not a conversion of CPSC into a university and does not alter the composition of its Board of Trustees. It strengthens the existing State College by modernizing its academic mandate and authorizing it to retain its current programs and, when justified, establish additional technical-vocational, undergraduate, graduate, postgraduate, professional, continuing-education, and flexible-learning programs within its competence and areas of specialization. The authority to offer additional programs is not automatic or unlimited. A program may open only after demonstrated local or regional need, inclusion in the institutional development plan, availability of funds, recommendation through the appropriate academic process, and full 1 compliance with the policies, standards, and requirements of the Commission on Higher Education, the Professional Regulation Commission, and other competent authorities. Programs requiring licensure, laboratories, clinical training, internships, affiliations, accreditation, or specialized facilities may not admit students until the necessary faculty, curriculum, facilities, equipment, learning resources, and regulatory authority are in place. Academic authority must be matched by institutional capacity. The bill accordingly provides a legal basis for the phased construction, repair, renovation, upgrading, and maintenance of classrooms, laboratories, simulation and clinical-training facilities, workshops, libraries, research and innovation centers, digital systems, student-support facilities, accessibility features, safety systems, and disaster-resilient infrastructure. It also supports the acquisition and maintenance of books, databases, software, medical and laboratory equipment, instructional technologies, and other learning resources. Implementation will follow institutional priorities and available appropriations and will remain subject to procurement, property, budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws. The measure also recognizes that facilities alone cannot sustain quality education. CPSC must be able to maintain a sufficient complement of qualified faculty members, researchers, specialists, librarians, laboratory and clinical personnel, information-technology personnel, student-support personnel, and administrative personnel. The College must likewise support graduate study, professional certification, licensure, clinical or industry exposure, research training, and other forms of faculty and personnel development. These investments are essential to regulatory compliance, program accreditation, instructional quality, research, extension, and student welfare. To support orderly implementation, the bill requires an updated institutional development plan, phased program development, and coordination with CHED, the Department of Budget and Management, and other concerned agencies. It modernizes selected powers and procedures of the Board, facilitates institutional partnerships and lawful resource sharing, and updates the appropriations provision so that additional academic programs, facilities, equipment, plantilla requirements, faculty development, research, scholarships, student support, accreditation, and regulatory compliance may be properly considered in the annual national budget. Amending the charter will enable CPSC to respond to student aspirations and the human- resource requirements of Camiguin and Northern Mindanao without compromising academic quality or fiscal responsibility. It will give the College the legal and institutional framework to expand carefully, accommodate more qualified students as capacity permits, and deliver programs supported by the personnel, facilities, equipment, and public funding necessary for their success. In view of the foregoing, immediate approval of this bill is earnestly sought. JURDIN JESUS M. label: HB 11659
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE ANGAT - SAN RAFAEL ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF ANGAT, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the Angat - San Rafael Road, located in the Municipality of Angat, Province of Bulacan, into a national road. The Angat - San Rafael Road spans approximately 11.85 kilometers. It serves as a crucial arterial route connecting the municipalities of Angat and San Rafael, facilitating the movement of people, agricultural produce, commercial goods, and public services across eastern Bulacan. Due to increasing traffic volume and the growing economic activities in the region, the local government unit faces significant financial constraints in maintaining, expanding, and upgrading this road to meet safety and structural standards. Converting this local road into a national road will transfer its repair, maintenance, and future improvement under the jurisdiction and funding of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This development will enhance regional connectivity, lower transportation costs, ensure public safety, and bolster economic growth not only for the Municipality of Angat but for the entire Province of Bulacan. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11660
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE NEW BAGBAGUIN BYPASS ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria in the Province of Bulacan serves as a major industrial, commercial, and agricultural hub in Central Luzon. Due to its strategic location and proximity to Metro Manila, the municipality experiences high volumes of daily vehicular traffic, ranging from light passenger vehicles to heavy cargo trucks transporting agricultural and manufactured goods. To alleviate severe traffic congestion along major thoroughfares, particularly within the urban center and major arterial roads, the local government and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) undertook the construction and development of the New Bagbaguin Bypass Road. Stretching approximately two (2) kilometers, this bypass road provides a critical alternative route, diverting heavy traffic away from congested residential and commercial centers, reducing travel time, and improving overall logistical efficiency in the province. While the New Bagbaguin Bypass Road serves a vital regional function in supporting interstate trade and transport, its maintenance, repair, and future improvement currently rest on local government funds. Given the heavy volume and high axle loads of commercial traffic utilizing this bypass, local funding constraints hamper continuous, optimal maintenance and necessary upgrades. Converting the New Bagbaguin Bypass Road into a National Road will transfer its administration, maintenance, and further development under the responsibility of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This will guarantee standard quality maintenance, enhance road safety, and ensure long-term sustainability to keep up with regional economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11661
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE CITYLAND – PEREZ ROAD IN BARANGAY PULONG BUHANGIN, MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria, Bulacan, has undergone rapid urbanization and commercial expansion over recent years, driven by its strategic location and growing population. Barangay Pulong Buhangin, one of the largest and most populous barangays in the municipality, serves as a major hub for residential communities, educational institutions, commercial establishments, and local trade. Connecting to primary transportation arteries, the Cityland – Perez Road in Barangay Pulong Buhangin spans approximately 3.78 kilometers. It plays a crucial role in facilitating the daily movement of commuters, agricultural goods, and commercial transport within Santa Maria and neighboring municipalities in Bulacan. However, the continuous increase in traffic volume, heavy vehicle loads, and local economic development have placed a heavy financial and operational strain on the local government’s road maintenance capacity. Classifying this key thoroughfare as a local road limits the resources available for necessary repairs, drainage improvements, and safety upgrades. Converting the Cityland – Perez Road into a National Road will transfer its maintenance, repair, and improvement responsibilities to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This shift will ensure the upgrading of the road to national engineering standards to handle high traffic density and heavy freight safely. In view of the foregoing benefits to the community and the region, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11662
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE MEYCAUAYAN-SANTA MARIA BYPASS ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Meycauayan-Santa Maria Bypass Road, stretching approximately 4.53 kilometers within the Municipality of Santa Maria, Province of Bulacan, serves as a vital transportation artery connecting key municipalities in eastern Bulacan to major thoroughfares, including the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX). As the Municipality of Santa Maria and surrounding areas continue to experience rapid economic growth, industrial expansion, and population increases, local traffic congestion has intensified. The bypass road was constructed to relieve traffic along inner municipal roads, facilitate the seamless movement of goods and agricultural products, and improve travel time for commuter and commercial traffic across the province. However, the maintenance, repair, and upgrade requirements of a heavy-traffic arterial road pose a continuous financial burden on the local government unit (LGU). Converting the Meycauayan-Santa Maria Bypass Road into a National Road will transfer its maintenance, repair, and future improvements under the supervision and funding of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This shift ensures that the road complies with national safety standards, receives dedicated annual budget allocations, and continues to sustain regional economic growth without overburdening local municipal funds. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11663
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE NORZAGARAY–SAN JOSE ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF NORZAGARAY, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the Norzagaray–San Jose Road, located in the Municipality of Norzagaray, Province of Bulacan, into a national road under the jurisdiction and supervision of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). Spanning approximately 11.46 kilometers, the Norzagaray–San Jose Road serves as a vital arterial route within Bulacan. It facilitates the movement of people, agricultural produce, industrial supplies, and essential goods between local communities and neighboring commercial centers. Norzagaray is host to vital national infrastructure, including major water reservoirs and quarrying/cement manufacturing hubs, making its road network integral not only to municipal commerce but to regional trade and economic activity. Despite its strategic importance, the continuous maintenance and upgrade of this 11.46-kilometer stretch place a significant financial burden on the local government unit (LGU) of Norzagaray. Municipal funding limitations often restrict the LGU's capacity to undertake comprehensive road widenings, structural reinforcements, and routine rehabilitation necessary to support heavy vehicular traffic and adverse weather conditions. Converting the Norzagaray–San Jose Road into a national road will transfer its control, maintenance, and improvement to the DPWH. This ensures regular budget allocation under the General Appropriations Act (GAA), bringing the road up to national standards, enhancing road safety, and boosting regional socio- economic growth. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE SANTA MARIA - PANDI BYPASS ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria in the Province of Bulacan is a rapidly growing urban and commercial hub in Central Luzon. Its strategic location serves as a primary gateway connecting neighboring municipalities to the North Luzon Expressway (NLEX) and major economic centers. Due to continuous industrialization and population growth, local traffic density has increased significantly. The Santa Maria - Pandi Bypass Road, spanning approximately three (3) kilometers within the territorial jurisdiction of Santa Maria, was constructed to alleviate heavy traffic congestion along the town center and facilitate smoother transit between Santa Maria and the Municipality of Pandi. Despite its vital function as an arterial bypass, the maintenance, repair, and operational upkeep of the Santa Maria - Pandi Bypass Road currently burden the local government unit (LGU) funds. Converting this local road into a national road will transfer its supervision and maintenance to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This shift ensures continuous funding for infrastructure maintenance, improvement, and safety upgrades under the National Expenditure Program (NEP). Furthermore, integrating this bypass road into the national road network will enhance regional connectivity, lower transportation costs for agricultural and commercial goods, boost local economic activity, and support public safety and disaster response mobility. In view of the foregoing considerations, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE SANTA MARIA–SAN JOSE ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE This bill seeks to convert the Santa Maria–San Jose Road, located in the Municipality of Santa Maria, Province of Bulacan, into a National Road under the jurisdiction and maintenance of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). Spanning approximately 8.96 kilometers, the Santa Maria–San Jose Road serves as a vital arterial route connecting key barangays within Santa Maria and providing strategic linkages to neighboring municipalities in Bulacan. It functions as a heavily traversed corridor for the transport of agricultural produce, commercial goods, industrial materials, and daily commuters traveling toward regional economic hubs and major expressways. Despite its critical economic and social function, the continuous maintenance of this 8.96-kilometer stretch pose a significant financial burden on the local government unit (LGU) of Santa Maria. Local budget limitations restrict the municipal government's capacity to execute essential structural reinforcements, drainage system improvements, and routine maintenance necessary to support growing traffic volumes and severe weather conditions. Converting the Santa Maria–San Jose Road into a national road will transfer its supervision, maintenance, and rehabilitation to the DPWH. This will ensure regular funding from the national budget, raise safety and engineering standards, reduce traffic congestion, and unlock further economic potential for Santa Maria and the Province of Bulacan as a whole. In view of the foregoing, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought. SALVADOR A. PLEYTO, SR. label: HB 11666
title: AN ACT CONVERTING THE SANTA MARIA RIVER SIDE ROAD IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF SANTA MARIA, PROVINCE OF BULACAN, INTO A NATIONAL ROAD AND APPROPRIATING FUNDS THEREFOR
explanatory_note: EXPLANATORY NOTE The Municipality of Santa Maria in the Province of Bulacan is a rapidly expanding suburban and commercial hub in Central Luzon. Serving as a crucial gateway between Metro Manila and inner Bulacan municipalities, its road networks experience an increasingly heavy volume of daily vehicular traffic, ranging from private vehicles to commercial trucks carrying agricultural goods. The Santa Maria River Side Road, which spans a length of 2.18 kilometers within the municipality, serves as a critical bypass and feeder road that helps decongest primary arterial roads, facilitates faster local transportation, and connects surrounding barangays to vital economic centers, public markets, and schools. However, due to its current status as a municipal road, maintenance and repair are funded solely through the limited local government budget. Given the high traffic density and environmental exposure along the river basin, the road requires continuous structural upgrades, concrete re-paving, adequate drainage infrastructure, and regular safety enhancements that exceed the financial capacity of the local government unit. Converting the Santa Maria River Side Road into a National Road will transfer its maintenance, repair, and future improvement responsibilities to the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH). This transition will ensure a higher standard of road quality, enhanced safety features, and sustained national infrastructure funding In view of the foregoing urgent considerations, the immediate passage of this bill is earnestly sought.
